(p-98)In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Commentary on Surat al-Baqarah

This surah is Medinan. It was revealed in various periods, and among it is the last verse revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah; then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged﴾ [al-Baqarah: 281]. Surat al-Baqarah is called "the tent-pole of the Qur'an" (fusṭāṭ al-Qur'ān) because of its greatness and splendour, and because of the legal rulings and admonitions it contains. ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both, learned it, along with its jurisprudence and all the knowledge it contains, over eight years. It contains five hundred rulings and fifteen parables. al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Which part of the Qur'an is most excellent?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Surat al-Baqarah." Then he said: "And which verse of it is most excellent?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The Verse of the Throne (Āyat al-Kursī)."

It is said that the meanings of the verses of mercy, hope and punishment in it reach three hundred and sixty meanings. It is also narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I was given Surat al-Baqarah from the first Remembrance (al-Dhikr al-Awwal), and I was given Ṭā-Hā and the Ṭawāsīn from the Tablets of Moses, and I was given the Opening of the Book (Fātiḥat al-Kitāb) and the final verses of Surat al-Baqarah from beneath the Throne."

In the authentic hadith from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Al-Baqarah and Āl ʿImrān will come on the Day of Resurrection as if they were two canopies with light between them, or two dark clouds, or as if they were two flocks of birds in ranks, pleading on behalf of their companion." In al-Bukhari, he, peace be upon him, said: "Whoever recites the two verses from the end of Surat al-Baqarah at night, they will suffice him."

(p-99)Abu Hurayrah narrated from him ﷺ that he said: "The house in which Surat al-Baqarah is recited, the Devil does not enter." It is also narrated from him, peace be upon him, that he said: "Everything has a hump, and the hump of the Qur'an is Surat al-Baqarah. In it is a verse which is the chief of the verses of the Qur'an: it is the Verse of the Throne."

The number of verses of Surat al-Baqarah is two hundred and eighty-five. It is said: two hundred and eighty-six. It is said: two hundred and eighty-seven.

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾

Scholars have differed concerning the letters that occur at the beginnings of the surahs, on two views. ash-Shaʿbi, ʿAmir ibn Sharahil, Sufyan ath-Thawri, and a group of the hadith scholars said: they are the secret of Allah in the Qur'an, and they are among the ambiguous (mutashabih) matters of which Allah alone has knowledge. One is not obliged to speak about them; rather, one believes in them and they pass as they came.

(p-100)The majority of scholars said: rather, one must speak about them, seek out the benefits beneath them and the meanings that may be derived from them. They differed about this in twelve views.

ʿAli ibn Abi Talib and Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the disjointed letters in the Qur'an are the Greatest Name of Allah, except that we do not know how it is composed from them.

Ibn ʿAbbas also said: they are names of Allah which He swore by.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: they are names of the surahs.

Qatadah said: they are names of the Qur'an, like al-Furqan and al-Dhikr.

Mujahid said: they are openings of the surahs.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Just as they say at the beginning of a recitation of famous poems, "bal wa-la bal," so Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Akhfash took this approach.

Some people said: they are the reckoning of "Abu Jad," to indicate the duration of the community (millah) of Muhammad ﷺ, as occurs in the hadith of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and this is the view of Abu al-ʿAliyah Rafiʿ and others.

Qutrub and others said: they are an indication of the letters of the alphabet, as if he says to the Arabs: "I have challenged you only with a composition of these letters which you know." So his saying "Alif Lam Mim" is like your saying "alif, ba, ta, tha," to indicate by them the twenty-nine letters.

Some people said: they are a sign which Allah had placed for the People of the Book, that He would send down to Muhammad a book at the beginning of whose surahs are disjointed letters.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: they are letters which indicate "Anā Allāhu aʿlam" (I am Allah, the Most Knowing), "Anā Allāhu arā" (I am Allah, the Seeing), "Anā Allāhu ufaṣṣil" (I am Allah, who explains in detail).

(p-101)Ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, said: each of them is a letter from: either a name of the names of Allah, or a blessing from His blessings, or from the name of an angel among His angels, or a prophet among His prophets.

Some people said: they are an alerting device, like the ya in calling out (in nidaʾ).

Some people said: it has been narrated that when the polytheists turned away from listening to the Qur'an in Makkah, these letters were revealed so that they would find them strange and thus open their ears to them, and then they would hear the Qur'an after them, so that the proof would be established against them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is what the majority said: that these letters should be explained and that an interpretation should be sought for them, because we find that the Arabs have spoken with disjointed letters, arranging them and using them in place of the words which these letters form part of, like the saying of the poet:

"We said to her, 'Stop (qifī),' and she said: 'Qāf...'" 

He meant: she said: "I have stopped (waqafat)." And like the saying of the speaker:

"With goodness there is goodness, and if evil, then fā (...) and I do not want evil except that you tā (...)"

He meant: "wa-in sharran fa-sharrun" (and if evil, then it is evil), and he meant: "illā an tashā" (except that you wish). The examples of this are numerous. So their presence in the Qur'an is not something the Arabs would reject in their language. Therefore, when it is part of the known discourse of the Arabs, it is appropriate to seek its interpretation and to look for its meaning.

(p-102)Stopping on these letters is on sukūn because they are incomplete, except when you make a predication about them or conjoin them, in which case you inflect them (tuʿrabuhā). The grammatical position of "Alif Lam Mim": it is in the nominative (rafʿ), being either the predicate of an implied subject (mubtadaʾ muḍmar), or the subject (mubtadaʾ) itself; or in the accusative (naṣb) by an implied verb; or in the genitive (khafḍ) by oath. This analysis makes the nominative possible in some of the views mentioned earlier about the letters, the accusative in some, and the genitive according to the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they are names of Allah which He swore by.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 2:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿That is the Book; there is no doubt in it; it is guidance for those who are mindful of God﴾

The noun "dhalika" (that) consists of the dhal and the alif. It has also been said: the dhal alone, with the alif as reinforcement. The lam is for the distance of the thing pointed to, and for emphasis, and the kaf is for addressing (the second person). The position of "dhalika" is nominative, as if it were the predicate of a subject (mubtada'), or it is a subject whose predicate follows it.

Scholars differed about "dhalika" here. It has been said: it means "this" (hadha), and the pointing is to these letters from the Qur'an. This is because "dhalika" may be used to point to a present thing to which some absence is attached, while "hadha" is used for an absent thing that is of the same level of established presence and nearness.

It has also been said: it retains its own usage as a pointing to an absent thing. They differed about this absent thing. It has been said: it is what of the Qur'an had already been sent down. It has been said: the Torah and the Gospel. It has been said: the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), that is, the Book which is the Decree (al-qadar). It has been said: God had promised His Prophet that He would send down to him a book which water would not erase, so He pointed to that promise. Al-Kisa'i said: "dhalika" is a pointing to the Qur'an which is in heaven and had not yet been sent down. It has been said: God had promised the People of the Book that He would send down to Muhammad a book, so the pointing is to that promise. It has been said: the pointing is to the letters of the alphabet in the statement of the one who said "Alif Lam Mim": the letters of the alphabet with which I have challenged you to produce arrangement from them.

The word "al-kitab" (the Book) is derived from "katabtu al-shay'" when I gathered it and joined part of it to part, like the "kutab" of beads (kutab al-kharz, with the kaf dammed and the ta' fatha) and the "kutab" of a she-camel (kutab al-naqah).

The raising of "al-kitab" may be taken as an apposition (badal), or as the predicate of the subject, or as an explicative apposition ('atf al-bayan).

As for "la raywa fihi" (there is no doubt in it), its meaning is: there is no doubt in it and no uncertainty about it. The meaning is that in its essence there is no doubt in it, even if doubt has occurred among the disbelievers.

A group said: the wording of His saying "la raywa fihi" is the wording of a report, but its meaning is a prohibition. A group said: it is a generality by which the particular is intended, that is, among the believers; and this is weak.

Al-Zuhri, Ibn Muhaysin, Muslim ibn Jundub and 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr read "fihi" with the h dammed, and likewise "ilayhi" and "alayhi" and "bihi", and "nassilhi" and "nuwallihi", and whatever is similar to that wherever it occurs, following the original form. Ibn Ishaq read "fayhwa" with the h dammed and connected it with a waw.

"Hudan" (guidance) means: right direction and clarification. As to its place in grammar, it is in the nominative, as the predicate of "dhalika", or the predicate of an implied subject, or a subject whose predicate is the prepositional phrase before it. It is permissible that its position be accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "dhalika" or of "al-kitab", the governing element being the sense of pointing; or of the pronoun in "fihi", the governing element being the sense of settledness; and there is weakness in this view.

As for His saying "lil-muttaqin" (for those who are mindful): the word is derived from waqa, and its verb is ittaqa on the pattern of ifta'ala. Its origin was "lil-muwtaqiyin"; the kasra was found heavy on the ya', so it was made quiescent and deleted for the sake of the meeting of two quiescents; the waw was changed to ta' according to their usage when waw and ta' come together; and the ta' was assimilated into the ta', so it became "lil-muttaqin". The meaning is: for those who are mindful of God, Exalted is He, by carrying out His commands and avoiding His disobediences; this becomes a protection between them and the punishment of God.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 3:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Those who believe in the unseen, establish the prayer, and spend out of what We have provided for them.﴾

"Yu'minun" (they believe) means "yusaddiqun" (they affirm as true). It takes the preposition "bi" (in), and it may also take "li" (for/to), as in His, the Exalted, words: (p-105) ﴿And do not believe except those who follow your religion﴾ [Al 'Imran: 73], and as in His words: ﴿But none believed in Musa﴾ [Yunus: 83]. There is a difference between the two constructions: the construction with "li" implies, within it, a construction with "bi" that is understood from the meaning.

The reciters differed over the hamza in "yu'minun." Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i pronounced the hamza in "yu'minun" and similar forms, such as "ya'kulun" (they eat), "ya'muruna" (they command), and "yu'tuna" (they give), and likewise when the hamza is vowelled, as in "yu'akhkhirukum" (He delays you) and "ya'uduhu" (it burdens him). However, Hamza preferred to omit the hamza when pausing, while the others pause with the hamza. Warsh related from Nafi' the omission of the hamza in all of these cases. It has been related from 'Asim that he did not pronounce the hamza when it was silent (sakin). Abu 'Amr, when he joined the recitation (idraj) or recited in the prayer, did not pronounce every silent hamza, except that he pronounced certain silent letters in specific instances, which we will mention in their proper places, God willing.

When the silence of the hamza marks the jussive (jazm), one does not drop its hamza, as in "nunsa'uha" (We cause it to be forgotten) and "hayyi' lana" (prepare for us), and what is similar to them.

As for His words "bil-ghayb" (in the unseen): one group said its meaning is that they affirm when they are absent and alone, unlike the hypocrites who believe when they are present and disbelieve when they are absent. Others said: they affirm what is hidden from them of what the revealed laws (shara'i') have reported. The commentators differed in expressing examples of this. One group said: the unseen in this verse is God, the Mighty and Majestic. Others said: divine decree and predestination (al-qada' wal-qadar). Others said: the Qur'an and what it contains of unseen matters. Others said: the Gathering (al-hashr), the Bridge (al-sirat), the Balance (al-mizan), Paradise and Hell. These statements do not contradict one another; rather, the term "the unseen" applies to all of them.

Linguistically, "al-ghayb" is what is hidden from you of a matter, and also the sunken depression of the land in which its interior is concealed.

(p-106) As for His words "yuqimun" (they establish): it means they make it manifest and firm, as one says "uqimat al-suq" (the market was set up). This is a figure of speech drawn from standing up from a state of concealment, such as sitting or otherwise. From this is the verse of the poet:

"When it is said, 'You have come,' they do not leave until the horses set up the market of spear-thrusting."

And from it is the verse of another poet:

"We set up for the people of the two 'Iraqs the market of striking, and they retreated and turned away, all of them."

The origin of "yuqimun" is "yaqumun." The vowel of the waw was moved to the qaf, and it was changed into a ya' because the kasra preceded it. As for "al-salat" (the prayer), it is derived from "salla yusalli," meaning "to supplicate." As the poet said:

"Upon you is like what you have prayed for, so close your eyes to sleep, for the side of a man has a place to lie down."

And from it is the verse of another:

"For her is a guardian who never leaves her house, and if she is slaughtered, he prays over her and over Zamzam."

Since "salat" in the Shari'a is supplication, and to it were added specific forms and recitation, all of that was named by the name of supplication. (p-107) Some people said: it is derived from "al-sala," which is a vein in the middle of the back that divides at the joint and encloses it. From this the one who runs second in a horse race takes its name (al-musalli), because he comes alongside the two hindquarters (salwa) of the leader, so "salat" was derived from it, either because it came second after faith and was likened to the second horse, or because the bower and the prostrator bend their hindquarters (salawan).

The view that it derives from supplication is the better one.

As for His words, the Exalted: ﴿and spend out of what We have provided for them﴾, "mimma" is written joined, and "ma" in the sense of "alladhi" (that which) should have been written separately, but the preposition and its object are treated as one thing. Also, since the nun of "min" was hidden in pronunciation, it was dropped in writing. "Ar-rizq" (provision), according to the People of the Sunna, is whatever benefit is validly obtained from, whether lawful or unlawful, unlike the statement of the Mu'tazila that what is unlawful is not provision. "Yunfiqun" (they spend) here means: they give what the Shari'a has obligated them to pay of zakat, and what it has encouraged them to give beyond that.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "yunfiqun" means they give zakat, seeking reward for it. Others said: the verse concerns spending in jihad.

Al-Dahhak said: it is spending that they used to draw near to God, the Mighty and Majestic, according to their means. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas also said: it is a man's spending on his family. The verse encompasses all of this, and these statements are examples, not contradictions.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 4–5:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, words:

﴿And who believe in what has been sent down to you, and what was sent down before you, and in the Hereafter they are certain.﴾ ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord, and those are the successful.﴾

(p-108) The interpreters (al-mutawwilun) differed about who is meant by this verse and the one before it. Some said: both verses are about all believers. Others said: they are about the believers among the People of the Book. Others said: the first verse is about the believing Arabs and the second is about the believing People of the Book, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, and it was concerning him that it was revealed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These views conflict. Whoever makes the two verses refer to one category, then the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "alladhina" is in the genitive by way of 'atf (conjunction). It is also permissible for it to be in the nominative by way of istinaf (resumption), meaning: "and they are those who..." Whoever makes the two verses refer to two categories, then the i'rab of "alladhina" is nominative by way of ibtida' (inchoative), and its predicate is ﴿those are upon guidance﴾.

His words ﴿what has been sent down to you﴾ mean the Qur'an, and ﴿what was sent down before you﴾ mean the earlier books. Abu Haywa and Yazid ibn Qatib read "bima anzala" and "ma anzala" with a fatha on the hamza in both places only. On this reading the verb may be attributed to Allah, the Exalted, or to Jibril. The first is more evident and more binding.

As for "bil-akhira" (in the Hereafter), it has been said its meaning is "with the Last Abode," and it has been said: "with the Last Creation."

As for "yuqinun" (they are certain), its meaning is: they know with a knowledge firmly settled in their souls. Certainty (yaqin) is the highest rank of knowledge, the kind that cannot admit doubt in any respect.

As for the saying of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him: "He swears by his certainty, then the matter turns out to be contrary to that," it is a figurative expression in accordance with the Arab custom of figurative speech, and he did not intend to define the discussion of certainty.

(p-109) His, the Exalted, words "ulaika" (those) are a demonstrative referring to those mentioned. "Ula'" is the plural of "dha," and it is built on kasra, because it is weak in its vagueness compared with the strength of nouns. The original of building is sukun, but it was given a vowel because two unvowelled letters came together (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). The "ka" is for address. "Al-huda" here means guidance. The second "ulaika" is an inchoative, and "al-muflihun" is its predicate. "Hum" is a separating pronoun (fasl), because it falls between two definites. It is also permissible for "hum" to be the inchoative and "al-muflihun" its predicate, with the whole clause being the predicate of "ulaika."

Al-falh is attaining the object of one's desire and reaching one's hope. From it is the saying of Labid:

"Understand, if you are yet understanding, for he has truly prospered who has intellect."

Poems of the Arabs have also come in which falah carries the meaning of survival, such as his saying:

"......................................... and we hope for survival after 'Ad and Himyar."

And like the saying of al-Adbat:

"For every care among cares there is a space, while morning and evening have no falah with them."

Survival encompasses attaining hope and succeeding in one's aim, since it is the head of that and its foundation. Al-Khalil reported falah with both meanings.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, words:

"......................................... and we hope for survival after 'Ad and Himyar."

(p-110) The words of His Majesty, the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering; and for them is a great punishment.﴾

The meaning of kufr (disbelief) is derived from their saying "kafr" when something covers and conceals. From it is the saying of the poet:

﴿...................................... in a night of kafr of the stars, its clouds⦆

That is, its concealing. From it the night was named "kafir" (covering) because it covers everything with its darkness. The poet said:

﴿So she remembers a heavy, slow burden after she had cast the brightness of her right hand into the kafir⦆

From it the farmers were called "kuffar," because they cover the seed.

As for "kafara" in religion, its meaning is: he covered his heart with rust (rain) so that it is kept away from faith, or he covered the truth with his sayings and his actions.

There is disagreement regarding who this verse was revealed about, after agreement that it is not general, since some disbelievers embraced Islam after it. One group said: it concerns those whom Allah knew beforehand would not believe; Allah the Exalted wished to make known that among people there are those whose state is this, without anyone being aided. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and their like. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it was revealed concerning the leaders of the confederates, who are the people of the well at Badr.

(p-111) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view has been related like this, and it is an error, because many of the leaders of the confederates embraced Islam, and the arrangement of the verse concerns the companions of the well. The first view among those we have related is the one relied upon. Whoever specifies a particular person is only giving an example of one whose death in disbelief has been revealed to him by the unseen, that he is included within the verse.

His saying: ﴿it is the same for them﴾, meaning: it is equal to them. From it is the saying of the poet:

﴿And a night of which people say, from its darknesses, it is equal, the sound of eyes and their blind⦆

Abu 'Ali said: the word has four dialects: "siwa" with a kasra on the sin, "sawa'" with a fatha and a long vowel, and these two are the well-known dialects. Among the Arabs are those who put a kasra on the sin and lengthen it, and among them are those who put a damma on its first letter and shorten it; these two dialects are less common than those two. It is said "siyyi" with the meaning of "sawa'," as they said "qi" and "qiwa'".

"Sawa'" is in the nominative as the predicate of inna, or it is in the nominative as a subject whose predicate follows, and the clause is the predicate of inna. It is valid for the predicate of inna to be "la yu'minun" (they will not believe). Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Nafi' recited "a-andharta-hum" with a lengthened hamza, and likewise whatever resembles it throughout the Qur'an. This was also the recitation of al-Kisa'i when he eased it, except that Abu 'Amr's lengthening is longer than Ibn Kathir's, because he inserts an alif between the two hamzas, while Ibn Kathir does not do that. Qalun and Isma'il ibn Ja'far related from Nafi' the insertion of an alif between the two hamzas with easing of the second; Warsh related from him easing the second between-between without inserting an alif between the two hamzas. As for 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i when he makes it clear, and Ibn 'Amir, it is with two hamzas: "a-andharta-hum," and what is like it throughout the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited with both hamzas made clear and an alif inserted between them. al-Zuhri and Ibn Muhaysin recited "andharat-hum" with the first hamza dropped, and "am" indicates the dropped alif.

Makki has greatly lengthened on this verse by mentioning permissible readings he did not recite, and relating such things in books of tafsir is a burden.

Indhar is informing with intimidation; this is its definition. Andhara is a verb that takes two objects. Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Then say: I have warned you of a thunderbolt like the thunderbolt of 'Ad and Thamud﴾ [Fussilat: 13], and He said: ﴿Indeed We have warned you of a near punishment﴾ [An-Naba': 40]. One of the two objects in this verse is omitted, because the meaning indicates it. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a-andharta-hum am lam tundhir-hum﴾ has the wording of a question, but its meaning is a statement. It took the form of a question because it contains equality, which is found in a question. Do you not see that when you say, informing: "It is the same for me whether you sat or went," and when you say, asking: "Did Zayd go out or stand?", the two matters are equal for you; these two are in statement and those two in question, and the non-knowledge of one of them specifically. When equality encompasses both, the wording of question was applied to this statement because it shares with it in the indefiniteness. Every question is an equalization, though not every equalization is a question.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has set a seal﴾ is derived from "khatm," which is the stamping, and "al-khatim" is the stamp. A group among the interpreters went to the view that this is literal, and that the heart is in the shape of a palm that contracts with increased misguidance and aversion finger by finger. Others said: this is figurative, and what Allah created in their hearts of disbelief, misguidance and aversion from faith He named a seal. Others who took it as figurative said: the seal is here ascribed to Allah the Exalted because the disbelievers disbelieved in Him and turned away from worshipping Him and affirming His oneness, as one says: "wealth destroyed so-and-so," whereas it was his poor handling of it that destroyed him.

The majority recited "wa-'ala sam'ihim," and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited "wa-'ala asma'ihim." In the majority's recitation it is a verbal noun which applies to the few and the many. Also, since it is added to a plural pronoun, the added-to indicates the intended meaning. It is possible that the intended meaning is "upon the places of their hearing," so the added word was omitted and the added-to word was put in its place.

"Al-ghisha wa" is the covering that is placed over and conceals. From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

﴿Would that you had asked the Banu Dhubyan what my lineage is, when the smoke covers the white-haired old man⦆

And the other said:

﴿I followed you when upon my eye was a ghisha, but when it was cleared away I cut off my breath, blaming it﴾

"Ghisha'a" is in the nominative as a subject, and what precedes it is its predicate. 'Asim, as related by al-Mufaddal al-Dabbi from him, recited "ghishatan" with the accusative, on the estimate: "and He placed upon their eyes a covering." The seal then applies to the hearts and hearing, and the covering to the eyes, with the pause at His saying "wa-'ala sam'ihim." The rest recited "ghisha'un" with the nominative. Abu 'Ali said: the nominative recitation is better, because the accusative either makes you take it as a seal on what is apparent, and it would then be objectionable that you have placed a barrier between the conjunction and what it conjoins, and this in our view is only permitted in poetry; or you take it as a verb indicated by "seal," estimated as: "and He placed upon their eyes," and the speech then comes in the manner of:

﴿...................................... girded with a sword and a spear⦆

And the saying of the other:

﴿...................................... I fed her chaff and cold water⦆

and you hardly find this usage in a state of ease and choice. So the nominative recitation is better, and the waw is conjunctive joining one sentence to another. He said: I have not heard from "ghisha" a conjugated verb with waw; when this is not found, and its meaning is that of a root whose lam is ya' from "ghashiya yaghsha," as indicated by their saying "al-ghashayan," then "ghisha'a" from "ghashiya" is like "jaba'a" from "jaba'tu," in that the waw is as if a replacement for the ya', since no verb has been conjugated from it, just as none has been conjugated from "jiba'a."

Some interpreters said: the covering is upon the hearing and the sight, and the pause is at His saying "upon their hearts." Others said: the seal is on all of them, and the covering is the seal itself.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: We have already mentioned Abu 'Ali's objection to this view.

Abu Haywa recited "ghashwa" with a fatha on the ghayn and the nominative, which is the recitation of al-A'mash. al-Thawri said: the companions of 'Abd Allah used to recite it "ghashya" with a fatha on the ghayn and the ya' and the nominative. al-Hasan recited "ghushawa" with a damma on the ghayn, and it was also read "ghashawa" with a fatha on the ghayn. The most correct of these readings is the one recited by the seven, with a kasra on the ghayn in the pattern of "imama," since things which always contain something follow this pattern, like "dimama," "imama," "kitaba," " 'isaba," "rababa," and others.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and for them is a great punishment﴾ means: because of your opposition, O Muhammad, and their disbelief in Allah, they deserved that. "Great" means, in relation to a punishment lesser than it which has intervals of slackening; and by this conceivable interval it is valid that two accidents may differ in intensity, like two blacknesses, one of which is more intense than the other, since the other has been interrupted by something that is not blackness.

(p-110) The words of His Majesty, the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe.﴾ ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a covering; and for them is a great punishment.﴾

The meaning of kufr (disbelief) is derived from their saying "kafr" when something covers and conceals. From it is the saying of the poet:

﴿...................................... in a night of kafr of the stars, its clouds⦆

That is, its concealing. From it the night was named "kafir" (covering) because it covers everything with its darkness. The poet said:

﴿So she remembers a heavy, slow burden after she had cast the brightness of her right hand into the kafir⦆

From it the farmers were called "kuffar," because they cover the seed.

As for "kafara" in religion, its meaning is: he covered his heart with rust (rain) so that it is kept away from faith, or he covered the truth with his sayings and his actions.

There is disagreement regarding who this verse was revealed about, after agreement that it is not general, since some disbelievers embraced Islam after it. One group said: it concerns those whom Allah knew beforehand would not believe; Allah the Exalted wished to make known that among people there are those whose state is this, without anyone being aided. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse was revealed concerning Huyayy ibn Akhtab, Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf and their like. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it was revealed concerning the leaders of the confederates, who are the people of the well at Badr.

(p-111) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view has been related like this, and it is an error, because many of the leaders of the confederates embraced Islam, and the arrangement of the verse concerns the companions of the well. The first view among those we have related is the one relied upon. Whoever specifies a particular person is only giving an example of one whose death in disbelief has been revealed to him by the unseen, that he is included within the verse.

His saying: ﴿it is the same for them﴾, meaning: it is equal to them. From it is the saying of the poet:

﴿And a night of which people say, from its darknesses, it is equal, the sound of eyes and their blind⦆

Abu 'Ali said: the word has four dialects: "siwa" with a kasra on the sin, "sawa'" with a fatha and a long vowel, and these two are the well-known dialects. Among the Arabs are those who put a kasra on the sin and lengthen it, and among them are those who put a damma on its first letter and shorten it; these two dialects are less common than those two. It is said "siyyi" with the meaning of "sawa'," as they said "qi" and "qiwa'".

"Sawa'" is in the nominative as the predicate of inna, or it is in the nominative as a subject whose predicate follows, and the clause is the predicate of inna. It is valid for the predicate of inna to be "la yu'minun" (they will not believe). Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir and Nafi' recited "a-andharta-hum" with a lengthened hamza, and likewise whatever resembles it throughout the Qur'an. This was also the recitation of al-Kisa'i when he eased it, except that Abu 'Amr's lengthening is longer than Ibn Kathir's, because he inserts an alif between the two hamzas, while Ibn Kathir does not do that. Qalun and Isma'il ibn Ja'far related from Nafi' the insertion of an alif between the two hamzas with easing of the second; Warsh related from him easing the second between-between without inserting an alif between the two hamzas. As for 'Asim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i when he makes it clear, and Ibn 'Amir, it is with two hamzas: "a-andharta-hum," and what is like it throughout the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Abi Ishaq recited with both hamzas made clear and an alif inserted between them. al-Zuhri and Ibn Muhaysin recited "andharat-hum" with the first hamza dropped, and "am" indicates the dropped alif.

The Arabic word *nun* in *min* (from) should originally be vowelled with a kasra because of the two consecutive unvowelled letters, but it is opened before the *alif-lam* (the definite article). Whoever says that two kasras would be heavy in a word of two letters is challenged by their saying *min ibnika* ("from your son"), *min ismika* ("from your name") and similar forms. The grammarians differed over the word *al-nas* ("the people"). One group said it derives from *nasiya* (to forget): the original *nasiya* was transposed to *niys*, the *ya* moved and was preceded by an open vowel, so it became an *alif*, giving *nas*, and then the *alif-lam* was added. Others said *nas* is a collective noun that took the *alif-lam* without this derivation. Others said the original is *unas*, the *alif-lam* was added to *al-unas*, the *hamza* was dropped, giving *al-nas*, and the *lam* was assimilated into the *nun* because their articulation points are close.

This verse was revealed about the hypocrites (*munafiqun*).

His words, "Among the people are those who say, 'We believe in God'" (﴿مَن يَقُولُ آمَنّا بِاللهِ﴾), shift from the singular to the plural in accordance with the wording and meaning of *man* (whoever). This is acceptable because the singular precedes the plural in rank. But a speaker may not move from a plural form to a singular one. If you said, "Among the people are those who stand and speaks" (in mixed number), it would not be permitted. God Most High named the Day of Resurrection "the Last Day" (*al-yawm al-akhir*) because there is no night after it, and "day" (*yawm*) is only applied to a period preceded by night. Then God negated faith from the hypocrites. In this there is a refutation of the Karramiyya (a sect holding that faith is merely verbal profession, even without belief in the heart), in their saying, "Faith is only speech with the tongue, even if one does not believe in the heart."

The commentators differed over His words, "They seek to deceive God" (﴿يُخادِعُونَ اللهَ﴾). Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said the meaning is "they seek to deceive the Messenger of God," and God is named because of the closeness of His Messenger to Him. Their deception consists in their attempt to make the Messenger of God and the believers disclose their secrets, so that they may guard against what they dislike and take precautions against harm from the believers to what they love. A group of commentators said: rather, they deceive God and the believers, by displaying faith contrary to what they conceal of unbelief, in order to protect their blood, safeguard their property, and think that they have escaped, deceived and succeeded. But they only deceive themselves, for they are going to be in punishment, and they are not aware of it.

The reciters differed over the second "they deceive" (*yukhadi'una*). Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited *yukhadi'una*. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited *wa-ma yakhda'una* ("and they deceive not"). Abu Talut 'Abd al-Salam ibn Shaddad and al-Jarud ibn Abi Sabra recited *yakhda'una* with a *ya* vowelled with a *damma*. Qatada and Muraq al-'Ijli recited *yukhaddi'una* (with the *ya* vowelled with a *damma*, the *kha* with a *fatha*, the *dal* with a kasra and shaddah). The justification for the reading of Ibn Kathir and those mentioned with him is preserving the consistency of the wording, and that the second verb be named with the name of the first verb that caused it. This occurs as the poet said:

"Let no one act ignorantly towards us, lest we act with ignorance more than that of the ignorant."

So his retaliation was called ignorance. This line of reasoning is supported in this verse by the fact that *fa'ala* (the form with an *alif* between the first two radicals) may come from a single agent, as in *'aqabtu al-lissa* ("I punished the thief") and *tara'qtu al-na'l* ("I patched the sandal"). This reading is also justified by the thought that comes to mind and the suggestions that occur to them about entering the religion, hypocrisy within it, and unbelief in the matter and its opposite. In this sense it is like the dialogue of two strangers, so the verb becomes as if it were from two parties. The poet has said:

"Remember from where and from where his drink came, / he consults his two selves like the camel with a herd."

Ibn al-A'rabi recited:

"You did not know what you were saying, and you are not one who says it, / may your life be long, as long as you live, to eternity. / You did not consult your two selves, doubting / about it and its sister, and you were not stingy."

Another said:

"He consults his two selves, while in life there is ample room; / does the melting (of fat) return, or does it not dissolve it?"

Tha'lab recited, from Ibn al-A'rabi:

"I was like the one with the sickness, you did not know when it was afflicted; / she consults her two selves: should she be stolen from or should she commit adultery?"

The justification for the reading of 'Asim and those mentioned with him is that this action is a deception of themselves which is carried out upon them. You say *khadaʿtu al-rajul* meaning "I employed trickery upon the man," and *khadaʿtuhu* meaning "the trick was completed upon him and the purpose was carried out in him." The verbal noun is *khid'* with a kasra on the *kha*, and *khadi'a*. Abu Zayd reported this. So the meaning of the verse is: they only execute evil upon themselves and within themselves.

The justification for the reading of Abu Talut is one of two things. Either the sentence is to be understood as *wa-ma yakhda'una illa 'an anfusihim* ("they deceive none but from their own selves"), in which the preposition is dropped and the verb is connected directly, as in His words, "And Moses chose his people" (﴿واخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ﴾, 7:155), meaning "from among his people." Or *yakhda'una* is treated as if it had the sense of *yantaqisuna* (they diminish), since the meaning is: they do not diminish or despoil anyone except themselves. A similar usage is God's words, "It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast" (﴿لَيْلَةَ الصِيامِ الرَفَثُ إلى نِسائِكُمْ﴾, 2:187). One does not say *rafathtu ila al-mar'a* ("I had sexual relations with the woman"), but since *rafath* has the sense of "going in to," the construction is permitted. Among this type is His words, "Would you like to purify yourself?" (﴿هَلْ لَكَ إلى أنْ تَزَكّى﴾, 79:18). One usually says *hal laka fi kadha* ("would you like such-and-such"), but since the meaning is "I draw you towards purifying yourself," the construction is permitted and fine. This is a noble feature of eloquent speech. Among this type is the words of al-Farazdaq:

"How do you see me, a shield-bearer? / God has killed Ziyad on my behalf."

Here *qatala* (killed) has come to include the meaning of *sarafa* (turned away), so the construction with *'an* is used. Another example is the saying of another:

"If the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me, / by God's life, their pleasure delights me."

Here *radiyat* (were pleased) has come to include the sense of *aqbalat 'alayya* ("turned towards me"). As for al-Kisa'i, he said about this line: the verb *radiya* was connected with the opposite of its meaning, which is *sakhita* (was angry). Matters in speech are sometimes treated as their opposites.

The justification for the reading of Qatada is the intensification of deception, since it leads to the punishment of God.

Al-Khalil said: it is said *khada'a* from one party, because in deception there is a respite, just as one says *'alajtu al-mari'a* ("I treated the patient") because of the respite involved.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy upon him, said:

This is from his subtle insight. It seems he returns the *fa'ala* form to two parties, and there must be in it a respite, a resistance and a delay. Thus he is, in meaning, opposing the sense in which *fa'ala* occurs.

His words, "and they are not aware" (﴿وَما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾), mean: "and they do not know with the knowledge of perception and attentiveness." The word is derived from *shi'ar* (undergarment), as if the thing perceived by the self is a garment for the self. The *shi'ar* is the garment next to the human body, and it derives from *sha'r* (hair). Likewise the poet who is perceptive of strange meanings. The saying *layta shi'ri* ("would that I knew") means "would that my perception were grasped." From this meaning is the poet's saying:

"They raided with an arrow, and no one perceived it, / then they returned and said: 'How good is the milk!'"

There is disagreement about what God negated of them regarding perceiving it. One group said: "and they do not perceive that the harm of this deception returns upon them, because they will remain eternally in the Fire." Others said: "and they do not perceive that God reveals to you their secret and their deception in their saying, 'We believe.'"

"I was like the one with the sickness, you did not know when it was afflicted; / she consults her two selves: should she be stolen from or should she commit adultery?"

The justification for the reading of 'Asim and those mentioned with him is that this action is a deception of themselves which is carried out upon them. You say *khadaʿtu al-rajul* meaning "I employed trickery upon the man," and *khadaʿtuhu* meaning "the trick was completed upon him and the purpose was carried out in him." The verbal noun is *khid'* with a kasra on the *kha*, and *khadi'a*. Abu Zayd reported this. So the meaning of the verse is: they only execute evil upon themselves and within themselves.

The justification for the reading of Abu Talut is one of two things. Either the sentence is to be understood as *wa-ma yakhda'una illa 'an anfusihim* ("they deceive none but from their own selves"), in which the preposition is dropped and the verb is connected directly, as in His words, "And Moses chose his people" (﴿واخْتارَ مُوسى قَوْمَهُ﴾, 7:155), meaning "from among his people." Or *yakhda'una* is treated as if it had the sense of *yantaqisuna* (they diminish), since the meaning is: they do not diminish or despoil anyone except themselves. A similar usage is God's words, "It is made lawful for you to go in to your wives on the night of the fast" (﴿لَيْلَةَ الصِيامِ الرَفَثُ إلى نِسائِكُمْ﴾, 2:187). One does not say *rafathtu ila al-mar'a* ("I had sexual relations with the woman"), but since *rafath* has the sense of "going in to," the construction is permitted. Among this type is His words, "Would you like to purify yourself?" (﴿هَلْ لَكَ إلى أنْ تَزَكّى﴾, 79:18). One usually says *hal laka fi kadha* ("would you like such-and-such"), but since the meaning is "I draw you towards purifying yourself," the construction is permitted and fine. This is a noble feature of eloquent speech. Among this type is the words of al-Farazdaq:

"How do you see me, a shield-bearer? / God has killed Ziyad on my behalf."

Here *qatala* (killed) has come to include the meaning of *sarafa* (turned away), so the construction with *'an* is used. Another example is the saying of another:

"If the Banu Qushayr are pleased with me, / by God's life, their pleasure delights me."

Here *radiyat* (were pleased) has come to include the sense of *aqbalat 'alayya* ("turned towards me"). As for al-Kisa'i, he said about this line: the verb *radiya* was connected with the opposite of its meaning, which is *sakhita* (was angry). Matters in speech are sometimes treated as their opposites.

The justification for the reading of Qatada is the intensification of deception, since it leads to the punishment of God.

Al-Khalil said: it is said *khada'a* from one party, because in deception there is a respite, just as one says *'alajtu al-mari'a* ("I treated the patient") because of the respite involved.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy upon him, said:

This is from his subtle insight. It seems he returns the *fa'ala* form to two parties, and there must be in it a respite, a resistance and a delay. Thus he is, in meaning, opposing the sense in which *fa'ala* occurs.

His words, "and they are not aware" (﴿وَما يَشْعُرُونَ﴾), mean: "and they do not know with the knowledge of perception and attentiveness." The word is derived from *shi'ar* (undergarment), as if the thing perceived by the self is a garment for the self. The *shi'ar* is the garment next to the human body, and it derives from *sha'r* (hair). Likewise the poet who is perceptive of strange meanings. The saying *layta shi'ri* ("would that I knew") means "would that my perception were grasped." From this meaning is the poet's saying:

"They raided with an arrow, and no one perceived it, / then they returned and said: 'How good is the milk!'"

There is disagreement about what God negated of them regarding perceiving it. One group said: "and they do not perceive that the harm of this deception returns upon them, because they will remain eternally in the Fire." Others said: "and they do not perceive that God reveals to you their secret and their deception in their saying, 'We believe.'"

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 10–12:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿In their hearts is a disease, so Allah increased them in disease. And for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth," they say, "We are only reformers."﴾ ﴿Unquestionably, they are the corrupters, but they do not perceive.﴾

(p-120) "Disease" (marad) is a metaphorical expression for the corruption that exists in the beliefs of these hypocrites. This is either doubt, or denial due to their envy, while knowing the truth of what they deny. The interpreters (al-mu'awwilun) explained it along these lines. Some people said: the disease is grief over the manifestation of the matter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Al-Asma'i reported from Abu 'Amr the reading "marḍ" with a sukun on the ra', which is a dialectal form of the verbal noun. Abu al-Fath said: this is not a case of lightening (takhfif).

The interpreters differed about the meaning of His words: ﴿so Allah increased them in disease﴾. It was said: it is a supplication against them. It was said: it is a report that Allah has done this to them. This increase is by what is sent down of revelation and what becomes manifest of proofs; so for these hypocrites it is blindness, and whenever they lie, the disease increases. Hamzah read "fa-zādahum" with a kasra on the zay, and Ibn 'Amir likewise; Nafi' used the "ishmam" (a hint of kasra) on the zay; the rest read it with a fatha.

"Alim" means "mu'lim" (painful), as the poet said, and he is 'Amr ibn Ma'di Karib:

"Does Rayhana's caller, the hearing one..."

meaning "musmi'" (one who makes hear).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "yukadhdhibun" with a damma on the ya' and tashdid on the dhal, and the rest read it with a fatha on the ya' and takhfif on the dhal. The reading with tathqil is supported by His earlier words: ﴿and they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8], for this is a report that they lie. The reading with takhfif is supported by the fact that the context of the verses is a report of their lying, and the threat of the painful punishment is directed at the lying, and at lying in such a matter, since it encompasses disbelief. The reading with tathqil is preferable.

("Idha") is an adverb of time. It is related from al-Mubarrad that in your saying in the sense of suddenness, "kharajat fa-idha Zayd" ("I went out, and suddenly Zayd"), it is an adverb of place because it contains a body; this is rejected, because the meaning is: "I went out, and suddenly there was the presence of Zayd." It therefore contains a verbal noun, as other time adverbs require, and from it is their saying: "Today is wine, and tomorrow is a matter," meaning the existence of wine and the occurrence of a matter. The governing element of "idha" in this verse is "qalu" (they say). The origin of "qila" is "qawl"; the vowel of the waw was moved to the qaf, and it was changed into a ya' because of the kasra preceding it. Al-Kisa'i read "qila, wa-ghida, wa-si'a, wa-si'at, wa-hila, wa-suqa, wa-ji'a" with a damma on the initial letter of all of these; this is also reported from Ibn 'Amir. It is also reported from him that he read with a kasra "ghila, qila, and ji'a" (the ghayn, qaf and jim) wherever they occur in the Qur'an. Nafi' applied a damma to two of these, "si'a" and "si'at," and a kasra to the rest. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah used a kasra on the initial letters of all of these.

The pronoun in "lahum" refers back to the hypocrites mentioned earlier. Some people said: the reference here is to the hypocrites among the Jews. Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him) said in explaining this verse: "These have not yet come"; and the meaning of his words "they have not died out" is that rather, they keep coming in every age.

﴿Do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ means: by disbelief and allying with disbelievers. "Nahnu" is a pronoun of the nominative category, built on damma, since it is a strong pronoun used for a single honored person, for two, and for a group; it was given the most complete of the vowels. Also, since it is in most cases a plural pronoun, and the plural pronoun in apparent nouns takes a waw, it was given the damma, since it is the sister of the waw.

For the hypocrites' saying ﴿We are only reformers﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: they deny that they cause corruption, and this is their continued persistence in hypocrisy. The second: that they acknowledge allying with the disbelievers, but claim that this is reform, since they are kin who are to be kept in contact. The third: that they are reformers between the disbelievers and the believers, and for this reason they mix with the disbelievers.

"Ala" is an opening particle of speech, and "inna" with a kasra on the alif is a resumptive beginning. The second "hum" is a nominative in the position of the subject, "al-mufsidun" is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "inna." It may be a separating pronoun (fasl), which the Kufans call "'imad"; in that case "al-mufsidun" is the predicate of "inna," and "hum" has no place in the i'rab. It may also be an emphatic restatement of the pronoun in "innahum," in which case its position is in the accusative.

The definite article in His words "al-mufsidun" entered because the word had been mentioned earlier in "la tufsidu" (do not cause corruption), so it is as if it were a kind of known reference. Had the report about them come without the word having been mentioned before, it would have been "ala innahum mufsidun," as al-Jurjani said.

The shaykh, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this definite article contains emphasis, as you say, "Zayd is the man," meaning: Zayd has the qualities of the man; so it may dispense with an introduction that requires a prior reference.

"Lakin," with its whole form, is a particle of contrast (istidrak). It may be intended here: "they do not realize that they are corrupters," and it may be intended: "they do not realize that Allah will expose them." This is alongside the possibility that their saying "We are only reformers" is pure denial of corruption. The first possibility is that their saying "We are only reformers" is a belief on their part that it is good in the bond of kinship, or a reconciliation between the believers and the disbelievers.

[p. 123] The Exalted's saying:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed," they say, "Shall we believe as the foolish have believed?" Verily, it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know.﴾ ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." But when they go off alone to their devils, they say, "Verily, we are with you; we were only mocking."﴾

The meaning: Believe in Muhammad ﷺ and his law, just as the emigrants (muhajirun) and the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) among the people of Yathrib believed. They said: "Shall we be like those whose intellects are light?" *Al-safah* (foolishness) is lightness and thinness that calls to lightness. It is said of a garment, *thawb safih*, when it is thin and loosely woven. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rumma:

"They advance as spears sway when the tips of their shafts are swept by the passing of the spring breezes."

This saying they used to utter in secret, so God made His Prophet and the believers aware of it. He established that foolishness, thinness of judgment, and corruption of insight are in their very domain and are their attribute. He informed that they do not know that they are the foolish, because of the rust (*al-rayn*) that is upon their hearts.

Some said: the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites of the Jews, and by "the people" is meant Abd Allah ibn Salam and those of the Children of Israel who embraced Islam.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is a specification for which there is no evidence. The original form of *laqu* (they met) is *laqiyu*; the damma was felt heavy upon the ya', so it was made quiescent, and two quiescent letters came together, so the ya' was deleted.

Ibn al-Samayfa' recited: *laqawu alladhina* (لاقَوُا الَّذِينَ).

Such was the state of the hypocrites: they displayed faith to the believers and displayed disbelief in their private gatherings with one another. The believers would be deceived by them on account of kinship. Thus proofs (*al-shahadat*) were not sought against them, and their identification as hypocrites was not established with a certainty that would, by its clarity, require the ruling of their execution. What they displayed of faith protected their blood. The Messenger of God ﷺ would turn away from them and leave them in the confusion of doubt, fearing that it might be said of him that he kills his companions, and people would then flee from him. This accords with what [the Prophet] ﷺ said to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, when he said to him, at the time of the saying of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, "*They will surely expel the mightier from it the meaner*" (al-Munafiqun 8)—the story goes on—"Leave me, O Messenger of God, that I may strike the neck of this hypocrite." He said: "Leave him, lest people say that Muhammad kills his companions."

This is the position of the companions of Malik, may God be pleased with him, concerning the meaning of the Messenger of God ﷺ restraining himself from killing the hypocrites, despite his knowledge of their disbelief in general. This was stated by Muhammad ibn al-Jahm, Isma'il al-Qadi, al-Abhari, and Ibn al-Majishun, and they argued from the saying of the Exalted: "*If the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease and the agitators in the city do not desist, We will surely incite you against them; then they will not remain your neighbours therein except briefly. Cursed; wherever they are found, they will be seized and slain with [intense] slaying*" (al-Ahzab 60–61).

Qatada said its meaning is: when they openly declare hypocrisy.

Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: Hypocrisy in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ is what among us today is *zandaqa* (heresy, covert unbelief, the zindiq being the one who professes it). Thus the *zindiq* is killed if testimony is given against him for it, without being asked to repent (*istitaba*), because he does not display what he would be asked to repent of. The Messenger of God ﷺ restrained himself from [killing] the hypocrites only to establish a sunna for his community that a ruler does not judge by his own knowledge when he has not witnessed [the offence] against the hypocrites.

The judge Isma'il said: Against Abd Allah ibn Ubayy only Zayd ibn Arqam testified, alone; and against al-Jullas ibn Suwayd only Umayr ibn Sa'd, his stepson, testified, alone. Had two men testified against any of them for his disbelief and hypocrisy, he would have been killed.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Stronger than the singular testimony of Zayd and others is that the utterance was not a clear statement of disbelief, but disbelief is only understood from its implications. Verily, it is they who are the foolish, but they do not know.﴾ ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe." But when they go off alone to their devils, they say, "Verily, we are with you; we were only mocking."﴾

The meaning: Believe in Muhammad ﷺ and his law, just as the emigrants (muhajirun) and the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) among the people of Yathrib believed. They said: "Shall we be like those whose intellects are light?" *Al-safah* (foolishness) is lightness and thinness that calls to lightness. It is said of a garment, *thawb safih*, when it is thin and loosely woven. From this is the verse of Dhu al-Rumma:

"They advance as spears sway when the tips of their shafts are swept by the passing of the spring breezes."

This saying they used to utter in secret, so God made His Prophet and the believers aware of it. He established that foolishness, thinness of judgment, and corruption of insight are in their very domain and are their attribute. He informed that they do not know that they are the foolish, because of the rust (*al-rayn*) that is upon their hearts.

Some said: the verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites of the Jews, and by "the people" is meant Abd Allah ibn Salam and those of the Children of Israel who embraced Islam.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is a specification for which there is no evidence. The original form of *laqu* (they met) is *laqiyu*; the damma was felt heavy upon the ya', so it was made quiescent, and two quiescent letters came together, so the ya' was deleted.

Ibn al-Samayfa' recited: *laqawu alladhina* (لاقَوُا الَّذِينَ).

Such was the state of the hypocrites: they displayed faith to the believers and displayed disbelief in their private gatherings with one another. The believers would be deceived by them on account of kinship. Thus proofs (*al-shahadat*) were not sought against them, and their identification as hypocrites was not established with a certainty that would, by its clarity, require the ruling of their execution. What they displayed of faith protected their blood. The Messenger of God ﷺ would turn away from them and leave them in the confusion of doubt, fearing that it might be said of him that he kills his companions, and people would then flee from him. This accords with what [the Prophet] ﷺ said to Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, when he said to him, at the time of the saying of Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, "*They will surely expel the mightier from it the meaner*" (al-Munafiqun 8)—the story goes on—"Leave me, O Messenger of God, that I may strike the neck of this hypocrite." He said: "Leave him, lest people say that Muhammad kills his companions."

Qatada said its meaning is: when they openly declare hypocrisy.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 15–16:

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Allah mocks them and extends them in their transgression, wandering blindly.﴾ ﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, but their commerce has not profited them, and they were not [rightly] guided.﴾

The exegetes differed concerning this "mockery" (istihza'). The majority of scholars said: it is the naming of the punishment by the name of the sin, and the Arabs use this often. From it is the poet's saying:

"Let no one among us act ignorantly against us, lest we act with ignorance beyond the ignorance of the ignorant."

Others said: Allah, exalted is He, does to them acts which, in human reflection, are a form of mockery, according to what is related: "Indeed the Fire freezes as fat freezes, so they walk upon it, thinking it a means of deliverance, and then it swallows them up." And what is related: "Indeed the gates of the Fire are opened for them, so they go toward the exit..." Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan took this line.

(p-129) Others said: His mockery of them is His gradual leading of them on from where they do not know, for by the abundance of Allah's worldly blessings upon them, they think that He is pleased with them, while He, exalted is He, has decreed their punishment. This, in human reflection, is as if it were mockery.

"Yamuddu-hum" means: He increases them in transgression. Mujahid said: "Its meaning is: He gives them respite (yumli)." Yunus ibn Habib said: it is said "madda fi al-sharr" (he extended in evil) and "amadda fi al-khayr" (he extended in good). Others said: "madda al-shay'" means to extend a thing with something of its own kind and nature, while "amadda-hu" means to extend it with something different from it. One says: "madda al-nahr" (the river swelled), and another river "madda-hu" (extended it). It is also said "amadda-hu." Al-Lihyani said: for everything into which its like enters and multiplies it, one says "madda-hu yamuddu-hu madda." In the Revelation: ﴿And the sea, after it, is extended by seven seas﴾ [Luqman: 27].

The "madda" (supply) of a thing is what extends it; the ha' is added for emphasis.

Ibn Qutayba and others said: "madadtu al-dawa" and "amdadtu-ha" have the same meaning.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems that "madadtu-ha" means I made another ink added to its ink, and "amdadtu-ha" means I made it possessed of ink, like "qabara" and "aqbara" (to bury), and "hasara" and "ahsara" (to confine). And "madadna al-qawm" means we became helpers to them, and "amdadnahum bi-ghayrina" means we supplied them with others. Al-Lihyani also related: "amadda al-amir jundahu bi-l-khayl" (the commander supplied his army with horses). In the Revelation: ﴿And We have supplied you with wealth and children﴾ [al-Isra': 6].

(p-130) Some linguists said: ﴿wa-yamuddu-hum fi tughyanihim﴾ means: He gives them respite and makes them persist. The word may be from "madd," which is prolongation and extension, as it is explained in: ﴿in extended columns﴾ [al-Humaza: 9]. It may also mean an increase in the transgression itself. "Tughyan" is excess and overstepping the limit, as one says: "taghā al-ma'" (the water rose beyond its bounds), and "taghat al-nar" (the fire blazed out of control). It is related from al-Kisa'i that he read "tughyanihim" with imala (vowel inclination). "Ya'mahun" means: they wander bewildered. "Al-'amah" is bewilderment in terms of sight, and the common meaning is one who seems not to see, being perplexed in darkness, or in a wilderness, or in distress.

His statement "Ulaika" is a demonstrative referring to those previously mentioned; it is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and "alladhina" is its predicate (khabar). "Ishtarawu" is a relative clause (sila) of "alladhina." Its original form was "ishtariyu": the yā' moved and the letter before it was open, so it became an alif, which was then dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters. It was also said: the damma was felt heavy on the yā', so it became unvocalized and was dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters, and then the wāw was given a vowel because it met the unvocalized letter after it. It was specifically given damma for several reasons: among them, that damma is the sister of wāw and the lightest of the vowels upon it; among them, that since it is the wāw of the plural, it was given damma as was done with the nūn in "naḥnu"; and among them, that it was given damma to follow the vowel of the dropped yā' before it. Abu 'Ali said: damma became preferable in it, to distinguish it from the wāw of "aw" and "law," since those are vowelled with kasra. Abu al-Sammal Qu'nub al-'Adawi read "ishtarawa al-dalala" with a fatha on the wāw, and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read it with a kasra on the wāw. "Al-dalala" and "al-dalal" mean perdition, the opposite of guidance (huda), which is rightly reaching the goal.

The wording of the exegetes differed regarding the meaning of His statement: ﴿ishtarawu al-dalala bi-l-huda﴾.

Some said: they took error and left guidance. Others said: they preferred error (istahabbu al-dalala) (p-131) and shunned guidance, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat: 17]. Others said: "shira'" (purchase) here is a metaphor and comparison: when they abandoned guidance, which was offered to them, and fell into error instead of it, choosing it, they were likened to those who purchase, as if they had pushed their guidance away into error, since it had been available for them to take. On this meaning Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, relied in prohibiting that a man buy on the condition that he may choose among all the individual items of a kind whose members differ, where excess (tafadul) is not permitted in it.

Some said: the verse concerns those among the hypocrites who had believed, then apostatized inwardly and in their conviction. On this view, the purchase comes close to its literal sense.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿fa-ma ribiat tijaratuhum﴾ concludes the parable with something resembling its beginning in the word "purchase." He attributed the profit to the commerce, as they say: "laylun qa'im wa-nahar sa'im" (a standing night and a fasting day). The meaning is: they did not profit in their commerce. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "fa-ma ribiat tijaratuhum" in the plural.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿wa-ma kanu muhtadin﴾ — it was said: the meaning is in this purchase of theirs; it was said: it is absolute; and it was said: it is in Allah's prior knowledge. The wording admits all of these.

Others said: "shira'" (purchase) here is a metaphor and comparison: when they abandoned guidance, which was offered to them, and fell into error instead of it, choosing it, they were likened to those who purchase, as if they had pushed their guidance away into error, since it had been available for them to take. On this meaning Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, relied in prohibiting that a man buy on the condition that he may choose among all the individual items of a kind whose members differ, where excess (tafadul) is not permitted in it.

Some said: the verse concerns those among the hypocrites who had believed, then apostatized inwardly and in their conviction. On this view, the purchase comes close to its literal sense.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿fa-ma ribiat tijaratuhum﴾ concludes the parable with something resembling its beginning in the word "purchase." He attributed the profit to the commerce, as they say: "laylun qa'im wa-nahar sa'im" (a standing night and a fasting day). The meaning is: they did not profit in their commerce. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "fa-ma ribiat tijaratuhum" in the plural.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿wa-ma kanu muhtadin﴾ — it was said: the meaning is in this purchase of theirs; it was said: it is absolute; and it was said: it is in Allah's prior knowledge. The wording admits all of these.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 17–18:

(p-132) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Their parable is like that of one who kindled a fire; but when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darkness, unable to see.﴾ ﴿Deaf, dumb, and blind, so they will not return.﴾

"Al-mathal", "al-mathl", and "al-mathil" are one and the same, meaning: likeness. So have the people of lexicography stated. "Al-mutamāthilān" are two things that resemble each other. The likeness of a thing may be a body like it, and it may be what the mind comprehends and imagines of a thing as a parable for it. So His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Their parable is like that of﴾, means: what takes shape in the mind of the one who considers their affair is like what takes shape in the mind of the one who considers the affair of the one who kindled the fire. By this, the difficulty is removed that arises in the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the parable of Paradise﴾ [al-Ra'd: 35], and in the interpretation of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11], because what the intellect attains of oneness and eternity, and of negating what is not permissible for Him, is that nothing resembles Him in it. That attained meaning is the "highest parable" in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest parable﴾ [al-Nahl: 60]. It has been related in its interpretation: "that there is no god but Allah," so it is explained in terms of oneness.

As for His saying "mathaluhum" (their parable), it is in the nominative as the subject of the inchoative, and the predicate is in the kāf. On this view the kāf is a noun, as it is in the verse of al-A'sha:

؎ Will you desist, when he who forbids the wicked will not desist? Like the spear-thrust from which oil and twisted wick flow out.

It is permissible that the predicate be omitted, its estimate being: "their parable is a settled thing like the parable of," and then the kāf on this view is a particle (p-133). This is not permissible in the verse of al-A'sha, because the omitted element is an agent whose estimate is "a thing like the spear-thrust," and according to the majority of the Basran grammarians the agent may not be omitted, whereas omitting the predicate of the inchoative is permitted when the speech indicates it. Al-Akhfash permitted omitting the agent, and that the kāf in the verse of al-A'sha be a particle.

He used the singular "alladhī" because He did not intend to liken a group to a group; rather the intent is that each one of the hypocrites, his act is like the act of the one who kindled the fire. And "alladhī" is also not a reference to one specific individual necessarily; rather to this act, which occurred from one person or from a group. The grammarians said: "alladhī" is an ambiguous noun that applies to the singular and the plural. "Istawqada" is said to mean "awqada" (kindled), and that is like "ʿajiba" and "istaʿjaba" having the same meaning. Abu ʿAli said: and like "hazi'a" and "istahza'a," "sakhira" and "istaskhara," "waqqara" and "istaqarra," "ʿalā qarnahu" and "ista'lāhu." The form istaf'ala has also come with the meaning of af'ala: "ajāba" and "istajāba." From this is the poet's saying:

؎ A caller called, "O you who answer to generosity," but none answered him at that moment.

And "akhlafa li-ahlihi" and "istakhlafa" when he brought them water. From this is the poet's saying:

؎ And waterers from a desert land, their jaws yellowed, their gullets red.

And from this is the other's saying:

؎ ...................................... He gave it drink and sated it with water, one who causes water to come.

(p-134) From this is "awqada" and "istawqada," as Abu Zayd said. It was also said: "istawqada" is meant to seek from another that he kindle for him, according to the well-known pattern of istaf'ala. That requires his need for the fire, and its extinguishing, along with his need for it, is more painful to him.

Scholars differed regarding "adā'at." It was said that it is transitive, because it is derived with the hamza from "ḍā'a." From this is the saying of al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib about the Prophet ﷺ:

؎ When you were born, the earth shone, and the horizon was illuminated by your light.

On this view, "mā" in His saying "mā ḥawlahu" is the object. It was also said that "adā'at" is not transitive, because it is said "ḍā'a" and "adā'a" with the same meaning, so "mā" is superfluous and "ḥawlahu" is an adverbial of place.

The interpreters differed regarding the act of the hypocrites that resembles the act of the one who kindled the fire. One group said: it concerns one who believed and then disbelieved by way of hypocrisy; his faith is like the fire when it illuminates, and his subsequent disbelief is like its extinguishing and the departure of the light. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others said: what the hypocrite displays of faith in this world, by which he protects his blood, secures his property, marries, and mingles, is like the fire that illuminated what was around him (p-135). When he dies, he goes to the painful punishment; that is like its extinguishing and his remaining in darkness. Another group said: the hypocrites' approach to the Muslims and their speech with them is like the fire, and their turning back to their rebellious companions and their relapse among them is like its going out. Another group, among them Qatada, said: their uttering "There is no god but Allah" and the Qur'an is like the illumination of the fire, and their holding disbelief in their hearts is like its extinguishing. Most of the grammarians said: the response to "lamma" is "dhahaba," and the pronoun in "nūrihim" in this view returns to "alladhī." The verse may be compared to the poet's saying:

؎ Indeed, those whose blood was spilled at Fulj, they are the people, all of the people, O Umm Khalid.

On this view the likening of the hypocrite to the one who kindled the fire is complete, because the kindler's remaining in darkness, unable to see, is like the hypocrite's remaining, according to the difference previously mentioned. Some said: the response to "lamma" is implied, and it is "ṭafi'at" (it went out), and the pronoun in "nūrihim" on this view refers to the hypocrite, and the report of this is about a state that will be in the Hereafter, namely His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So a wall with a gate will be set up between them﴾ [al-Hadid: 13]. This view is not strong.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Abu al-Sammal read "fī ẓulumātin" with a sukun on the lam, and a group read "ẓulamātin" with a fatha on the lam.

(p-136) Abu al-Fath said: for "ẓulumātin" and "kisrāt" there are three dialects: imitation of the ḍamma by the ḍamma, and of the kasra by the kasra; or lightening by shifting to fatha in the second; or lightening by making the second sukun. All of these are permissible and good. As for the pattern fi'lah with fatha, it necessarily requires heaviness by imitation, so one says tamrah and tamarāt. Some who read "ẓulamātin" with a fatha on the lam held that it is the plural of ẓulm, so it is a plural of a plural.

"Al-aṣamm" is the one who does not hear; "al-abkam" is the one who does not speak and does not understand; if he understands, he is "al-akhras" (the mute). It was also said: "al-abkam" and "al-akhras" are the same. He described them with these attributes because their deeds of error and their scarcity of response are like the deeds of one with this description. "Ṣummun" is in the nominative as a predicate of an inchoative; either this is by estimating the repetition of "ulā'ika," or by implying "hum." ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud and Hafsa, the Mother of the Believers, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "ṣummān, bukman, ʿumyan" in the accusative. Its accusative is as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) of the pronoun in "muhtadīn." It was also said that it is an accusative of censure, but this is weak. As for one who makes the pronoun in "nūrihim" refer to the hypocrites and not to the kindlers, then the accusative of these attributes is as a circumstantial accusative of the pronoun in "tarakahum." Some of the exegetes said: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿so they will not return﴾ is a report from Him, exalted is He, that they will not believe in any way.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This would only be valid if the verse were about specific individuals. Others said: its meaning is "so they will not return" as long as they remain in the state He described them with; and this is the correct view, because the verse is not specific, and all of them are exposed to returning and are called to it.
