**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 19–20:**

God the Exalted said:

﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, in which are darknesses, thunder, and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And God encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it; and when darkness falls over them, they stand still. Had God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight. Indeed God has power over everything.﴾

(p-137) "Aw" (or) is used for giving a choice. Its meaning is: "Liken them to this, or to that," not that one must be limited to one of the two. His words, ﴿or like a rainstorm﴾, are coordinated with ﴿like the one who﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. Al-Tabari said: "Aw" here means "wa" (and).

(p-138) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a foreign usage (ʿujma) [in the sense of being a non-Arabic or unusual expression]. "Al-sayyib" means rain, from *ṣāba yaṣūbu*, meaning to descend from a height to a lower place. From this is the saying of 'Alqama ibn 'Abada:

> As if a cloud had poured down upon them,
> whose thunderbolts for its birds are a soft murmur.

And the saying of another:

> So you are not of mankind, but of an angel
> who has descended from the air of the sky, pouring down.

The original form of *ṣayyib* is *ṣayyūb*. The waw and the yaʾ came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into a yaʾ and the two were assimilated (idgham), as happened in *sayyid* and *mayyit*. Some of the Kufan grammarians said: the original form of *ṣayyib* is *ṣuwayb* on the pattern of *faʿīl*. It would then have been required that it not be altered, just as *ṭawīl* was not altered; therefore this view is weak. His words, the Exalted, ﴿darknesses﴾ in the plural, indicate the darkness of the night and the darkness of the thick cloud. Because these pile up upon one another and increase, it is expressed in the plural. The darkness of a thick cloud is a terror and a grief to the soul, unlike a cloud and rain when its thickness has cleared, for then it is pleasant and delightful.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

> No garden of the gardens of the sandgrouse
> whose lamps are its hawdhan (flowers) is more beautiful than it,
> nor a cloud of rain, its darknesses (adjan) having cleared, in a dewy morning.

(p-139) The scholars differed concerning "al-ra'd" (thunder). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Shahr ibn Hawshab and others said: it is an angel who drives the clouds with this audible sound. Whenever a cloud strays, he cries out to it; and when his anger intensifies, fire flies from his mouth, and these are the thunderbolts. The name of this angel is "al-Ra'd." It was also said: "al-Ra'd" is an angel, and this sound is his glorification (tasbih). It was also said: "al-Ra'd" is the name of the audible sound. This was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and this is what is known in the language of the Arabs. Labid said in the Jahiliyya:

> The thunder and the thunderbolts stunned me
> on the day of the hateful battle of Najd (with the Fawaris).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "al-Ra'd" is a wind that is choked among the clouds, so it produces that sound. It was also said: "al-Ra'd" is the striking together of the bodies of the clouds. Most scholars hold that the thunder is an angel, and that its sound is his glorification and his driving of the clouds.

They differed concerning "al-barq" (lightning). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is an iron whip in the hand of the angel with which he drives the clouds. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a whip of light in the hand of the angel with which he drives the clouds onward. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that lightning is an angel who appears (yatarā'ā). Some people said: lightning is water, and this is a weak view.

As for "al-sa'iqa" (thunderbolt): al-Khalil said: it is a severe strike resulting from the sound of the thunder, sometimes accompanied by a piece of fire. It is said that it is from the whip that is in the hand of the angel. As for the piece of fire, it was said: it is what comes out of the angel's mouth at the time of his anger.

(p-140) Al-Khalil also related from some Arab tribes the form "al-sa'iqa" with a sin. Al-Naqqash said: it is said *ṣā'iqa*, *ṣa'qa* and *ṣāqi'a* with one meaning. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "min al-sawāqi'" with the qaf placed before the ʿayn [i.e., transposed]. Abu 'Amr said: this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim recited "ḥadhāra al-mawt" with a kasra on the ḥa' and with an alif.

The interpreters differed about the purpose of this parable, and how the states of the hypocrites are arranged to correspond to what is in the parable of darknesses, thunder, lightning and thunderbolts. The majority of the exegetes said: Allah, the Exalted, likened the Qur'an to the rainstorm, because of the confusion it causes for them; the blindness is the darknesses, and what is in it of threat; the warning is the thunder; the clear proofs and brilliant evidences in it which almost dazzle them are the lightning; their being frightened, alarmed and warned is the placing of their fingers in their ears; and the exposure of their hypocrisy, the publicizing of their disbelief, and the legal obligations which they dislike, such as jihad, zakat and the like, are the thunderbolts.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is sound and clear. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Two men among the hypocrites fled from the Prophet (ﷺ) to the polytheists, and this rain which Allah mentioned befell them. They became certain of destruction and said: 'Would that we had woken up and come to Muhammad, and placed our hands in his hand!' They woke up, came to him, and their Islam was good. So Allah struck, with what befell them, a parable for the hypocrites." He also said, Ibn Mas'ud: the hypocrites in the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to put their fingers in their ears so that they would not hear the Qur'an. So Allah struck the parable for them. This agrees with the view of the majority which we have mentioned.

Some people said: the thunder and the lightning are in the position of the Qur'an's warning and threat.

﴿Muhit bil-kafirin﴾ (encompasses the disbelievers) means: by His punishment and His seizing of them. It is said: "The ruler encompassed so-and-so" when he seized him with a seizure that besieges him from every side. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. So in the speech there is an omission of a noun in the genitive construction (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "encompasses the disbelievers by His punishment." "Yakādu" (nearly/almost) is a verb which negates the meaning when affirmed, and affirms it when negated. So here the lightning did not snatch away their sight; and "al-khatf" means taking away with speed.

The recitation differed regarding this word. The majority of the people recited ﴿yakhṭifu abṣārahum﴾ with a fatha on the yaʾ and the ṭāʾ and a sukun on the khāʾ, following their saying in the past tense *khaṭifa* with a kasra on the ṭāʾ; this is the most eloquent of the Arabic dialects, and it is Qurashi. ʿAli ibn al-Husayn and Yahya ibn Wathhab recited *yakhṭifu* with a fatha on the yaʾ, a sukun on the khāʾ, and a kasra on the ṭāʾ, following the saying of some Arabs in the past tense *khaṭafa* with a fatha on the ṭāʾ. Al-Mahdawi attributed this recitation to al-Hasan and Abu Raja', and that is a mistake. Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', 'Asim al-Jahdari and Qatada recited *yakhiṭṭifu* with a fatha on the yaʾ, a kasra on the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ, and a shadda on the ṭāʾ. Its original form is *yakhtatifu*: the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ, and the khāʾ was given a kasra because of the meeting of two sukuns. Ibn Mujahid related a recitation which he did not attribute to anyone: *yakhaṭṭifu* with a fatha on the yaʾ and the khāʾ, and a shadda on the kasra-marked ṭāʾ. Abu al-Fath said: its original form is *yakhtatifu*; the vowel of the tāʾ was moved to the khāʾ, and the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ. Abu ʿAmr al-Dani related from al-Hasan also that he recited *yakhaṭṭifu* with a fatha on the yaʾ, the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ, and with a shadda on it. **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 19–20:**

God the Exalted said:

﴿Or like a rainstorm from the sky, in which are darknesses, thunder, and lightning. They put their fingers in their ears against the thunderbolts, for fear of death. And God encompasses the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight. Whenever it lights up for them, they walk in it; and when darkness falls over them, they stand still. Had God willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight. Indeed God has power over everything.﴾

(p-137) "Aw" (or) is used for giving a choice. Its meaning is: "Liken them to this, or to that," not that one must be limited to one of the two. His words, ﴿or like a rainstorm﴾, are coordinated with ﴿like the one who﴾ [al-Baqarah: 17]. Al-Tabari said: "Aw" here means "wa" (and).

(p-138) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a foreign usage (ʿujma) [in the sense of being a non-Arabic or unusual expression]. "Al-sayyib" means rain, from *ṣāba yaṣūbu*, meaning to descend from a height to a lower place. From this is the saying of 'Alqama ibn 'Abada:

> As if a cloud had poured down upon them,
> whose thunderbolts for its birds are a soft murmur.

And the saying of another:

> So you are not of mankind, but of an angel
> who has descended from the air of the sky, pouring down.

The original form of *ṣayyib* is *ṣayyūb*. The waw and the yaʾ came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukun, so the waw was changed into a yaʾ and the two were assimilated (idgham), as happened in *sayyid* and *mayyit*. Some of the Kufan grammarians said: the original form of *ṣayyib* is *ṣuwayb* on the pattern of *faʿīl*. It would then have been required that it not be altered, just as *ṭawīl* was not altered; therefore this view is weak. His words, the Exalted, ﴿darknesses﴾ in the plural, indicate the darkness of the night and the darkness of the thick cloud. Because these pile up upon one another and increase, it is expressed in the plural. The darkness of a thick cloud is a terror and a grief to the soul, unlike a cloud and rain when its thickness has cleared, for then it is pleasant and delightful.

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

> No garden of the gardens of the sandgrouse
> whose lamps are its hawdhan (flowers) is more beautiful than it,
> nor a cloud of rain, its darknesses (adjan) having cleared, in a dewy morning.

(p-139) The scholars differed concerning "al-ra'd" (thunder). Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Shahr ibn Hawshab and others said: it is an angel who drives the clouds with this audible sound. Whenever a cloud strays, he cries out to it; and when his anger intensifies, fire flies from his mouth, and these are the thunderbolts. The name of this angel is "al-Ra'd." It was also said: "al-Ra'd" is an angel, and this sound is his glorification (tasbih). It was also said: "al-Ra'd" is the name of the audible sound. This was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, and this is what is known in the language of the Arabs. Labid said in the Jahiliyya:

> The thunder and the thunderbolts stunned me
> on the day of the hateful battle of Najd (with the Fawaris).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "al-Ra'd" is a wind that is choked among the clouds, so it produces that sound. It was also said: "al-Ra'd" is the striking together of the bodies of the clouds. Most scholars hold that the thunder is an angel, and that its sound is his glorification and his driving of the clouds.

They differed concerning "al-barq" (lightning). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: it is an iron whip in the hand of the angel with which he drives the clouds. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is a whip of light in the hand of the angel with which he drives the clouds onward. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that lightning is an angel who appears (yatarā'ā). Some people said: lightning is water, and this is a weak view.

As for "al-sa'iqa" (thunderbolt): al-Khalil said: it is a severe strike resulting from the sound of the thunder, sometimes accompanied by a piece of fire. It is said that it is from the whip that is in the hand of the angel. As for the piece of fire, it was said: it is what comes out of the angel's mouth at the time of his anger.

(p-140) Al-Khalil also related from some Arab tribes the form "al-sa'iqa" with a sin. Al-Naqqash said: it is said *ṣā'iqa*, *ṣa'qa* and *ṣāqi'a* with one meaning. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "min al-sawāqi'" with the qaf placed before the ʿayn [i.e., transposed]. Abu 'Amr said: this is the dialect of Tamim. Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim recited "ḥadhāra al-mawt" with a kasra on the ḥa' and with an alif.

The interpreters differed about the purpose of this parable, and how the states of the hypocrites are arranged to correspond to what is in the parable of darknesses, thunder, lightning and thunderbolts. The majority of the exegetes said: Allah, the Exalted, likened the Qur'an to the rainstorm, because of the confusion it causes for them; the blindness is the darknesses, and what is in it of threat; the warning is the thunder; the clear proofs and brilliant evidences in it which almost dazzle them are the lightning; their being frightened, alarmed and warned is the placing of their fingers in their ears; and the exposure of their hypocrisy, the publicizing of their disbelief, and the legal obligations which they dislike, such as jihad, zakat and the like, are the thunderbolts.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is sound and clear. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "Two men among the hypocrites fled from the Prophet (ﷺ) to the polytheists, and this rain which Allah mentioned befell them. They became certain of destruction and said: 'Would that we had woken up and come to Muhammad, and placed our hands in his hand!' They woke up, came to him, and their Islam was good. So Allah struck, with what befell them, a parable for the hypocrites." He also said, Ibn Mas'ud: the hypocrites in the assembly of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to put their fingers in their ears so that they would not hear the Qur'an. So Allah struck the parable for them. This agrees with the view of the majority which we have mentioned.

Some people said: the thunder and the lightning are in the position of the Qur'an's warning and threat.

﴿Muhit bil-kafirin﴾ (encompasses the disbelievers) means: by His punishment and His seizing of them. It is said: "The ruler encompassed so-and-so" when he seized him with a seizure that besieges him from every side. From this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and his fruit was encompassed﴾ [al-Kahf: 42]. So in the speech there is an omission of a noun in the genitive construction (hadhf mudaf), meaning: "encompasses the disbelievers by His punishment." "Yakādu" (nearly/almost) is a verb which negates the meaning when affirmed, and affirms it when negated. So here the lightning did not snatch away their sight; and "al-khatf" means taking away with speed.

The recitation differed regarding this word. Al-Mahdawi attributed this recitation to al-Hasan and Abu Raja', and that is a mistake. (p-143) His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿O people, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become mindful of Him.﴾ ﴿He who made the earth a bed for you, and the sky a canopy, and sent down water from the sky and brought forth with it fruits as provision for you. So do not set up rivals to God while you know.﴾

"Yā" is the particle of address, and it carries an alerting force. "Ayyu" is the one addressed (al-munādā). Abu 'Ali said: "Ayyu" is brought in after the vocative particle when the noun that follows has the definite article (*al*), because the vocative particle already gives definiteness, so two definitions would otherwise combine. "Hā" is an alerting particle and a pointer to the intended addressee, and it stands in the same position as *dhā* in the singular. "Al-nās" (the people) is an obligatory epithet (na't lāzim) of "ayyu." Mujahid said: wherever "Yā ayyuhā al-nās" occurs in the Qur'an, it is Meccan, and "Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū" is Medinan.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It has already been mentioned at the beginning of the surah that the whole surah is Medinan. "Yā ayyuhā al-nās" may occur in a Medinan passage, but as for his statement regarding "Yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū," it is correct.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿worship your Lord﴾ means: affirm His oneness and single Him out for worship. He mentioned His creating them from among His other attributes, since the Arabs acknowledged that God created them, so He cited that as proof against them. Regarding "la'alla" in this verse, many of the exegetes (mufassirūn, scholars of tafsir) said: it carries the sense of making taqwa (God-consciousness) obligatory, and it is not, when from God, a sense of hope or expectation. Sibawayh and the leading authorities of the Arabic language said: it retains its original meaning, and hope and expectation belong only to the realm of humans. That is, when you reflect on your condition together with the worship of your Lord, you hope for taqwa for yourselves. "La'allakum" is connected to His saying ﴿worship your Lord﴾. It is also possible to connect it to "khalaqakum" (He created you), meaning: since every newborn is born upon the fitra (natural disposition), whoever reflects on it expects and hopes that it will become God-conscious. "Tattaqūn" is derived from *wiqāya* (protection), and its underlying form is *tūtaqayūna*. The vowel of the *yā'* was moved to the *qāf* and the *yā'* was deleted because of the meeting with the quiescent *wāw*, and the first *wāw* was assimilated into the *tā'*.

His saying ﴿alladhī ja'ala﴾ is in the accusative as a follow-on (ittibā') to the preceding "alladhī." It may also be in the nominative by cutting off (qat'), and what Makki mentioned, namely an implied "a'nī" (I mean), or that it is the object of "tattaqūn," is weak. "Ja'ala" in this verse means "ṣayyara" (made, rendered), because it takes two objects. "Firāshan" means: you spread it and settle upon it. Whatever is on the earth that is not a bed, such as the mountains and seas, belongs to the benefits of what is spread out from it, because the mountains are like pegs, and one travels by sea to its various benefits.

As for "al-samā'" (the sky): it is said to be a singular noun whose plural is *samawāt*, and it is said to be a plural whose singular is *samāwa*. Everything that rises above you in the air is "samā'," and the air itself, in its height, is called "samā'." From it comes the hadith: "God created Adam; his height in the sky was sixty cubits." The word derives from *sumūw* (elevation) and its derivatives.

His saying ﴿binā'an﴾ is a figurative comparison to what is understood, as He said: ﴿And the sky We built with might, and indeed We are expanding it﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 51:47]. Some of the Companions said: He built it over the earth like a dome.

His saying ﴿and sent down from the sky﴾ means the clouds. It was so named metaphorically because it is what is adjacent to the sky and close to it. They also called rain "sky" by association, and from it is the line of the poet:

*When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry.*

(p-145) Then, by the same figure, "ra'aynāhu" (we grazed it) is used metaphorically. Through the intermediary of the rain, he made the sky into herbage. The root of "mā'an" (water) is *mawah*, which is indicated by their saying in the plural *miyāh* and *amwāh*, and in the diminutive *muwayh*. The term "rizq" (provision) applies to what comes out of the fruits before it is owned; that is, they are prepared so that benefit from them is valid, and therefore they are provision. Some people cited this verse against the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who say that provision is what may validly be owned, and that what is unlawful is not provision.

The singular of "andād" (rivals) is "nidd." It means one who opposes and resembles, whether by similitude, opposition, or contrariety. Insofar as it opposes and resembles, a certain similarity has been established. Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar and al-Mufaddal said: "al-ḍidd" (opposite) is "al-nidd." This specification by these two is an illustration, not a restriction.

The commentators differed over who is addressed in this verse. A group of exegetes said: the addressees are all the polytheists. On this view, His saying ﴿while you know﴾ means the specific knowledge that God created, sent down water, and brought forth provision; and the verse does not deny ignorance to the unbelievers. It was also said: the intended are the unbelieving Children of Israel, and the meaning is: you know from the books that are with you that God has no rival. (p-146) Ibn Fawrak said: it is possible that the verse addresses the believers, so the meaning is: do not apostatize, O believers, and set up rivals to God after your knowledge, which is the negation of ignorance, that God is one.

This verse indicates that God, the Exalted, has made a person independent of every created being through these blessings. Whoever makes himself need another human like himself, because of greed, hope and desire for the adornments of this world, has taken the paths of those who set up rivals to God. May God, the Exalted, protect us by His grace, and restrict our hopes to Him by His favor and bounty; there is no lord but Him.

His saying ﴿binā'an﴾ is a figurative comparison to what is understood, as He said: ﴿And the sky We built with might, and indeed We are expanding it﴾ [al-Dhāriyāt 51:47]. Some of the Companions said: He built it over the earth like a dome.

His saying ﴿and sent down from the sky﴾ means the clouds. It was so named metaphorically because it is what is adjacent to the sky and close to it. They also called rain "sky" by association, and from it is the line of the poet:

*When the sky descends upon the land of a people, we graze upon it, even if they are angry.*

(p-145) Then, by the same figure, "ra'aynāhu" (we grazed it) is used metaphorically. Through the intermediary of the rain, he made the sky into herbage. The root of "mā'an" (water) is *mawah*, which is indicated by their saying in the plural *miyāh* and *amwāh*, and in the diminutive *muwayh*. The term "rizq" (provision) applies to what comes out of the fruits before it is owned; that is, they are prepared so that benefit from them is valid, and therefore they are provision. Some people cited this verse against the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), who say that provision is what may validly be owned, and that what is unlawful is not provision.

The singular of "andād" (rivals) is "nidd." It means one who opposes and resembles, whether by similitude, opposition, or contrariety. Insofar as it opposes and resembles, a certain similarity has been established. Abu 'Ubayda Ma'mar and al-Mufaddal said: "al-ḍidd" (opposite) is "al-nidd." This specification by these two is an illustration, not a restriction.

The commentators differed over who is addressed in this verse. A group of exegetes said: the addressees are all the polytheists. On this view, His saying ﴿while you know﴾ means the specific knowledge that God created, sent down water, and brought forth provision; and the verse does not deny ignorance to the unbelievers. It was also said: the intended are the unbelieving Children of Israel, and the meaning is: you know from the books that are with you that God has no rival. (p-146) Ibn Fawrak said: it is possible that the verse addresses the believers, so the meaning is: do not apostatize, O believers, and set up rivals to God after your knowledge, which is the negation of ignorance, that God is one.

This verse indicates that God, the Exalted, has made a person independent of every created being through these blessings. Whoever makes himself need another human like himself, because of greed, hope and desire for the adornments of this world, has taken the paths of those who set up rivals to God. May God, the Exalted, protect us by His grace, and restrict our hopes to Him by His favor and bounty; there is no lord but Him.

"Al-Rayb" means doubt. This verse indicates that the preceding address was to the group of polytheists (al-mushrikun) who were challenged, and the explanation of the word "surah" was given at the beginning of this commentary. (p-147)

Yazid ibn Qatib read "anzalna" with an alif. The commentators differed over what the pronoun in His words ﴿from its like﴾ refers to. The majority of scholars said it refers to the Qur'an. They then differed. Most said: "from the like of its composition (nazm), its arrangement, and the eloquence of its meanings, which they recognize. Nothing incapacitates them except the unique composition (ta'lif) with which the Qur'an was distinguished, and by it the inimitability (i'jaz) occurred, according to the view of the expert scholars of reasoning." Some said: "﴿from its like﴾ refers to its unseen matters (ghuyub), its truthfulness, and its antiquity (qidam)." According to these, the challenge (tahaddi) occurred through its antiquity. The first view is clearer. On this view, "min" is either redundant (za'ida) or indicates kind (bayan al-jins). On the first view, it is either partitive (li-l-tab'id) or indicates kind. A group said: the pronoun in ﴿from its like﴾ refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). Then they differed. One group said: "from an unlettered truthful man like him." Another group said: "from a sorcerer, a soothsayer, or a poet like him, according to your claim, O polytheists." Another group said the pronoun in "its like" refers to the earlier scriptures: the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms.

His words ﴿and call your witnesses﴾ mean a call for help (du'a' istis'rakh). "Shuhada'" (witnesses) are those who attend and are present with them, as helpers and supporters; this is what Ibn 'Abbas said. It was also said, from Mujahid, that the meaning is a call for summoning (du'a' istihdar). "Shuhada'" is the plural of "shahid," meaning those who testify for you that you have produced an equal. This view is weak. Al-Farra' said: "your witnesses" refers to their gods.

His words ﴿if you are truthful﴾ mean: in what you have said of doubt. This is the view of some exegetes. Others said: in what you have said, namely that you are able to produce an equal. This view is supported by His words in another verse, ﴿Had we willed, we would have said the like of this﴾ [al-Anfal: 31].

His words ﴿But if you do not﴾: "in" (in) was joined to "lam" (lam), because "lam tafʿalu" means "you have left off doing," so "in" has no effect on it, just as it has no effect on past-tense verbs. "Taf'alu" is jussive (majzum) by "lam," and "lam" governs the jussive because it resembles "la" in exoneration, in that both negate. Just as "la" deletes the tanwin of the noun, so "lam" deletes the vowel or the sign from the verb.

His words ﴿and never will you do﴾: it is put in the subjunctive (nusibat) by "lan." Some Arabs put it in the jussive with "lan"; this was reported by Abu 'Ubayda.

From this is the verse of al-Nabigha in some transmissions:

"So I will not present — may you not be cursed — with the gift."

And in the hadith about the dream of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar: "It was said to me: 'You will not graze.'" This is according to that dialect. His words ﴿never will you do﴾ arouse their resolve and stir their souls, so that their incapacity afterward is more wondrous. It is also one of the unseen matters (ghayb) which the Qur'an announced before they occurred.

His words ﴿then fear the Fire﴾ are a command to faith and obedience to God; it came out in these warning words. The majority read "waquduha" with a fatha on the waw. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Mujahid, Talha ibn Musarrif, and Abu Haywa read "wuquduha" with a damma on the waw throughout the Qur'an, except that Talha excepted the word in Surat al-Buruj. "With fatha on the waw" means the firewood, and "with damma" means the verbal noun (masdar). Both have been reported for firewood, and both have been reported for the verbal noun. Ibn Jinni said: whoever reads with damma on the waw, it is by omitting a modifier (mudaf), its estimated form being "possessor of its fuel," because "al-wuqud" with damma is a verbal noun and not "the people." "Al-waqud" with fatha has also come from them as a verbal noun, and similarly "wuli'tu bihi wulu'an" with fatha on the waw. All of this is anomalous (shadh), and the rule is damma. (p-149)

His words "the people" are a general term (umum) whose meaning is specific to those among whom the decree of entering it has preceded. It was reported from Ibn Mas'ud concerning "the stones" that they are sulphur stones, and they were singled out for this because they exceed all other stones in five kinds of torment: the speed of their kindling, the stench of their smell, the abundance of their smoke, the intensity of their adhesion to bodies, and the strength of their heat when heated.

His words ﴿it has been prepared﴾ are a rebuttal of those who said that the Fire has not yet been created, a view in which Mundhir ibn Sa'id fell into error.

Some commentators held that this Fire specified with stones is the Fire of unbelievers specifically, and that others are for the disobedient. The majority said: rather, the reference is to the whole Fire, not to a specific Fire. He mentioned "the unbelievers" only so that those addressed would be included in the threat, since their deed is disbelief; as if He said: it is prepared for one who does your deed. This does not imply that no one else enters it. Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "a'addaha Allahu lil-kafirin" (God has prepared it for the unbelievers). (p-150)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 25:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow. Whenever they are provided with a fruit therefrom, they say, "This is what we were provided with before," and they are given it in semblance. And for them therein are pure spouses, and they will abide therein eternally.﴾

"Bashshir" (give good tidings) is derived from "al-bushra" (the skin of the face), because what gives a person tidings of good or evil leaves a visible effect on the skin of the face. The usual use of "bishara" (good tidings) is for good, though it may be used for evil when restricted to it explicitly, as in Allah's words: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾ [al-Inshiqaq: 24]. Whenever the word "bishara" is used without qualification, it is understood to mean good.

In His words ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾ is a refutation of those who say that the word "iman" (faith), by itself, entails acts of obedience, for if that were so, He would not have repeated it. "Anna" (that) is in a position of accusative after "bashshir," and it has been said that it is in a position of genitive by the implied preposition "bi" (with). "Jannat" is the plural of "jannah" (garden), which is an orchard of trees and palms; an orchard of vines is also called "al-firdaws." It was named "jannah" because it covers (tujinnu) whoever enters it, i.e., conceals him. From the same root come "al-mijann" (shield), "al-janan" (heart/inner part), and "jinn al-layl" (the darkness of night).

﴿Min tahtiha﴾ means: from beneath the trees mentioned in the reference to the garden. It has been said that His words ﴿min tahtiha﴾ mean "alongside it," as you say, "My house is beneath the house of so-and-so." This view is weak. "Al-anhar" (rivers) are waters in their channels that are long and wide, because the word is derived from "anharat," meaning it widened. From this is the verse of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"I held it in my hand and widened its opening,
so a standing man could see beyond it what lies behind it."

From the same root is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whatever causes blood to flow (unhira) and over which the name of Allah has been mentioned, eat it." Its meaning is: whatever the slaughter cuts open widely until blood flows like a river. He attributed flowing to the river, though it is really water alone that flows, as a figurative usage, as He said: ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82], and as the poet said:

"I have been told that after you the fire was kindled,
and after you, O Kulayb, the assembly fell into disorder."

It is narrated that the rivers of Paradise are not in trenches; rather, they flow on the surface of the land of Paradise in a regulated manner.

His words "kullama" (whenever) are an adverb that implies restriction (al-hasr).

In this verse there is a refutation of those who say that a condition for provision (rizq) is ownership (tamalluk). Some of the usulis (jurists of legal theory) mentioned this, but it is not clear to me.

[p. 152] Their saying "hadha" (this) refers to the kind: that is, "this is of the kind of which we were provided before." The statement may be an expression of wonder, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. It may also be a report from some of them to others, as a group of commentators have said. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: they are given the fruit, and then after it they are given something of the same form, while the taste differs, so they wonder at this and inform one another. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is nothing in Paradise of what is in this world except the names; as for the realities, they are different. Some interpreters said: the meaning is that they see the fruit and distinguish its kinds, as its appearance resembles what was in this world, so they say, "This is what we were provided with before, in this world."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The saying of Ibn 'Abbas that was accepted refutes this view to some extent. Some commentators said: the meaning is "this is what we were promised in this world," so it is as if they had been provided it in this world, since Allah's promise is fulfilled. Others said: when some of the fruit of Paradise is plucked, another like it emerges immediately in its place, so "this" refers to what emerges in the place of what was plucked. The majority of people read "wa-utu" with a damma on the hamza and on the ta', while Harun al-A'war read "wa-ataw" with a fatha on the hamza and the ta', and the subject in this reading is the youths and the servants. The form "utu" in the reading of the majority originally was "utiyu"; the vowel of the ya' was moved to the ta', then the ya' was dropped due to the meeting of two unvocalized letters.

As for His words "mutashabihan" (in semblance), Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and others said its meaning is: some of it resembles other parts in appearance, while differing in taste. 'Ikrima said: its meaning is that it resembles the fruit of this world in appearance, while differing from it in most attributes. Qatada said: "mutashabihan" means excellent, with nothing inferior in it, as in His words: ﴿a Book consistent in its parts [kitaban mutashabihan]﴾ [al-Zumar: 23].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It seems he means "mutanasiban" (in proportion), in that each kind is the best of its genus; this is a kind of resemblance. It has also been said that "mutashabihan" means that it resembles the fruit of this world in name, but not in other respects, [p. 153] such as form and taste. "Azwaj" is the plural of "zawj" (spouse). A woman is a man's "zawj," and a man is a woman's "zawj." For a woman "zawja" is also said, and from this is the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Whoever strives to corrupt my wife
is like one who approaches a lion's den to steal from it."

'Ammar ibn Yasir, concerning 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "By Allah, I know that she is his wife in this world and the Hereafter, but Allah has tested you." Al-Bukhari and others narrated the hadith in full. "Mutahhara" (purified) is more emphatic than "tahira" (pure). The meaning of this purity is freedom from menstruation, saliva, and all other impurities of human women. It has also been said that it means freedom from sins. "Al-khulud" means lasting in life, or in possession and the like. One says "khalada bi-l-makan" when residence in a place continues. Khulud may be used figuratively for what is long-lasting, but what is in this verse is eternal in reality.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 26:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example, [even] of a gnat or what is above it. As for those who believed, they know that it is the truth from their Lord. But as for those who disbelieved, they say, "What did Allah intend by this as an example?" He leads many astray thereby and guides many thereby, and He leads astray thereby only the defiantly disobedient.﴾

The exegetes (al-mufassirun) mention that when Allah, the Exalted, had struck the two examples mentioned earlier in this surah, the disbelievers said: "What are these examples? Allah is too exalted to strike such examples." So the verse was revealed.

Ibn Qutayba said: "It was revealed only because the disbelievers denied the striking of examples in other than this surah, with the fly and the spider. And some people said that this verse is an example of this world."

(p-154) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak; the arrangement of the speech and the coherence of the meaning reject it.

And "yastahyi" (is ashamed) originally is yastahyiyu. Its middle and last radicals are both weak letters (ḥarfa 'illa). The final radical was altered by the dammah being deemed heavy on the yā', so it became sukun. Ibn Kathir in one of the transmissions from him, and Ibn Muhaysin, and others, read "yastahi" with a kasra on the ḥā', which is a dialect of Tamim: the vowel of the first yā' was transferred to the ḥā', which became sukun; then the dammah on the second yā' was deemed heavy and it became sukun, so one of the two was deleted because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters.

The interpreters differed on the meaning of "yastahyi" in this verse. Al-Tabari preferred that it means "yakhsha" (fears), and others said it means "yatruku" (leaves off). This latter is the preferable one. Whoever says it means "yamtani'u" (refrains) or "yamna'uhu al-ḥayā'" (shyness prevents him), it is "yatruku" or close to it.

Since the one of great rank among people is not prevented from engaging in base speech except by shame concerning that, Allah, by His saying ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed﴾, responded to those who said: "How does Allah strike an example with the fly or the like?" That is: these things are not of base speech, since they are among the eloquent in meaning, conveying the speaker's purposes to the listener's soul, so they are not among the things one is ashamed of. Al-Mahdawi related that the shame in this verse refers to people, but this is not acceptable.

As for His, the Exalted, saying ﴿an example [of]﴾: "an" (أنّ) with the verb is in the position of the accusative, as if it were a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of the object. The meaning of ﴿strike an example﴾ is: "yubayyinu ḍarban min al-amthal", that is, a kind of examples, as you say: "this is of the kind (ḍarb) of this." The ḍarīb is the like. It may be that it is like the kind (ḍarb) of resurrection and the kind of humiliation, so the meaning becomes: to impose the proof with an example.

(p-155) And "mathalan" (an example) is the object. It has been said that it is the first object, and it has been said that it is the second, placed before it while it is intended to be after it, because "ḍaraba" in this meaning is transitive to two objects.

They differed concerning His saying ﴿mā baʿūḍatan﴾ (of a gnat). Some people said: "mā" is an extra (ṣila) particle that adds only some emphasis. It has been said: "mā" is an indefinite noun in the position of the accusative by way of apposition (badal), because of its vagueness. Al-Mahdawi related this view from al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Tha'lab. And other than this has been said, which is confusion prompted by the assumption that "ḍaraba" is transitive to only one object. Some of the Kufans said: the accusative of "baʿūḍatan" is by way of dropping the preposition, and the meaning is: "an yaḍriba mathalan mā min baʿūḍatin" (that He strike an example of [any] gnat). It is related from the Arabs: "lahu ʿishrūna mā nāqatan fa-jamalan" (he has twenty of [any] she-camel, then a male camel), and Abu al-ʿAbbas denied this view.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What is preferred is that "mā" is a qualifying descriptive (ṣifa mukhaṣṣiṣa), as you say: "jiʾtuka fī amrin mā" (I came to you about a certain matter), so it makes the indefinite specific and approximate. From this is the saying of Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt:

﻿"Salaʿun mā wa-mithluhu ʿushara mā, ʿāʾilun mā wa-ʿālat al-bayqūrā"

(p-156) And "baʿūḍatan" on this view is the second object. Some people said: "mā" is indefinite, as if he said: "shay'an" (a thing). The verse in this respect resembles the saying of Hassan ibn Thabit:

"Fa-kafā bi-nā faḍlan ʿalā man ghayrinā ḥubbu al-nabiyyi Muḥammadin iyyānā"

This view has already been mentioned in a similar form. The resemblance to the verse is not sound in my opinion.

"Baʿūḍa" is on the pattern fa'ūla, from "baḍʿ" (a part), when it cuts the flesh. It is said "biḍʿ" and "baḍʿ" have the same meaning. On this basis they interpreted the poet's saying:

"La-niʿma al-bayt bayt Abi Dithār, idhā mā khāfa baʿḍu al-qawmi baʿḍā"

Al-Daḥḥak, Ibrahim ibn Abi ʿAbla, and Ru'ba ibn al-ʿAjjaj read "baʿūḍatun" with the nominative. Abu al-Fath said: the basis of this is that "mā" is a noun in the position of "alladhī" (who), meaning: He is not ashamed to strike as an example that which is a gnat. So the returning pronoun to the relative was deleted, and it is the subject of the predicate. A similar case is the reading of some: "tamāman ʿalā alladhī aḥsana" (completion upon him who did well), meaning: "ʿalā alladhī huwa aḥsanu" (upon him who is best). Sibawayh related: "mā anā bi-alladhī qā'ilun laka shay'an", meaning: "huwa qā'ilun" (he is one who says to you something).

As for His, the Exalted, saying ﴿fa-mā fawqahā﴾ (or what is above it): whoever makes the first "mā" an extra particle, then the second "mā" is conjoined to "baʿūḍatin". Whoever makes "mā" a noun, then the second "mā" is conjoined to it.

Al-Kisa'i, Abu ʿUbayda and others said: the meaning is "fa-mā fawqahā fī al-ṣighar" (or what is above it in smallness). Qatada, Ibn Jurayj and others said: the meaning is "fī al-kibar" (in largeness).

(p-157) The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Both are possible. The pronoun in "annahu" refers to the example.

The grammarians differed concerning "mādhā". It has been said: it is in the position of a single noun, meaning "ayyu shay'in arada Allahu" (what thing did Allah intend)? It has been said: "mā" is a noun and "dhā" is another noun meaning "alladhī" (who/which), so "mā" is in the nominative position as the subject, and "dhā" is its predicate. The meaning of their speech here is denial in the form of a question. And His saying "mathalan" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz). The reading of the majority of the community in this verse is "yuḍillu" with a damma on the yā' in both places. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that he read in the first place "yuḍillu" with a damma on the yā', and in the second "wa-mā yaḍillu" with a fatḥa on the yā', "bihi illā al-fāsiqūna". **Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 2, verses 27–29**

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿Those who break the covenant of God after its ratification, and sever what God has commanded to be joined, and cause corruption on earth—those are the losers.﴾ ﴿How can you disbelieve in God, when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then give you life again, then to Him you will be returned.﴾ ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on earth, then turned to the heaven and made it seven heavens. And He is Knower of all things.﴾

*Naqd* (نقض) means reversing what has been firmly established back to its original state, so that it is no longer firm. *Al-'ahd* (العهد) in this verse means a prior commitment to something and an enjoining of it.

The interpreters differed over the meaning of this covenant. Some of the commentators said: it is the covenant God took from the children of Adam when He brought them forth from the loins of their father Adam like specks (*adh-dharr*). Others said: rather, it is the proofs God set up for His oneness in the heavens, the earth, and the rest of His creation; these are in the position of a covenant. Others said: rather, this covenant is the one God took from His servants through His messengers: that they should affirm His oneness and not worship anything besides Him. Others said: rather, this covenant is the one God took concerning following the messengers and the revealed books: that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and not conceal his matter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

According to this last view, the verse concerns the People of the Book. The apparent context before and after it, however, indicates that it concerns all the disbelievers. Qatadah said: this verse concerns those who had believed in the Prophet (peace be upon him), then disbelieved in him and broke the covenant.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: al-Tabari did not attribute any of these opinions to anyone specific.

Every lawful covenant among the Muslims: breaking it is not made permissible by this verse. The pronoun in *mithaqihi* (ميثاقه, "its ratification") may refer back to "the covenant" or to the Name of God, the Exalted. *Mithaq* (ميثاق) is on the pattern *mif'al* from *al-wathaqah*, which is the tightening and binding of a contract or the like. In this verse it is a noun in the place of a verbal noun (masdar), as the poet 'Amr ibn Shubaym said:

> "Do you disbelieve after the death was turned back from me, and after your giving me the hundred camels?"

He meant: after your giving (*ba'd i'tail*, بعد إعطائك).

God's words, *"mā amara Allāhu bihi an yūṣal"* (﴿ما أمر الله به أن يوصل﴾, "what God has commanded to be joined"): *mā* (ما) is in the place of the accusative, governed by *yaqta'ūna* ("they sever"). Scholars differed over what the thing is that He commanded to be joined. Qatadah said: it is the ties of kinship in general among people. Others said: specifically among those who believe in Muhammad, as if the disbelievers were severing their kinship ties. The majority of the people of knowledge said: the reference in this verse is to the religion of God and His worship on earth, the establishment of His laws, and the preservation of His limits. This is the truth, and kinship ties are a part of this. *"An"* (أن) is in the place of the accusative, either as a substitute for *mā* or as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*). It has also been said that *an* is in the place of the genitive, as a substitute for the pronoun in *bihi* ("with it"), and this is the more fitting view.

*"Wa yufsidūna fī al-ardi"* (﴿ويفسدون في الأرض﴾, "and cause corruption on earth"): they worship other than God, and they act unjustly in their deeds, since these are according to their desires. *Al-khāsir* (الخاسر, "the loser") is the one who has diminished his soul's share of success and triumph. *Al-khusran* (الخسران, "loss") is a deficiency, whether in a balance or otherwise.

God's words, *"kayfa takfurūna"* (﴿كيف تكفرون﴾, "how can you disbelieve"): its form is interrogative, but it is not really an interrogation; it is an affirmation and a rebuke. That is, how can you disbelieve in God and His blessings upon you and this power of His? *Kayfa* (كيف) is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and what governs it is *takfurūna*. Its estimated sense is: "Do you disbelieve while denying?" or "Do you disbelieve while refusing?" *Kayfa* is indeclinable, and it was given the *fatha* vowel because of its lightness. As for those who said that *kayfa* here conveys affirmation and wonder, its meaning is: if this matter occurs, it is right to be astonished at it because of its strangeness and its remoteness from the familiar gratitude owed to a benefactor. The *wāw* in His words *"wa kuntum"* (﴿وكنتم﴾, "when you were") is the *wāw* of circumstance (*wāw al-hāl*).

The interpreters differed over the order of these two deaths and two lives. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, and Mujahid said: the meaning is that you were dead, nonexistent before you were created, effaced, just as a thing that has been effaced is called "dead." Then you were created and brought out into this world, and He gave you life. Then the death known to all caused you to die; then He will give you life again for the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment.

Others said: "you were dead" refers to Adam having been of clay and dead before he came to life; then He breathed the spirit into him, and He gave you life through the life of Adam; then He causes you to die, and then gives you life again, according to what has preceded. Qatadah said: "you were dead" refers to being in the loins of your fathers; then you were brought out into the world, and He gave you life; then as previously described. Others said: "you were dead" refers to being in the wombs before the breathing of the spirit; then He gave you life by bringing you out into the world; then as previously described.

Ibn Zayd said: God, may He be exalted, brought out the souls (*nisam*) of the children of Adam like specks; then He caused them to die after that, and this is His words "and you were dead"; then He gave them life by bringing them out into the world; then as previously described. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih said: "you were dead" refers to the death known to all; then He gave you life for questioning in the graves; then He caused you to die in them; then He gave you life for the Resurrection. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "and you were dead" means dead in obscurity; then He gave you life by making you remembered and honored through this religion and the Prophet who came to you.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

The first opinion is the best of these views, because it is the one the disbelievers cannot escape acknowledging in the first arrangement of it. Moreover, His first words "you were dead" and His attributing the causing of death to Him at the end strengthen this opinion. When the souls of the disbelievers submit to the fact that they were dead and nonexistent, then to being given life in this world, then to being caused to die in it, the necessity of another giving of life becomes binding upon them; and their denial of it is a claim without any proof.

The pronoun in *"ilayhi"* (إليه, "to Him") refers back to God, the Exalted, meaning to His reward or His punishment. It has been said that it refers back to the living, but the first is more apparent.

The majority of the reciters read *"turja'ūna"* (ترجعون, "you will be returned") with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and a *fatḥa* on the *jīm*. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Ya'mur, Salam, al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan, and Ya'qub al-Hadrami read *"yarji'ūna, wa tarji'ūna"* (يرجعون، وترجعون, "they will be returned" / "you will be returned") with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and the *tā'* wherever it occurs.

*Khalaqa* (خلق) means to invent and bring into existence after non-existence. It may also be said of a human being that he created (*khalaqa*) something after composing it, and from this is the poet's verse:

> "Indeed you smooth out what you have made, while some people are made and then do not smooth"

And from another's verse:

> "Whoever makes what he has made strong, my resource against it is small"

*Lakum* (لكم, "for you") means: for consideration (*li'l-i'tibar*), and what precedes and follows it in the accusative indicates this. The lessons (*al-'ibar*) are the giving of life, the causing of death, the creating, the turning to the heaven, and the making of it level. Some people said: rather, the meaning of *lakum* is the permitting of things and their being made one's property. This is the view of those who say that before revelation things were permitted by default, which this verse clarifies. The advocates of prohibition by default and the advocates of suspension of judgment disagreed with them in this interpretation. Most of the advocates of prohibition by default excepted matters whose nature, with the existence of a human being, required permissibility, such as breathing and movement. Against the advocates of prohibition: every prohibition in the Qur'an; and against the advocates of permissibility: every permission and allowance in the Qur'an. Suspension of judgment is preferred when we assume a new case in which there is no revealed text and which is not connected to one. The meaning of suspension is that it is the exhaustion of the examiner's effort concerning the new events that arise. Ibn Furak related from Ibn al-Sa'igh that he said: the intellect has never been free of revelation, and there is no new event without some revealed text in it; the first of these has a connection to it, and the first is a condition that is to be maintained. He said: one should rely on this and dispense with examining prohibition, permissibility, and suspension. *Jamī'an* (جميعًا, "all") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

God's words, *"thumma istawā"* (﴿ثم استوى﴾, "then He turned"): *thumma* (ثم) here is for the sequence of reports, not for the sequence of the matter itself. *Istawā* (استوى): some people said its meaning is "He rose above," without modality and without delimitation. This is the choice of al-Tabari, and the estimated sense is: His command, His power, and His dominion rose above. Ibn Kaysan said: its meaning is that He directed Himself to the heaven, that is, with His creating and His originating. It has been said: its meaning is that His making was completed in it, as you say "the matter became level (*istawā al-amr*)."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: this is unsettling.

Al-Tabari related from some people that the meaning is "He turned toward," and he rejected this.

It is related from some people that the one who "turned" is the smoke, and this too is rejected by the arrangement of the speech. It has been said that the meaning is "He prevailed (*istawlā*)," as the poet said:

> "Bishr has prevailed over Iraq, without a sword and without spilled blood"

This only applies to God's words *"'alā al-'arshi istawā"* (﴿على العرش استوى﴾, "He established Himself on the Throne," Ta-Ha 5). The principle in this verse and its like is the rejection of movement and the inhering of temporal events, and the istiwa' of power and dominion remains.

*"Sawwāhunna"* (سواهن, "and made them"): it has been said that the meaning is that He made them equal (*sawā'*); it has been said that He leveled their surfaces by smoothing them. *"Sab'a"* (سبع, "seven") is in the accusative, either as a substitute for the pronoun or as an object of *sawwā*, with the preposition removed from the pronoun, as if He had said: "so He made from them seven." It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. And His saying *"sawwāhunna"*: either because "the heaven" is a plural noun, or because it is a singular collective noun (*ism jins*), which indicates plurality.

God's words, *"wa huwa bi-kulli shay'in 'alīm"* (﴿وهو بكل شيء عليم﴾, "and He is Knower of all things"): its meaning is with respect to existent things; and His knowledge of non-existent things is established by other verses.

This verse implies that the earth and what is in it were created before the heaven, and this is correct. Then the earth was spread out (*duhiyat*) after the creation of the heaven. By this, the meanings of these verses agree with those in Surah *al-Mu'min* and in *al-Nazi'at*.
