Others said: rather, it is the proofs God set up for His oneness in the heavens, the earth, and the rest of His creation; these are in the position of a covenant. Others said: rather, this covenant is the one God took from His servants through His messengers: that they should affirm His oneness and not worship anything besides Him. Others said: rather, this covenant is the one God took concerning following the messengers and the revealed books: that they should believe in Muhammad (ﷺ) and not conceal his matter.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

According to this last view, the verse concerns the People of the Book. The apparent context before and after it, however, indicates that it concerns all the disbelievers. Qatadah said: this verse concerns those who had believed in the Prophet (peace be upon him), then disbelieved in him and broke the covenant.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: al-Tabari did not attribute any of these opinions to anyone specific.

Every lawful covenant among the Muslims: breaking it is not made permissible by this verse. The pronoun in *mithaqihi* (ميثاقه, "its ratification") may refer back to "the covenant" or to the Name of God, the Exalted. *Mithaq* (ميثاق) is on the pattern *mif'al* from *al-wathaqah*, which is the tightening and binding of a contract or the like. In this verse it is a noun in the place of a verbal noun (masdar), as the poet 'Amr ibn Shubaym said:

> "Do you disbelieve after the death was turned back from me, and after your giving me the hundred camels?"

He meant: after your giving (*ba'd i'tail*, بعد إعطائك).

God's words, *"mā amara Allāhu bihi an yūṣal"* (﴿ما أمر الله به أن يوصل﴾, "what God has commanded to be joined"): *mā* (ما) is in the place of the accusative, governed by *yaqta'ūna* ("they sever"). Scholars differed over what the thing is that He commanded to be joined. Qatadah said: it is the ties of kinship in general among people. Others said: specifically among those who believe in Muhammad, as if the disbelievers were severing their kinship ties. The majority of the people of knowledge said: the reference in this verse is to the religion of God and His worship on earth, the establishment of His laws, and the preservation of His limits. This is the truth, and kinship ties are a part of this. *"An"* (أن) is in the place of the accusative, either as a substitute for *mā* or as an object of purpose (*maf'ul min ajlihi*). It has also been said that *an* is in the place of the genitive, as a substitute for the pronoun in *bihi* ("with it"), and this is the more fitting view.

*"Wa yufsidūna fī al-ardi"* (﴿ويفسدون في الأرض﴾, "and cause corruption on earth"): they worship other than God, and they act unjustly in their deeds, since these are according to their desires. *Al-khāsir* (الخاسر, "the loser") is the one who has diminished his soul's share of success and triumph. *Al-khusran* (الخسران, "loss") is a deficiency, whether in a balance or otherwise.

God's words, *"kayfa takfurūna"* (﴿كيف تكفرون﴾, "how can you disbelieve"): its form is interrogative, but it is not really an interrogation; it is an affirmation and a rebuke. That is, how can you disbelieve in God and His blessings upon you and this power of His? *Kayfa* (كيف) is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*), and what governs it is *takfurūna*. Its estimated sense is: "Do you disbelieve while denying?" or "Do you disbelieve while refusing?" *Kayfa* is indeclinable, and it was given the *fatha* vowel because of its lightness. As for those who said that *kayfa* here conveys affirmation and wonder, its meaning is: if this matter occurs, it is right to be astonished at it because of its strangeness and its remoteness from the familiar gratitude owed to a benefactor. The *wāw* in His words *"wa kuntum"* (﴿وكنتم﴾, "when you were") is the *wāw* of circumstance (*wāw al-hāl*).

The interpreters differed over the order of these two deaths and two lives. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, and Mujahid said: the meaning is that you were dead, nonexistent before you were created, effaced, just as a thing that has been effaced is called "dead." Then you were created and brought out into this world, and He gave you life. Then the death known to all caused you to die; then He will give you life again for the Resurrection on the Day of Judgment.

Others said: "you were dead" refers to Adam having been of clay and dead before he came to life; then He breathed the spirit into him, and He gave you life through the life of Adam; then He causes you to die, and then gives you life again, according to what has preceded. Qatadah said: "you were dead" refers to being in the loins of your fathers; then you were brought out into the world, and He gave you life; then as previously described. Others said: "you were dead" refers to being in the wombs before the breathing of the spirit; then He gave you life by bringing you out into the world; then as previously described.

Ibn Zayd said: God, may He be exalted, brought out the souls (*nisam*) of the children of Adam like specks; then He caused them to die after that, and this is His words "and you were dead"; then He gave them life by bringing them out into the world; then as previously described. Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Salih said: "you were dead" refers to the death known to all; then He gave you life for questioning in the graves; then He caused you to die in them; then He gave you life for the Resurrection. It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "and you were dead" means dead in obscurity; then He gave you life by making you remembered and honored through this religion and the Prophet who came to you.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

The first opinion is the best of these views, because it is the one the disbelievers cannot escape acknowledging in the first arrangement of it. Moreover, His first words "you were dead" and His attributing the causing of death to Him at the end strengthen this opinion. When the souls of the disbelievers submit to the fact that they were dead and nonexistent, then to being given life in this world, then to being caused to die in it, the necessity of another giving of life becomes binding upon them; and their denial of it is a claim without any proof.

The pronoun in *"ilayhi"* (إليه, "to Him") refers back to God, the Exalted, meaning to His reward or His punishment. It has been said that it refers back to the living, but the first is more apparent.

The majority of the reciters read *"turja'ūna"* (ترجعون, "you will be returned") with a *ḍamma* on the *tā'* and a *fatḥa* on the *jīm*. Ibn Abi Ishaq, Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Ya'mur, Salam, al-Fayyad ibn Ghazwan, and Ya'qub al-Hadrami read *"yarji'ūna, wa tarji'ūna"* (يرجعون، وترجعون, "they will be returned" / "you will be returned") with a *fatḥa* on the *yā'* and the *tā'* wherever it occurs.

*Khalaqa* (خلق) means to invent and bring into existence after non-existence. It may also be said of a human being that he created (*khalaqa*) something after composing it, and from this is the poet's verse:

> "Indeed you smooth out what you have made, while some people are made and then do not smooth"

And from another's verse:

> "Whoever makes what he has made strong, my resource against it is small"

*Lakum* (لكم, "for you") means: for consideration (*li'l-i'tibar*), and what precedes and follows it in the accusative indicates this. The lessons (*al-'ibar*) are the giving of life, the causing of death, the creating, the turning to the heaven, and the making of it level. Some people said: rather, the meaning of *lakum* is the permitting of things and their being made one's property. This is the view of those who say that before revelation things were permitted by default, which this verse clarifies. The advocates of prohibition by default and the advocates of suspension of judgment disagreed with them in this interpretation. Most of the advocates of prohibition by default excepted matters whose nature, with the existence of a human being, required permissibility, such as breathing and movement. Against the advocates of prohibition: every prohibition in the Qur'an; and against the advocates of permissibility: every permission and allowance in the Qur'an. Suspension of judgment is preferred when we assume a new case in which there is no revealed text and which is not connected to one. The meaning of suspension is that it is the exhaustion of the examiner's effort concerning the new events that arise. Ibn Furak related from Ibn al-Sa'igh that he said: the intellect has never been free of revelation, and there is no new event without some revealed text in it; the first of these has a connection to it, and the first is a condition that is to be maintained. He said: one should rely on this and dispense with examining prohibition, permissibility, and suspension. *Jamī'an* (جميعًا, "all") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state.

God's words, *"thumma istawā"* (﴿ثم استوى﴾, "then He turned"): *thumma* (ثم) here is for the sequence of reports, not for the sequence of the matter itself. *Istawā* (استوى): some people said its meaning is "He rose above," without modality and without delimitation. This is the choice of al-Tabari, and the estimated sense is: His command, His power, and His dominion rose above. Ibn Kaysan said: its meaning is that He directed Himself to the heaven, that is, with His creating and His originating. It has been said: its meaning is that His making was completed in it, as you say "the matter became level (*istawā al-amr*)."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said: this is unsettling.

Al-Tabari related from some people that the meaning is "He turned toward," and he rejected this.

It is related from some people that the one who "turned" is the smoke, and this too is rejected by the arrangement of the speech. It has been said that the meaning is "He prevailed (*istawlā*)," as the poet said:

> "Bishr has prevailed over Iraq, without a sword and without spilled blood"

This only applies to God's words *"'alā al-'arshi istawā"* (﴿على العرش استوى﴾, "He established Himself on the Throne," Ta-Ha 5). The principle in this verse and its like is the rejection of movement and the inhering of temporal events, and the istiwa' of power and dominion remains.

*"Sawwāhunna"* (سواهن, "and made them"): it has been said that the meaning is that He made them equal (*sawā'*); it has been said that He leveled their surfaces by smoothing them. *"Sab'a"* (سبع, "seven") is in the accusative, either as a substitute for the pronoun or as an object of *sawwā*, with the preposition removed from the pronoun, as if He had said: "so He made from them seven." It has been said that it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state. And His saying *"sawwāhunna"*: either because "the heaven" is a plural noun, or because it is a singular collective noun (*ism jins*), which indicates plurality.

God's words, *"wa huwa bi-kulli shay'in 'alīm"* (﴿وهو بكل شيء عليم﴾, "and He is Knower of all things"): its meaning is with respect to existent things; and His knowledge of non-existent things is established by other verses.

This verse implies that the earth and what is in it were created before the heaven, and this is correct. Then the earth was spread out (*duhiyat*) after the creation of the heaven. By this, the meanings of these verses agree with those in Surah *al-Mu'min* and in *al-Nazi'at*.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 30–32 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And [mention] when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will place upon the earth a successive authority (khalifa)." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said, "Indeed, I know that which you do not know."﴾ ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said, "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿They said, "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the Knowing, the Wise."﴾

Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna said: "Idh" (when) is superfluous (za'ida), and the implied meaning is: "And your Lord said." Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: This is an audacity (ijtira') from Abu 'Ubayda, and all the exegetes refuted him on this point. The majority said: It is not superfluous; rather it is connected to an implied verb, its implied meaning being: "And mention when He said." Also, His saying: ﴿He created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqara: 29], the verse, requires that the implied meaning be: "And the beginning of your creation when your Lord said to the angels." The addressing of "Rabb" (Lord) to Muhammad ﷺ, and the addressing of him with the "kaf" (second person pronoun), is an honouring from Him to him and a manifestation of his being specially singled out by it.

The word "malaika" (angels): its singular is "malak," originally "mal'ak," on the pattern "maf'al," from "la'aka" meaning to send. Its plural is "malaika" on the pattern "mufa'ala." Some said: the original of "malak" is "ma'lak," from "alaka" meaning to send, and from it is the saying of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

"Convey to al-Nu'man from me a messenger (ma'lak), that my imprisonment and my waiting have lasted long."

Both forms are attested: "la'aka" and "alaka," the hamza having been transposed after the lam, so its pattern becomes "ma'al" and its plural "malaika," its pattern "mu'afala." Ibn Kaysan said: it is from "malaka yamliku," and the hamza in it is augmental, as it was added in "sha'mal" from "shamila," so its pattern is "fa'al," and the pattern of its plural is "fa'a'ila." It may come in poetry in its original form, as he said:

"I am not for a human, but for an angel (la-mal'akin) who descended from the air of the sky, descending."

In ordinary speech, the hamza was eased and its vowel was dropped onto the lam, or onto the 'ayn according to Ibn Kaysan's view, so it is said "malak." The "ha'" in "malaika" is for the feminization of non-real (ghayr haqiqi) plurals. It was said that it is for emphasis (mubalagha), like 'allama and nassaba. The first view is clearer. Abu 'Ubayda said: the hamza in "malaika" is added, because its singular is "malak."

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is what Ibn Kaysan inclined to.

"Ja'il" (placing/making) in this verse means "khaliq" (creating); al-Tabari mentioned it from Abu Rawq, and its transitivity to one object supports this. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: "ja'il" means "fa'il" (doing). Ibn Sabit reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: the "earth" here means Makkah, because the earth was spread out from beneath it, and because it is the place of residence of the prophets whose peoples were destroyed, and that the grave of Nuh, Hud and Salih is between the Maqam and the Rukn.

"Khalifa" means one who succeeds. Ibn 'Abbas said: The jinn were in the earth before the children of Adam, and they caused corruption and shed blood; so Allah sent to them a company of angels who killed them, and drove their remnant to the islands of the seas and the summits of the mountains, and made Adam and his offspring a successor (khalifa). Al-Hasan said: Allah only named the children of Adam a successor because each generation succeeds the one before it, generation after generation.

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this view it is possible that it means "khalifa" in the sense of one who succeeds (khalifa), and in the sense of one who is succeeded (makhluqa). Ibn Mas'ud said: its meaning is only: a successor from Me in judging among My servants with truth and with My commands, meaning by that Adam, peace be upon him, and whoever stood in his place after him from his offspring. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "khaliqa" with the qaf.

His exalted saying: ﴿They said, "Will You place therein..."﴾, the verse. We know with certainty that the angels do not know the unseen, and do not speak before (Him) in word; and that is general for all the angels, because His saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27] came in the manner of praise for them. The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib said: "This is the indicator of generality, so it is not sound, with these two conditions, unless they had some information and a preliminary (muqaddima) about the corruption of the creation in the earth." Ibn Zayd and others said: "Allah the Exalted informed them that the successor would be from his offspring a people who would cause corruption and shed blood, so they made this statement on account of that."

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is either by way of wonder at Allah's appointing as successor one who disobeys Him, or at the disobedience of one whom Allah appoints as successor in His earth and whom He favours with that; or it is by way of grave magnification of both matters together: the appointing as successor and the disobedience. Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab and others said: The angels had seen and known what the jinn had done of corruption and shedding of blood in the earth, so their statement ﴿Will You place therein...﴾, the verse, came by way of pure interrogation: is this successor on the path of those who preceded from the jinn or not? Others said: Allah the Exalted had informed the angels that He would create in the earth a creation who would cause corruption and shed blood; so when He said to them afterwards: ﴿Indeed, I will place﴾, they said: ﴿Will You place therein...﴾, the verse, by way of seeking guidance and information: is this successor the one He had informed them of before, or another?

"Al-Safk" is the pouring of blood; this is its common usage, and it may be said: "safaka kalamahu fi kadha" when he rendered his speech in such a matter (sarada). The reading of the majority is with a kasra on the fa'; Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yasfiku" with a damma on the fa'; Ibn Hurmuz read "wa-yasfika" with the nasb (accusative) by the waw of conjunction in the sense of "al-sarf" (turning away), as if he said: one who combines causing corruption and shedding. Al-Mahdawi said: it is in the nasb as an answer to the interrogation. The first is better.

Their saying: ﴿while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You﴾. Some of the interpreters said: it is by way of interrogation, as if they meant: "And we exalt You with praise, the verse; or shall we change from this state?"

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him:
This is good along with the view of pure interrogation in their saying "Will You place".

Others said: its meaning is self-praise and description of their state, and that is permissible for them, as Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 55]. This is good along with the wonder and grave magnification in their saying "Will You place", that Allah would appoint as successor one who disobeys Him?

On this view He taught them manners with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know.﴾

Others said: the meaning of the verse is: "And we, if You had placed us in the earth and made us successors, would exalt You with praise." This too is good along with the wonder and grave magnification in their saying "Will You place?" The meaning of ﴿exalt You with praise﴾ is: we declare You free of what is not fitting for You and Your attributes. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said: the glorification of the angels is their prayer to Allah. Qatada said: the glorification of the angels is their saying "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah), according to its usage in the language.

"Bihamdika" means: we mix glorification with praise and join it to it. It is possible that His saying "bihamdika" is a parenthetical insertion between the two statements, as if they said: "(And we glorify and sanctify)," then they interjected by way of submission, meaning: and You are the One praised for guiding to that.

﴿And sanctify You﴾: al-Dahhak and others said: its meaning is: we purify our selves for You, seeking Your good pleasure; and taqdis is purification without dispute, and from it comes "al-ard al-muqaddasa," meaning the purified land, and from it "Bayt al-Maqdis," and from it "al-qudus" by which one purifies oneself. Others said: ﴿and sanctify You﴾ means: we magnify You, and purify Your remembrance from what is not fitting for it. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Salih and others. Some said: "nuqaddisu laka" means: we pray to You; this is weak.

His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know.﴾ The more apparent view is that "a'lamu" is a verb in the imperfect, and "ma" is in the accusative position governed by it. It was said: "a'lamu" is a noun, and "ma" is in the genitive position by annexation (idafa), and there is no dispute among the grammarians that it cannot take tanwin (be declined), and the disagreement lies only in "af'al" when it is named with it and is indefinite: Sibawayh and al-Khalil do not decline it, and al-Akhfash declines it.

The people of interpretation differed concerning what is meant by His saying: ﴿that which you do not know.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: Iblis, may Allah curse him, had become conceited and pride entered him when Allah made him the guardian of the lowest heaven and honoured him. It was also said: rather, when Allah sent him to kill the jinn who had caused corruption in the earth, and he defeated them and killed them with his troops; this too was said by Ibn 'Abbas. He believed that this was due to a merit of his own, and he made light of disbelief and disobedience on Adam's side, peace be upon him. He said: when the angels said ﴿while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You﴾, and they did not know that within Iblis's self there was something contrary to that, Allah said to them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾, meaning what is within Iblis's self. Qatada said: when the angels said: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein﴾, and Allah the Exalted knew that among those He would appoint as successors in the earth would be prophets, excellent ones and people of obedience, He said to them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾, meaning: the deeds of the excellent among the children of Adam.

His exalted saying: "wa-'allama" means: he made known. The teaching of Adam here, according to some, is the inspiration of knowledge to him by necessity. Others said: rather it is teaching by speech, either through an intermediary angel, or by speaking to him before his descent to the earth; so it does not share with Musa, peace be upon him, in his special distinction. Al-Yamani read "wa-'ullima" with a damma on the 'ayn, making the verb passive, with "Adamu" in the nominative. Abu al-Fath said: this is the reading of Yazid al-Barbari. "Adam" is an af'al form derived from "al-udma," which is a redness inclining toward blackness; its plural is "udm" and "awadim," like "humr" and "ahamir." It is not declined in any way. It was also said: the pattern of Adam is "fa'il," derived from "adim al-ard" (the surface of the earth), as if the angel made it its surface; its plural is "adamun" and "awadim," and the one who says this must decline it. Al-Tabari said: "Adam" is a quadriliteral verb that was named with.

It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Allah created Adam from the surface of the whole earth, so his offspring came out according to its nature: among them the white and the black and the reddish, the easy and the rough, and the good and the wicked."

The interpreters differed concerning His saying: "al-asma'" (the names). The majority of the community said: He taught him the designations (al-tasmiyat). Some said: He presented to him the persons (al-ashkhas). The first is clearer, and the wording "'allama" indicates that.

Then the majority differed as to which names He taught him. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid said: He taught him the name of every thing among all created beings, the minute and the great. Hamid al-Shami said: He taught him only the names of the stars. Al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym said: He taught him only the names of the angels. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: He taught him only the names of his offspring. Al-Tabari said: He taught him the names of his offspring and the angels, and he chose this and preferred it by His saying: ﴿then He presented them to the angels﴾. Al-Naqqash reported from Ibn 'Abbas that He taught him one word by which he knew all the names. Others said: He taught him the names of the kinds, such as mountains, horses, valleys and the like, without specifying what his offspring named of them. Ibn Qutayba said: He taught him the names of what He created in the earth. Some said: He taught him the names in one language, then the convention arose among his offspring regarding other languages. Some others said: rather He taught him the names in every language his offspring would speak. Some people went to excess in this meaning, to the point that Ibn Jinni reported from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi that he said: Allah taught Adam everything, so that he was proficient in grammar as well as Sibawayh was; and sayings of this kind are clearly erroneous in several respects.

Most scholars said: He taught him the benefits of everything and what is suitable for it. Some said: He presented the persons to him at the time of the teaching. Others said: rather He described them to him without presenting persons.

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All of these are possibilities; people have spoken according to them.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "thumma 'aradaha" (then He presented them, feminine), and Ibn Mas'ud read: "thumma 'aradahunna" (then He presented them, feminine plural).

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 30–32 (part 2 of 2):

The interpreters (al-mu'awwilun) differed: did He present to the angels the persons (ashkhas) of the names, or the names without the persons? Ibn Mas'ud and others said: He presented the persons. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: He presented the names. Whoever says, regarding the names, that they are general to everything, says: He presented them community by community and kind by kind. Whoever says that the names are the namings (al-tasmiyat) finds it consistent with the reading of Ubayy, "'aradaha" (He presented it). As for the reading of whoever reads "'aradahum" (He presented them), we say that the word al-asma' (the names) indicates the persons, and therefore it was permissible to say "'aradahum" of the names.

And "anbi'uni" (inform me) means: tell me. Al-naba' is the news (al-khabar), and from it comes al-Nabi (the Prophet). Some people said: from this matter, by way of the informing, the imposition of what cannot be borne is excluded, and its permissibility is established, because He, exalted is He, knew that they would not know. The verifying scholars among the people of interpretation (al-muhaqqiqun min ahl al-ta'wil) said: this is not by way of imposition (al-taklif), but by way of affirmation (al-taqrir) and questioning (al-tawqif).

His saying, exalted is He, "ha'ula'" (these): its apparent meaning is the presence of persons, and that is at the presentation before the angels. There is nothing in this verse that requires that the name was intended to refer to the named (al-musamma), as Makki and al-Mahdawi maintained. Whoever says that He presented persons to the angels finds it consistent with the word "ha'ula'". Whoever says that He presented only names makes the indication by "ha'ula'" refer to the persons of the names, which are absent, since what is part of them has come present by means of a cause, namely their names; and it is as if He said to them, regarding each name: whose is this for which person?

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears is that Allah, exalted is He, taught Adam the names, and presented along with that to him the kinds as persons; then He presented those to the angels and asked them about their namings which Adam had learned. Then Adam said to them: this, its name is so-and-so, and this, its name is so-and-so. "Ha'ula'" is a word built on the kasra, and its shortened form (al-qasr) is the dialect of Tamim and some of Qays and Asad. al-A'sha said:

"Ha'ula thumma ha'ula kullan u'tiya
na'alan mahdhuwwatan bi-na'al"

"Kuntum" is in the place of jazm by the condition (al-shart), and the answer (al-jawab) according to Sibawayh is what precedes it, while according to al-Mubarrad it is omitted, and the estimate is: "in kuntum sadiqin fa-anbi'uni" (if you are truthful, then inform me). Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, and some of the companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: the meaning of the verse is: if you are truthful that the khalifa will corrupt and shed blood. Others said: truthful in that if I appoint you as successors, you will glorify Me with My praise and sanctify for Me. al-Hasan and Qatada said: it is narrated that when Allah created Adam, the angels said: let our Lord create whatever He wills; He will not create a creature more knowledgeable than us, nor more honored by Him. So Allah, exalted is He, intended to show them, from Adam's knowledge and honor, the opposite of what they supposed. So the meaning is: if you are truthful in your claim to knowledge. Others said: the meaning of the verse is: if you are truthful in answering the question, knowing the names. They said: (p-173) for this reason it was not permissible for the angels to exercise ijtihad, and they said: "Subhanaka." This was related by al-Naqqash, who said: had He not required of them truthfulness in the informing, ijtihad would have been permissible for them, just as it was permissible for the one whom Allah caused to die for a hundred years, when He said to him: "kam labithta" (how long have you remained) [al-Baqara: 259], and did not require of him correctness, so he said and did not hit the mark, and he was not reproved. All of this is possible. al-Tabari related that some exegetes said: the meaning of "in kuntum" is "idh kuntum" (since you are); al-Tabari said: this is an error.

If someone asks: what is the wisdom in Allah's saying to the angels, "Inni ja'ilun" (Indeed I am making...), and so on? It is said: this is a test for them and an examination, so that what happened from them would occur, and He, exalted is He, would discipline them through the teaching and honoring of Adam with what He disciplined them. "Subhanaka" is put in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). al-Kisa'i said: it is put in the accusative as a construct vocative (munada mudaf).

al-Zahrawi said: the place of "ma" in their saying, "ma 'allamtana" (what You taught us), is in the accusative by "'allamtana", and the predicate of the negation of the genus (khabar al-tabri'a) is in "lana" (for us). It is possible that the place of "ma" is in the nominative, as a substitute (badal) from the predicate of the negation of the genus, as you say: "la ilaha illa Allah", that is: there is no god in existence except Allah. "Anta" is in the place of the accusative as an emphatic (ta'kid) for the pronoun in "innaka", or in the place of the nominative by way of the inchoative (ibtida'), and "al-'Alim" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "inna", or it is a parenthetical clause (fasila) with no place in the grammatical structure (la mawdi'a laha min al-i'rab). "Al-'Alim" means al-'alim (the knowing), but it adds a meaning of intensity and abundance in the number of known things with respect to Allah, mighty and majestic is He. "Al-Hakim" means al-hakim (the judge), and between them is the distinction of intensification. It is also said: its meaning is al-muhkam (the perfected), as 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib said:

"Amin rayhana al-da'i al-sami'"

That is: al-musmi' (the one who makes hear). The speech according to this is among the attributes of the act. Others said: al-Hakim is the one who prevents corruption, and from it comes "hakamat al-faras" (the bridle of the horse, which restrains it). And from it is the saying of Jarir:

"Abni Hanifa ahkimu sufahaakum
inni akhafu 'alaykum an aghdaba"

(p-174) "O sons of Hanifa, restrain your foolish ones; indeed I fear for you that I will become angry."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 30–32 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And [mention] when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed, I will place upon the earth a successive authority (khalifa)." They said, "Will You place upon it one who causes corruption therein and sheds blood, while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You?" He said, "Indeed, I know that which you do not know."﴾ ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them; then He presented them to the angels and said, "Inform Me of the names of these, if you are truthful."﴾ ﴿They said, "Glory be to You; we have no knowledge except what You have taught us. Indeed, You are the Knowing, the Wise."﴾

Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna said: "Idh" (when) is superfluous (za'ida), and the implied meaning is: "And your Lord said." Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: This is an audacity (ijtira') from Abu 'Ubayda, and all the exegetes refuted him on this point. The majority said: It is not superfluous; rather it is connected to an implied verb, its implied meaning being: "And mention when He said." Also, His saying: ﴿He created for you all that is in the earth﴾ [al-Baqara: 29], the verse, requires that the implied meaning be: "And the beginning of your creation when your Lord said to the angels." The addressing of "Rabb" (Lord) to Muhammad ﷺ, and the addressing of him with the "kaf" (second person pronoun), is an honouring from Him to him and a manifestation of his being specially singled out by it.

The word "malaika" (angels): its singular is "malak," originally "mal'ak," on the pattern "maf'al," from "la'aka" meaning to send. Its plural is "malaika" on the pattern "mufa'ala." Some said: the original of "malak" is "ma'lak," from "alaka" meaning to send, and from it is the saying of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

"Convey to al-Nu'man from me a messenger (ma'lak), that my imprisonment and my waiting have lasted long."

Both forms are attested: "la'aka" and "alaka," the hamza having been transposed after the lam, so its pattern becomes "ma'al" and its plural "malaika," its pattern "mu'afala." Ibn Kaysan said: it is from "malaka yamliku," and the hamza in it is augmental, as it was added in "sha'mal" from "shamila," so its pattern is "fa'al," and the pattern of its plural is "fa'a'ila." It may come in poetry in its original form, as he said:

"I am not for a human, but for an angel (la-mal'akin) who descended from the air of the sky, descending."

In ordinary speech, the hamza was eased and its vowel was dropped onto the lam, or onto the 'ayn according to Ibn Kaysan's view, so it is said "malak." The "ha'" in "malaika" is for the feminization of non-real (ghayr haqiqi) plurals. It was said that it is for emphasis (mubalagha), like 'allama and nassaba. The first view is clearer. Abu 'Ubayda said: the hamza in "malaika" is added, because its singular is "malak."

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is what Ibn Kaysan inclined to.

"Ja'il" (placing/making) in this verse means "khaliq" (creating); al-Tabari mentioned it from Abu Rawq, and its transitivity to one object supports this. Al-Hasan and Qatada said: "ja'il" means "fa'il" (doing). Ibn Sabit reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: the "earth" here means Makkah, because the earth was spread out from beneath it, and because it is the place of residence of the prophets whose peoples were destroyed, and that the grave of Nuh, Hud and Salih is between the Maqam and the Rukn.

"Khalifa" means one who succeeds. Ibn 'Abbas said: The jinn were in the earth before the children of Adam, and they caused corruption and shed blood; so Allah sent to them a company of angels who killed them, and drove their remnant to the islands of the seas and the summits of the mountains, and made Adam and his offspring a successor (khalifa). Al-Hasan said: Allah only named the children of Adam a successor because each generation succeeds the one before it, generation after generation.

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this view it is possible that it means "khalifa" in the sense of one who succeeds (khalifa), and in the sense of one who is succeeded (makhluqa). Ibn Mas'ud said: its meaning is only: a successor from Me in judging among My servants with truth and with My commands, meaning by that Adam, peace be upon him, and whoever stood in his place after him from his offspring. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "khaliqa" with the qaf.

His exalted saying: ﴿They said, "Will You place therein..."﴾, the verse. We know with certainty that the angels do not know the unseen, and do not speak before (Him) in word; and that is general for all the angels, because His saying: ﴿They do not precede Him in speech﴾ [al-Anbiya: 27] came in the manner of praise for them. The Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Tayyib said: "This is the indicator of generality, so it is not sound, with these two conditions, unless they had some information and a preliminary (muqaddima) about the corruption of the creation in the earth." Ibn Zayd and others said: "Allah the Exalted informed them that the successor would be from his offspring a people who would cause corruption and shed blood, so they made this statement on account of that."

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is either by way of wonder at Allah's appointing as successor one who disobeys Him, or at the disobedience of one whom Allah appoints as successor in His earth and whom He favours with that; or it is by way of grave magnification of both matters together: the appointing as successor and the disobedience. Ahmad ibn Yahya Tha'lab and others said: The angels had seen and known what the jinn had done of corruption and shedding of blood in the earth, so their statement ﴿Will You place therein...﴾, the verse, came by way of pure interrogation: is this successor on the path of those who preceded from the jinn or not? Others said: Allah the Exalted had informed the angels that He would create in the earth a creation who would cause corruption and shed blood; so when He said to them afterwards: ﴿Indeed, I will place﴾, they said: ﴿Will You place therein...﴾, the verse, by way of seeking guidance and information: is this successor the one He had informed them of before, or another?

"Al-Safk" is the pouring of blood; this is its common usage, and it may be said: "safaka kalamahu fi kadha" when he rendered his speech in such a matter (sarada). The reading of the majority is with a kasra on the fa'; Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "yasfiku" with a damma on the fa'; Ibn Hurmuz read "wa-yasfika" with the nasb (accusative) by the waw of conjunction in the sense of "al-sarf" (turning away), as if he said: one who combines causing corruption and shedding. Al-Mahdawi said: it is in the nasb as an answer to the interrogation. The first is better.

Their saying: ﴿while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You﴾. Some of the interpreters said: it is by way of interrogation, as if they meant: "And we exalt You with praise, the verse; or shall we change from this state?"

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him:
This is good along with the view of pure interrogation in their saying "Will You place".

Others said: its meaning is self-praise and description of their state, and that is permissible for them, as Yusuf, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed, I am a knowing guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 55]. This is good along with the wonder and grave magnification in their saying "Will You place", that Allah would appoint as successor one who disobeys Him?

On this view He taught them manners with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know.﴾

Others said: the meaning of the verse is: "And we, if You had placed us in the earth and made us successors, would exalt You with praise." This too is good along with the wonder and grave magnification in their saying "Will You place?" The meaning of ﴿exalt You with praise﴾ is: we declare You free of what is not fitting for You and Your attributes. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud said: the glorification of the angels is their prayer to Allah. Qatada said: the glorification of the angels is their saying "Subhan Allah" (Glory be to Allah), according to its usage in the language.

"Bihamdika" means: we mix glorification with praise and join it to it. It is possible that His saying "bihamdika" is a parenthetical insertion between the two statements, as if they said: "(And we glorify and sanctify)," then they interjected by way of submission, meaning: and You are the One praised for guiding to that.

﴿And sanctify You﴾: al-Dahhak and others said: its meaning is: we purify our selves for You, seeking Your good pleasure; and taqdis is purification without dispute, and from it comes "al-ard al-muqaddasa," meaning the purified land, and from it "Bayt al-Maqdis," and from it "al-qudus" by which one purifies oneself. Others said: ﴿and sanctify You﴾ means: we magnify You, and purify Your remembrance from what is not fitting for it. This was said by Mujahid, Abu Salih and others. Some said: "nuqaddisu laka" means: we pray to You; this is weak.

His exalted saying: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know.﴾ The more apparent view is that "a'lamu" is a verb in the imperfect, and "ma" is in the accusative position governed by it. It was said: "a'lamu" is a noun, and "ma" is in the genitive position by annexation (idafa), and there is no dispute among the grammarians that it cannot take tanwin (be declined), and the disagreement lies only in "af'al" when it is named with it and is indefinite: Sibawayh and al-Khalil do not decline it, and al-Akhfash declines it.

The people of interpretation differed concerning what is meant by His saying: ﴿that which you do not know.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: Iblis, may Allah curse him, had become conceited and pride entered him when Allah made him the guardian of the lowest heaven and honoured him. It was also said: rather, when Allah sent him to kill the jinn who had caused corruption in the earth, and he defeated them and killed them with his troops; this too was said by Ibn 'Abbas. He believed that this was due to a merit of his own, and he made light of disbelief and disobedience on Adam's side, peace be upon him. He said: when the angels said ﴿while we exalt You with praise and sanctify You﴾, and they did not know that within Iblis's self there was something contrary to that, Allah said to them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾, meaning what is within Iblis's self. Qatada said: when the angels said: ﴿Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein﴾, and Allah the Exalted knew that among those He would appoint as successors in the earth would be prophets, excellent ones and people of obedience, He said to them: ﴿Indeed, I know that which you do not know﴾, meaning: the deeds of the excellent among the children of Adam.

His exalted saying: "wa-'allama" means: he made known. The teaching of Adam here, according to some, is the inspiration of knowledge to him by necessity. Others said: rather it is teaching by speech, either through an intermediary angel, or by speaking to him before his descent to the earth; so it does not share with Musa, peace be upon him, in his special distinction. Al-Yamani read "wa-'ullima" with a damma on the 'ayn, making the verb passive, with "Adamu" in the nominative. Abu al-Fath said: this is the reading of Yazid al-Barbari. "Adam" is an af'al form derived from "al-udma," which is a redness inclining toward blackness; its plural is "udm" and "awadim," like "humr" and "ahamir." It is not declined in any way. It was also said: the pattern of Adam is "fa'il," derived from "adim al-ard" (the surface of the earth), as if the angel made it its surface; its plural is "adamun" and "awadim," and the one who says this must decline it. Al-Tabari said: "Adam" is a quadriliteral verb that was named with.

It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Allah created Adam from the surface of the whole earth, so his offspring came out according to its nature: among them the white and the black and the reddish, the easy and the rough, and the good and the wicked."

The interpreters differed concerning His saying: "al-asma'" (the names). The majority of the community said: He taught him the designations (al-tasmiyat). Some said: He presented to him the persons (al-ashkhas). The first is clearer, and the wording "'allama" indicates that.

Then the majority differed as to which names He taught him. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Mujahid said: He taught him the name of every thing among all created beings, the minute and the great. Hamid al-Shami said: He taught him only the names of the stars. Al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym said: He taught him only the names of the angels. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd said: He taught him only the names of his offspring. Al-Tabari said: He taught him the names of his offspring and the angels, and he chose this and preferred it by His saying: ﴿then He presented them to the angels﴾. Al-Naqqash reported from Ibn 'Abbas that He taught him one word by which he knew all the names. Others said: He taught him the names of the kinds, such as mountains, horses, valleys and the like, without specifying what his offspring named of them. Ibn Qutayba said: He taught him the names of what He created in the earth. Some said: He taught him the names in one language, then the convention arose among his offspring regarding other languages. Some others said: rather He taught him the names in every language his offspring would speak. Some people went to excess in this meaning, to the point that Ibn Jinni reported from Abu 'Ali al-Farisi that he said: Allah taught Adam everything, so that he was proficient in grammar as well as Sibawayh was; and sayings of this kind are clearly erroneous in several respects.

Most scholars said: He taught him the benefits of everything and what is suitable for it. Some said: He presented the persons to him at the time of the teaching. Others said: rather He described them to him without presenting persons.

The author, al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All of these are possibilities; people have spoken according to them.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "thumma 'aradaha" (then He presented them, feminine), and Ibn Mas'ud read: "thumma 'aradahunna" (then He presented them, feminine plural).

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 30–32 (part 2 of 2):

The interpreters (al-mu'awwilun) differed: did He present to the angels the persons (ashkhas) of the names, or the names without the persons? Ibn Mas'ud and others said: He presented the persons. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: He presented the names. Whoever says, regarding the names, that they are general to everything, says: He presented them community by community and kind by kind. Whoever says that the names are the namings (al-tasmiyat) finds it consistent with the reading of Ubayy, "'aradaha" (He presented it). As for the reading of whoever reads "'aradahum" (He presented them), we say that the word al-asma' (the names) indicates the persons, and therefore it was permissible to say "'aradahum" of the names.

And "anbi'uni" (inform me) means: tell me. Al-naba' is the news (al-khabar), and from it comes al-Nabi (the Prophet). Some people said: from this matter, by way of the informing, the imposition of what cannot be borne is excluded, and its permissibility is established, because He, exalted is He, knew that they would not know. The verifying scholars among the people of interpretation (al-muhaqqiqun min ahl al-ta'wil) said: this is not by way of imposition (al-taklif), but by way of affirmation (al-taqrir) and questioning (al-tawqif).

His saying, exalted is He, "ha'ula'" (these): its apparent meaning is the presence of persons, and that is at the presentation before the angels. There is nothing in this verse that requires that the name was intended to refer to the named (al-musamma), as Makki and al-Mahdawi maintained. Whoever says that He presented persons to the angels finds it consistent with the word "ha'ula'". Whoever says that He presented only names makes the indication by "ha'ula'" refer to the persons of the names, which are absent, since what is part of them has come present by means of a cause, namely their names; and it is as if He said to them, regarding each name: whose is this for which person?

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears is that Allah, exalted is He, taught Adam the names, and presented along with that to him the kinds as persons; then He presented those to the angels and asked them about their namings which Adam had learned. Then Adam said to them: this, its name is so-and-so, and this, its name is so-and-so. "Ha'ula'" is a word built on the kasra, and its shortened form (al-qasr) is the dialect of Tamim and some of Qays and Asad. al-A'sha said:

"Ha'ula thumma ha'ula kullan u'tiya
na'alan mahdhuwwatan bi-na'al"
