Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 35–36:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat therefrom in abundance wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it and removed them from that in which they had been. And We said, "Go down, [all of you], as enemies to one another, and for you on the earth is a place of settlement and provision for a time."﴾

"Uskun" (dwell) means: remain in residence. Its form is that of an imperative, but its meaning is permission. "Anta" (you) is an emphasis for the pronoun in "uskun," and "zawjuka" (your wife) is coordinated with it. "Al-zawj" is the wife of a man, and this is more common than "zawja," which has already been discussed. "Al-Jannah" is an orchard with a enclosure around it.

Scholars differed concerning the Garden in which Adam was made to dwell: is it the Garden of Eternity (jannat al-khuld) or a garden prepared for the two of them? Those who did not make it the Garden of Eternity held that whoever enters the Garden of Eternity does not leave it. This is not impossible. However, the transmitted text reports that whoever enters it as a reward does not leave it, whereas whoever enters it from the beginning, as Adam did, is not impossible, and no transmitted text states that he does not leave it.

They also differed as to when Eve was created from the rib of Adam, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Abbas said: when he informed the angels of the names and they were commanded to prostrate to him, sleep was cast upon him and Eve was created. He awoke and she was at his side, and he said, as they claim: "Flesh of my flesh and blood of my blood," and he found tranquillity in her. The angels then went to test his knowledge, and they said to him, "O Adam, what is her name?" He said, "Hawwa'." They said, "And why?" He said, "Because she was created from a living thing." Then Allah said to him: ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas also said: When Adam was made to dwell in the Garden, he walked in it feeling lonely. When he slept, Eve was created from his short rib, so that he might find tranquillity in her and be at ease with her. When he awoke he saw her and said, "Who are you?" She said, "A woman created from your rib so that you may find tranquillity in me."

"Kula" (eat) has dropped its nun for the imperative, and the first alif was dropped for the vowel of the kaf, when the second was dropped because of the meeting of two identical letters; this deletion is irregular. The meaning of this imperative with "kula" is permission, by the indication of His saying: ﴿wherever you wish﴾. The pronoun in "minha" refers back to "the Garden."

Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read "raghadan" with a sukun on the ghayn, while the majority read it with a fatha. "Al-raghad" is a comfortable, abundant, pleasant life free of hardship, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is seen by you living in comfort, secure from calamities, in a raghad life."

"Raghadan" is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; it was also said that it is an accusative of the verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause. "Haythu" is built on damma; some Arabs build it on fatha, and some Arabs inflect it according to its position, in the nominative, accusative and genitive, as in His saying: ﴿We will draw them on step by step from where they do not know﴾ [al-A'raf: 182]. Some Arabs say "hawth."

"Shi'tuma" originally was "shay'atuma," transformed into "fa'altuma"; its yā' moved and the letter before it was opened, so it became "sha'atuma," the unvocalized extended alif was dropped for the meeting of the two sukuns, and the shin was kasra to indicate the yā', so "shi'tuma" came about. This is the explanation of al-Mubarrad. As for Sibawayh, the original form in his view is "shiy'atuma" with a kasra on the yā', the vowel of the yā' was transferred to the shin, and the yā' was dropped afterward.

His exalted saying: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ means: do not approach it by eating, because permission was given regarding it. One of the skilled scholars said: when Allah wished to forbid eating from the tree, He forbade it with a expression that implies eating and what leads to it, which is approaching.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a clear example of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i'). Ibn Muhaysin read "hadhi" according to the original form, and the ha' in "hadhihi" is a substitute for the yā'. There is no feminine ha' in the speech preceded by a kasra other than this one. This demonstrative may refer to one specific tree or to a kind. Harun al-A'war related from some scholars the reading "al-shijrah" with a kasra on the shin. "Al-shajar" is every plant that stands on a stalk.

They differed about what this tree was that He forbade. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the vine, and for this reason wine was forbidden to us. Ibn Jurayj related from some Companions: it is the fig tree. Ibn 'Abbas also, Abu Malik, 'Atiyya and Qatadah said: it is the ear of grain, whose grain is like the kidneys of a cow, sweeter than honey and softer than butter. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the tree of knowledge, which bears the fruit of everything. This is weak and is not authentically from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Tabari related from Ya'qub ibn 'Utbah that it is the tree by which the angels used to rub the mouths of the children for eternity; this too is weak. He said: The Jews claim it is the colocynth, and say: it was sweet, and became bitter from that time.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is nothing in any of these identifications that is supported by a report. Rather, the correct position is to believe that Allah, exalted is He, forbade Adam a tree, and he disobeyed and transgressed by eating from it.

In Allah's prohibition to Adam of the tree there is an indication that his dwelling in the Garden was not permanent, because the one who is eternal is not forbidden anything, nor commanded or prohibited. It was also said: this tree had been singled out to cause whoever ate it to need to relieve himself, and therefore it was forbidden; when he ate and the Garden was not a place for relieving oneself, he was sent down to the earth.

His saying "fa-takuna" (so that you become) is in the jussive position by coordination with "la taqraba." It may also be in the accusative as a response. The governing particle, according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is the implied "an," and according to al-Jarmi, it is the fa'.

"Al-zalim" in the language is one who places a thing in other than its place; from it is their saying: "whoever resembles his father has not wronged." From it also comes "al-mazlumah al-jald," because the rain did not come to it at its time. From it also is the saying of 'Amr ibn Qami'ah:

"The valleys were wronged by the flowing of a greedy one, and the pure water became clear for it after the cloud had ceased."

"Zulm" in the rulings of the Sharia has degrees: the highest of them is shirk, then the wrong of sins, which are also degrees.

In this verse it indicates that His saying "wa la taqraba" is by way of obligation, not recommendation, because whoever abandons the recommended is not called a wrongdoer; so the word "zulm" implies the strength of the prohibition.

"Azallahuma" is derived from "zalal," and in the verse it is metaphorical, because it concerns opinion and reflection; the true meaning of "zalal" is in the feet. Abu 'Ali said: "fa-azallahuma" admits two interpretations: one is that they acquired the slip; the other is that it is from zalla, meaning to stumble. Hamzah read "fa-azalahuma," derived from al-zawal (removal), as if he were the one who removes, since his seduction led to removal; this is the reading of al-Hasan and Abu Raja'.

There is no disagreement among the scholars that Iblis the accursed is the one who undertook the seduction of Adam.

They differed regarding the manner: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and the majority of scholars said: he seduced them face to face, and the evidence for this is His saying: "And he swore to them" (wa qasamahuma), and swearing to them apparently means speaking directly. Others said: when Iblis entered upon Adam he spoke to him about his condition, saying: "O Adam, how fine this would be, if there were eternity," and Iblis found a way to seduce him. He said: "Shall I guide you to the tree of eternity?" Others said: he entered the Garden within the mouth of the serpent, which had four legs like the Bactrian camel, after presenting himself to many animals and none would admit him except the serpent. He came out to Eve and took something from the tree and said: "Look how fine this is," and he seduced her until she ate; then he seduced Adam. Eve said to him: "Eat, for I have eaten and it did not harm me," so he ate, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they were in the state of sin. The serpent was cursed, its legs were returned into its belly, and enmity was placed between it and the children of Adam.

It was said to Eve: just as you caused the tree to bleed, so blood will afflict you every month, and likewise you will carry in hardship and give birth in hardship, approaching death repeatedly through it. al-Tabari and al-Naqqash added: and you will be foolish, though you were forbearing.

Another group said: Iblis did not enter the Garden to Adam after he had been removed from it; rather he seduced Adam with his devil, his authority and his whisperings which Allah had given him, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Satan flows through the son of Adam as the blood flows." The pronoun in "anha" refers to "the tree" according to the reading of whoever read "azallahuma," and it may refer to "the Garden." As for whoever read "azalahuma," it refers only to "the Garden." Here there is an omitted element indicated by the context, its estimate being "so they ate from the tree." Some people said: they ate from a tree other than the one indicated, so they did not understand the prohibition to apply to its whole species. Others said: they interpreted the prohibition as recommendation.

Ibn al-Musayyib said: Adam only ate after Eve had given him wine to drink, so he was not in his right mind.

His exalted saying: ﴿So He removed them from that in which they had been﴾ admits several meanings: it was said he removed them from obedience to disobedience; it was said from the blessing of the Garden to the misery of this world; it was said from the elevation of station to the lowest place of sin. All of this is close in meaning. Abu Haywah read "ihbitu" with a damma on the ba', and "yaf'alu" is common in the intransitive, and "habata" is intransitive. Al-hubut is descent from a height to a lower place.

They differed as to who is addressed by the descent: al-Suddi and others said: Adam, Eve, Iblis and the serpent. al-Hasan said: Adam, Eve and the whisperer. Others said: and the serpent, because Iblis had already been sent down earlier at his disobedience.

And ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase. The word "'aduww" is used in the singular in view of the word "ba'd," and "ba'd" and "kull" function as singular; and in view of the word "'aduww," which is used for the singular and the plural. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4].

And ﴿for you on the earth is a place of settlement﴾ means: a place of residence; this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd. al-Suddi said: the intended meaning is residence in graves.

"Al-mata'" is what is enjoyed: of food, clothing, life, conversation, companionship and other things. Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, when he stood at the grave of his son Ayyub after burying him, recited:

"I stood at a strange grave in 'Afrah, a little enjoyment from a departed beloved."

The interpreters differed about "al-hin" here. One group said: until death; this is the view of those who say that the settlement is the stay in this world. Another group said: "ila hin" means until the Day of Resurrection; this is the view of those who say the settlement is in the graves. It also follows, on the view that the settlement is in this world, that by His saying "wa lakum" is meant: for your kinds in this world there is settlement and enjoyment, generation after generation, until the Day of Resurrection. "Al-hin" is a long period of time; its shortest, in oaths and obligations, is a year. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It gives its produce at every time by the permission of its Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 25]. It has also been said its shortest is six months, because some palm trees bear fruit every six months; and "hin" is sometimes used in conversation for a short period of time. In His exalted saying "ila hin" there is a benefit for Adam, peace be upon him, so that he may know that he will not remain in it and will move to the Garden which he was promised to return to; and for others than Adam it indicates the return (al-ma'ad).

It is narrated that Adam descended upon a mountain of the mountains of Sarandib, that Eve descended at Jeddah, that the serpent descended at Isfahan, and it was said at Maysan, and that Iblis descended upon al-Ubullah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 35–36:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden, and eat therefrom in abundance wherever you wish, but do not approach this tree, lest you be among the wrongdoers."﴾ ﴿Then Satan caused them to slip from it and removed them from that in which they had been. And We said, "Go down, [all of you], as enemies to one another, and for you on the earth is a place of settlement and provision for a time."﴾

"Uskun" (dwell) means: remain in residence. Its form is that of an imperative, but its meaning is permission. "Anta" (you) is an emphasis for the pronoun in "uskun," and "zawjuka" (your wife) is coordinated with it. "Al-zawj" is the wife of a man, and this is more common than "zawja," which has already been discussed. "Al-Jannah" is an orchard with a enclosure around it.

Scholars differed concerning the Garden in which Adam was made to dwell: is it the Garden of Eternity (jannat al-khuld) or a garden prepared for the two of them? Those who did not make it the Garden of Eternity held that whoever enters the Garden of Eternity does not leave it. This is not impossible. However, the transmitted text reports that whoever enters it as a reward does not leave it, whereas whoever enters it from the beginning, as Adam did, is not impossible, and no transmitted text states that he does not leave it.

They also differed as to when Eve was created from the rib of Adam, peace be upon him. Ibn 'Abbas said: when he informed the angels of the names and they were commanded to prostrate to him, sleep was cast upon him and Eve was created. He awoke and she was at his side, and he said, as they claim: "Flesh of my flesh and blood of my blood," and he found tranquillity in her. The angels then went to test his knowledge, and they said to him, "O Adam, what is her name?" He said, "Hawwa'." They said, "And why?" He said, "Because she was created from a living thing." Then Allah said to him: ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾.

Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas also said: When Adam was made to dwell in the Garden, he walked in it feeling lonely. When he slept, Eve was created from his short rib, so that he might find tranquillity in her and be at ease with her. When he awoke he saw her and said, "Who are you?" She said, "A woman created from your rib so that you may find tranquillity in me."

"Kula" (eat) has dropped its nun for the imperative, and the first alif was dropped for the vowel of the kaf, when the second was dropped because of the meeting of two identical letters; this deletion is irregular. The meaning of this imperative with "kula" is permission, by the indication of His saying: ﴿wherever you wish﴾. The pronoun in "minha" refers back to "the Garden."

Ibn Wathhab and al-Nakha'i read "raghadan" with a sukun on the ghayn, while the majority read it with a fatha. "Al-raghad" is a comfortable, abundant, pleasant life free of hardship, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"While a man is seen by you living in comfort, secure from calamities, in a raghad life."

"Raghadan" is in the accusative as an adjective of an omitted verbal noun; it was also said that it is an accusative of the verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial clause. "Haythu" is built on damma; some Arabs build it on fatha, and some Arabs inflect it according to its position, in the nominative, accusative and genitive, as in His saying: ﴿We will draw them on step by step from where they do not know﴾ [al-A'raf: 182]. Some Arabs say "hawth."

"Shi'tuma" originally was "shay'atuma," transformed into "fa'altuma"; its yā' moved and the letter before it was opened, so it became "sha'atuma," the unvocalized extended alif was dropped for the meeting of the two sukuns, and the shin was kasra to indicate the yā', so "shi'tuma" came about. This is the explanation of al-Mubarrad. As for Sibawayh, the original form in his view is "shiy'atuma" with a kasra on the yā', the vowel of the yā' was transferred to the shin, and the yā' was dropped afterward.

His exalted saying: ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾ means: do not approach it by eating, because permission was given regarding it. One of the skilled scholars said: when Allah wished to forbid eating from the tree, He forbade it with a expression that implies eating and what leads to it, which is approaching.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a clear example of blocking the means (sadd al-dhara'i'). Ibn Muhaysin read "hadhi" according to the original form, and the ha' in "hadhihi" is a substitute for the yā'. There is no feminine ha' in the speech preceded by a kasra other than this one. This demonstrative may refer to one specific tree or to a kind. Harun al-A'war related from some scholars the reading "al-shijrah" with a kasra on the shin. "Al-shajar" is every plant that stands on a stalk.

They differed about what this tree was that He forbade. Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the vine, and for this reason wine was forbidden to us. Ibn Jurayj related from some Companions: it is the fig tree. Ibn 'Abbas also, Abu Malik, 'Atiyya and Qatadah said: it is the ear of grain, whose grain is like the kidneys of a cow, sweeter than honey and softer than butter. It is also related from Ibn 'Abbas that it is the tree of knowledge, which bears the fruit of everything. This is weak and is not authentically from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Tabari related from Ya'qub ibn 'Utbah that it is the tree by which the angels used to rub the mouths of the children for eternity; this too is weak. He said: The Jews claim it is the colocynth, and say: it was sweet, and became bitter from that time.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

There is nothing in any of these identifications that is supported by a report. Rather, the correct position is to believe that Allah, exalted is He, forbade Adam a tree, and he disobeyed and transgressed by eating from it.

In Allah's prohibition to Adam of the tree there is an indication that his dwelling in the Garden was not permanent, because the one who is eternal is not forbidden anything, nor commanded or prohibited. It was also said: this tree had been singled out to cause whoever ate it to need to relieve himself, and therefore it was forbidden; when he ate and the Garden was not a place for relieving oneself, he was sent down to the earth.

His saying "fa-takuna" (so that you become) is in the jussive position by coordination with "la taqraba." It may also be in the accusative as a response. The governing particle, according to al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is the implied "an," and according to al-Jarmi, it is the fa'.

"Al-zalim" in the language is one who places a thing in other than its place; from it is their saying: "whoever resembles his father has not wronged." From it also comes "al-mazlumah al-jald," because the rain did not come to it at its time. From it also is the saying of 'Amr ibn Qami'ah:

"The valleys were wronged by the flowing of a greedy one, and the pure water became clear for it after the cloud had ceased."

"Zulm" in the rulings of the Sharia has degrees: the highest of them is shirk, then the wrong of sins, which are also degrees.

In this verse it indicates that His saying "wa la taqraba" is by way of obligation, not recommendation, because whoever abandons the recommended is not called a wrongdoer; so the word "zulm" implies the strength of the prohibition.

"Azallahuma" is derived from "zalal," and in the verse it is metaphorical, because it concerns opinion and reflection; the true meaning of "zalal" is in the feet. Abu 'Ali said: "fa-azallahuma" admits two interpretations: one is that they acquired the slip; the other is that it is from zalla, meaning to stumble. Hamzah read "fa-azalahuma," derived from al-zawal (removal), as if he were the one who removes, since his seduction led to removal; this is the reading of al-Hasan and Abu Raja'.

There is no disagreement among the scholars that Iblis the accursed is the one who undertook the seduction of Adam.

They differed regarding the manner: Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and the majority of scholars said: he seduced them face to face, and the evidence for this is His saying: "And he swore to them" (wa qasamahuma), and swearing to them apparently means speaking directly. Others said: when Iblis entered upon Adam he spoke to him about his condition, saying: "O Adam, how fine this would be, if there were eternity," and Iblis found a way to seduce him. He said: "Shall I guide you to the tree of eternity?" Others said: he entered the Garden within the mouth of the serpent, which had four legs like the Bactrian camel, after presenting himself to many animals and none would admit him except the serpent. He came out to Eve and took something from the tree and said: "Look how fine this is," and he seduced her until she ate; then he seduced Adam. Eve said to him: "Eat, for I have eaten and it did not harm me," so he ate, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they were in the state of sin. The serpent was cursed, its legs were returned into its belly, and enmity was placed between it and the children of Adam.

It was said to Eve: just as you caused the tree to bleed, so blood will afflict you every month, and likewise you will carry in hardship and give birth in hardship, approaching death repeatedly through it. al-Tabari and al-Naqqash added: and you will be foolish, though you were forbearing.

Another group said: Iblis did not enter the Garden to Adam after he had been removed from it; rather he seduced Adam with his devil, his authority and his whisperings which Allah had given him, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed Satan flows through the son of Adam as the blood flows." The pronoun in "anha" refers to "the tree" according to the reading of whoever read "azallahuma," and it may refer to "the Garden." As for whoever read "azalahuma," it refers only to "the Garden." Here there is an omitted element indicated by the context, its estimate being "so they ate from the tree." Some people said: they ate from a tree other than the one indicated, so they did not understand the prohibition to apply to its whole species. Others said: they interpreted the prohibition as recommendation.

Ibn al-Musayyib said: Adam only ate after Eve had given him wine to drink, so he was not in his right mind.

His exalted saying: ﴿So He removed them from that in which they had been﴾ admits several meanings: it was said he removed them from obedience to disobedience; it was said from the blessing of the Garden to the misery of this world; it was said from the elevation of station to the lowest place of sin. All of this is close in meaning. Abu Haywah read "ihbitu" with a damma on the ba', and "yaf'alu" is common in the intransitive, and "habata" is intransitive. Al-hubut is descent from a height to a lower place.

They differed as to who is addressed by the descent: al-Suddi and others said: Adam, Eve, Iblis and the serpent. al-Hasan said: Adam, Eve and the whisperer. Others said: and the serpent, because Iblis had already been sent down earlier at his disobedience.

And ﴿some of you are enemies to others﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase. The word "'aduww" is used in the singular in view of the word "ba'd," and "ba'd" and "kull" function as singular; and in view of the word "'aduww," which is used for the singular and the plural. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They are the enemy, so beware of them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 4].

And ﴿for you on the earth is a place of settlement﴾ means: a place of residence; this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah and Ibn Zayd. al-Suddi said: the intended meaning is residence in graves.

"Al-mata'" is what is enjoyed: of food, clothing, life, conversation, companionship and other things. Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik, when he stood at the grave of his son Ayyub after burying him, recited:

"I stood at a strange grave in 'Afrah, a little enjoyment from a departed beloved."

The interpreters differed about "al-hin" here. One group said: until death; this is the view of those who say that the settlement is the stay in this world. Another group said: "ila hin" means until the Day of Resurrection; this is the view of those who say the settlement is in the graves. It also follows, on the view that the settlement is in this world, that by His saying "wa lakum" is meant: for your kinds in this world there is settlement and enjoyment, generation after generation, until the Day of Resurrection. "Al-hin" is a long period of time; its shortest, in oaths and obligations, is a year. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿It gives its produce at every time by the permission of its Lord﴾ [Ibrahim: 25]. It has also been said its shortest is six months, because some palm trees bear fruit every six months; and "hin" is sometimes used in conversation for a short period of time. In His exalted saying "ila hin" there is a benefit for Adam, peace be upon him, so that he may know that he will not remain in it and will move to the Garden which he was promised to return to; and for others than Adam it indicates the return (al-ma'ad).

It is narrated that Adam descended upon a mountain of the mountains of Sarandib, that Eve descended at Jeddah, that the serpent descended at Isfahan, and it was said at Maysan, and that Iblis descended upon al-Ubullah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 37–39:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He relented toward him. Indeed, He is the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful.﴾ ﴿We said, "Go down from it, all of you. And when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance – there will be no fear for them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs – those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾

The meaning: Adam received (talaqqa) the words, and Allah relented toward him at that time. "Adam" is the subject (marfu') of "talaqqa," and "words" (kalimat) is its object (mansub) by it. The receiving (talaqqi) from Adam is turning toward them, accepting them, and understanding them. Makki transmitted an opinion that they were inspired to him and he benefited from them. Ibn Kathir read "Adam" in the accusative and "from His Lord, words" in the nominative, so the receiving of the words is Adam's attaining, through them, Allah's mercy and His acceptance of his repentance.

The commentators differed concerning "the words." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: they are His saying, ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23], to the end of the verse. Mujahid said: they are that Adam said, "Glory be to You, O Allah, there is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me. Indeed, You are the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful."

Ibn 'Abbas said: they are that Adam said: "My Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you see, if I repent and obey, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes."

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: Adam said: "My Lord, do you see what I disobeyed You in: is it something You had written upon me, or something You initiated?" He said: "Rather, it is something I had written upon you." He said: "My Lord, as You wrote it upon me, so forgive me."

Qatada said: the words are that Adam said: "My Lord, do you see if I repent and make amends?" He said: "Then I will admit you to the Garden."

A group said: the intended meaning of "the words" is his regret, his seeking forgiveness, and his grief. He called them "words" metaphorically, since they issue from creation as words, and in each of them is "Be" (kun). This view implies that Adam said nothing except the well-known seeking of forgiveness.

Some of the righteous predecessors of the Muslims were asked what the sinner should say. He said: he should say what his parents said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23], what Musa said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16], and what Yunus said: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed, I was among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87].

"And He relented toward him" means: He returned to him with it. Repentance (tawba) from Allah the Exalted is His turning toward His servant with mercy and enabling; repentance from the servant is his turning back from disobedience, with regret for the sin together with abandoning it in what follows. Allah the Exalted specified Adam by mention here in the receiving and the repentance, while Eve shared with him in that by consensus, because he was the one addressed at the beginning of the story with His saying: ﴿Dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden﴾ [al-Baqara: 35]. Therefore the story was completed by mentioning him alone. Also, because the woman is a matter of sanctity and is veiled, Allah wished to conceal her; for this reason He did not mention her in the disobedience in His saying: ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and erred﴾ [Ta-Ha: 121]. It is narrated that Allah relented toward Adam on the Day of 'Ashura'.

Adam's kunya was Abu Muhammad, and it was said: Abu al-Bashar. The majority read "innahu" with a kasra on the alif, as a fresh sentence (al-qat'). Ibn Abi 'Aqrab read "annahu" with a fatha on the hamza, meaning "because He." The form "al-Tawwab" is for emphasis and intensification.

In His saying, ﴿Indeed, He is the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾, there is an emphasis whose benefit is that repentance granted to the servant is only a blessing from Allah, not from the servant alone, so that the penitent does not become self-admiring; rather, what is obligatory upon him is to thank Allah the Exalted for His having relented toward him.

He repeated the command to descend when He attached to each of the two commands a ruling different from the other's: He attached enmity to the first, and to the second the coming of guidance. It was also said: He repeated the command to descend as a way of stressing and emphasizing the matter, as you say to a man: "Stand up, stand up."

Al-Naqqash transmitted that the second descent is from the Garden to the heaven, while the first, in the order of the verse, is to the earth, which is the latter in occurrence; so there is no repetition in the command according to this view.

"Jami'an" (all of you) is a state (hal) from the pronoun in "ihbitu" (go down). It is neither a verbal noun nor an active participle, but it stands in place of them and indicates them, as if he said: "descent, all of you," or "descending, all of you."

Concerning the intended addressees of this address, it was differed: it was said: Adam, Eve, Iblis and their offspring. It was said: its apparent meaning is generality, but its meaning is specific to Adam and Eve, because guidance does not come to Iblis. They were addressed with the plural form to honor them both. The first view is more sound, because Iblis is addressed with faith by consensus.

The "inna" in His saying "fa-imma" is the conditional particle, and "ma" entered upon it as an emphasizer so that the heavy nun could be attached; it is like the oath-lam that comes so that the nun may come. In His saying, "minni" (from Me), there is an indication that the actions of the servants are the creation of Allah the Exalted. The commentators differed concerning the meaning of His saying "huda" (guidance): it was said: clarification and guidance.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The correct view is to say: clarification and invitation. A group said: "guidance" means the messengers, who are to Adam from the angels, and to his children from humankind, and whoever came after him.

His saying, ﴿whoever follows My guidance﴾, is a conditional clause whose response is ﴿there will be no fear for them﴾. Sibawayh said: the second condition and its response are both the response of the first, in His saying: ﴿then if there comes to you...﴾. It is related from al-Kisa'i that His saying ﴿there will be no fear for them﴾ is the response to both conditions together.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is related, but it is open to question, and it is not appropriate to oppose Sibawayh here. The disagreement concerns verses like His saying: ﴿But if he is among those brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 88], ﴿then rest and bounty﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 89], where Sibawayh says it is the response of both conditions. As for this verse, the meaning prevents ﴿there will be no fear﴾ from being the response to both conditions.

al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "huda" (with the alif, as "hudan" in the accusative pattern of the dialect), and this is the dialect of Hudhayl. Abu Dhu'ayb said, lamenting his sons:

They raced to their desire and bent to their passion, so they were carried off, and every side has its place of fall.

Likewise they say "'asiyya" and similar forms. The reason for this dialect is that the ya of possession normally requires the preceding letter to be kasra; since in this pattern the kasra on the quiescent alif is not valid, it was replaced with ya and assimilated.

al-Zuhri, Ya'qub and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "fala khawfa 'alayhim" with the accusative, in the sense of generic negation (tabri'a). Its aspect is that it is more general and more emphatic in negating fear. The aspect of the nominative is that it is more balanced in wording, so that the nominative in "hum yahzanun" is coordinated with a nominative. In the nominative reading, "la" functions as "laysa" does. Ibn Muhayşin, with a variant from him, read "fala khawfun" with the nominative and without tanwin; this is on the basis that "la" acts as "laysa," but he dropped the tanwin for lightness because of frequent use.

His saying ﴿neither fear shall be upon them﴾ [Yunus: 62] may mean: concerning what lies before them of the world. ﴿Nor shall they grieve﴾ over what has escaped them of it. It may also mean: on the Day of Resurrection, there is no fear for them, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ therein. It may also mean that He will admit them to the Garden, where there is no fear and no grief.

His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved﴾ is a conjunction of a nominal clause over a nominal clause. He said "and they denied," and disbelief alone would have sufficed; for the word "kafaru" is shared by the disbelief of ingratitude for blessings and the disbelief of sins, and by this alone eternal abiding is not necessitated. So He made clear that disbelief here is polytheism, by His saying ﴿and denied Our signs﴾. "Ayat" here may mean the recited revelation, or it may mean the placed sign. The discussion of the word "ayah" has already preceded at the beginning of this book.

"Ulā'ika" is nominative as the subject, and "ashab" is its predicate. Companionship (suhba) is being joined to a thing in a state, at some time; if the joining and close association are constant, it is the perfection of companionship, and so is the companionship of the people of the Fire with it. By this statement the disagreement over naming the Companions (sahaba), may Allah be pleased with them, is resolved, because their ranks are varied: the least of them is joining in Islam and time, and the most is close association and constant companionship.

﴿And they therein abide eternally﴾ [al-Baqara: 25]: a nominal clause, subject and predicate, in the position of a circumstantial clause.

It was also said: He repeated the command to descend as a way of stressing and emphasizing the matter, as you say to a man: "Stand up, stand up."

Al-Naqqash transmitted that the second descent is from the Garden to the heaven, while the first, in the order of the verse, is to the earth, which is the latter in occurrence; so there is no repetition in the command according to this view.

"Jami'an" (all of you) is a state (hal) from the pronoun in "ihbitu" (go down). It is neither a verbal noun nor an active participle, but it stands in place of them and indicates them, as if he said: "descent, all of you," or "descending, all of you."

Concerning the intended addressees of this address, it was differed: it was said: Adam, Eve, Iblis and their offspring. It was said: its apparent meaning is generality, but its meaning is specific to Adam and Eve, because guidance does not come to Iblis. They were addressed with the plural form to honor them both. The first view is more sound, because Iblis is addressed with faith by consensus.

The "inna" in His saying "fa-imma" is the conditional particle, and "ma" entered upon it as an emphasizer so that the heavy nun could be attached; it is like the oath-lam that comes so that the nun may come. In His saying, "minni" (from Me), there is an indication that the actions of the servants are the creation of Allah the Exalted. The commentators differed concerning the meaning of His saying "huda" (guidance): it was said: clarification and guidance.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The correct view is to say: clarification and invitation. A group said: "guidance" means the messengers, who are to Adam from the angels, and to his children from humankind, and whoever came after him.

His saying, ﴿whoever follows My guidance﴾, is a conditional clause whose response is ﴿there will be no fear for them﴾. Sibawayh said: the second condition and its response are both the response of the first, in His saying: ﴿then if there comes to you...﴾. It is related from al-Kisa'i that His saying ﴿there will be no fear for them﴾ is the response to both conditions together.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is related, but it is open to question, and it is not appropriate to oppose Sibawayh here. The disagreement concerns verses like His saying: ﴿But if he is among those brought near﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 88], ﴿then rest and bounty﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 89], where Sibawayh says it is the response of both conditions. As for this verse, the meaning prevents ﴿there will be no fear﴾ from being the response to both conditions.

al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi Ishaq read "huda" (with the alif, as "hudan" in the accusative pattern of the dialect), and this is the dialect of Hudhayl. Abu Dhu'ayb said, lamenting his sons:

They raced to their desire and bent to their passion, so they were carried off, and every side has its place of fall.

Likewise they say "'asiyya" and similar forms. The reason for this dialect is that the ya of possession normally requires the preceding letter to be kasra; since in this pattern the kasra on the quiescent alif is not valid, it was replaced with ya and assimilated.

al-Zuhri, Ya'qub and 'Isa al-Thaqafi read "fala khawfa 'alayhim" with the accusative, in the sense of generic negation (tabri'a). Its aspect is that it is more general and more emphatic in negating fear. The aspect of the nominative is that it is more balanced in wording, so that the nominative in "hum yahzanun" is coordinated with a nominative. In the nominative reading, "la" functions as "laysa" does. Ibn Muhayşin, with a variant from him, read "fala khawfun" with the nominative and without tanwin; this is on the basis that "la" acts as "laysa," but he dropped the tanwin for lightness because of frequent use.

His saying ﴿neither fear shall be upon them﴾ [Yunus: 62] may mean: concerning what lies before them of the world. ﴿Nor shall they grieve﴾ over what has escaped them of it. It may also mean: on the Day of Resurrection, there is no fear for them, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾ therein. It may also mean that He will admit them to the Garden, where there is no fear and no grief.

His saying ﴿And those who disbelieved﴾ is a conjunction of a nominal clause over a nominal clause. He said "and they denied," and disbelief alone would have sufficed; for the word "kafaru" is shared by the disbelief of ingratitude for blessings and the disbelief of sins, and by this alone eternal abiding is not necessitated. So He made clear that disbelief here is polytheism, by His saying ﴿and denied Our signs﴾. "Ayat" here may mean the recited revelation, or it may mean the placed sign. The discussion of the word "ayah" has already preceded at the beginning of this book.

"Ulā'ika" is nominative as the subject, and "ashab" is its predicate. Companionship (suhba) is being joined to a thing in a state, at some time; if the joining and close association are constant, it is the perfection of companionship, and so is the companionship of the people of the Fire with it. By this statement the disagreement over naming the Companions (sahaba), may Allah be pleased with them, is resolved, because their ranks are varied: the least of them is joining in Islam and time, and the most is close association and constant companionship.

﴿And they therein abide eternally﴾ [al-Baqara: 25]: a nominal clause, subject and predicate, in the position of a circumstantial clause.

Mujahid said: they are that Adam said, "Glory be to You, O Allah, there is no god but You. I have wronged myself, so forgive me. Indeed, You are the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful."

Ibn 'Abbas said: they are that Adam said: "My Lord, did You not create me with Your hand?" He said: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, did You not breathe into me of Your spirit?" He said: "Yes." He said: "My Lord, did You not settle me in Your Garden?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Do you see, if I repent and obey, will You return me to the Garden?" He said: "Yes."

'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: Adam said: "My Lord, do you see what I disobeyed You in: is it something You had written upon me, or something You initiated?" He said: "Rather, it is something I had written upon you." He said: "My Lord, as You wrote it upon me, so forgive me."

Qatada said: the words are that Adam said: "My Lord, do you see if I repent and make amends?" He said: "Then I will admit you to the Garden."

A group said: the intended meaning of "the words" is his regret, his seeking forgiveness, and his grief. He called them "words" metaphorically, since they issue from creation as words, and in each of them is "Be" (kun). This view implies that Adam said nothing except the well-known seeking of forgiveness.

He said: he should say what his parents said: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 23], what Musa said: ﴿My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me﴾ [al-Qasas: 16], and what Yunus said: ﴿There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed, I was among the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87].

Therefore the story was completed by mentioning him alone. It is narrated that Allah relented toward Adam on the Day of 'Ashura'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 40–41:

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and fulfil My covenant, and I shall fulfil your covenant, and fear Me alone.﴾ ﴿And believe in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you, and do not be the first to disbelieve in it, and do not exchange My signs for a small price, and fear Me alone, so be mindful of Me.﴾

"Yā" is a vocative particle (ḥarf nidā') that carries the meaning of calling attention. Al-Khalīl said: the governing element of the vocative is a hidden verb, as if he were saying, "I want" or "I call." Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: the governing element is the vocative particle itself, which was made to carry the meaning of the hidden verb, so it grew strong and governed. This is supported by the fact that among the particles of meaning, only the vocative particle joins with nouns by itself. "Banī" is a vocative construct phrase (munādā muḍāf), and "Isrā'īl" is Yaʿqūb son of Isḥāq son of Ibrāhīm, peace be upon them all. It is a non-Arabic name, and it is said as "Isrā'il," "Isrā'īl," and the Tamīm say "Isrā'īn." In Hebrew, "Isrā" means "servant" and "Īl" is a name of God the Exalted, so its meaning is "servant of God." Al-Mahdawī related that "Isrā" is derived from "al-shiddah fi'l-asr" (strength in binding), as if he is the one whose binding God strengthened and whose creation He fortified. It is reported from Nāfiʿ, al-Ḥasan, al-Zuhrī, and Ibn Abī Isḥāq that they omitted the hamza in "Isrāʾīl."

"Dhikr" in the speech of the Arabs has several meanings, and this is one of them: the remembrance of the heart, which is the opposite of forgetting. "Niʿmah" here is a collective noun (ism al-jins), so it is singular in form but has the meaning of plural. The yā' in "niʿmatiya" is vocalised because it met the definite article "al-," and it is permissible to make it quiescent; when it is quiescent it is elided for the sake of avoiding two consecutive quiescent letters. Its vocalisation (with fatḥah) is better, because it adds a letter to the Book of God, the Exalted. Some scholars specified the favour in this verse. Al-Ṭabarī said: the sending of messengers from among them, the sending down of manna and quails, their deliverance from the torment of the family of Pharaoh, and the gushing of water from the stone. Others said: the favour here is that He let them live to the time of Muḥammad (ﷺ). Others said: it is that He granted them knowledge of the Torah and made them its people and its bearers. These are views given as examples, and generality in the word is the better view. Makkī related that the ones addressed among the Children of Israel by this address are the believers in Muḥammad (ﷺ), because the disbeliever has no favour of God upon him.

Ibn ʿAbbās and the majority of scholars said: the address is to all the Children of Israel in the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him, both their believers and their disbelievers.

The pronoun in "ʿalaykum" is intended to refer to your forefathers, as the Arabs say: "Did we not defeat you on such and such a day?" concerning a battle that took place between the forefathers and grandfathers. And whoever said that only the believers in Muḥammad (ﷺ) were addressed, the pronoun in "ʿalaykum" is consistent, and every command that follows comes in the sense of continuity.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿and fulfil My covenant, I shall fulfil your covenant﴾. It is a command and its answer. Al-Khalīl said: the jussive of the answer following a command has the meaning of a conditional. Fulfilment of the covenant is committing to what it includes of action. Al-Zuhrī recited "ʾuwaffi" with a fatḥah on the wāw and a shaddah on the fā', for intensification.

The interpreters differed about this covenant made to them. The majority said: it is general to all His commands, prohibitions, and injunctions, so the mention of Muḥammad (ﷺ) in the Torah enters into it. It was said: the covenant is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63], etc. Ibn Jurayj said: the covenant is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And God certainly took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 12], etc. Their covenant is that He will admit them into Paradise, and their fulfilment of the covenant of God is a sign of God's fulfilment of His covenant to them. It is not a cause for it, because a cause does not precede the effect it produces.

His statement: ﴿and fear Me alone﴾. The word is "iyyā," and the yā' is a pronoun like the kāf of the addressee. It was also said that "iyyāya" as a whole is the noun, and it is in the accusative by a hidden verb placed after it, its estimate being: "And fear Me alone, fear" then "fear Me." It is impossible to estimate it as preceding, because when the verb precedes, only a light pronoun may suitably attach to it, and so it would have come as "wa-rhabūni."

The fear that the command to it includes has the meaning of a threat. The yā' after the nūn fell away because it is the end of a verse (ra's āyah). Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with the yā'.

"Āminū" means "believe," and "muṣaddiqan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in "anzaltu," and it was said that it is from "mā," and the governing element of it is "āminū." "Mā anzaltu" is a metaphor for the Qur'an, and "limā maʿakum" means from the Torah.

His statement: ﴿and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾. This is from the implicit meaning of the discourse (mafhūm al-khiṭāb), in which what is stated and what is left unstated share the same ruling. The first, the second, and others are included in the prohibition. However, warn them against rushing to disbelief in it, since on the first one there is a share of the sin of the one who is followed. "Awwal" is in the accusative as the predicate of "kāna" (khabar kāna).

Sībawayh said: "awwal" is of the form "afʿal" and has no verb, due to the weakness of its first and middle radicals. Other than Sībawayh said: it is from "awwal" meaning "he was saved," with the hamza softened, changed into a wāw, and assimilated; and it was said: it is from "āla," so it was "ʾaʾwal," which was transposed to become "aʿfal," and it was made easy, changed, and assimilated.

He made "kāfir" singular while it has the sense of plural, because when "afʿal" is annexed to a noun derived from a verb, it is permissible to use the singular of that noun while meaning the plural. The poet said:

"And when they eat, the basest of eaters is one of them; and when they go hungry, the worst of the hungry is one of them."

Sībawayh holds that it is an indefinite noun abbreviated from a definite one, as if he said: "and do not be the first of the disbelievers in it." It was also said that its meaning is: "and do not be the first group that disbelieves."

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Before them the disbelievers of Quraysh had already disbelieved, so its meaning is: from among the People of the Book, since they are the ones looked to in such matters, because they are a proof whose knowledge is presumed to be held.

It is disputed to whom the pronoun in "bihi" refers. It was said: it refers to Muḥammad, peace be upon him. It was said: it refers to the Torah, since the phrase "limā maʿakum" includes it. On this view, "awwal kāfir bihi" stands plainly in its literal sense regarding priority. It was also said: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an, since "bimā anzaltu" includes it.

The interpreters differed about the price which they were forbidden to take in exchange for the signs. One group said: the rabbis used to teach their religion for a wage, so they were forbidden from that. In their books is written: "Teach freely as you were taught freely," that is, in vain, without wage. Others said: the rabbis had a regular allowance which they consumed in return for knowledge, like a salary, so they were forbidden from that. Others said: the rabbis took bribes to alter the story of Muḥammad, peace be upon him, in the Torah, and concerning that He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾. Others said: the meaning of the verse is: do not exchange My commands, My prohibitions, and My signs for a small price, meaning this world and its duration, and the livelihood which is meagre and has no worth. The parallel of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and fear Me alone﴾ has already been mentioned. Between "ittaqūni" and "irhabūni" there is a difference: fear (rahbah) is associated with a binding threat.

It was said: the covenant is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾ [al-Baqarah: 63], etc. Ibn Jurayj said: the covenant is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And God certainly took the covenant of the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 12], etc. Their covenant is that He will admit them into Paradise, and their fulfilment of the covenant of God is a sign of God's fulfilment of His covenant to them. It is not a cause for it, because a cause does not precede the effect it produces.

His statement: ﴿and fear Me alone﴾. The word is "iyyā," and the yā' is a pronoun like the kāf of the addressee. It was also said that "iyyāya" as a whole is the noun, and it is in the accusative by a hidden verb placed after it, its estimate being: "And fear Me alone, fear" then "fear Me." It is impossible to estimate it as preceding, because when the verb precedes, only a light pronoun may suitably attach to it, and so it would have come as "wa-rhabūni."

The fear that the command to it includes has the meaning of a threat. The yā' after the nūn fell away because it is the end of a verse (ra's āyah). Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited it with the yā'.

"Āminū" means "believe," and "muṣaddiqan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the pronoun in "anzaltu," and it was said that it is from "mā," and the governing element of it is "āminū." "Mā anzaltu" is a metaphor for the Qur'an, and "limā maʿakum" means from the Torah.

His statement: ﴿and do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾. This is from the implicit meaning of the discourse (mafhūm al-khiṭāb), in which what is stated and what is left unstated share the same ruling. The first, the second, and others are included in the prohibition. However, warn them against rushing to disbelief in it, since on the first one there is a share of the sin of the one who is followed. "Awwal" is in the accusative as the predicate of "kāna" (khabar kāna).

Sībawayh said: "awwal" is of the form "afʿal" and has no verb, due to the weakness of its first and middle radicals. Other than Sībawayh said: it is from "awwal" meaning "he was saved," with the hamza softened, changed into a wāw, and assimilated; and it was said: it is from "āla," so it was "ʾaʾwal," which was transposed to become "aʿfal," and it was made easy, changed, and assimilated.

He made "kāfir" singular while it has the sense of plural, because when "afʿal" is annexed to a noun derived from a verb, it is permissible to use the singular of that noun while meaning the plural. The poet said:

"And when they eat, the basest of eaters is one of them; and when they go hungry, the worst of the hungry is one of them."

Sībawayh holds that it is an indefinite noun abbreviated from a definite one, as if he said: "and do not be the first of the disbelievers in it." It was also said that its meaning is: "and do not be the first group that disbelieves."

The judge Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: Before them the disbelievers of Quraysh had already disbelieved, so its meaning is: from among the People of the Book, since they are the ones looked to in such matters, because they are a proof whose knowledge is presumed to be held.

It is disputed to whom the pronoun in "bihi" refers. It was said: it refers to Muḥammad, peace be upon him. It was said: it refers to the Torah, since the phrase "limā maʿakum" includes it. On this view, "awwal kāfir bihi" stands plainly in its literal sense regarding priority. It was also said: the pronoun in "bihi" refers to the Qur'an, since "bimā anzaltu" includes it.

The interpreters differed about the price which they were forbidden to take in exchange for the signs. One group said: the rabbis used to teach their religion for a wage, so they were forbidden from that. In their books is written: "Teach freely as you were taught freely," that is, in vain, without wage. Others said: the rabbis had a regular allowance which they consumed in return for knowledge, like a salary, so they were forbidden from that. Others said: the rabbis took bribes to alter the story of Muḥammad, peace be upon him, in the Torah, and concerning that He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and do not exchange My signs for a small price﴾. Others said: the meaning of the verse is: do not exchange My commands, My prohibitions, and My signs for a small price, meaning this world and its duration, and the livelihood which is meagre and has no worth. The parallel of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and fear Me alone﴾ has already been mentioned. Between "ittaqūni" and "irhabūni" there is a difference: fear (rahbah) is associated with a binding threat.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 2, verses 42–46:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿And do not mix up the truth with falsehood, nor conceal the truth while you know it.﴾ ﴿And establish prayer, give zakah, and bow with those who bow.﴾ ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves, though you recite the Book? Do you not then reason?﴾ ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, it is difficult except for the humble.﴾ ﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord and that to Him they will return.﴾

The meaning: "Do not mix" (wa-la talbisu). It is said: "labastu al-amr" (with the vowel fatha on the ba'), "albasuhu," when I mixed it, and I blended its clear part with its unclear part, its truth with its falsehood. As for the poet's words:

*"And a battalion I mixed with another battalion..."*

the apparent meaning is that it derives from this sense, though it may also be from the sense of "clothing" (libas).

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed regarding what is meant by His words "the truth with falsehood." Abu al-'Aliyah said: The Jews said, "Muhammad is a prophet sent, but to other than us." So their acknowledgment that he was sent is truth, and their denial that he was sent to them is falsehood. Al-Tabari said: Among the Jews there were hypocrites, so what they displayed of faith was truth, and what they concealed of disbelief was falsehood. Mujahid said: Its meaning is: do not mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam.

Ibn Zayd said: What is meant by the truth is the Torah, and the falsehood is what they altered in it of the mention of Muhammad (peace be upon him). "Talbisu" is in the jussive mood by the prohibition, and "taktumu" is coordinated with it in a jussive position. It may also be in the accusative position by the implied "an" (that). When "an" is assumed, it forms with "taktumu" a verbal noun (masdar) construction, and the waw is coordinating upon an implied masdar from "talbisu," as if the sentence were: "And let there not be your mixing of the truth with falsehood, and your concealing of the truth." The Kufans said: "Taktumu" is in the accusative by the waw of accompaniment (waw al-sarf). And "the truth" here refers to the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

His words, "while you know," are a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). He, the Exalted, did not testify to them as having knowledge; rather He forbade them from concealing what they knew. It may also be a testimony against them regarding knowledge of a specific truth, concerning the matter of Muhammad (peace be upon him), and not a testimony to them of knowledge in an absolute sense. According to this view, the clause is not in the position of a circumstantial phrase. In these words is evidence of the gravity of the sin for one who commits it knowingly, and that he is more disobedient than the ignorant one.

"Establish prayer" (aqimu al-salah) [al-An'am: 72] means: display its form and maintain it with its conditions. This is a figurative comparison to the seated person being raised to a standing position of visibility. From this is the poet's words:

*"And when it is said, 'You have come,' they do not depart until the horses establish the market of battle."*

The discussion of "al-salah" has already preceded.

"Zakah" in this verse is the obligatory zakah, by the indication of the consensus (ijma') of the Community on the obligation of enjoining it. "Zakah" is derived from "zaka al-shay'," when a thing grows and increases. The expenditure from wealth is called zakah, though it is a reduction from it, in that it grows by blessing, or by the reward which Allah bestows upon the one who pays zakah. It was also said that "zakah" is derived from purification, as one says "zaka fulan," meaning he became pure of the stain of blame or neglect. So it is as if what is expended from wealth purifies one from the liability of the right which Allah placed in it for the poor. Do you not see that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) called what is expended in zakah "the dirt of people"?

His, the Exalted, words, "and bow with those who bow." Some said: Because bowing is one of the pillars of prayer, He made bowing a term for the whole prayer. Others said: He singled out bowing for mention because the Children of Israel had no bowing in their prayer. Another group said: He said "with" (ma'a) because the initial command to prayer did not require attending congregation, so He commanded them with the word "with," to attend congregation. Bowing (ruku') in the language is bending the body. Labid said:

*"I narrate the reports of the generations that have passed, I bow as if, whenever I stand, I am bowing."*

It is also used metaphorically for a decline in rank. Al-Adba' ibn Qari' said:

*"Do not be hostile to the weak, lest one day you bow (decline), while time has raised him."*

His, the Exalted, words, "Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people," came in the form of a question, and its meaning is reproach. "Al-birr" (righteousness) encompasses all aspects of good and acts of obedience, and the name "birr" applies to each one of them. "Tansawna" means: you are left (abandoned), as Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67].

The commentators differed about the intended meaning of this verse. Ibn 'Abbas said: The rabbis used to command their followers and imitators to follow the Torah, while they themselves contradicted it in denying from it the description of Muhammad (ﷺ). Another group said: When any of the Arabs sought guidance from the rabbis regarding following Muhammad, they would point them in a direction, while they themselves did not do it. Ibn Juraij said: The rabbis used to urge people to obey Allah, while they themselves committed sins. Another group said: They used to urge people to give charity while they themselves were miserly.

His words, "while you recite the Book," mean: you study and read. It may also mean: you follow, i.e., in taking it as a model. "The Book" is the Torah, which forbids them from the blameworthy attribute they are upon.

His words, "Do you not then reason?" mean: Will you not restrain yourselves from engaging in this destructive state that is harmful to you? "Al-'aql" (reason) is the perception that prevents error. It is derived from it "'iqal al-ba'ir" (the camel's tether), meaning that which restrains it from moving freely. And from it: "al-ma'qil," meaning the place of refuge.

His words, "And seek help through patience and prayer."

Muqatil said its meaning is: in seeking the Hereafter. Others said: The meaning is: seek help through patience in obedience and against desires, in attaining the pleasure of Allah, and through prayer in attaining the pleasure and erasing of sins, and against the calamities of time as well. From this is the hadith: "When a matter distressed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he would turn to prayer." And from this is what is reported that 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas was informed of the death of his brother Qutham while he was on a journey. He said "inna lillah" and turned aside from the road, prayed, then returned to his mount while reciting: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾.

Mujahid said: Patience (sabr) in this verse is fasting, and from this Ramadan was called "the month of patience." On this view, fasting and prayer are singled out for mention because of their correspondence in that fasting restrains desires and makes one ascetic regarding this world, and prayer forbids indecency and wrongdoing, and produces humility, and in it the Qur'an is recited, which reminds one of the Hereafter. Others said: "Patience" is in its ordinary sense, and "prayer" is supplication. According to this view, this verse resembles His words, ﴿When you encounter a company, stand firm and remember Allah﴾ [al-Anfal: 45], because steadfastness is patience, and remembrance of Allah is supplication.

The commentators differed regarding His words, "And indeed, it is difficult," as to what the pronoun refers. It was said: it refers to "prayer." It was said: it refers to the seeking of help implied by His words, "and seek help." It was said: it refers to the worship implicitly included in the meaning of "patience and prayer." Another group said: it refers to the answering of Muhammad (ﷺ), but this is weak, because there is no evidence from the verse for it. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the Ka'bah, because the command to prayer is directed toward it, but this is weaker than what preceded. "Kabirah" means: heavy, burdensome.

"Al-khashi'un" are the humble, the lowly and submissive. "Khushu'" is a state in the soul, from which there appears upon the limbs stillness and humility.

As for "yazunnun" in this verse, the majority said: its meaning is "they are certain" (yuqinun). Al-Mahdawi and others related that the zann (supposition) here may validly retain its original sense, and an implicit element is understood in the sentence, with their sins, as if they anticipate meeting Him as sinners.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a forced interpretation. In Arabic speech, the basic sense of zann is doubt with an inclination toward one of the two beliefs, though zann may be used in place of certainty concerning matters that are established. But it is not used regarding what has already become perceptible to the senses. The Arabs do not say, regarding a visible, present man: "I suppose this is a human being." The usage is found only regarding what has not yet become perceptible, as in this verse, and as in His words, ﴿So they supposed that they would be plunged into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53], and as in the words of Durayd ibn al-Simmah:

*"I said to them: 'Suppose (that you face) two thousand armored men, whose chiefs are with the Persian-woven coats of mail.'"*

His, the Exalted, words, "that they will meet their Lord" — "anna" and its clause fill the place of the two objects of "zann." "Al-mulaqah" (meeting) is either for punishment or reward, so there is an omitted noun in the sentence (meeting the reckoning of their Lord). It is valid that the meeting here is by seeing (ru'yah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, and mutawatir (widely transmitted) hadith has come with it. Al-Mahdawi related that "mulaqah" here is a construction of the form "fa'ala" from one party, like "'afaka Allah" (may Allah grant you wellness), but this is weak, because "laqiya" includes the meaning of "laqa," and not all verbs are so, rather "fa'ala" is the opposite of "fa'il" in meaning. "Mulaqu" its origin is "mulaqun," because it has the meaning of encountering, so the nun was dropped for lightness, and when it was dropped, the genitive construction (idafah) became firmly established by its resemblance to nouns. And it is an idafah that is not pure (ghayr mahdah), because it is not definite.

The Kufans said: What is in the active participle which has the meaning of coming from the verb requires the retention of the nun and its governing function. Its being, together with what follows it, two nouns, requires the deletion of the nun and the idafah.

"Raji'un": it was said its meaning is "by death." It was said: "by resurrection and going forth to the reckoning and the presentation." The preceding verse strengthens this view.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Then He causes you to die, then brings you to life, then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to the Lord, the Exalted. It was also said it refers to the meeting implied by "mulaqu."
