The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is a forced interpretation. In Arabic speech, the basic sense of zann is doubt with an inclination toward one of the two beliefs, though zann may be used in place of certainty concerning matters that are established. But it is not used regarding what has already become perceptible to the senses. The Arabs do not say, regarding a visible, present man: "I suppose this is a human being." The usage is found only regarding what has not yet become perceptible, as in this verse, and as in His words, ﴿So they supposed that they would be plunged into it﴾ [al-Kahf: 53], and as in the words of Durayd ibn al-Simmah:

*"I said to them: 'Suppose (that you face) two thousand armored men, whose chiefs are with the Persian-woven coats of mail.'"*

His, the Exalted, words, "that they will meet their Lord" — "anna" and its clause fill the place of the two objects of "zann." "Al-mulaqah" (meeting) is either for punishment or reward, so there is an omitted noun in the sentence (meeting the reckoning of their Lord). It is valid that the meeting here is by seeing (ru'yah), which is the position of the People of the Sunnah, and mutawatir (widely transmitted) hadith has come with it. Al-Mahdawi related that "mulaqah" here is a construction of the form "fa'ala" from one party, like "'afaka Allah" (may Allah grant you wellness), but this is weak, because "laqiya" includes the meaning of "laqa," and not all verbs are so, rather "fa'ala" is the opposite of "fa'il" in meaning. "Mulaqu" its origin is "mulaqun," because it has the meaning of encountering, so the nun was dropped for lightness, and when it was dropped, the genitive construction (idafah) became firmly established by its resemblance to nouns. And it is an idafah that is not pure (ghayr mahdah), because it is not definite.

The Kufans said: What is in the active participle which has the meaning of coming from the verb requires the retention of the nun and its governing function. Its being, together with what follows it, two nouns, requires the deletion of the nun and the idafah.

"Raji'un": it was said its meaning is "by death." It was said: "by resurrection and going forth to the reckoning and the presentation." The preceding verse strengthens this view.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿Then He causes you to die, then brings you to life, then to Him you will be returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. The pronoun in "ilayhi" refers to the Lord, the Exalted. It was also said it refers to the meeting implied by "mulaqu."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 47–49:**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul at all, nor will intercession be accepted from it, nor will any compensation be taken from it, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh, who afflicted you with the worst torment, slaughtering your sons and sparing your women; and in that was a great trial from your Lord.﴾

This call and this reminder of the favour have been repeated. The benefit of this is that the first address may be for the believers, and it may also be for the disbelievers among them. This repeated address is only for the disbelievers, as indicated by what follows it. Also, in it there is a strengthening of the admonition, an emphasis on urging them to remember the blessings of Allah, and a graceful way of addressing them with His words: ﴿I preferred you over the worlds﴾, because the preference given to their forefathers and ancestors is a preference for them as well. The speech here is broad. Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, Ibn Jurayj and others said: the meaning is "over the worlds of their time," in which there were repeated prophethood and kingship, because Allah, the Exalted, says to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿You are the best community brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

(p-204) As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day﴾, "a Day" (yawman) is in the accusative governed by "guard yourselves" (ittaqu) by way of extension (*sa'a*), and the implied meaning is "the punishment of a Day" or "the terror of a Day"; then that was omitted and the Day was put in its place. It is also possible that its accusative is as an adverb of time (*zarf*), not as the object of "guard yourselves," because the Day of Resurrection is not a day of action; rather its meaning is: "Come forth as those who guard themselves against a Day." And "lā tajzī" means "will not avail." Al-Suddi said its meaning is "will not decide," and this is strengthened by His saying "shay'an" (anything). It was also said: the meaning is "will not compensate." It is said that *jaza* and *ajza'a* have one meaning.

Some people distinguished between them, saying: *jaza* means "to judge" and "to repay," while *ajza'a* means "to suffice" and "to be enough." Abu al-Sammal recited "tujzi'" with a damma on the *ta'* and a *hamza*. In the statement there is an ellipsis. The Basrans said the estimated reading is "lā tajzī fīhi" (will not avail in it), then "fīhi" was omitted. Others said a pronoun attached to "tajzī" was omitted, its estimate being "lā tajzihi," although omitting this pronoun in the predicate is ugly; it is only good in the relative clause (ṣila). Some Basrans said: the estimate is "lā tajzī fīhi," so the preposition was omitted and the pronoun became attached, then the pronoun was gradually omitted.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And intercession will not be accepted from it﴾, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a *ta'* (tu-qbalu), and the rest read it with a *ya'* from below (yu-qbalu), (p-205) according to the meaning, since the feminine form of *shafā'a* (intercession) is not real. *Shafā'a* is derived from *shaf'* and they are "two," because the intercessor and the one interceded for form a pair; likewise the intercessor is (a pair) in what has not been divided.

The cause of this verse: the Children of Israel said, "We are the sons of Allah and the sons of His prophets, and our fathers will intercede for us." So Allah, the Exalted, informed them about the Day of Resurrection that intercession will not be accepted on it: ﴿no soul will avail another soul﴾. This applies only to the disbelievers, by consensus (*ijma'*), while the hadith concerning intercession for the believers is widely transmitted (*mutawatir*).

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾, Abu al-'Aliyah said: *'adl* means ransom.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: *'adl* of a thing is that which equals it in value and quantity, even if it is not of its kind, while *'idl* (with a kasra on the 'ayn) is that which equals the thing of its own kind and substance. Al-Tabari related that some Arabs pronounce the 'ayn with a kasra in the meaning of ransom, but the singular of *a'dāl* (plural) is with a kasra only.

The pronoun in His saying "nor are they" (wa lā hum) refers to the disbelievers whom the verse implies, and it may also refer to the two souls mentioned earlier, because "two" is a plural, or because "soul" (nafs) is a generic noun, which is plural in meaning.

This verse covers the matters that the children of Adam are accustomed to in this world, for one who is in distress with a human being can only be freed by having that person intercede for him, or by being helped, or by ransom.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾, that is, We rescued you. "Āl" originally is "ahl" (people), the *ha'* was changed into an *alif*, as was done in "mā'" (water). For this reason, diminutive forms restore it to its origin, so one says "uhayl" and "muwayh." It has also been said about "āl" that it is a noun other than "ahl," its origin being "awl," and its diminutive "uwayyil." He attributed the act to "the people of Pharaoh" although they were doing it by his command and authority, because they took that task upon themselves. Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this implies that whoever is ordered by a tyrant to kill someone, and the one ordered kills him, is the one held responsible for it.

(p-206) The "āl" of a man are his kin, his supporters and his followers. From this is the saying of Urakah al-Thaqafi:

*So do not weep for a dead man after a dead man, whom 'Ali and 'Abbas and the family of Abu Bakr have buried.*

He means the believers who buried the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The most well-known usage is that "āl" is added to personal names, not to places and lands, though it is sometimes said "āl Makkah" and "āl al-Madinah." "Fir'awn" (Pharaoh) is a name for every one of the Amalekites who ruled Egypt. As for the Pharaoh of Moses, it was said his name was Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan; Ibn Ishaq said his name was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab, and it is related that he was from Istakhr, and he returned to Egypt and kingship came to him there. The origin of the presence of the Children of Israel in Egypt was the settling of Israel there in the time of his son Yusuf, peace be upon them both.

"Yasumunakum" means: they impose it upon you and compel you to it, and from this comes "musāwama" (bargaining over goods), and one says "sāmahu khasfa" (he made him endure a humiliating condition). The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "yasumūnakum" is in the nominative, as a new sentence (isti'nāf). The clause is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: imposing upon you the worst torment, and it is permissible not to estimate a state in it, and it is a descriptive clause of a past state. "Sū' al-'adhāb" means its worst and hardest form. Al-Suddi said: he assigned them to the filthiest works, and slaughtered the sons and spared the women. Others said: he assigned them to tasks: plowing, farming, building and other things, and his people were soldiers and kings.

The majority recited "yudhabbihūna" with a doubled *ba'* (kasra) for emphasis, while Ibn Muhaysin recited "yadhbahūna" without doubling; the first is more preferred, since slaughtering is repeated.

It is related that Pharaoh had seen in his dream a fire that came out of Bayt al-Maqdis and burned the houses of Egypt, and his dream was interpreted for him: that a male child from the Children of Israel would grow up and destroy the kingship of Pharaoh at his hands. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn 'Abbas and others said: the soothsayers and astrologers said to Pharaoh: "The time of a boy from the Children of Israel who will destroy your kingdom has drawn near." (p-207) Ibn 'Abbas also said: Pharaoh and his people discussed the promise of Allah to Ibrahim that He would place in his descendants prophets and kings, so at that point he ordered the slaughter of the male infants among the Children of Israel, and he appointed a man for every ten women to watch whoever of them became pregnant. It was also said that he appointed midwives for this purpose.

Some said: the meaning of ﴿they slaughter your sons﴾ is that they slaughter the men, and they are called "sons" because they were in that state. This speaker cited the words of Allah, the Exalted: "your women."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the correct interpretation is that "the sons" are the male children, and "the women" are the female children. He referred to them by the name of women in their future state, and so that he would make them use the name appropriate to their time: they would be employed and humiliated. The very act of sparing them is not a torment, but the torment came about because of it. And "yudhabbihūna" is a substitute (badal) for "yasumūnakum."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in that was a trial﴾, "dhālikum" refers to the whole matter, since it is a report, so it is like a singular present (object). "Balā'" means test and examination, and "balā'" may be used for both good and evil. Some people said the reference of "dhālikum" is to the deliverance, so "balā'" in this view is for good and evil alike, meaning: in your deliverance there is a favour from Allah upon you. The majority of people said the reference is to the slaughter and the like, and "balā'" here is for evil, and the meaning is: in the slaughter there is hardship and a test.

Al-Tabari and others related regarding the manner of their deliverance: that Moses, peace be upon him, was inspired to travel out of Egypt with the Children of Israel, so Moses commanded them to borrow jewelry and goods from the Copts, and Allah made that lawful for the Children of Israel. Moses set out with them at the beginning of the night, and Pharaoh was informed, so he said: "No one shall follow them until the roosters crow." But no rooster crowed in Egypt that night until morning, and Allah caused many of the sons of the Copts to die (p-208) that night, so they busied themselves with burial, and the Israelites went out following in the morning. Moses went toward the sea until he reached it. The number of the Children of Israel was over six hundred thousand, and the number of Pharaoh's army was one million and two hundred thousand. Other accounts have been related, which I have abridged because of their weak authentication.

When Pharaoh caught up with Moses, the Children of Israel thought they would not be saved. Yusha' ibn Nun said to Moses: "Where were you commanded?" He said: "Here," and pointed to the sea. Yusha' spurred his horse into it until it reached the depths, then he returned and said to Moses: "Where were you commanded? By Allah, you have not lied, nor have you been lied to." So he pointed to the sea. Allah, the Exalted, inspired him: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], and inspired the sea: "Part for Moses when he strikes you." The sea remained agitated that night, and when morning came Moses struck the sea and called it "Abu Khalid," and it parted. That was on the day of 'Ashura'.

This applies only to the disbelievers, by consensus (*ijma'*), while the hadith concerning intercession for the believers is widely transmitted (*mutawatir*).

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor will any compensation be taken from it﴾, Abu al-'Aliyah said: *'adl* means ransom.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: *'adl* of a thing is that which equals it in value and quantity, even if it is not of its kind, while *'idl* (with a kasra on the 'ayn) is that which equals the thing of its own kind and substance. Al-Tabari related that some Arabs pronounce the 'ayn with a kasra in the meaning of ransom, but the singular of *a'dāl* (plural) is with a kasra only.

The pronoun in His saying "nor are they" (wa lā hum) refers to the disbelievers whom the verse implies, and it may also refer to the two souls mentioned earlier, because "two" is a plural, or because "soul" (nafs) is a generic noun, which is plural in meaning.

This verse covers the matters that the children of Adam are accustomed to in this world, for one who is in distress with a human being can only be freed by having that person intercede for him, or by being helped, or by ransom.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We delivered you from the people of Pharaoh﴾, that is, We rescued you. "Āl" originally is "ahl" (people), the *ha'* was changed into an *alif*, as was done in "mā'" (water). For this reason, diminutive forms restore it to its origin, so one says "uhayl" and "muwayh." It has also been said about "āl" that it is a noun other than "ahl," its origin being "awl," and its diminutive "uwayyil." He attributed the act to "the people of Pharaoh" although they were doing it by his command and authority, because they took that task upon themselves. Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this implies that whoever is ordered by a tyrant to kill someone, and the one ordered kills him, is the one held responsible for it.

(p-206) The "āl" of a man are his kin, his supporters and his followers. From this is the saying of Urakah al-Thaqafi:

*So do not weep for a dead man after a dead man, whom 'Ali and 'Abbas and the family of Abu Bakr have buried.*

He means the believers who buried the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The most well-known usage is that "āl" is added to personal names, not to places and lands, though it is sometimes said "āl Makkah" and "āl al-Madinah." "Fir'awn" (Pharaoh) is a name for every one of the Amalekites who ruled Egypt. As for the Pharaoh of Moses, it was said his name was Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan; Ibn Ishaq said his name was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab, and it is related that he was from Istakhr, and he returned to Egypt and kingship came to him there. The origin of the presence of the Children of Israel in Egypt was the settling of Israel there in the time of his son Yusuf, peace be upon them both.

"Yasumunakum" means: they impose it upon you and compel you to it, and from this comes "musāwama" (bargaining over goods), and one says "sāmahu khasfa" (he made him endure a humiliating condition). The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of "yasumūnakum" is in the nominative, as a new sentence (isti'nāf). The clause is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: imposing upon you the worst torment, and it is permissible not to estimate a state in it, and it is a descriptive clause of a past state. "Sū' al-'adhāb" means its worst and hardest form. Al-Suddi said: he assigned them to the filthiest works, and slaughtered the sons and spared the women. Others said: he assigned them to tasks: plowing, farming, building and other things, and his people were soldiers and kings.

The majority recited "yudhabbihūna" with a doubled *ba'* (kasra) for emphasis, while Ibn Muhaysin recited "yadhbahūna" without doubling; the first is more preferred, since slaughtering is repeated.

It is related that Pharaoh had seen in his dream a fire that came out of Bayt al-Maqdis and burned the houses of Egypt, and his dream was interpreted for him: that a male child from the Children of Israel would grow up and destroy the kingship of Pharaoh at his hands. Ibn Ishaq, Ibn 'Abbas and others said: the soothsayers and astrologers said to Pharaoh: "The time of a boy from the Children of Israel who will destroy your kingdom has drawn near." (p-207) Ibn 'Abbas also said: Pharaoh and his people discussed the promise of Allah to Ibrahim that He would place in his descendants prophets and kings, so at that point he ordered the slaughter of the male infants among the Children of Israel, and he appointed a man for every ten women to watch whoever of them became pregnant. It was also said that he appointed midwives for this purpose.

Some said: the meaning of ﴿they slaughter your sons﴾ is that they slaughter the men, and they are called "sons" because they were in that state. This speaker cited the words of Allah, the Exalted: "your women."

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the correct interpretation is that "the sons" are the male children, and "the women" are the female children. He referred to them by the name of women in their future state, and so that he would make them use the name appropriate to their time: they would be employed and humiliated. The very act of sparing them is not a torment, but the torment came about because of it. And "yudhabbihūna" is a substitute (badal) for "yasumūnakum."

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And in that was a trial﴾, "dhālikum" refers to the whole matter, since it is a report, so it is like a singular present (object). "Balā'" means test and examination, and "balā'" may be used for both good and evil. Some people said the reference of "dhālikum" is to the deliverance, so "balā'" in this view is for good and evil alike, meaning: in your deliverance there is a favour from Allah upon you. The majority of people said the reference is to the slaughter and the like, and "balā'" here is for evil, and the meaning is: in the slaughter there is hardship and a test.

Al-Tabari and others related regarding the manner of their deliverance: that Moses, peace be upon him, was inspired to travel out of Egypt with the Children of Israel, so Moses commanded them to borrow jewelry and goods from the Copts, and Allah made that lawful for the Children of Israel. Moses set out with them at the beginning of the night, and Pharaoh was informed, so he said: "No one shall follow them until the roosters crow." But no rooster crowed in Egypt that night until morning, and Allah caused many of the sons of the Copts to die (p-208) that night, so they busied themselves with burial, and the Israelites went out following in the morning. Moses went toward the sea until he reached it. The number of the Children of Israel was over six hundred thousand, and the number of Pharaoh's army was one million and two hundred thousand. Other accounts have been related, which I have abridged because of their weak authentication.

When Pharaoh caught up with Moses, the Children of Israel thought they would not be saved. Yusha' ibn Nun said to Moses: "Where were you commanded?" He said: "Here," and pointed to the sea. Yusha' spurred his horse into it until it reached the depths, then he returned and said to Moses: "Where were you commanded? By Allah, you have not lied, nor have you been lied to." So he pointed to the sea. Allah, the Exalted, inspired him: ﴿Strike the sea with your staff﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63], and inspired the sea: "Part for Moses when he strikes you." The sea remained agitated that night, and when morning came Moses struck the sea and called it "Abu Khalid," and it parted. That was on the day of 'Ashura'.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 50–53:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when We parted the sea for you and saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh while you were looking on.﴾ ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights, then you took the calf [for worship] after him, while you were wrongdoers.﴾ ﴿Then We pardoned you after that, that you might be grateful.﴾ ﴿And when We gave Moses the Scripture and the Criterion, that you might be guided.﴾

"Faraqna" means: We made it split (farqan). Al-Zuhri recited "farraqna" with the letter ra' doubled. As for "bikum" (p-209), it means "because of you." It has also been said: since they were between the divided parts at the time of their crossing, it was as if the division was with them. It has also been said that it means "for you," with the preposition bi- standing in place of li-, but this is weak.

"Al-bahr" (the sea) is the Sea of al-Qulzum (the Red Sea). The sea was not split across its width, from one bank to the other. Rather, it was split from one place to another place on the same shore. That division was near the place of deliverance, and one could not reach it by land except after many days because of intervening mountains and rough terrain. Al-Amiri mentioned that the place where they emerged from the sea was near the desert of Palestine, and that it was their route.

It has also been said that the sea split across its width, and that the sea split into twelve paths, one path for each tribe. When they entered them, each group said: "Our companions have drowned," and they panicked. Moses said: "O God, help me against their evil characters." God revealed to him: "Strike your staff upon the sea." He struck it, and in the water there became openings like arches, so that they could see one another and crossed over. Gabriel (ﷺ) was at their rear, on a mare, urging the Children of Israel on, and saying to the family of Pharaoh: "Wait, until the last of you joins the first of you." When Pharaoh reached the sea and wanted to enter, his horse shied, so Gabriel confronted him with the mare, and the horse followed her. The family of Pharaoh entered, with Michael urging them on. When only Michael remained at the rear of them on the bank alone, the sea closed over them and they drowned.

As for "tanzurun" (you were looking on), it has been said that it means "with your eyes," because they were close to one another. It has been said that it means "with your insight," for reflection, since they were occupied and not standing and looking with their eyes. It has also been said that the people of Pharaoh floated on the water and they looked at them. It has also been said that the meaning is: "while you were in the state of one who looks, were he to look," as you say: "this matter is from you in sight and hearing," meaning in a state where you can see it and hear it if you wish.

Al-Tabari, may God have mercy on him, said: The Qur'an's report, on the tongue of Muhammad (ﷺ), of these unseen matters, which were not part of the knowledge of the Arabs and occurred only within the hidden knowledge of the Children of Israel, is a clear proof for the Children of Israel, and a binding evidence against them, of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Jumhur recited "wa'adna" (with alif, "we appointed"), while Abu 'Amr recited "wa'adna" (p-210) without alif ("We promised"). Abu 'Ubayd preferred this reading, and said: appointment (mu'adah) only occurs from humans.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is not correct, because Moses' acceptance of God's promise, his commitment to it, and his waiting for it, resembles mu'adah (mutual appointment).

"Musa" (Moses) is a non-Arabic name that is not declined, because of its foreignness and definiteness. The Copts, according to what is reported, call water "mu" and trees "sa." When Moses was found in the chest by water and a tree, he was named Musa.

Ibn Ishaq said: He is Musa son of 'Imran son of Yasjar son of Qahat son of Lawi son of Ya'qub son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim the Friend (al-Khalil).

"Arba'in" (forty) is in the accusative as the second object. It is not permissible to make it an adverbial accusative of time in this context. According to what is related, these were Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. He singled out the nights for mention rather than the days, since the night is older than the day and precedes it in rank, and for this reason dating is done by it.

Al-Naqqash said: In this there is an indication of the connection to fasting, because if He had mentioned the days, it would have been possible to think that he broke his fast at night. When He specified the nights, the force of the speech required that he, peace be upon him, fasted continuously for forty nights with their days.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: My father, may God be pleased with him, related to me, saying: I heard the ascetic shaykh, the imam, the preacher Abu al-Fadl ibn al-Jawhari, may God have mercy on him, admonishing people with this meaning, regarding seclusion with God and drawing near to Him in prayer and the like, and that this occupies one from every food and drink. He would say: "Where is the state of Moses in nearness to God, and in continuity for eighty years?" And from his saying, when he set out to al-Khidr, to his young man at some point in the day: "Bring us our morning meal."

All the exegetes agree that all forty [nights] were the appointed term. Some of the Basrans said: He promised him at the head of the forty nights, but this is weak. His saying: "Then you took" (thumma ittakhadhtum): most of the Seven read it with idgham (assimilation of the dhal into the tha'), while Ibn Kathir and 'Asim in Hafs's transmission from him read it with the dhal made clear. Thumma indicates a time lapse, and to show that taking [the calf] was after the appointment. Ittakhadha, its pattern is if'tala from al-akhdh (taking). Abu 'Ali said: it is from "takhidha," not from "akhadha," and he cited al-Mumazzaq:

"And I have taken my leg to a side, its sinew thin like the hollow of a sand-grouse's nest."

"Al-'ijl" (the calf) is in the accusative governed by "ittakhadhtum," and the second object is omitted: you took the calf as a god. Ittakhadha may be transitive to one object, as in His saying: "Would that I had taken a way with the Messenger" (25:27), and it may be transitive to two objects, one of which is the same as the other in meaning, as in His saying: "They have taken their oaths as a shield" (58:16), and as in this verse and others. The pronoun in "ba'dihi" (after him) refers to Moses. It has been said that it refers to his departure for speaking [with God], since the appointment requires it. It has also been said that it refers to the promise.

(p-212) The narrative of this verse: when Moses, peace be upon him, brought the Children of Israel out of Egypt, he said to them: "God, Exalted, will deliver you from the family of Pharaoh, and will grant you their ornaments and goods which He had commanded you to borrow." It is reported that they borrowed them of their own accord, and God granted them this as a spoil after their departure. Moses said to them, on behalf of God, Exalted: "He will send down to me a Book containing the lawful and the unlawful, and guidance for you." When they crossed the sea, they demanded from Moses what he had told them about the Book. He went out to his Lord's appointment alone, and he had informed them of the forty nights. They counted twenty days as twenty nights, then said: "These are forty of the days, and we have broken the appointment." Their obstinacy and opposition appeared. The Samiri was a man from the Children of Israel named Musa ibn Zufar. It has been said that he was not from the Children of Israel; he was a stranger among them. He had recognized Gabriel, peace be upon him, at the time they crossed the sea. One group said: he noticed his form and knew that he was an angel. Another group said: the mother of the Samiri had given birth to him in the year of the slaughter of children, so she placed him in a cave and closed it over him, and Gabriel (ﷺ) nourished him with the fingers of his own hand, so he found in one finger milk, in one finger honey, and in one finger butter. When he saw him at the time of the crossing of the sea, he recognized him, took a handful of dust from beneath the hoof of his horse, and it was inspired in his heart that he would not cast it upon anything and say to it "Be," except that it would be. When Moses went out for his appointment, Aaron said to the Children of Israel: "That ornament and goods which you borrowed from the Copts are not lawful for you. So bring them, until the fire that used to descend upon the sacrifices consumes them." It has also been said: rather, he kindled a fire for them and ordered them to throw all of that into it, so they began casting it in. It has also been said: rather, he ordered them to place it in a pit without fire until Moses came. The Samiri came and cast the handful and said: "Be a calf."

It has been said that the Samiri was originally from a people who worshipped cows, and that this pleased him. It has also been said: the Children of Israel had passed with Moses by a people who worshipped cows, and they said: "O Moses, make for us a god as they have gods." The Samiri took note of this and knew that they would be tempted from that direction, so the Children of Israel were tempted by the calf. A group of them continued worshipping it, and Aaron withdrew from them with those who followed him. Moses came from his appointment and became angry, as its narrative will come in its places in the Qur'an, if God wills. (p-213) Then God revealed to him that He would not accept the repentance of the Children of Israel until they killed themselves, and the Children of Israel did that.

It is reported that they put on weapons, those who had worshipped and those who had not, and God cast darkness upon them, so that they killed one another: a father killed his son and a brother his brother. When the killing intensified among them and reached seventy thousand, God pardoned them, made those who died among them martyrs, and accepted the repentance of the rest. That is His saying: "Then We pardoned you."

Some exegetes said: Those who had worshipped the calf stood in a row, and those who had not worshipped it entered upon them with weapons and killed them. Another group said: Those who had worshipped sat in their courtyards, and Joshua son of Nun went out calling: "Cursed is whoever loosens his sitting cloth," and those who had not worshipped began killing them. Moses, in the midst of this, was praying for his people and longing for their pardon. The reason those who had not worshipped were punished by killing themselves, according to one opinion, or by killing their relatives according to the other opinions, is that they did not change the wrong when they worshipped the calf; they merely withdrew, and it was obligatory upon them to fight those who worshipped it.

"And you were wrongdoers" is a subject and predicate in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the explanation of "dhulm" (wrongdoing) has already been given.

"Al-'Afw" (pardon) is the covering of a trace and the removal of a former state resulting from a sin or other matter. The word 'afw is used in the sense of forgiveness (safh) only with regard to sin. "Then We pardoned you" means: He pardoned those among them who remained and were not killed. "La'allakum" (that you may) expresses hope on their part and anticipation from them, not in regard to God, Mighty and Majestic, because He knows what will come from them.

His, Exalted, saying: "And when We gave Moses..." — the verse. "Idh" (when) is conjoined to what was mentioned of the favours. "Al-Kitab" (the Scripture) is the Torah, by consensus of the interpreters. There was disagreement about "al-Furqan" here. Al-Zajjaj and others said: it is the Torah; the meaning is repeated because the wording differs, and because it adds the meaning of distinguishing between truth and falsehood, which the word "Kitab" does not express. Others said: al-Kitab is the Torah, and al-Furqan is the rest of the signs given to Moses, peace be upon him, because they distinguished between truth and falsehood. Others said: (p-214) al-Furqan is the victory that distinguished between their condition and the condition of the family of Pharaoh, by deliverance and drowning. Ibn Zayd said: al-Furqan is the parting of the sea for him, until it became a division. Al-Farra' and Qutrub said: the meaning of this verse is: We gave Moses the Scripture, and Muhammad the Criterion.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is weak.

"And that you may be guided" is an expression of hope and anticipation, like the first.

Al-Amiri mentioned that the place where they emerged from the sea was near the desert of Palestine, and that it was their route.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on 2:54–55**

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿And when Moses said to his people, "O my people, you have wronged yourselves by taking the calf [for worship], so repent to your Creator and kill yourselves. That is better for you in the sight of your Creator." Then He accepted your repentance; indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And when you said, "O Moses, we will never believe you until we see Allah plainly," the thunderbolt seized you while you were looking on.﴾

This statement from Moses (ﷺ) was by command of Allah, the Exalted. The yā' is omitted in "yā qawmī" because the vocative is a place of elision and lightening. The pronoun in "ittikhādikum" is in a position of genitive (khafḍ) according to the wording, and in a position of nominative (raf') according to the meaning. "Al-'ijl" is an Arabic word meaning the young of a cow. Some said it was called "calf" because it hurried (ista'jala) before Moses (peace be upon him) came, but this view is worthless. People differed over whether the calf remained made of gold. The majority said it did, while al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said it became flesh and blood. The first view is more sound. "Tūbū" means: return from disobedience to obedience.

The majority read "bāri'ikum" with the hamza pronounced and vowelled. Abū 'Amr read "bāri'ikum" with the hamza vowel-less (sukūn). It is reported from Sībawayh that he preferred the rapid, nearly-silent vowel (ikhtilās al-ḥaraka), which is the best. This sukūn is acceptable in a sequence of vowels. Al-Mubarrad said that sukūn is not permitted in a sequence of vowels on the letter of i'rab (the final letter that marks grammatical case, i'rab), and that Abū 'Amr's reading "bāri'ikum" is a grammatical error (laḥn).

(p-215) The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It has been transmitted from the Arabs that sukūn occurs on the letter of i'rab. The poet said:

"When they swerved, I said, 'O companion of the people...'"

And Imru' al-Qays said:

"So today I drink, not carrying a sin from Allah, nor as an uninvited guest."

Another said:

"Sulaymā said, 'Buy us some sawīq (a porridge of ground grain)...'"

Another said:

"...and your thigh has appeared from the waistwrap."

Jarīr said:

"...and the River Tīrī, and the Arabs do not know you."

And Waḍḍāḥ al-Yaman said:

"Indeed my poetry is honey that has been mixed with sesame."

Whoever denies sukūn on the letter of i'rab argues that it is not permitted, since that letter is the marker of i'rab. Abū 'Alī (may Allah have mercy on him) said: As for the vowel of construction (ḥarakat al-binā'), the grammarians have not differed over the permissibility of its sukūn in a sequence of vowels.

al-Zuhrī read "bārīkum" with a kasra on the yā' and without a hamza, and this was also transmitted from Nāfi'. Qatādah read "fa-aqīlū anfusakum" and said it is from al-istiqāla (seeking to be excused). Abū al-Fatḥ said: "iqtāla" here is ifta'ala, and its middle radical may be a wāw, as in iqtāda, or a yā', as in iqtāsa.

Morphologically, it is weak that it derives from al-istiqāla, but one should think well of Qatādah, may Allah have mercy on him, that he did not report this except with a proof in his possession.

As for His statement, "fa-tāba 'alaykum": before it there is an omitted element, its estimate being "fa-fa'altum" (so you did it). His statement "'alaykum" means "upon the remaining ones." Allah made killing a martyrdom for those who were killed, accepted the repentance of the rest, and pardoned them. Some people said: "fa-qtulū" in this verse means by repentance and by extinguishing the attributes of the soul, such as desire, obstinacy and anger. They cited his (ﷺ) saying about garlic and onions: "Then let him cook them until they die (fa-l-tumit-humā ṭabkhan)."

And by the verse of Ḥassān:

"...you were killed, you were killed, so bring it, you will not be killed."

His statement, "wa-idh qultum yā Mūsā," means the seventy whom Moses chose. There was a difference (p-217) over the time of their selection. Most exegetes related that this was after the worship of the calf: he chose them to ask forgiveness for the Children of Israel. al-Naqqāsh and others related that he chose them when he came out of the sea and asked for the appointed time. The first is more sound.

The story of the seventy is that when Moses (ﷺ) returned from speaking with Allah and found that the calf had been worshipped, a group among those who had not worshipped the calf said to him: "We did not disbelieve, and we are your companions, but let us hear the speech of your Lord." So Allah revealed to him to choose seventy elders from among them, but he found only sixty. Allah revealed to him to choose ten from the youths, and he did so, and they became elders. He had chosen six from each tribe, and they exceeded seventy by two, so they disputed over who would stay behind. Allah revealed to him that whoever stayed behind would have a reward like that of those who had gone before. So Yūsha' ibn Nūn and Ṭālūt ibn Yūqinā stayed behind. Moses (peace be upon him) went with the seventy after commanding them to abstain from women for three days and to bathe on the third day. He appointed Hārūn over his people and went on until he came to the mountain, and the cloud was cast over them. al-Naqqāsh and others said: a cloud covered them, and a light was placed between them and Moses, so they fell prostrate. al-Suddī and others said: they heard the speech of Allah commanding and forbidding, but they could not bear hearing it, their minds were confused, and they wished that Moses would hear and relay it to them, so he did. When he finished and they came out, a group of them altered what they had heard of Allah's speech. This is His statement, "And there was a group among them who heard the speech of Allah and then distorted it" (2:75).

Their faith was unsettled, and Allah tested them with this. They said, "We will never believe you until we see Allah plainly." They did not ask for something impossible in seeing Him. As for the matter, according to the People of the Sunnah it is impossible in this world by way of revelation (al-sam').

Then the thunderbolt seized them, and they were burned and died a death of stupor (humūd) by which others take heed. Qatādah said: they died and their souls departed, then they were returned to complete their terms. When they were in that stupor (p-218), Moses began to plead with his Lord on their behalf, saying: "O Lord, how shall I return to the Children of Israel without them? They will perish and never believe in me, and they went out with me, and they were the good ones?"

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He means: they were in a state of goodness at the time of departure.

Others said: Moses (peace be upon him) thought the seventy had been punished because of the worship of the calf. That is His statement, "Will You destroy us for what the foolish among us did?" (7:155), meaning the worshippers of the calf.

Ibn Fūrak said: It is possible that the punishment of the seventy was because they, by saying to Moses "Show us," took the request to see Allah out of its proper course, and this is not within Moses's power (peace be upon him).

"Jahratan" is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl). The clearer view is that it is from the pronoun in "narā." It was said it is from the pronoun in "nu'mina," and it was said it is from the pronoun in "qultum." Al-jahra means openness, and from it comes al-jahr, the opposite of secrecy; jahara al-rajul al-amr means he revealed the matter.

Sahl ibn Shu'ayb and Ḥumayd ibn Qays read "jahratan" with a fatḥa on the hā'. This is an attested dialect among the Basrans in cases where a throat letter is quiescent and the preceding letter is vowelled with fatḥa. The Kufans permit fatḥa there even if they did not hear it. It is possible that "jahratan" is the plural of jāhir, meaning: until we see Allah uncovering this matter.

'Umar and 'Alī, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "fa-akhadhatkumu al-ṣa'qah." The meaning of "al-ṣā'iqah" was discussed at the beginning of the surah, and "al-ṣa'qah" is what happens to a person from the thunderbolt. "Tanẓurūn" means: at your condition.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: until the punishment transformed them and removed their sight.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 56–58:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Then We revived you after your death, that perhaps you would be grateful.﴾ ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you the manna and the quails. "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating and say, 'Hittah (forgiveness),' and We will forgive you your sins and increase the doers of good.'"﴾

(p-219) God, exalted is He, answered Moses's (peace be upon him) desire regarding them, and He revived them from that stupor or death so that they might complete their terms, and He accepted their repentance. Here "ba'th" (raising up) means arousal, as in the words: ﴿Who has raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52]. Some people said: when they were revived and blessed with repentance, they asked Moses (peace be upon him) that God make them prophets; this is His saying: ﴿Then We raised you after your death﴾, that is, as prophets, ﴿that perhaps you would be grateful﴾, that is, for this blessing. The expression "perhaps" (la'alla) applies only with respect to humans. The Tablets containing the Torah were sent down to Moses during that period; this is the view of a group. Others said: the Tablets were sent down during his first going up alone.

The exegetes mentioned regarding the shading by clouds that when the Children of Israel had done what they did of killing, and some of them remained, they ended up in the open plain of the Wilderness (al-Tih) between Egypt and Syria. They were commanded to fight the giants, but they disobeyed and said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. Moses then invoked against them, and they were punished by remaining in that plain for forty years, wandering about in an area of five or six farsakhs. It is narrated that they would walk all day and then descend to spend the night, and in the morning they would find themselves where they had been the day before. Moses (peace be upon him) then regretted his invocation against them, and it was said to him: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26]. It is also narrated that they all died in the open plain of the Wilderness, and their sons grew up in the best obedience; they are the ones who came out of the open plain of the Wilderness and fought the giants.

When all of them were in the Wilderness, they said to Moses: "Who will provide us with food?" He said: "God." So God sent down upon them the manna and the quails. They said: "Who will protect us from the heat of the sun?" So He shaded them with the clouds. They said: "With what shall we light ourselves at night?" So He set up for them a pillar of light in the middle of their encampment. Makki mentioned a pillar of fire. They said: "Who will give us water?" So Moses was commanded to strike the rock. They said: "Who will provide us with clothing?" So they were granted that their garments would not wear out, nor decay, nor become soiled, and that their young would grow in proportion to the growth of children.

The meaning of "zallalna" (We shaded) is: We made it into shades. "Al-ghamam" means the clouds, because it covers (ghamma) the face of the sky, that is, it conceals it. Mujahid said: it is cooler than clouds, finer and purer, and it is the one in which God will come on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: His command, His authority and His decree will come. It has also been said: "al-ghamam" is what is white of the clouds. "Al-mann" is a sweet gum; this is the view of one group. It has been said: it is honey. It has been said: a sweet drink. It has been said: what falls today on trees.

It has also been said: "al-mann" is thin bread like the purest flour; it has been said: it is zanjabin (a sweet confection of ginger), and it has been said: ginger; and in some sayings, more. It has been said: "al-mann" is a verbal noun, by which is meant all that God bestowed upon them in summary. The Prophet ﷺ said in the Sahih of Muslim: « "The mushroom" is among what God bestowed upon the Children of Israel, and its water is a cure for the eye. » It was said: he (peace be upon him) meant that the mushroom itself is of a kind that was sent down upon the Children of Israel. It was also said: he meant that there is no toil in the mushroom, nor pounding, nor harvesting; so it is a favor without effort, of a kind that was among the Children of Israel, in that it required no effort.

It is narrated that "al-mann" would descend upon them from the break of dawn until sunrise, like snow, and a man would take from it what sufficed him for his day. If he stored it, it would spoil for him, except on Friday, when they would store it for Saturday, and it would not spoil for them, because Saturday was a day of worship. "Al-mann" here is a collective noun with no singular form from its own wording.

"Al-salwa" is a bird, by the consensus of the exegetes; so said Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others. It has been said: it is the very quail (al-sumana). It has been said: a bird inclining to red, like the quail. It has been said: a bird like the pigeon, which the south wind gathers for them. Al-Akhfash said: "al-salwa" is both its plural and its singular, with one wording. Al-Khalil said: its plural is salwat-, its singular being salwat. Al-Kisa'i said: "al-salwa" is a singular whose plural is salawa. "Al-salwa" is a defective noun (ism maqsur) in which the i'rab does not appear, because its last letter is an alif, and the alif is an airy letter resembling a vowel, so its vowel becomes impossible; and if it were vowelled it would revert to another letter. Al-Hudhali exaggerated and said:

She swore to him by God an oath: "You are sweeter than the salwa when its honey is drawn out."

He thought that "al-salwa" is honey.

As for His saying, exalted is He, "Eat" — the meaning is: And We said: "Eat," and it was omitted for brevity, since the context indicates it. "Al-tayyibat" (the good things) here encompasses both the lawful and the delicious.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾, there is to be understood before it: "so they disobeyed," and they did not requite the blessings with gratitude. The meaning: they did not place their act where it harmed Us, but they placed it where it harmed them, where it was not due. Some exegetes said: "they did not wrong Us" means "they did not diminish Us," and the meaning returns to what we have summarized.

"Al-qaryah" is the town, named so because it gathers (taqarrat), that is, it is assembled, and from it comes "qariyat al-ma'" in the (p-222) basin, that is, it gathered the water. The reference of "this" is to Jerusalem according to the majority; it has been said: to Jericho (Arihā), which is near Jerusalem. 'Umar ibn Shabbah said: it was a capital and the dwelling of kings. When the offspring of the Children of Israel came out of the Wilderness, they were commanded to enter the town indicated, while the elders died in it. It is narrated that Moses (peace be upon him) died in the Wilderness, and likewise Aaron (peace be upon him). Al-Zajjaj related from some people that Moses and Aaron were not in the Wilderness, because it was a punishment; but the first view is the more widespread. "Kulu" (eat) is a permission. The meaning of "raghadan" (in abundance) has already been explained; it is a blessed land of great produce, and therefore He said: "raghadan."

As for "al-bab" (the gate): Mujahid said: it is a gate in the city of Jerusalem known to this day as Bab Hittah. It has been said: it is the gate of the dome at which Moses (peace be upon him) used to pray. It is also narrated from Mujahid that it is a gate in the mountain upon which Moses spoke, like a narrow pass. As for "sujjadan" (prostrating), Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said its meaning is: bowing (ruku'). It has been said: humbly submitting, not in a specific posture. Prostration encompasses all of this, because it is humility; and from it is the saying of the poet:

You see the hills in it prostrating before the hooves.

It is narrated that the gate was lowered for them so that it would be low and they would enter it humbly.

As for "hittah": it is a form (fi'lah) from hatta yahuttu, and it is raised as the predicate of an implied subject, as if they said: "Our request is hittah for our sins." This is the estimation of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. Al-Tabari said: the estimation is "our entering the gate as we were commanded, (a request for) hittah." It has been said: they were commanded to say it in the raised form with this wording.

'Ikrimah and others said: they were commanded to say: "There is no god but God," so that their sins would be removed by it. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were told: "Seek forgiveness, and say what removes your sins." Others said: they were told to say that this command is true, as He informed us. These three views require the accusative (nasb), and Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah read "hittatan" in the accusative.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud and others that they were commanded to prostrate and to say "hittah," but they entered crawling on their buttocks and saying: "Hintah habbah hamra'u fi sha'rah" (a wheat grain, red, in a hair), and other words are reported. Nafi' read "yughfar" with a yā' below, vowelled with a ḍammah; Ibn 'Amir read "tughfar" with a tā' above, vowelled with a ḍammah; Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "wa-yaghfir" with a fatḥah on the yā', meaning God forgives; and the rest read "nughfir" with the nūn. A group read "tughfar," as if hittah were the cause of forgiveness.

The seven readers read "khaṭāyākum," except that al-Kisa'i inclined it. Al-Jahdari read "tughfar lakum khaṭī'atukum" with a ḍammah on the tā' above and the raising of khaṭī'ah. Al-A'mash read "yaghfira" with a yā' below and a fatḥah, "khaṭī'atikum" in the accusative. Qatadah read like al-Jahdari, and it is reported from him that he read with a yā' below and a ḍammah, "khaṭī'atukum" in the nominative. Al-Hasan al-Basri read "yaghfiru lakum khaṭī'atikum," meaning God forgives. Abu Haywah read "tughfaru" with a tā' above, raised, "yaghfiru lakum khaṭī'atikum" in the plural with the raising of the tā'. Al-Ahwazi related that it was read "khata'ayakum" with a hamzah on the first alif and a sukun on the last, and it is also related that it was read with a sukun on the first and a hamzah on the last. Al-Farra' said: khaṭāyā is the plural of khaṭiyyah, without a hamzah, like hadiyyah and hadāyā, and rakiyyah and rakāyā.

Al-Khalil said: it is the plural of khaṭī'ah with a hamzah, and its origin is khaṭāyi'; the hamzah was moved before the yā', so it became khaṭā'i; the yā' was replaced by an alif as a necessary substitution, and the hamzah before it was given a fatḥah, so it became khaṭā'a, a hamzah between two alifs, and it belongs to the category of both, so it is as if there were three alifs; then the hamzah was changed into a yā', so it became khaṭāyā. Sibawayh said: its origin is khaṭāyi'a; the hamzah of the yā' was made a hamzah as in madā'in and katā'ib, so two hamzahs came together, and the second was changed into a yā', and then it was given the treatment described above.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will increase the doers of good﴾: the sense of the promise is that when the sins are forgiven through your entering and your saying, increase is granted after that to whoever does good. Some of the Children of Israel entered as they were commanded and said: "There is no god but God," and it is said that these are the ones intended by "the doers of good" here.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 56–58:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Then We revived you after your death, that perhaps you would be grateful.﴾ ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds and sent down upon you the manna and the quails. "Eat of the good things with which We have provided you." And they did not wrong Us, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ ﴿And when We said, "Enter this town and eat from it wherever you wish, in abundance, and enter the gate prostrating and say, 'Hittah (forgiveness),' and We will forgive you your sins and increase the doers of good.'"﴾

(p-219) God, exalted is He, answered Moses's (peace be upon him) desire regarding them, and He revived them from that stupor or death so that they might complete their terms, and He accepted their repentance. Here "ba'th" (raising up) means arousal, as in the words: ﴿Who has raised us from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52]. Some people said: when they were revived and blessed with repentance, they asked Moses (peace be upon him) that God make them prophets; this is His saying: ﴿Then We raised you after your death﴾, that is, as prophets, ﴿that perhaps you would be grateful﴾, that is, for this blessing. The expression "perhaps" (la'alla) applies only with respect to humans. The Tablets containing the Torah were sent down to Moses during that period; this is the view of a group. Others said: the Tablets were sent down during his first going up alone.

The exegetes mentioned regarding the shading by clouds that when the Children of Israel had done what they did of killing, and some of them remained, they ended up in the open plain of the Wilderness (al-Tih) between Egypt and Syria. They were commanded to fight the giants, but they disobeyed and said: ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 24]. Moses then invoked against them, and they were punished by remaining in that plain for forty years, wandering about in an area of five or six farsakhs. It is narrated that they would walk all day and then descend to spend the night, and in the morning they would find themselves where they had been the day before. Moses (peace be upon him) then regretted his invocation against them, and it was said to him: ﴿So do not grieve over the defiant people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 26]. It is also narrated that they all died in the open plain of the Wilderness, and their sons grew up in the best obedience; they are the ones who came out of the open plain of the Wilderness and fought the giants.

When all of them were in the Wilderness, they said to Moses: "Who will provide us with food?" He said: "God." So God sent down upon them the manna and the quails. They said: "Who will protect us from the heat of the sun?" So He shaded them with the clouds. They said: "With what shall we light ourselves at night?" So He set up for them a pillar of light in the middle of their encampment. Makki mentioned a pillar of fire. They said: "Who will give us water?" So Moses was commanded to strike the rock. They said: "Who will provide us with clothing?" So they were granted that their garments would not wear out, nor decay, nor become soiled, and that their young would grow in proportion to the growth of children.

The meaning of "zallalna" (We shaded) is: We made it into shades. "Al-ghamam" means the clouds, because it covers (ghamma) the face of the sky, that is, it conceals it. Mujahid said: it is cooler than clouds, finer and purer, and it is the one in which God will come on the Day of Resurrection.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: His command, His authority and His decree will come. It has also been said: "al-ghamam" is what is white of the clouds. "Al-mann" is a sweet gum; this is the view of one group. It has been said: it is honey. It has been said: a sweet drink. It has been said: what falls today on trees.

It has also been said: "al-mann" is thin bread like the purest flour; it has been said: it is zanjabin (a sweet confection of ginger), and it has been said: ginger; and in some sayings, more. It has been said: "al-mann" is a verbal noun, by which is meant all that God bestowed upon them in summary. The Prophet ﷺ said in the Sahih of Muslim: « "The mushroom" is among what God bestowed upon the Children of Israel, and its water is a cure for the eye. » It was said: he (peace be upon him) meant that the mushroom itself is of a kind that was sent down upon the Children of Israel. It was also said: he meant that there is no toil in the mushroom, nor pounding, nor harvesting; so it is a favor without effort, of a kind that was among the Children of Israel, in that it required no effort.

It is narrated that "al-mann" would descend upon them from the break of dawn until sunrise, like snow, and a man would take from it what sufficed him for his day. If he stored it, it would spoil for him, except on Friday, when they would store it for Saturday, and it would not spoil for them, because Saturday was a day of worship. "Al-mann" here is a collective noun with no singular form from its own wording.

"Al-salwa" is a bird, by the consensus of the exegetes; so said Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' ibn Anas and others. It has been said: it is the very quail (al-sumana). It has been said: a bird inclining to red, like the quail. It has been said: a bird like the pigeon, which the south wind gathers for them. Al-Akhfash said: "al-salwa" is both its plural and its singular, with one wording. Al-Khalil said: its plural is salwat-, its singular being salwat. Al-Kisa'i said: "al-salwa" is a singular whose plural is salawa. "Al-salwa" is a defective noun (ism maqsur) in which the i'rab does not appear, because its last letter is an alif, and the alif is an airy letter resembling a vowel, so its vowel becomes impossible; and if it were vowelled it would revert to another letter. Al-Hudhali exaggerated and said:

She swore to him by God an oath: "You are sweeter than the salwa when its honey is drawn out."

He thought that "al-salwa" is honey.

As for His saying, exalted is He, "Eat" — the meaning is: And We said: "Eat," and it was omitted for brevity, since the context indicates it. "Al-tayyibat" (the good things) here encompasses both the lawful and the delicious.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they did not wrong Us﴾, there is to be understood before it: "so they disobeyed," and they did not requite the blessings with gratitude. The meaning: they did not place their act where it harmed Us, but they placed it where it harmed them, where it was not due. Some exegetes said: "they did not wrong Us" means "they did not diminish Us," and the meaning returns to what we have summarized.

"Al-qaryah" is the town, named so because it gathers (taqarrat), that is, it is assembled, and from it comes "qariyat al-ma'" in the (p-222) basin, that is, it gathered the water. The reference of "this" is to Jerusalem according to the majority; it has been said: to Jericho (Arihā), which is near Jerusalem. 'Umar ibn Shabbah said: it was a capital and the dwelling of kings. When the offspring of the Children of Israel came out of the Wilderness, they were commanded to enter the town indicated, while the elders died in it. It is narrated that Moses (peace be upon him) died in the Wilderness, and likewise Aaron (peace be upon him). Al-Zajjaj related from some people that Moses and Aaron were not in the Wilderness, because it was a punishment; but the first view is the more widespread. "Kulu" (eat) is a permission. The meaning of "raghadan" (in abundance) has already been explained; it is a blessed land of great produce, and therefore He said: "raghadan."

As for "al-bab" (the gate): Mujahid said: it is a gate in the city of Jerusalem known to this day as Bab Hittah. It has been said: it is the gate of the dome at which Moses (peace be upon him) used to pray. It is also narrated from Mujahid that it is a gate in the mountain upon which Moses spoke, like a narrow pass. As for "sujjadan" (prostrating), Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, said its meaning is: bowing (ruku'). It has been said: humbly submitting, not in a specific posture. Prostration encompasses all of this, because it is humility; and from it is the saying of the poet:

You see the hills in it prostrating before the hooves.

It is narrated that the gate was lowered for them so that it would be low and they would enter it humbly.

As for "hittah": it is a form (fi'lah) from hatta yahuttu, and it is raised as the predicate of an implied subject, as if they said: "Our request is hittah for our sins." This is the estimation of al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. Al-Tabari said: the estimation is "our entering the gate as we were commanded, (a request for) hittah." It has been said: they were commanded to say it in the raised form with this wording.

'Ikrimah and others said: they were commanded to say: "There is no god but God," so that their sins would be removed by it. Ibn 'Abbas said: they were told: "Seek forgiveness, and say what removes your sins." Others said: they were told to say that this command is true, as He informed us. These three views require the accusative (nasb), and Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Ablah read "hittatan" in the accusative.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud and others that they were commanded to prostrate and to say "hittah," but they entered crawling on their buttocks and saying: "Hintah habbah hamra'u fi sha'rah" (a wheat grain, red, in a hair), and other words are reported. Nafi' read "yughfar" with a yā' below, vowelled with a ḍammah; Ibn 'Amir read "tughfar" with a tā' above, vowelled with a ḍammah; Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "wa-yaghfir" with a fatḥah on the yā', meaning God forgives; and the rest read "nughfir" with the nūn. A group read "tughfar," as if hittah were the cause of forgiveness.

The seven readers read "khaṭāyākum," except that al-Kisa'i inclined it. Al-Jahdari read "tughfar lakum khaṭī'atukum" with a ḍammah on the tā' above and the raising of khaṭī'ah. Al-A'mash read "yaghfira" with a yā' below and a fatḥah, "khaṭī'atikum" in the accusative. Qatadah read like al-Jahdari, and it is reported from him that he read with a yā' below and a ḍammah, "khaṭī'atukum" in the nominative. Al-Hasan al-Basri read "yaghfiru lakum khaṭī'atikum," meaning God forgives. Abu Haywah read "tughfaru" with a tā' above, raised, "yaghfiru lakum khaṭī'atikum" in the plural with the raising of the tā'. Al-Ahwazi related that it was read "khata'ayakum" with a hamzah on the first alif and a sukun on the last, and it is also related that it was read with a sukun on the first and a hamzah on the last. Al-Farra' said: khaṭāyā is the plural of khaṭiyyah, without a hamzah, like hadiyyah and hadāyā, and rakiyyah and rakāyā.

Al-Khalil said: it is the plural of khaṭī'ah with a hamzah, and its origin is khaṭāyi'; the hamzah was moved before the yā', so it became khaṭā'i; the yā' was replaced by an alif as a necessary substitution, and the hamzah before it was given a fatḥah, so it became khaṭā'a, a hamzah between two alifs, and it belongs to the category of both, so it is as if there were three alifs; then the hamzah was changed into a yā', so it became khaṭāyā. Sibawayh said: its origin is khaṭāyi'a; the hamzah of the yā' was made a hamzah as in madā'in and katā'ib, so two hamzahs came together, and the second was changed into a yā', and then it was given the treatment described above.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will increase the doers of good﴾: the sense of the promise is that when the sins are forgiven through your entering and your saying, increase is granted after that to whoever does good. Some of the Children of Israel entered as they were commanded and said: "There is no god but God," and it is said that these are the ones intended by "the doers of good" here.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 59–60:

His saying, may He be Mighty and Majestic:

﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, so We sent upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they used to defy (Our command).﴾ ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people, We said: Strike the rock with your staff. And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place. Eat and drink of the provision of Allah, and do not go about in the earth spreading corruption.﴾

It is narrated that when they came to the gate, they entered backwards (from its rear, al-qahqara). In a hadith it is said that they entered crawling on their buttocks (asti'a-him), and they substituted, saying "ḥabba fi sha'ra" (a grain in a hair). It was also said that they said: "ḥinṭa ḥabba ḥamra'" (a red wheat grain) in which there is a hair; and it was said: "shu'ayra" (a barley grain). al-Ṭabarī related that they said: "ḥaṭṭī shamaqāthā azibah," and its interpretation is what has preceded. And ar-rijz (the punishment) means the torment.

Ibn Zayd, Muqatil and others said: Allah the Exalted sent upon those who substituted and entered in a manner other than what they had been commanded, the plague (ṭā'ūn), and it removed from them seventy thousand. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah caused to die from them in a single hour more than twenty thousand. Ibn Muhaysin read "rijzan" with a ra' having a sukun (ar-rijz), which is a dialect for the torment; and ar-rijz is also the name of a famous idol. The ba' in His saying "bima" is connected to "fa-anzalna" and is the ba' of causation.

"Yafsuqun" means they go out of obedience to Allah. An-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read "yafsiqun" with a kasra on the sin, it is said: fasaqa yafsuqu and yafsiqu, with a dammah or kasra on the sin. "Idh" is connected to a hidden verb whose estimate is "udhkur" (remember). "Istasqa" means: he asked for water. The form istaf'ala here means seeking a thing, though it has come in other senses, like His saying: ﴿And Allah is Rich (wa-staghna Allahu)﴾ [at-Taghabun: 6], meaning "ghaniyy" (Rich); and their saying "ista'jaba" meaning "a'jaba" (to amaze). Some people gave as an example their saying "istansara al-bughath" and "istanwaqa al-jamal," since it means moving from one state to another. This water-seeking took place in the plain of the Wandering (fahṣ al-tīh), so Allah the Exalted commanded him to strike the rock as a sign from Him. The rock was from the mountain of Ṭūr, the size of a sheep's head, placed in a sack-fold and carried with them; when they halted it was placed in the middle of their camp, and Moses struck it.

It is mentioned that they did not carry the rock, but they would find it at every stage in its place at the first stage, and this is greater in the sign.

There is no disagreement that it was a separate, square rock, from each side of which three springs gushed forth when Moses ﷺ struck it, and when they had no need of water and departed, the springs dried up.

There is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: he struck it, "fa-infajarat" (so there gushed forth). Infijar is the splitting of one thing from another, and from it comes al-fajr (dawn); and inbijas in water is less than infijar.

"Ithnatā" is declined differently from its sisters for the sake of the soundness of the meaning of duality, since only one is built with one; here it is two with one, so if it were built, three would make one of them ineffective. The joining of the two feminine markers in His saying "ithnata 'ashrata" is permitted because the marker is far from the marker, and because they are in two things; that is prevented in one thing, such as "muslimat" and others. Ibn Wathhab, Ibn Abi Layla and others read "'ashrata" with a kasra on the shin; this is narrated from Abu 'Amr, though the more famous from him is sukun, and it is the dialect of Tamim, and it is rare, because they lighten it much but make this one heavy. al-A'mash read "'ashara" with a fatha on the shin, which is a weak dialect; it is narrated from him that it is kasra and sukun, and sukun is the dialect of the Hijaz. "'Aynan" is put in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), and "ayn" is a homonymous noun, and here it means the source of water. "Unas" is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, and its meaning here is: every tribe (sibt), because the tribes among the Children of Israel were like the clans among the Arabs, and they are the descendants of the twelve sons of Ya'qub ('alayhi as-salam). The mashrab is the place of drinking, like the mashra' is the place of going down to the water; and each tribe had a spring from those springs that it did not exceed.

In the speech there is an omitted element, its estimate being: and We said to them: Eat al-mann and al-salwa, and drink the water gushing from the separated rock. With these states the attribution of provision to Allah is fitting; otherwise all are provided by Him, even though there is acquisition (taksub) for the servant in it.

"Wa-la ta'thaw" means: and do not go to extremes in corruption. It is said: 'atha ar-rajul ya'thi 'athwan and 'athiya ya'tha 'uthyan when he corrupts to the utmost degree of corruption. The first is the dialect of the Qur'an, and the second is anomalous.

The Arabs say: 'athā ya'thū 'athwan, and he was not read with this dialect, because it would require a dammah on the tha' of "ta'thaw." The Arabs say: 'āka ya'īthu when he corrupts, and 'ath-tha ya'ithhu likewise, and from it comes 'athhat as-sūf, which is the moth that gnaws it. "Mufsidin" is a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The meaning is repeated for the difference of wording.

In these words there is: the permissibility of blessings, enumerating them, and the warning against sins and the prohibition of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 59–60:

His saying, may He be Mighty and Majestic:

﴿But those who did wrong substituted a word other than that which had been said to them, so We sent upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky because they used to defy (Our command).﴾ ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people, We said: Strike the rock with your staff. And there gushed forth from it twelve springs. Every people knew its drinking place. Eat and drink of the provision of Allah, and do not go about in the earth spreading corruption.﴾

It is narrated that when they came to the gate, they entered backwards (from its rear, al-qahqara). In a hadith it is said that they entered crawling on their buttocks (asti'a-him), and they substituted, saying "ḥabba fi sha'ra" (a grain in a hair). It was also said that they said: "ḥinṭa ḥabba ḥamra'" (a red wheat grain) in which there is a hair; and it was said: "shu'ayra" (a barley grain). al-Ṭabarī related that they said: "ḥaṭṭī shamaqāthā azibah," and its interpretation is what has preceded. And ar-rijz (the punishment) means the torment.

Ibn Zayd, Muqatil and others said: Allah the Exalted sent upon those who substituted and entered in a manner other than what they had been commanded, the plague (ṭā'ūn), and it removed from them seventy thousand. Ibn 'Abbas said: Allah caused to die from them in a single hour more than twenty thousand. Ibn Muhaysin read "rijzan" with a ra' having a sukun (ar-rijz), which is a dialect for the torment; and ar-rijz is also the name of a famous idol. The ba' in His saying "bima" is connected to "fa-anzalna" and is the ba' of causation.

"Yafsuqun" means they go out of obedience to Allah. An-Nakha'i and Ibn Wathhab read "yafsiqun" with a kasra on the sin, it is said: fasaqa yafsuqu and yafsiqu, with a dammah or kasra on the sin. "Idh" is connected to a hidden verb whose estimate is "udhkur" (remember). "Istasqa" means: he asked for water. The form istaf'ala here means seeking a thing, though it has come in other senses, like His saying: ﴿And Allah is Rich (wa-staghna Allahu)﴾ [at-Taghabun: 6], meaning "ghaniyy" (Rich); and their saying "ista'jaba" meaning "a'jaba" (to amaze). Some people gave as an example their saying "istansara al-bughath" and "istanwaqa al-jamal," since it means moving from one state to another. This water-seeking took place in the plain of the Wandering (fahṣ al-tīh), so Allah the Exalted commanded him to strike the rock as a sign from Him. The rock was from the mountain of Ṭūr, the size of a sheep's head, placed in a sack-fold and carried with them; when they halted it was placed in the middle of their camp, and Moses struck it.

It is mentioned that they did not carry the rock, but they would find it at every stage in its place at the first stage, and this is greater in the sign.

There is no disagreement that it was a separate, square rock, from each side of which three springs gushed forth when Moses ﷺ struck it, and when they had no need of water and departed, the springs dried up.

There is an omission in the speech, its estimate being: he struck it, "fa-infajarat" (so there gushed forth). Infijar is the splitting of one thing from another, and from it comes al-fajr (dawn); and inbijas in water is less than infijar.

"Ithnatā" is declined differently from its sisters for the sake of the soundness of the meaning of duality, since only one is built with one; here it is two with one, so if it were built, three would make one of them ineffective. The joining of the two feminine markers in His saying "ithnata 'ashrata" is permitted because the marker is far from the marker, and because they are in two things; that is prevented in one thing, such as "muslimat" and others. Ibn Wathhab, Ibn Abi Layla and others read "'ashrata" with a kasra on the shin; this is narrated from Abu 'Amr, though the more famous from him is sukun, and it is the dialect of Tamim, and it is rare, because they lighten it much but make this one heavy. al-A'mash read "'ashara" with a fatha on the shin, which is a weak dialect; it is narrated from him that it is kasra and sukun, and sukun is the dialect of the Hijaz. "'Aynan" is put in the accusative as a specification (tamyīz), and "ayn" is a homonymous noun, and here it means the source of water. "Unas" is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, and its meaning here is: every tribe (sibt), because the tribes among the Children of Israel were like the clans among the Arabs, and they are the descendants of the twelve sons of Ya'qub ('alayhi as-salam). The mashrab is the place of drinking, like the mashra' is the place of going down to the water; and each tribe had a spring from those springs that it did not exceed.

In the speech there is an omitted element, its estimate being: and We said to them: Eat al-mann and al-salwa, and drink the water gushing from the separated rock. With these states the attribution of provision to Allah is fitting; otherwise all are provided by Him, even though there is acquisition (taksub) for the servant in it.
