The Arabs say: 'athā ya'thū 'athwan, and he was not read with this dialect, because it would require a dammah on the tha' of "ta'thaw." The Arabs say: 'āka ya'īthu when he corrupts, and 'ath-tha ya'ithhu likewise, and from it comes 'athhat as-sūf, which is the moth that gnaws it. "Mufsidin" is a circumstantial state (ḥāl). The meaning is repeated for the difference of wording.

In these words there is: the permissibility of blessings, enumerating them, and the warning against sins and the prohibition of them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 61:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And when you said, "O Musa, we will not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord for us to bring forth for us from what the earth grows: its herbs, its cucumbers, its garlic, its lentils, and its onions." He said, "Would you exchange what is lower for what is better? Go down to a city, for indeed you will have what you ask." And they were struck with humiliation and poverty, and they returned with anger from Allah. That was because they had been disbelieving in the signs of Allah and killing the prophets without right. That was because they disobeyed and were transgressing.﴾

This saying of theirs was during the wandering (al-tih), when they grew weary of the manna and the quails, and remembered their former life in Egypt. He referred to the manna and the quails as "one kind of food" (ṭaʿām wāḥid), though they were two foods, because they were eaten at one time, and because their repetition was always the same; so they were called one food.

The dialect of the Banu 'Amir reads "fa-ud'u" with a kasra on the ʿayn. "Yukhrij" is in the jussive (majzūm) by what the command contains of the meaning of a conditional, and by the command itself according to the view of Abu 'Umar al-Jarmi. The object, according to the view of Sibawayh, is implied, its estimate being: "eaten, of what the earth grows." Al-Akhfash said that "min" in His saying "mimmā" is superfluous and "mā" is the object. Sibawayh refused that "min" be made void except in negation, as in their saying: "mā ra'aytu min aḥad" (I did not see anyone).

"Min" in His saying ﴿min baqlihā﴾ is for specifying the kind, and "baqlihā" is a substitute (badal) with the particle repeated. The baql (herbs) is every thing the earth produces of [...] al-najm (p-228). The qiththa' is the plural of qathaʾa. Ṭalḥa ibn Muṣarrif and Yaḥyā ibn Wathhāb read "qiththa'ihā" with a ḍamma on the qāf. Ibn 'Abbas and most of the exegetes said: al-fūm is wheat. Mujahid said: al-fūm is bread. ʿAṭāʾ and Qatada said: al-fūm is all the grains that can be baked, such as wheat, fava beans, lentils, and the like. al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: al-fūm is garlic, and it is the reading of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud with the letter thāʾ; this was also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. The thāʾ is substituted for the fāʾ, as they said: maghāthīr and maghāfīr, and jadath and jadaf, and "waqaʿū fī ʿāthūr sharr" and "ʿāfūr sharr," though substitution is not analogical. The first is more correct: that it is wheat. Ibn 'Abbas recited the verse of Uhayha ibn al-Jallah:

Indeed I was the richest of people in person, a single one, who came to Madina from the cultivation of fūm.

He means wheat. Ibn Duraid said: al-fūm is the crop or wheat. The people of Azd al-Sarāh call the ear of grain fūm.

Al-istibdāl is seeking to place one thing in the place of another. "Adnā" is taken, according to Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj (p-229), from al-dunuww, meaning nearness in value. ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān said: it is hamzated from al-danīʾ, the clearly base, in the sense of the lowest, except that its hamza was lightened. Others said: it is taken from al-dūn, meaning the lowest, so its origin is adwan, af'al, which was transposed to become afal‘, and the waw was changed to alif because it is final. Zuhayr, for al-Kisa'i, read "adnaʾ".

The meaning of the verse: Would you exchange the herbs, the cucumbers, the fūm, the lentils, and the onions, which are the lower, for the manna and the quails, which are the better?

The aspect that makes the manna and quails superior to what they requested may be that they are superior in value, since these herbs have no worth; this is the saying of al-Zajjaj. It may be that the manna and quails are preferred because they are the food with which Allah favored them and commanded them to eat, and in continuing the command of Allah Most High and thanking His blessing there is reward and treasure in the Hereafter; and what they sought lacks these qualities, so it is lower from this aspect. It may be that they are preferred in goodness and pleasure, and herbs are without doubt lower from this aspect. It may be that they are preferred in the goodness and benefit of nourishment, so the manna and quails are without doubt better in this aspect. It may be that they are preferred because there is no burden or toil in them, while what they sought comes only with tilling, farming and toil, so it is "lower" in this aspect. It may be that they are preferred in that there is no doubt about their lawfulness and purity, since they descend from Allah, whereas grains and land are subject to sales and usurpations, and doubts enter them, so they are "lower" in this aspect.

(p-230) The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The superiority of the manna and quails is established by all of these aspects.

In the speech there is an ellipsis; its estimate: Musa called upon his Lord, and He answered him, and he said to them: "Go down." The meaning of descending has been mentioned before, and it is as if one who arrives at a land that is lowered upon it, so it is from the direction of descent.

Most people read "miṣran" with tanwin, and this is the orthography of the muṣḥaf, except what is related from some of the muṣḥafs of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him. Mujahid and others, among those who gave it tanwin, meant a miṣr (city) from the cities, unspecified, and they cited what the Qur'an implies of their command to enter the town, and what the reports consistently attest: that they settled in Syria after the wandering. Another group said: whoever gave it tanwin meant the Miṣr of Pharaoh itself, specifically, and they cited what the Qur'an says, that Allah made the Children of Israel inherit the dwellings and traces of the people of Pharaoh. They permitted its tanwin. al-Akhfash said: because of its lightness and its resemblance to Hind and Da'd. Sibawayh did not permit this. Other than al-Akhfash said: he meant a place, so he gave it tanwin.

al-Ḥasan, Abān ibn Taghlib, and others read "ihbiṭū Miṣra" without tanwin, and likewise it is in the muṣḥaf of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb. They said: it is Miṣr of Pharaoh. al-Aʿmash said: it is the Miṣr over which Ṣāliḥ ibn ʿAlī was governor. Ashhab said: Malik said to me: "It is, in my view, Miṣr, your town, the dwelling of Pharaoh."

His Exalted saying ﴿fa-inna lakum mā sa'altum﴾ requires that He left them to themselves. al-Nakhaʿī and Ibn Wathhāb read "saʾaltum" with a kasra on the sīn, and it is a dialect. ﴿And humiliation and poverty were struck upon them﴾ (p-231) its meaning: they were made to adhere to them, and it was decreed upon them, as one says: the commander struck the expedition; and as the Arabs said: "ḍarbat lāzib," that is, an obligation of an obligated or obliging one, so the verbal noun is attributed to the object by meaning; and as one says: the judge struck upon the hand, that is, he restrained and obligated; and from it: "ḍaraba al-dahru ḍarabātihi," that is, time imposed its impositions.

"Dhilla" is a form (fiʿla) from dhull, as if it were the state and condition. "Maskana" is from miskīn. al-Zajjaj said: it is taken from sukūn (stillness). It here is the garb of poverty and its submissiveness, and if a wealthy Jew is found, he is not free of the garb of poverty and its humiliation. al-Ḥasan and Qatāda said: al-maskana is the kharāj, that is, the jizya. Abu al-ʿĀliya said: al-maskana is destitution and need.

﴿And they returned with anger from Allah﴾ its meaning: they passed, bearing it; one says: "bu't bi-kadhā" when I bore it, and from it is the saying of Muhalhil to Yahyā ibn al-Ḥārith ibn ʿAbbād: "Bu' bi-shisʿ naʿl Kulayb" (bear the thong of Kulayb's sandal).

Anger, in the sense of will, is an attribute of essence; in the sense of its manifestation upon the servant by punishment, it is an attribute of act. The reference by "dhalika" is to the striking of humiliation and what follows it.

The bāʾ in "bi-annahum" is the bāʾ of cause. al-Mahdawi said: the bāʾ is in the sense of the lām, and the meaning: "li-annahum" (because they). The signs here may be understood to mean the nine signs and others that break custom, which are proof of the truthfulness of the one who brings them; and it may be understood to mean the signs of the Torah, which are like the signs of the Qur'an.

al-Ḥasan ibn Abi al-Ḥasan read "wa-taqtulūna" with the tāʾ, referring back to their address; and it was also reported from him with the yāʾ (p-232). Nāfiʿ read "al-nabiʾīn" with a hamza, and likewise wherever it occurs in the Qur'an except in two places: in Surat al-Aḥzāb, ﴿if a woman gives herself to the Prophet, if the Prophet wishes﴾ [33:50] without madd or hamza, and ﴿do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you﴾ [33:53]. He left the hamza out of these two because of the meeting of two kasra hamzas of one kind. The rest omitted the hamza in all of that. As for the one who used the hamza, it is in his view from "anba'a" when he informs, and its active participle is munbi'; so "nabbi'" is in the sense of munbi', as "samīʿ" is in the sense of musmi'. They cited that what came of its plural is "nibāʾ." The poet said:

O seal of the prophets (nibāʾ), indeed you are sent with the truth; every guidance of God is your guidance.

This is like the plural of fa'īl in the sound form, such as ẓarīf and ẓurafāʾ and its like. Abu ʿAlī said: Sibawayh claimed that they say, in diminishing prophethood: "Musaylima's prophethood was a bad prophetess (nabīʾa sūʾ)." And all of them say: "Musaylima prophesied (tanabbaʾa)," so their agreement on that is evidence that the lām is a hamza.

Those who said to leave the hamza differed about nabīʾ. Some of them derived it as those who hamzated did, then lightened the hamza. Others said: it is derived from nabā yanbū, when it appears, so the nabī is the clear road, and the prophet of God is as the clear road from God, the path of guidance and salvation. The poet said:

When we arrived at a clear (nabiyyan) road, and it was made firm for us, a wide-stepping (muskhanfar) one like the traces of the flowing water, scraped away.

They argued that the more usual plural of anbiyāʾ is like fa'īl in the weak (mu'tall) forms, such as walī and awliyāʾ, and ṣafī (p-233) and aṣfiyāʾ. al-Zahrāwī related that one says: "nabūʾa" when it appears, so he is "nabīʾ," and the clear road is "nabīʾ" with a hamza. It was reported that a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Peace be upon you, O Nabī of Allah," and he hamzated; the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "I am not Nabīʾ of Allah" — and he hamzated — "but I am Nabī of Allah" — and he did not hamzate. Abu ʿAlī said: the chain of this hadith is weak. What further weakens it is that the Prophet ﷺ was recited to by the panegyrist:

O seal of the prophets (nubāʾ).

No objection was recorded regarding that, and the plural is like the singular.

His Exalted saying ﴿bi-ghayr al-ḥaqq﴾ is an amplification of the heinousness and the sin they committed. It is known that no prophet is killed rightly; but from the standpoint that someone may imagine a reason for it, His saying ﴿without right﴾ clarifies the heinousness and clarity of the sin, and no prophet ever committed what would necessitate his killing. Allah Most High only permitted those of them who were killed, and empowered over them, as an honour for them and an increase in their ranks, like the one among the believers who is killed in the way of Allah. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: none of the prophets was ever killed except one who had not been commanded to fight, and everyone who was commanded to fight was victorious. His Exalted saying "dhalika" is a return to the first and an emphasis of the reference to it. The bāʾ in "bi-mā" is the bāʾ of cause. "Yaʿtadūn" means they transgress the limits; and i'tidā' is exceeding the bound in everything, and its customary usage is in injustice and sins.

[p-234]

The Exalted and Majestic says:

﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who were Jews, and the Christians, and the Sabians, whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds, for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿And [recall] when We took your covenant and raised the mount above you, [saying], "Take what We have given you with strength, and remember what is in it, that you may be righteous."﴾ ﴿Then you turned away after that, and were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you and His mercy, you would have been among the losers.﴾

The commentators differed about what is meant by ﴿those who believed﴾ in this verse. Sufyan al-Thawri said: they are the hypocrites within the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is as if He said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ outwardly, and He paired them with the Jews, the Christians and the Sabians. Then He explained the ruling for whoever among all of them believes in Allah and the Last Day. So the meaning of His words ﴿whoever believes﴾ refers, among the believers mentioned, to whoever is sincere and pure, and among the other groups mentioned, to whoever entered into faith.

A group said: ﴿those who believed﴾ are the truly faithful who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), and His words ﴿whoever believes in Allah﴾ apply to them in the sense of whoever persists and continues, and to the other groups in the sense of whoever entered into it.

al-Suddi said: they are the people of the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic creed of Abraham) who did not live to see Muhammad (ﷺ), such as Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Qass ibn Sa'ida, and Waraqa ibn (p-235) Nawfal. ﴿And those who were Jews﴾ likewise refers to those who did not live to see Muhammad (ﷺ), except whoever disbelieved in 'Isa (peace be upon him). "And the Christians" likewise refers to those who did not live to see Muhammad (ﷺ). "And the Sabians" likewise. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the companions of Salman al-Farisi. al-Tabari mentioned for him a long story, which Ibn Ishaq also related, and its implication is that he accompanied some Christian worshippers, and their last one said to him: "The time of a prophet has drawn near. If you reach him, believe in him." He saw from them great worship. When he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embraced Islam, he told him of their condition and asked him about them, and this verse was revealed.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse was revealed at the beginning of Islam, and by it Allah established that whoever believed in Muhammad (ﷺ), and whoever remained upon his Judaism, Christianity or Sabianism while believing in Allah and the Last Day, has his reward. Then He abrogated what He had established in this by His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85], and all the sharia were brought back to the sharia of Muhammad (ﷺ).

(p-236) ﴿And those who were Jews﴾ are the Jews, and they were named thus because of their saying: ﴿Indeed, we have turned back to You﴾ [al-A'raf: 156], meaning: we have repented. So their name, according to this, is from hada, yahudu (to repent, to return).

The poet said:

"Indeed I am a man who, from my praise, is repentant (hā'id)"

meaning: penitent. It was also said that they were attributed to Yahudha ibn Ya'qub, and when the name was Arabized it underwent alteration, as the Arabs alter some of what they Arabize from the language of others. al-Zahrawi related that tahwid means speaking with calm, dignity and softness, and he recited:

"And a tender one among those who listen at the forenoon, whose recitation of verses is sung in a melodious, soft chant"

He said: from this the Jews were named. Abu al-Samal read "hādū" with a fatha on the dal.

"And the Christians" is a word derived from naṣr (help). Either because their town is called Nāṣira, and it is said Naṣriyā and Naṣrat; or because they helped one another (tanāṣarū); or because of the saying of 'Isa (peace be upon him): ﴿Who are my helpers toward Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52]. Sibawayh said: its singular is naṣrān and naṣrāna, like nadmān and nadmāna and nadāmā. He recited:

"Both of them fell, and she bowed her head, as a Christian woman bows, not inclining"

al-Tabari recited:

"He remains, when the evening has come, bent over, and at the forenoon he is before her, a Christian [of the sun], bright"

(p-237) Sibawayh said: except that it is not used in speech except with the ya' of relative attribution. al-Khalil said: the singular of the Christians is naṣrī, like mahrī and mahārā.

In the language, al-ṣābi' is one who leaves one religion for another, and for this reason the Arabs used to say of one who embraced Islam: "qad ṣaba'" (he has become a ṣābi'). It was also said that they were named thus when they denied the gods, comparing them to the Sabians of Mosul, who had no piety except their saying: "There is no god but Allah." A group pronounced it with a hamza and made it from ṣaba'at al-nujūm when they rise, and ṣaba'at thaniyyat al-ghulām when it comes out. Abu 'Ali said: it is said ṣaba'a 'alā al-qawm, meaning ṭara'a (came upon), so the ṣābi' is one who abandons his religion in which he was legislated to another religion, just as the ṣābi' 'alā al-qawm abandons his land and moves to another. The readers other than Nafi' recited it with the hamza, for he did not pronounce the hamza. Whoever does not pronounce the hamza makes it from ṣabā yaṣbū, when he inclines, or makes the hamza into a ya'. Sibawayh does not permit this except in poetry.

As for those referred to by His words, the Exalted: ﴿and the Sabians﴾, al-Suddi said: they are a sect of the People of the Book. Mujahid said: they are a people with no religion, neither Jews nor Christians. Ibn Abi Najih said: they are a people whose religion is a mixture between Judaism and Magianism, whose slaughtered animals may not be eaten. Ibn Zayd said: they are a people who say: "There is no god but Allah," but have no works and no book; they were in the region of Mosul. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Qatada said: they are a people who worship the angels, pray toward the qibla, pray the five prayers, and recite the Zabur. Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan saw them and wished to impose the jizya (poll tax) on them lift from them, until he understood that they worship the angels.

The word "man" in His words ﴿whoever believes in Allah﴾ is in the accusative position as a substitution (badal) for "alladhina" (those who). The fa' in (p-238) His words "fa-lahum" is introduced because of the indefiniteness in "man." And "lahum ajruhum" is a subject and predicate, in the position of the predicate of "inna." It is also permissible, and it is good, that "man" be in the nominative position as a subject, meaning the conditional, and the fa' in His words "fa-lahum" is introductory to the consequent, and "lahum ajruhum" is the predicate of "man," and the whole sentence is the predicate of "inna." The returning pronoun referring to "alladhina" is omitted and must be supplied, and its supplying is: ﴿whoever of them believes in Allah﴾ [al-Baqara: 126]. So it is permissible for what follows it to come singular according to its wording, or dual or plural according to its meaning, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [Yunus: 42], where He used the plural according to the meaning; and as in His words: ﴿And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, He will admit him into gardens﴾ [al-Nisa': 13], then He said: ﴿abiding therein﴾ [al-Nisa': 13], where He used the plural according to the meaning. al-Farazdaq said:

"Come, if you pledge to me that you will not betray me, we will be like those two, O wolf, who keep company"

where he used the dual according to the meaning. When what follows "man" comes according to the wording, it is permissible to change to the meaning afterward; but when what follows it comes according to the meaning, it is not used to change afterward to the wording, because confusion enters the speech.

al-Hasan recited "wa-la khawfa" with the accusative, as a negation of genus; the nominative is as a subject. The discussion of a verse like this has already preceded.

As for His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And [recall] when We took your covenant﴾, "idh" is coordinated with what precedes it. The mīthāq is a mif'āl from waththaqa, yathiqu, like mīzān from wazana, yazinu. "Al-ṭūr" is the name of the mountain on which Moses (p-239) was spoken to, as said by Ibn 'Abbas. Mujahid, 'Ikrima, Qatada and others said: "al-ṭūr" is the name of every mountain. This is evidenced by the verse of al-'Ajjaj:

"He drew near his wings from the ṭūr, and passed, hastening, as a falcon hastens when it swoops down"

Ibn 'Abbas also said: al-ṭūr is every mountain that has vegetation; every mountain without vegetation is not a ṭūr.

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: all of this is on the basis that the word is Arabic. Abu al-'Aliya and Mujahid said: it is Syriac, the name of every mountain.

The narrative of this verse is that when Moses, peace be upon him, came to the Children of Israel from Allah, the Exalted, with the tablets in which was the Torah, he said to them: "Take them and hold fast to them." They said: "No, unless Allah speaks to us with them as He spoke to you." So they were struck senseless, then they were revived. He said to them: "Take them." They said: "No." So Allah, the Exalted, commanded the angels, who uprooted a mountain from the mountains of Palestine, its length a farsakh by the like of it, and their army was like that. So it was placed over them like a canopy. Allah, the Exalted, brought out the sea behind them and kindled a fire before them, so His wrath encompassed them. It was said to them: "Take them, and upon you is the covenant that you will not neglect them, or else the mountain will fall upon you, the sea will drown you, and the fire will burn you." So they prostrated in repentance to Allah, and took the Torah with the covenant. al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said, from some scholars: had they taken it the first time, there would not have been a covenant upon them, and their prostration would have been on one side, because they were watching the mountain in fear. But when Allah had mercy on them, they said: "There is no prostration better than a prostration which Allah accepted and by which He showed mercy." So they made their prostration on one side.

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: what cannot be authentic other than this is that Allah, at the time of their prostration, produced faith in their hearts, for they believed under compulsion while their hearts were not at rest. (p-240) I have abridged what was related in the narrative of this verse, and I aimed at its soundest form, the one that the wording of the verse requires. Some people confused the swooning of this story with the swooning of the seventy.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾: in the speech there is an omission, its supplied form being: "And We said: take." "Ataynakum" means: We gave you. "Bi-quwwa" (with strength): Ibn 'Abbas said its meaning is with earnestness and diligence. It was said: with much study. Ibn Zayd said its meaning is with affirmation and verification. al-Rabi' said its meaning is with obedience to Allah. ﴿And remember what is in it﴾, that is, reflect upon it, preserve its commands and its warnings, and do not forget it or neglect it. The pronoun returns to ﴿what We have given you﴾, meaning the Torah. The supplied complement of "ma" is: "remember what has been established in it." And ﴿that you may be righteous﴾ is an expression of hope regarding humankind.

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Then you turned away after that﴾, the verse. "Tawalla" is on the pattern of "tafa''ala", and its origin is turning away from a thing physically, and turning one's back. Then it was used figuratively and broadly for turning away from matters, religions and beliefs.

﴿The bounty of Allah﴾ is in the nominative as a subject, and the predicate is omitted according to Sibawayh, and it is not permissible to state it because it is not needed. Its supplied form is: "Were it not for the bounty of Allah upon you, it would have rescued you." "And His mercy" is coordinated with "bounty." Qatada said: the bounty of Allah is Islam, and His mercy is the Qur'an.

The qāḍī Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is on the basis that the addressee of His words "upon you," in wording and meaning, is those who lived in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ). The majority hold that the meaning intended is those who preceded. "Lakuntum" is the answer to "lawla," and ﴿among the losers﴾ is the predicate of "kana," and "al-khusran" is loss.

Their turning away after that: either by sins, so the bounty of Allah was in repentance and in granting them respite to repent; or their turning away was by disbelief, so the bounty of Allah was that He did not hasten to destroy them, so that among their descendants there would be one who believes. Or the intended meaning is whoever reached Muhammad (ﷺ), and some people said this, and on it the saying of Qatada is directed: (p-241) that the bounty is Islam and the mercy is the Qur'an. It is also directed that the bounty and mercy be understood as their attaining the time of Muhammad (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 65–67:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And you have certainly known those who transgressed among you in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and driven away."﴾ ﴿And We made it a deterrent punishment for those present and those after them, and an admonition to the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾

"عَلِمْتُمُ" (ʿalimtum) means "you recognized" (ʿaraftum), as you say ʿalimtu Zaydan, meaning ʿarraftuhu (I knew Zayd). Thus al-ʿilm (knowledge) does not transitively take more than one object. "اعْتَدَوْا" (iʿtadaw) means "they went beyond the limit," a derivative of al-iʿtidaʾ (transgression). "فِي السَبْتِ" (fi as-sabt) means "on the day of Saturday," though it may be understood as "in the ruling of the Sabbath." "السَبْتُ" (as-sabt) is derived either from al-subut, which is rest and repose, or from al-sabt, which is cutting, because things were completed and their creation finished on it.

The story of their transgression concerning it is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded Moses, peace be upon him, concerning Friday and informed him of its virtue, as He commanded all the prophets. Moses, peace be upon him, conveyed that to the Children of Israel from Allah and commanded them to observe it, but they refused and moved it to Saturday. So Allah revealed to Moses that he should leave them and what they had chosen from that, and He tested them concerning it by commanding them to abstain from work, and He forbade them to hunt fish, and He intensified the trial for them by making the fish come on Saturday until they came out onto the open areas. This was related by al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. It was also said: until they brought out their snouts from the water. That was either by inspiration from Allah, the Exalted, or by a command whose reason is not explained. Or it was that they understood the sense of security that is in the day, through its repetition, until they understood that. Do you not see that Allah, the Exalted, has inspired animals with the sense of fear that is in Friday from the matter of the Resurrection? The saying of the Prophet ﷺ supports this: "There is no animal except that it is attentive on Friday out of fear of the Hour." And the doves of Makkah have understood the sense of security, though its connection is close to their understanding.

The matter of the Children of Israel was at Aylah on the sea. When Saturday passed, the fish would depart and not appear until the next Saturday. They remained in this state for a time until they desired fish. A man deliberately, on Saturday, tied a fish with a rope and drove a stake for it at the shore. When Saturday passed, he came and took it. A group heard of his deed and did the same. It was also said: rather, a man dug a pit on a day other than Saturday, into which the sea would flow. When it was Saturday, the fish came out and got into the pit. When the sea receded, the water left by the channel of the pit and the fish remained, so he came after Saturday and took it. A group did the same, and this became widespread until they hunted it openly on Saturday and sold it in the markets. This was among the greatest transgressions. Among the Children of Israel there was a group that forbade this and was saved from the punishment. There was a group among them that neither disobeyed nor forbade. It was said: it was saved along with those who forbade, and it was said: it perished along with the disobedient.

"كُونُوا" (kūnū) is an imperative word, the imperative of creation, like His saying, Exalted, to everything: "Be, and it is" (kun fayakūn). They were not commanded, in the transition to the state of transformation, to do anything, nor did they have any acquisition in it. "خاسِئِينَ" (khāsiʾīn) means "distanced, humiliated, abased," as is said to a dog and to the one who is driven away: "ukhsa'" (begone). You say "khasa'tuhu fakhasaʾa" (I drove him off and he went off). Its place in grammar is the accusative, either as a circumstantial state or as a second predicate after a predicate.

It is related in their narrative that Allah, the Exalted, transformed the disobedient into apes at night. The saved ones woke in the morning and went to their mosques and gathering places, and they did not see any of the perished. They said, "Surely something has happened to the people," so they opened the doors upon them as they had been closed at night, and they found them "apes," recognizing the man and the woman. It was also said: the saved ones had divided the town between themselves and the disobedient with a wall, as a disavowal of them. They woke in the morning and the city of the perished had not been opened, so they climbed over the wall, and behold, they were apes leaping upon one another.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is established, that the transformed one does not have offspring, does not eat, does not drink, and does not live longer than three days. And there occurs in the Sahih of Muslim from him, peace be upon him: "A nation among the nations was lost, and I think it was the mice." The apparent meaning of this is that the transformed ones have offspring. If he intended this, then it was a presumption on his part, peace be upon him, in a matter that has no bearing on conveying the message, and then it was revealed to him afterwards that the transformed one does not have offspring. A parallel to what we have said is his, peace be upon him, descent at the waters of Badr and his command to abandon the pollination of palms, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "If I inform you of an opinion in worldly matters, then I am only a human being." It is related from Mujahid, concerning the interpretation of this verse, that only their hearts were transformed, and their understandings were returned like the understandings of apes. The first view is stronger and more apparent. The pronoun in "فَجَعَلْناها" (fajaʿalnāhā) may refer to the transformation and the punishment, may refer to the nation that was transformed, may refer to the apes, and may refer to the town, since the meaning of the speech requires it. It was also said it refers to the fish, but in this view there is distance.

"النَكالُ" (nakāl) is deterrence through punishment, and "النَكْلِ" and "الأنْكالِ" are iron fetters. So nakāl is a punishment by which someone other than the one punished is deterred from doing the same act. Al-Suddi said: "what is before it" means what preceded it of the sins of the people, and "what is after it" means for whoever sins after it with similar sins. This is a good view. Others said: "what is before it" means those who were present among the saved, and "what is after it" means those who come after. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "for what is before it" means for the people after them, so that they may be warned and guard themselves, and "what is after it" means for those who remained of them as a lesson.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I do not think this is authentically from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, because the indication of "what is before the hand" is not like that in speech. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: "for what is before it and what is after it" means from the towns. This is an arrangement of crimes, not an arrangement in time. "مَوْعِظَةً" (mawʿiẓa) is a noun of place or instrument derived from being admonished and restrained. "لِلْمُتَّقِينَ" (lil-muttaqīn) means "for those who were forbidden and were saved." A group said: it means for the community of Muhammad ﷺ. The wording encompasses every God-fearing person from every nation.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And when Moses said﴾ to the end of the verse. "إذْ" (idh) is conjoined to what preceded, and the purpose is to remind them of their ancestors' breaking of the covenant. Abu ʿAmr recited "يَأْمُرُكُمْ" (yaʾmurukum) with the letter rāʾ sukūn, and it is related from him that he elided the vowel. The discussion of a similar form has already passed in "بارِئِكُمْ" (bāriʾikum).

The occasion of this verse, as is related, is that a man from the Children of Israel grew old and had wealth, and his nephew was impatient for his death. It was said: his brother, or his two paternal cousins, or heirs in number, unspecified. He killed him so that he would inherit, and threw him into a tribe other than his own in order to take his blood-money and stain them with his blood. It was also said: the Children of Israel were in two neighboring towns, and he threw him at the gate of one of the two cities, the one in which he was not killed. Then he and his tribe began searching for him until they found him slain, and they laid the charge on the tribe or on the inhabitants of the town where the corpse was found. They denied killing him, and a dispute arose among the Children of Israel about it until they took up weapons. The people of wisdom among them said: "Shall we fight while the Messenger of Allah is among us?" So they went to Moses, peace be upon him, related the story to him, and asked him for clarification. Allah revealed to him that they should slaughter a cow, and the corpse would be struck with a part of it, and it would come to life and report its killer. So he said to them: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, and their reply was: ﴿Do you take us in ridicule?﴾

Al-Jahdari recited "أيَتَّخِذُنا" (ayattakhidhunā) with a yāʾ, meaning "Does Allah take us [in ridicule]?" Hamzah recited "هُزُؤًا" (huzuʾan) with sukūn on the zāy and the hamza, which is a dialect form. ʿAsim recited "هُزُؤٌ" (huzuʾun) with ḍammah on the zāy, the hāʾ, and the hamza, and also recited without hamza "هُزُوًا" (huzūan), as transmitted by Abu ʿAli. A group of reciters recited with ḍammah on the hāʾ and the zāy, with the hamza between-between, and it is related from Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba the ḍammah on the hāʾ and the shadda on the zāy, "هُزًّا" (huzzan).

This statement by the Children of Israel apparently indicates corruption of belief in the one who said it, and faith is not valid for one who says to a prophet whose miracles have become manifest, and who said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, "Do you take us in ridicule?" Had anyone said this today about some statement of the Prophet ﷺ, it would be obligatory to declare him a disbeliever. A group went to the view that this came from them out of coarseness of disposition, harshness, and disobedience, in the manner of what the one who said to the Prophet ﷺ regarding the division of the spoils of Hunayn said: "Indeed this is a division not intended for the sake of Allah," and as the other said to him: "Be just, O Muhammad." Each is possible, and Allah knows best.

Moses's saying, peace be upon him: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾ may bear two meanings: one of them is seeking refuge from ignorance in that he would report about Allah, the Exalted, mockingly; and the other is from the ignorance, as they were ignorant in their saying ﴿Do you take us in ridicule?﴾ toward one who informs them about Allah, the Exalted.

Moses's saying, peace be upon him: ﴿I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant﴾ may bear two meanings: one of them is seeking refuge from ignorance in that he would report about Allah, the Exalted, mockingly; and the other is from the ignorance, as they were ignorant in their saying ﴿Do you take us in ridicule?﴾ toward one who informs them about Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 65–67:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And you have certainly known those who transgressed among you in the matter of the Sabbath, so We said to them, "Be apes, despised and driven away."﴾ ﴿And We made it a deterrent punishment for those present and those after them, and an admonition to the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow." They said, "Do you take us in ridicule?" He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾

"عَلِمْتُمُ" (ʿalimtum) means "you recognized" (ʿaraftum), as you say ʿalimtu Zaydan, meaning ʿarraftuhu (I knew Zayd). Thus al-ʿilm (knowledge) does not transitively take more than one object. "اعْتَدَوْا" (iʿtadaw) means "they went beyond the limit," a derivative of al-iʿtidaʾ (transgression). "فِي السَبْتِ" (fi as-sabt) means "on the day of Saturday," though it may be understood as "in the ruling of the Sabbath." "السَبْتُ" (as-sabt) is derived either from al-subut, which is rest and repose, or from al-sabt, which is cutting, because things were completed and their creation finished on it.

The story of their transgression concerning it is that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, commanded Moses, peace be upon him, concerning Friday and informed him of its virtue, as He commanded all the prophets. Moses, peace be upon him, conveyed that to the Children of Israel from Allah and commanded them to observe it, but they refused and moved it to Saturday. So Allah revealed to Moses that he should leave them and what they had chosen from that, and He tested them concerning it by commanding them to abstain from work, and He forbade them to hunt fish, and He intensified the trial for them by making the fish come on Saturday until they came out onto the open areas. This was related by al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan. It was also said: until they brought out their snouts from the water. That was either by inspiration from Allah, the Exalted, or by a command whose reason is not explained. Or it was that they understood the sense of security that is in the day, through its repetition, until they understood that. Do you not see that Allah, the Exalted, has inspired animals with the sense of fear that is in Friday from the matter of the Resurrection? The saying of the Prophet ﷺ supports this: "There is no animal except that it is attentive on Friday out of fear of the Hour." And the doves of Makkah have understood the sense of security, though its connection is close to their understanding.

The matter of the Children of Israel was at Aylah on the sea. When Saturday passed, the fish would depart and not appear until the next Saturday. They remained in this state for a time until they desired fish. A man deliberately, on Saturday, tied a fish with a rope and drove a stake for it at the shore. When Saturday passed, he came and took it. A group heard of his deed and did the same. It was also said: rather, a man dug a pit on a day other than Saturday, into which the sea would flow. When it was Saturday, the fish came out and got into the pit. When the sea receded, the water left by the channel of the pit and the fish remained, so he came after Saturday and took it. A group did the same, and this became widespread until they hunted it openly on Saturday and sold it in the markets. This was among the greatest transgressions. Among the Children of Israel there was a group that forbade this and was saved from the punishment. There was a group among them that neither disobeyed nor forbade. It was said: it was saved along with those who forbade, and it was said: it perished along with the disobedient.

"كُونُوا" (kūnū) is an imperative word, the imperative of creation, like His saying, Exalted, to everything: "Be, and it is" (kun fayakūn). They were not commanded, in the transition to the state of transformation, to do anything, nor did they have any acquisition in it. "خاسِئِينَ" (khāsiʾīn) means "distanced, humiliated, abased," as is said to a dog and to the one who is driven away: "ukhsa'" (begone). You say "khasa'tuhu fakhasaʾa" (I drove him off and he went off). Its place in grammar is the accusative, either as a circumstantial state or as a second predicate after a predicate.

It is related in their narrative that Allah, the Exalted, transformed the disobedient into apes at night. The saved ones woke in the morning and went to their mosques and gathering places, and they did not see any of the perished. They said, "Surely something has happened to the people," so they opened the doors upon them as they had been closed at night, and they found them "apes," recognizing the man and the woman. It was also said: the saved ones had divided the town between themselves and the disobedient with a wall, as a disavowal of them. They woke in the morning and the city of the perished had not been opened, so they climbed over the wall, and behold, they were apes leaping upon one another.

It is related from the Prophet ﷺ, and it is established, that the transformed one does not have offspring, does not eat, does not drink, and does not live longer than three days. And there occurs in the Sahih of Muslim from him, peace be upon him: "A nation among the nations was lost, and I think it was the mice." The apparent meaning of this is that the transformed ones have offspring. If he intended this, then it was a presumption on his part, peace be upon him, in a matter that has no bearing on conveying the message, and then it was revealed to him afterwards that the transformed one does not have offspring. A parallel to what we have said is his, peace be upon him, descent at the waters of Badr and his command to abandon the pollination of palms, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "If I inform you of an opinion in worldly matters, then I am only a human being." It is related from Mujahid, concerning the interpretation of this verse, that only their hearts were transformed, and their understandings were returned like the understandings of apes. The first view is stronger and more apparent. The pronoun in "فَجَعَلْناها" (fajaʿalnāhā) may refer to the transformation and the punishment, may refer to the nation that was transformed, may refer to the apes, and may refer to the town, since the meaning of the speech requires it. It was also said it refers to the fish, but in this view there is distance.

"النَكالُ" (nakāl) is deterrence through punishment, and "النَكْلِ" and "الأنْكالِ" are iron fetters. So nakāl is a punishment by which someone other than the one punished is deterred from doing the same act. Al-Suddi said: "what is before it" means what preceded it of the sins of the people, and "what is after it" means for whoever sins after it with similar sins. This is a good view. Others said: "what is before it" means those who were present among the saved, and "what is after it" means those who come after. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "for what is before it" means for the people after them, so that they may be warned and guard themselves, and "what is after it" means for those who remained of them as a lesson.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: I do not think this is authentically from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, because the indication of "what is before the hand" is not like that in speech. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: "for what is before it and what is after it" means from the towns. This is an arrangement of crimes, not an arrangement in time. "مَوْعِظَةً" (mawʿiẓa) is a noun of place or instrument derived from being admonished and restrained. "لِلْمُتَّقِينَ" (lil-muttaqīn) means "for those who were forbidden and were saved." A group said: it means for the community of Muhammad ﷺ. The wording encompasses every God-fearing person from every nation.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And when Moses said﴾ to the end of the verse. "إذْ" (idh) is conjoined to what preceded, and the purpose is to remind them of their ancestors' breaking of the covenant. Abu ʿAmr recited "يَأْمُرُكُمْ" (yaʾmurukum) with the letter rāʾ sukūn, and it is related from him that he elided the vowel. The discussion of a similar form has already passed in "بارِئِكُمْ" (bāriʾikum).

The occasion of this verse, as is related, is that a man from the Children of Israel grew old and had wealth, and his nephew was impatient for his death. It was said: his brother, or his two paternal cousins, or heirs in number, unspecified. He killed him so that he would inherit, and threw him into a tribe other than his own in order to take his blood-money and stain them with his blood. It was also said: the Children of Israel were in two neighboring towns, and he threw him at the gate of one of the two cities, the one in which he was not killed. Then he and his tribe began searching for him until they found him slain, and they laid the charge on the tribe or on the inhabitants of the town where the corpse was found. They denied killing him, and a dispute arose among the Children of Israel about it until they took up weapons. The people of wisdom among them said: "Shall we fight while the Messenger of Allah is among us?" So they went to Moses, peace be upon him, related the story to him, and asked him for clarification. Allah revealed to him that they should slaughter a cow, and the corpse would be struck with a part of it, and it would come to life and report its killer. So he said to them: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, and their reply was: ﴿Do you take us in ridicule?﴾

Al-Jahdari recited "أيَتَّخِذُنا" (ayattakhidhunā) with a yāʾ, meaning "Does Allah take us [in ridicule]?" Hamzah recited "هُزُؤًا" (huzuʾan) with sukūn on the zāy and the hamza, which is a dialect form. ʿAsim recited "هُزُؤٌ" (huzuʾun) with ḍammah on the zāy, the hāʾ, and the hamza, and also recited without hamza "هُزُوًا" (huzūan), as transmitted by Abu ʿAli. A group of reciters recited with ḍammah on the hāʾ and the zāy, with the hamza between-between, and it is related from Abu Jaʿfar and Shayba the ḍammah on the hāʾ and the shadda on the zāy, "هُزًّا" (huzzan).

This statement by the Children of Israel apparently indicates corruption of belief in the one who said it, and faith is not valid for one who says to a prophet whose miracles have become manifest, and who said: ﴿Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow﴾, "Do you take us in ridicule?" Had anyone said this today about some statement of the Prophet ﷺ, it would be obligatory to declare him a disbeliever. A group went to the view that this came from them out of coarseness of disposition, harshness, and disobedience, in the manner of what the one who said to the Prophet ﷺ regarding the division of the spoils of Hunayn said: "Indeed this is a division not intended for the sake of Allah," and as the other said to him: "Be just, O Muhammad." Each is possible, and Allah knows best.

[Quran 2:68–70 as quoted in the commentary]

**﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what she is." He said: "Indeed, He says she is a cow neither old (fari') nor virgin (bikr), but middle-aged (awan) between that. So do what you are commanded."﴾**

**﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what her color is." He said: "Indeed, He says she is a cow, bright yellow (safra'), her color vivid, pleasing to the beholders."﴾**

**﴿They said: "Call upon your Lord for us, that He may make clear to us what she is. Indeed, cows have become confused to us, and we, if God wills, will surely be guided."﴾**

This is their (the Children of Israel's) obstinacy and their lack of obedience. Had they complied with the command and taken any cow and slaughtered it, they would have fulfilled what they were commanded. But they made it difficult, so God made it difficult for them. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliya, and others.

The dialect of the Banu 'Amir pronounces "ud'u" (call) with a kasra on the 'ayn. "Ma" is an interrogative (istifham) in the nominative as the subject (mubtada', the topic of the sentence), and "hiya" is its predicate (khabar). "Fari'un" is in the nominative as an adjective (na't, descriptive modifier) of "baqara" (cow), according to the view of al-Akhfash, or as the predicate of an implied subject, its implied form being "la hiya fari'un" (she is not old).

Al-fari' is the aged, decrepit cow that no longer bears young. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Mujahid, and others.

One says "faradat" (she became old), in the present "tafridu," with the 'ayn vowelled with fatha, and the verbal noun is "furuwdan." It is also said "furidat" with the 'ayn vowelled with damma. Anything that has passed and whose time has become long is called "fari'." A poet said:

> O many a one who bears a grudge against me, an old enmity, for him are cycles like the cycles of a menstruating woman.

Al-bikr among cattle is the one that has not borne young since she was young. Ibn Qutayba related that it is the one that has borne only one calf. Al-bikr among women is the one who has not been touched by a man. Al-bikr among children is the first-born. Among things that are new, it is the first. Al-'awan is the one that has borne young repeatedly, time after time. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Akhfash, and the lexicographers have transmitted it. From it comes the Arab saying: "The awan does not need to be taught the (wine) cup." And a war described as "harbun 'awan" is one in which fighting has taken place two times or more. "Awan" is in the nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, its implied form being "hiya 'awan" (she is middle-aged). Its plural is "'awn" with the waw sukun, and "'awun" with the waw vowelled with damma has been heard.

"Bayn" (between) by rule is supposed to be followed by two items, but here it is followed by "dhalika" (that). This is because "dhalika" is used to point to things that have been stated in general terms. According to Sibawayh, "dhalika" takes the place of what was mentioned, so it refers to a singular item in its usual sense, and although two (qualities) were mentioned, "bayn" is still used in its usual way.

His words, ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, are a renewal of the command, an emphasis, and an admonition to abandon obstinacy. But they did not abandon it. "Ma" is in the nominative as the subject, and "lawnuha" (its color) is its predicate.

Ibn Zayd and the majority of people said regarding His words "safra'" (yellow) that she was entirely yellow. Makki, may God have mercy on him, related from some of them: even the horns and hooves. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said she was yellow only in her horns and hooves. Al-Hasan also said: "Safra'" means "black." This is an anomalous view that is not used figuratively except for camels, and the statement of al-A'sha, Maymun ibn Qays, was interpreted in this way:

> Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts; they are yellow, their young like raisins.

Al-fuqu' is an adjective specific to yellow, just as "ahmar" (red) is specific to "qani'" (bright red), "aswad" (black) to "halik" (deep black), "abyad" (white) to "nasi'" (pure white), and "akhdar" (green) to "nadir" (fresh green). "Lawnuha" is the subject of "faqi'" (intensely), and ﴿tasurru al-nathirin﴾ (pleasing to the beholders). Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "It was as if the rays of the sun were coming out of its skin." So its meaning is that it pleases the onlookers. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "Yellow pleases the soul." Ibn 'Abbas urged the wearing of yellow shoes, as related from him by al-Naqqash. It is also reported that Ibn al-Zubayr and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir forbade the wearing of black shoes, because they cause worry. Abu al-'Aliya and al-Suddi said: ﴿tasurru al-nathirin﴾ means in her fatness and her entire appearance. After all this, they asked Him about what she was, asking like people who were bewildered, who had already sensed the evil of disobedience.

"Al-baqar" is the plural of "baqara," and it is also pluralized as "baqir." Ibn Yamur and 'Ikrima recited it this way, and as far as I know they did not recite it with the other forms, "buqayr" or "bayqur."

The Seven (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers) recited "tashabaha" as a past-tense verb. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj recited "tashshabahu," with the shin doubled and the ha' vowelled with damma. The original form is "tatashabahu," which was assimilated. This is also the recitation of Yahya ibn Ya'mur. They also recited "tushabihu," with the shin lightened by dropping the second ta'. Ibn Mas'ud recited "yushabihu" with a ya' and assimilation of the ta'. Al-Mahdawi related from al-Mu'ayti "tashshabbaha" with the shin and ba' doubled and no alif. Abu 'Amr al-Dani related the recitation "mutashabbih" as an active participle from "tashabbaha." It is also related as "yatashabahu."

In their exception (istithna', saying "in sha' Allah") in this final question there is a sign of repentance, submission, regret, and eagerness to comply with the command. It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Had they not made that exception, they would never have been guided to it." The pronoun in "inna" is the subject of "inna," and "muhtadun" is its predicate. The "lam" is for emphasis. The exception is a parenthetical interjection, placed before the mention of guidance to give it emphasis.

Its plural is "'awn" with the waw sukun, and "'awun" with the waw vowelled with damma has been heard.

"Bayn" (between) by rule is supposed to be followed by two items, but here it is followed by "dhalika" (that). This is because "dhalika" is used to point to things that have been stated in general terms. According to Sibawayh, "dhalika" takes the place of what was mentioned, so it refers to a singular item in its usual sense, and although two (qualities) were mentioned, "bayn" is still used in its usual way.

His words, ﴿So do what you are commanded﴾, are a renewal of the command, an emphasis, and an admonition to abandon obstinacy. But they did not abandon it. "Ma" is in the nominative as the subject, and "lawnuha" (its color) is its predicate.

Ibn Zayd and the majority of people said regarding His words "safra'" (yellow) that she was entirely yellow. Makki, may God have mercy on him, related from some of them: even the horns and hooves. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said she was yellow only in her horns and hooves. Al-Hasan also said: "Safra'" means "black." This is an anomalous view that is not used figuratively except for camels, and the statement of al-A'sha, Maymun ibn Qays, was interpreted in this way:

> Those are my horses from him, and those are my mounts; they are yellow, their young like raisins.

Al-fuqu' is an adjective specific to yellow, just as "ahmar" (red) is specific to "qani'" (bright red), "aswad" (black) to "halik" (deep black), "abyad" (white) to "nasi'" (pure white), and "akhdar" (green) to "nadir" (fresh green). "Lawnuha" is the subject of "faqi'" (intensely), and ﴿tasurru al-nathirin﴾ (pleasing to the beholders). Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "It was as if the rays of the sun were coming out of its skin." So its meaning is that it pleases the onlookers. For this reason Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "Yellow pleases the soul." Ibn 'Abbas urged the wearing of yellow shoes, as related from him by al-Naqqash. It is also reported that Ibn al-Zubayr and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir forbade the wearing of black shoes, because they cause worry. Abu al-'Aliya and al-Suddi said: ﴿tasurru al-nathirin﴾ means in her fatness and her entire appearance. After all this, they asked Him about what she was, asking like people who were bewildered, who had already sensed the evil of disobedience.

"Al-baqar" is the plural of "baqara," and it is also pluralized as "baqir." Ibn Yamur and 'Ikrima recited it this way, and as far as I know they did not recite it with the other forms, "buqayr" or "bayqur."

The Seven (al-Sab'a, the seven canonical readers) recited "tashabaha" as a past-tense verb. Al-Hasan and al-A'raj recited "tashshabahu," with the shin doubled and the ha' vowelled with damma. The original form is "tatashabahu," which was assimilated. This is also the recitation of Yahya ibn Ya'mur. They also recited "tushabihu," with the shin lightened by dropping the second ta'. Ibn Mas'ud recited "yushabihu" with a ya' and assimilation of the ta'. Al-Mahdawi related from al-Mu'ayti "tashshabbaha" with the shin and ba' doubled and no alif. Abu 'Amr al-Dani related the recitation "mutashabbih" as an active participle from "tashabbaha." It is also related as "yatashabahu."

In their exception (istithna', saying "in sha' Allah") in this final question there is a sign of repentance, submission, regret, and eagerness to comply with the command. It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Had they not made that exception, they would never have been guided to it." The pronoun in "inna" is the subject of "inna," and "muhtadun" is its predicate. The "lam" is for emphasis. The exception is a parenthetical interjection, placed before the mention of guidance to give it emphasis.

[p-250] "Dhalul" means a cow made submissive through work and training. One says *baqara dhalul*, meaning a cow that is clearly tame, with the *dhal* vowelled with a kasra. *Rajul dhalul* (a man who is clearly humble) is said with a damma on the *dhal*. *Dhalul* is an adjective (na't) for *baqara* ("cow"), or it is taken as implying a pronoun meaning "it" (hiya). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read *la dhalula* with a fatha on the *lam*.

*Tuthir al-ard* means "she plows the earth" through tillage. According to some, this clause is in a position of raised case (raf') as a description of the cow, meaning: "not tame, plowing." Others said that *tuthir* is a new independent verb (fi'l mustani'af), and the meaning is that she is obliged to plow, and that she used to plow and not irrigate. This clause cannot be in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because it follows an indefinite noun (nakira).

*Tasqi al-harth* means "she irrigates the tilled land," by means of a water-wheel (saniya) or other implements. *Al-harth* is what has been plowed and sown. *Musallama* is an intensive form (bina' mubalagha) from *salama* ("soundness"). Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliya said it means free from defects. Mujahid and Qatada said it means free from markings and colours. Others said it means free from work. *La shiyata fiha* means there is no variation in its colour: it is entirely yellow, with no white, no red and no black. This was said by Ibn Zayd and others. *Al-mushi* is one of mixed colours, and from it comes *wushiya al-thawb*, meaning the cloth was decorated with colours. From it also comes *al-washi* (the slanderer), because he decorates his lies with colourful speech. *Al-thawr al-ashyah* is the bull that has a spot (balqa). One says: a horse *ablaq*, a ram *akhraj*, a he-goat *abraq*, a dog *abqa'*, and a bull *ashyu'*. All of these mean "having a spot."

These descriptions of the cow have a cause: they were strict, so God was strict with them. The religion of God is ease, and excessive probing in questioning the Prophets (peace be upon them) is blameworthy.

The story of the origin of this cow, as it is related, is that a man from the Children of Israel had a son, and he had a young cow. He released it into a thicket and said: "O God, I entrust to You this calf for this child." Then the man died. When the boy grew up, his mother said to him: "Your father entrusted a calf to God for you. Go and take it." He went, and when the cow saw him, she came to him until he took hold of her horns. She had been wild, but he began to lead her toward his mother. The Children of Israel met him and found his cow in the description they had been commanded.

A group related that there was a man among the Children of Israel who was dutiful to his father. One day his father slept, and under his head were the keys to their dwelling. A jewel merchant passed by him and offered to buy it for sixty thousand. The son of the sleeper said to him: "Wait until my father wakes, and I will take it from you for seventy thousand." The jewel merchant said to him: "Wake your father, and I will give it to you for fifty thousand." They kept doing this until the price reached one hundred thousand, and the jewel merchant lowered it to thirty thousand. The son of the sleeper said to him: "By God, I will not buy it from you for anything." Out of dutifulness to his father, God compensated him by making the cow come into his possession.

Others said it was found with an old woman who was supporting orphans, and the cow belonged to them. There are other differences in its story, this being its general meaning. When the cow was found, they bargained with its owner, and he overcharged them. Its value, as related from 'Ikrima, was three dinars. They brought him to Musa (peace be upon him) and said: "This man has overcharged us." He said to them: "Satisfy him regarding his property, and buy it from him for its weight once." This was said by 'Ubayda al-Salmani. It was also said: for its weight twice. Al-Suddi said: for its weight ten times. Mujahid said: it belonged to a man who was dutiful to his mother, and they took it from him for dinars equal to the amount of its hide filled with them. Makki related that this cow descended from heaven and was not one of the cattle of the earth. Al-Tabari related from al-Hasan that it was wild.

*Al-'An* (now) is built on fatha. It is not made definite by this alif and lam. Do you not see that they never separate from it in usage? It was made indeclinable because it has taken on the meaning of the definite particle, and because it occupies the position of an indefinite, since its meaning is "this time." It refers to the period between the past and the future. It was read *qalu al-'an* with a sukun on the *lam* and a hamza after it; *qalu al-'an* with a long vowel on the waw and a fatha on the *lam* without hamza; *qalu al-'an* with the waw dropped from pronunciation and no hamza; and *qalu al-'an* with the first alif cut (pronounced as a hamza) even though it is an alif of connection, just as one says *ya Allahu*.

*Ji'ta bil-haqq* (you have brought the truth), according to those who regarded them as disobedient, means: you have made clear to us the utmost clarity. *Ji'ta bil-haqq* (you have brought the truth) which we sought, not that he used to come before that with something other than the truth. According to Ibn Zayd, who interpreted their conversation as disbelief, it means: now you have spoken truly, and they submitted in this situation when it was made clear to them that it was sound. It was also said that they identified it with these descriptions and said: this is the cow of such-and-such a person. This verse indicates that slaughter is the basic rule for cattle, and if it is slaughtered by cutting the throat (nahr), it is also valid.

God's words, ﴿and they almost did not do it﴾, are an expression of their hesitation in slaughtering it and their slowness in hastening to the command of God. Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: that was on their part because of the high price of the cow and the greatness of its cost. Others said: it was out of fear of disgrace concerning the matter of the killer. It was also said: it was according to their known habit of little obedience and their obstinacy toward the Prophets. The story of the slain man, which is meant by God's words ﴿and when you killed a soul﴾, has already been mentioned. The meaning is: We said to them, remember when "you killed" and "disputed about it." *Idda'ara'tum* originally was *tadara'tum*. Then the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*, so beginning with an assimilated letter became impossible, and an alif of connection was brought in. Its meaning is "you pushed away from one another," that is, some of you pushed the killing of the slain man onto others. The poet said:

*"The flood's repelling met a repelling that pushes it back..."*

Another said:

*"A man who repels the adversaries with speech, like the edge of the Hindi Samsama sword."*

The pronoun in His words "in it" refers to the soul; it was also said to refer to the killers. Abu Haywa and Abu al-Sawwar al-Ghanawi read *"wa idh qatalatum nasamatan fa-idda'ara'tum"*. A group read *"fa-tadara'tum"* according to the original form. The position of *ma* is in the accusative, governed by *mukhrijun*, and what is concealed is the matter of the slain man. As for His words ﴿Strike him with part of it﴾, this is a sign from God Most High through the hands of Musa (peace be upon him): He commanded them to strike the slain man with part of the cow, and he would come to life and tell who his killer was. It was said: they struck him. It was also said: they struck his grave, because Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that the matter of the slain man occurred before crossing the sea, and that they continued seeking the cow for forty years. Al-Qurazi said: they were commanded to seek it when it was not yet in the loins or the womb. Al-Suddi said: he struck with the fleshy part between the shoulders. Mujahid, Qatada and 'Ubayda al-Salmani said: he struck with the thigh. It was also said he struck with the tongue, and it was said: with the tail. Abu al-'Aliya said: with one of its bones.

God's words ﴿Thus God brings the dead to life﴾, the verse: the demonstrative *dhalika* ("thus") refers to the bringing to life contained in the story of the verse, since in the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimated meaning being: they struck him, and he came to life. In this verse there is an exhortation to take lesson, and an indication of resurrection in the Hereafter. Its apparent meaning is that it is an address to the Children of Israel at that time, and it was related to Muhammad (ﷺ) so that he might take lesson from it until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari held that it is an address to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that it is separated from His words ﴿Strike him with part of it﴾. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) used this incident as evidence for permitting the testimony of the slain man, and that the procedure of *qasama* (the oath-taking procedure in homicide cases, where the claimants swear to establish blame) may apply together with it.
