Then the *ta'* was assimilated into the *dal*, so beginning with an assimilated letter became impossible, and an alif of connection was brought in. Its meaning is "you pushed away from one another," that is, some of you pushed the killing of the slain man onto others. The poet said:

*"The flood's repelling met a repelling that pushes it back..."*

Another said:

*"A man who repels the adversaries with speech, like the edge of the Hindi Samsama sword."*

The pronoun in His words "in it" refers to the soul; it was also said to refer to the killers. Abu Haywa and Abu al-Sawwar al-Ghanawi read *"wa idh qatalatum nasamatan fa-idda'ara'tum"*. A group read *"fa-tadara'tum"* according to the original form. The position of *ma* is in the accusative, governed by *mukhrijun*, and what is concealed is the matter of the slain man. As for His words ﴿Strike him with part of it﴾, this is a sign from God Most High through the hands of Musa (peace be upon him): He commanded them to strike the slain man with part of the cow, and he would come to life and tell who his killer was. It was said: they struck him. It was also said: they struck his grave, because Ibn 'Abbas mentioned that the matter of the slain man occurred before crossing the sea, and that they continued seeking the cow for forty years. Al-Qurazi said: they were commanded to seek it when it was not yet in the loins or the womb. Al-Suddi said: he struck with the fleshy part between the shoulders. Mujahid, Qatada and 'Ubayda al-Salmani said: he struck with the thigh. It was also said he struck with the tongue, and it was said: with the tail. Abu al-'Aliya said: with one of its bones.

God's words ﴿Thus God brings the dead to life﴾, the verse: the demonstrative *dhalika* ("thus") refers to the bringing to life contained in the story of the verse, since in the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimated meaning being: they struck him, and he came to life. In this verse there is an exhortation to take lesson, and an indication of resurrection in the Hereafter. Its apparent meaning is that it is an address to the Children of Israel at that time, and it was related to Muhammad (ﷺ) so that he might take lesson from it until the Day of Resurrection. Al-Tabari held that it is an address to the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ), and that it is separated from His words ﴿Strike him with part of it﴾. Malik (may Allah have mercy on him) used this incident as evidence for permitting the testimony of the slain man, and that the procedure of *qasama* (the oath-taking procedure in homicide cases, where the claimants swear to establish blame) may apply together with it.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAtiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah 2, verses 74–75:**

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Then your hearts hardened after that, so they were like stones, or even harder. And indeed, among stones are those from which rivers gush forth, and indeed, among them are those that split open so water comes out of them, and indeed, among them are those that fall down from fear of Allah. And Allah is not unaware of what you do.﴾ ﴿Do you then hope that they will believe in you, when a group of them used to hear the speech of Allah and then distort it after they had understood it, while they knew?﴾

"Qasat" means it became hard and dry. It is an expression for their hearts being empty of turning back (*inabah*) to Allah and submission (*idhʿan*) to the signs of Allah the Exalted. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the intended meaning is the hearts of the heirs of the murdered man, because when he came back to life and said that they had killed him, and then returned to the state of his death, they denied his killing and said, "He lied," even though they had seen this great sign. But the judgment of Allah the Exalted was carried out against them by their being killed. ʿUbayda al-Salmani said: from that time on, no killer inherited.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Our law has come with something similar. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, related in the *al-Muwaṭṭaʾ* that the story of Uhayha ibn al-Jallah concerning his paternal uncle was the reason that a killer does not inherit, and that this was established in Islam, just as many of the disputes of the Jahiliyya were established. Abu al-ʿAliya, Qatada and others said: Allah intended the hearts of the Children of Israel all together, in their disobedience and in what they committed after that.

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿so they were like stones﴾ and the rest of the verse: the *kaf* (like) is in the position of the predicate of *hiya* (they), its estimated form being: "so they are like stones." ﴿Or even harder﴾ is in the nominative by coordination with the *kaf* ("like"), with *aw* (or) acting upon the predicate of the inchoative, with the estimate of repeating *hiya*. And *qaswatan* is in the accusative as a specification (*tamyīz*). The customary use of *aw* is for doubt, and that is not valid in this verse. The meaning of *aw* here has been disputed. One group said: it has the meaning of *wa* (and), as He the Exalted said: ﴿a sinner or a disbeliever﴾ [al-Insan: 24], meaning "and a disbeliever." As the poet said:

*He attained the caliphate, or it was for him as a destiny,*
*just as Moses came to his Lord at an appointed measure.*

meaning "and it was for him." Another group said: it has the meaning of *bal* (rather), as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], meaning "rather they are more." Another group said: its meaning is choice, i.e., "liken them to stones, you will hit the mark, or to something harder than stones, you will hit the mark." Another group said: it retains its meaning of doubt, and its meaning, in your view, O addressees, and in your estimation, is that if you witnessed their hardness, you would doubt: "Are they like stones, or harder than stones?" Another group said: it is for the sake of obscuring the matter to the listener, and from this is the saying of Abu al-Aswad al-Duʾali:

*I love Muhammad with an intense love,*
*and ʿAbbas and Hamza, or ʿAli.*

Abu al-Aswad did not doubt; he only intended to obscure the matter for the listener. Abu al-Aswad was challenged on this and it was argued from the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And indeed we or you are surely upon guidance, or in manifest error﴾ [Saba: 24]. This verse is different from the verse of Abu al-Aswad, and the meaning of the verse is not complete except with *aw*. Another group said: Allah the Exalted intended that among them is one whose heart is like a stone, and among them is one whose heart is harder than a stone. So the meaning is that they are two groups like stones, or harder. A similar example is your saying: "I fed you the sweet or the sour," meaning that what you fed him did not go outside these two. Another group said: the Exalted and Majestic intended that they were like stones, whose returning and turning back could be hoped for, just as rivers gush forth and water comes out of stones. Then after that their hearts increased in hardness, to the point that they reached the state of one whose turning back is not hoped for. So they became harder than stones. Thus they were never free of being like stones at times, or harder at other times. Abu Hayya recited *qasawatan*, and the meaning is the same.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And indeed, among stones﴾ and the rest of the verse, it is an excuse for the stones and a preference for them over their hearts in terms of the lesser degree of hardness. Qatada said: Allah the Exalted excused the stones and did not excuse the wretched of the sons of Adam. Qatada recited *wa-inna* with the light form (*mukhaffafa*) of the heavy one, and likewise in the second and third occurrences. He distinguished it from the negating *in* by the emphatic *lam* in *lamma*, and *ma* is in the position of the accusative noun of *inna*. The *lam* entered upon the subject of *inna* because the prepositional phrase came between them, and if the noun had been directly joined to *inna*, the entry of the *lam* would not have been valid, because of the heaviness of combining two emphatics. Malik ibn Dinar recited *yanfajiru* with a *nun* and a *yaʾ* before it from below, and with a kasra on the *jim*. He made the pronoun in *minhu* singular, treating it according to the wording of *ma*. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and al-Dahhak recited *minha al-anhar* treating it as referring to the stones. *Al-anhar* is the plural of *nahr*, which is that whose water is abundant and flows from trenches.

Talha ibn Musarrif recited *lamma* with a doubled *mim* in both places, but this recitation is not well-founded. *Yashshaqqaqu* originally was *yatashaqqaqu*, the *ta* being assimilated into the *shin*. This is an expression for springs that have not grown large enough to become rivers, or for stones that split even if no water flows widely. Ibn Musarrif recited *yanshaqqu* with the *nun*. As for the falling of stones, it has been said: it is the shifting of their shadows. It has also been said: the intended meaning is the mountain that Allah made crumble to dust. It has also been said: Allah the Exalted creates in some stones fear and life, by which they descend from a height in humility.

A parallel to this life is the life of the stone that greeted the Prophet ﷺ, and the life of the trunk that moaned at the absence of the Prophet ﷺ. It has been said: the word *hubut* (falling) is metaphorical. This is because, since hearts take lessons from their creation and are humbled by some of their sights, the humility of the one who looks at them is attributed to them, just as the Arabs said: "a she-camel that trades," meaning one that prompts whoever sees her to buy her. Mujahid said: "No stone has fallen from the top of a mountain, no river has gushed from a stone, and no water has come out of it, except from fear of Allah." The Qur'an was revealed with this. Ibn Jurayj said the same. Al-Tabari related from a group that the fear attributed to the stones is figurative, just as will (*irada*) is attributed to a wall in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that wants to collapse﴾ [al-Kahf: 77], and just as Zayd al-Khayl said:

*With a gathering in whose chambers the piebald horses go astray,*
*you see the hills in it prostrating to the hooves.*

And just as Jarir said:

*…………………………… and the humbled mountains.*

meaning: whoever sees the stone falling imagines fear in it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is a weak view, because the excellence of the meaning of the verse is undermined by it. Rather, the stronger view is that Allah the Exalted creates for the stones a certain measure of perception by which fear and movement occur.

*Bi-ghafilin* is in the position of the accusative, being the predicate of *ma*, because it is the Hijazi usage. This is strengthened by the entry of the *ba* into the predicate, although the *ba* may come irregularly with the Tamimi usage.

Ibn Kathir recited *yaʿmalūna* with a *yaʾ*, and in this case the address is to Muhammad ﷺ.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do you then hope that they will believe in you﴾ and the rest of the verse: the address is to the believers among the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ. The reason is that the Ansar had a desire for the Jews to become Muslim, because of the alliance and neighborhood that existed between them. The meaning of this address is a reproach concerning a matter that is far-fetched, since the forefathers of these Jews had already committed evil deeds, and these were following the same course. *Al-fariq* is a collective noun with no singular from its own form, like *al-hizb*. Mujahid and al-Suddi said: by *al-fariq* here is meant the rabbis who distorted the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad ﷺ.

It has been said: the intended meaning is everyone who distorted something in the Torah, whether a ruling or other than it, as in their act concerning the verse of stoning and similar things. Ibn Ishaq and al-Rabiʿ said: what is meant is the seventy who heard with Moses, and then altered after that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is weakness in this view. Whoever says that the seventy heard what Moses heard has erred, and has removed the excellence of Moses, peace be upon him, and his particular privilege of direct speech. Al-Aʿmash recited *kalima Allah* (the word of Allah). Altering (*tahrif*) a thing means turning it from one state to another. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, held that their distortion and alteration was only through interpretation, while the wording of the Torah remained. A group of scholars held that they changed words of their own accord, and that this is possible in the Torah because they were entrusted with preserving it, but it is not possible in the Qur'an, because Allah the Exalted guaranteed its preservation.

The Almighty's saying:

﴿When they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"; but when they are alone with one another, they say, "Do you speak to them of what God has disclosed to you, so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord? Will you not then understand?" Do they not know that God knows what they conceal and what they reveal?﴾ ﴿And among them are unlettered folk who know not the Book, but only wishful fancies, and they merely conjecture.﴾

The meaning: They also do this when they "meet" [the believers], so how could one hope for their faith? It is possible that this statement is a new, independent sentence, cut off from the sense of hope, and in it is an exposure of their inner secrets. It is related in the tafsir that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let no one enter upon us at the outskirts of Madinah except a believer." Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Wahb ibn Yahuda and their likes said: "Go and seek out news of those who have believed in Muhammad, and say to them, 'We believe,' and disbelieve when you return." Thereupon this verse was revealed. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning hypocrites among the Jews. It is also related from him that it was revealed concerning a group of Jews who said to some of the believers: "We affirm that he is a prophet, but he is not for us; he is only for you in particular." Then, when they were alone, some of them said: "Why do you acknowledge his prophethood, when we used to seek victory through him before?" So this is what God has disclosed to them of His knowledge. The root of "khala" (alone) is "khalaw"; the waw moved and the letter before it was open, so it became an alif.

Abu al-'Aliya and Qatada said: some Jews spoke of what was in the Torah concerning the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the disbelieving rabbis said to them: "Do you speak to them of what God has disclosed to you?" That is, He has informed you of the description of Muhammad, so that they argue against you, since you acknowledge it [in the Torah] (p-261) and yet do not believe in him? Al-Suddi said: some Jews recounted to some Muslims the punishment with which their forefathers had been chastised, and some of the rabbis said: "Do you speak to them of what God has disclosed to you" of the punishment, so that they argue against you and say: "We are more honoured by God, since He has not done to us the like of this?" And "fataha" in this interpretation means "judged."

Mujahid said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to the Banu Qurayza: 'O brothers of the apes and swine!' Then the rabbis said to their followers: 'He knew this only from you. Will you speak to them?'" Ibn Zayd said: when they were asked about something, they would say: "In the Torah it is thus and thus." The rabbis disliked this and forbade them to do so when alone, and concerning this the verse was revealed.

"Al-fath" in the language divides into categories, which are gathered by the meaning of expansion and removal of ambiguity, and to this the judgement and other meanings return. And "al-fattah" is the judge in the dialect of Yemen. "Yuhajjukum" is from "hujja" (argument), and its root is from "hajja," meaning he intended, because each of the two disputants intends the victory of the other. And "ʿinda rabbikum" means in the Hereafter. It was also said that "ʿinda" carries the sense of "fi" (in), that is, "in your Lord," so they would be more entitled to it. It was also said: the meaning is "at the mention of your Lord." As for His saying, exalted is He, "Will you not then understand?", it was said that it is from the words of the rabbis to the followers; it was also said that it is an address from God to the believers, that is: "Will you not understand that the Children of Israel will not believe while they are in these states?" And "al-ʿaql" (understanding) is necessary knowledge.

The majority read "Awa la ya'lamun" with the yā' from below (third person), while Ibn Muhaysin read "Aw la ta'lamun" with the tā' as an address to the believers.

(p-262) What they concealed is their disbelief, and what they disclosed is their saying "We believe"; this is concerning the Jews in general. What the rabbis concealed is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and knowledge of him, and what they disclosed is the denial of him. The wording of the verse encompasses all of them. "Ummiyyun" here is an expression for those ignorant of the Torah. Abu al-'Aliya, Mujahid and others said: the meaning is "and among these Jews mentioned." So the verse alerts to their common people and followers, that is, they are among those in whose faith one does not hope, because of the misguidance that has overwhelmed them. It was also said: what is meant here by the Ummiyyin is a people whose scribes were removed because of sins they committed, so they remained unlettered. 'Ikrima and al-Dahhak said: they are, in the verse, the Christian Arabs. It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, that he said: "They are the Magians." The pronoun in "minhum" according to these sayings refers to all the disbelievers. The saying of Abu al-'Aliya and Mujahid is the most probable of these sayings. Abu Haywa and Ibn Abi 'Abla read "ummiyyun" with the mīm lightened. The "ummiyy" in the language is one who does not write nor read in a book; it is attributed to "umm" (mother), either because he is in the state of his mother in lacking the Book, not in the state of his father, since women are not those occupied with the Book, as al-Tabari said; or because he is in a state in which his mother bore him, not moving away from it; and it was said: it is attributed to "umma" (community) and its form and creation, as if he has nothing of the human beings except that; and it was said: it is attributed to the "umma" in its simplicity before the knowledge of sciences became known, for it neither reads nor writes. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) said about the Arabs: "We are an unlettered community, we neither reckon nor write," the hadith. The definite article in "al-Kitab" is for prior reference, and by it is meant the Torah, according to the saying of Abu al-'Aliya and Mujahid.

"Al-amani" is the plural of "umniyya." Abu Ja'far, Shayba and Nafi' in some of what is related from him read "amani" with the yā' lightened. The original of "umniyya" is "umnuwiyya" on the pattern of "uf'ula," and this pattern is pluralised as "af'ila"; on this basis the yā' must be lightened, and it is pluralised as "af'ili," so this becomes "amaniyi," and the yā' is assimilated into the yā', giving "amanniyy." (p-263) People differed about the meaning of "amaniyy." One group said: here it is from "tamanna al-rajul" (a man wished) when he hoped, so its meaning is that among them is one who neither writes nor reads, but merely says by his supposition something he heard, wishing that it is from the Book. Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Wahb ibn Yahuda and their likes said: "Go and seek out news of those who have believed in Muhammad, and say to them, 'We believe,' and disbelieve when you return." Thereupon this verse was revealed. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed concerning hypocrites among the Jews. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 79–82:

(p-264) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿So woe to those who write the Scripture with their own hands, then say, "This is from Allah," that they may trade it for a little price. So woe to them for what their hands have written, and woe to them for what they earn.﴾ ﴿And they say, "The Fire will not touch us except for a number of days." Say, "Have you taken a covenant with Allah, so that Allah will not break His covenant? Or do you say about Allah what you do not know?"﴾ ﴿Yes! Whoever earns an evil deed and his sin encompasses him, those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾ ﴿But those who believe and do righteous deeds, those are the companions of Paradise; they will abide therein forever.﴾

"Those who" (alladhina) in this verse refers to the rabbis and leaders. Al-Khalil said: al-wayl (woe) is the intensity of evil. Al-Asma'i said: al-wayl is ugliness. It is a verbal noun (masdar) with no verb of its own, and its plural is waylat. The best reading of it when it is separated (from what follows) is the nominative (raf'), because it implies an occurrence; the accusative (nasb) is also valid with the meaning of supplication, i.e., "May Allah impose woe upon him."

Wayl, wayh, ways, and wayb are close in meaning, and some people have distinguished between them. Sufyan and 'Ata' ibn Yasar related that al-wayl in this verse is a valley that flows at the courtyard of Hell with the pus of the people of the Fire. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri related from the Prophet ﷺ that it is "a valley in Hell between two mountains, into which the one who falls will plunge for forty autumns." Abu 'Iyad said: it is a cistern in Hell. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) related from the Prophet ﷺ that it is "a mountain from the mountains of Fire." Al-Zahrawi reported from others that it is a gate of the gates of Hell. And "those who write" (alladhina yaktubuna) are the rabbis who altered the Torah. His saying "with their own hands" is an explanation of their crime and an affirmation of their open defiance of Allah.

(p-265) He distinguished between the one who writes and the one who orders, since the one who undertakes the act is more culpable than one who does not undertake it, even if it was his opinion. Ibn al-Sarraj said: it is a metaphor meaning that it was from their own invention, without being sent down to them, even if it was not literally in the books written by their hands.

What they altered was the description of the Prophet ﷺ, in order to perpetuate their leadership and their gains. Ibn Ishaq said: his description in the Torah was "dark-skinned, of medium height," so they changed it to "tall and fair-skinned." Al-Suddi mentioned that they used to write books in which they altered the description of the Prophet ﷺ, and they would sell them to the Bedouins, spread them among their followers, and say: "This is from Allah." The coherence of this verse with the one before it indicates that this writing and alteration were for the unlettered followers who know nothing except what is read to them.

As for the price (thaman), it has been said: it is the goods of this world; and it has been said: it is the bribes and the food that they received. Describing it as "little" is either because it perishes, or because it is unlawful. The word "woe" is repeated because of the repetition of the states for which they deserved it. "Earn" (yaksibuna) means from sins and transgressions; it has been said: it means from the wealth implied by the mention of the price.

As for His saying, the Exalted, ﴿The Fire will not touch us﴾ and the rest of the verse: Ibn Zayd and others related that its cause was that "the Prophet ﷺ said to the Jews: 'Who are the people of the Fire?' They said: 'We are, then you will succeed us.' He said to them: 'You have lied; you know that we will not succeed you.' So this verse was revealed." It is also said that the cause was that the Jews said: Allah, the Exalted, swore that He would enter them into the Fire for forty days, the number of days they worshipped the calf. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and 'Ata'.

(p-266) A group said: the Jews said: "In the Torah it is written that the length of Hell is a forty-year journey, and that they will cross one year each day until they complete it, and Hell will be gone." Ibn 'Abbas also said, and Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj, that they said: "The duration of this world is seven thousand years, and Allah, the Exalted, will punish them one day for every thousand years."

"Attakhadhtum" originally was: "a'-ittakhadhtum," its form being "af'altum" from "al-akhdh" (taking). The second hamza was softened because it is impermissible to have two hamzas together, so it became "ay-ittakhadhtum." The yā' fluctuated in conjugation: it became an alif in "yittakhadhu" and a waw in "muttakhadh," so it was replaced by a firm consonant, which is the tā', and was assimilated. When the interrogative alif entered this verse, the alif of connection was dispensed with. The view of Abu 'Ali is that "a-ittakhadhtum" is from "takhidha," not from "akhadha," and this has been mentioned previously.

The people of tafsir said: "covenant" (ʿahd) from Allah, the Exalted, in this verse means the pledge and the promise. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: its meaning is "Have you said: there is no god but Allah, and believed, and obeyed, so that you claim by that and know that you will come out of the Fire?" According to the first interpretation, the meaning is: "Has Allah made a covenant with you concerning what you claim?" According to the second: "Have you sent ahead with Allah deeds that necessitate what you claim?"

His saying: ﴿then Allah will not break His covenant﴾ is a parenthetical interjection within the speech.

"Bala" (yes indeed) is a response after a negation, in the position of "na'am" after an affirmation. The Kufans said: its origin is "bal," which is used for turning away from the first statement, and a yā' was added to it so that stopping on it would be smooth; the yā' carries the meaning of affirmation and emphasis with what comes after it. Sibawayh said: it is a particle like "bal" and others, and in this verse it is a rejection of the saying of the Children of Israel: ﴿The Fire will not touch us﴾, so Allah rejected it for them, and made clear that abiding in (p-267) the Fire and the Garden is according to disbelief and faith. "Man" is a conditional in the place of nominative by inception, and "ulaika" is a second inception, and "ashab" is its predicate; the clause is the predicate of the first, and the "fa'" (in "fa-ulaika") is a preparatory particle, making the clause the answer of the condition. A group said: the "sayyi'ah" (evil deed) is shirk, like His saying: ﴿And whoever comes with an evil deed, their faces will be thrown into the Fire﴾ [an-Naml: 90]; and the "khati'at" (sins) are the major sins. Some said "khati'atuhu" is in the singular form; others said: the "sayyi'ah" here is the major sins, and it is given in the singular though it has the sense of the plural, since it denotes a category, like His saying: ﴿And if you count the favor of Allah﴾ [an-Nahl: 18]. And "khati'ah" is disbelief; the word "ihatah" (encompassing) strengthens this view, and it is derived from the wall surrounding a thing.

Al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, al-A'mash, al-Suddi, and others said: the meaning of the verse is: "He died with sins from which he did not repent." Al-Rabi' also said: "He died upon his disbelief." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and al-Suddi said: "Every sin for which Allah has threatened the Fire is the encompassing sin."

The "khulud" (abiding) in this verse is absolute and eternal regarding the polytheists, and is used metaphorically in the sense of long duration regarding the disobedient, even if its cessation is known, as one says: "a khalid king," and the king is prayed for with "al-khuld" (long life).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But those who believe﴾ and the rest of the verse: this division indicates that His saying "whoever earns an evil deed" refers to the disbelievers, not the disobedient. It also indicates this by His saying "and it encompasses him," because the disobedient believer is not encompassed by his sin. It also indicates this because the response was directed at disbelievers who claimed that the Fire would not touch them except for a number of days; they are the ones meant by the abiding. And Allah knows best.

"Then you are those who kill yourselves and expel a group of you from their homes, supporting one another against them in sin and aggression. And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them, while their expulsion is forbidden to you. Do you then believe in part of the Book and disbelieve in part? So what is the recompense of those among you who do that, except disgrace in the life of this world? And on the Day of Resurrection they will be returned to the most severe punishment. And Allah is not unaware of what you do."

"Hā'ulā'" (these) indicates that the address is to those present, and does not allow it to be traced back to their forefathers. It was said: the sentence is to be understood as "yā hā'ulā'" (O you), so the particle of address was omitted; but according to Sibawayh, omitting it is not good with demonstratives: one does not say "hādhā aqbal" (this one comes). It was also said: its implied sense is "a'nī hā'ulā'" (I mean these). And it was said: "hā'ulā'" carries the meaning of "alladhīna" (those who), so the sense is "thumma antum alladhīna taqtulūna" (then you are those who kill), and "taqtulūna" is the relative clause of "hā'ulā'" and the like. Yazīd ibn Mufarrigh al-Ḥimyarī said:

؎ ʿAdas, what authority has ʿAbbād over you? You escaped, and this one, the one you carry, is released.

Our eminent teacher Abū al-Ḥasan ibn Aḥmad, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "hā'ulā'" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), "antum" is the predicate placed before it (khabar muqaddam), and "taqtulūna" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl); with it the meaning is complete, and it was the intended element, so it is not dispensable, though it came after the predication and the subject were complete, as you say: "hādhā Zayd muntaliqan" (this is Zayd going out), where you intend to inform of his going out, not of the fact that this is Zayd. This verse is an address to Qurayẓa, al-Naḍīr, and Banū Qaynuqā', because al-Naḍīr and Qurayẓa were allied with al-Aws, and Banū Qaynuqā' were allied with al-Khazraj; so whenever war broke out between the Banū Qaylah, each group of the Children of Israel went out with its allies, and some of them killed others and expelled others from their homes; yet they would also ransom each other's captives, following the ruling of the Torah, while they had themselves violated it by fighting and expulsion.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read "tuqattilūna" with a damma on the first tā' and a kasra on the second, with its shadda, for emphasis. "Diyār" means the dwelling-places of residence; al-Khalīl said: the encampment of a people is their dār. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read "tuẓāhirūna" with a light ẓā', which is by dropping the second tā' from "tataẓāharūna." The remaining seven read "taẓẓāharūna" with a heavy ẓā', by assimilating the tā' into the ẓā'. Abū Ḥaywah read "tuẓāhirūna" with a damma on the tā' and a kasra on the hā'. Mujāhid and Qatādah read "taẓẓahharūna" with a fatḥa on the tā', a shadda on the ẓā', and the hā' fatḥah without an alif; this was transmitted from Abū ʿAmr. The meaning in every reading is: "tata'āwanūna" (you help one another), and it is derived from "al-ẓahr" (the back), as if each of the two who support one another leans his back against the other. "Al-ithm" (sin) is the constant obligation upon the servant from acts of disobedience, and the meaning is the sins one has acquired; "al-'udwān" is transgressing the limits and wrongdoing. The wording "al-ityān" (coming) is fine, insofar as it stands in contrast to "al-ikhrāj" (expulsion), so the antithesis showing the ugliness of their act in expulsion becomes apparent.

Ḥamzah read "asrā tafdūhum," Nāfi', ʿĀṣim and al-Kisā'ī read "asārā tufādūhum," Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Ibn Kathīr read "asārā tafdūhum," and some read "asrā tufādūhum." "Asārā" is the plural of "asīr" (captive), and "asīr" is derived from "al-asar," which is binding; he was so named because he is bound (yu'sar), that is, tied with cords, and then its use became frequent until it became fixed, even where there is no tying or binding. "Asīr" is on the pattern "fa'īl" in the sense of "maf'ūl," and it is not pluralized with the sound masculine suffix of wāw and nūn; it is broken only into "asrā" and "asārā," and the more analogous form is "asrā," because "fa'īl" in the sense of "maf'ūl" originally takes the plural "fa'lā," like "qatlā" and "jarḥā." The original pattern of "fa'lān" is to be pluralized into "fa'ālā" with a fatḥa on the fā', and "fu'ālā" with a ḍamma on it, like "sakrān," "maskalān," "sukārā" and "kusālā." Sibawayh said: they said in the plural of "kaslān": "kaslā," assimilating it to "asrā," just as they said "asārā," assimilating it to "kusālā"; the point of resemblance being that captivity befalls a man against his will, just as laziness befalls him, while "fa'ālā" is used for what is like a calamity that befalls a person.

"Tufādūhum," in linguistic meaning, is that you release them after taking something from them; this is what Abū ʿAlī said. "Fādaytu nafsī" means I released myself after paying something. Thus it may come in the sense of "fadaytu," that is, I paid from my own wealth in it. From this is the statement of al-ʿAbbās to the Prophet ﷺ: "Give me, for I ransomed myself and I ransomed ʿAqīl." Both are verbs that take two objects, the second of which is with a preposition: you say "fadaytu Zaydan bi-māl" and "fādaytuhu bi-māl." Some said that in the reading "tufādūhum" it is a construction of mutual action (mufā'alah): "asrā bi-asrā" (captive for captive). Abū ʿAlī said: each of the two parties does an action: the capture is the seizing of the captive, and the one seized is also a giving, either of a captive or of something else; the second object is omitted.

Allah's words: ﴿wa-huwa muḥarramun﴾ (while it is forbidden). It was said regarding "huwa": it is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-amr), its implied sense being "wa-al-amru muḥarramun ʿalaykum" (and the matter is forbidden to you), and "ikhrājuhum" in this view is an apposition (badal) to "huwa." It was also said: "huwa" is a separator (fāṣilah), and this is the doctrine of the Kufans; it is not here the one functioning as a copula ('imād). "Muḥarram" in this view is the subject (mubtada') and "ikhrājuhum" its predicate. It was said: it is the pronoun implied in "muḥarram," placed first and made explicit. It was said: it is the pronoun of expulsion, its implied sense being "wa-ikhrājuhum muḥarramun ʿalaykum" (and their expulsion is forbidden to you).

Allah's words: ﴿afa-tu'minūna bi-ba'ḍi al-kitāb﴾ (Do you then believe in part of the Book): this means the Torah. What they believed in is the ransoming of captives, and what they disbelieved in is killing some of them by others and expelling them from their homes; this is a rebuke to them and a clarification of the ugliness of their act.

It is related that ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām passed by the Exilarch (Ra's al-Jālūt) in Kufa, while he was ransoming some of the women whom the Arabs had not taken, and not ransoming those whom they had taken. Ibn Salām said to him: "Indeed it is written in your book that you must ransom all of them." Then Allah, exalted and majestic, threatened them. "Khizy" means disgrace and punishment; it is said: "khazia al-rajulu yakhzā khiz'an" when a man is humiliated through disgrace, and "khazia yakhzā khazāyatan" when he feels shame.

The people differed about what is meant by "khizy" here. It was said: retaliation (qiṣāṣ) against whoever killed; it was said: imposing the jizyah upon them for ever; and it was said: the killing of Qurayẓa and the exile of al-Naḍīr. "Al-dunyā" is derived from "dana yadnū," and its original letter is a wāw, but it was changed into a yā' to distinguish nouns from adjectives.

"Ashadd al-ʿadhāb" (the most severe punishment) is eternal abiding in Jahannam. Al-Ḥasan and Ibn Hurmuz read "turaddūna" with a tā'.

Allah's words: ﴿wa-mā Allāhu bi-ghāfilin ʿammā taʿmalūn﴾ (And Allah is not unaware of what you do). Nāfiʿ and Ibn Kathīr read "ya'malūna" with a yā', as a reference to the third person; the address of the verse is then to the community of Muhammad ﷺ, and the verse is an admonition to them in meaning, since Allah is on watch over every disbeliever and sinner. The rest read it with a tā', as an address which may be part of the continuing discourse of the verse, and this is the more apparent; it may also be understood as addressing the community of Muhammad ﷺ. It is related that ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Children of Israel have passed away, and you are the ones meant by this, O community of Muhammad."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 86–88:**

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Those are the ones who have bought the worldly life in exchange for the Hereafter. So their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿And We certainly gave Moses the Book and followed him with messengers after him. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit. Is it that whenever a messenger came to you with what your souls did not desire, you became arrogant? So you denied some and killed others.﴾ ﴿And they said, "Our hearts are wrapped." Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief, so little is it that they believe.﴾

Allah made abandoning the Hereafter, and taking the world while they were able to hold fast to the Hereafter, equivalent to one who took something and then sold it for worldly gain. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, applied this same notion in the jurisprudence of sales (fiqh al-buyu'). It is not permissible to buy on the basis that the buyer may choose among items whose individual qualities differ, and excess (al-tafadul) is not permitted in such transactions, as with slaughtered partridges (al-hijal al-madhbuha) and others. "Their punishment will not be lightened in the Hereafter, nor will they be helped," neither in this world nor in the Hereafter.

"Al-Kitab" refers to the Torah, and it is in the accusative as the second object of "atayna" (We gave). "Qaffayna" (We followed) is derived from "al-qafa" (the back of the neck). You say: "qaffaytu fulanan bi-fulan" when you bring the one from behind his back. From this comes "qafa yaqfu," meaning he followed. This verse is like the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:44]. Every messenger who came after Moses came only to confirm the Torah and to command adherence to it, until the time of Jesus, peace be upon him.

Al-Hasan and Yahya ibn Ya'mur read "bil-rusl" with a sukun on the sin. Abu 'Amr agreed with them when it is attached to a pronoun, as in "rusulina" and "rusulihim." [p. 278] "Al-bayyinat" (the clear proofs) are the evidences that Allah gave to Jesus. It was also said they are his signs, such as giving life, healing, and fashioning a bird. It was also said they are the Gospel (al-Injil). The verse includes all of these.

"Wa-ayyadnahu" means "We strengthened him," and "al-ayd" means strength. Ibn Muhaysin, al-A'raj, and Humayd read "ayyadnahu" (with a different form). Ibn Kathir and Mujahid read "ruh al-qudsi" with a sukun on the dal. The majority read it with a damma on the qaf and the dal, and there is a dialect of reading both with a fatha. Abu Haywa read "bi-ruhi al-qudusi" with a waw.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "Ruh al-qudus" is the Name by which he used to bring the dead to life. Ibn Zayd said: it is the Gospel, just as Allah the Exalted called the Qur'an a spirit. Al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, al-Rabi', and Qatadah said: "Ruh al-qudus" is Gabriel, peace be upon him. This is the most authentic of the opinions. The Prophet ﷺ said to Hassan ibn Thabit: "Satirize Quraysh, and the Holy Spirit is with you," and at another time he said to him: "And Gabriel is with you."

Al-Rabi' and Mujahid said: "al-qudus" is one of the Names of Allah the Exalted, like "al-Quddus," and the idafa (construct) on this view is like the idafa of "al-Malik" (the King) to "al-Malik" (the Owner). It is ascribed to Gabriel, peace be upon him, because of his being one of the servants of Allah the Exalted. It was also said: "al-qudus" means purity, and it was said: "al-qudus" means blessing.

"Kullama" is an adverbial of time (zarf), and the element that governs it is "istakbartum" (you became arrogant). The apparent form of the speech is interrogative, and its meaning is rebuke and affirmation [p. 279], and it also includes a statement about them. The intended people in this verse are the Children of Israel. It is related that the Children of Israel used to kill three hundred prophets in a single day, and then their markets would be set up at the end of the day. It is also related: seventy prophets, and then the market of their vegetables would be set up at the end of the day.

In "tahwa" there is a pronoun referring back to the relative "ma," because of the length of the phrase. "Al-hawa" (desire) is most often used for what is not true, and this verse is of that kind, because they were only pursuing desires. It may also be used for what is true. From this is the statement of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, in the story of the captives of Badr: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ inclined toward what Abu Bakr said, and did not incline toward what I said." "Istakbartum" is from "al-kibr" (arrogance). "Fariqan" is a direct object placed before its verb.

The majority of the reciters read "ghulf" with a sukun on the lam, as the plural of "aghlaf," like "humr" and "sufr." The meaning is: "Our hearts are upon them wrapped and covered, so they do not understand." This is what Ibn 'Abbas said. Qatadah said the meaning is: "upon them is a seal." Another group said: "ghulf" with a sukun on the lam is the plural of "ghilaf," originally "ghullf" with a doubled lam, which was lightened. This is rarely used except in poetry. Al-A'mash, al-A'raj, and Ibn Muhaysin read "ghullun" with a doubled lam, the plural of "ghilaf." It is also narrated from [p. 280] Abu 'Amr. Then the meaning is: they are containers for knowledge and understanding, according to their claim, so they have no need for the knowledge of Muhammad. It was also said the meaning is: "How could the knowledge of Muhammad ﷺ be hidden from them?" Allah the Exalted refuted them with His words: ﴿Rather, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief﴾. "Bal" (rather) in this verse cancels the first statement and turns away from it. Then Allah the Exalted explained that the cause of their aversion to faith is that they were cursed for the disbelief and transgression that preceded it. This is the recompense for sin, so the sin is greater than it. "Al-la'n" means distancing and expelling.

"Qalilan" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, whose estimate is: "faiman qalilan ma yu'minun" (little faith they have). The pronoun in "yu'minun" refers to those present in the time of Muhammad ﷺ. The paucity of this faith may be understood in several ways. Either because those among them who believed in Muhammad were few, so it was little because of the fewness of men. Qatadah said this meaning. Or because the time of their belief, at the time when they used to seek victory by him before his mission, was brief, since they disbelieved after that. Or because after their disbelief they retained only a tawhid not in its proper form, since they were anthropomorphists, so they diminished it by their denial of the Messenger and their denial of the Torah. It is little only in the sense that it does not benefit them. On this interpretation the estimate is "faiman qalilan." On the one before it, it is "waqtan qalilan" (a brief time), and on the one before that, "'adadan mina al-rijal qalilan" (a small number of men). The "ma" in "ma yu'minun" is an extra, emphasizing particle, and "qalilan" is in the accusative by "yu'minun."

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 89–91:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿When there came to them a Book from Allah, confirming what was with them, and before that they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved, yet when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it. So the curse of Allah is upon the disbelievers.﴾ ﴿Wretched is that for which they have sold themselves: that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down, out of envy that Allah should send down of His bounty upon whom He wills of His servants. So they earned wrath upon wrath, and for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us," and they disbelieve in what is beyond it, while it is the truth confirming what is with them. Say, "Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before, if you were believers?"﴾

Allah Exalted described the Qur'an as being the truth.

*Muṣaddiqan* (confirming) is a emphatic circumstantial state (*ḥāl mu'akkida*) according to Sibawayh, and it is not a transferable state. Its meaning has already been mentioned in the speech, and there remains for it only the meaning of emphasis. Sibawayh cited as an example of an emphatic state:

*I am the son of Dara, known by her is my lineage; and is there, O people, any shame upon Dara?*

*Limā ma'ahum* (for what is with them) means the Torah.

His saying, Exalted is He: *Qul fa-lima taqtulūna* (Say: "Why then do you kill") is a verse of refutation from Allah Exalted against them, regarding their claim that they believed in what was sent down to them, and it is a denial from Him to them in that matter, and an argument against them.

It is not permissible to pause on *falima* because of the deficiency of a single letter, except that al-Bazzi paused on it with the *hā'* (*falimah*), while the rest of the reciters paused with the mīm silent.

Allah addressed those present among the Children of Israel at the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) by saying that they killed the prophets, since that was the act of their forefathers.

*Taqtulūna* (you kill) came in the form of the future tense, while it has the meaning of the past, since the difficulty is removed by His saying *min qablu* (before). When there is no difficulty, it is permissible to use the past with the meaning of the future, and to use the future with the meaning of the past. Al-Hutay'a said:

*Al-Hutay'a bore witness on the day he meets his Lord that al-Walid is more deserving of excuse.*

(p-285) The benefit of using the past in the place of the future is to indicate that it is in its certainty like the past which has already occurred. The benefit of using the future in the meaning of the past is to inform that the matter is continuous. Do you not see that when the contemporaries of Muhammad (ﷺ) were content with the deeds of their forefathers, a portion of the killing of the prophets remained with them?

*In kuntum* (if you were) is a conditional clause (*sharṭ*), and the response (*jawāb*) precedes it. A group said: *in* is a negating particle with the meaning of *mā*.

His words, ﴿then you took﴾: the "then" (thumma) indicates that they did this after a delay of reflection on the signs, and that is more grave in their sin. The story of their taking the calf has already been mentioned. The pronoun in His words ﴿after him﴾ refers to Moses, peace be upon him, meaning after him, when he was absent from you during the private conversation (with Allah). It is also possible that the pronoun in "ba'dihi" refers to the coming (al-majī'). This verse refutes them, in that whoever believes in what was revealed to him does not take the calf. The mention of the taking of the covenant and the raising of the mount has already passed.

It does not merely mean to perceive speech. Some of the exegetes said that they actually ﴿said, "We hear and we disobey,"﴾ and uttered these words, exaggerating in their obstinacy and disobedience. Another group said that this is a figure of speech, and they did not literally utter "We hear and we disobey," but their deed required it, as the poet said:

*The basin is full, and it says, "Enough, I am full!"*

This is also an argument against them regarding the falsity of their statement: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91].

His Most High words ﴿and they were made to drink into their hearts [the love of] the calf﴾: the estimated (implied) word is "love" (hubb), so the meaning is: their hearts were made to drink it. This is a metaphor and figure of speech, an expression of how firmly the matter of the calf was fixed in their hearts. Some people said that the meaning of His words ﴿and they were made to drink into their hearts the calf﴾ is their drinking the water into which Moses had cast the filings of the calf. That is because he had ground it with a file and thrown it into the water, and the Children of Israel were told: "Drink from that water." So all of them drank, and whoever loved the calf had the gold filings appear on his lips. This view is refuted by His Most High words ﴿in their hearts﴾. It is reported that those among whom the love of the calf became evident were afflicted by the jinn from that water.

His Most High words "bi-kufrihim" (because of their disbelief) may be the "ba'" of causation, and it may be in the sense of "ma'a" (with).

His Most High words ﴿Say, "How wretched is…"﴾, the verse: He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to rebuke them, that these things which you did, and what your faith enjoins upon you, the faith you claimed in your saying, ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], are wretched. The "ma" is in the position of nominative, and the estimated meaning is: "The wretched thing is the killing, the taking of a calf, and the saying ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾." It is also permissible that "ma" be in the accusative position, and ﴿if you are believers﴾ is a conditional clause. The conditional may come while the one stating the condition knows that the matter is on one of the two sides, as Allah the Most High said concerning 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and 'Isa, peace be upon him, knew that he had not said it. Likewise: ﴿if you are believers﴾, and the speaker knows that they are not believers, but it is the establishment of proof by clear reasoning. Some people said: "in" (if) here is a negation, in the position of "ma," like the one that preceded. Al-Hasan and Muslim ibn Jundub read "bi-huwa iman-ukum" with the "ha'" in the nominative.

His Most High words ﴿Say, "If the Last Abode is yours with Allah exclusively…"﴾, the verse: a command to Muhammad (ﷺ) to rebuke them. The meaning is: if its bliss, its portion, and its good are yours, then that requires your eagerness to reach it: ﴿then wish for death.﴾ "Al-dar" is the subject of "kanat," "khalisatan" is its predicate, and it is permissible that the accusative of "khalisatan" be a circumstantial accusative (hal). "'Inda Allah" is the predicate of "kanat." As for ﴿apart from the people﴾, it may be intended that "the people" means Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who followed him, and it may be intended as complete generality, which is the statement of the Jews as transmitted from them. Ibn Abi Ishaq read "tamannaw" with a kasra on the waw because of the meeting of two consonants. Al-Ahwazi reported from Abu 'Amr that he read "tumannu al-mawt" with a fatha on the waw, and it is reported from others that they elided the vowel in the nominative. The reading of the majority is with a damma on the waw.

This is a clear sign which Allah gave to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Jews said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and similar statements. So Allah commanded His Prophet to invite them to wish for death, and to inform them that whoever among them wished for it would die. The Prophet (ﷺ) did so, and the Jews knew his truthfulness, so they refrained from wishing for it, out of fear of Allah because of the ugliness of their deeds and their knowledge of their own lying in their saying ﴿We are the children of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and out of eagerness for life. It was also said that Allah prevented them from wishing and restricted them to refraining from it, so that the sign would be manifest to His Prophet (ﷺ).

What is meant by His words "tumannu" (wish for it) is: desire it with your hearts and ask for it. This is the view of a group of exegetes. Ibn 'Abbas said: what is meant is only asking, even if not with the heart. He and others also said: they were only commanded to pray for death upon the worse of the two parties, whether of the believers or of them.

Another group said that this is a figure of speech, and they did not literally utter "We hear and we disobey," but their deed required it, as the poet said:

*The basin is full, and it says, "Enough, I am full!"*

This is also an argument against them regarding the falsity of their statement: ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91].

His Most High words ﴿and they were made to drink into their hearts [the love of] the calf﴾: the estimated (implied) word is "love" (hubb), so the meaning is: their hearts were made to drink it. This is a metaphor and figure of speech, an expression of how firmly the matter of the calf was fixed in their hearts. Some people said that the meaning of His words ﴿and they were made to drink into their hearts the calf﴾ is their drinking the water into which Moses had cast the filings of the calf. That is because he had ground it with a file and thrown it into the water, and the Children of Israel were told: "Drink from that water." So all of them drank, and whoever loved the calf had the gold filings appear on his lips. This view is refuted by His Most High words ﴿in their hearts﴾. It is reported that those among whom the love of the calf became evident were afflicted by the jinn from that water.

His Most High words "bi-kufrihim" (because of their disbelief) may be the "ba'" of causation, and it may be in the sense of "ma'a" (with).

His Most High words ﴿Say, "How wretched is…"﴾, the verse: He commanded Muhammad (ﷺ) to rebuke them, that these things which you did, and what your faith enjoins upon you, the faith you claimed in your saying, ﴿We believe in what was revealed to us﴾ [al-Baqarah: 91], are wretched. The "ma" is in the position of nominative, and the estimated meaning is: "The wretched thing is the killing, the taking of a calf, and the saying ﴿We hear and we disobey﴾." It is also permissible that "ma" be in the accusative position, and ﴿if you are believers﴾ is a conditional clause. The conditional may come while the one stating the condition knows that the matter is on one of the two sides, as Allah the Most High said concerning 'Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116], and 'Isa, peace be upon him, knew that he had not said it. Likewise: ﴿if you are believers﴾, and the speaker knows that they are not believers, but it is the establishment of proof by clear reasoning. Some people said: "in" (if) here is a negation, in the position of "ma," like the one that preceded. Al-Hasan and Muslim ibn Jundub read "bi-huwa iman-ukum" with the "ha'" in the nominative.

His Most High words ﴿Say, "If the Last Abode is yours with Allah exclusively…"﴾, the verse: a command to Muhammad (ﷺ) to rebuke them. The meaning is: if its bliss, its portion, and its good are yours, then that requires your eagerness to reach it: ﴿then wish for death.﴾ "Al-dar" is the subject of "kanat," "khalisatan" is its predicate, and it is permissible that the accusative of "khalisatan" be a circumstantial accusative (hal). "'Inda Allah" is the predicate of "kanat." As for ﴿apart from the people﴾, it may be intended that "the people" means Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who followed him, and it may be intended as complete generality, which is the statement of the Jews as transmitted from them. Ibn Abi Ishaq read "tamannaw" with a kasra on the waw because of the meeting of two consonants. Al-Ahwazi reported from Abu 'Amr that he read "tumannu al-mawt" with a fatha on the waw, and it is reported from others that they elided the vowel in the nominative. The reading of the majority is with a damma on the waw.

This is a clear sign which Allah gave to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), because the Jews said: ﴿We are the children of Allah and His beloved﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and similar statements. So Allah commanded His Prophet to invite them to wish for death, and to inform them that whoever among them wished for it would die. The Prophet (ﷺ) did so, and the Jews knew his truthfulness, so they refrained from wishing for it, out of fear of Allah because of the ugliness of their deeds and their knowledge of their own lying in their saying ﴿We are the children of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18], and out of eagerness for life. It was also said that Allah prevented them from wishing and restricted them to refraining from it, so that the sign would be manifest to His Prophet (ﷺ).

What is meant by His words "tumannu" (wish for it) is: desire it with your hearts and ask for it. This is the view of a group of exegetes. Ibn 'Abbas said: what is meant is only asking, even if not with the heart. He and others also said: they were only commanded to pray for death upon the worse of the two parties, whether of the believers or of them.

Al-Mahdawi and others mentioned that this verse applied during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ) and was lifted with his death. The correct view is that this incident, in which those who wish for death die, occurred for many days at the time the verse was revealed, and it is like his (ﷺ) calling the Christians of Najran to mubahala (mutual invocation of curse). A group said: the reason for this invitation to wish for death was that the Prophet (ﷺ) intended by it the destruction of the lying group, or the cutting off of their argument, not that its cause was their saying ﴿We are the children of Allah﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 18].

Then Allah the Most High informed about them that they are incapable, and that they will never wish for it. "Abadan" is an adverb of time. When "ma" means "alladhi" (that which), it requires a returning pronoun, estimated as: "qaddamat-hu" (it sent ahead). When "ma" with "qaddamat" is like a verbal noun, it does not need a pronoun. This is the view of Sibawayh, while al-Akhfash holds that there is a pronoun in the verbal-noun sense. He attributed their sins and crimes to the hands, and ascribed the sending ahead to them, since most of a servant's earning of good and evil is by his own hands, so he applied all things to that. His Most High words ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers﴾: its apparent meaning is a report, and its implication is a warning, because Allah knows the wrongdoers and others, so the benefit of specifying them is the occurrence of the warning.

[p. 290] "Wajada" (he found) in this sense takes two objects, because it is a verb of the inner self (af'al al-nafs). For this reason its object may be the first-person pronoun, as in the verse of the poet:

*He turned toward the tribe until I found myself,*
*and I went hungry from listening, [starved of] the līt and the akhda'.*

(Līt and akhda' are two parts of the neck.)

The Prophet (ﷺ) said about the dabb (a lizard): "It was not in the land of my people, so I find myself averse to it."

Their eagerness for life is because they know their sins, and that there is no good for them with Allah, exalted is He.

His words, "and of those who associate partners [with Allah]" (﴿وَمِنَ الَّذِينَ أشْرَكُوا﴾): it is said the meaning is "and [more eager] than those who associate partners," because the polytheist Arabs know only this worldly life. Consider the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*Enjoy the world, for you are mortal...*

The pronoun in "aḥaduhum" (one of them) in this view refers to the Jews. It is also said that the sentence was complete at "ḥayāt" (life), and then a new statement begins about a group of polytheists, that "one of them wishes", and they are the Magians (al-Majūs), because their greeting to a sneezer is a word in their language meaning "live a thousand years." So it is as if the statement is: "and among the polytheists are a people, one of whom wishes..." In this view, the Children of Israel are compared to this sect of polytheists. The mention of the thousand is specific, because it is the end of the unit of counting (al-'aqd) in reckoning.

His words, "but being granted such a life will not remove him" (﴿وَما هو بِمُزَحْزِحِهِ﴾): the grammarians differed about "huwa" (it/he). It is said it is a pronoun referring to the preceding "aḥad" (one), so the sense is: "and none of them will be removed from it," with the predicate of the subject in the prepositional phrase (al-majrūr), and "an yu'ammara" (that he be granted life) is the subject (fā'il) of "bi-muzaḥzihihi." Another group said it is a pronoun for the act of granting long life, so the sense is: "and the granting of long life will not remove him," the predicate is in the prepositional phrase, and "an ya'mura" is a substitute (badal) for "al-ta'mīr" in this view. Another group said "huwa" is a pronoun of the matter and affair (ḍamīr al-amr wal-sha'n, the dummy pronoun), but this view has been rejected on the basis of what is preserved from the grammarians, that the matter and affair is only explained by a full clause not preceded by a preposition.

Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) permitted this in some of his questions in the Ḥalabiyyāt.

Al-Tabari related from a group that they said: it is an 'imād (a dummy pronoun). It is also said: "mā" is a Ḥijāzī-type negator (its subject is "huwa" and its predicate is in "bi-muzaḥzihihi"). "Al-zaḥzaḥa" means removal and distancing.

His words, "and Allah is Seeing of what they do" (﴿واللهُ بَصِيرٌ بِما يَعْمَلُونَ﴾), is a threat. The majority read "ya'malūna" with the yā' (third person). Qatada, al-A'raj and Ya'qub read "ta'malūna" with the tā' (second person), and this is a return to addressing the threatened ones among the Children of Israel.

His words, "Say: whoever is an enemy to Gabriel" (﴿قُلْ مَن كانَ عَدُوًّا لِجِبْرِيلَ﴾) and the verse: it was revealed on a cause that had not been mentioned earlier in the preceding verses. But the people of exegesis (ahl al-tafsīr, the scholars of Qur'anic interpretation) agree that the Jews said: "Gabriel is our enemy." The manner of this is disputed. It is said: the Jews of Fadak said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We will ask you about four things, and if you know them, we will follow you." They asked him about the resemblance of the child, and he said: "Whichever water prevails, the resemblance is to it." They asked him about his sleep, and he said: "My eye sleeps but my heart does not sleep." They asked him about who comes to him of the angels, and he said: "Gabriel." When he named him, they said: "He is our enemy, for he is the angel of war, of hardship and of drought. If the one who comes to you were Michael, the angel of mercy, of fertility and of rain, we would follow you."

It is also said: 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) used to frequent the House of Study (bayt al-madāris, the Jewish schools), and one day he made them swear by Him who sent down the Torah to Moses at Mount Sinai: "Do you know that Muhammad is a prophet?" They said, "Yes." He said, "Then why do you perish by denying him?" They said, "His companion is Gabriel, and he is our enemy." It is mentioned that they stated the cause of their enmity toward him: that he protected (ḥamā) Bukhtnaṣṣar (Nebuchadnezzar) when they were sent to him before he ruled, when someone was about to kill him. So this verse was revealed in response to their statement.

There are dialects for "Jibrīl" (Gabriel): "Jibrīl," with kasra on the jīm and rā' without hamza, and by this Nāfi' recited. "Jabrīl," with fatḥa on the jīm and kasra on the rā' without hamza, and by this Ibn Kathīr recited. It is related from him that he said: "I saw the Prophet (ﷺ) in a dream reciting 'Jibrīl' and 'Mīkāl,' so I have continued to recite them thus ever since." "Jabra'il," with fatḥa on the jīm and rā', a hamza between the rā' and the lām, and by this 'Āṣim recited. "Jabra'īl," with fatḥa on the jīm and rā', a hamza after the rā', and a yā' between the hamza and the lām, and by this Ḥamza and al-Kisā'ī recited; al-Kisā'ī related it from 'Āṣim. "Jabrā'il," with an alif after the rā' then a hamza, and by this 'Ikrima recited. "Jibrā'īl," with a yā' added after the hamza. "Jibrāyīl," with two yā's, and by this al-A'mash recited. "Jabra'l," with fatḥa on the jīm and rā', a hamza, and a shaddated lām, and by this Yaḥyā ibn Ya'mur recited. "Jabrāl" is also a dialect of it. And "Jibrīn," with kasra on the jīm and rā', a yā' and a nūn. Al-Tabari said: it is the dialect of the Banū Asad, and no one recited with it.

"Jibrīl" is a non-Arabic (a'jamī) name that the Arabs Arabicized, so they have these dialects for it. Some of these forms exist in Arabic word patterns, and those are more readily Arabicized, like "Jibrīl," which is like "qindīl" (lamp). Others are outside the patterns of Arabic, like the way the Arabs Arabicized words without putting them into a pattern, such as "ibrīsam" (silk), "Fīrind," "ājir" (brick) and similar.

Ibn 'Abbas and others mentioned that "Jabr," "Mīk," and "Sarāf" are all in the non-Arabic (a'jamiyya) language meaning "servant" and "slave," and "Īl" is the name of Allah, the Exalted; it is also said "Il," and from it is the words of Abu Bakr al-Ṣiddīq (may Allah be pleased with him) when he heard the rhymed prose (saj') of Musaylima: "This is speech that did not come out of Il!"

His words, "then indeed He has sent it down upon your heart" (﴿فَإنَّهُ نَزَّلَهُ عَلى قَلْبِكَ﴾): the pronoun in "fa-innahu" refers to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and the pronoun in "nazzalahu" refers to Gabriel (ﷺ). The meaning is with the Qur'an and the rest of the revelation. It is also said: the pronoun in "innahu" refers to Gabriel, and in "nazzalahu" to the Qur'an. The heart is singled out for mention because it is the place of intellect, knowledge and the reception of realities.

The address with the second-person pronoun in "qalbika" (your heart) comes as a broadening of expression, since there is no one whom the Prophet (ﷺ) would address with this "ka"; rather the wording would be: "then indeed He has sent it down upon my heart." But this is good because in the speech of the Arabs it is good to preserve the wording that the one commanded to speak says, and it is also good to intend the meaning he is to say and to deliver it as an address to him, as you say to a man: "Say to your people, 'Do not humiliate you'." Thus is this verse. A similar example is the words of al-Farazdaq:

*Did you not see that on the day of Jaww Suwayqa*
*I wept, and Hunayda called to me, "What is with you?"*

He kept the meaning and departed from the call of Hunayda, who said, "What is with you?"

"Bi-idhni Allah" (by the permission of Allah) means: by His knowledge and His enabling him to this rank. "Muṣaddiqan" (confirming) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun of the Qur'an in "nazzalahu." "Mā bayna yadayhi" (what is before it) is what preceded it of the Books of Allah, the Exalted. "Hudan" (guidance) is direction. "Bushrā" (good tidings) is used most often for good; it does not come for evil except when restricted by a qualifier. The purpose of this verse is to honour Gabriel (ﷺ) and to blame his opponents.

His words, "Whoever is an enemy to Allah" (﴿مَن كانَ عَدُوًّا لِلَّهِ﴾) and the verse: it is a threat and a blame directed at the opponents of Gabriel, peace be upon him, and an announcement that the enmity of some implies Allah's enmity toward them. The servant's enmity toward Allah is his disobedience and his turning away from obeying Him, and opposing His friends. Allah's enmity toward the servant is His punishing him and manifesting the effect of enmity upon him.

The mention of Gabriel and Michael, though the angels were already mentioned generally, is to honour them both. It is also said they were singled out because the Jews mentioned them, and the verse was revealed because of them, so mentioning them is necessary, lest the Jews say, "We did not oppose Allah and all His angels." Nāfi' read "Mīkā'īl" with a hamza and no yā'. Ibn Kathīr also read it this way as related from him. Ibn 'Āmir, Ibn Kathīr also, Ḥamza, and al-Kisā'ī read "Mīkā'īl" with a yā' after the hamza. Abu 'Amr and 'Āṣim read "Mīkāl." It was related from Ibn Kathīr since he saw it in the dream, as we mentioned. Ibn Muḥaysin read "Mīka'il" with a hamza and no alif. Al-A'mash read "Mīkāyīl" with two yā's.

The noun (the name Allah) appears explicitly in His words, "then indeed Allah" (﴿فَإنَّ اللهَ﴾), so that the return of the pronoun is not ambiguous.

The expression came with the general term "the disbelievers" because a pronoun returning to "man" (من) would be ambiguous, whether you make it singular or plural. And if we did not care about the ambiguity and said, "the meaning indicates to the hearer the intended sense," it would necessitate specifying a particular group as having Allah's enmity. It is possible that Allah, the Exalted, knew that some of them would believe, so it is not fitting to apply "Allah's enmity" to a specific person regarding his final outcome.

It is related that a man from the Jews met 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and said to him: "Have you considered Gabriel, whom your companion claims comes to him? That is our enemy." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "Whoever is an enemy to Allah..." to the end of the verse, and so it was revealed upon the tongue of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him).

The Qāḍī Abu Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: this report is weak in terms of its meaning.

His words, "And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs" (﴿وَلَقَدْ أنْزَلْنا إلَيْكَ آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ﴾): al-Tabari mentioned that Ibn Ṣūriyā said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, you have not brought a clear sign." So this verse was revealed. "Al-fāsiqūn" (the defiantly disobedient) here means those who go outside faith, so it is the disobedience of disbelief. The sense is: "none disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient," because the affirmative (al-ījāb) does not come except after the completion of a negative clause.

It is possible that Allah, the Exalted, knew that some of them would believe, so it is not fitting to apply "Allah's enmity" to a specific person regarding his final outcome.

It is related that a man from the Jews met 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and said to him: "Have you considered Gabriel, whom your companion claims comes to him? That is our enemy." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "Whoever is an enemy to Allah..." to the end of the verse, and so it was revealed upon the tongue of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him).

The Qāḍī Abu Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: this report is weak in terms of its meaning.

His words, "And We have certainly sent down to you clear signs" (﴿وَلَقَدْ أنْزَلْنا إلَيْكَ آياتٍ بَيِّناتٍ﴾): al-Tabari mentioned that Ibn Ṣūriyā said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "O Muhammad, you have not brought a clear sign." So this verse was revealed. "Al-fāsiqūn" (the defiantly disobedient) here means those who go outside faith, so it is the disobedience of disbelief. The sense is: "none disbelieves in them except the defiantly disobedient," because the affirmative (al-ījāb) does not come except after the completion of a negative clause.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 100–102:

(p-296) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Is it that every time they make a covenant, a party of them throws it aside? Rather, most of them do not believe.﴾ ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger from Allah, confirming what was with them, a party of those who were given the Book threw the Book of Allah behind their backs, as if they did not know.﴾ ﴿And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Sulayman. Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery, and [they followed] what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut.﴾

Sibawayh said: the waw is the waw of conjunction, and the interrogative alif has entered upon it. Al-Akhfash said: it is extra (za'ida). Al-Kisa'i said: it is "aw" (or), and it was vocalized with a fatha for ease of pronunciation. A group recited it as "aw" with a sukun on the waw, so that it comes to mean "bal" (rather), like the speaker who says "I will surely strike you," and the one who replies, "Or Allah will suffice."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: all of this is far-fetched (mutakallif), and "aw" in this example is firmly in the sense of division (taqsim). The correct view is the view of Sibawayh. It was also read "'ahidu 'ahdan" (ʿahidū ʿahdan). Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "'uhidu" (ʿūhidū). "'Ahdan" is a verbal noun (masdar); it is also said to be an object in the sense of "they gave a covenant." Al-Nabdh means throwing down and casting away, and from it come nabidh and manbudh. For this reason the abundance of those who cast it aside was explained by His saying: "Rather, most of them," since the word "fariq" could be taken to mean the minority. The pronoun may also refer back to the party, or to all the Children of Israel, and the latter is more disparaging to them. The covenant they cast aside is what was taken from them in the Torah concerning the matter of Muhammad ﷺ. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "a party broke it" (naqada-hu).

(p-297) And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad ﷺ. "What was with them" is the Torah, and "confirming" (musaddiq) is an adjective (na't) of "a Messenger." Ibn Abi 'Abla read "musaddiqan" with a fatha. "Lamma" (when) is one by which something is made necessary because of the necessity of something else; it is a temporal adverb, and its response clause is "nabadha," which comes next. "Al-kitab" which they were given is the Torah, and "Kitaba Allah" is the object of "nabadha." The intended meaning is the Qur'an, because denying it is casting it aside. It is also said that the intended meaning is the Torah, because opposing it and disbelieving what was taken from them in it is casting it aside.

And ﴿behind their backs﴾ is a metaphor, because what is placed behind the back has been removed from sight entirely. The Arabs say: "This matter was placed behind his back and the back of his ear." Al-Farazdaq said:

"Tamim ibn Zayd, do not let my need be behind the back, lest its answer be a burden upon me."

And ﴿as if they did not know﴾ is a comparison with one who does not know, since they acted the act of the ignorant, so the wording implies that they disbelieved while knowing.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾, the verse, meaning the Jews. Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning is those who were in the time of Sulayman. Ibn 'Abbas said: the intended meaning is those who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. It is also said that it includes all of them. "Tatlu": 'Ata' said its meaning is "taqra'" (recite), from recitation. Ibn 'Abbas said: "tatlu" means "tatba'" (follow), as you say: "The people came, one following (yatlu) another." "Tatlu" can mean "talat" (it recited), so the present tense is placed in the position of the past. The Kufans said the meaning is "kanat tatlu" (it used to recite). Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "al-Shayatun" with a waw. His saying: ﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ means during the time of the reign of Sulayman. It is also said the meaning is "in the kingdom of Sulayman," in the sense of "in his stories, attributes and reports." Al-Tabari said: "ittaba'u" means "faddalu" (they preferred), and ﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ means over his law, his prophethood and his condition.

As for what the devils recited, it is said that they used to convey to the soothsayers a word of truth, accompanied by a hundred falsehoods, until that became their knowledge. Sulayman gathered it and buried it beneath his throne. When he died, the devils said: "That was the knowledge of Sulayman." It is also said: rather, what the devils recited was sorcery and its teaching, and Sulayman, peace be upon him, gathered it as was previously mentioned. It is also said that Sulayman, peace be upon him, used to dictate his knowledge to his scribe Asaf ibn Barkhiya and store it, and when he died the jinn brought it out and wrote between every two lines a line of sorcery, then attributed that to Sulayman. It is also said that Asaf colluded with devils to write sorcery and attribute it to Sulayman after his death. It is also said that the jinn wrote that after Sulayman's death, fabricated it and attributed it to him. It is also said that when the kingdom of Sulayman departed from him, some of the jinn and humans adopted sorcery and soothsaying as knowledge; when Sulayman returned to his kingdom, he sought out their books throughout the lands and buried them. When he died, a devil said to the Children of Israel: "Shall I guide you to the treasure of Sulayman, by which the jinn and the wind were subjected to him? It is this sorcery." So the Children of Israel extracted it, it spread among them, and they attributed Sulayman to sorcery, and disbelieved in that, until Allah cleared him through the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ.

It has been narrated that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned Sulayman among the prophets, some of the Jews said: "Look at Muhammad, he mentions Sulayman among the prophets, and he was only a sorcerer." His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Sulayman did not disbelieve﴾ is an absolution from Allah, Exalted is He, of Sulayman. No one had previously been mentioned in the verses as attributing disbelief to him, but this verse (p-299) was revealed concerning the earlier matter, that the Jews attributed him to sorcery, and sorcery and practicing it is disbelief.
