Al-Shafi'i said: he is questioned about his sorcery; if it is disbelief, he is asked to repent, and if he repents, well, otherwise he is killed. Malik said, regarding one who ties knots against men from women: he is punished and not killed. There is disagreement concerning the sorcerer of the People of the Covenant (dhimmi). It was said he is killed. Malik said: he is not killed unless he kills by his sorcery, and he must pay compensation for what he caused, and he is killed if he brings about what he did not agree to.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "lakinna" with a shadda on the nun, and "al-shayatina" in the accusative. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir read with a light nun and "al-shayatinu" in the nominative. Some of the Kufans said: the shadda is more beloved to me when the waw enters upon it, because the light form is in the position of "bal," and "bal" is not preceded by waw. Abu 'Ali said: the entry of the waw upon it does not imply a meaning that requires the shadda; it is heavy and light with one meaning, except that it does not govern when lightened.

The disbelief of the devils is either by teaching them sorcery, or by knowing it, or by declaring Sulayman a disbeliever because of it, and all of that occurred. The people who taught were followers of the devils among the Children of Israel. (p-300) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this view, teaching is merely a brief introduction to its principles.

It is also said that "ma" is conjoined to the "ma" in His saying: ﴿what they recited﴾. It is also said: "ma" is negating, a rejection of His saying: ﴿and Sulayman did not disbelieve﴾, because the Jews said: "Allah sent down Jibril and Mikail with sorcery," and Allah negated that.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abza read "al-malakayni" with a kasra on the lam. Ibn Abza said: they are Dawud and Sulayman, and according to this view too "ma" is negating. Al-Hasan said: they were two small men (ilj) who were kings in Babylon, so "ma" according to this view is not negating. Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali read them thus as well and said: they are Harut and Marut, which is like the view of al-Hasan. "Babil" is not declined because of femininity and definiteness; it is a region of the earth. It was disputed where it is. Some said it is in Iraq and what borders it. Ibn Mas'ud said to the people of Kufa: "You are between al-Hira and Babil." Qatada said: it is from Nasibin to Ra's al-'Ayn. Some said it is in the west, and this is weak. Some said it is the mountain of Damawand.

"Harut and Marut" is an apposition (badal) of "al-malakayni" according to the one who said they are two angels. Whoever read "malakayni" with a kasra on the lam and made them Dawud and Sulayman, or made the two angels Jibril and Mikail, made "Harut and Marut" an apposition of "the devils" in His saying: ﴿but the devils﴾, and said: they are two devils.

(p-301) "Yu'allimuna" comes either because the two is treated as plural, or by assuming followers for these two devils, who are the leaders. Whoever said they were two small men said: "Harut and Marut" is an apposition of his saying "al-malakayni."

It is also said: they are an apposition of "the people" in His saying: ﴿teaching people﴾. Allah said to them: "Choose two angels who will judge among the people." They chose Harut and Marut, and they judged. A woman came to them with a dispute, and they were tempted by her; they sought her, but she refused unless they drank wine and killed a man. They did so. She asked them about the Name by which they ascend to heaven, and they taught it to her; she spoke it and ascended, and was transformed into a star, and she is Venus (al-Zuhra). Ibn 'Umar used to curse her.

(p-302) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak, and it is far-fetched to attribute it to Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It is narrated that Venus descended to them in the form of a Persian woman, and what was mentioned happened between them. Allah then made the angels aware of what had happened with Harut and Marut, and they were astonished. They remained on earth because they were given the choice between the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of this world, and they chose the punishment of this world. So they are in a cavity of the earth, suspended, clapping their wings.

A group recited it as "aw" with a sukun on the waw, so that it comes to mean "bal" (rather), like the speaker who says "I will surely strike you," and the one who replies, "Or Allah will suffice."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: all of this is far-fetched (mutakallif), and "aw" in this example is firmly in the sense of division (taqsim). The correct view is the view of Sibawayh. It was also read "'ahidu 'ahdan" (ʿahidū ʿahdan). Al-Hasan and Abu Raja' read "'uhidu" (ʿūhidū). "'Ahdan" is a verbal noun (masdar); it is also said to be an object in the sense of "they gave a covenant." Al-Nabdh means throwing down and casting away, and from it come nabidh and manbudh. Al-Fariq is a collective noun (ism jam') with no singular from its own form, and it applies to a few or many of a group. For this reason the abundance of those who cast it aside was explained by His saying: "Rather, most of them," since the word "fariq" could be taken to mean the minority. In this interpretation, "they do not believe" is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "aktharuhum." The pronoun may also refer back to the party, or to all the Children of Israel, and the latter is more disparaging to them. The covenant they cast aside is what was taken from them in the Torah concerning the matter of Muhammad ﷺ. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "a party broke it" (naqada-hu).

(p-297) And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when there came to them a Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad ﷺ. "What was with them" is the Torah, and "confirming" (musaddiq) is an adjective (na't) of "a Messenger." Ibn Abi 'Abla read "musaddiqan" with a fatha. "Lamma" (when) is one by which something is made necessary because of the necessity of something else; it is a temporal adverb, and its response clause is "nabadha," which comes next. "Al-kitab" which they were given is the Torah, and "Kitaba Allah" is the object of "nabadha." The intended meaning is the Qur'an, because denying it is casting it aside. It is also said that the intended meaning is the Torah, because opposing it and disbelieving what was taken from them in it is casting it aside.

And ﴿behind their backs﴾ is a metaphor, because what is placed behind the back has been removed from sight entirely. The Arabs say: "This matter was placed behind his back and the back of his ear." Al-Farazdaq said:

"Tamim ibn Zayd, do not let my need be behind the back, lest its answer be a burden upon me."

And ﴿as if they did not know﴾ is a comparison with one who does not know, since they acted the act of the ignorant, so the wording implies that they disbelieved while knowing.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited﴾, the verse, meaning the Jews. Ibn Zayd said: the intended meaning is those who were in the time of Sulayman. Ibn 'Abbas said: the intended meaning is those who were in the time of the Prophet ﷺ. It is also said that it includes all of them. "Tatlu": 'Ata' said its meaning is "taqra'" (recite), from recitation. Ibn 'Abbas said: "tatlu" means "tatba'" (follow), as you say: "The people came, one following (yatlu) another." "Tatlu" can mean "talat" (it recited), so the present tense is placed in the position of the past. The Kufans said the meaning is "kanat tatlu" (it used to recite). Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak read "al-Shayatun" with a waw. His saying: ﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ means during the time of the reign of Sulayman. It is also said the meaning is "in the kingdom of Sulayman," in the sense of "in his stories, attributes and reports." Al-Tabari said: "ittaba'u" means "faddalu" (they preferred), and ﴿over the kingdom of Sulayman﴾ means over his law, his prophethood and his condition.

As for what the devils recited, it is said that they used to convey to the soothsayers a word of truth, accompanied by a hundred falsehoods, until that became their knowledge. Sulayman gathered it and buried it beneath his throne. When he died, the devils said: "That was the knowledge of Sulayman." It is also said: rather, what the devils recited was sorcery and its teaching, and Sulayman, peace be upon him, gathered it as was previously mentioned. It is also said that Sulayman, peace be upon him, used to dictate his knowledge to his scribe Asaf ibn Barkhiya and store it, and when he died the jinn brought it out and wrote between every two lines a line of sorcery, then attributed that to Sulayman. It is also said that Asaf colluded with devils to write sorcery and attribute it to Sulayman after his death. It is also said that the jinn wrote that after Sulayman's death, fabricated it and attributed it to him. It is also said that when the kingdom of Sulayman departed from him, some of the jinn and humans adopted sorcery and soothsaying as knowledge; when Sulayman returned to his kingdom, he sought out their books throughout the lands and buried them. When he died, a devil said to the Children of Israel: "Shall I guide you to the treasure of Sulayman, by which the jinn and the wind were subjected to him? It is this sorcery." So the Children of Israel extracted it, it spread among them, and they attributed Sulayman to sorcery, and disbelieved in that, until Allah cleared him through the tongue of Muhammad ﷺ.

It has been narrated that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ mentioned Sulayman among the prophets, some of the Jews said: "Look at Muhammad, he mentions Sulayman among the prophets, and he was only a sorcerer." His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Sulayman did not disbelieve﴾ is an absolution from Allah, Exalted is He, of Sulayman. No one had previously been mentioned in the verses as attributing disbelief to him, but this verse (p-299) was revealed concerning the earlier matter, that the Jews attributed him to sorcery, and sorcery and practicing it is disbelief.

According to Malik, the sorcerer is killed as an unbeliever and is not given the chance to repent, like the zindiq. Al-Shafi'i said: he is questioned about his sorcery; if it is disbelief, he is asked to repent, and if he repents, well, otherwise he is killed. Malik said, regarding one who ties knots against men from women: he is punished and not killed. There is disagreement concerning the sorcerer of the People of the Covenant (dhimmi). It was said he is killed. Malik said: he is not killed unless he kills by his sorcery, and he must pay compensation for what he caused, and he is killed if he brings about what he did not agree to.

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "lakinna" with a shadda on the nun, and "al-shayatina" in the accusative. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ibn 'Amir read with a light nun and "al-shayatinu" in the nominative. Some of the Kufans said: the shadda is more beloved to me when the waw enters upon it, because the light form is in the position of "bal," and "bal" is not preceded by waw. Abu 'Ali said: the entry of the waw upon it does not imply a meaning that requires the shadda; it is heavy and light with one meaning, except that it does not govern when lightened.

The disbelief of the devils is either by teaching them sorcery, or by knowing it, or by declaring Sulayman a disbeliever because of it, and all of that occurred. The people who taught were followers of the devils among the Children of Israel. "Al-sihr" is the second object of "yu'allimuna," and the position of "yu'allimuna" is accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), or nominative as a second predicate.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and what was sent down to the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut﴾. "Ma" is conjoined to "al-sihr," so it is in the accusative position. This is according to the view that Allah, Exalted is He, sent down sorcery to the two angels as a trial for people, so that whoever followed it would disbelieve, and whoever abandoned it would believe; or according to the view of Mujahid and others: Allah, Exalted is He, sent down to the two angels the thing by which one separates a man from his wife, not sorcery; or according to the view that He, Exalted is He, sent down sorcery upon them so that it might be known by way of warning against it and forbidding it.

(p-300) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

According to this view, teaching is merely a brief introduction to its principles.

It is also said that "ma" is conjoined to the "ma" in His saying: ﴿what they recited﴾. It is also said: "ma" is negating, a rejection of His saying: ﴿and Sulayman did not disbelieve﴾, because the Jews said: "Allah sent down Jibril and Mikail with sorcery," and Allah negated that.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak and Ibn Abza read "al-malakayni" with a kasra on the lam. Ibn Abza said: they are Dawud and Sulayman, and according to this view too "ma" is negating. Al-Hasan said: they were two small men (ilj) who were kings in Babylon, so "ma" according to this view is not negating. Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali read them thus as well and said: they are Harut and Marut, which is like the view of al-Hasan. "Babil" is not declined because of femininity and definiteness; it is a region of the earth. It was disputed where it is. Some said it is in Iraq and what borders it. Ibn Mas'ud said to the people of Kufa: "You are between al-Hira and Babil." Qatada said: it is from Nasibin to Ra's al-'Ayn. Some said it is in the west, and this is weak. Some said it is the mountain of Damawand.

"Harut and Marut" is an apposition (badal) of "al-malakayni" according to the one who said they are two angels. Whoever read "malakayni" with a kasra on the lam and made them Dawud and Sulayman, or made the two angels Jibril and Mikail, made "Harut and Marut" an apposition of "the devils" in His saying: ﴿but the devils﴾, and said: they are two devils.

(p-301) "Yu'allimuna" comes either because the two is treated as plural, or by assuming followers for these two devils, who are the leaders. Whoever said they were two small men said: "Harut and Marut" is an apposition of his saying "al-malakayni."

It is also said: they are an apposition of "the people" in His saying: ﴿teaching people﴾. Al-Zuhri read "Harutu wa Marutu" with a raf', and its basis is an apposition of "the devils" in His saying: ﴿what the devils recited﴾, or of the second "shayatin" according to the reading of the one who lightened "lakin" and put it in the nominative, or as the predicate of an implied subject whose estimate is: "they are Harut and Marut." Those who said they were two angels narrated that the angels abhorred the rulers of the children of Adam and claimed that if they were in the same remoteness from Allah as they were, they would obey Him with the truest obedience. Allah said to them: "Choose two angels who will judge among the people." They chose Harut and Marut, and they judged. A woman came to them with a dispute, and they were tempted by her; they sought her, but she refused unless they drank wine and killed a man. They did so. She asked them about the Name by which they ascend to heaven, and they taught it to her; she spoke it and ascended, and was transformed into a star, and she is Venus (al-Zuhra). Ibn 'Umar used to curse her.

(p-302) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of this is weak, and it is far-fetched to attribute it to Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them. It is narrated that Venus descended to them in the form of a Persian woman, and what was mentioned happened between them. Allah then made the angels aware of what had happened with Harut and Marut, and they were astonished. They remained on earth because they were given the choice between the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of this world, and they chose the punishment of this world. So they are in a cavity of the earth, suspended, clapping their wings.

(p-303) A group narrated that they taught sorcery at that very place, and they were bound by a covenant not to teach anyone until they said to him: ﴿We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.﴾ This narrative increases in some reports and decreases in others, and nothing of it is certain; therefore I have abridged it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 103–104:**

The words of the Most High:

﴿They taught no one until they had said, "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." From them people learned what would cause division between a man and his wife, though they could not harm anyone thereby except by God's permission. They learned what harmed them and did not benefit them. They certainly knew that whoever purchased it would have no share in the Hereafter. Wretched is what they sold themselves for, if only they knew.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 102] ﴿And if they had believed and been mindful of God, a reward from God would have been far better, if only they knew.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, do not say "Ra'ina" but say "Unzurna," and listen. For the disbelievers there is a painful punishment.﴾

Ibn al-A'rabi mentioned in al-Yaqutah that "yu'allimani" means "ya'lamani" (they know) and "yash'uran" (they perceive), as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

؎ Know, Messenger of God, that you will overtake me, and that a threat from you is like seizing by the hand

He took this verse to mean that the two angels descended only to teach people magic and to forbid it.

The majority said: rather, teaching is in its usual sense. As for "do not disbelieve": one group said it means by learning magic, and another group said it means by practicing it. Al-Mahdawi related that their saying "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve" [al-Baqarah: 102] was mockery, since they only say it to someone whose misguidance they have already confirmed.

The "min" in "min ahadin" (from anyone) [al-Baqarah: 102] is extra (za'idah) after a negation. As for His words "fa-yata'allamun" (so they learn), Sibawayh said the implied sense is "fa-hum yata'allamun" (so they, they learn). It was also said that it is conjoined to His words "yu'allimuna al-nas" (they teach people) [al-Baqarah: 102], but al-Zajjaj rejected this. It was also said that it is conjoined to the position (mawdi') of "ma yu'allimani" (what the two teach), because His words "wa-ma yu'allimani" (and they do not teach), though the negative "ma" enters upon it, imply affirmation in teaching. It was also said the implied sense is "fa-ya'tuna fa-yata'allamun" (so they come and learn), and al-Zajjaj preferred this.

The pronoun in "yu'allimani" refers to Harut and Marut, the two angels, or to the two foreign men (al-'ilajayn), as previously mentioned. The pronoun in "minhuma" (from them) is said to refer to the two, and it is also said to refer to magic and to what was sent down upon the two angels.

"Yufarriquna" (they cause division) means the dissolution of the marriage bond. It was also said it means that they bind a man from his wife so that he cannot have intercourse with her, which is also a form of separation.

Al-Hasan, al-Zuhri and Qatadah read "al-marr" with a short ra' kasrah, and it is related from al-Zuhri that the ra' was doubled. Ibn Abi Ishaq read "al-mar'" with a damma on the mim and a hamzah, which is the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-Ash'hab al-'Uqayli read "al-mir'" with a kasrah on the mim and a hamzah, and this is related from al-Hasan. The majority of people read "al-mar'a" with a fatha on the mim and a hamzah.

"Zawj" here means a man's wife, and each of the two is the zawj of the other. A woman is also called zawjah. al-Farazdaq said:

؎ Indeed, he who strives to corrupt my wife is like one who runs to a lion's thicket, seeking to take her

The majority read "bi-darrina" (with harming ones). Al-A'mash read "bi-dari bihi min ahad." It was said the nun was dropped for lightness, and it was said it was dropped for the idafah (construct) to "ahad," with the genitive phrase placed between the mudaf and the mudaf ilayhi.

"Bi-idhni Allah" means by His knowledge and His permission. "Yadhurruhum" means in the Hereafter, and "wa-la yanfa'uhum" likewise refers to the Hereafter, even if it benefits them in this world through gains. What is considered is the matter of the Hereafter. The pronoun in "'alimu" (they knew) refers to the Children of Israel according to the pronouns preceding it. It was also said it refers to the devils, and it was said to the two angels, who are a dual but are referred to in plural. He said "ishtarahu" (whoever purchased it), because they used to be given a wage on condition that they teach. "Khalaq" means portion and share, and here it means standing and rank. The lam in His words "la-man" (indeed whoever) [al-Baqarah: 102] is the lam of oath, indicating that the speech is an oath and not a conditional.

The discussion on "bi'sama" has already been given, and "shara'u" means "they sold," and a similar case has already been mentioned. The pronoun in "yu'allimun" refers to the Children of Israel by consensus. Whoever said that the pronoun in "'alimu" refers to them has taken this second instance as metaphorical: since they acted like one who does not know, they were as if they did not know. Whoever said the pronoun in "'alimu" refers to the devils or to the two angels said: those (the devils or angels) knew that there is no portion for whoever purchases it, and these (the Children of Israel) did not know, so it is literal.

Makki said: the pronoun in "'alimu" refers to the scholars of the People of the Book, and in His words "law kanu ya'lamun" (if only they knew) it refers to those among them who were learning.

His words "wa-law annahum amanu" (and if they had believed) — the position of "anna" is nominative (raf'), meaning: if their faith had occurred. It refers to those who purchased magic. "Law" requires an answer. One group said its answer is "la-mathubatun" (a reward), because it is a verbal noun (masdar) that occurs for the past and the future, while the answer to "law" must be past or have the sense of past. Al-Akhfash said: "law" has no explicit answer in this verse, but it is implied, meaning: if they had believed they would have been rewarded.

Qatadah, Abu al-Simal and Ibn Buraydah read "lamathwabatun" with a sukun on the tha' and a fatha on the waw, and this too is a verbal noun, like mashurah and mashwarah. "Mathubah" is nominative as the subject, "khayr" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "anna." Among most people "mathubah" means reward and recompense, and this is the correct view. Others said its meaning is return to God, from "thaba yathubu" when he returned. The lam in it is the lam of oath, because the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida') is dispensable, while this lam is not.

His words "law kanu ya'lamun" (if only they knew) may mean the negation of knowledge from them, or it may mean: if only they knew knowledge that benefits.

The majority read "ra'ina" from al-muraa'ah (attentiveness), in the sense of "fa'ilna," meaning: "ra'ina" — "look after us and we will look after you." In this there is rudeness (jafa'), in that anyone would address his Prophet with it, and God has urged lowering the voice in his presence, supporting him, and honoring him. Whoever took this meaning said: God forbade the believers from it for this reason, and on this interpretation the Jews have no place in this verse. Rather, it is a prohibition of every address that implies equality with the Prophet ﷺ.

A group said it is a dialect that the Ansar used to say, and Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut said it to the Prophet ﷺ, twisting it with his tongue and as a slander, just as it was said: "Listen, without being listened to." So God forbade the believers from saying this expression.

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi (may God have mercy on him) said: restricting this dialect to the Ansar is a shortcoming; rather, it is the dialect of all the Arabs, an active participle from al-muraa'ah. The Jews, however, turned it toward ru'unah (foolishness), showing that they meant attentiveness, while concealing that they meant ru'unah, which is ignorance.

Al-Mahdawi related from some people that this verse, on this interpretation, abrogates (naskh) an act that had been permissible. (Naskh here means abrogation: the lifting of a previously valid ruling by a later revelation.) But the conditions of abrogation are not met in this verse, because the earlier ruling was not an established law.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Haywah read "ra'inan" with tanwin, and this carries the meaning of ignorance. This is taken to mean that the Jews used to say it, so God forbade the believers from saying a permissible expression as a means of blocking (sadd dhari'ah, blocking the means to what is forbidden), lest the Jews use it as a way to the prohibited, since the believers used to say "ra'ina" without tanwin. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it is "ra'awna," which is an irregular reading (shadhdhah), and its explanation is that they used to address the Prophet ﷺ as a group is addressed, showing him honor, while in their hearts they meant fa'ul (a form) from ru'unah.

"Unzurna," with a damma on the alif and the zay, means: "intazirna" (wait for us) and "amhil 'alayna" (be patient with us). It may also mean "tafqidna" (look upon us) from al-nazar (looking). This word is sincere in honoring the Prophet ﷺ on both meanings.

The apparent meaning to me is a request for the look of the eye combined with reflecting on the state (of the one addressed), and this is the meaning of "ra'ina." So the expression was changed for the believers so that the Jews' connection to it would be removed. Al-A'mash and others read "anzirna" with the alif cut and the zay kasrah, meaning: delay us and give us time until we understand from you and receive from you.

When God the Most High in this verse forbade and commanded, He then urged listening, which implies obedience. Know that for whoever opposes His command and disbelieves there is a painful punishment (adhab alim), which is the painful. "Isma'u" (listen) is conjoined to "quluu" (say), not to its governed element.

"Mathubah" is nominative as the subject, "khayr" is its predicate, and the sentence is the predicate of "anna." Among most people "mathubah" means reward and recompense, and this is the correct view. Others said its meaning is return to God, from "thaba yathubu" when he returned. The lam in it is the lam of oath, because the lam of the beginning (lam al-ibtida') is dispensable, while this lam is not.

His words "law kanu ya'lamun" (if only they knew) may mean the negation of knowledge from them, or it may mean: if only they knew knowledge that benefits.

The majority read "ra'ina" from al-muraa'ah (attentiveness), in the sense of "fa'ilna," meaning: "ra'ina" — "look after us and we will look after you." In this there is rudeness (jafa'), in that anyone would address his Prophet with it, and God has urged lowering the voice in his presence, supporting him, and honoring him. Whoever took this meaning said: God forbade the believers from it for this reason, and on this interpretation the Jews have no place in this verse. Rather, it is a prohibition of every address that implies equality with the Prophet ﷺ.

A group said it is a dialect that the Ansar used to say, and Rifa'ah ibn Zayd ibn al-Tabut said it to the Prophet ﷺ, twisting it with his tongue and as a slander, just as it was said: "Listen, without being listened to." So God forbade the believers from saying this expression.

Abu Muhammad al-Qadi (may God have mercy on him) said: restricting this dialect to the Ansar is a shortcoming; rather, it is the dialect of all the Arabs, an active participle from al-muraa'ah. The Jews, however, turned it toward ru'unah (foolishness), showing that they meant attentiveness, while concealing that they meant ru'unah, which is ignorance.

Al-Mahdawi related from some people that this verse, on this interpretation, abrogates (naskh) an act that had been permissible. (Naskh here means abrogation: the lifting of a previously valid ruling by a later revelation.) But the conditions of abrogation are not met in this verse, because the earlier ruling was not an established law.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Haywah read "ra'inan" with tanwin, and this carries the meaning of ignorance. This is taken to mean that the Jews used to say it, so God forbade the believers from saying a permissible expression as a means of blocking (sadd dhari'ah, blocking the means to what is forbidden), lest the Jews use it as a way to the prohibited, since the believers used to say "ra'ina" without tanwin. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud it is "ra'awna," which is an irregular reading (shadhdhah), and its explanation is that they used to address the Prophet ﷺ as a group is addressed, showing him honor, while in their hearts they meant fa'ul (a form) from ru'unah.

"Unzurna," with a damma on the alif and the zay, means: "intazirna" (wait for us) and "amhil 'alayna" (be patient with us). It may also mean "tafqidna" (look upon us) from al-nazar (looking). This word is sincere in honoring the Prophet ﷺ on both meanings.

The apparent meaning to me is a request for the look of the eye combined with reflecting on the state (of the one addressed), and this is the meaning of "ra'ina." So the expression was changed for the believers so that the Jews' connection to it would be removed. Al-A'mash and others read "anzirna" with the alif cut and the zay kasrah, meaning: delay us and give us time until we understand from you and receive from you.

When God the Most High in this verse forbade and commanded, He then urged listening, which implies obedience. Know that for whoever opposes His command and disbelieves there is a painful punishment (adhab alim), which is the painful. "Isma'u" (listen) is conjoined to "quluu" (say), not to its governed element.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 105–106 (part 1 of 2):

His the Mighty and Majestic's saying:
﴿Those who disbelieve among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not wish that any good should be sent down to you from your Lord. But Allah singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty.﴾ ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten, We bring one better than it or the like of it. Do you not know that Allah is over all things competent?﴾

The estimated sense: "nor [from] the polytheists," and "those who disbelieve" is general. Then He specified their kinds: from the Jews, the Christians, and the worshippers of idols, to make clear that the alif and lam in "those who" (alladhina) are not for a specific reference (al-'ahd), meaning a particular individual.

The meaning of the verse: what We have commanded you, namely to glorify your Prophet, is better than the gift from Allah that He bestows upon you, and the disbelievers do not wish for that. Then the wording encompasses every good other than this. The "an" with the verb is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), and the "min" is superfluous (za'idah) according to some of them. Since the desire for the descent of good is negated, this stands in the place of the negation which must precede the superfluous "min" according to Sibawayh and al-Khalil; as for al-Akhfash, he permits its superfluity in an affirmative context.

Some said: "min" is partitive (li-l-tab'id), because they wish that no good, little or much, should descend upon the believers. Had the partitive sense been removed, it would be permissible for a speaker to say: "We wish that no complete good should descend, and we do not dislike that some part should descend." Then, when the desire for the descent of a part is negated, that is all the more fitting for the descent of a complete good.

The mercy in this verse is general, encompassing all its kinds which Allah has granted to His servants, past and present. Some said: the mercy is the Qur'an; some said: the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ. These are parts of the general mercy contained in the wording of the verse.

As for His exalted saying: ﴿Whatever sign We abrogate or cause to be forgotten﴾ – the verse. Naskh (abrogation, lit. "annulment/transcription") in the language of the Arabs has two senses: the first is transfer (naql), like copying a book from another; the second is removal (izalah). The first has no place in this verse, and it occurs in the Book of Allah in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We were having copied what you used to do﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 29]. The second, which is removal, is the one in this verse, and it is divided linguistically into two kinds: one that establishes the abrogating (nasikh) after the abrogated (mansukh), like their saying: "the sun abrogated the shadow" (nasakhat al-shamsu al-zill); and another that does not establish, like their saying: "the wind abrogated the trace" (nasakhat al-rih al-athar).

The naskh in the Sharia occurs in accordance with these two kinds. The abrogating in reality is Allah, the Exalted, and the legal address is called "abrogating" since by it abrogation occurs.

The definition of the nasikh according to the skilled scholars of Ahl al-Sunnah (huddhaq ahl al-sunnah) is: the address indicating the lifting of a ruling established by a prior address, in such a way that, were it not for it, the ruling would remain established even with its delay from it.

Naskh is possible for Allah, the Exalted, by reason, for nothing impossible follows from it, nor a change of any of His attributes, the Exalted. Commands are not tied to will (irada), so it would not follow from abrogation that the will changed; nor is abrogation due to the arising of knowledge (tuaruy 'ilm). Rather Allah, the Exalted, knows until what time His command with the first ruling ends, and He knows its abrogation by the second.

Al-bada' (change of mind/manifestation of a new decision) is not permissible for Allah, the Exalted, because it occurs only through the arising of knowledge or the change of will, and that is impossible with regard to Allah, the Exalted. The Jews made naskh and bada' one and the same, and therefore they did not permit naskh, and thus they went astray.

The mansukh according to our imams is the ruling established itself, not what the Mu'tazilah held, that it is like the established ruling in what is to come. What led them to that is their doctrine that commands are willed, and that the good is an essential attribute of goodness, and the will of Allah, the Exalted, is good. Evidence has established that commands are not connected to will, and that goodness and badness in the rulings derive only from the Sharia, not from an essential attribute.

Specification (takhsis) from the general (al-'umum) gives the impression that it is abrogation, but it is not, because the specified item was never encompassed by the general. Had it been definitively established that the general encompassed a certain thing, and then that thing was removed from the generality, it would be abrogation, not specification. Abrogation is not permitted in reports (akhbar); it is specific to commands and prohibitions. Some objectors returned a command to a report by saying: "Does its meaning not amount to: it is obligatory upon you to do such-and-such?" This is a report. The answer is to say: indeed, within the meaning is [the implication]: "unless I abrogate it for you and lift it." Just as the wording of the command included that report, so this exception is included.

The forms of naskh vary:
Sometimes the heavier is abrogated into the lighter, like the abrogation of the requirement of ten [to stand firm] by the requirement of two.
Sometimes the lighter is abrogated into the heavier, like the abrogation of the day of 'Ashura' and the numbered days by Ramadan.
Sometimes a like is abrogated by its like in heaviness and lightness, like the kiss.
Sometimes a thing is abrogated without a replacement, like the charity before private consultation (sadaqat al-najwa).

Complete abrogation is when both the recitation and the ruling are abrogated, and that is frequent. Among it is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "We used to recite: 'Do not turn away from your fathers, for that is disbelief.'"

Sometimes the recitation is abrogated but not the ruling, like the verse of stoning.

Sometimes the ruling is abrogated but not the recitation, like the charity before private consultation, and like His saying: ﴿And if any of your wives has gone over to the disbelievers, and you have had a victory, then give those whose wives have gone the like of what they had spent﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 11]. The recitation and the ruling are two rulings, so it is permissible to abrogate one of them without the other. The Qur'an is abrogated by the Qur'an, and the Sunnah by the Sunnah. This expression means the mutawatir report which is definitive. The report of a single narrator (khabar al-wahid) is abrogated by the report of a single narrator. All of this is agreed upon. The skilled imams hold that the Qur'an is abrogated by the Sunnah, and that exists in His saying ﷺ: "There is no bequest to an heir," and this is the apparent position of the questions of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, while al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, rejected that. The proof against him is from his own position of dropping the lashing in the punishment for adultery upon the married person who is stoned, for there is nothing that removes that except the Sunnah, the action of the Prophet ﷺ.

Likewise the skilled imams hold that the Sunnah is abrogated by the Qur'an. That exists in the matter of the qiblah, for prayer toward Syria was never in the Book of Allah; and in His saying: ﴿Then do not return them to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], for their return was only by the treaty of the Prophet ﷺ with Quraysh.

The skilled scholars agree that the abrogation of the Qur'an by a single-narrator report is rationally permissible, and they differed whether it has occurred in the Sharia. Abu al-Ma'ali and others held that it occurred in the incident of the mosque of Quba', regarding the turning toward the qiblah; and some rejected that.

It is not valid to abrogate a text by analogy (qiyas), since among the conditions of analogy is that it not contradict a text. All of this is during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. As for after his death and the establishment of the Sharia, the Community agreed that there is no abrogation. For this reason consensus (ijma') neither abrogates nor is abrogated, because it is only formed after the Prophet ﷺ. So when we find a consensus that contradicts a text, we know that the consensus was based on an abrogating text which we do not know.

Some speakers of kalam said: established abrogation is fixed with regard to everyone, whether or not one knows the abrogating text. What the skilled scholars hold is that whoever has not received the abrogating text is worshipping by the first ruling, and when the abrogating text reaches him, the judgment of abrogation comes upon him. The skilled scholars hold the permissibility of abrogating a ruling before it is acted upon, and that exists in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, in the story of the one to be sacrificed.

The majority of people read: "ma nansakh" with a fatha on the nun, from nasakha. A group read "nunsikh," with a damma on the nun, from ansakha, and with it Ibn 'Amir alone among the Seven read.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is not a dialect, because one does not say nusikha and ansakha with the same meaning; nor is it for transitivity, because the meaning would come out: "what We write of a sign," i.e., what We send down, so the whole Qur'an would be abrogated on this reading, and that is not the case. So it remains only that the meaning is: "what We find abrogated," as you say: "ahmadtu al-rajul" and "abkhaltuhu," meaning you found him praiseworthy or stingy. Abu 'Ali said: We do not find it abrogated except by Our abrogating it, so the two readings agree in meaning though they differ in wording.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The reciters of this reading have construed the meaning in two ways. One is that the meaning is: "what We write and send down from the Preserved Tablet, or what We defer in it and leave aside, so We do not send it down," meaning that is Our action, for We bring something better than the deferred and left aside, or its like; so the two pronouns in "minha" or "mithliha" return to the pronoun in "nansa'uha."

The other meaning: that "nansakh" is from naskh in the sense of removal, and the sense is: "what We abrogate for you," i.e., We permit you to abrogate it. As if, when Allah abrogated it, He permitted His Prophet to leave it by that abrogation, and so He called that permission "insakh." "Ma" is conditional, and it is the object of "nansakh," and "nansakh" is apocopated by the condition. The reciters differed regarding the reading of His saying "nunsiha." Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, and the majority of people read "nansaha" with a damma on the first nun, a sukun on the second, a kasra on the sin, and without the hamza; this is from ansa, the transmitted form of nasiya. A group read it as above except that they hamzaed after the sin, and this has the meaning of delay; the Arabs say: "ansa'tu al-dayn wa ghayrahu, unsi'uhu insa'an" when I delayed it. A group read: "aw nansaha" with a fatha on the first nun, a sukun on the second, and a fatha on the sin, and this has the meaning of leaving; Makki mentioned it without attributing it, and Abu 'Ubayd al-Bakri mentioned it in the book "al-La'ali" from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and I think he erred. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas read "aw tansaha" with a ta' addressing the Prophet ﷺ, a nun after it with a sukun, and a fatha on the sin; so said Abu al-Fath and Abu 'Amr al-Dani. It was said to Sa'd: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib reads it with a damma on the first nun and a kasra on the sin," and he said: "The Qur'an was not revealed to al-Musayyib nor to the family of al-Musayyib," and he recited: ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6], and ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾ [al-Kahf: 24].

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, as also reported from him, read "aw tunsaha" with a damma on the ta' first, a fatha on the sin, and a sukun on the nun between them; this is from forgetting (nisyan). Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim and Abu Raja' read "nunassiha" with a damma on the first nun, a fatha on the second, and a kasra on the sin, shaddah; this too is from forgetting. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read "nansa'uha" with a fatha on the first nun, another after it with a sukun, a fatha on the sin, and an alif after it followed by a hamza; this is from delay. The Arabs say: "nasa'tu al-ibil 'an al-hawd, unsi'uha nas'an," meaning I delayed them; and likewise it is said: "anса'a al-ibil" when he increases their thirst by a day or two or more, meaning he delayed them from the watering.

A group read the same reading as this, except that it has a ta' with a fatha first, addressing the Prophet ﷺ and attributing the verb to him. Abu Haywah read the same, except that he damma'd the first ta'. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "aw nunsika" with a damma on the first nun, a sukun on the second, a kasra on the sin, and a kaf addressing (the Prophet). In the codex of Salim, mawla of Abu Hudhayfah, it is "aw nunsikaha," like Ubayy's reading except that it added the pronoun of the verse. Al-A'mash read "ma nunsika min ayatin aw nansakhha najii'u bi-mithliha," and so it is established in the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: These readings, each of them, cannot be free of being either from al-naskh or al-insa' in the sense of delay, or from forgetting (nisyan).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 105–106 (part 2 of 2):

Forgetting (al-nisyan) in the speech of the Arabs usually comes as the opposite of remembering (al-dhikr), and it may also come in the sense of leaving (al-tark). The three meanings are all attributed to these readings. Whatever of these readings fits the word *nisyan*, which is the opposite of remembering, then the meaning of the verse is: "Whatever sign We abrogate, or cause you to forget it, so that you forget it until it is entirely removed and gone, We bring something better than it for you or its equal in benefit." Whatever of these readings is understood in the sense of leaving, then the verse, with that sense, admits four meanings. The first: "Whatever We abrogate, in its various forms of abrogation (al-naskh), or leave without sending it down to you, We will surely send down, out of mercy to you, something better than it or its like, so that the religion does not fall short of the limit of its perfection." The second meaning: "Or We leave its recitation (tilawa) [though We abrogate its ruling]." Then abrogation, on this reading, is the removal of both recitation and ruling. The third meaning: "Or We leave its ruling [though We remove its recitation]." Abrogation on this reading is also the removal of both recitation and ruling. The fourth meaning: "Or We leave it neither abrogated in its ruling nor in its recitation." Abrogation on this meaning is in all its forms.

The two pronouns in "minha" (from it) or "mithliha" (its like) refer only to the abrogated verse. It is as though the statement says: "Whether We abrogate or leave it, We bring something better than the abrogated verse or its like."

Whatever of these readings is understood in the sense of postponement (al-ta'khir), then the verse with it admits the same four meanings as in leaving. The first: "Whatever We abrogate or postpone sending down." The second: "Whatever We abrogate, the more perfect abrogation, or postpone its ruling, though We leave its recitation." The third: "Whatever We abrogate, the more perfect abrogation, or postpone its recitation, though We leave its ruling." The fourth: "Whatever We abrogate or postpone, keeping it established, not abrogating it." The two pronouns refer as we mentioned under leaving.

Some of these meanings are stronger than others, but we have mentioned all of them because they are admissible, and the scholars have stated all of them, either explicitly or by allusion, so we have completed them.

Al-Zajjaj said: The reading "aw nunsiha" (with a *damma* on the *nun*, a sukun on the second letter, and a *kasra* on the *sin*) does not admit the sense of leaving, because one does not say *ansa* in the sense of *taraka* (to leave). Abu 'Ali and others said: That is admissible, because it means "We make you leave it." Al-Zajjaj also weakened the view that the verse be understood as forgetting in the sense opposite to remembering, and said: This did not happen to the Prophet ﷺ, nor did he forget any Qur'an. Abu 'Ali and others said: That is permissible, and it has occurred, and there is no difference between a verse being removed by abrogation or by causing it to be forgotten. Al-Zajjaj argued with the words of the Most High: ﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾ [al-Isra: 86], meaning: We did not do it. Abu 'Ali said: We did not take away all of it.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: [This is] in the sense of removing the blessing, as He threatened. Al-Tabari related the view from someone earlier than al-Zajjaj and refuted it. The correct view in this matter is that the Prophet ﷺ forgetting what Allah the Most High willed that he forget, and did not will to establish as Qur'an, is permissible.

As for forgetting that is a human weakness, the Prophet ﷺ is protected from it before conveying and after conveying, as long as no one among the Companions has memorized it. As for after it has been memorized, then what is permissible for humans is permissible for him, because he has conveyed and fulfilled the trust. From this is the hadith: "When he dropped a verse, and after finishing the prayer he said: 'Is Ubayy among the people?' He said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Why did you not remind me?' He said: 'I thought it had been abrogated.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'It was not abrogated, but I forgot it.'"

The word "khayr" (better) in the verse is a comparative adjective (sifat tafdil). The meaning: "more beneficial for you, O people, in the immediate, if the abrogating verse is lighter, and in the deferred, if it is heavier, and its equal if it is equal." Some said: "khayr" in the verse is a verbal noun (masdar), and "min" indicates the starting point of the end (li-ibtida' al-ghaya).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view is troubled by His words "or its like," unless the "mithl" is conjoined to the pronoun in "minha" without repeating the preposition, and that is objectionable.

His words, the Most High: ﴿Do you not know that﴾, apparently are interrogative, but their meaning is affirmation (taqrir). Affirmation requires a counterpart (mu'adil), as pure interrogation does. The counterpart here, according to a group, is ﴿Or do you wish﴾ [al-Baqara: 108]. Some said: "am" here is disjunctive (munqati'a), so its counterpart according to them is omitted, its estimate being: "Or do you know?" All of this is on the basis that the address to the Prophet ﷺ is an address to his community. If he alone is addressed, the counterpart is omitted and nothing else, and both views are transmitted.

The meaning of the verse: Allah the Most High abrogates what He wills, establishes what He wills, and does with His rulings what He wills. He is capable of that and of everything. This is directed at the Jews' denial of abrogation. His words, ﴿of everything﴾, have a general form whose meaning is specific, since the eternal attributes are not included in it by the evidence of reason, nor are impossibilities, because they are not "things." In the speech of the Arabs, "shay'" (thing) means what exists. "Qadir" (capable) is an active participle in the intensive form from "qadara" with a *fatha* on the 'ayn, "yaqdiru" with a *kasra*. Some Arabs say "qadira" with a *kasra* on the 'ayn, "yaqdaru" with a *fatha*.

Just as the wording of the command included that report, so this exception is included.

The forms of naskh vary:
Sometimes the heavier is abrogated into the lighter, like the abrogation of the requirement of ten [to stand firm] by the requirement of two.
Sometimes the lighter is abrogated into the heavier, like the abrogation of the day of 'Ashura' and the numbered days by Ramadan.
Sometimes a like is abrogated by its like in heaviness and lightness, like the kiss.
Sometimes a thing is abrogated without a replacement, like the charity before private consultation (sadaqat al-najwa).

Complete abrogation is when both the recitation and the ruling are abrogated, and that is frequent. Among it is the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "We used to recite: 'Do not turn away from your fathers, for that is disbelief.'"

Sometimes the recitation is abrogated but not the ruling, like the verse of stoning.

Sometimes the ruling is abrogated but not the recitation, like the charity before private consultation, and like His saying: ﴿And if any of your wives has gone over to the disbelievers, and you have had a victory, then give those whose wives have gone the like of what they had spent﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 11]. The recitation and the ruling are two rulings, so it is permissible to abrogate one of them without the other. The Qur'an is abrogated by the Qur'an, and the Sunnah by the Sunnah. This expression means the mutawatir report which is definitive. The report of a single narrator (khabar al-wahid) is abrogated by the report of a single narrator. All of this is agreed upon. The skilled imams hold that the Qur'an is abrogated by the Sunnah, and that exists in His saying ﷺ: "There is no bequest to an heir," and this is the apparent position of the questions of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, while al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, rejected that. The proof against him is from his own position of dropping the lashing in the punishment for adultery upon the married person who is stoned, for there is nothing that removes that except the Sunnah, the action of the Prophet ﷺ.

Likewise the skilled imams hold that the Sunnah is abrogated by the Qur'an. That exists in the matter of the qiblah, for prayer toward Syria was never in the Book of Allah; and in His saying: ﴿Then do not return them to the disbelievers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 10], for their return was only by the treaty of the Prophet ﷺ with Quraysh.

The skilled scholars agree that the abrogation of the Qur'an by a single-narrator report is rationally permissible, and they differed whether it has occurred in the Sharia. Abu al-Ma'ali and others held that it occurred in the incident of the mosque of Quba', regarding the turning toward the qiblah; and some rejected that.

It is not valid to abrogate a text by analogy (qiyas), since among the conditions of analogy is that it not contradict a text. All of this is during the lifetime of the Prophet ﷺ. As for after his death and the establishment of the Sharia, the Community agreed that there is no abrogation. For this reason consensus (ijma') neither abrogates nor is abrogated, because it is only formed after the Prophet ﷺ. So when we find a consensus that contradicts a text, we know that the consensus was based on an abrogating text which we do not know.

Some speakers of kalam said: established abrogation is fixed with regard to everyone, whether or not one knows the abrogating text. What the skilled scholars hold is that whoever has not received the abrogating text is worshipping by the first ruling, and when the abrogating text reaches him, the judgment of abrogation comes upon him. The skilled scholars hold the permissibility of abrogating a ruling before it is acted upon, and that exists in the Book of Allah, the Exalted, in the story of the one to be sacrificed.

The majority of people read: "ma nansakh" with a fatha on the nun, from nasakha. A group read "nunsikh," with a damma on the nun, from ansakha, and with it Ibn 'Amir alone among the Seven read.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: it is not a dialect, because one does not say nusikha and ansakha with the same meaning; nor is it for transitivity, because the meaning would come out: "what We write of a sign," i.e., what We send down, so the whole Qur'an would be abrogated on this reading, and that is not the case. So it remains only that the meaning is: "what We find abrogated," as you say: "ahmadtu al-rajul" and "abkhaltuhu," meaning you found him praiseworthy or stingy. Abu 'Ali said: We do not find it abrogated except by Our abrogating it, so the two readings agree in meaning though they differ in wording.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The reciters of this reading have construed the meaning in two ways. One is that the meaning is: "what We write and send down from the Preserved Tablet, or what We defer in it and leave aside, so We do not send it down," meaning that is Our action, for We bring something better than the deferred and left aside, or its like; so the two pronouns in "minha" or "mithliha" return to the pronoun in "nansa'uha."

The other meaning: that "nansakh" is from naskh in the sense of removal, and the sense is: "what We abrogate for you," i.e., We permit you to abrogate it. As if, when Allah abrogated it, He permitted His Prophet to leave it by that abrogation, and so He called that permission "insakh." "Ma" is conditional, and it is the object of "nansakh," and "nansakh" is apocopated by the condition. The reciters differed regarding the reading of His saying "nunsiha." Nafi', Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, and the majority of people read "nansaha" with a damma on the first nun, a sukun on the second, a kasra on the sin, and without the hamza; this is from ansa, the transmitted form of nasiya. A group read it as above except that they hamzaed after the sin, and this has the meaning of delay; the Arabs say: "ansa'tu al-dayn wa ghayrahu, unsi'uhu insa'an" when I delayed it. A group read: "aw nansaha" with a fatha on the first nun, a sukun on the second, and a fatha on the sin, and this has the meaning of leaving; Makki mentioned it without attributing it, and Abu 'Ubayd al-Bakri mentioned it in the book "al-La'ali" from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, and I think he erred. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas read "aw tansaha" with a ta' addressing the Prophet ﷺ, a nun after it with a sukun, and a fatha on the sin; so said Abu al-Fath and Abu 'Amr al-Dani. It was said to Sa'd: "Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib reads it with a damma on the first nun and a kasra on the sin," and he said: "The Qur'an was not revealed to al-Musayyib nor to the family of al-Musayyib," and he recited: ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget﴾ [al-A'la: 6], and ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget﴾ [al-Kahf: 24].

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, as also reported from him, read "aw tunsaha" with a damma on the ta' first, a fatha on the sin, and a sukun on the nun between them; this is from forgetting (nisyan). Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim and Abu Raja' read "nunassiha" with a damma on the first nun, a fatha on the second, and a kasra on the sin, shaddah; this too is from forgetting. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Mujahid, 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, Ibn Kathir, and Abu 'Amr read "nansa'uha" with a fatha on the first nun, another after it with a sukun, a fatha on the sin, and an alif after it followed by a hamza; this is from delay. The Arabs say: "nasa'tu al-ibil 'an al-hawd, unsi'uha nas'an," meaning I delayed them; and likewise it is said: "anса'a al-ibil" when he increases their thirst by a day or two or more, meaning he delayed them from the watering.

A group read the same reading as this, except that it has a ta' with a fatha first, addressing the Prophet ﷺ and attributing the verb to him. Abu Haywah read the same, except that he damma'd the first ta'. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "aw nunsika" with a damma on the first nun, a sukun on the second, a kasra on the sin, and a kaf addressing (the Prophet). In the codex of Salim, mawla of Abu Hudhayfah, it is "aw nunsikaha," like Ubayy's reading except that it added the pronoun of the verse. Al-A'mash read "ma nunsika min ayatin aw nansakhha najii'u bi-mithliha," and so it is established in the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: These readings, each of them, cannot be free of being either from al-naskh or al-insa' in the sense of delay, or from forgetting (nisyan).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 105–106 (part 2 of 2):

Forgetting (al-nisyan) in the speech of the Arabs usually comes as the opposite of remembering (al-dhikr), and it may also come in the sense of leaving (al-tark). The three meanings are all attributed to these readings. Whatever of these readings fits the word *nisyan*, which is the opposite of remembering, then the meaning of the verse is: "Whatever sign We abrogate, or cause you to forget it, so that you forget it until it is entirely removed and gone, We bring something better than it for you or its equal in benefit." Whatever of these readings is understood in the sense of leaving, then the verse, with that sense, admits four meanings. The first: "Whatever We abrogate, in its various forms of abrogation (al-naskh), or leave without sending it down to you, We will surely send down, out of mercy to you, something better than it or its like, so that the religion does not fall short of the limit of its perfection." The second meaning: "Or We leave its recitation (tilawa) [though We abrogate its ruling]." Then abrogation, on this reading, is the removal of both recitation and ruling. The third meaning: "Or We leave its ruling [though We remove its recitation]." Abrogation on this reading is also the removal of both recitation and ruling. The fourth meaning: "Or We leave it neither abrogated in its ruling nor in its recitation." Abrogation on this meaning is in all its forms.

The two pronouns in "minha" (from it) or "mithliha" (its like) refer only to the abrogated verse. It is as though the statement says: "Whether We abrogate or leave it, We bring something better than the abrogated verse or its like."

Whatever of these readings is understood in the sense of postponement (al-ta'khir), then the verse with it admits the same four meanings as in leaving. The first: "Whatever We abrogate or postpone sending down." The second: "Whatever We abrogate, the more perfect abrogation, or postpone its ruling, though We leave its recitation." The third: "Whatever We abrogate, the more perfect abrogation, or postpone its recitation, though We leave its ruling." The fourth: "Whatever We abrogate or postpone, keeping it established, not abrogating it." The two pronouns refer as we mentioned under leaving.

Some of these meanings are stronger than others, but we have mentioned all of them because they are admissible, and the scholars have stated all of them, either explicitly or by allusion, so we have completed them.

Al-Zajjaj said: The reading "aw nunsiha" (with a *damma* on the *nun*, a sukun on the second letter, and a *kasra* on the *sin*) does not admit the sense of leaving, because one does not say *ansa* in the sense of *taraka* (to leave). Abu 'Ali and others said: That is admissible, because it means "We make you leave it." Al-Zajjaj also weakened the view that the verse be understood as forgetting in the sense opposite to remembering, and said: This did not happen to the Prophet ﷺ, nor did he forget any Qur'an. Abu 'Ali and others said: That is permissible, and it has occurred, and there is no difference between a verse being removed by abrogation or by causing it to be forgotten. Al-Zajjaj argued with the words of the Most High: ﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾ [al-Isra: 86], meaning: We did not do it. Abu 'Ali said: We did not take away all of it.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: [This is] in the sense of removing the blessing, as He threatened. Al-Tabari related the view from someone earlier than al-Zajjaj and refuted it. The correct view in this matter is that the Prophet ﷺ forgetting what Allah the Most High willed that he forget, and did not will to establish as Qur'an, is permissible.

As for forgetting that is a human weakness, the Prophet ﷺ is protected from it before conveying and after conveying, as long as no one among the Companions has memorized it. As for after it has been memorized, then what is permissible for humans is permissible for him, because he has conveyed and fulfilled the trust. From this is the hadith: "When he dropped a verse, and after finishing the prayer he said: 'Is Ubayy among the people?' He said: 'Yes, O Messenger of Allah.' He said: 'Why did you not remind me?' He said: 'I thought it had been abrogated.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'It was not abrogated, but I forgot it.'"

The word "khayr" (better) in the verse is a comparative adjective (sifat tafdil). The meaning: "more beneficial for you, O people, in the immediate, if the abrogating verse is lighter, and in the deferred, if it is heavier, and its equal if it is equal." Some said: "khayr" in the verse is a verbal noun (masdar), and "min" indicates the starting point of the end (li-ibtida' al-ghaya).

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This view is troubled by His words "or its like," unless the "mithl" is conjoined to the pronoun in "minha" without repeating the preposition, and that is objectionable.

His words, the Most High: ﴿Do you not know that﴾, apparently are interrogative, but their meaning is affirmation (taqrir). Affirmation requires a counterpart (mu'adil), as pure interrogation does. The counterpart here, according to a group, is ﴿Or do you wish﴾ [al-Baqara: 108]. Some said: "am" here is disjunctive (munqati'a), so its counterpart according to them is omitted, its estimate being: "Or do you know?" All of this is on the basis that the address to the Prophet ﷺ is an address to his community. If he alone is addressed, the counterpart is omitted and nothing else, and both views are transmitted.

The meaning of the verse: Allah the Most High abrogates what He wills, establishes what He wills, and does with His rulings what He wills. He is capable of that and of everything. This is directed at the Jews' denial of abrogation. His words, ﴿of everything﴾, have a general form whose meaning is specific, since the eternal attributes are not included in it by the evidence of reason, nor are impossibilities, because they are not "things." In the speech of the Arabs, "shay'" (thing) means what exists. "Qadir" (capable) is an active participle in the intensive form from "qadara" with a *fatha* on the 'ayn, "yaqdiru" with a *kasra*. Some Arabs say "qadira" with a *kasra* on the 'ayn, "yaqdaru" with a *fatha*.

[p. 315] [p. 316] [p. 317]

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 107–109:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Did you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and that you have, apart from Allah, no protector or helper?﴾ ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before? Whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the right way.﴾ ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back into disbelievers after your faith, out of envy from themselves, after the truth has become clear to them. So pardon and overlook, until Allah brings His command. Indeed, Allah is over all things competent.﴾

Al-mulk (dominion): authority, the executive power of command, and the will. The plural pronoun in "lakum" (to you) indicates that the address to the Prophet ﷺ is meant as an address to his community (ummah).

Al-wali (protector): a form (fa'il) from waliya, meaning to be adjacent and to cling close. So the helper (al-nasir), the assister (al-mu'in), the one who takes charge of a matter (al-qa'im bil-amr), and the guardian (al-hafiz) are all, in some respect, close to one another. Al-nasir (helper) is a form from al-nasr (help), and is more intensive in meaning than naasara.

As for His saying, ﴿Or do you wish﴾ (Am turidun): One group said that "am" is a response to the first interrogation, so it is its counterpart (mu'adilah). Another group said that "am" here is an interrogative particle cut off from the first, as if he had said: "Do you wish?" This usage exists in the speech of the Arabs. Another group said that "am" here means "bal" (rather), together with the interrogative alif. Makki and others said: this is weak, because "am" does not occur with the meaning of "bal" except when doubt has seized the speaker regarding what he is presenting.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: That is not as Makki said, may Allah have mercy on him, because "bal" may be used to turn away from the first wording rather than from its meaning. What Makki said applies only to one of the two meanings of "bal", namely turning away from both the wording and the meaning. Sibawayh's statement is correct: "bal" is used to leave off one speech and begin another.

Abu al-'Aliyah said: This verse was revealed when some of the Companions said to the Prophet ﷺ: "Would that our sins took the same course as the sins of the Children of Israel, with punishment hastened in this world." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah has given you better than what He gave the Children of Israel." And he recited: ﴿And whoever does wrong or wrongs himself, then seeks forgiveness of Allah, will find Allah Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [an-Nisa': 110]. On this view, the attribution of the Messenger ﷺ to the community comes according to the matter in itself, and according to their acknowledgment.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Rafi' ibn Huraymalah the Jew asked the Prophet ﷺ to make springs gush forth, and other things." It was also said: the disbelievers of Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ to bring them Allah openly (jahratan). It was also said: they asked him to bring them Allah and the angels as a tribe (qabilan). Mujahid said: they asked him to turn al-Safa into gold. He said to them: "Take that, like the Table for the Children of Israel." But they refused and drew back.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: On these reports, the attribution of the Messenger to them comes according to the matter in itself, not according to their acknowledgment.

What Moses, peace be upon him, was asked was that he see Allah openly. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and others read "sila" with a kasra on the sin and a ya'. This is a dialect in which one says "salta, asalu" (I asked). It is possible that it derives from a hamza, with the hamza replaced by ya' without regular analogy, and then the sin was given a kasra because of the ya'. Some readers pronounced the hamza as an intermediate sound between hamza and ya', with the sin pronounced with a damma. Turning away from faith and turning towards disbelief is expressed by "tabdil" (exchange). Abu al-'Aliyah said: "kufr" (disbelief) here means hardship, and "iman" (faith) means ease. This is weak, unless one means both as metaphors: hardship upon oneself and ease for it are expressions for punishment and bliss. As for the commonly understood hardships and ease of worldly affairs, the verse is not to be interpreted by them.

"Dalla" (strayed) means he missed the road. "As-sawa'" (the middle) of anything is its centre and its core. From this is His saying: ﴿in the midst of Hell﴾ [as-Saffat: 55]. 'Isa ibn 'Umar said: "I wrote until my middle (sawa'i) was cut off." Hassan ibn Thabit, in his elegy for the Prophet ﷺ, as reported by Ibn Ishaq and others:

"Alas for the helpers of the Prophet and his kin, after his setting, in the middle of the grave."

Abu 'Ubayd said: the one meant is 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, and he thinks this is a mistake on his part. "As-sabil" (the way) is an expression for the Sharia which Allah sent down to His servants. Since it is like the means to attaining His mercy, it is like the path to it.

As for His saying, ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish﴾: "kathir" (many) is raised as the subject of "wadda" (wished). It is an adjective of an indefinite noun, and omitting an indefinite modified noun is rare, but it is permitted here because it is an established adjective which removes ambiguity, in the position of "fariq" (a group). Al-Zuhri said: by "kathir" he meant one person, namely Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. This is an unfair judgment. His saying "yaruddunakum" (they would turn you back) refers back to it. Ibn 'Abbas said: the intended ones are the two sons of Akhtab, Huyayy and Abu Yasir.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Implicitly, the followers are included, so the expression comes out firmly. "Al-Kitab" (the Book) here is the Torah. "Law" (if/would that) here has the function of "an" (that) and does not need an answer. It was said that its answer is implied in "wadda": the estimate is "if they turned you back, they would wish that," so "wadda" indicates the answer, because the one whose condition is that he should come later than "law" [i.e., the answer is after the conditional particle]. "Kuffaran" (as disbelievers) is a second object, and it may be a circumstantial accusative (hal). "Hasadan" (out of envy) is an object of cause, and it was said it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative.

There is disagreement about the attachment of His saying, ﴿out of envy from themselves﴾. It was said that it attaches to "wadda", because it means "they wished". It was said that it attaches to "hasadan", and so the pause falls on "kuffaran". On both of these views the meaning is: they did not find this in any Book, nor were they commanded it; it comes from themselves. The word "hasad" (envy) indicates this, so ﴿from themselves﴾ came as emphasis and binding, as in His saying: ﴿they say with their mouths﴾ [Al 'Imran: 167], ﴿they write the Book with their hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79], and ﴿nor a bird that flies with its two wings﴾ [al-An'am: 38]. It was also said that it attaches to "yaruddunakum" (they would turn you back). The meaning is that they wished the turning back to be in addition to coming from themselves, that is, by their own seduction and beautifying.

There is disagreement about the cause of this verse. It was said: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman and 'Ammar ibn Yasir came to the House of Study, and the Jews wished to divert them from their religion, but both held firm, and the verse was revealed. It was also said: this verse is in meaning a continuation of what preceded it, namely Allah's prohibition against following the Jews' words regarding "ra'ina" and other things, and that they do not wish any good to descend, and they wish to turn the believers back into disbelievers.

"Al-haqq" (the truth) meant in this verse is the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ and the correctness of what the Muslims hold to. This verse is among the clear indications of the possibility of disbelief through obstinacy. The people of the Sunnah differed on whether that is permissible. The sound view, in my opinion, is that it is permissible rationally and has occurred in fact. In every verse that requires it, it follows that knowledge is stripped away at a second stage of obstinacy. "Al-'afw" (pardon) is leaving off punishment, and it derives from "‘iffat al-athar" (the effacing of traces). "Al-safh" (overlooking) is turning away from the sinner, as if he turns the side of his neck (safhat al-'unuq) away.

Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Fight those who do not believe﴾ [at-Tawbah: 29], up to His saying "sagharun" (humbled). It was also said it is abrogated by the statement: "Kill the polytheists." Some people said: this is not the definition of abrogation (naskh), because in the matter itself, the time limit for it was determined by revelation.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This applies to one who takes "the awaited command" to mean the commands of the Sharia, or the killing of Qurayzah and the expulsion of al-Nadir, and the matter of one who takes it to mean the appointed terms of the children of Adam. The abrogation then falls upon this very verse, because there is no disagreement that the verses of unrestricted truce have all been abrogated, and abrogation is the coming of the command in these restricted verses. It was said: the coming of the command is the imposition of fighting. It was said: it is the killing of Qurayzah and the expulsion of al-Nadir. Abu 'Ubaydah said regarding this verse: it is abrogated by fighting, because every verse which contains the abandonment of fighting is Meccan and abrogated. His ruling that this verse is Meccan is weak, because the Jews' obstinate opposition was in Medina.

His saying, ﴿Indeed, Allah is over all things competent﴾, its implication in this context is a promise to the believers.

"Alas for the helpers of the Prophet and his kin, after his setting, in the middle of the grave."

Al-Zuhri said: by "kathir" he meant one person, namely Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf. This is an unfair judgment. His saying "yaruddunakum" (they would turn you back) refers back to it. Ibn 'Abbas said: the intended ones are the two sons of Akhtab, Huyayy and Abu Yasir.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Implicitly, the followers are included, so the expression comes out firmly. "Al-Kitab" (the Book) here is the Torah. "Hasadan" (out of envy) is an object of cause, and it was said it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative.

There is disagreement about the attachment of His saying, ﴿out of envy from themselves﴾. It was said that it attaches to "wadda", because it means "they wished". On both of these views the meaning is: they did not find this in any Book, nor were they commanded it; it comes from themselves. Some people said: this is not the definition of abrogation (naskh), because in the matter itself, the time limit for it was determined by revelation.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This applies to one who takes "the awaited command" to mean the commands of the Sharia, or the killing of Qurayzah and the expulsion of al-Nadir, and the matter of one who takes it to mean the appointed terms of the children of Adam.
