**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 110–113:**

(p-322) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And establish prayer and give zakah. And whatever good you put forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian." That is their wishful thinking. Say, "Produce your proof, if you should be truthful."﴾ ﴿Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good will have his reward with his Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿And the Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not upon anything," while they recite the Scripture. Likewise said those who do not know the like of their saying. So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾

Some of the jurists said: the saying of the Exalted, "And establish prayer," is general (ʿumum). Another group said it is among the ambiguous (mujmal) parts of the Qur'an. The preferred view is that it is general from one aspect and ambiguous from another. It is general in that the prayer is (linguistically) supplication (duʿaʾ), so taking it in its literal sense is possible, while the Law has specified it with particular postures, actions and words. It is ambiguous in respect of its times and the number of its units (rakʿat), which are not understood from the word itself; rather the hearer is in need of an explanation. All of this applies to "establish prayer." As for zakah, it is wholly ambiguous and nothing more.

Al-Tabari said: Allah only commanded prayer and zakah here in order to erase what preceded of their inclination toward the sayings of the Jews, "Ra'ina" (a word that was used with a mocking double meaning), because that is a prohibition of its kind. Then the believers were commanded with that which erases it.

The good that is put forward is past, since it has been done. So the meaning of "you will find it" is: you will find its reward and recompense, and that is equivalent to its existence. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, is a statement in form, but its meaning is promise and warning.

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise"﴾, its meaning: the Jews said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew," and the Christians said, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Christian." So He combined their saying, and the separation of their two categories indicates the divergence of their two sayings. This is the concision (ijaz) and the wrapping-up (laff) of the speech. (p-323) "Hud" is the plural of ha'id, like ʿaʾid and ʿud, and its meaning is "the one who repents and returns." Similar to it in the plural are bazil and bazl, ha'il and hawl, and ba'ir and bur. It has also been said that it is a verbal noun (masdar) used as a description for both the singular and the plural, like fatar, ʿadl and ridaʾ.

Al-Farra' said: its origin is yahudiyy, whose two yaʾs were deleted contrary to analogy. Ubayy ibn Kaʿb recited: "except one who was a Jew" (yahudiyyan). Allah refuted them and made their saying a mere wish (umniyya). They had already been cut off earlier by His saying, ﴿so wish for death﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:94]. Muhammad ﷺ was commanded to call them to bring forth proof.

It has been said that the ha' in "hatu" (bring) is original, from "hata, yuhatii" (a verb that has fallen out of use in all its conjugations except the imperative). It has also been said that it is a substitute for the hamza of "ataa" (to give). It has also been said that ha is an interjection of alerting, and the hamza of "ataa" was obligatorily deleted. Burhan (proof) is the evidence that produces certainty.

Al-Tabari said: the demand for proof here requires the establishment of rational reflection (nazar) and refutes the one who denies it. The statement of the Jews, "lan" (never), is a negation after which "bala" (yes) is appropriate, since it is a rejection with affirmation in answer to a negation; it is a particle coined for this purpose. It has also been said that it is "bal" (rather) to which a yaʾ has been added, to dissociate it in the manner of the conjunction found in "bal."

"Aslama" means: submitted, humbled oneself, and obeyed. From it is the saying of Zayd ibn ʿAmr ibn Nufayl:

*And I have submitted my face to Him to whom the clouds have submitted,*
*carrying sweet, pure water.*

The "face" is singled out for mention because it is the noblest part of the human being that is seen and the place of the senses, and in it appear honour and humiliation. For this reason one says "the face of the matter," meaning its main and noblest part. Al-Aʿsha said:

*I interpret the judgment according to its face;*
*my judgment is not by a tyrannical whim.*

It is also possible that "face" in this verse means the aim (maqsid). ﴿while being a doer of good﴾ is a clause in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). The pronoun in "lahu" (for him) returns to the wording of "man" (whoever), and so does the pronoun in "ajruhu" (his reward). In "ʿalayhim" (upon them) and "yahzanun" (they grieve), the pronoun returns to the meaning (plural).

Ibn Muhaysin recited "fala khawfa" (no fear) without tanwin on the raised fa'. It was said that this is a lightening, and it was said that the intended meaning is "fala al-khawf" (no [the] fear), so the alif and lam were deleted. Fear (khawf) is for what is anticipated, and grief (huzn) is for what has already occurred.

The saying of the Exalted, ﴿And the Jews say﴾ and the verse, means: each group claimed that it had more right to the mercy of Allah than the other. The occasion of revelation of the verse was that the Christians of Najran gathered with the Jews of Medina before the Prophet ﷺ, and they reviled one another. The Jews disbelieved in Jesus, his religion and the Gospel, and the Christians disbelieved in Moses and the Torah. In this act of theirs there was each group's disbelief in the other's scripture, because the Gospel includes the truthfulness of Moses and the confirmation of the Torah, and the Torah includes the good tidings of Jesus and the soundness of his prophethood, and both include the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ. So Allah rebuked them for their lying, while in their books is the opposite of what they said.

In the saying of the Exalted, ﴿while they recite the Scripture﴾, there is an admonition to the community of Muhammad ﷺ to be constant in the Qur'an and to stop at its limits, just as al-Hurr ibn Qays said about ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, who was careful (waqqaf) with (p-325) the Book of Allah. The Scripture that they recite was said to be the Torah and the Gospel, so the alif and lam are for the genus. It was said to be the Torah alone, because the Christians follow it, so the alif and lam are for a known referent (ʿahd).

Scholars differed about who is meant by the saying of the Exalted, ﴿those who do not know﴾. The majority said: it refers to the pagans of the Arabs, because they had no scripture. ʿAta' said: the intended are nations that existed before the Jews and the Christians. Some said: the intended are the Jews, and it is as if their saying was repeated, but this view is weak. He, the Exalted, informed them that ﴿He will judge between them﴾, meaning by rewarding the one who was upon some truth, whatever that truth was, and punishing the one who was upon nothing. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that He will show them with their own eyes who enters Paradise and who enters the Fire. ﴿The Day of Resurrection﴾ is named after the rising of people from the graves, since that is the beginning of everything in the day and in what continues after it. His saying "kanu" (they used to be), in the past form, is good in consideration of the judgment, and this is not placing the past in the position of the future, because their disagreement was not on that day but in the world.

(p-322) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾ ﴿And they say, "None will enter Paradise except one who is a Jew or a Christian." That is their wishful thinking. Say, "Produce your proof, if you should be truthful."﴾ ﴿Yes, whoever submits himself to Allah while being a doer of good will have his reward with his Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿And the Jews say, "The Christians are not upon anything," and the Christians say, "The Jews are not upon anything," while they recite the Scripture. Likewise said those who do not know the like of their saying. So Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ.﴾

Some of the jurists said: the saying of the Exalted, "And establish prayer," is general (ʿumum). Another group said it is among the ambiguous (mujmal) parts of the Qur'an. The preferred view is that it is general from one aspect and ambiguous from another. It is general in that the prayer is (linguistically) supplication (duʿaʾ), so taking it in its literal sense is possible, while the Law has specified it with particular postures, actions and words. It is ambiguous in respect of its times and the number of its units (rakʿat), which are not understood from the word itself; rather the hearer is in need of an explanation. All of this applies to "establish prayer." As for zakah, it is wholly ambiguous and nothing more.

The good that is put forward is past, since it has been done. So the meaning of "you will find it" is: you will find its reward and recompense, and that is equivalent to its existence. The saying of the Exalted, ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾, is a statement in form, but its meaning is promise and warning.

(p-٣٢٦)

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned therein and strives for their ruin? Those would not have entered them except in fear. For them in this world is disgrace, and for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment.﴾ ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah. Indeed, Allah is all-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

As for His words, ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ (to the end of the verse): "man" (who) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada', inchoative), and "aẓlamu" (more unjust) is its predicate (khabar). The meaning is: no one is more unjust.

The commentators differed about who is meant by this category of wrongdoers. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it refers to the Christians who used to harm those who prayed in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and would throw filth into it. Qatada and al-Suddi said: it refers to the Romans who assisted Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) in destroying Bayt al-Maqdis, when the Children of Israel had killed Yahya ibn Zakariyya (peace be upon him). It was also said: the one meant is Bukht Nassar. (p-٣٢٦) Ibn Zayd said: it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh when they barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from al-Masjid al-Haram.

This verse encompasses everyone who prevents anyone from a mosque until the Day of Resurrection, or who ruins a city of Islam, because it (the city) contains mosques, even if they are not endowed (as waqf), since the entire earth is a mosque for this Ummah. The commonly known form is "masjid" with a kasra on the jim, but some of the Arabs say "masjad" with a fatha on it.

"An yudhkara" (that His name be mentioned) is in the accusative position, either by assuming the deletion of "min" (from) and the verb's governing directly, or as a substitute (badal) for "al-masajid" (the mosques), and this is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition, a substitute that is connected to and belongs to what it substitutes, or is characterized by a describing attribute). It is also permissible for "an" to be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), and it is permissible for it to be in the genitive position by dropping the preposition, as mentioned by Sibawayh.

Those among the exegetes who said that the verse is about Bayt al-Maqdis made the actual existing ruin the "ruin" (in the verse). Those who said it is about al-Masjid al-Haram made preventing its construction a "ruin," since it calls to that. Those who made the verse about the Christians narrated that a time passed after that when no Christian could enter Bayt al-Maqdis without being beaten severely; this was said by Qatada and al-Suddi. Those who made it about Quraysh said: it was similarly proclaimed by the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) that no polytheist should perform Hajj. "Khaifina" (in fear) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

This verse is not a clear command to prevent them from the mosques, but it is an indication of that, and a disavowal; in it is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers.

(p-٣٢٧) As for those who made the verse about the Christians, they said: the disgrace is the killing of the combatant (harbi) and the jizya (poll tax) of the protected non-Muslim (dhimmi). It was also said: it is the conquests that took place in Islam, such as 'Amuriyya and Hiraqla and others. As for those who made it about Quraysh, they made the disgrace their defeat in the conquest and their being killed, and the punishment in the Hereafter is for whoever among them died as a disbeliever. "Khizyun" (disgrace) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in the prepositional phrase that follows.

"Al-mashriq" is the place of sunrise, and "al-maghrib" is the place of sunset; that is, both belong to Him, and what lies between them of directions and creatures. He singled them out for mention even though the totality of creation is like this, because the occasion of the verse required it.

"Ayna ma" is a conditional particle, and "tuwallu" is in the jussive mood (jazm) because of it. The response (jawab) is in His words "fa-thamma" (then there). The meaning is: wherever you turn toward it and to it. For "tawalla," though its most common usage is "turned away," it implies that one moves toward a direction. You say: "wallaytu 'an kadha" (I turned away from such-and-such) and "wallaytu ila kadha" (I turned toward such-and-such). Al-Hasan recited "tawallaw" with a fatha on the ta' and the lam; "thumma" is built on the fatha and is in the accusative position as an adverb of place (zarf). "Wajhu Allah" (the Face of Allah) means "that toward which He directed us," as you say: "I traveled in the direction of such-and-such," meaning toward such-and-such a side.

The people differed about the interpretation of "the Face" which is attributed to Allah the Exalted in several places (p-٣٢٨) of the Qur'an. The skilled scholars (al-huddhaq) said: this refers back to existence, and the expression of it as "the Face" is a figurative (majaz) usage of the Arabic language, since the face is the most apparent and most honored of the limbs in what is witnessed. Some of the Imams said: that is an attribute established by revelation (sam'), additional to what the intellects require of the attributes of the Eternal, the Exalted. Abu al-Ma'ali weakened this view.

In some places, like this verse, it is plausible that "the Face" means the direction in which His pleasure lies and upon which His reward is, as you say: "I gave charity for the Face of Allah, the Exalted." And specifically in this verse, it is plausible that "the Face" means the direction toward which we were turned in the qibla, according to one of the views that will come. Abu Mansur said in al-Muqni': it is possible that what is meant by "the Face" here is status (jah), as you say: "So-and-so is the face of the people," meaning the place of their honor. So the implication is: there is the majesty of Allah and His greatness.

The exegetes differed about the occasion of revelation of this verse. Qatada said: by this verse Allah permitted His Prophet (ﷺ) that the Muslims should pray wherever they wished, and the Prophet (ﷺ) then chose Bayt al-Maqdis; then all of that was abrogated (naskh) by the transfer to the Ka'ba. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its meaning is an indication toward the Ka'ba, that is: wherever you are, from east or west, you are able to face the Ka'ba, which is "the Face of Allah" to which He directed you; and on this view it abrogates Bayt al-Maqdis. Ibn Zayd said: the Jews had admired the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis and said: "He was guided only by us." When he was turned toward the Ka'ba, the Jews said: "What turned them from their qibla?" So the verse was revealed: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west﴾ (to the end of the verse). Ibn 'Umar said: this verse was revealed concerning voluntary prayer while traveling, wherever the rider's mount turns the person. Al-Nakha'i said: the verse is general: wherever you turn in your dealings and your pursuits, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾, that is, the place of His pleasure and His reward, the direction of His mercy to which one is reached through obedience. (p-٣٢٩) 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'a said: it was revealed concerning one who strove in determining the qibla and erred. A hadith transmitted about this was narrated by 'Amir ibn Rabi'a, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey on a dark night, and a group sought the qibla and set up markers. When they awoke in the morning, they saw that they had missed it, so they informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of that, and this verse was revealed." Some people narrated this hadith as though the Prophet (ﷺ) had not been with the people on that journey, and that is an error.

Qatada also said: this verse was revealed concerning the Negus (al-Najashi), because when he died, the Prophet (ﷺ) called the Muslims to pray over him. Some people said: "How can one pray over someone who never prayed toward the qibla at all?" So this verse was revealed. That is, the Negus was intending the Face of Allah even though he had not been informed of turning toward the qibla.

Ibn Jubayr said: the verse was revealed concerning supplication, when the verse was revealed: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. The Muslims said: "To where do we call?" So this verse was revealed: ﴿so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾.

Al-Mahdawi said: it was also said: this verse is connected in meaning to the one before it, that is: the ruin of a mosque should not prevent you from performing acts of worship, for if the mosque specifically designated for prayer is ruined, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾ present wherever you turn. He also said: it was said that the verse was revealed when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was barred from the House.

"Wasi'un" (All-Encompassing) means "of expansive mercy," and "'Alim" (All-Knowing) means "knowing where to place it." It was also said: "wasi'" here means that He widens (the scope of the ruling) upon His servants; His religion is easy, and He is "'Alim" with the intentions, which are the essence of the deed, even if its outward forms differ regarding the qibla and similar matters.

(p-٣٢٦)

Indeed, Allah is all-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾

As for His words, ﴿And who is more unjust﴾ (to the end of the verse): "man" (who) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada', inchoative), and "aẓlamu" (more unjust) is its predicate (khabar). The meaning is: no one is more unjust.

The commentators differed about who is meant by this category of wrongdoers. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: it refers to the Christians who used to harm those who prayed in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) and would throw filth into it. Qatada and al-Suddi said: it refers to the Romans who assisted Bukht Nassar (Nebuchadnezzar) in destroying Bayt al-Maqdis, when the Children of Israel had killed Yahya ibn Zakariyya (peace be upon him). It was also said: the one meant is Bukht Nassar. (p-٣٢٦) Ibn Zayd said: it refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh when they barred the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from al-Masjid al-Haram.

This verse encompasses everyone who prevents anyone from a mosque until the Day of Resurrection, or who ruins a city of Islam, because it (the city) contains mosques, even if they are not endowed (as waqf), since the entire earth is a mosque for this Ummah. The commonly known form is "masjid" with a kasra on the jim, but some of the Arabs say "masjad" with a fatha on it.

"An yudhkara" (that His name be mentioned) is in the accusative position, either by assuming the deletion of "min" (from) and the verb's governing directly, or as a substitute (badal) for "al-masajid" (the mosques), and this is a badal al-ishtimal (inclusive apposition, a substitute that is connected to and belongs to what it substitutes, or is characterized by a describing attribute). It is also permissible for "an" to be an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), and it is permissible for it to be in the genitive position by dropping the preposition, as mentioned by Sibawayh.

Those among the exegetes who said that the verse is about Bayt al-Maqdis made the actual existing ruin the "ruin" (in the verse). Those who said it is about al-Masjid al-Haram made preventing its construction a "ruin," since it calls to that. Those who made the verse about the Christians narrated that a time passed after that when no Christian could enter Bayt al-Maqdis without being beaten severely; this was said by Qatada and al-Suddi. Those who made it about Quraysh said: it was similarly proclaimed by the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) that no polytheist should perform Hajj. "Khaifina" (in fear) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal).

This verse is not a clear command to prevent them from the mosques, but it is an indication of that, and a disavowal; in it is a promise to the believers and a warning to the disbelievers.

(p-٣٢٧) As for those who made the verse about the Christians, they said: the disgrace is the killing of the combatant (harbi) and the jizya (poll tax) of the protected non-Muslim (dhimmi). It was also said: it is the conquests that took place in Islam, such as 'Amuriyya and Hiraqla and others. As for those who made it about Quraysh, they made the disgrace their defeat in the conquest and their being killed, and the punishment in the Hereafter is for whoever among them died as a disbeliever. "Khizyun" (disgrace) is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is in the prepositional phrase that follows.

"Al-mashriq" is the place of sunrise, and "al-maghrib" is the place of sunset; that is, both belong to Him, and what lies between them of directions and creatures. He singled them out for mention even though the totality of creation is like this, because the occasion of the verse required it.

"Ayna ma" is a conditional particle, and "tuwallu" is in the jussive mood (jazm) because of it. The response (jawab) is in His words "fa-thamma" (then there). The meaning is: wherever you turn toward it and to it. For "tawalla," though its most common usage is "turned away," it implies that one moves toward a direction. You say: "wallaytu 'an kadha" (I turned away from such-and-such) and "wallaytu ila kadha" (I turned toward such-and-such). Al-Hasan recited "tawallaw" with a fatha on the ta' and the lam; "thumma" is built on the fatha and is in the accusative position as an adverb of place (zarf). "Wajhu Allah" (the Face of Allah) means "that toward which He directed us," as you say: "I traveled in the direction of such-and-such," meaning toward such-and-such a side.

The people differed about the interpretation of "the Face" which is attributed to Allah the Exalted in several places (p-٣٢٨) of the Qur'an. The skilled scholars (al-huddhaq) said: this refers back to existence, and the expression of it as "the Face" is a figurative (majaz) usage of the Arabic language, since the face is the most apparent and most honored of the limbs in what is witnessed. Some of the Imams said: that is an attribute established by revelation (sam'), additional to what the intellects require of the attributes of the Eternal, the Exalted. Abu al-Ma'ali weakened this view.

In some places, like this verse, it is plausible that "the Face" means the direction in which His pleasure lies and upon which His reward is, as you say: "I gave charity for the Face of Allah, the Exalted." And specifically in this verse, it is plausible that "the Face" means the direction toward which we were turned in the qibla, according to one of the views that will come. Abu Mansur said in al-Muqni': it is possible that what is meant by "the Face" here is status (jah), as you say: "So-and-so is the face of the people," meaning the place of their honor. So the implication is: there is the majesty of Allah and His greatness.

The exegetes differed about the occasion of revelation of this verse. Qatada said: by this verse Allah permitted His Prophet (ﷺ) that the Muslims should pray wherever they wished, and the Prophet (ﷺ) then chose Bayt al-Maqdis; then all of that was abrogated (naskh) by the transfer to the Ka'ba. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: its meaning is an indication toward the Ka'ba, that is: wherever you are, from east or west, you are able to face the Ka'ba, which is "the Face of Allah" to which He directed you; and on this view it abrogates Bayt al-Maqdis. Ibn Zayd said: the Jews had admired the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis and said: "He was guided only by us." When he was turned toward the Ka'ba, the Jews said: "What turned them from their qibla?" So the verse was revealed: ﴿And to Allah belong the east and the west﴾ (to the end of the verse). Ibn 'Umar said: this verse was revealed concerning voluntary prayer while traveling, wherever the rider's mount turns the person. Al-Nakha'i said: the verse is general: wherever you turn in your dealings and your pursuits, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾, that is, the place of His pleasure and His reward, the direction of His mercy to which one is reached through obedience. (p-٣٢٩) 'Abdullah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'a said: it was revealed concerning one who strove in determining the qibla and erred. A hadith transmitted about this was narrated by 'Amir ibn Rabi'a, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) on a journey on a dark night, and a group sought the qibla and set up markers. When they awoke in the morning, they saw that they had missed it, so they informed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of that, and this verse was revealed." Some people narrated this hadith as though the Prophet (ﷺ) had not been with the people on that journey, and that is an error.

Qatada also said: this verse was revealed concerning the Negus (al-Najashi), because when he died, the Prophet (ﷺ) called the Muslims to pray over him. Some people said: "How can one pray over someone who never prayed toward the qibla at all?" So this verse was revealed. That is, the Negus was intending the Face of Allah even though he had not been informed of turning toward the qibla.

Ibn Jubayr said: the verse was revealed concerning supplication, when the verse was revealed: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60]. The Muslims said: "To where do we call?" So this verse was revealed: ﴿so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾.

Al-Mahdawi said: it was also said: this verse is connected in meaning to the one before it, that is: the ruin of a mosque should not prevent you from performing acts of worship, for if the mosque specifically designated for prayer is ruined, ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾ present wherever you turn. He also said: it was said that the verse was revealed when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was barred from the House.

"Wasi'un" (All-Encompassing) means "of expansive mercy," and "'Alim" (All-Knowing) means "knowing where to place it." It was also said: "wasi'" here means that He widens (the scope of the ruling) upon His servants; His religion is easy, and He is "'Alim" with the intentions, which are the essence of the deed, even if its outward forms differ regarding the qibla and similar matters.

(p-٣٣٠) All the reciters read this verse as "وَقالُوا" (wa-qālū), with a *wāw* linking the sentence to the one before it, or as a conjunction following "سعى" (sa'ā).

Ibn 'Āmir and others read "قالُوا" (qālū) without the *wāw*. Abū 'Alī (al-Fārisī) said: "It is also written this way in the codices of the people of Syria." Dropping the *wāw* can be justified in two ways. First, this sentence is connected in meaning to the one before it, so that connection makes the *wāw* unnecessary. Second, the sentence is begun afresh (*isti'nāf*) without regard to its connection with what came before.

Scholars differed over whom the pronoun in "قالُوا" refers to. It is said to refer to the Christians, because they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and mentioning them fits the context of the verse better. It is also said to refer to the Jews, because they said, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah." And it is said to refer to the pagan Arabs, because they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah."

"سُبْحانَهُ" (Subḥānahu) is a verbal noun meaning His exaltation above, and His freedom from, what they say. "ما" (mā) is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is the prepositional phrase that follows, or else the implied verb of being (*al-istiqrār al-muqaddar*). The meaning is: all of that belongs to Him in ownership. What they claim, that Allah has taken a son, falls within what is "in the heavens and the earth." A son can only be of the same kind as the father, not one of the created, owned beings.

"القُنُوتُ" (qunūt) in the language means obedience. It also means prolonged standing in worship, and from this comes the *qunūt* in (p-٣٣١) the prayer. So the meaning of the verse is that all created things are devoutly obedient to Allah, that is, they submit and obey. The disbelievers and inanimate things show their *qunūt* in the way the craftsmanship of the Creator is manifest upon them and in them.

It is also said: the disbeliever's shadow prostrates, while he himself is unwilling.

"بَدِيعٌ" (badī') is derived from *mubdi'* (the one who originates), as *baṣīr* is from *mubṣir* (the one who sees). A similar usage is the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"Does Rayḥāna the summoner, the hearer...?"

Here it means *al-musmi'* (the one who makes hear). *Al-mubdi'* means the one who invents and brings into being. From this root comes *ahl al-bid'a* (the people of innovation). And from this root comes the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) about the Ramadan prayer: "What a fine innovation this is!"

The heavens and the earth are singled out for mention because they are the greatest of His creations that we see, exalted is He.

"قَضى" (qaḍā) means "decreed" (*qadar*), and it can also mean "executed" (*amḍā*). Both meanings are possible in this verse. According to the doctrine of the *Ahl al-Sunna* (the people of the Sunna), He decreed it from eternity and executed it in that decree. According to the Mu'tazila, He executes it at the time of creation and bringing into existence.

"الأمْرُ" (al-amr) is the singular of "الأُمُورُ" (al-umūr, affairs). It is not here the verbal noun of "أمَرَ يَأْمُرُ" (amara ya'muru, to command). "وَيَكُونُ" (wa-yakūnu) is in the nominative as a new sentence. Sībawayh said: its meaning is "so it comes to be." Others said: "يَكُونُ" is conjoined to "يَقُولُ" (yaqūlu). Al-Ṭabarī chose and affirmed this view. But it is wrong in terms of meaning, because it implies that the saying occurs together with the bringing into being and existence. (p-٣٣٢) Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī spoke on this question with something corrupt from the Mu'tazila, not from the perspective of Arabic grammar.

Ibn 'Āmir read "فَيَكُونُ" (fa-yakūnu) in the accusative. Abū 'Alī judged this weak. Its justification, despite its weakness, is that it may be supported by a similarity in wording. Aḥmad ibn Mūsā said about Ibn 'Āmir's reading: "This is a grammatical error (*laḥn*)."

The *qāḍī* Abū Muḥammad (Ibn 'Aṭiyya) — may Allah have mercy on him — said: The *fā'* (fa) does not govern the response to an imperative unless both are verbs in which the sense of a conditional (*shart*) consistently applies. You say: "Honour Zayd, and he will honour you," meaning: "If you honour Zayd, he will honour you." In this verse this does not work, because its implied form would be: "If you are, he is," and there is no sense in that. What consistently carries the sense of a conditional is when the two agents or the two verbs differ. The first: "Honour Zayd, and he will honour you." The second: "Honour Zayd, and you will be chief."

The summary of the belief in this verse is that Allah, exalted and majestic, has never ceased to command the non-existent things on condition of their existence, to be capable though the capable things are not yet, and to know though the known things have not yet occurred. Thus everything in the verse that implies the future is according to what is commanded, since created things come into being after they were not. And everything that is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, of power, knowledge and command, is eternal and has never ceased.

Whoever among the exegetes makes "قَضى" mean "executed" at the time of creation and bringing into being, then the manifestation of the created things at their appointed times is as if it were a saying to them: "Be!" For reflection requires this, in the manner of the poet's words:

(p-٣٣٣) "And the relatives said to the womb, 'Be true!'..."

All of this runs along with the view of the Mu'tazila. But the meaning that the expression "كُنْ" (kun, be) indicates is eternal, subsisting in His essence. Full clarity on this question requires more explanation than this.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَقالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("And those who do not know said..."), al-Rabī' and al-Suddī said: they are the pagan Arabs. 'Abd Allah ibn Abī Umayya and others had asked the Prophet ﷺ for something similar to this. So He denied them knowledge, because they had neither a Book nor adherence to a prophethood. Mujāhid said: they are the Christians, because they are the ones mentioned in the verse at its beginning. Al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. Ibn 'Abbās said: what is meant are those Jews who were alive in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because Rāfi' ibn Ḥuraymila said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Let us hear the speech of Allah." It was also said: the reference in His words "لا يَعْلَمُونَ" (those who do not know) is to all of these groups, because all of them said this statement or something like it. Then ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ ("those before them") means the people of Noah, 'Ād, Thamūd and others.

"لَوْلا" (lawlā) here is a particle of exhortation (*taḥḍīḍ*), meaning "why not" (*hallā*), as al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla said:

"You count the slaughter of the she-camel as the best of your glory, O sons of Ḍawṭarā, rather than the brave one wearing a helmet."

This "لَوْلا" is not the one that gives the sense of prevention of one thing by the necessity of another. The difference between them is that in the exhortation sense it is followed only by a verb, either expressed or implied, whereas in its sense of prevention through necessity it is followed by a nominal sentence (*ibtidā'*), and it is customary to omit the predicate.

The word "الآيَةُ" (āya) here means the sign that points to something. Its wording has already been discussed. ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ means the Jews and Christians according to the view that ﴿الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ refers to the pagan Arabs; they are the earlier nations according to the view that ﴿الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ refers to the pagan Arabs and Christians; and they are the Jews according to the view that ﴿الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ refers to the Arabs, Christians and Jews together. The first *kāf* in "كَذَلِكَ" (kadhālika, "thus") is an adjective (*na't*) for an implied verbal noun. "مِثْلَ" (mithla, "like") is an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, and it is permissible for "قالَ" (qāla) to govern it. The "similarity of the hearts" here refers to seeking what is not valid, or to disbelief, even though their outward appearances differ. Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Abū Ḥaywa read "تَشّابَهَتْ" (tashshābahat) with a doubled *shīn*. Abū 'Amr al-Dānī said: this is not permissible, because it is a past-tense verb.

As for His words, ﴿قَدْ بَيَّنّا الآياتِ لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ﴾ ("We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain"): since mention had already been made of those whom Allah led astray, so that they disbelieved in the prophets and sought what was not permissible for them, He followed this with mention of those for whom He made clear what benefits and establishes proof. But the clarification took place and was acquired by those who have certainty, so He singled them out for mention. It is also possible that the meaning is: "We have made clear the clarification that is the creation of guidance," so that the sense is: "We have guided whom We guided."

When certainty (*yaqīn*) is attributed to knowledge ('ilm), it specifies it and carries it to the utmost firmness.

His saying, "بَيَّنّا" (bayyannā, "We have made clear"), is an indication that certainty is an attribute of their knowledge. A second indication is that the speech is praising them. As for certainty in the usage of the jurists, when it is not attributed to knowledge, it is lower than knowledge. For them, knowledge is the recognition of the known as it actually is, whereas certainty is a belief held by the certain person which is held firmly, even though the thing may be contrary to his belief. An example is the statement that the follower is certain of the existence of the Creator. From this comes Mālik's saying (may Allah have mercy on him) in the *Muwaṭṭā'*, on the question of one who swears an oath about something he is certain of while the thing in itself is (p-٣٣٥) otherwise. As for the reality of the matter, certainty is the more specific term: it is knowledge in the form that cannot possibly be other than what it is.

"مِثْلَ" (mithla, "like") is an adjective for an omitted verbal noun, and it is permissible for "قالَ" (qāla) to govern it. The "similarity of the hearts" here refers to seeking what is not valid, or to disbelief, even though their outward appearances differ. Ibn Abī Isḥāq and Abū Ḥaywa read "تَشّابَهَتْ" (tashshābahat) with a doubled *shīn*. Abū 'Amr al-Dānī said: this is not permissible, because it is a past-tense verb.

As for His words, ﴿قَدْ بَيَّنّا الآياتِ لِقَوْمٍ يُوقِنُونَ﴾ ("We have made the signs clear for a people who are certain"): since mention had already been made of those whom Allah led astray, so that they disbelieved in the prophets and sought what was not permissible for them, He followed this with mention of those for whom He made clear what benefits and establishes proof. But the clarification took place and was acquired by those who have certainty, so He singled them out for mention. It is also possible that the meaning is: "We have made clear the clarification that is the creation of guidance," so that the sense is: "We have guided whom We guided."

When certainty (*yaqīn*) is attributed to knowledge ('ilm), it specifies it and carries it to the utmost firmness.

His saying, "بَيَّنّا" (bayyannā, "We have made clear"), is an indication that certainty is an attribute of their knowledge. A second indication is that the speech is praising them. As for certainty in the usage of the jurists, when it is not attributed to knowledge, it is lower than knowledge. For them, knowledge is the recognition of the known as it actually is, whereas certainty is a belief held by the certain person which is held firmly, even though the thing may be contrary to his belief. An example is the statement that the follower is certain of the existence of the Creator. From this comes Mālik's saying (may Allah have mercy on him) in the *Muwaṭṭā'*, on the question of one who swears an oath about something he is certain of while the thing in itself is (p-٣٣٥) otherwise. As for the reality of the matter, certainty is the more specific term: it is knowledge in the form that cannot possibly be other than what it is.

(p-٣٣٠) All the reciters read this verse as "وَقالُوا" (wa-qālū), with a *wāw* linking the sentence to the one before it, or as a conjunction following "سعى" (sa'ā).

Ibn 'Āmir and others read "قالُوا" (qālū) without the *wāw*. Abū 'Alī (al-Fārisī) said: "It is also written this way in the codices of the people of Syria." Dropping the *wāw* can be justified in two ways. First, this sentence is connected in meaning to the one before it, so that connection makes the *wāw* unnecessary. Second, the sentence is begun afresh (*isti'nāf*) without regard to its connection with what came before.

Scholars differed over whom the pronoun in "قالُوا" refers to. It is said to refer to the Christians, because they said, "The Messiah is the son of Allah," and mentioning them fits the context of the verse better. It is also said to refer to the Jews, because they said, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah." And it is said to refer to the pagan Arabs, because they said, "The angels are the daughters of Allah."

"سُبْحانَهُ" (Subḥānahu) is a verbal noun meaning His exaltation above, and His freedom from, what they say. "ما" (mā) is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is the prepositional phrase that follows, or else the implied verb of being (*al-istiqrār al-muqaddar*). The meaning is: all of that belongs to Him in ownership. What they claim, that Allah has taken a son, falls within what is "in the heavens and the earth." A son can only be of the same kind as the father, not one of the created, owned beings.

"القُنُوتُ" (qunūt) in the language means obedience. It also means prolonged standing in worship, and from this comes the *qunūt* in (p-٣٣١) the prayer. So the meaning of the verse is that all created things are devoutly obedient to Allah, that is, they submit and obey. The disbelievers and inanimate things show their *qunūt* in the way the craftsmanship of the Creator is manifest upon them and in them.

It is also said: the disbeliever's shadow prostrates, while he himself is unwilling.

"بَدِيعٌ" (badī') is derived from *mubdi'* (the one who originates), as *baṣīr* is from *mubṣir* (the one who sees). A similar usage is the verse of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib:

"Does Rayḥāna the summoner, the hearer...?"

Here it means *al-musmi'* (the one who makes hear). *Al-mubdi'* means the one who invents and brings into being. From this root comes *ahl al-bid'a* (the people of innovation). And from this root comes the saying of 'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allah be pleased with him) about the Ramadan prayer: "What a fine innovation this is!"

The heavens and the earth are singled out for mention because they are the greatest of His creations that we see, exalted is He.

"قَضى" (qaḍā) means "decreed" (*qadar*), and it can also mean "executed" (*amḍā*). Both meanings are possible in this verse. According to the doctrine of the *Ahl al-Sunna* (the people of the Sunna), He decreed it from eternity and executed it in that decree. According to the Mu'tazila, He executes it at the time of creation and bringing into existence.

"الأمْرُ" (al-amr) is the singular of "الأُمُورُ" (al-umūr, affairs). It is not here the verbal noun of "أمَرَ يَأْمُرُ" (amara ya'muru, to command). "وَيَكُونُ" (wa-yakūnu) is in the nominative as a new sentence. Sībawayh said: its meaning is "so it comes to be." Others said: "يَكُونُ" is conjoined to "يَقُولُ" (yaqūlu). Al-Ṭabarī chose and affirmed this view. But it is wrong in terms of meaning, because it implies that the saying occurs together with the bringing into being and existence. (p-٣٣٢) Abū 'Alī al-Fārisī spoke on this question with something corrupt from the Mu'tazila, not from the perspective of Arabic grammar.

Ibn 'Āmir read "فَيَكُونُ" (fa-yakūnu) in the accusative. Abū 'Alī judged this weak. Its justification, despite its weakness, is that it may be supported by a similarity in wording. Aḥmad ibn Mūsā said about Ibn 'Āmir's reading: "This is a grammatical error (*laḥn*)."

The *qāḍī* Abū Muḥammad (Ibn 'Aṭiyya) — may Allah have mercy on him — said: The *fā'* (fa) does not govern the response to an imperative unless both are verbs in which the sense of a conditional (*shart*) consistently applies. You say: "Honour Zayd, and he will honour you," meaning: "If you honour Zayd, he will honour you." In this verse this does not work, because its implied form would be: "If you are, he is," and there is no sense in that. What consistently carries the sense of a conditional is when the two agents or the two verbs differ. The first: "Honour Zayd, and he will honour you." The second: "Honour Zayd, and you will be chief."

The summary of the belief in this verse is that Allah, exalted and majestic, has never ceased to command the non-existent things on condition of their existence, to be capable though the capable things are not yet, and to know though the known things have not yet occurred. Thus everything in the verse that implies the future is according to what is commanded, since created things come into being after they were not. And everything that is attributed to Allah, the Exalted, of power, knowledge and command, is eternal and has never ceased.

Whoever among the exegetes makes "قَضى" mean "executed" at the time of creation and bringing into being, then the manifestation of the created things at their appointed times is as if it were a saying to them: "Be!" For reflection requires this, in the manner of the poet's words:

(p-٣٣٣) "And the relatives said to the womb, 'Be true!'..."

All of this runs along with the view of the Mu'tazila. But the meaning that the expression "كُنْ" (kun, be) indicates is eternal, subsisting in His essence. Full clarity on this question requires more explanation than this.

As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَقالَ الَّذِينَ لا يَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("And those who do not know said..."), al-Rabī' and al-Suddī said: they are the pagan Arabs. 'Abd Allah ibn Abī Umayya and others had asked the Prophet ﷺ for something similar to this. So He denied them knowledge, because they had neither a Book nor adherence to a prophethood. Mujāhid said: they are the Christians, because they are the ones mentioned in the verse at its beginning. Al-Ṭabarī preferred this view. Ibn 'Abbās said: what is meant are those Jews who were alive in the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, because Rāfi' ibn Ḥuraymila said to the Prophet ﷺ, "Let us hear the speech of Allah." It was also said: the reference in His words "لا يَعْلَمُونَ" (those who do not know) is to all of these groups, because all of them said this statement or something like it. Then ﴿الَّذِينَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ﴾ ("those before them") means the people of Noah, 'Ād, Thamūd and others.

"لَوْلا" (lawlā) here is a particle of exhortation (*taḥḍīḍ*), meaning "why not" (*hallā*), as al-Ashhab ibn Rumayla said:

"You count the slaughter of the she-camel as the best of your glory, O sons of Ḍawṭarā, rather than the brave one wearing a helmet."

This "لَوْلا" is not the one that gives the sense of prevention of one thing by the necessity of another. The difference between them is that in the exhortation sense it is followed only by a verb, either expressed or implied, whereas in its sense of prevention through necessity it is followed by a nominal sentence (*ibtidā'*), and it is customary to omit the predicate.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 119–121:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good news and a warner, and you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿And the Jews will never be pleased with you, nor the Christians, until you follow their religion. Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance." And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have from Allah no protector and no helper.﴾ ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it with its true recitation. Those believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers.﴾

The meaning: "bringer of good news" to whoever believes, and "warner" to whoever disbelieves. Nafi' alone read "wa-la tas'al" with a jazm (jussive), as a prohibition, and in this there are two meanings. One is: "do not ask" in the sense of magnifying their condition of punishment, as you say, "So-and-so, do not ask about him," meaning that he is at an extreme, whether in good or in bad.

The second meaning has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I wish I knew what my two parents did?" Then it was revealed: "and you will not be questioned." Al-Mahdawi, may Allah have mercy on him, related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I wish I knew which of my two parents died more recently?" Then it was revealed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an error on the part of whoever narrated it or assumed it, because his father died while he was in his mother's womb. It was said that he was a month old, and it was said two months old. His mother died five years after that, while returning with him from Madinah from a visit to his maternal uncles. So this is something that cannot be supposed to have been hidden from him ﷺ.

The rest of the Seven read "wa-la tas'alu" with a damma on the ta' and the lam. A group read "wa-la tas'al" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the lam. In these two readings two meanings are possible: one is a report, that he is not asked about them, or he does not ask about them; the other is that it conveys the sense of a circumstantial clause, as if he said: "and not one to be questioned about them" or "not one who asks about them," coordinated with His saying: ﴿bringer of good news and a warner﴾.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa-ma tas'al," and Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-lan tas'al." These two readings support the meaning of definitive statement and resumption (isti'naf) in the other readings.

Al-Jahim is one of the layers of the Fire.

It is said: radiya yarda ridan, ridan and ridwanan (رضي يرضى رضى ورضا ورضوانا); and ridа' mamdudan (رضاء ممدودا) is also reported. He said "their religion" (ملتهم), and they are two different religions. The meaning is: the Jews will not be pleased until you follow their religion, and the Christians will not be pleased until you follow their religion; so He combined them for brevity, because that is understood.

Al-millah (ملة) means the path, and the word has become specific to the sacred laws and religion. A "path that has been worn" (طريق مملّ) means one on which walking has left its mark.

It is reported that the cause of this verse is that the Jews and the Christians asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a truce, and they promised him that they would follow him after a period, as a deception from them. So Allah, Exalted, informed him that giving them a truce would not benefit with them, and He made him aware of the secret of their deception.

(p-337) And His saying, Exalted: ﴿Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance"﴾ means: what you are upon, O Muhammad, of the guidance of Allah, which He places in the heart of whomever He wills, is the true guidance, not what these people claim. Then Allah, Exalted, said to His Prophet: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ — the verse. This is a conditional addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and his community is included with him in it.

"Ahwa'" (أهواء) is the plural of hawa (هوى). Since they were varied, it was made plural; had it been taken in the singular of "religion," it would have said "hawahum." The wali (ولي) is the one who undertakes reform, protection, victory and assistance. "Nasir" (نصير) is an intensive form of the active participle from nasara.

And His saying, Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ — the verse. "Alladhina" is in the nominative by being the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿We have given them the Book﴾ is its relative clause. Qatadah said: what is meant by "alladhina" in this place is those from the community of Muhammad ﷺ who embraced Islam. And "al-Kitab" on this interpretation is the Torah, and "ataynahum" means "We gave them." Others said: this is specific to the forty who came with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, in the ship, and Allah praised them. It is also possible that "alladhina" is meant generally, covering the believers among the Children of Israel and the believers among the Arabs, and "al-Kitab" is then a generic noun. "Yatlunahu" means: they follow it truly, by carrying out its commands and prohibitions. It was also said: "yatlunahu" means: they recite it with its true recitation. This too implies following and acting upon it. And "yatlunahu," if "alladhina" is meant specifically of those who were guided, may be the predicate of the subject, and it may be in the place of a circumstantial clause, with the predicate being "ulaika." If "alladhina" is meant generally, the predicate can only be "ulaika," and "yatlunahu" is a circumstantial clause that cannot be dispensed with, and it carries a benefit, because if the predicate were "yatlunahu," it would necessarily follow that every believer recites the Book ﴿with its true recitation﴾.

"Haqqa" (حق) is a verbal noun, and the operator on it is a hidden verb which has the sense of af'ala. It is not permissible to make it a genitive construct with a definite noun (p-338), but it is permissible here because making "recitation" definite by attaching it to a pronoun is not a complete definiteness; it is rather like their saying: "ra'jul wahid ummah" (a man who alone is a community) and "nasij wahdah" (a weaver who alone is a whole cloth). The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "al-Kitab." It was also said that it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, because the followers of the Torah find him mentioned in it, and so they believe in him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In my view it is also possible that the pronoun refers to the guidance mentioned earlier. This is because the disbelieving Jews and Christians were mentioned at the beginning of the verse, and He warned His Messenger against following their desires, and informed him that "the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance," which He gave him and sent him with. Then He mentioned to him that the believers who recite the Book of Allah are the ones who believe in that guidance and are guided by its lights. The pronoun in "yakfur bihi" may admit the same reference as the first. And ﴿Then those are the losers﴾ is a subject, a supporting pronoun (imad) and a predicate, or a subject, a subject and a predicate, the second subject with its predicate being the predicate of the first. Al-khusran (الخسران) is the loss of one's share.

Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance." And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, you would have from Allah no protector and no helper.﴾ ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it with its true recitation. Those believe in it. And whoever disbelieves in it, those are the losers.﴾

The meaning: "bringer of good news" to whoever believes, and "warner" to whoever disbelieves. Nafi' alone read "wa-la tas'al" with a jazm (jussive), as a prohibition, and in this there are two meanings. One is: "do not ask" in the sense of magnifying their condition of punishment, as you say, "So-and-so, do not ask about him," meaning that he is at an extreme, whether in good or in bad.

The second meaning has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I wish I knew what my two parents did?" Then it was revealed: "and you will not be questioned." Al-Mahdawi, may Allah have mercy on him, related that the Prophet ﷺ said: "I wish I knew which of my two parents died more recently?" Then it was revealed.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is an error on the part of whoever narrated it or assumed it, because his father died while he was in his mother's womb. It was said that he was a month old, and it was said two months old. His mother died five years after that, while returning with him from Madinah from a visit to his maternal uncles. So this is something that cannot be supposed to have been hidden from him ﷺ.

The rest of the Seven read "wa-la tas'alu" with a damma on the ta' and the lam. A group read "wa-la tas'al" with a fatha on the ta' and a damma on the lam. In these two readings two meanings are possible: one is a report, that he is not asked about them, or he does not ask about them; the other is that it conveys the sense of a circumstantial clause, as if he said: "and not one to be questioned about them" or "not one who asks about them," coordinated with His saying: ﴿bringer of good news and a warner﴾.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa-ma tas'al," and Ibn Mas'ud read "wa-lan tas'al." These two readings support the meaning of definitive statement and resumption (isti'naf) in the other readings.

Al-Jahim is one of the layers of the Fire.

It is said: radiya yarda ridan, ridan and ridwanan (رضي يرضى رضى ورضا ورضوانا); and ridа' mamdudan (رضاء ممدودا) is also reported. He said "their religion" (ملتهم), and they are two different religions. The meaning is: the Jews will not be pleased until you follow their religion, and the Christians will not be pleased until you follow their religion; so He combined them for brevity, because that is understood.

Al-millah (ملة) means the path, and the word has become specific to the sacred laws and religion. A "path that has been worn" (طريق مملّ) means one on which walking has left its mark.

It is reported that the cause of this verse is that the Jews and the Christians asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for a truce, and they promised him that they would follow him after a period, as a deception from them. So Allah, Exalted, informed him that giving them a truce would not benefit with them, and He made him aware of the secret of their deception.

(p-337) And His saying, Exalted: ﴿Say: "Indeed, the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance"﴾ means: what you are upon, O Muhammad, of the guidance of Allah, which He places in the heart of whomever He wills, is the true guidance, not what these people claim. Then Allah, Exalted, said to His Prophet: ﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ — the verse. This is a conditional addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, and his community is included with him in it.

"Ahwa'" (أهواء) is the plural of hawa (هوى). Since they were varied, it was made plural; had it been taken in the singular of "religion," it would have said "hawahum." The wali (ولي) is the one who undertakes reform, protection, victory and assistance. "Nasir" (نصير) is an intensive form of the active participle from nasara.

And His saying, Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ — the verse. "Alladhina" is in the nominative by being the subject (mubtada'), and ﴿We have given them the Book﴾ is its relative clause. Qatadah said: what is meant by "alladhina" in this place is those from the community of Muhammad ﷺ who embraced Islam. And "al-Kitab" on this interpretation is the Torah, and "ataynahum" means "We gave them." Others said: this is specific to the forty who came with Ja'far ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, in the ship, and Allah praised them. It is also possible that "alladhina" is meant generally, covering the believers among the Children of Israel and the believers among the Arabs, and "al-Kitab" is then a generic noun. "Yatlunahu" means: they follow it truly, by carrying out its commands and prohibitions. It was also said: "yatlunahu" means: they recite it with its true recitation. This too implies following and acting upon it. And "yatlunahu," if "alladhina" is meant specifically of those who were guided, may be the predicate of the subject, and it may be in the place of a circumstantial clause, with the predicate being "ulaika." If "alladhina" is meant generally, the predicate can only be "ulaika," and "yatlunahu" is a circumstantial clause that cannot be dispensed with, and it carries a benefit, because if the predicate were "yatlunahu," it would necessarily follow that every believer recites the Book ﴿with its true recitation﴾.

"Haqqa" (حق) is a verbal noun, and the operator on it is a hidden verb which has the sense of af'ala. It is not permissible to make it a genitive construct with a definite noun (p-338), but it is permissible here because making "recitation" definite by attaching it to a pronoun is not a complete definiteness; it is rather like their saying: "ra'jul wahid ummah" (a man who alone is a community) and "nasij wahdah" (a weaver who alone is a whole cloth). The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "al-Kitab." It was also said that it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, because the followers of the Torah find him mentioned in it, and so they believe in him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In my view it is also possible that the pronoun refers to the guidance mentioned earlier. This is because the disbelieving Jews and Christians were mentioned at the beginning of the verse, and He warned His Messenger against following their desires, and informed him that "the guidance of Allah is the [true] guidance," which He gave him and sent him with. Then He mentioned to him that the believers who recite the Book of Allah are the ones who believe in that guidance and are guided by its lights. The pronoun in "yakfur bihi" may admit the same reference as the first. And ﴿Then those are the losers﴾ is a subject, a supporting pronoun (imad) and a predicate, or a subject, a subject and a predicate, the second subject with its predicate being the predicate of the first. Al-khusran (الخسران) is the loss of one's share.

(p-٣٣٩) The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿O Children of Israel, remember My favour which I bestowed upon you, and that I preferred you over the worlds.﴾ ﴿And fear a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything, nor will any compensation be accepted from it, nor will intercession (shafa'a) benefit it, nor will they be helped.﴾ ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with words, and he fulfilled them, He said: "Indeed I will make you a leader (imam) for mankind." He said: "And from my offspring?" He said: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers."﴾

Al-Hasan and others read "ni'mati" with a sukun on the ya' for lightness (takhfif), because its original form is with a vowel, like the vowels of the pronoun suffixes in laka and bika. Then al-Hasan elided it because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters (iltiqa' al-sakinayn). Among the Seven (al-Sab'a, the canonical readers), some vowel the ya' and some make it unvowelled.

If we consider the excellence of the Children of Israel to be specific, by the abundance of prophets and other things, then "al-'alamun" (the worlds) is a general, unrestricted term. If we consider their preference to be absolute, then "al-'alimun" means the people of their own time, because the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) is better than them by explicit text. The discussion of a verse like this has already been given up to His words "they will not be helped."

The meaning of ﴿nor will intercession benefit it﴾ is: there is none there (ayy laysat thumma). The meaning is not that someone will intercede for them and it is rejected. Rather, it negates that there would be intercession in the manner it exists in this world. As for the intercession which is for hastening the reckoning, it does not benefit these disbelievers in particular. As for the last intercession, which is by permission of Allah the Exalted for the sinners among the believers, it comes after punishment has taken its due; and these threatened disbelievers have no share of it.

(p-٣٤٠) The governing element (al-'amil) of "idh" is a verb, its estimated form being "and remember when." "Abtala" means "tested." As for "Ibrahim," it is said that its interpretation in Arabic is "a compassionate father."

Ibn 'Amir read "Abrahām" throughout Surat al-Baqara. The object was placed before the agent (fa'il) for emphasis, since the fact that the Lord is the one who tests is known, so the listener is concerned with who was tested. The fact that the object pronoun is attached to the agent necessitates placing the object first, so the speech was built on this emphasis.

The commentators differed about "the words" (al-kalimat). Ibn 'Abbas said: they are thirty portions (sahm), which are the whole of Islam, and no one completed them fully except Ibrahim, may the blessings of Allah be upon him: ten of them are in Bara'a (Surat al-Tawba): ﴿the repentant, the worshippers﴾ [al-Tawba 9:112], and so on; ten are in al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed the Muslim men and Muslim women﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:35]; and ten are in: ﴿A questioner asked﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:1].

(p-٣٤١) Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Qatada: "the words" are ten characteristics (khisal), five of which are on the head: rinsing the mouth (madmada), sniffing water into the nose (istinshaq), trimming the moustache, using the tooth-stick (siwak), and parting the hair. It was said that instead of parting the hair, it is letting the beard grow. And five are on the body: trimming the nails, shaving the pubic area, plucking the armpit hair, cleansing oneself with water (istinja'), and circumcision.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: they are ten characteristics, six in the body and four in the Hajj (pilgrimage): circumcision, shaving the pubic area, plucking the armpits, trimming the nails, trimming the moustache, ghusl (full washing) on Friday, tawaf around the House, sa'y (going between Safa and Marwa), stoning the jamarat, and al-ifada (the departure from 'Arafat).

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: they are the six traits by which he was tested: the star, the moon, the sun, the fire, the emigration (hijra), and circumcision. It was said that instead of emigration it is slaughter. A group said they are specifically the rites of the Hajj. It is narrated that Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Purify yourself, then rinse your mouth; then purify yourself, then sniff water; then purify yourself, then use the siwak; then purify yourself, then trim your moustache; then purify yourself, then part your hair; then purify yourself, then cleanse yourself with water; then purify yourself, then shave your pubic area; then purify yourself, then pluck your armpits; then purify yourself, then trim your nails; then purify yourself," and he turned to his body, looking at what it was doing, and he was circumcised after a hundred and twenty years. In al-Bukhari it is narrated that he was circumcised when he was eighty years old, with an adze (bi-l-qadum).

(p-٣٤٢) The narrator said: Allah then revealed to him: ﴿Indeed I make you a leader for mankind﴾, meaning they follow you in these characteristics, and the righteous are guided by you.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is the strongest of the opinions in the interpretation of this verse; and according to all these opinions, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, is the one who fulfilled them.

Mujahid and others said: the words are that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Ibrahim: "I am going to test you with a matter; what is it?" Ibrahim said: "You make me a leader for mankind." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "You make the House a place of return (mathaba)." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "And [make it] a place of security (amn)." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "And show us our rites and accept our repentance." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "You make this city secure." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "And provide its people with fruits." Allah said: "Yes."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: according to this view, it is Allah the Exalted who fulfilled them. The commentators have elaborated on this at length and mentioned many things beyond it, which I have abridged.

These characteristics were called "words" because commands accompanied them, and those commands are words. It is narrated that when Ibrahim (ﷺ) completed these words, or when Allah completed them for him, Allah wrote for him freedom from the Fire (al-bara'a min al-nar). That is His saying, ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [al-Najm 53:37].

The imam is the exemplar (al-qudwa). From the same root, a building string is called imam. Here it is a singular noun. Elsewhere it was said that it is a plural of amm, whose pattern is fa'il, its original form being amam, so it is like qa'im and qiyam, ja'i' andji'a', and na'im and niyam. Allah the Exalted made Ibrahim an imam for the people of His obedience, and therefore the nations agreed in claiming him. Allah informed that he was a hanif (one who turns purely to the truth).

Ibrahim's saying, ﴿and from my offspring (dhurriyyati)﴾ is in the form of supplication and desire directed to Allah, meaning: "And from my offspring, O Lord, then make [them imams also]." It was said that this from him is in the form of a question about them, meaning: "And from my offspring, O Lord, what will become of them?"

The word dhurriyya is derived from dhara yadhru, or dhara yadhri, or dhar yadhar, or dhara'a yadhra'u. These verbs have close meanings. Abu al-Fath elaborated at length in explaining its derivation, and gave a satisfying account.

As for His saying, ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach [the wrongdoers]﴾, that is, Allah said. Regarding the meaning of "covenant" ('ahd): Mujahid said it is the imamate; al-Suddi said it is prophethood; Qatada said it is security from the punishment of Allah; al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak said the covenant is the religion, the religion of Allah the Exalted. Ibn 'Abbas said the meaning of the verse is: there is no covenant for a wrongdoer that you should obey him. The accusative of "al-zalimin" is because the covenant "yanal" (attains) just as it is "yunal" (is attained). Qatada, Abu Raja' and al-A'mash read "al-zalimun" in the nominative.

If we interpret the covenant as the religion, or as security, or as meaning that there is no obedience to a wrongdoer, then the wrongdoing in the verse is the wrongdoing of disbelief, because the sinful believer does attain religion and security from the punishment of Allah, and obedience to him is required if he holds authority. If we interpret the covenant as prophethood or as the imamate in religion, then the wrongdoing is the wrongdoing of sins and what is beyond them.
