It is narrated that Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "Purify yourself, then rinse your mouth; then purify yourself, then sniff water; then purify yourself, then use the siwak; then purify yourself, then trim your moustache; then purify yourself, then part your hair; then purify yourself, then cleanse yourself with water; then purify yourself, then shave your pubic area; then purify yourself, then pluck your armpits; then purify yourself, then trim your nails; then purify yourself," and he turned to his body, looking at what it was doing, and he was circumcised after a hundred and twenty years. In al-Bukhari it is narrated that he was circumcised when he was eighty years old, with an adze (bi-l-qadum).

(p-٣٤٢) The narrator said: Allah then revealed to him: ﴿Indeed I make you a leader for mankind﴾, meaning they follow you in these characteristics, and the righteous are guided by you.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this is the strongest of the opinions in the interpretation of this verse; and according to all these opinions, Ibrahim, peace be upon him, is the one who fulfilled them.

Mujahid and others said: the words are that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Ibrahim: "I am going to test you with a matter; what is it?" Ibrahim said: "You make me a leader for mankind." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "You make the House a place of return (mathaba)." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "And [make it] a place of security (amn)." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "And show us our rites and accept our repentance." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "You make this city secure." Allah said: "Yes." Ibrahim said: "And provide its people with fruits." Allah said: "Yes."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: according to this view, it is Allah the Exalted who fulfilled them. The commentators have elaborated on this at length and mentioned many things beyond it, which I have abridged.

These characteristics were called "words" because commands accompanied them, and those commands are words. It is narrated that when Ibrahim (ﷺ) completed these words, or when Allah completed them for him, Allah wrote for him freedom from the Fire (al-bara'a min al-nar). That is His saying, ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [al-Najm 53:37].

The imam is the exemplar (al-qudwa). From the same root, a building string is called imam. Here it is a singular noun. Elsewhere it was said that it is a plural of amm, whose pattern is fa'il, its original form being amam, so it is like qa'im and qiyam, ja'i' andji'a', and na'im and niyam. Allah the Exalted made Ibrahim an imam for the people of His obedience, and therefore the nations agreed in claiming him. Allah informed that he was a hanif (one who turns purely to the truth).

Ibrahim's saying, ﴿and from my offspring (dhurriyyati)﴾ is in the form of supplication and desire directed to Allah, meaning: "And from my offspring, O Lord, then make [them imams also]." It was said that this from him is in the form of a question about them, meaning: "And from my offspring, O Lord, what will become of them?"

The word dhurriyya is derived from dhara yadhru, or dhara yadhri, or dhar yadhar, or dhara'a yadhra'u. These verbs have close meanings. Abu al-Fath elaborated at length in explaining its derivation, and gave a satisfying account.

As for His saying, ﴿He said: My covenant does not reach [the wrongdoers]﴾, that is, Allah said. Regarding the meaning of "covenant" ('ahd): Mujahid said it is the imamate; al-Suddi said it is prophethood; Qatada said it is security from the punishment of Allah; al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak said the covenant is the religion, the religion of Allah the Exalted. Ibn 'Abbas said the meaning of the verse is: there is no covenant for a wrongdoer that you should obey him. The accusative of "al-zalimin" is because the covenant "yanal" (attains) just as it is "yunal" (is attained). Qatada, Abu Raja' and al-A'mash read "al-zalimun" in the nominative.

If we interpret the covenant as the religion, or as security, or as meaning that there is no obedience to a wrongdoer, then the wrongdoing in the verse is the wrongdoing of disbelief, because the sinful believer does attain religion and security from the punishment of Allah, and obedience to him is required if he holds authority. If we interpret the covenant as prophethood or as the imamate in religion, then the wrongdoing is the wrongdoing of sins and what is beyond them.

[p. 343] Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a sanctuary, and [said], "Take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer." And We charged Abraham and Ismael: "Purify My House for those who circle it, those who stay in it, and those who bow and prostrate."﴾ ﴿And when Abraham said: "My Lord, make this land secure, and provide its people with fruits, those of them who believe in Allah and the Last Day." He said: "As for him who disbelieves, I will let him enjoy [life] for a little, then I will drive him to the punishment of the Fire, and what a wretched destination it is."﴾

"وَإذْ" is coordinated with the preceding "إذِ" (when). "البَيْتَ" (the House) is the Ka'bah. "مَثابَةً" may derive from ثاب (to return), since people return to it, i.e., go back to it again and again. It may also derive from الثَّوابُ (reward), meaning that they are rewarded there. Al-Akhfash said: the ـة (ta' marbuta) was added for emphasis, because of the great number of those who return. Rarely does anyone leave the House without feeling that he has not had his fill of it. So it is like نَسّابَة (genealogist) and عَلّامَة (very learned). Others said: the ـة is the feminine suffix of the verbal noun, so it is a مَفْعَلَة (maf'alah) form, originally مَثُوبَة, whose vowel was moved from the waw to the thaa', and the waw then became an alif because the letter before it was open. It is also said that it is the feminine form in reference to the spot (بُقْعَة), as one says مَقام and مَقامَة.

Al-A'mash read "مَثاباتٌ" in the plural. Waraqah ibn Nawfal said about the Ka'bah:

*A place of return for all the tribes from every side, to which the swift, lean camels hasten.*

"أمْنًا" means that people raid and kill around Mecca, while it is secure from that. A man could meet the killer of his father there and not stir against him, because Allah, the Exalted, placed a sanctity in hearts for it, and made it a sanctuary for people, birds and beasts. The Law made an exception to this for the five vermin, as related from the Prophet (ﷺ).

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "وَاتَّخِذُوا" with a kasrah on the kha' (as an imperative). Anas ibn Malik and others said its meaning is what was related from 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), that he said: "I agreed with my Lord in three matters: regarding the veil, and regarding ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you﴾ [al-Tahrim: 5], and I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you would take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer,' and then ﴿And take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer﴾ was revealed." So this is a command to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Mahdawi said: it was also said that it is coordinated with His saying "remember" (اذْكُرُوا), so this is a command to the Children of Israel. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: this is a command to Abraham and his followers, and so it is among the "words" (of the test), as if He said: "I am making you an imam for the people," and "take [it]." Al-Mahdawi, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned that it is coordinated with the command implied by His saying ﴿We made the House a place of return﴾, because the meaning is "return (to it)."

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "وَاتَّخَذُوا" with a fathah on the kha', as a statement about those among the followers of Abraham who took it, and it is coordinated with His saying "And when We made", as if He said: "And when they took." It is also said that it is coordinated with "جَعَلْنا" without the assumption of إذْ, so it is one clause; and with the assumption of إذْ, it is two clauses.

The interpretation of ﴿the station of Abraham﴾ has differed. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah and others, and al-Bukhari transmitted it, said that it is the stone on which Abraham stood when he became too weak to lift the stones that Ismael was handing him in the building of the House, and his feet sank into it. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: it is a stone which his wife brought him, and he washed himself upon it while riding; it was brought to him from one side, then from another side, and his two feet sank into it when he leaned on it.

[p. 345] A group of scholars said: "the station" is the Sacred Mosque. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "the station" is 'Arafat, Muzdalifah and the jamarat. Ibn 'Abbas said: its station is all the standing places of the Hajj. Mujahid said: its station is the whole Sacred Precinct (al-Haram). "مُصَلًّى" is a place of prayer. This is according to the view of one who says that the station is the stone. As for one who says otherwise, he says "مُصَلًّى" is a claim, according to the root meaning of prayer (ṣalāh, supplication).

Allah's saying "وَعَهِدْنا" (We charged): ʿahd in the language has several senses, and this is one of them: a command in the sense of an instruction. "أنْ" is in the accusative position, with the assumption of بِأنْ (that), with the preposition omitted. Sibawayh said: it has the sense of أيْ (namely), explanatory, so it has no place in i'rab (grammatical analysis).

"طَهِّرا" (purify): it is said that it means: build it and found it upon purity and the intention of purity, so it is like His saying ﴿founded upon piety﴾ [al-Tawbah: 108]. Mujahid said it is a command to purify it from the worship of idols. It is also said: from dung and blood; but this is weak, not supported by reports. It is also said: from shirk.

Allah attributed the House to Himself to honor it. It is the attribution of a created thing to its Creator, and of a possession to its Owner. "لِلطّائِفِينَ" (for those who circle it): its apparent meaning is the people who perform ṭawāf (circumambulation), as said by 'Ata' and others. Ibn Jubayr said: it means the strangers who arrive at Mecca.

"العاكِفِينَ" (those who stay in it): Ibn Jubayr said: they are the people of the city who reside there. 'Ata' said: they are those who live as neighbors in Mecca. Ibn 'Abbas said: those who pray. Others said: those who seclude themselves (i'tikaf).

In the language, ʿukūf means attachment to a thing and remaining upon it, as the poet said:

*…… the Nabataeans kept themselves busy playing al-fanzaj.*

So its meaning is: for those who devote themselves to the House, seeking the face of the Mighty Allah.

﴿And those who bow and prostrate﴾: those who pray. Bowing and prostration were singled out for mention because they are the closest states of the worshipper to Allah, the Exalted. Every person who stays near the House of Allah seeks the Essence of Allah, so he is never free of one of these three ranks: either he is in prayer, or in circumambulation. If he is occupied with some matter of his worldly life, his state of devotion to dwelling near the House does not leave him.

Allah's saying "وَإذْ قالَ إبْراهِيمُ" (And when Abraham said), the verse: Abraham, peace be upon him, supplicated for his descendants and others in Mecca for security and abundant living. The word "اجْعَلْ" (make) is grammatically an imperative, but with respect to Allah, the Exalted, it expresses desire and supplication. "آمِنًا" (secure) means: safe from tyrants and rulers, from an enemy who utterly destroys, and from the calamities that befall lands. At that time Mecca and its surroundings were a barren waste with no water and no vegetation. So Allah blessed what was around it, such as al-Ta'if and other places, and all kinds of fruits grew in it.

It is related that when Abraham made this supplication, Allah, the Exalted, commanded Gabriel, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, and he uprooted Palestine, and it is said a piece of al-Urdunn, and carried it around the House seven times and set it down at Wajj, so al-Ta'if was named for that circling (ṭawāf).

Scholars differed about when Mecca was made sacred. One group said: Allah made it sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth. Another group said: Abraham made it sacred.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The first was said by the Prophet (ﷺ) in his sermon on the second day of the Conquest, and the second was also said by the Prophet (ﷺ). In the Sahih it is related from him: "O Allah, indeed Abraham made Mecca sacred [p. 347], and I have made Medina sacred; what lies between its two lava plains is sacred."

There is no contradiction between the two reports, because the first is an announcement of Allah's prior knowledge and decree concerning it, and that its sanctity was in effect from the time of Adam and during the periods when the region was populated with faith; and the second is an announcement of Abraham's renewal of its sanctity and his making it manifest after it had been effaced.

Each of these two statements is fitting in its own context. He (ﷺ) magnified the sanctity on the second day of the Conquest for the believers, by attributing the prohibition to Allah, the Exalted. Abraham, when declaring Medina sacred, mentioned Mecca as an example for himself. There is no doubt that the sanctity of Medina also comes from Allah, the Exalted, and from His all-effective decree and His prior knowledge.

"مَن" (those who) is a substitute for "أهْلَهُ" (its people), and Abraham singled out the believers for his supplication.

Allah's saying "وَمَن كَفَرَ" (as for him who disbelieves): Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Ishaq and others said: this statement is from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, to Abraham. They read "فَأُمَتِّعُهُ" with a ḍammah on the hamzah, a fathah on the mim, and a shaddah on the ta', and "ثُمَّ اضْطَرَّهُ" with the hamzah of the alif cut off and a ḍammah on the ra'. The Seven readers also read this way, except Ibn 'Amir, who read "فَأُمَتِّعُهُ" with a ḍammah on the hamzah, a sukun on the mim, and a lightened ta', and "ثُمَّ أضْطَرَّهُ" with the hamzah of the alif cut off. Yahya ibn Wathhab read "فَأُمَتِّعُهُ" as Ibn 'Amir did, and "ثُمَّ اضْطَرَّهُ" with a kasrah on the hamzah, following the dialect of Quraysh in their saying لا إخالُ (I do not think). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "فَنُمَتِّعُهُ" and "ثُمَّ نَضْطَرُّهُ". "مَن" is a conditional particle, and the apodosis is "فَأُمَتِّعُهُ".

The position of "مَن" is nominative, as subject and predicate. It may also be accusative, with the assumption: "and I will provide for him who disbelieves", and then it is not a conditional particle. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said: this statement is from Abraham, peace be upon him, and they read "فَأُمَتِّعُهُ" with a fathah on the hamzah and a sukun on the mim, and "ثُمَّ اضْطَرَّهُ" with a connecting alif and a fathah on the ra'. It was also read with a kasrah, and a ḍammah is permissible. Ibn Muhaysin read "ثُمَّ اطَّرُّهُ" by assimilating the ḍad into the ṭa'. Yazid ibn Abi Habib read "ثُمَّ اضْطَرَّهُ" with a ḍammah on the ṭa'.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is as if Abraham, peace be upon him, supplicated for the believers and against the disbelievers.

"قَلِيلًا" (a little) means the duration of life, because the enjoyment of this world is little. It is an adjective either of a verbal noun, as if He said "enjoyment, a little," or of a time, as if He said "a little time" or "a short period."

"المَصِيرُ" (destination) is a noun of place (mafʿil) like مَوْضِعٌ (place) from صارَ يَصِيرُ (to become). بِئْسَ (wretched) originally was بِئْسَ, and it has been discussed under بِيسَما.

"أُمَتِّعُهُ" means: I give him the enjoyment of the world and let him remain in it for a little while, because it is perishing and ending.

The original meaning of matāʿ is provision. Then it was used for whatever is the final outcome of a person, or his gift, or his actions. The poet said:

*I stood at the grave of a stranger in a desert, a little enjoyment from a beloved who has departed.*

From this comes the giving of provision (tamtīʿ) to wives. And Allah drives the disbeliever into the Fire as recompense for his disbelief.

Yahya ibn Wathhab read "فَأُمَتِّعُهُ" as Ibn 'Amir did, and "ثُمَّ اضْطَرَّهُ" with a kasrah on the hamzah, following the dialect of Quraysh in their saying لا إخالُ (I do not think). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "فَنُمَتِّعُهُ" and "ثُمَّ نَضْطَرُّهُ". "مَن" is a conditional particle, and the apodosis is "فَأُمَتِّعُهُ".

The position of "مَن" is nominative, as subject and predicate. It may also be accusative, with the assumption: "and I will provide for him who disbelieves", and then it is not a conditional particle. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and others said: this statement is from Abraham, peace be upon him, and they read "فَأُمَتِّعُهُ" with a fathah on the hamzah and a sukun on the mim, and "ثُمَّ اضْطَرَّهُ" with a connecting alif and a fathah on the ra'. It was also read with a kasrah, and a ḍammah is permissible. Ibn Muhaysin read "ثُمَّ اطَّرُّهُ" by assimilating the ḍad into the ṭa'. Yazid ibn Abi Habib read "ثُمَّ اضْطَرَّهُ" with a ḍammah on the ṭa'.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is as if Abraham, peace be upon him, supplicated for the believers and against the disbelievers.

"قَلِيلًا" (a little) means the duration of life, because the enjoyment of this world is little. It is an adjective either of a verbal noun, as if He said "enjoyment, a little," or of a time, as if He said "a little time" or "a short period."

"أُمَتِّعُهُ" means: I give him the enjoyment of the world and let him remain in it for a little while, because it is perishing and ending.

The original meaning of matāʿ is provision. Then it was used for whatever is the final outcome of a person, or his gift, or his actions. The poet said:

*I stood at the grave of a stranger in a desert, a little enjoyment from a beloved who has departed.*

From this comes the giving of provision (tamtīʿ) to wives. And Allah drives the disbeliever into the Fire as recompense for his disbelief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 127–129:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿And when Abraham and Ishmael were raising the foundations of the House, [they said]: "Our Lord, accept from us. Indeed You are the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and make us submissive to You, and of our descendants a community submissive to You. And show us our rites, and turn to us in forgiveness. Indeed You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful."﴾ ﴿"Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses, and teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them. Indeed You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise."﴾

The meaning: "Idh" (when) is to be understood as a reference back to a past event: remember when... "Al-qawa'id" is the plural of qa'ida, which means the foundation. Al-Farra' said it means the walls, but this is a metaphorical usage. "Al-qawa'id min al-nisa'" (the women past childbearing) is the plural of qa'id, referring to those who have ceased to bear children; the feminine ta' was dropped because the masculine has no part in this. This is the view of some grammarians, though dropping the ta' while the masculine is also included is an anomaly, as in the phrase "naqatun damir" (a lean she-camel). According to al-Khalil's view, whenever the ta' of femininity is dropped, the adjective ceases to be applied to the verb and becomes a relative (nisba) form.

"Al-Bayt" (the House) here is unanimously the Ka'bah. Some narrators of stories differed. It is said that Adam ordered its construction and built it, then it was obliterated and effaced until Abraham was guided to it and raised its foundations. It is said that Adam brought it down from Paradise. It is said that when he felt lonely on earth, after his stature had diminished and he had lost the voices of the angels, it was sent down to him, and it was like a pearl; some say like a ruby. It is said that the House was a red mound, and some say a white one, and from beneath it the earth was spread out, and that Abraham began its construction by God's command and raised its foundations.

What is sound from all of this is that God commanded Abraham to raise the foundations of the House. Its being ancient is possible, and it is also possible that this was a new beginning. None of these views is to be preferred except by a chain of transmission that removes all excuse.

(p-350) 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr said: Abraham and Ishmael raised it together. Ibn 'Abbas said: Abraham and Ishmael raised it, with Ishmael handing him the stones. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib said: Abraham and Ishmael raised it while Ishmael was a small child. This is not authentically reported from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), because the verse and the reports reject it.

"Ismail" is conjoined to "Ibrahim" (ʿaṭf). It is also said that it is a new sentence (in the nominative, mubtada'), whose predicate comes afterward. Al-Mawardi said: "Isma'il" originally was "isma' ya Ā'īl" (hear, O God), but this is weak. The sense of the sentence is: they both say, "Our Lord, accept." This is also how it is read in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b and 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, with "yaqulan" (they say) explicitly present. A group said the intended meaning is: "And Ishmael says: Our Lord," and it was omitted because the context indicates it. All of this shows that Ishmael was not a child at that time.

These two attributes were specified because they suit their situation: the All-Hearing of our supplication and the All-Knowing of our intentions. Their saying "ij'alna" (make us) means "sayyirna" (make us become), and it takes two objects; "muslimayn" (submissive) is the second object. Likewise they were. They only desired steadfastness and continuity. Islam in this place means faith and deeds together. Ibn 'Abbas and 'Awf read "muslimin" in the plural. The "min" in His saying "wa min dhurriyyatina" (and of our descendants) is partitive; He specified some of the descendants because God had informed him that among them were wrongdoers. "Umma" means a community. Al-Tabari reports that he meant by it the Arabs specifically; this is weak, because his call became manifest among the Arabs and among others who believed from outside them.

Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "arina" with a kasra on the ra'. Ibn Kathir read "arina" with a sukun on the ra'. Abu 'Amr read between sukun and kasra, with ikhtilas (a rapid, partial vowel). The original form was "ar'iina"; the yā' was dropped for the jazm, the vowel of the hamza was moved onto the ra', and the hamza was dropped for lightness. Those who made the ra' sukun then found the kasra heavy, as it is heavy in "fakhidh" (thigh), but here there is more elision than in "fakhdh". Some said "arina" is from seeing with the eye; others said from seeing with the heart, and this is the more correct view. It requires that the verb extend to three objects, and it is answered that it is found transitive by the hamza from seeing with the heart just as the non-transitive form is. Hatit ibn Ya'fur, brother of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur, said:

"Show me a steed that died of emaciation, for I see what you see, or a stingy one that is eternal."

Qatada said: "al-manasik" are the landmarks of the pilgrimage. It is reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: when Abraham finished building the House and made this supplication, Allah sent Gabriel to him and he performed the pilgrimage with him. Ibn Jurayj said: "al-manasik" are the slaughtering places, that is, the places of sacrifice. A group of scholars said: "al-manasik" are all acts of worship; from this comes "nasik", meaning worshipper. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa arihim manasikahum" (and show them their rites), as if he meant the descendants.

(p-352) Tawba is return. Legally it is defined as return from evil to good. God's turning to the servant is His returning him (to mercy) and guiding him. Scholars differed about the meaning of their asking for repentance while they were prophets, protected from sin. One group said they asked for steadfastness and continuity. It is also said they meant their descendants after them, as when you say: "So-and-so was kind to me and honoured me," while you mean your children and descendants. And it is said, and this is the best in my view, that when they knew the rites, built the House and obeyed, they wished to establish for people that this standing place and these locations are places of disavowal of sins and seeking repentance.

Al-Tabari said: there is no one among God's creation except that between him and God there are states that ought to be better than they are. The community agreed on the infallibility of the prophets with respect to conveying the message, and from major sins, and from minor sins that involve baseness. Opinions differ regarding other minor sins. What I say is that they are protected from all of these. The Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Indeed I repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness seventy times a day" refers only to his return from one state to a higher one, so that his knowledge and awareness of God's command increase; he advances from one station to another. Repentance here is in the linguistic sense.

His Exalted saying: "Our Lord, and raise among them a messenger from among them," to the end of the verse. This is what the Prophet ﷺ meant by his saying: "I am the answer to my father Abraham's prayer, and the glad tidings of Jesus." The meaning of "minhum" (from among them) is that they would know him, realise his virtue, that he would be compassionate and concerned for them. "Yatlu" (recite) is in the accusative as an attribute of "rasul," meaning reciting to them; it can also be in the position of a circumstantial clause. "Al-ayat" are the verses of the Qur'an, and "al-Kitab" is the Qur'an. He attributed the teaching (p-353) to the Prophet ﷺ in that he gives the matters he considers and knows the methods of reasoning through what God casts into him and reveals to him. Qatada said: "al-hikma" is the Sunna and the Prophet's ﷺ explanation of the laws. Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that wisdom is understanding of the religion, and the understanding that is an innate disposition and a light from God. "Yuzakkihim" means He purifies them and causes them to grow in goodness; the meaning of zakat does not depart from purification or growth. "Al-'Aziz" is the One who prevails, whose purpose is accomplished and is not turned back. "Al-Hakim" is the One who places the act in the right place, the act being firmly made for it.

﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself? We had chosen him in this world, and in the Hereafter he is indeed among the righteous. When his Lord said to him, "Submit," he said, "I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds." The meaning is: he renounces it, and holds himself above it. "Millah" (الملة) means the sacred law and the way. "Safiha" (سَفِهَ) derives from safah (السفه), whose meaning is weakness of judgment and lightness.

There is disagreement regarding the accusative case of "nafsahu" (نَفْسَهُ). Al-Zajjaj said: "safiha" (سَفِهَ) means "jahila" (جَهِلَ, to be ignorant), and it is made transitive by interpretation (ʿaddāhu bi-l-maʿnā). Others said: "safiha" means "uhlika" (أُهْلِكَ, to be destroyed). Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad related that "safiha" with a kasra on the fa' (سَفِهَ) is transitive like "safaha" (سَفَهَ) with a fatḥa on the fa' and its doubling, and it was related from Abu al-Khattab that this is a dialect. Al-Farra' said: its accusative is by way of specification (tamyīz, a grammatical term for a noun clarifying the vagueness of a preceding word).

In my view, this definition is not pure, because the pronoun in it carries the same vagueness as in "man," so the sentence is as though it said: "except one who makes a fool of a self." The Basrans said: specification is not permitted with this definition, and the accusative is only on the assumption that the preposition "fī" (فِي, "in") has been deleted; when the preposition was deleted, the verb became strong. This follows the view of Sībawayh regarding what he related of their saying: "Fulān struck the back and the belly," meaning "in the back and the belly."

Makkī related that the implied meaning is "except one who makes a fool of his self" (إلّا مَن سَفِهَ قَوْلَه نَفْسَهُ), with "nafsahu" as an emphatic (ta'kīd), the emphasized element having been deleted and the emphasis placed in its position, by analogy with the adjective and the noun it modifies (al-naʿt wa-l-manʿūt). This is an overstrained view.

"Iṣṭafā" (اصطفى) is of the pattern "iftaʿala" (افتعل) from ṣafwah (الصفوة, the pure or best part), meaning: he chose the best. The tā' was changed to ṭā' (طاء) to harmonize with the ṣād (صاد) in emphatic articulation (iṭbāq). The meaning of this choosing is that He gave him prophethood and took him as a close friend (khalīl).

"Fī al-ākhirah" (فِي الْآخِرَةِ, "in the Hereafter") is connected to an implied active participle derived from ṣalāḥ (الصلاح, righteousness). It cannot be connected to "al-ṣāliḥīn" (الصالِحِينَ, "the righteous"), because the relative clause (ṣilah) does not precede the relative pronoun, on the condition that the alif and lām (الألف واللام) are in the sense of "alladhī" (الذي, "who"). Some said: the alif and lām here are for definiteness, and the sentence is sound. It was also said: the meaning is that in the works of the Hereafter he is "among the righteous," so the sentence has an elided genitive (ḥadhf muḍāf, omission of a noun governing another noun).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When his Lord said to him, "Submit,"﴾: the governing element (al-ʿāmil) of "idh" (إذ, "when") is "iṣṭafaynāhu" (اصطفيناه, "We chose him"). This statement came from Allah when He tested him with the star, the moon and the sun. Islam here is in its most complete aspects.

The pronoun in "bihā" (بِها, "with it") refers to his word which is: ﴿I have submitted to the Lord of the worlds﴾. It was also said that it refers to the previously mentioned religion, and the first is more correct because it is the nearest antecedent. ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid al-Aswārī read "wa-yaʿqūba" (ويَعْقُوبَ) in the accusative, on the basis that Jacob is included among those who were instructed. The alif and lām in "al-dīn" (الدِينَ, "the religion") are for a known referent, because they had already known it. Ibn Masʿūd and al-Ḍaḥḥāk read "an yā banīya" with "an" retained.

His saying: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ is an eloquent conciseness, because its purpose is to command them to Islam and to persistence in it. He expressed this with a concise wording that conveys the intended meaning and includes admonition and reminder (p-356) of death, because a person is certain that he will die but does not know when. So when he is commanded with a command such that death does not reach him except while he is upon it, then from the time of the command he is continuously and inescapably directed toward it. Sībawayh related, in something resembling this meaning, their saying: "I will not let you see me here," whereas it is not up to the one addressed to prevent him from perceiving the command; rather the intent is: "Go away and leave this place," but it was expressed with wording that adds the meaning of anger and aversion. "Wa-antum muslimūn" (وَأنْتُمْ مُسْلِمُونَ, "while you are Muslims") is a nominal sentence consisting of subject and predicate (ibtidāʾ wa-khabar), in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 133–135:

The Almighty and Majestic's words:

﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we are Muslims."﴾ ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided." Say, "Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf (one who turns away from false religions toward the truth), and he was not of the polytheists."﴾

This address is to the Jews and the Christians who claimed the Prophets (may God's blessings be upon them) and attributed them to Judaism and Christianity. God rejected them, declared them liars, and informed them that they were upon the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic religion) and Islam. He said to them, by way of rebuke and reproach: "Were you present with Ya'qub, and did you know what he enjoined, that you claim it with knowledge?" That is, you were not present; rather, you are inventing falsehoods. The particle "am" (or) can mean the interrogative alif at the beginning of a statement, a Yemeni usage. al-Ṭabarī related that "am" may be used interrogatively in the middle of a speech whose beginning has already been given, and this is one such case, as in His words: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [Yunus: 38]. Some said that "am" means "bal" (rather), and the meaning is: "Rather, your forefathers witnessed Ya'qub, and you knew from them what he enjoined, but you disbelieved out of denial, and you attributed them to other than the ḥanīfiyya out of obstinacy."

The most apparent view is that it has the meaning of "bal" together with the interrogative alif combined. "Shuhadā'" is the plural of "shāhid," meaning present (ḥāḍir). The meaning of the verse: Ya'qub came to the first stages of death, for if death had fully arrived he could not have said anything. "Ya'qub" is placed first as a matter of giving precedence to what is most important, and the governing element of "idh" (when) is "shuhadā'." "Idh qāla" is a substitute for the first "idh." He expressed the object of worship with "mā" (what) as a test for them, and did not say "man" (who), so that it would not open a way for them to be guided. He only intended to test them. Also, the commonly known objects of worship apart from God the Exalted are inanimate things such as idols, fire, the sun, and stones, so he asked them about what they worship of these. "Min ba'dī" means after my death. It is related that when Ya'qub was given the choice, as the Prophets are given it, he chose death and said: "Give me time until I counsel my sons and family." So he gathered them and said this to them, and they were guided. Then "They said, 'We will worship your God'" is the verse, and so they showed him their steadfastness in the religion and their knowledge of God the Exalted. Isma'il is included among the fathers because he was an uncle. The Prophet (ﷺ) said about al-Abbas: "Return my father (abī) to me, for I fear that Quraysh will do to him what Thaqīf did to 'Urwa ibn Mas'ūd," and he said about him on another occasion: "This is the remnant of my fathers." From this is his (peace be upon him) saying: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones," according to the well-known view that Ishaq is the one sacrificed.

al-Ḥasan, Ibn Ya'mur, al-Jaḥdarī, and Abū Rajā' read: "wa-ilāha abīka" (the God of your father). Then the scholars differed. It was said that it is a singular noun, and by it they meant Ibrahim alone. Others said it is the sound plural (jam' salāma), and Sībawayh related: ab, abawn, abayn. The poet said:

"When they recognized our voices, they wept, and ransomed us with the fathers (al-abyan)."

Ibn Zayd said: it is said that Isma'il was mentioned first because he was older than Ishaq. "Ilāh" is a substitute for "ilāhaka," and he repeated it for the benefit of the attribute of oneness.

It was also said that "ilāhan" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and this is a good view, because the purpose is to establish the state of oneness. "Wa-naḥnu lahu muslimūn" is a nominal sentence (mubtada' and khabar), meaning: thus we were and thus we are. It may also be in the position of a circumstantial clause, with "na'budu" as its governing element, but the first interpretation is more praiseworthy.

God's words "qad khalat" (has passed away) are in the position of a nominative attribute (na't) for "ummah" (nation). Its meaning: they died and went to the emptiness of the earth. By "the nation" He means the Prophets mentioned. The addressees in this verse are the Jews and Christians, that is, you, O you who attribute to them Judaism and Christianity: that will not benefit you, because every soul ﴿has what it earned﴾ of good and evil, so their goodness will not benefit you if you have earned evil. In this verse there is a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists) who say there is no acquisition (kasb) for the servant. ﴿And you will not be asked about what they used to do﴾, so that you may claim their religion for yourselves.

Their saying: ﴿Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided﴾ is similar to their saying: ﴿None will enter Paradise except those who are Jews or Christians﴾ [al-Baqara: 111].

"Millata" is put in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: rather, we follow the religion (millata). It was said that it is accusative by way of incitement (ighrā'). al-A'raj and Ibn Abī 'Abla read "bal millatu" in the nominative, and the implied meaning is: rather, guidance is a religion. "Ḥanīfan" is a circumstantial clause. It was said that it is accusative by an implied verb, because the circumstantial clause is connected to the genitive noun. Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 133–135:

The Almighty and Majestic's words:

﴿Or were you witnesses when death approached Ya'qub, when he said to his sons, "What will you worship after me?" They said, "We will worship your God and the God of your fathers, Ibrahim and Isma'il and Ishaq, one God, and to Him we are Muslims."﴾ ﴿That is a nation that has passed away. For it is what it earned, and for you is what you have earned. And you will not be asked about what they used to do.﴾ ﴿And they say, "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided." Say, "Rather, [we follow] the religion of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf (one who turns away from false religions toward the truth), and he was not of the polytheists."﴾

This address is to the Jews and the Christians who claimed the Prophets (may God's blessings be upon them) and attributed them to Judaism and Christianity. God rejected them, declared them liars, and informed them that they were upon the ḥanīfiyya (the pure monotheistic religion) and Islam. He said to them, by way of rebuke and reproach: "Were you present with Ya'qub, and did you know what he enjoined, that you claim it with knowledge?" That is, you were not present; rather, you are inventing falsehoods. The particle "am" (or) can mean the interrogative alif at the beginning of a statement, a Yemeni usage. al-Ṭabarī related that "am" may be used interrogatively in the middle of a speech whose beginning has already been given, and this is one such case, as in His words: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [Yunus: 38]. Some said that "am" means "bal" (rather), and the meaning is: "Rather, your forefathers witnessed Ya'qub, and you knew from them what he enjoined, but you disbelieved out of denial, and you attributed them to other than the ḥanīfiyya out of obstinacy."

The most apparent view is that it has the meaning of "bal" together with the interrogative alif combined. "Shuhadā'" is the plural of "shāhid," meaning present (ḥāḍir). The meaning of the verse: Ya'qub came to the first stages of death, for if death had fully arrived he could not have said anything. "Ya'qub" is placed first as a matter of giving precedence to what is most important, and the governing element of "idh" (when) is "shuhadā'." "Idh qāla" is a substitute for the first "idh." قوله عزّ وجلّ:

﴿قُولُوا آمَنَّا بِاللهِ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَالْأَسْبَاطِ وَمَا أُوتِيَ مُوسَى وَعِيسَى وَمَا أُوتِيَ النَّبِيُّونَ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ﴿فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا وَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإِنَّمَا هُمْ فِي شِقَاقٍ فَسَيَكْفِيكَهُمُ اللهُ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ﴾ ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللهِ وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللهِ صِبْغَةً وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾

هَذَا الْخِطَابُ لِأُمَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ)، عَلَّمَهُمُ اللهُ الْإِيمَانَ.

﴿وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْنَا﴾ يَعْنِي بِهِ الْقُرْآنَ، وَصَحَّتْ إِضَافَةُ الْإِنْزَالِ إِلَيْهِمْ مِنْ حَيْثُ هُمُ الْمَأْمُورُونَ وَالْمَنْهِيُّونَ فِيهِ.

وَ(إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ) يَجْمَعَانِ "بَرَاهِيمَ وَسَمَاعِيلَ"، هَذَا هُوَ اخْتِيَارُ سِيبَوَيْهِ (Sibawayh) وَالْخَلِيلِ (al-Khalil). وَقَالَ قَوْمٌ: "بَرَاهِمُ وَسَمَاعِلُ"، وَقَالَ الْكُوفِيُّونَ: "بَرَاهِمَةُ وَسَمَاعِلَةُ"، وَقَالَ الْمُبَرِّدُ (al-Mubarrad): "أَبَارِهُ وَأَسَامِعُ"، وَأَجَازَ ثَعْلَبٌ (Tha'lab) "بَرَّاهُ"، كَمَا يُقَالُ فِي التَّصْغِيرِ "بُرَيِّهِ". وَ"الْأَسْبَاطِ" هُمْ وُلْدُ يَعْقُوبَ، وَهُمْ: رُوبِيلُ، وَشَمْعُونُ، وَلَاوِي، وَيَهُوذَا، وَرَبَالُونُ، وَيَشْحُرُ، وَدِنِيَّةُ بِنْتُهُ، وَأُمُّهُمْ لِيَّا، ثُمَّ خَلَفَ عَلَى أُخْتِهَا رَاحِيلُ فَوَلَدَتْ لَهُ يُوسُفَ وَبِنْيَامِينَ، وَوُلِدَ لَهُ مِنْ سَرِيَّتَيْنِ: ذَانُ، وَتَفْتَالِي، وَجَادُ، وَأَشْرُو. وَالسِّبْطُ فِي بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْقَبِيلَةِ فِي وَلَدِ إِسْمَاعِيلَ، فَسُمُّوا الْأَسْبَاطَ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ مِنْ كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ سِبْطٌ.

(p-٣٦١)﴿وَمَا أُوتِيَ مُوسَى﴾ هُوَ التَّوْرَاةُ وَآيَاتُهُ، وَ(مَا أُوتِيَ عِيسَى) هُوَ الْإِنْجِيلُ وَآيَاتُهُ. فَالْمَعْنَى: إِنَّا نُؤْمِنُ بِجَمِيعِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ لِأَنَّ جَمِيعَهُمْ جَاءَ بِالْإِيمَانِ بِاللهِ، فَدِينُ اللهِ وَاحِدٌ وَإِنِ اخْتَلَفَتْ أَحْكَامُ الشَّرَائِعِ. وَ﴿لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ﴾ أَيْ: لَا نُؤْمِنُ بِبَعْضٍ وَنَكْفُرُ بِبَعْضٍ كَمَا تَفْعَلُونَ. وَفِي الْكَلَامِ حَذْفٌ تَقْدِيرُهُ: بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ وَبَيْنَ نَظِيرِهِ، فَاخْتُصِرَ لِفَهْمِ السَّامِعِ. وَالضَّمِيرُ فِي "لَهُ" عَائِدٌ عَلَى اسْمِ اللهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ الْآيَةُ. خِطَابٌ لِمُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ) وَأُمَّتِهِ، وَالْمَعْنَى: إِنْ صَدَّقُوا تَصْدِيقًا مِثْلَ تَصْدِيقِكُمْ، فَالْمُمَاثَلَةُ وَقَعَتْ بَيْنَ الْإِيمَانَيْنِ، هَذَا قَوْلُ بَعْضِ الْمُتَأَوِّلِينَ.

وَقِيلَ: الْبَاءُ زَائِدَةٌ مُؤَكِّدَةٌ، وَالتَّقْدِيرُ: آمَنُوا مِثْلُ، وَالضَّمِيرُ فِي "بِهِ" عَائِدٌ كَالضَّمِيرِ فِي "لَهُ"، فَكَأَنَّ الْكَلَامَ: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِاللهِ مِثْلَ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ. وَيَظْهَرُ عَوْدُ الضَّمِيرِ عَلَى "مَا". وَقِيلَ: "مِثْلِ" زَائِدَةٌ كَمَا هِيَ فِي قَوْلِهِ: ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ [الشورى: ١١]. وَقَالَتْ فِرْقَةٌ: هَذَا مِنْ مَجَازِ الْكَلَامِ (figurative usage)، تَقُولُ: هَذَا أَمْرٌ لَا يَفْعَلُهُ مِثْلُكَ، أَيْ لَا تَفْعَلُهُ أَنْتَ، فَالْمَعْنَى: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِالَّذِي آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ. هَذَا قَوْلُ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، وَقَدْ حَكَاهُ عَنْهُ الطَّبَرِيُّ (al-Tabari) قِرَاءَةً، ثُمَّ أُسْنِدَ إِلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: "لَا تَقُولُوا: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ، فَإِنَّهُ لَا مَثَلَ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى، وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِالَّذِي آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ أَوْ بِمَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ".

قَالَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ: وَهَذَا عَلَى جِهَةِ التَّفْسِيرِ، أَيْ هَكَذَا فَلْيُتَأَوَّلْ، (p-٣٦٢) وَحَكَاهُمَا أَبُو عَمْرٍو الدَّانِيُّ (Abu 'Amr al-Dani) قِرَاءَتَيْنِ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، فَاللهُ أَعْلَمُ.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ أَيْ أَعْرَضُوا، يَعْنِي بِهِ الْيَهُودَ وَالنَّصَارَى. وَالشِّقَاقُ: الْمُشَاقَّةُ وَالْمُحَادَّةُ وَالْمُخَالَفَةُ، أَيْ فِي شِقَاقٍ لَكَ، هُمْ فِي شِقٍّ وَأَنْتَ فِي شِقٍّ. وَقِيلَ: الشِّقَاقُ مَعْنَاهُ أَنَّ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ شَقَّ وَصَلَ مَا بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ صَاحِبِهِ. ثُمَّ وَعَدَهُ تَعَالَى أَنَّهُ سَيَكْفِيهِ إِيَّاهُمْ وَيُغَلِّبُهُ عَلَيْهِمْ، فَكَانَ ذَلِكَ فِي قَتْلِ بَنِي قَيْنُقَاعَ وَبَنِي قُرَيْظَةَ وَإِجْلَاءِ النَّضِيرِ، وَهَذَا الْوَعْدُ وَانْتِجَازُهُ مِنْ أَعْلَامِ نُبُوَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ). وَ"السَّمِيعُ" لِقَوْلِ كُلِّ قَائِلٍ، "الْعَلِيمُ" بِمَا يَجِبُ أَنْ يَنْفُذَ فِي عِبَادِهِ.

وَ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللهِ﴾ شَرِيعَتُهُ وَسُنَّتُهُ وَفِطْرَتُهُ، وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ النَّصَارَى لَهُمْ مَاءٌ يَصْبُغُونَ فِيهِ أَوْلَادَهُمْ، فَهَذَا يَنْظُرُ إِلَى ذَلِكَ. وَقِيلَ: سُمِّيَ الدِّينُ "صِبْغَةً" اسْتِعَارَةً (metaphor) مِنْ حَيْثُ تَظْهَرُ أَعْمَالُهُ وَسَمْتُهُ عَلَى الْمُتَدَيِّنِ كَمَا يَظْهَرُ الصَّبْغُ فِي الثَّوْبِ وَغَيْرِهِ.

وَنَصْبُ "الصِّبْغَةِ" عَلَى الْإِغْرَاءِ (exhortation, i.e., the grammatical construction of urging someone to take hold of something), وَقِيلَ: بَدَلٌ مِنْ "مِلَّةَ"، وَقِيلَ: نُصِبَ عَلَى الْمَصْدَرِ الْمُؤَكِّدِ (emphatic infinitive) لِأَنَّ مَا قَبْلَهُ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا﴾ هُوَ فِي مَعْنَى "يَلْبَسُونَ" أَوْ "يَتَجَلَّلُونَ صِبْغَةَ اللهِ". وَقِيلَ: التَّقْدِيرُ: ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ صِبْغَةُ اللهِ، فَهِيَ مُتَّصِلَةٌ بِالْآيَةِ الْمُتَقَدِّمَةِ. وَقَالَ الطَّبَرِيُّ: "مَنْ قَرَأَ بِرَفْعِ 'مِلَّةَ' قَرَأَ بِرَفْعِ 'صِبْغَةَ'".

قَالَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ:

وَقَدْ ذَكَرْتُهَا عَنِ الْأَعْرَجِ (al-A'raj) وَابْنِ أَبِي عَبْلَةَ (Ibn Abi 'Ablah): ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾ ابْتِدَاءٌ وَخَبَرٌ.

قوله عزّ وجلّ:

﴿قُولُوا آمَنَّا بِاللهِ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَالْأَسْبَاطِ وَمَا أُوتِيَ مُوسَى وَعِيسَى وَمَا أُوتِيَ النَّبِيُّونَ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ﴿فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا وَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإِنَّمَا هُمْ فِي شِقَاقٍ فَسَيَكْفِيكَهُمُ اللهُ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ﴾ ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللهِ وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللهِ صِبْغَةً وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾

هَذَا الْخِطَابُ لِأُمَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ)، عَلَّمَهُمُ اللهُ الْإِيمَانَ.

﴿وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْنَا﴾ يَعْنِي بِهِ الْقُرْآنَ، وَصَحَّتْ إِضَافَةُ الْإِنْزَالِ إِلَيْهِمْ مِنْ حَيْثُ هُمُ الْمَأْمُورُونَ وَالْمَنْهِيُّونَ فِيهِ.

وَ(إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ) يَجْمَعَانِ "بَرَاهِيمَ وَسَمَاعِيلَ"، هَذَا هُوَ اخْتِيَارُ سِيبَوَيْهِ (Sibawayh) وَالْخَلِيلِ (al-Khalil). وَقَالَ قَوْمٌ: "بَرَاهِمُ وَسَمَاعِلُ"، وَقَالَ الْكُوفِيُّونَ: "بَرَاهِمَةُ وَسَمَاعِلَةُ"، وَقَالَ الْمُبَرِّدُ (al-Mubarrad): "أَبَارِهُ وَأَسَامِعُ"، وَأَجَازَ ثَعْلَبٌ (Tha'lab) "بَرَّاهُ"، كَمَا يُقَالُ فِي التَّصْغِيرِ "بُرَيِّهِ". وَ"الْأَسْبَاطِ" هُمْ وُلْدُ يَعْقُوبَ، وَهُمْ: رُوبِيلُ، وَشَمْعُونُ، وَلَاوِي، وَيَهُوذَا، وَرَبَالُونُ، وَيَشْحُرُ، وَدِنِيَّةُ بِنْتُهُ، وَأُمُّهُمْ لِيَّا، ثُمَّ خَلَفَ عَلَى أُخْتِهَا رَاحِيلُ فَوَلَدَتْ لَهُ يُوسُفَ وَبِنْيَامِينَ، وَوُلِدَ لَهُ مِنْ سَرِيَّتَيْنِ: ذَانُ، وَتَفْتَالِي، وَجَادُ، وَأَشْرُو. وَالسِّبْطُ فِي بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْقَبِيلَةِ فِي وَلَدِ إِسْمَاعِيلَ، فَسُمُّوا الْأَسْبَاطَ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ مِنْ كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ سِبْطٌ.

(p-٣٦١)﴿وَمَا أُوتِيَ مُوسَى﴾ هُوَ التَّوْرَاةُ وَآيَاتُهُ، وَ(مَا أُوتِيَ عِيسَى) هُوَ الْإِنْجِيلُ وَآيَاتُهُ. فَالْمَعْنَى: إِنَّا نُؤْمِنُ بِجَمِيعِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ لِأَنَّ جَمِيعَهُمْ جَاءَ بِالْإِيمَانِ بِاللهِ، فَدِينُ اللهِ وَاحِدٌ وَإِنِ اخْتَلَفَتْ أَحْكَامُ الشَّرَائِعِ. وَ﴿لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ﴾ أَيْ: لَا نُؤْمِنُ بِبَعْضٍ وَنَكْفُرُ بِبَعْضٍ كَمَا تَفْعَلُونَ. وَفِي الْكَلَامِ حَذْفٌ تَقْدِيرُهُ: بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ وَبَيْنَ نَظِيرِهِ، فَاخْتُصِرَ لِفَهْمِ السَّامِعِ. وَالضَّمِيرُ فِي "لَهُ" عَائِدٌ عَلَى اسْمِ اللهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ الْآيَةُ. خِطَابٌ لِمُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ) وَأُمَّتِهِ، وَالْمَعْنَى: إِنْ صَدَّقُوا تَصْدِيقًا مِثْلَ تَصْدِيقِكُمْ، فَالْمُمَاثَلَةُ وَقَعَتْ بَيْنَ الْإِيمَانَيْنِ، هَذَا قَوْلُ بَعْضِ الْمُتَأَوِّلِينَ.

وَقِيلَ: الْبَاءُ زَائِدَةٌ مُؤَكِّدَةٌ، وَالتَّقْدِيرُ: آمَنُوا مِثْلُ، وَالضَّمِيرُ فِي "بِهِ" عَائِدٌ كَالضَّمِيرِ فِي "لَهُ"، فَكَأَنَّ الْكَلَامَ: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِاللهِ مِثْلَ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ. وَيَظْهَرُ عَوْدُ الضَّمِيرِ عَلَى "مَا". وَقِيلَ: "مِثْلِ" زَائِدَةٌ كَمَا هِيَ فِي قَوْلِهِ: ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ [الشورى: ١١]. وَقَالَتْ فِرْقَةٌ: هَذَا مِنْ مَجَازِ الْكَلَامِ (figurative usage)، تَقُولُ: هَذَا أَمْرٌ لَا يَفْعَلُهُ مِثْلُكَ، أَيْ لَا تَفْعَلُهُ أَنْتَ، فَالْمَعْنَى: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِالَّذِي آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ. هَذَا قَوْلُ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، وَقَدْ حَكَاهُ عَنْهُ الطَّبَرِيُّ (al-Tabari) قِرَاءَةً، ثُمَّ أُسْنِدَ إِلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: "لَا تَقُولُوا: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ، فَإِنَّهُ لَا مَثَلَ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى، وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِالَّذِي آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ أَوْ بِمَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ".

قَالَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ: وَهَذَا عَلَى جِهَةِ التَّفْسِيرِ، أَيْ هَكَذَا فَلْيُتَأَوَّلْ، (p-٣٦٢) وَحَكَاهُمَا أَبُو عَمْرٍو الدَّانِيُّ (Abu 'Amr al-Dani) قِرَاءَتَيْنِ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، فَاللهُ أَعْلَمُ.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ أَيْ أَعْرَضُوا، يَعْنِي بِهِ الْيَهُودَ وَالنَّصَارَى. وَالشِّقَاقُ: الْمُشَاقَّةُ وَالْمُحَادَّةُ وَالْمُخَالَفَةُ، أَيْ فِي شِقَاقٍ لَكَ، هُمْ فِي شِقٍّ وَأَنْتَ فِي شِقٍّ. وَقِيلَ: الشِّقَاقُ مَعْنَاهُ أَنَّ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ شَقَّ وَصَلَ مَا بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ صَاحِبِهِ. ثُمَّ وَعَدَهُ تَعَالَى أَنَّهُ سَيَكْفِيهِ إِيَّاهُمْ وَيُغَلِّبُهُ عَلَيْهِمْ، فَكَانَ ذَلِكَ فِي قَتْلِ بَنِي قَيْنُقَاعَ وَبَنِي قُرَيْظَةَ وَإِجْلَاءِ النَّضِيرِ، وَهَذَا الْوَعْدُ وَانْتِجَازُهُ مِنْ أَعْلَامِ نُبُوَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ). وَ"السَّمِيعُ" لِقَوْلِ كُلِّ قَائِلٍ، "الْعَلِيمُ" بِمَا يَجِبُ أَنْ يَنْفُذَ فِي عِبَادِهِ.

وَ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللهِ﴾ شَرِيعَتُهُ وَسُنَّتُهُ وَفِطْرَتُهُ، وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ النَّصَارَى لَهُمْ مَاءٌ يَصْبُغُونَ فِيهِ أَوْلَادَهُمْ، فَهَذَا يَنْظُرُ إِلَى ذَلِكَ. وَقِيلَ: سُمِّيَ الدِّينُ "صِبْغَةً" اسْتِعَارَةً (metaphor) مِنْ حَيْثُ تَظْهَرُ أَعْمَالُهُ وَسَمْتُهُ عَلَى الْمُتَدَيِّنِ كَمَا يَظْهَرُ الصَّبْغُ فِي الثَّوْبِ وَغَيْرِهِ.

وَنَصْبُ "الصِّبْغَةِ" عَلَى الْإِغْرَاءِ (exhortation, i.e., the grammatical construction of urging someone to take hold of something), وَقِيلَ: بَدَلٌ مِنْ "مِلَّةَ"، وَقِيلَ: نُصِبَ عَلَى الْمَصْدَرِ الْمُؤَكِّدِ (emphatic infinitive) لِأَنَّ مَا قَبْلَهُ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا﴾ هُوَ فِي مَعْنَى "يَلْبَسُونَ" أَوْ "يَتَجَلَّلُونَ صِبْغَةَ اللهِ". وَقِيلَ: التَّقْدِيرُ: ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ صِبْغَةُ اللهِ، فَهِيَ مُتَّصِلَةٌ بِالْآيَةِ الْمُتَقَدِّمَةِ. وَقَالَ الطَّبَرِيُّ: "مَنْ قَرَأَ بِرَفْعِ 'مِلَّةَ' قَرَأَ بِرَفْعِ 'صِبْغَةَ'".

قَالَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ:

وَقَدْ ذَكَرْتُهَا عَنِ الْأَعْرَجِ (al-A'raj) وَابْنِ أَبِي عَبْلَةَ (Ibn Abi 'Ablah): ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾ ابْتِدَاءٌ وَخَبَرٌ.

قوله عزّ وجلّ:

﴿قُولُوا آمَنَّا بِاللهِ وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْنَا وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَى إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ وَإِسْحَاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ وَالْأَسْبَاطِ وَمَا أُوتِيَ مُوسَى وَعِيسَى وَمَا أُوتِيَ النَّبِيُّونَ مِنْ رَبِّهِمْ لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ ﴿فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا وَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا فَإِنَّمَا هُمْ فِي شِقَاقٍ فَسَيَكْفِيكَهُمُ اللهُ وَهُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ﴾ ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللهِ وَمَنْ أَحْسَنُ مِنَ اللهِ صِبْغَةً وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾

هَذَا الْخِطَابُ لِأُمَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ)، عَلَّمَهُمُ اللهُ الْإِيمَانَ.

﴿وَمَا أُنْزِلَ إِلَيْنَا﴾ يَعْنِي بِهِ الْقُرْآنَ، وَصَحَّتْ إِضَافَةُ الْإِنْزَالِ إِلَيْهِمْ مِنْ حَيْثُ هُمُ الْمَأْمُورُونَ وَالْمَنْهِيُّونَ فِيهِ.

وَ(إِبْرَاهِيمَ وَإِسْمَاعِيلَ) يَجْمَعَانِ "بَرَاهِيمَ وَسَمَاعِيلَ"، هَذَا هُوَ اخْتِيَارُ سِيبَوَيْهِ (Sibawayh) وَالْخَلِيلِ (al-Khalil). وَقَالَ قَوْمٌ: "بَرَاهِمُ وَسَمَاعِلُ"، وَقَالَ الْكُوفِيُّونَ: "بَرَاهِمَةُ وَسَمَاعِلَةُ"، وَقَالَ الْمُبَرِّدُ (al-Mubarrad): "أَبَارِهُ وَأَسَامِعُ"، وَأَجَازَ ثَعْلَبٌ (Tha'lab) "بَرَّاهُ"، كَمَا يُقَالُ فِي التَّصْغِيرِ "بُرَيِّهِ". وَ"الْأَسْبَاطِ" هُمْ وُلْدُ يَعْقُوبَ، وَهُمْ: رُوبِيلُ، وَشَمْعُونُ، وَلَاوِي، وَيَهُوذَا، وَرَبَالُونُ، وَيَشْحُرُ، وَدِنِيَّةُ بِنْتُهُ، وَأُمُّهُمْ لِيَّا، ثُمَّ خَلَفَ عَلَى أُخْتِهَا رَاحِيلُ فَوَلَدَتْ لَهُ يُوسُفَ وَبِنْيَامِينَ، وَوُلِدَ لَهُ مِنْ سَرِيَّتَيْنِ: ذَانُ، وَتَفْتَالِي، وَجَادُ، وَأَشْرُو. وَالسِّبْطُ فِي بَنِي إِسْرَائِيلَ بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْقَبِيلَةِ فِي وَلَدِ إِسْمَاعِيلَ، فَسُمُّوا الْأَسْبَاطَ لِأَنَّهُ كَانَ مِنْ كُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ سِبْطٌ.

(p-٣٦١)﴿وَمَا أُوتِيَ مُوسَى﴾ هُوَ التَّوْرَاةُ وَآيَاتُهُ، وَ(مَا أُوتِيَ عِيسَى) هُوَ الْإِنْجِيلُ وَآيَاتُهُ. فَالْمَعْنَى: إِنَّا نُؤْمِنُ بِجَمِيعِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ لِأَنَّ جَمِيعَهُمْ جَاءَ بِالْإِيمَانِ بِاللهِ، فَدِينُ اللهِ وَاحِدٌ وَإِنِ اخْتَلَفَتْ أَحْكَامُ الشَّرَائِعِ. وَ﴿لَا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ﴾ أَيْ: لَا نُؤْمِنُ بِبَعْضٍ وَنَكْفُرُ بِبَعْضٍ كَمَا تَفْعَلُونَ. وَفِي الْكَلَامِ حَذْفٌ تَقْدِيرُهُ: بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْهُمْ وَبَيْنَ نَظِيرِهِ، فَاخْتُصِرَ لِفَهْمِ السَّامِعِ. وَالضَّمِيرُ فِي "لَهُ" عَائِدٌ عَلَى اسْمِ اللهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ﴾ الْآيَةُ. خِطَابٌ لِمُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ) وَأُمَّتِهِ، وَالْمَعْنَى: إِنْ صَدَّقُوا تَصْدِيقًا مِثْلَ تَصْدِيقِكُمْ، فَالْمُمَاثَلَةُ وَقَعَتْ بَيْنَ الْإِيمَانَيْنِ، هَذَا قَوْلُ بَعْضِ الْمُتَأَوِّلِينَ.

وَقِيلَ: الْبَاءُ زَائِدَةٌ مُؤَكِّدَةٌ، وَالتَّقْدِيرُ: آمَنُوا مِثْلُ، وَالضَّمِيرُ فِي "بِهِ" عَائِدٌ كَالضَّمِيرِ فِي "لَهُ"، فَكَأَنَّ الْكَلَامَ: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِاللهِ مِثْلَ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ. وَيَظْهَرُ عَوْدُ الضَّمِيرِ عَلَى "مَا". وَقِيلَ: "مِثْلِ" زَائِدَةٌ كَمَا هِيَ فِي قَوْلِهِ: ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ [الشورى: ١١]. وَقَالَتْ فِرْقَةٌ: هَذَا مِنْ مَجَازِ الْكَلَامِ (figurative usage)، تَقُولُ: هَذَا أَمْرٌ لَا يَفْعَلُهُ مِثْلُكَ، أَيْ لَا تَفْعَلُهُ أَنْتَ، فَالْمَعْنَى: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِالَّذِي آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ. هَذَا قَوْلُ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، وَقَدْ حَكَاهُ عَنْهُ الطَّبَرِيُّ (al-Tabari) قِرَاءَةً، ثُمَّ أُسْنِدَ إِلَيْهِ أَنَّهُ قَالَ: "لَا تَقُولُوا: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِمِثْلِ مَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ، فَإِنَّهُ لَا مَثَلَ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى، وَلَكِنْ قُولُوا: فَإِنْ آمَنُوا بِالَّذِي آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ أَوْ بِمَا آمَنْتُمْ بِهِ".

قَالَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ: وَهَذَا عَلَى جِهَةِ التَّفْسِيرِ، أَيْ هَكَذَا فَلْيُتَأَوَّلْ، (p-٣٦٢) وَحَكَاهُمَا أَبُو عَمْرٍو الدَّانِيُّ (Abu 'Amr al-Dani) قِرَاءَتَيْنِ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ، فَاللهُ أَعْلَمُ.

وَقَوْلُهُ تَعَالَى: ﴿وَإِنْ تَوَلَّوْا﴾ أَيْ أَعْرَضُوا، يَعْنِي بِهِ الْيَهُودَ وَالنَّصَارَى. وَالشِّقَاقُ: الْمُشَاقَّةُ وَالْمُحَادَّةُ وَالْمُخَالَفَةُ، أَيْ فِي شِقَاقٍ لَكَ، هُمْ فِي شِقٍّ وَأَنْتَ فِي شِقٍّ. وَقِيلَ: الشِّقَاقُ مَعْنَاهُ أَنَّ كُلَّ وَاحِدٍ شَقَّ وَصَلَ مَا بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ صَاحِبِهِ. ثُمَّ وَعَدَهُ تَعَالَى أَنَّهُ سَيَكْفِيهِ إِيَّاهُمْ وَيُغَلِّبُهُ عَلَيْهِمْ، فَكَانَ ذَلِكَ فِي قَتْلِ بَنِي قَيْنُقَاعَ وَبَنِي قُرَيْظَةَ وَإِجْلَاءِ النَّضِيرِ، وَهَذَا الْوَعْدُ وَانْتِجَازُهُ مِنْ أَعْلَامِ نُبُوَّةِ مُحَمَّدٍ (ﷺ). وَ"السَّمِيعُ" لِقَوْلِ كُلِّ قَائِلٍ، "الْعَلِيمُ" بِمَا يَجِبُ أَنْ يَنْفُذَ فِي عِبَادِهِ.

وَ﴿صِبْغَةَ اللهِ﴾ شَرِيعَتُهُ وَسُنَّتُهُ وَفِطْرَتُهُ، وَذَلِكَ أَنَّ النَّصَارَى لَهُمْ مَاءٌ يَصْبُغُونَ فِيهِ أَوْلَادَهُمْ، فَهَذَا يَنْظُرُ إِلَى ذَلِكَ. وَقِيلَ: سُمِّيَ الدِّينُ "صِبْغَةً" اسْتِعَارَةً (metaphor) مِنْ حَيْثُ تَظْهَرُ أَعْمَالُهُ وَسَمْتُهُ عَلَى الْمُتَدَيِّنِ كَمَا يَظْهَرُ الصَّبْغُ فِي الثَّوْبِ وَغَيْرِهِ.

وَنَصْبُ "الصِّبْغَةِ" عَلَى الْإِغْرَاءِ (exhortation, i.e., the grammatical construction of urging someone to take hold of something), وَقِيلَ: بَدَلٌ مِنْ "مِلَّةَ"، وَقِيلَ: نُصِبَ عَلَى الْمَصْدَرِ الْمُؤَكِّدِ (emphatic infinitive) لِأَنَّ مَا قَبْلَهُ مِنْ قَوْلِهِ: ﴿فَقَدِ اهْتَدَوْا﴾ هُوَ فِي مَعْنَى "يَلْبَسُونَ" أَوْ "يَتَجَلَّلُونَ صِبْغَةَ اللهِ". وَقِيلَ: التَّقْدِيرُ: ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ مُسْلِمُونَ﴾ صِبْغَةُ اللهِ، فَهِيَ مُتَّصِلَةٌ بِالْآيَةِ الْمُتَقَدِّمَةِ. وَقَالَ الطَّبَرِيُّ: "مَنْ قَرَأَ بِرَفْعِ 'مِلَّةَ' قَرَأَ بِرَفْعِ 'صِبْغَةَ'".

قَالَ الْقَاضِي أَبُو مُحَمَّدٍ رَحِمَهُ اللهُ:

وَقَدْ ذَكَرْتُهَا عَنِ الْأَعْرَجِ (al-A'raj) وَابْنِ أَبِي عَبْلَةَ (Ibn Abi 'Ablah): ﴿وَنَحْنُ لَهُ عَابِدُونَ﴾ ابْتِدَاءٌ وَخَبَرٌ.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 2, verses 139–141:

Allah the Exalted says:

﴿Say, "Do you argue with us about Allah, when He is our Lord and your Lord? For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds, and we are sincere to Him alone."﴾ ﴿Or do you say that Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes were Jews or Christians?" Say, "Are you more knowing, or is Allah? And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah? Allah is not unaware of what you do."﴾ ﴿That is a community that has passed away. For them is what they earned, and for you is what you earn. You will not be questioned about what they used to do.﴾

The meaning of the verse: Say, O Muhammad, to these Jews and Christians, who claim that they are the sons of Allah and His beloved, and who assert that they have a greater right to Allah than you, because their religions and scriptures are older: ﴿Do you argue with us about Allah?﴾ That is, do you contest with us the proof of your claim? The Lord, exalted is He, is one, and each person is recompensed for his own deed, so what effect does the antiquity of a religion have? Then they are rebuked by His saying: ﴿and we are sincere to Him alone﴾, that is: why, you yourselves are not sincere? So how do you claim what we have a greater right to than you?

Ibn Muhaysin recited أتُحاجُّونّا with the nun assimilated into the nun (idgham), and the meeting of two consonants (al-jam' bayna sakinayn) was made light, because the first is a letter of elongation and softness (harf madd wa-leen), so the elongation functions like a vowel. From this category are دابَّةٌ and شابَّةٌ. The phrase في الله means: in His religion, in nearness to Him, and in favour with Him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Am taqooloon﴾ is a conjunction (atf) upon the preceding interrogative alif. This reading with the taa' from above was recited by Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited أمْ يَقُولُونَ with the yaa' from below. On this reading, أم is disjunctive (maqta'a), as mentioned by al-Tabari. It is also reported from some grammarians that it is not disjunctive, because when you say: أتَقُومُ أمْ يَقُومُ عَمْرٌو؟ the meaning is: Would this happen or that?

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This example is not a good one, because the speaker in it is one and the addressee is one, whereas in the verse the speaking is by two parties and the addressees are two different parties.
