Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 142–143 (part 1 of 2):

The Most High said:
﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from their qiblah (direction of prayer) which they used to face?" Say: "To God belong the East and the West; He guides whom He wills to a straight path."﴾ ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you. We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels. It was indeed a great thing, except for those whom God has guided. God would never make your faith (îmân) to be lost. Indeed God is Most Kind and Merciful to the people.﴾

God, exalted is He, informed in this verse that they would say, concerning the change of direction of the believers from Syria to the Ka'bah: "What has turned them away?" The "foolish" (al-sufahâ') are those who are light in their judgments and minds. Safah means lightness and flimsiness. A "safîh" garment is one that is not finely woven. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"They walk like spears swaying, whose tops are made light (tasaffahat) by the gusts of the spring winds."

That is, the winds made them light. He specified "from the people" because foolishness can occur in inanimate things and animals as well. The intended meaning of "the foolish" here is all who said "What has turned them away?" Different groups said it, and there is disagreement about who they were. Ibn 'Abbas said: the rabbis among them said it, because they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, what has turned you away from our qiblah? Return to it and we will believe in you." They intended to tempt him. Al-Suddi said: some of the Jews and hypocrites said it mockingly, because they said: "The man has longed for his homeland."

A group said: it was said by the Quraysh disbelievers, because they said: "What has turned him away from his qiblah? He only returned to us because he knows that we are upon the truth, and he will return to our whole religion." The meaning of "turned them away" (wallâhum) is "redirected them." The qiblah is a form (fi'lah) denoting the manner of facing something, like the qa'dah (manner of sitting) and the izrah (manner of wearing a waist-wrap).

The future tense is used in "will say" in place of the past, indicating the continuation of that and that they would persist in that saying. Ibn 'Abbas and others stated explicitly that the verse was revealed after their saying.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Say: To God belong the East and the West﴾ are an establishment of proof, meaning: to Him belongs the dominion of the easts and the wests and what is between them. ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ is an indication of God's guidance of this community to the qiblah of Abraham. The "sirât" is the path. The scholars differed over whether the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) was by a command of God in the Qur'an, or by a revelation that was not recited (wahy ghayr matlu, i.e., revelation not part of the recited Qur'an). Ibn Fawrak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The first thing abrogated (nusikha, naskh meaning abrogation) from the Qur'an was the qiblah." The majority said: rather, the command concerning the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis was by an unrecited revelation. Al-Rabi' said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) chose among the directions, and chose Bayt al-Maqdis in order to win over the People of the Book. Those who said it was by unrecited revelation said: this was so that God might test those among the Arabs who believed, because they were attached to the Ka'bah and averse to Bayt al-Maqdis and other places.

It was disputed how long he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis. In al-Bukhari it is sixteen or seventeen months. It is reported from Anas ibn Malik nine or ten months, and reported from others thirteen months.

Makki related from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq that he said: "The first ordinance of prayer was that it was prescribed in Makkah as two rak'ahs at the beginning of the day and two rak'ahs at its end. Then came the Isra' (night journey) on the night of the seventeenth of Rabi' al-Akhir, a year before the Hijrah, and the five prayers were prescribed, and Jibril (peace be upon him) led them, and the first prayer was the Zuhr. The Prophet (ﷺ) faced Bayt al-Maqdis. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) migrated to Madinah in Rabi' al-Awwal, and he continued facing Bayt al-Maqdis until Rajab of the second year." It was said: until Jumada; it was said: until the middle of Sha'ban.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾: the kaf (the "thus") is connected to the meaning in His words ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾, meaning: just as We guided you to the qiblah of Abraham and his law, thus We made you a nation (ummah). "Ummatan" is the second object, and "wasatan" is an adjective. "Ummah" means generations of people. "Wasatan" means "just" ('udûlan). This was transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the wording of the exegetes agrees on it.

The wasat means the best and highest of a thing, as you say: "the middle of the people" (wasat al-qawm), "the middle pearl of the necklace" (wasitat al-qilâdah) meaning the most precious stone in it, and "the leader is the middle of the army." Like the Most High's saying: ﴿The best of them said﴾ (al-Qalam: 28). The wasat with a sukun on the sin (wasṭ) is an indeclinable adverb of place built on fatha. It has come declinable in some transmissions in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"She brought a bridled horse whose forehead is like a saddle-cloth of safflower dyed, and its middle split open."

With a damma on the ta' (wasṭuhâ), the pronoun refers to the saddle-cloth (salâ'ah). It was also transmitted with a fatha on the ta' (wasaṭuhâ), and the pronoun then refers to the female (al-jâ'iyah). When you say "I dug the middle of the house" (wasṭ al-dâr) or "the middle of the house" (wasaṭ al-dâr), the meaning differs.

Some scholars said: the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not exceed in religion as the Jews did, nor did it slacken as the Christians did; rather it is moderate, so it is the highest and best of nations from this aspect.

The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of matters are their middles" means: their best.

Excellence and goodness in a thing may be either because it is the most precious of its kind, or because it lies between excess and deficiency; so it is best from this aspect. "Shuhada'" is the plural of shahid (witness).

The exegetes differed over what is meant by "the people" in this place. One group said: it is the entire human race. The nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) will testify on the Day of Resurrection for the prophets against their peoples, regarding conveyance of the message. That is because Noah's people will deny that he conveyed it, so the nation of Muhammad will say to him: "We bear witness for you," and they will testify. God will say to them: "How do you testify to what you did not witness?" They will say: "O our Lord, Your Messenger came to us and Your Book descended to us, so we testify to what You charged us with and informed us of." God, exalted is He, will say: "You have spoken the truth."

A sound hadith is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) to this meaning, and it is reported from him that "his nation will testify for every prophet whose people denied him." Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: you will testify for Muhammad (ﷺ) that he conveyed to the people in his time, among the Jews, Christians and Magians. Another group said: the meaning of the verse is: some of you will testify against others after death, as "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said when a funeral passed by him and he praised it with good, and he said: 'It is obligatory (wajabat),' then another passed by him and he praised it with evil, and he said: 'It is obligatory,' meaning Paradise and Hellfire. He was asked about that and said: 'You are the witnesses of God on earth.'" It is also reported in some chains that he recited: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾.

﴿And the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾: it was said: its meaning is: concerning your deeds on the Day of Resurrection. It was said: that he will testify against you regarding the conveyance to you. It was said: "'alaykum" here means "for you" (lakum), that is, he will testify for you regarding faith.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face﴾ (the verse). Qatadah, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and others said: the qiblah here is Bayt al-Maqdis, and the meaning is: We did not make it, when We first commanded you to it, except as a trial, so that We might know who follows you among the Arabs, who were only attached to the Masjid of Makkah, or among the Jews, as al-Dahhak said, that "the rabbis said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Bayt al-Maqdis is the qiblah of the prophets. If you pray toward it, we will follow you.' So God commanded him to pray toward it as a test for them, but they did not believe."

Some of those who held that the qiblah is Bayt al-Maqdis said: the meaning is: We did not make the turning away from the qiblah which you used to face, and its change, [except as a trial]. The genitive construction was elided and the mudaf ilayhi (the word in the genitive) was put in its place. Ibn 'Abbas said: the qiblah in the verse is the Ka'bah, and "you used to" (kunta) means "you" (anta), like His words: ﴿You were the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ (Al 'Imran: 110), meaning "you are." That is: We did not make it, and We turned you toward it, except as a trial.

It was reported concerning that: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was turned toward the Ka'bah, the Jews and hypocrites objected to it a great deal, and some of the believers doubted, until the verse was revealed." Ibn Jurayj said: it reached me that some people who had embraced Islam returned from Islam.

The meaning of His words "that We might know" is: that My Messenger and the believers with him might know. The attribution is made with the "we" of majesty, since they are His party and His elite. This is common in the speech of the Arabs, as you say: "'Umar conquered Iraq and collected its tribute," though it was his army and followers who did so. This is the aspect of metaphor when God's knowledge is described with a verb of future tense, because His knowledge is eternal and has never ceased.

Another aspect: God has known from eternity who will follow the Messenger, and that knowledge continued until they came into existence, and continued at the time of following and turning back, and will continue after that. God is described in all of that as knowing.

So by His words "that We might know" He intends the mention of His knowledge at the time they encounter obedience and disobedience, for reward and punishment are tied to that time. The meaning of "that We might know" is not that He begins knowing, but that He knows that existing.

Ibn Fawrak related that the meaning of "that We might know" is "that We might reward," so the meaning is: that We might know in a state in which they deserved reward. He tied knowledge to their actions so that the proof would be established and the certainty of what He knew would occur, not as a contest with them over it.

Ibn Fawrak also related: that the meaning of "that We might know" is "that We might distinguish," and al-Tabari mentioned it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Tabari also related that the meaning of "that We might know" is "that We might see." All of this is close in meaning, and the rule is the negation of the beginning of knowledge after it did not exist.

Al-Zuhri recited "liya'lama" (with the passive form), in the manner of the unnamed agent.

The phrase ﴿turns back on his heels﴾ is an expression for the apostate who returns from what he was in of faith, or of attachment, or other things. Returning on the heels is the worst condition of one who walks back from his direction, so the apostate in religion is likened to it. The apparent comparison is to one who retreats backward, which is the gait of an animal fleeing from something that has come close to it. It may also be that this comparison is to one who turns his back and walks on his tracks, for when he turns he indeed turns on his heels.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And indeed it was a great thing﴾ (the verse). The pronoun in "kânat" refers either to the qiblah, Bayt al-Maqdis, or to the change toward the Ka'bah, according to the disagreement about the qiblah which we mentioned. Ibn Zayd said: it refers to the prayer that was prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis. God, the Most High, testified in this verse for those who followed by guidance. "Kabîrah" here means: difficult and hard, weighing heavily upon the hearts. "In" here is the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and therefore the lâm (of emphasis) attaches to it, to remove the confusion between it and the negating "in" (nâfiyah). When the heaviness of "in" is apparent, the lâm may or may not attach to it. Al-Farra' said: "in" means "má" (what), and the lâm is in the position of "illâ" (except).

When the qiblah was changed, the Jews said: "O Muhammad, if the first was true, then you are now upon falsehood, and if this one is true, then you were in error in the first." Some of the believers' souls were troubled, and they feared for those who had died before the change, regarding their former prayers. So the verse was revealed: ﴿God would never make your faith to be lost.﴾

He addressed those present, and the intended meaning includes those who were present and those who had died, because the one present takes precedence, as the Arabs say: "Did we not kill you at such-and-such a place?" The one addressed was not killed, but the address prevailed because of his presence. Al-Dahhak read "liyudî'a" with a fatha on the dad and a shadda on the ya'.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and others said: faith (îmân) here means the prayer. He named the prayer "faith" because it proceeded from faith and affirmation, at the time of Bayt al-Maqdis and at the time of the change.

Since faith is the pivot upon which deeds revolve, and it was constant in the state of facing here, He mentioned it here, because it is the foundation to which one returns in prayer and other things, to what is commanded and forbidden.

Also, so that the prayers of the hypocrites toward Bayt al-Maqdis would not be included under the name of prayer, He mentioned the meaning which is the essence of the matter.

Furthermore, it was named faith because it is among the branches of faith.

Ra'fah (compassion) is the highest rank of mercy. Some read "la-ra'uf" in the pattern fa'ul, and from it is the saying of al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah:

"And the worst of the seekers, and do not be him, is the slayer of his paternal uncle, the compassionate and merciful one."

The Arabs say: ra'ūf, ra'ūf (with a longer vowel), ra'if on the pattern of ḥadhir, and ra'f. Abū Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited "la-ra'ūf" without a hamza, and in the same way he eased (sahhala) every hamza in the Book of God, whether it was quiescent (sākina) or vowelled (muta-ḥarrika).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 142–143 (part 1 of 2):

The Most High said:
﴿The foolish among the people will say: "What has turned them away from their qiblah (direction of prayer) which they used to face?" Say: "To God belong the East and the West; He guides whom He wills to a straight path."﴾ ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over the people, and the Messenger may be a witness over you. We did not make the qiblah which you used to face except that We might know who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels. It was indeed a great thing, except for those whom God has guided. God would never make your faith (îmân) to be lost. Indeed God is Most Kind and Merciful to the people.﴾

God, exalted is He, informed in this verse that they would say, concerning the change of direction of the believers from Syria to the Ka'bah: "What has turned them away?" The "foolish" (al-sufahâ') are those who are light in their judgments and minds. Safah means lightness and flimsiness. A "safîh" garment is one that is not finely woven. From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

"They walk like spears swaying, whose tops are made light (tasaffahat) by the gusts of the spring winds."

That is, the winds made them light. He specified "from the people" because foolishness can occur in inanimate things and animals as well. The intended meaning of "the foolish" here is all who said "What has turned them away?" Different groups said it, and there is disagreement about who they were. Ibn 'Abbas said: the rabbis among them said it, because they came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "O Muhammad, what has turned you away from our qiblah? Return to it and we will believe in you." They intended to tempt him. Al-Suddi said: some of the Jews and hypocrites said it mockingly, because they said: "The man has longed for his homeland."

A group said: it was said by the Quraysh disbelievers, because they said: "What has turned him away from his qiblah? He only returned to us because he knows that we are upon the truth, and he will return to our whole religion." The meaning of "turned them away" (wallâhum) is "redirected them." The qiblah is a form (fi'lah) denoting the manner of facing something, like the qa'dah (manner of sitting) and the izrah (manner of wearing a waist-wrap).

The future tense is used in "will say" in place of the past, indicating the continuation of that and that they would persist in that saying. Ibn 'Abbas and others stated explicitly that the verse was revealed after their saying.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Say: To God belong the East and the West﴾ are an establishment of proof, meaning: to Him belongs the dominion of the easts and the wests and what is between them. ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾ is an indication of God's guidance of this community to the qiblah of Abraham. The "sirât" is the path. The scholars differed over whether the Prophet's (ﷺ) prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) was by a command of God in the Qur'an, or by a revelation that was not recited (wahy ghayr matlu, i.e., revelation not part of the recited Qur'an). Ibn Fawrak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The first thing abrogated (nusikha, naskh meaning abrogation) from the Qur'an was the qiblah." The majority said: rather, the command concerning the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis was by an unrecited revelation. Al-Rabi' said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) chose among the directions, and chose Bayt al-Maqdis in order to win over the People of the Book. Those who said it was by unrecited revelation said: this was so that God might test those among the Arabs who believed, because they were attached to the Ka'bah and averse to Bayt al-Maqdis and other places.

It was disputed how long he prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis. In al-Bukhari it is sixteen or seventeen months. It is reported from Anas ibn Malik nine or ten months, and reported from others thirteen months.

Makki related from Ibrahim ibn Ishaq that he said: "The first ordinance of prayer was that it was prescribed in Makkah as two rak'ahs at the beginning of the day and two rak'ahs at its end. Then came the Isra' (night journey) on the night of the seventeenth of Rabi' al-Akhir, a year before the Hijrah, and the five prayers were prescribed, and Jibril (peace be upon him) led them, and the first prayer was the Zuhr. The Prophet (ﷺ) faced Bayt al-Maqdis. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) migrated to Madinah in Rabi' al-Awwal, and he continued facing Bayt al-Maqdis until Rajab of the second year." It was said: until Jumada; it was said: until the middle of Sha'ban.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾: the kaf (the "thus") is connected to the meaning in His words ﴿He guides whom He wills﴾, meaning: just as We guided you to the qiblah of Abraham and his law, thus We made you a nation (ummah). "Ummatan" is the second object, and "wasatan" is an adjective. "Ummah" means generations of people. "Wasatan" means "just" ('udûlan). This was transmitted from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the wording of the exegetes agrees on it.

The wasat means the best and highest of a thing, as you say: "the middle of the people" (wasat al-qawm), "the middle pearl of the necklace" (wasitat al-qilâdah) meaning the most precious stone in it, and "the leader is the middle of the army." Like the Most High's saying: ﴿The best of them said﴾ (al-Qalam: 28). The wasat with a sukun on the sin (wasṭ) is an indeclinable adverb of place built on fatha. It has come declinable in some transmissions in the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"She brought a bridled horse whose forehead is like a saddle-cloth of safflower dyed, and its middle split open."

With a damma on the ta' (wasṭuhâ), the pronoun refers to the saddle-cloth (salâ'ah). It was also transmitted with a fatha on the ta' (wasaṭuhâ), and the pronoun then refers to the female (al-jâ'iyah). When you say "I dug the middle of the house" (wasṭ al-dâr) or "the middle of the house" (wasaṭ al-dâr), the meaning differs.

Some scholars said: the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) did not exceed in religion as the Jews did, nor did it slacken as the Christians did; rather it is moderate, so it is the highest and best of nations from this aspect.

The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The best of matters are their middles" means: their best.

Excellence and goodness in a thing may be either because it is the most precious of its kind, or because it lies between excess and deficiency; so it is best from this aspect. "Shuhada'" is the plural of shahid (witness).

The exegetes differed over what is meant by "the people" in this place. One group said: it is the entire human race. The nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) will testify on the Day of Resurrection for the prophets against their peoples, regarding conveyance of the message. That is because Noah's people will deny that he conveyed it, so the nation of Muhammad will say to him: "We bear witness for you," and they will testify. God will say to them: "How do you testify to what you did not witness?" They will say: "O our Lord, Your Messenger came to us and Your Book descended to us, so we testify to what You charged us with and informed us of." God, exalted is He, will say: "You have spoken the truth."

A sound hadith is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) to this meaning, and it is reported from him that "his nation will testify for every prophet whose people denied him." Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: you will testify for Muhammad (ﷺ) that he conveyed to the people in his time, among the Jews, Christians and Magians. Another group said: the meaning of the verse is: some of you will testify against others after death, as "the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said when a funeral passed by him and he praised it with good, and he said: 'It is obligatory (wajabat),' then another passed by him and he praised it with evil, and he said: 'It is obligatory,' meaning Paradise and Hellfire. He was asked about that and said: 'You are the witnesses of God on earth.'" It is also reported in some chains that he recited: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾.

﴿And the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾: it was said: its meaning is: concerning your deeds on the Day of Resurrection. It was said: that he will testify against you regarding the conveyance to you. It was said: "'alaykum" here means "for you" (lakum), that is, he will testify for you regarding faith.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you used to face﴾ (the verse). Qatadah, al-Suddi, 'Ata' and others said: the qiblah here is Bayt al-Maqdis, and the meaning is: We did not make it, when We first commanded you to it, except as a trial, so that We might know who follows you among the Arabs, who were only attached to the Masjid of Makkah, or among the Jews, as al-Dahhak said, that "the rabbis said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Bayt al-Maqdis is the qiblah of the prophets. If you pray toward it, we will follow you.' So God commanded him to pray toward it as a test for them, but they did not believe."

Some of those who held that the qiblah is Bayt al-Maqdis said: the meaning is: We did not make the turning away from the qiblah which you used to face, and its change, [except as a trial]. The genitive construction was elided and the mudaf ilayhi (the word in the genitive) was put in its place. Ibn 'Abbas said: the qiblah in the verse is the Ka'bah, and "you used to" (kunta) means "you" (anta), like His words: ﴿You were the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ (Al 'Imran: 110), meaning "you are." That is: We did not make it, and We turned you toward it, except as a trial.

It was reported concerning that: "When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was turned toward the Ka'bah, the Jews and hypocrites objected to it a great deal, and some of the believers doubted, until the verse was revealed." Ibn Jurayj said: it reached me that some people who had embraced Islam returned from Islam.

The meaning of His words "that We might know" is: that My Messenger and the believers with him might know. The attribution is made with the "we" of majesty, since they are His party and His elite. This is common in the speech of the Arabs, as you say: "'Umar conquered Iraq and collected its tribute," though it was his army and followers who did so. This is the aspect of metaphor when God's knowledge is described with a verb of future tense, because His knowledge is eternal and has never ceased.

Another aspect: God has known from eternity who will follow the Messenger, and that knowledge continued until they came into existence, and continued at the time of following and turning back, and will continue after that. God is described in all of that as knowing.

So by His words "that We might know" He intends the mention of His knowledge at the time they encounter obedience and disobedience, for reward and punishment are tied to that time. The meaning of "that We might know" is not that He begins knowing, but that He knows that existing.

Ibn Fawrak related that the meaning of "that We might know" is "that We might reward," so the meaning is: that We might know in a state in which they deserved reward. He tied knowledge to their actions so that the proof would be established and the certainty of what He knew would occur, not as a contest with them over it.

Ibn Fawrak also related: that the meaning of "that We might know" is "that We might distinguish," and al-Tabari mentioned it from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Tabari also related that the meaning of "that We might know" is "that We might see." All of this is close in meaning, and the rule is the negation of the beginning of knowledge after it did not exist.

Al-Zuhri recited "liya'lama" (with the passive form), in the manner of the unnamed agent.

The phrase ﴿turns back on his heels﴾ is an expression for the apostate who returns from what he was in of faith, or of attachment, or other things. Returning on the heels is the worst condition of one who walks back from his direction, so the apostate in religion is likened to it. The apparent comparison is to one who retreats backward, which is the gait of an animal fleeing from something that has come close to it. It may also be that this comparison is to one who turns his back and walks on his tracks, for when he turns he indeed turns on his heels.

The words of the Most High: ﴿And indeed it was a great thing﴾ (the verse). The pronoun in "kânat" refers either to the qiblah, Bayt al-Maqdis, or to the change toward the Ka'bah, according to the disagreement about the qiblah which we mentioned. Ibn Zayd said: it refers to the prayer that was prayed toward Bayt al-Maqdis. God, the Most High, testified in this verse for those who followed by guidance. "Kabîrah" here means: difficult and hard, weighing heavily upon the hearts. "In" here is the lightened form of the heavy (mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and therefore the lâm (of emphasis) attaches to it, to remove the confusion between it and the negating "in" (nâfiyah). When the heaviness of "in" is apparent, the lâm may or may not attach to it. Al-Farra' said: "in" means "má" (what), and the lâm is in the position of "illâ" (except).

When the qiblah was changed, the Jews said: "O Muhammad, if the first was true, then you are now upon falsehood, and if this one is true, then you were in error in the first." Some of the believers' souls were troubled, and they feared for those who had died before the change, regarding their former prayers. So the verse was revealed: ﴿God would never make your faith to be lost.﴾

He addressed those present, and the intended meaning includes those who were present and those who had died, because the one present takes precedence, as the Arabs say: "Did we not kill you at such-and-such a place?" The one addressed was not killed, but the address prevailed because of his presence. Al-Dahhak read "liyudî'a" with a fatha on the dad and a shadda on the ya'.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Qatadah, al-Suddi, al-Rabi' and others said: faith (îmân) here means the prayer. He named the prayer "faith" because it proceeded from faith and affirmation, at the time of Bayt al-Maqdis and at the time of the change.

Since faith is the pivot upon which deeds revolve, and it was constant in the state of facing here, He mentioned it here, because it is the foundation to which one returns in prayer and other things, to what is commanded and forbidden.

Also, so that the prayers of the hypocrites toward Bayt al-Maqdis would not be included under the name of prayer, He mentioned the meaning which is the essence of the matter.

Furthermore, it was named faith because it is among the branches of faith.

Ra'fah (compassion) is the highest rank of mercy. Some read "la-ra'uf" in the pattern fa'ul, and from it is the saying of al-Walid ibn 'Uqbah:

"And the worst of the seekers, and do not be him, is the slayer of his paternal uncle, the compassionate and merciful one."

The Arabs say: ra'ūf, ra'ūf (with a longer vowel), ra'if on the pattern of ḥadhir, and ra'f. Abū Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' recited "la-ra'ūf" without a hamza, and in the same way he eased (sahhala) every hamza in the Book of God, whether it was quiescent (sākina) or vowelled (muta-ḥarrika).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 144–145:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, words:

﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven. So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with. So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram. And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it. And indeed, those who were given the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what they do.﴾ ﴿And if you were to bring those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qiblah, nor are you a follower of their qiblah, nor are some of them followers of the qiblah of others. And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you, indeed you would then be of the wrongdoers.﴾

The purpose: the turning of the sight. The face is mentioned because it is more general and more noble, and it is the term used in seeking desires. You say: "I exerted my face in such-and-such," and "I did such-and-such for the face of so-and-so." Among this is the words of the poet:

"I returned with what I sought, and my face with its water..."

Also, the face turns with the turning of the sight. Qatadah, al-Suddi and others said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would turn his face in supplication to Allah the Exalted, asking that He turn it to the qiblah of Makkah." It was also said: "He would turn it so that he might be given permission in supplication."

The meaning of turning toward the heaven is that the heaven is a direction from which the learned are accustomed to receive mercy, such as rain, lights and revelation, so they direct their desire wherever blessings continuously come. "Tarduha" means: you love it and your eye is comforted by it.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved the Ka'bah and the change away from Bayt al-Maqdis for three reasons that have been related. Mujahid said: because of the Jews' saying: "Muhammad did not know his religion until he followed us." Ibn 'Abbas said: and so that he might hit the qiblah of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). al-Rabi' and al-Suddi said: and so that he might win over the Arabs through their love for the Ka'bah. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his ummah were directed only opposite the spout (mizab) of the Ka'bah. Ibn 'Abbas and others said: rather, he was directed to the whole House.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The mizab is the qiblah of Madinah and Syria, and there is the qiblah of the people of al-Andalus without doubt. And there is no disagreement that the Ka'bah is the qiblah from every horizon.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿So turn your face toward al-Masjid al-Haram﴾, the verse, is a command to change and an abrogation of the qiblah of Syria.

It was said: "That was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was in the noon prayer, after two rak'ahs of it, so he turned in the prayer." Abu al-Faraj mentioned that 'Abbad ibn Nahik was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in this prayer. It was also said: this verse was revealed outside of a prayer, and the first prayer toward the Ka'bah was the 'Asr. "Shatra" is in the accusative as an adverb of place, and it resembles the object because the verb falls upon it; its meaning is: toward and facing.

Ibn Ahmar said:

"It carries us toward a gathering, while it is bound, its tether having worn thin from its long journeys."

Another said:

"I say to Umm Zinba': set the chests of the camels facing toward the Banu Tamim."

Laqit said:

"And there has overshadowed you from the direction of your frontier a terror whose darkness covers you in pieces."

Another said:

"Is there no messenger to convey to 'Amr, and does the message not avail toward 'Amr?"

﴿And wherever you are, turn﴾ is a command to the ummah, abrogating. Dawud ibn Abi Hind said: in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud is "So turn your face toward the presence of al-Masjid al-Haram." Muhammad ibn Talhah said: in it is "So turn your faces toward it." Ibn Abi 'Ablah read: "So turn your faces toward it (tilqa'ahu)." And ﴿those who were given the Scripture﴾ are the Jews and Christians. al-Suddi said: the intended are the Jews; the first is more apparent. The meaning: the Jews and Christians know that the Ka'bah is the qiblah of Ibrahim, the leader of the nations, and that facing it is the truth obligatory upon all, following Muhammad (ﷺ) whom they find in their books. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "ta'malun" (you do) with a ta' in address, either intending the People of the Book or the ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ); on both readings it is an information that Allah the Exalted does not neglect the servants nor is unaware of them, and it contains a warning. The rest read with ya' from below.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And if you bring﴾, the verse: Allah the Exalted informed His Prophet when the Jews said to him: "Return to Bayt al-Maqdis and we will believe in you," a deception from them, that they do not follow his qiblah, meaning all of them, since some did follow, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and others; and that they do not adopt his religion. That is, do not incline to them.

The verse here means: the sign. The answer to "la'in" is like the answer to "law," and it is its opposite in that "law" requires the past and occurrence while "in" requires the future, because both are preceded by the sense of an oath, so the answer belongs to the oath, not that one of the two particles takes the place of the other. This is the statement of Sibawayh.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿nor are you a follower of their qiblah﴾, is a declarative form that implies a command, meaning: do not incline to anything of that.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿nor are some of them﴾, the verse: al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: the Jews do not follow the qiblah of the Christians, nor do the Christians follow the qiblah of the Jews; this is an information of their disagreement, their enmity, and their misguidance. Others said: the meaning of the verse: nor is any among them who has embraced Islam with you a follower of the qiblah of those who have not embraced it, nor is anyone who has not embraced it a follower of the qiblah of those who have embraced it. The first is more apparent regarding the parts.

The qiblah of the Christians is the rising of the sun (east), and the qiblah of the Jews is Bayt al-Maqdis.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And if you were to follow﴾, the verse, is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) while the intended is his ummah. Whatever comes of this type that gives the impression of a supposed wrong from the Prophet (ﷺ) is to be understood as intending his ummah, due to the Prophet's (ﷺ) infallibility; and we are certain that this does not occur from him, so what is intended is whoever it is possible for this to occur from, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed to magnify the matter.

"Ahwa'" is the plural of "hawa," and it is not pluralized as "ahwiyah," although they have said "nada" and "andiyah"; the poet said:

"On a night of Jumada, one with dews, in whose darkness the dog cannot see the tent-pegs."

The desire of the soul is mostly used for what has no good in it, and it may be used for good when restricted to it, as "'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the captives of Badr: so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) inclined to what Abu Bakr said." And "idha" is a particle whose meaning is: that what was mentioned is established.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿nor are you a follower of their qiblah﴾, is a declarative form that implies a command, meaning: do not incline to anything of that.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿nor are some of them﴾, the verse: al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is: the Jews do not follow the qiblah of the Christians, nor do the Christians follow the qiblah of the Jews; this is an information of their disagreement, their enmity, and their misguidance. Others said: the meaning of the verse: nor is any among them who has embraced Islam with you a follower of the qiblah of those who have not embraced it, nor is anyone who has not embraced it a follower of the qiblah of those who have embraced it. The first is more apparent regarding the parts.

The qiblah of the Christians is the rising of the sun (east), and the qiblah of the Jews is Bayt al-Maqdis.

His, the Exalted, words: ﴿And if you were to follow﴾, the verse, is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ) while the intended is his ummah. Whatever comes of this type that gives the impression of a supposed wrong from the Prophet (ﷺ) is to be understood as intending his ummah, due to the Prophet's (ﷺ) infallibility; and we are certain that this does not occur from him, so what is intended is whoever it is possible for this to occur from, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was addressed to magnify the matter.

"Ahwa'" is the plural of "hawa," and it is not pluralized as "ahwiyah," although they have said "nada" and "andiyah"; the poet said:

"On a night of Jumada, one with dews, in whose darkness the dog cannot see the tent-pegs."

The desire of the soul is mostly used for what has no good in it, and it may be used for good when restricted to it, as "'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said regarding the captives of Badr: so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) inclined to what Abu Bakr said." And "idha" is a particle whose meaning is: that what was mentioned is established.

[p-378] "Alladhina" (those who) is in the nominative case as the subject (*mubtada'*, the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and the predicate (*khabar*) is "yaʻrifunahu" (they recognize it). It is also permissible for it to be in the genitive case as a qualifier (*na't*, an adjectival modifier) of "al-zalimin" (the wrongdoers), and "yaʻrifunahu" would then be in the accusative case as a circumstantial clause (*hal*, a clause describing the state of the subject).

The sons are singled out rather than the selves, although the self is closer, because a person passes through a period of his life in which he does not know himself, but no time passes over him in which he does not know his son. What is meant here is recognizing the face and distinguishing it, not knowing the true reality of lineage. 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, may Allah be pleased with him, has a digressive statement at this point, whose place will come, God willing.

The pronoun in "yaʻrifunahu" refers to the truth concerning the qibla (direction of prayer) and the change, by the command of Allah, to the Ka'ba. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj, and al-Rabi'.

Qatada also said, as did Mujahid and others, that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning they recognize his truthfulness and prophethood.

[p-379] "Al-fariq" means the group. It is singled out because some of them accepted Islam and did not conceal. The reference of "al-haqq" (the truth) is to what was mentioned earlier concerning the disagreement over the pronoun in "yaʻrifunahu", so it encompasses the truth in general as an exaggeration in censuring them. "Wa hum yaʻlamun" (while they know) clearly indicates that their disbelief is willful obstinacy.

As for Allah's statement, ﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾, "al-haqq" is in the nominative case by an implied subject, the sense being "it is the truth", though it is also permissible for it to be the subject with an implied predicate following it.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, read "al-haqqa" in the accusative, so that "yaʻlamun" governs it, and its accusative is also permissible with the implied sense: "Adhere to the truth."

﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant is his community. "Imtara fi al-shay'" means he doubted in the matter, and from it comes "al-miraʼ" (dispute), since one who disputes doubts the saying of the other. Al-Tabari cited as evidence that "al-mumtarin" means doubters a verse of al-A'sha:

They pour forth, at a gallop, over the shanks of those who press (their mares), when the mirage surges.

But he was mistaken in this, because Abu 'Ubayda and others said that "al-mumtarun" in the verse are those who press horses with their legs to make them run, as though they were milking the running from them. So there is no sense of doubt in the verse, as al-Tabari said.

As for Allah's statement, ﴿And for each there is a direction (wijha) toward which it turns﴾: "al-wijha" is a form (*fi'la*) from "al-muwajaha" (facing), like "al-qibla". The pronoun "huwa" (it) refers to the singular word "kull" (each), and what is meant by it is the groups. The meaning: for each possessor of a religion there is a direction, which he turns himself toward. This was said by al-Rabi', 'Ata', and Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn 'Amir alone among the seven readers read: "huwa muwallaha" (he is its one who turns it). Some said the pronoun "huwa" refers to Allah Most High, and the meaning is: Allah turns them toward it. Another group said the meaning of the verse is that each has a religion and a law, which is the religion of Allah and the religion of Muhammad, and He turns them to it; whoever follows it follows it, and whoever abandons it abandons it. Qatada said: what is meant by the verse is that prayer toward Syria and then prayer toward the Ka'ba, each of them is a direction, and Allah turns them toward it.

Al-Tabari reported that some people read: "li-kullin wijhatun" with "kull" in construct with "wijha", and al-Tabari considered this a mistake, though it is a valid reading, meaning: "So race to the good deeds, for each direction, and do not oppose what you are commanded in this and that; rather, you are only obligated to obey in all of it." He placed "li-kullin wijhatun" before the command "fastabiqu" (so race), for the sake of emphasizing the direction, just as the object is placed first. Abu 'Amr al-Dani cited this reading from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.

The waw in "wijha" remained intact and did not change as in "ʻidda" and "zinna", because "jiha" is a noun of place (*zarf*), and those (words) are verbal nouns (*masadir*), so it remained intact for the sake of distinction. Also, it completes the form of the state, as in "al-jilsa" (the manner of sitting). Abu ʻAli said: some people went to the view that it is a verbal noun that deviated from analogy and so remained intact, and others to the view that it is a noun other than a verbal noun. Others than Abu ʻAli said: when you want the verbal noun you say "jihatan", and "al-jiha" may be used for the place (*zarf*).

Al-Tabari related from Mansur that he said: "We read it: 'And for each We have made a qibla they are pleased with.'" Then Allah Most High commanded His servants to race toward good deeds and to hasten to the path of salvation. Then He admonished them by mentioning the gathering (on the Day of Resurrection), an admonition that contains threat and warning.

[p-381] As for Allah's statement, ﴿Wherever you are, Allah will bring you all together﴾, it means the resurrection from the graves. Then Allah Most High was described with power over everything that is within His power, to match the attribute with what was mentioned of bringing them together.

As for Allah's statement, ﴿And from wherever you go out﴾, its meaning is: wherever you are, and wherever you turn, from the east and west of the earth. Then this verse was repeated as an emphasis from Allah Most High, because the matter of the change was very difficult in their souls, so He confirmed the command so that people would see the seriousness of it, and it would become easier for them and their souls would be at rest with it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 150–151:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it, so that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong. So do not fear them, but fear Me, and so that I may complete My favour upon you and that you may be guided.﴾ ﴿Just as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves, who recites Our verses to you, purifies you, and teaches you the Book and wisdom, and teaches you what you did not know.﴾

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So turn your faces toward it﴾ is the obligation, upon those who pray, of facing the qibla (the direction of prayer). The obligation on one who prays, as long as he can see the Ka'bah, is that he should hit it by facing it. If it is hidden from him, then his obligation is to make ijtihad (independent juristic effort) in aiming at it. If he performed ijtihad and then it became clear to him that he had erred, then according to many scholars there is nothing upon him. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held that he should repeat the prayer within its time, in order to secure the virtue of facing the qibla.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾, the verse. Nafi' alone read "li-allā" (lām with the hamza softened, "li-ʾallā" pronounced with easing of the hamza), while the rest read "li-allā" with the hamza. The meaning: I have made known to you the correct direction of your qibla, and the proof in this is "li-allā". His words "to the people" are general, covering the Jews, the Arabs and others. It was said: what is meant by "the people" is the Jews, and then He excepted the disbelievers of the Arabs. His words "from among them" refute this interpretation.

A group said: "illā alladhīna" is an exception of the disconnected kind (istithnā' munqati'), and this is together with the people being the Jews only. We have mentioned the weakness of this view. The meaning: "but those who did wrong", meaning the disbelievers of Quraysh, in their saying: "Muhammad has returned to our qibla and will return to our religion entirely." Included in this is everyone other than the Jews who spoke about the incident.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 2, verses 152–157:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you. Give thanks to Me and do not deny Me.﴾ ﴿O you who believe, seek help through patience and prayer. Indeed, God is with the patient.﴾ ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God that they are dead. Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive.﴾ ﴿We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and a loss of wealth, lives and fruits. So give good tidings to the patient,﴾ ﴿who, when a calamity strikes them, say: "Indeed we belong to God, and to Him we will return."﴾ ﴿Those are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord and mercy, and those are the rightly guided.﴾

(p. 384) Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The meaning of the verse is: remember Me with obedience, and I will remember you with reward and forgiveness. That is, remember Me in all your affairs, so that my fear moves you to obedience, and then I will remember you with reward.

Al-Rabi' and al-Suddi said: The meaning is: remember Me with supplication, glorification and the like. In a hadith: "God, the Exalted, says: 'Son of Adam, remember Me in ease, and I will remember you in hardship.'" In another hadith: "God, the Exalted, says: 'When My servant remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a better gathering than theirs.'" It is also narrated that when a disbeliever remembers God, God remembers him with the curse and with eternal abiding in the Fire. Likewise, sinners take a share of this meaning. It is also narrated that God, the Exalted, revealed to Musa, peace be upon him: "Say to the disobedient: Do not remember Me."

﴿Wa-shkuru li﴾ (give thanks to Me) and ﴿washkurūnī﴾ (give thanks to Me) have one meaning, but "li" with "shukr" is more common and more eloquent. Its meaning is: My blessings and favours. Likewise when you say "shakartuka" (I thanked you), the meaning is: I thanked your deed and mentioned it. The omitted word here is the noun that is governed (mudaf, the first term of an idafa construction), since the meaning of thanks includes mention of the favour and mention of the one who bestowed it together. What is omitted in this way is an abbreviation, because what remains indicates what has been omitted.

And ﴿takfurūn﴾ (deny) means: My blessings and favours. The nūn of the plural was dropped because of the jussive (jazm, the apocopated mood), and this is the nūn of the first person singular (the speaker). The yā' that follows it was dropped for lightness, because it is the end of a verse (ra's āya). Had it been a prohibition against disbelief, the opposite of faith, it would have been "wa-lā takfurū" without the nūn.

The "yā" is the particle of address, "ayy" is the one addressed, and "hā" is for alerting. "Ayy" is brought in when the word has "al-" (the definite article), because the particle of address already conveys a certain definiteness, so if "ayy" were not brought in, there would be two definitives together.

Some people said: "al-ṣabr" (patience) means fasting, and from this it was said that Ramadan is "the month of patience." The meaning of seeking help through patience and prayer has already been discussed. Its summary is that both restrain from sins.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, God is with the patient﴾, its meaning is: by His assistance and support. It is therefore an omission of a mudaf (governed noun), as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to Hassan ibn Thabit: "Satirize them, and the Holy Spirit is with you." And as he said: "Shoot, and I am with the sons of so-and-so," in the hadith.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of God﴾ (the verse). Its occasion of revelation was that people said about those who were killed at Badr and Uhud: "So-and-so has died, and so-and-so has died." God disliked that the rank of the martyrs be lowered to the rank of others, so this verse was revealed. Also, the believers found it hard to part from their brothers and relatives, so the verse came to console them, magnifying the rank of the martyrs and informing them of the reality of their state, so that they became those to be envied, not those to be grieved for. This is shown by the hadith of Umm Haritha in the biography (al-sīra).

The difference between the martyr and others is only in provision (rizq). God, the Exalted, favoured them by the continuation (p. 386) of the state they had in this world, so He provides for them. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning this: "The souls of the martyrs are in the crops of green birds that feed on the fruit of Paradise." It is also narrated that they are in lamps of gold, and among many other such reports. There is no doubt that these are states for groups, or for all of them at different times. The majority of scholars hold that they are in Paradise, and this is supported by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Umm Haritha: "He is in the highest Firdaws." Mujahid said: they are outside Paradise and are hung from its trees.

"Amwātun" (dead) is in the nominative by an implied subject (idmār al-mubtada', i.e., the supposition of an implied subject), and the estimate is: "They are dead." The verb "qālū" (say) cannot govern it, because there is no connection between it and the verb, just as it is correct in your saying: "I said speech and an argument."

His saying: ﴿But you do not perceive﴾, that is, before We make you perceive.

His saying, Exalted is He: "And We will surely test you" (the verse). He, Exalted is He, commanded seeking help through patience and prayer, and informed that He is with the patient. Then the verse that follows gave, concerning the virtue of the martyrs, what strengthens patience regarding them and lightens the calamity. Then after that came these matters, which cannot be met except with patience, things that make known that this world is a house of trial and tribulations. That is, do not deny the parting from brothers and relatives. Then He promised the patient a reward.

Ata' and the majority said that the address in this verse is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said that the address is to Quraysh and what befell them, so it is a sign for the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p. 387) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

The first view is more apparent.

﴿And We will surely test you with something﴾ means: We will certainly examine you. The waw was vowelled because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). It was also said that the verb is built (mabnī) and, together with the heavy nūn, it is like "fifteen" (a compound).

"Al-khawf" (fear) means fear of enemies in wars. "Al-jū'" (hunger) means drought and famine. As for the need for food, its name is "al-gharth," though later writers used "al-jū'" loosely for it. "Naqṣ al-amwāl" (loss of wealth) is by calamities and disasters. "Al-anfus" (lives) is by death and killing. "Al-thamarāt" (fruits) is by blights and the removal of blessing.

So the intended meaning is: with something of this, and something of this. He was content with the first (mention) for brevity, and for that reason it is singular. Al-Dahhak read "bi-ashyā'" in the plural, and the meaning is close, one part to another.

Some scholars said: What is intended in this verse is the burdens and hardships of jihad. Fear is of the enemy, hunger is through it and through journeys to it, loss of wealth is through the expenses in it, lives are through killing, and fruits are through the enemy's striking them or through neglect of them because of jihad.

Then He, Exalted is He, described the patient whom He gave good tidings to, with His saying: ﴿Those who, when a calamity strikes them﴾ (the verse). He made these words a refuge for those afflicted by calamities and a protection for those being tested, because of the blessed meanings they gather: the Oneness of God, acknowledgment of His servanthood, and resurrection from the graves.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: These words were not given to any prophet before our Prophet. Had Ya'qub known them, he would not have said: "Alas for Yusuf!" It is narrated that the lamp of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out one night, and he said: (p. 388) "Indeed we belong to God, and to Him we will return." It was said: "Is it a calamity, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes. Everything that harms the believer is a calamity."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾ (the verse). "Ni'am" (blessings) from God upon the patient who say "Indeed we belong to God." The blessings of God upon His servant are His pardon, His mercy, His blessing, and His honouring him in this world and the Hereafter. He repeated "mercy" when the wording differed, for emphasis, and it is among the greatest parts of prayer from Him, Exalted is He.

He testified for them to being rightly guided. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), when he recited this verse, said: "What excellent two (things) and what excellent addition!" By the "two" he meant blessings and mercy, and by the "addition" he meant guidance.

Then the verse that follows gave, concerning the virtue of the martyrs, what strengthens patience regarding them and lightens the calamity. Then after that came these matters, which cannot be met except with patience, things that make known that this world is a house of trial and tribulations. That is, do not deny the parting from brothers and relatives. Then He promised the patient a reward.

Ata' and the majority said that the address in this verse is to the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was also said that the address is to Quraysh and what befell them, so it is a sign for the Prophet (ﷺ).

(p. 387) The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

The first view is more apparent.

﴿And We will surely test you with something﴾ means: We will certainly examine you. The waw was vowelled because of the meeting of two unvocalised letters (iltiqā' al-sākinayn). It was also said that the verb is built (mabnī) and, together with the heavy nūn, it is like "fifteen" (a compound).

"Al-khawf" (fear) means fear of enemies in wars. "Al-jū'" (hunger) means drought and famine. As for the need for food, its name is "al-gharth," though later writers used "al-jū'" loosely for it. "Naqṣ al-amwāl" (loss of wealth) is by calamities and disasters. "Al-anfus" (lives) is by death and killing. "Al-thamarāt" (fruits) is by blights and the removal of blessing.

So the intended meaning is: with something of this, and something of this. He was content with the first (mention) for brevity, and for that reason it is singular. Al-Dahhak read "bi-ashyā'" in the plural, and the meaning is close, one part to another.

Some scholars said: What is intended in this verse is the burdens and hardships of jihad. Fear is of the enemy, hunger is through it and through journeys to it, loss of wealth is through the expenses in it, lives are through killing, and fruits are through the enemy's striking them or through neglect of them because of jihad.

Then He, Exalted is He, described the patient whom He gave good tidings to, with His saying: ﴿Those who, when a calamity strikes them﴾ (the verse). He made these words a refuge for those afflicted by calamities and a protection for those being tested, because of the blessed meanings they gather: the Oneness of God, acknowledgment of His servanthood, and resurrection from the graves.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: These words were not given to any prophet before our Prophet. Had Ya'qub known them, he would not have said: "Alas for Yusuf!" It is narrated that the lamp of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out one night, and he said: (p. 388) "Indeed we belong to God, and to Him we will return." It was said: "Is it a calamity, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes. Everything that harms the believer is a calamity."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those are the ones upon whom are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾ (the verse). "Ni'am" (blessings) from God upon the patient who say "Indeed we belong to God." The blessings of God upon His servant are His pardon, His mercy, His blessing, and His honouring him in this world and the Hereafter. He repeated "mercy" when the wording differed, for emphasis, and it is among the greatest parts of prayer from Him, Exalted is He.

He testified for them to being rightly guided. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), when he recited this verse, said: "What excellent two (things) and what excellent addition!" By the "two" he meant blessings and mercy, and by the "addition" he meant guidance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 158–160:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols (sha'a'ir) of Allah. So whoever performs Hajj to the House or performs 'Umrah, there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them. And whoever volunteers good, indeed Allah is Appreciative and Knowing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance after We have made it clear to the people in the Scripture — those are the ones Allah curses, and the cursers curse them.﴾ ﴿Except those who repent, amend, and make clear. Those I will accept repentance from, and I am the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

﴿as-Safa and al-Marwah﴾: two small hills in Makkah.

"As-Safa" is the plural of ṣafāh, and it has been said it is a singular noun whose plural is ṣafan and aṣfā', meaning a great rock. The rajaz poet said:

...................................... the places where birds perch on the rocks

It has been said: among the characteristics of the Safa are whiteness and hardness.

"Al-Marwah": the singular of marw, which means small stones that have some softness in them.

From this is the saying of the companion whose sheep was about to die: "So you slaughtered it with a marwah." From this is also the saying of al-Amin: "Bring me out to my brother; if he kills me, then a marwah has broken a marwah, and a ṣamṣāmah has cut a ṣamṣāmah." It has also been said regarding al-marw that it means hard rocks. The poet said:

And he turned the land with a supple hoof, and when it met al-marw it crushed it.

The correct view is that al-marw is hard rock, both its hard and its soft kind, the kind that splits and whose edge is thin. In this sense it is said "al-marw is more common," though it may also be said of hard rock. Consider the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

Until it is as if I am a marwah for misfortunes, struck every day at Safa al-Mushaqqar.

The hill of Safa in Makkah is hard, while the hill of Marwah is soft and brittle, and by this they were named.

Some said: Safa was mentioned because Adam stood upon it, and Hawwa' (Eve) stood upon Marwah, so it was feminized for this reason.

Al-Sha'bi said: On Safa there was an idol called Isaf, and on Marwah there was an idol called Na'ila. So the masculine and feminine usage became consistent, and the masculine was placed first.

And ﴿from the symbols of Allah﴾ means: from His landmarks and places of worship. It is the plural of shu'ayrah or sha'arah. Mujahid said: this refers to speech, i.e., of what Allah has made you aware of by His favor, derived from tasha'artu, meaning "I sensed"; and sha'urat is derived from ash-shi'ar, which is the garment that is next to the body, and ash-shi'ar is derived from ash-shi'r (poetry).

From this same root comes the word poet (sha'ir).

"Hajj" means: to intend and to recur. From it is the saying of the poet:

And I witness from 'Awf many frequent gatherings, going to the insult of az-Zibriqan al-Mu'za'faran.

From it is also the saying of another:

He goes to the house (of the she-camel?) ...................................

"I'tamara" means to visit and to recur; it is derived from 'ammartu al-mawdi' (I cultivated the place).

And "al-junah" (blame): sin, and deviation from truth and obedience. From the same word comes al-janah (wing), because it is on one side; and from it the tent is called junah because of its swaying and because it resembles something with wings. From it is also: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61].

"Yatawwafa" originally is yatatawwafa; the ta' was made quiescent and assimilated into the ta' (ṭā'). Abu as-Sammal recited: "an yuṭāfa," whose origin is yaṭtūfu; the waw moved and the letter before it was open, so it became an alif, giving yaṭtāfu. The ta' was assimilated into the ta' after being made quiescent, according to the view of those who permit assimilating the second into the first, as in "muddakir." Those who do not permit this said: the ta' was changed into ṭā', then the ṭā' was assimilated into ṭā'. There is consideration in this, because the original letter was assimilated into the added one, and that is weak.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, and Shahr ibn Hawshab that they recited: "allā yattawwafa," and likewise in the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "allā yattawwafa." It has also been said: "allā yaṭūfa," with a damma on the ṭā' and sukun on the waw.

His saying, ﴿Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾, is a statement that implies the command to go around them as was established. His saying ﴿there is no blame﴾ does not intend to permit circumambulation for whoever wishes, because that after a command would not be consistent. Rather, its purpose is to remove what had settled in the hearts of some Arabs, that going back and forth between them was sinful, and to inform them that what had settled in their hearts was not correct.

There is disagreement about the manner of this. It is narrated that the jinn used to know and go back and forth between them in the Jahiliyyah, and a group from Tihamah did not go back and forth between them in the Jahiliyyah for this reason; when Islam came, they felt uneasy about going back and forth. It is also narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that this concerned the Ansar, because they used to pronounce the talbiyah for Manat, which was at al-Mushallal near Qudayd, and they revered it, so they did not go back and forth between Isaf and Na'ila out of reverence for that. When Islam came, they felt uneasy, and this verse was revealed. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that the Arabs who used to go around there believed that running between them was in reverence of Isaf and Na'ila, and the runner would touch Isaf, and when he reached Marwah he would touch Na'ila, and so on until he completed his rounds. When Islam came, they disliked running there, since it was because of the two idols. The scholars differed concerning the sa'y (running) between as-Safa and al-Marwah.

The view of Malik and al-Shafi'i is that it is an obligatory pillar of Hajj; whoever abandons it or forgets it cannot make it up except by returning to perform it. The view of al-Thawri and the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) is that a sacrifice (dam) suffices for one who abandons it, and if he returns, that is good; it is, according to them, recommended (nadb).

It is narrated from Abu Hanifah: if he abandons more than three rounds, then a dam is due; if he abandons three or fewer, then for each round he must feed one poor person. 'Ata' said: there is nothing due upon one who abandons it, neither a dam nor anything else. 'Ata' argued with what is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "allā yattawwafa bihimā," but this is a reading that contradicts the codices of Islam. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, rejected it in her saying to 'Urwah when he said to her: "Have you considered the saying of Allah: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾; so we see nothing upon anyone for not going back and forth between them?" She said: "O nephew, no! If that were the meaning, it would have said: 'there is no blame upon him for not going back and forth between them.'"

Also, what is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud returns to the meaning of "an yaṭūfa," and "lā" is an extra particle used for connection in speech, like His saying: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], and like the saying of the poet:

The Messenger of Allah did not approve of their action, nor the two good ones, Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

That is: and 'Umar.

And like the saying of another:

And I do not blame the fair ones for not mocking ...................................

The view of Malik and his companions regarding 'Umrah is that it is a sunnah, except Ibn Habib, who said it is obligatory.

Some of the seven reciters and others recited: "wa man yaṭṭawwa'" with the yā' at the beginning, in the imperfect/conditional form, and the answer (jawab) is in His saying "fa-inna."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim recited: "tatawwa'a," in its past tense form, so "man" in this reading means "the one who." The fa' entered into His saying "fa-inna" for the ambiguity that is in "man." This is related by Makki. Abu 'Ali said: "tatawwa'a" may be in a jussive position with "man" being conditional, and it may be that "man" means "the one who" and the verb is a relative clause with no place in the grammatical structure, and the fa' signals that the second thing is required because the first is required.

Whoever holds that running is obligatory says: the meaning of "tatawwa'a" is that he increased in righteousness beyond the obligatory, making it general in deeds. Some said: its meaning is: whoever volunteers with Hajj or 'Umrah after the obligatory Hajj.

Whoever does not hold running to be obligatory says: the meaning is whoever volunteers with running between them. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "fa-man taṭawwa'a bikhayr" (whoever volunteers good).

The meaning of "Shakir": He gives reward and recompense. "'Alim": knows the intentions and deeds; no deed of one who does righteousness, or any other, is lost in His sight.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal...﴾, the verse: those intended are the rabbis of the Jews and the monks of the Christians who concealed the matter of Muhammad ﷺ. al-Tabari said: It has been narrated that certain individuals among them were asked by some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ about what was in their books concerning his matter, and they concealed it, so this was revealed.

The verse further encompasses every person who conceals a knowledge of the religion of Allah that needs to be spread, and this is explained in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire." This applies when he is not afraid and there is no harm upon him in spreading it. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, had this verse in mind when he said: "Were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would not have narrated to you a single hadith." Abu Hurayrah abandoned this when he feared, and said: "I memorized from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ two vessels: as for one of them, I have spread it; as for the other, if I spread it, this throat would be cut." This verse was also in the mind of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, in his saying: "I will narrate to you a hadith which, were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would not have narrated it to you." Whoever narrated in the words of 'Uthman: "Were it not that it is in the Book of Allah," the meaning is other than this.

﴿The clear proofs and the guidance﴾ refers to the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and then it generalizes to everything good that one conceals.

Talhah ibn Musarrif recited: "min ba'di ma bayyanahu" in the singular.

﴿In the Scripture﴾ is intended to mean the Torah and the Gospel, according to the context of the cause of revelation, and that it concerns the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and then the Qur'an enters with the generalization of the verse. The meaning of cursing has already been mentioned. Scholars differed about the cursers. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: the angels and the believers; this is apparent, clear, and in accordance with the requirement of the speech. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: they are insects and beasts, who are afflicted with drought because of the sins of the evil scholars who concealed, so they curse them. They were described with the masculine plural (waw and nun), like those who have reason, because the act of those who have reason was attributed to them, as He said: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "the cursers" are all creatures except the two weighty ones, jinn and humans, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the disbeliever is struck in his grave and cries out, everyone hears it except the two weighty ones, and every hearer curses him." Ibn Mas'ud said: what is meant by it is what the Prophet ﷺ said: "When two people curse each other, if they deserve the curse it falls upon them, and if not, it returns upon the Jews." These three opinions are not required by the wording, and they are not established except by a chain of narration that removes all excuse.

Then Allah, Exalted, made an exception for those who repent, and the meaning of repentance has already been mentioned.

"Amended" means in their deeds and statements, "and made clear." Whoever interprets the verse in its general sense says: the meaning is that they made their repentance clear by manifest action and striving in it. Whoever interprets it as concerning those who concealed the matter of Muhammad ﷺ says: the meaning is they made clear the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, so the verse applies to those among the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam. The meaning of Allah's repentance upon His servant has already been mentioned: that it is His returning him from disobedience to obedience.
