Ibn Mas'ud said: what is meant by it is what the Prophet ﷺ said: "When two people curse each other, if they deserve the curse it falls upon them, and if not, it returns upon the Jews." These three opinions are not required by the wording, and they are not established except by a chain of narration that removes all excuse.

Then Allah, Exalted, made an exception for those who repent, and the meaning of repentance has already been mentioned.

"Amended" means in their deeds and statements, "and made clear." Whoever interprets the verse in its general sense says: the meaning is that they made their repentance clear by manifest action and striving in it. Whoever interprets it as concerning those who concealed the matter of Muhammad ﷺ says: the meaning is they made clear the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, so the verse applies to those among the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam. The meaning of Allah's repentance upon His servant has already been mentioned: that it is His returning him from disobedience to obedience.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 158–160:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols (sha'a'ir) of Allah. So whoever performs Hajj to the House or performs 'Umrah, there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them. And whoever volunteers good, indeed Allah is Appreciative and Knowing.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down of clear proofs and guidance after We have made it clear to the people in the Scripture — those are the ones Allah curses, and the cursers curse them.﴾ ﴿Except those who repent, amend, and make clear. Those I will accept repentance from, and I am the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

﴿as-Safa and al-Marwah﴾: two small hills in Makkah.

"As-Safa" is the plural of ṣafāh, and it has been said it is a singular noun whose plural is ṣafan and aṣfā', meaning a great rock. The rajaz poet said:

...................................... the places where birds perch on the rocks

It has been said: among the characteristics of the Safa are whiteness and hardness.

"Al-Marwah": the singular of marw, which means small stones that have some softness in them.

From this is the saying of the companion whose sheep was about to die: "So you slaughtered it with a marwah." From this is also the saying of al-Amin: "Bring me out to my brother; if he kills me, then a marwah has broken a marwah, and a ṣamṣāmah has cut a ṣamṣāmah." It has also been said regarding al-marw that it means hard rocks. The poet said:

And he turned the land with a supple hoof, and when it met al-marw it crushed it.

The correct view is that al-marw is hard rock, both its hard and its soft kind, the kind that splits and whose edge is thin. In this sense it is said "al-marw is more common," though it may also be said of hard rock. Consider the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

Until it is as if I am a marwah for misfortunes, struck every day at Safa al-Mushaqqar.

The hill of Safa in Makkah is hard, while the hill of Marwah is soft and brittle, and by this they were named.

Some said: Safa was mentioned because Adam stood upon it, and Hawwa' (Eve) stood upon Marwah, so it was feminized for this reason.

Al-Sha'bi said: On Safa there was an idol called Isaf, and on Marwah there was an idol called Na'ila. So the masculine and feminine usage became consistent, and the masculine was placed first.

And ﴿from the symbols of Allah﴾ means: from His landmarks and places of worship. It is the plural of shu'ayrah or sha'arah. Mujahid said: this refers to speech, i.e., of what Allah has made you aware of by His favor, derived from tasha'artu, meaning "I sensed"; and sha'urat is derived from ash-shi'ar, which is the garment that is next to the body, and ash-shi'ar is derived from ash-shi'r (poetry).

From this same root comes the word poet (sha'ir).

"Hajj" means: to intend and to recur. From it is the saying of the poet:

And I witness from 'Awf many frequent gatherings, going to the insult of az-Zibriqan al-Mu'za'faran.

From it is also the saying of another:

He goes to the house (of the she-camel?) ...................................

"I'tamara" means to visit and to recur; it is derived from 'ammartu al-mawdi' (I cultivated the place).

And "al-junah" (blame): sin, and deviation from truth and obedience. From the same word comes al-janah (wing), because it is on one side; and from it the tent is called junah because of its swaying and because it resembles something with wings. From it is also: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61].

"Yatawwafa" originally is yatatawwafa; the ta' was made quiescent and assimilated into the ta' (ṭā'). Abu as-Sammal recited: "an yuṭāfa," whose origin is yaṭtūfu; the waw moved and the letter before it was open, so it became an alif, giving yaṭtāfu. The ta' was assimilated into the ta' after being made quiescent, according to the view of those who permit assimilating the second into the first, as in "muddakir." Those who do not permit this said: the ta' was changed into ṭā', then the ṭā' was assimilated into ṭā'. There is consideration in this, because the original letter was assimilated into the added one, and that is weak.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, and Shahr ibn Hawshab that they recited: "allā yattawwafa," and likewise in the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "allā yattawwafa." It has also been said: "allā yaṭūfa," with a damma on the ṭā' and sukun on the waw.

His saying, ﴿Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah﴾, is a statement that implies the command to go around them as was established. His saying ﴿there is no blame﴾ does not intend to permit circumambulation for whoever wishes, because that after a command would not be consistent. Rather, its purpose is to remove what had settled in the hearts of some Arabs, that going back and forth between them was sinful, and to inform them that what had settled in their hearts was not correct.

There is disagreement about the manner of this. It is narrated that the jinn used to know and go back and forth between them in the Jahiliyyah, and a group from Tihamah did not go back and forth between them in the Jahiliyyah for this reason; when Islam came, they felt uneasy about going back and forth. It is also narrated from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that this concerned the Ansar, because they used to pronounce the talbiyah for Manat, which was at al-Mushallal near Qudayd, and they revered it, so they did not go back and forth between Isaf and Na'ila out of reverence for that. When Islam came, they felt uneasy, and this verse was revealed. It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that the Arabs who used to go around there believed that running between them was in reverence of Isaf and Na'ila, and the runner would touch Isaf, and when he reached Marwah he would touch Na'ila, and so on until he completed his rounds. When Islam came, they disliked running there, since it was because of the two idols. The scholars differed concerning the sa'y (running) between as-Safa and al-Marwah.

The view of Malik and al-Shafi'i is that it is an obligatory pillar of Hajj; whoever abandons it or forgets it cannot make it up except by returning to perform it. The view of al-Thawri and the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) is that a sacrifice (dam) suffices for one who abandons it, and if he returns, that is good; it is, according to them, recommended (nadb).

It is narrated from Abu Hanifah: if he abandons more than three rounds, then a dam is due; if he abandons three or fewer, then for each round he must feed one poor person. 'Ata' said: there is nothing due upon one who abandons it, neither a dam nor anything else. 'Ata' argued with what is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "allā yattawwafa bihimā," but this is a reading that contradicts the codices of Islam. 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, rejected it in her saying to 'Urwah when he said to her: "Have you considered the saying of Allah: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going back and forth between them﴾; so we see nothing upon anyone for not going back and forth between them?" She said: "O nephew, no! If that were the meaning, it would have said: 'there is no blame upon him for not going back and forth between them.'"

Also, what is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud returns to the meaning of "an yaṭūfa," and "lā" is an extra particle used for connection in speech, like His saying: ﴿What prevented you from not prostrating?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], and like the saying of the poet:

The Messenger of Allah did not approve of their action, nor the two good ones, Abu Bakr and 'Umar.

That is: and 'Umar.

And like the saying of another:

And I do not blame the fair ones for not mocking ...................................

The view of Malik and his companions regarding 'Umrah is that it is a sunnah, except Ibn Habib, who said it is obligatory.

Some of the seven reciters and others recited: "wa man yaṭṭawwa'" with the yā' at the beginning, in the imperfect/conditional form, and the answer (jawab) is in His saying "fa-inna."

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim recited: "tatawwa'a," in its past tense form, so "man" in this reading means "the one who." The fa' entered into His saying "fa-inna" for the ambiguity that is in "man." This is related by Makki. Abu 'Ali said: "tatawwa'a" may be in a jussive position with "man" being conditional, and it may be that "man" means "the one who" and the verb is a relative clause with no place in the grammatical structure, and the fa' signals that the second thing is required because the first is required.

Whoever holds that running is obligatory says: the meaning of "tatawwa'a" is that he increased in righteousness beyond the obligatory, making it general in deeds. Some said: its meaning is: whoever volunteers with Hajj or 'Umrah after the obligatory Hajj.

Whoever does not hold running to be obligatory says: the meaning is whoever volunteers with running between them. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "fa-man taṭawwa'a bikhayr" (whoever volunteers good).

The meaning of "Shakir": He gives reward and recompense. "'Alim": knows the intentions and deeds; no deed of one who does righteousness, or any other, is lost in His sight.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal...﴾, the verse: those intended are the rabbis of the Jews and the monks of the Christians who concealed the matter of Muhammad ﷺ. al-Tabari said: It has been narrated that certain individuals among them were asked by some of the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ about what was in their books concerning his matter, and they concealed it, so this was revealed.

The verse further encompasses every person who conceals a knowledge of the religion of Allah that needs to be spread, and this is explained in the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever is asked about knowledge and conceals it will be bridled on the Day of Resurrection with a bridle of fire." This applies when he is not afraid and there is no harm upon him in spreading it. Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, had this verse in mind when he said: "Were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would not have narrated to you a single hadith." Abu Hurayrah abandoned this when he feared, and said: "I memorized from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ two vessels: as for one of them, I have spread it; as for the other, if I spread it, this throat would be cut." This verse was also in the mind of 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, in his saying: "I will narrate to you a hadith which, were it not for a verse in the Book of Allah, I would not have narrated it to you." Whoever narrated in the words of 'Uthman: "Were it not that it is in the Book of Allah," the meaning is other than this.

﴿The clear proofs and the guidance﴾ refers to the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and then it generalizes to everything good that one conceals.

Talhah ibn Musarrif recited: "min ba'di ma bayyanahu" in the singular.

﴿In the Scripture﴾ is intended to mean the Torah and the Gospel, according to the context of the cause of revelation, and that it concerns the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, and then the Qur'an enters with the generalization of the verse. The meaning of cursing has already been mentioned. Scholars differed about the cursers. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: the angels and the believers; this is apparent, clear, and in accordance with the requirement of the speech. Mujahid and 'Ikrimah said: they are insects and beasts, who are afflicted with drought because of the sins of the evil scholars who concealed, so they curse them. They were described with the masculine plural (waw and nun), like those who have reason, because the act of those who have reason was attributed to them, as He said: ﴿I saw them prostrating to me﴾ [Yusuf: 4]. al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "the cursers" are all creatures except the two weighty ones, jinn and humans, because the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the disbeliever is struck in his grave and cries out, everyone hears it except the two weighty ones, and every hearer curses him." Ibn Mas'ud said: what is meant by it is what the Prophet ﷺ said: "When two people curse each other, if they deserve the curse it falls upon them, and if not, it returns upon the Jews." These three opinions are not required by the wording, and they are not established except by a chain of narration that removes all excuse.

Then Allah, Exalted, made an exception for those who repent, and the meaning of repentance has already been mentioned.

"Amended" means in their deeds and statements, "and made clear." Whoever interprets the verse in its general sense says: the meaning is that they made their repentance clear by manifest action and striving in it. Whoever interprets it as concerning those who concealed the matter of Muhammad ﷺ says: the meaning is they made clear the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, so the verse applies to those among the Jews and Christians who embraced Islam. The meaning of Allah's repentance upon His servant has already been mentioned: that it is His returning him from disobedience to obedience.

(p-٣٩٦) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved and died while they were disbelievers, upon them is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of mankind, all together.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein; their punishment will not be lightened, nor will they be reprieved.﴾ ﴿And your God is One God; there is no god but He, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.﴾ ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, and the ship which runs in the sea with what benefits mankind, and what Allah sends down from the sky of water, giving life thereby to the earth after its death, and dispersing therein every kind of moving creature, and the turning of the winds and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth, are signs for a people who use their reason.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved﴾ (the verse), is muhkam (clear and unabrogated) concerning those who died upon their disbelief. There is a difference of opinion regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿and mankind, all together﴾, since they (the disbelievers) do not curse themselves. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: the intended meaning of "mankind" is only the believers. Abu al-'Aliyah said: its meaning concerns the Hereafter, because the disbelievers curse themselves on the Day of Resurrection. A group said: its meaning is that the disbelievers say in this world, "May Allah curse the disbelievers," and so they curse themselves without realizing it.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read: "wal-malā'ikatu wal-nāsu ajma'ūna" (with the nominative case), on the assumption of: "Allah curses them."

The curse in this verse implies punishment, and therefore He said: ﴿abiding therein﴾. The pronoun refers back to the curse, and it was said that it refers to the Fire, even though it has not been mentioned, because it is established in meaning. Then He informed (p-٣٩٧) of the removal of every aspect of leniency from them, because if the punishment is neither lightened nor deferred, then it is the ultimate end.

"Yunzarūn" means they will not be given respite from the punishment. It may also be from "naẓar" (looking), like His saying: ﴿nor will He look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran 3:77). The first meaning is more apparent, because looking with the eye is transitive with ilā (to), except in rare poetic usage.

His saying: ﴿And your God is One God; there is no god but He﴾ (the verse) is an announcement of divine oneness (wahdāniyyah). The word "wāḥid" (one), as an attribute of Allah the Exalted, means the negation of any like, equal, or rival. Abu al-Ma'ali said: it means the negation of division and partitioning. 'Ata' said: When this verse was revealed in Medina, the disbelievers of Quraysh in Mecca said: "What is the proof of this? What is its sign and its indication?" Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: They said, "If this is so, O Muhammad, bring us a sign from Him that will be a mark of truthfulness," until they said, "Make al-Safa into gold for us." It was said to them: "That will be yours, but if you disbelieve after that, you will be punished." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ became concerned and said: "Leave me, I will give them a day after a day." Thereupon there was revealed His saying: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ (the verse).

The meaning of ﴿in the creation of the heavens﴾ is: in their origination and bringing into being. It was said that the meaning is that in His creation, i.e., the form of the heavens and the earth. "Ikhtilāf al-layl wal-nahār" (the alternation of night and day) means that this one succeeds that one, and that one succeeds this one; they are thus a succession (khilfah), as He said:

﴿And it is He who made the night and the day as a succession﴾ (Surah al-Furqan 25:62).

And as Zuhayr said:

Among them the wild cows and the female deer walk in succession, and their fawns rise up from every resting place.

(p-٣٩٨) And another said:

And for her at al-Matirun, when the ant has eaten what it gathered, there is succession, until when she has grown, she settles at the churches of Jilliq.

The alternation in this verse may also be understood as the alternation of attributes. "Al-layl" is the plural of "laylah" (night), and its plural is "layālī," with a yā' added to it, as in "karāhiyah" and "farāhiyah."

"Al-nahār" (day) is pluralized as "nuhur" and "anhirah," and it runs from the break of dawn until the setting of the sun. The saying of the Prophet ﷺ to 'Adi ibn Hatim supports this: "It is only the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night." This is the requirement of jurisprudence concerning oaths and similar matters. However, according to the apparent linguistic meaning, and its derivation from expansion, it begins from the time of dawn-brightening (isfār) when the time of day widens, as he said:

I held my hand over it and widened its opening; the one standing behind it sees what lies beyond.

Al-Zajjaj said in the book al-Anwā': The beginning of the day is the rising of the sun. He said: al-Nadr ibn Shumayl claimed that the beginning of the day is the start of the sunrise, and what comes before that is not counted as day.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The saying of the Prophet ﷺ is the ruling.

"Al-fulk" means ships. Its singular and plural share the same form, and those movements are not the same actual forms; rather, it is as if he formed the plural with a different pattern. This is shown by the medial vowel in the dual, as in their saying "falakān," and by "al-fulk" in the singular being masculine. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿in the laden ship﴾ (Surah Ya-Sin 36:41).

﴿What benefits mankind﴾ (Surah al-Ra'd 13:17) refers to trade and all the other needs for which one sails the sea, whether for raiding or pilgrimage. The blessing of the ship is when one benefits from it, and therefore the mention of benefit is singled out, since it may also carry one to harm.

﴿And what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾ means the rains by which the world is revived, plants and provisions are brought forth.

"Wa-baththa" means: He scattered and spread out. "Dābbah" (creature) includes all living animals. Some people have excluded birds from the category of dābbah. Al-A'sha said:

... the stepping of sandgrouse in the valley of al-Batha at every watering place.

And 'Alqamah ibn 'Abdah said:

... its thunderbolts for their birds, a stepping.

﴿And the turning of the winds﴾ means sending them as barren, or as bringers of destruction, or as ones that bring forth clouds, or as blasts of cold, or as sources of victory, or as destruction; and among them is sending them as southern and northern winds, and other kinds. "Al-riyāḥ" is the plural of "rīḥ" (wind). In the Qur'an, it appears in plural form when associated with mercy, and in singular form when associated with punishment, except in Surah Yunus in His saying: ﴿and they sailed with them in a good wind﴾ (Surah Yunus 10:22). This is the most common usage in speech.

(p-٤٠٠) In a hadith: "Whenever the wind blew, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would say: 'O Allah, make it winds (riyāḥan) and do not make it a wind (rīḥan).'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Because the wind of punishment is strong and its parts are tightly joined, as if it were one body, whereas the wind of mercy is gentle and broken up into parts; therefore it is called "riyāḥ," which means "scattered." It is also singular with the ships, because the wind that drives ships is a single continuous wind; then it is described as good, and thus its commonality with the wind of punishment is removed. It is a word from the "wāw" roots: one says "rīḥ" and "arwāḥ," and one does not say "aryāḥ." The form "riyāḥ" arose because of the kasrah (vowel) and the need for harmony with the yā'.

'Imarah ibn 'Aqil ibn Bilal committed a grammatical error in this word, using "aryāḥ" in his poetry. Abu Hatim said to him: "Aryāḥ is not permissible." He said: "Do you not hear their saying 'riyāḥ'?" Abu Hatim said: "This is contrary to that." He said: "You are right," and he retracted.

As for the seven readers (al-Qurrā' al-Sab'ah), they differed. Nafi' read "al-riyāḥu" (plural) in twelve places here, and in al-A'raf: ﴿He sends the winds﴾ (Surah al-A'raf 7:57); in Ibrahim: "the winds have blown violently upon him" (Surah Ibrahim 14:18); in al-Hijr: ﴿the winds as fertilizers﴾ (Surah al-Hijr 15:22); in al-Kahf: ﴿which the winds scatter﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:45); in al-Furqan: ﴿He sends the winds﴾ (Surah al-Furqan 25:48); in al-Naml: ﴿or who sends the winds﴾ (Surah al-Naml 27:63); in al-Rum in two places; in Fatir; in al-Jathiyah; and in 'Asaq: "the winds are still" (Surah al-Shura 42:33). Abu 'Amr, 'Asim, and Ibn 'Amir read in two of these places in the singular: in Ibrahim, and in Ha Mim 'Asaq. They read the rest as Nafi' did. Ibn Kathir read the plural in five places: here, in al-Hijr, in al-Kahf, in the first instance in al-Rum, and in al-Jathiyah: ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾; and the rest of the Qur'an in the singular. Hamzah read the plural in two places: in al-Furqan, and the first instance in al-Rum; and he read the rest of the Qur'an in the singular. al-Kisa'i read as Hamzah did, and added to it in al-Hijr: ﴿the winds as fertilizers﴾ (Surah al-Hijr 15:22).

They did not differ on the singular form of whatever does not contain the definite article "al-."

"Al-sahāb" (clouds) is the plural of "saḥābah" (a cloud). It is so named because it drags (yansahib) along, just as they said "ḥabā" (he crawled) because he crawls (yaḥbū); this was said by Abu 'Ali al-Farisi. "Taskhīr" (subjugation) of it means: sending it from one place to another.

These, then, are signs that the Creator exists, and the rational proof establishes that the Creator of the world can only be one, because two or more could differ.

Its interpretation: "And if you could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment, you would magnify what has befallen them", then he begins the information with His saying: ﴿that all power belongs to Allah﴾.

Another interpretation: "And if you could see those who did wrong when they see the punishment, saying: 'Indeed, all power belongs to Allah,' you would magnify their state."

and I have met my guests with a frowning face.

The linguistic meaning of "sabab" (means, cause) is the binding rope that connects, and it is said of anything one holds to that is a link between two things. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "al-asbāb" here means the kinship ties. Mujāhid said: they are the covenants. It is said: [p. 405] the affections. It is said: the dwellings that they had in this world. Ibn Zayd and al-Suddī said: they are the deeds, since the deeds of the believers are like the cause of their bliss, so their deeds are cut off from the wrongdoers.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who followed said﴾ (the verse), the meaning is: the followers who were disowned said: "If only we could be returned to this world until we do righteous deeds and disown them." "Al-karra" is the return to a state that had existed before. From this is the saying of Jarīr:

They inclined upon Fazāra with a turning
like the return of the mannīḥ, and they wandered, then a place for rest.

Here "al-manīḥ" is one of the blank arrows of the gambling game (maysir), for when it comes out of the ribāba (the bag), it is returned immediately, because there is no share in it and no ruling concerning it.

The "kāf" in His saying "kamā" (as) is in the position of an accusative, as a qualifier, either for a verbal noun or for a circumstantial clause, its implied form being: "disowning as". The "kāf" in His saying ﴿Thus Allah shows them﴾ is said to be in the position of a nominative, as the predicate of an inceptive, its implied form being: "the matter is thus." It is also said that it is a pure comparative "kāf", and the reference of "dhālika" (thus) is to their state at the time of their wishing for a return.

The seeing in the verse is seeing with the eye, and it is possible that it is seeing with the heart.

As for "aʿmālahum" (their deeds): al-Rabīʿ and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is the corrupt deeds which they committed, for which the Fire became due to them. Ibn Masʿūd and al-Suddī said: the meaning is the righteous deeds which they abandoned, so Paradise escaped them. Hadiths have been related in support of this view. These deeds are attributed to them from the standpoint that they were commanded to do them, while the attribution of the corrupt ones is from the standpoint that they did them.

[p. 406] "Ḥasarāt" (regrets) is a circumstantial clause if the seeing is visual, and an object if the seeing is of the heart. "Al-ḥasra" is the highest degree of remorse and grief over what has been lost. It is derived from a thing that is exhausted, whose strength has ended, like a camel or an eyesight. It is also said that it is from "ḥasr", meaning to uncover. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The Euphrates will uncover a mountain of gold."

﴿وَإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ اتَّبِعُوا ما أنْزَلَ اللهُ قالُوا بَلْ نَتَّبِعُ ما ألْفَيْنا عَلَيْهِ آباءَنا أوَلَوْ كانَ آباؤُهم لا يَعْقِلُونَ شَيْئًا ولا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers did not understand anything, nor were they guided?﴾

﴿وَمَثَلُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي يَنْعِقُ بِما لا يَسْمَعُ إلا دُعاءً ونِداءً صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهم لا يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve is that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and an cry. Deaf, dumb, blind, they do not understand.﴾

The address is general. "Mā" means "alladhī" (that which), and "ḥalālan" is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) from the pronoun returning to "mā." Makkī said it is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted object, its estimate being "shayʾan ḥalālan" (a lawful thing). This is remote, and likewise the purpose of the speech does not allow "ḥalālan" to be a direct object of "kulū" (eat). Reflect.

"Ṭayyiban" is a naʿt, and it is permissible for "ṭayyiban" to be a ḥāl from the pronoun in "kulū," its estimate being "mustaṭībīn" (seeking what is good). The ṭayyib (good) according to Mālik is the ḥalāl (lawful), so here it is an emphasis through variation of wording. According to al-Shāfiʿī, it is the mustaladhdh (pleasant), and for this reason he prohibits eating animals that are filthy and everything that is khabīth (foul).

"Khuṭuwāt" is the plural of khuṭwa, which is the distance between the two feet in walking. The meaning is a prohibition against following Satan and adopting his paths and ways. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "His khuṭuwāt are his deeds." Another said: (p-٤٠٧) "his traces." Mujāhid said: "his sins." Abū Mijlaz said: "They are vows and acts of disobedience." al-Ḥasan said: "It was revealed concerning what they instituted of the baḥīra (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released) and the sāʾiba (a freed camel) and the like." al-Naqqāsh said: "It was revealed concerning Thaqīf, Khuzāʿa, and the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb."

Ibn ʿĀmir and al-Kisāʾī read "khuṭuwātin" with a ḍamma on the khāʾ and the ṭāʾ. This was also narrated from ʿĀṣim and Ibn Kathīr with a variant. The rest read with sukūn on the ṭāʾ. Either they intended the ḍamma on the khāʾ and ṭāʾ and lightened it, since that is the pattern in the plural of fiʿla, as in ghurfa and ghurufāt; or they left it in the plural with the sukūn it has in the singular. Abū al-Samāl read "khaṭawātin" with a fatḥa on the khāʾ and ṭāʾ. It was narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, and Salām: "khuṭu'ātin" with a ḍamma on the khāʾ and ṭāʾ and a hamza on the wāw. Those who adopted this reading held that it is the plural of khaṭaʾa from khaṭaʾ (error), not from khaṭw (stepping).

Everything other than the sunan (established practices) and the sharāʾiʿ (laws) of blameworthy innovations and acts of disobedience is "khuṭuwāt al-shayṭān."

"ʿAduww" applies to the singular, dual, and plural.

God's words, "He only commands you," the verse: "innamā" is suited to restriction (ḥaṣr), and it may come without restricting, rather for emphasis, as when you say, "Innamā al-shujāʿu ʿAntara" (the brave one is only ʿAntara). It is as though you are attempting restriction or giving that impression. The meaning of "innamā" is known from the context in which it occurs, so in this verse it is restrictive. Satan's command is either through his words in the time of the soothsayers, where it is conceivable, or through his whispering; when he is obeyed, he carries out his command.

"Al-sūʾ" is a verbal noun from sāʾa yasūʾu, and it means acts of disobedience and what its consequence is bad. As for "al-faḥshāʾ," al-Suddī said: it is fornication. It was said: everything that reaches one of the ḥudūd (prescribed punishments), because it is then most flagrantly foul. It was said: what is grossly mentioned. The root of fuḥsh is the ugliness of appearance, as Imru al-Qays said:

"A neck like the neck of a gazelle, not unsightly when it is adorned, nor left bare."

Then the word was used for what is considered ugly in meaning. It is the Sharīʿa that makes things good and bad, so everything the Sharīʿa forbids is from the faḥshāʾ.

As for "mā lā taʿlamūn" (what you do not know), al-Ṭabarī said: it means what they forbade of the baḥīra and sāʾiba and the like, and made into law.

God's words, "And when it is said to them," mean the disbelievers of the Arabs. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it was revealed concerning the Jews. al-Ṭabarī said: the pronoun in "lahum" returns to "al-nās" in His words, "O mankind, eat." It was also said: it returns to "min" in His words, "And among mankind are those who take other than God as equals" (2:165).

"Ittabiʿū" means by action and acceptance. "Mā anzala Allāh" is the Qur'an and the Sharīʿa. "Alfaynā" means "wajadnā" (we found). The poet said:

"I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering God except a little."

The alif in His words "Awa-law" is an interrogative, and the wāw conjoins one sentence to another, because the utmost corruption in their adherence is that they say, "We follow our fathers even if they did not understand." So they affirmed this adherence of theirs, since this is the condition of their fathers.

The strength of the wording of this verse indicates the nullification of taqlīd (blind imitation), and the community has agreed on its nullification in matters of belief.

God's words, "And the likeness of those who disbelieve," the verse: the intent is to liken the preacher of the disbelievers and their caller, and the disbelievers who are admonished, to the shepherd who shouts to sheep or camels, so they hear nothing of his call and do not comprehend what he says. This is how Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, al-Suddī, and Sībawayh explained it. He mentioned part of this sentence and part of that, and what was mentioned indicates what was omitted. This is the utmost in brevity.

"Al-naʿīq" is the driving of sheep and calling to them. al-Akhṭal said:

"Shout to your sheep, O Jarīr, for your self has only deluded you into misguidance in the wilderness."

Some said: this comparison with the shepherd of sheep occurred because they are among the most stupid of animals, so they make their shepherd foolish. There is a proverb: "More foolish than a shepherd of eighty sheep."

Durayd said to Mālik ibn ʿAwf on the day of Hawāzin, "A shepherd of sheep, by God!" The poet said:

"I have become a mockery for the shepherd of sheep, who mocks me. What troubles you about me, O shepherd of sheep?"

So the meaning of the verse is that these disbelievers, the call passes over their ears without notice; they hear it but do not understand it, since they do not benefit from its understanding.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning in the verse is: the likeness of those who disbelieve in their following of their gods and their worship of them is like the likeness of one who shouts to what does not hear anything from him except an echo that does not benefit, meaning the echo that returns from the mountains.

al-Ṭabarī's interpretation of the verse is another meaning, which is that the intent is: the likeness of the disbelievers in their worship of their gods is like the likeness of one who shouts to something far from him, so it does not hear him because of the distance. The caller gets nothing from that except the call, which tires him and wearies him. In these two interpretations, the disbelievers are likened to the caller, and the idols to the one who is called to, and they are likened in deafness, dumbness, and blindness to one who has no sense, because they did not benefit from their senses, nor did they employ them in perceiving what they should. From this is the poet's saying:

"... deaf to what displeases him, hearing [only what pleases him]."

Since their lack of these senses is established, He decreed that they do not understand, because reason, as Abū al-Maʿālī and others said, is necessary knowledge that these senses provide, since in acquiring it the senses are indispensable. Reflect.

Either they intended the ḍamma on the khāʾ and ṭāʾ and lightened it, since that is the pattern in the plural of fiʿla, as in ghurfa and ghurufāt; or they left it in the plural with the sukūn it has in the singular. Abū al-Samāl read "khaṭawātin" with a fatḥa on the khāʾ and ṭāʾ. It was narrated from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Qatāda, al-Aʿmash, and Salām: "khuṭu'ātin" with a ḍamma on the khāʾ and ṭāʾ and a hamza on the wāw. Those who adopted this reading held that it is the plural of khaṭaʾa from khaṭaʾ (error), not from khaṭw (stepping).

Everything other than the sunan (established practices) and the sharāʾiʿ (laws) of blameworthy innovations and acts of disobedience is "khuṭuwāt al-shayṭān."

"ʿAduww" applies to the singular, dual, and plural.

God's words, "He only commands you," the verse: "innamā" is suited to restriction (ḥaṣr), and it may come without restricting, rather for emphasis, as when you say, "Innamā al-shujāʿu ʿAntara" (the brave one is only ʿAntara). It is as though you are attempting restriction or giving that impression. The meaning of "innamā" is known from the context in which it occurs, so in this verse it is restrictive. Satan's command is either through his words in the time of the soothsayers, where it is conceivable, or through his whispering; when he is obeyed, he carries out his command.

"Al-sūʾ" is a verbal noun from sāʾa yasūʾu, and it means acts of disobedience and what its consequence is bad. As for "al-faḥshāʾ," al-Suddī said: it is fornication. It was said: everything that reaches one of the ḥudūd (prescribed punishments), because it is then most flagrantly foul. It was said: what is grossly mentioned. The root of fuḥsh is the ugliness of appearance, as Imru al-Qays said:

"A neck like the neck of a gazelle, not unsightly when it is adorned, nor left bare."

Then the word was used for what is considered ugly in meaning. It is the Sharīʿa that makes things good and bad, so everything the Sharīʿa forbids is from the faḥshāʾ.

As for "mā lā taʿlamūn" (what you do not know), al-Ṭabarī said: it means what they forbade of the baḥīra and sāʾiba and the like, and made into law.

God's words, "And when it is said to them," mean the disbelievers of the Arabs. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it was revealed concerning the Jews. al-Ṭabarī said: the pronoun in "lahum" returns to "al-nās" in His words, "O mankind, eat." It was also said: it returns to "min" in His words, "And among mankind are those who take other than God as equals" (2:165).

"Ittabiʿū" means by action and acceptance. "Mā anzala Allāh" is the Qur'an and the Sharīʿa. "Alfaynā" means "wajadnā" (we found). The poet said:

"I found him not seeking to make amends, nor remembering God except a little."

The alif in His words "Awa-law" is an interrogative, and the wāw conjoins one sentence to another, because the utmost corruption in their adherence is that they say, "We follow our fathers even if they did not understand." So they affirmed this adherence of theirs, since this is the condition of their fathers.

The strength of the wording of this verse indicates the nullification of taqlīd (blind imitation), and the community has agreed on its nullification in matters of belief.

God's words, "And the likeness of those who disbelieve," the verse: the intent is to liken the preacher of the disbelievers and their caller, and the disbelievers who are admonished, to the shepherd who shouts to sheep or camels, so they hear nothing of his call and do not comprehend what he says. This is how Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, al-Suddī, and Sībawayh explained it. He mentioned part of this sentence and part of that, and what was mentioned indicates what was omitted. This is the utmost in brevity.

"Al-naʿīq" is the driving of sheep and calling to them. al-Akhṭal said:

"Shout to your sheep, O Jarīr, for your self has only deluded you into misguidance in the wilderness."

Some said: this comparison with the shepherd of sheep occurred because they are among the most stupid of animals, so they make their shepherd foolish. There is a proverb: "More foolish than a shepherd of eighty sheep."

Durayd said to Mālik ibn ʿAwf on the day of Hawāzin, "A shepherd of sheep, by God!" The poet said:

"I have become a mockery for the shepherd of sheep, who mocks me. What troubles you about me, O shepherd of sheep?"

So the meaning of the verse is that these disbelievers, the call passes over their ears without notice; they hear it but do not understand it, since they do not benefit from its understanding.

Ibn Zayd said: the meaning in the verse is: the likeness of those who disbelieve in their following of their gods and their worship of them is like the likeness of one who shouts to what does not hear anything from him except an echo that does not benefit, meaning the echo that returns from the mountains.

al-Ṭabarī's interpretation of the verse is another meaning, which is that the intent is: the likeness of the disbelievers in their worship of their gods is like the likeness of one who shouts to something far from him, so it does not hear him because of the distance. The caller gets nothing from that except the call, which tires him and wearies him. In these two interpretations, the disbelievers are likened to the caller, and the idols to the one who is called to, and they are likened in deafness, dumbness, and blindness to one who has no sense, because they did not benefit from their senses, nor did they employ them in perceiving what they should. From this is the poet's saying:

"... deaf to what displeases him, hearing [only what pleases him]."

Since their lack of these senses is established, He decreed that they do not understand, because reason, as Abū al-Maʿālī and others said, is necessary knowledge that these senses provide, since in acquiring it the senses are indispensable. Reflect.

﴿يا أيُّها الناسُ كُلُوا مِمّا في الأرْضِ حَلالا طَيِّبًا ولا تَتَّبِعُوا خُطُواتِ الشَيْطانِ إنَّهُ لَكم عَدُوٌّ مُبِينٌ﴾ ﴿O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good, and do not follow the steps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

﴿إنَّما يَأْمُرُكم بِالسُوءِ والفَحْشاءِ وأنْ تَقُولُوا عَلى اللهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality, and to say about God that which you do not know.﴾

﴿وَإذا قِيلَ لَهُمُ اتَّبِعُوا ما أنْزَلَ اللهُ قالُوا بَلْ نَتَّبِعُ ما ألْفَيْنا عَلَيْهِ آباءَنا أوَلَوْ كانَ آباؤُهم لا يَعْقِلُونَ شَيْئًا ولا يَهْتَدُونَ﴾ ﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what God has sent down," they say, "Rather, we will follow what we found our fathers upon." Even though their fathers did not understand anything, nor were they guided?﴾

﴿وَمَثَلُ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا كَمَثَلِ الَّذِي يَنْعِقُ بِما لا يَسْمَعُ إلا دُعاءً ونِداءً صُمٌّ بُكْمٌ عُمْيٌ فَهم لا يَعْقِلُونَ﴾ ﴿The likeness of those who disbelieve is that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing but a call and an cry. Deaf, dumb, blind, they do not understand.﴾

The address is general. "Mā" means "alladhī" (that which), and "ḥalālan" is a ḥāl (circumstantial qualifier) from the pronoun returning to "mā." Makkī said it is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted object, its estimate being "shayʾan ḥalālan" (a lawful thing). This is remote, and likewise the purpose of the speech does not allow "ḥalālan" to be a direct object of "kulū" (eat). Reflect.

"Ṭayyiban" is a naʿt, and it is permissible for "ṭayyiban" to be a ḥāl from the pronoun in "kulū," its estimate being "mustaṭībīn" (seeking what is good). The ṭayyib (good) according to Mālik is the ḥalāl (lawful), so here it is an emphasis through variation of wording. According to al-Shāfiʿī, it is the mustaladhdh (pleasant), and for this reason he prohibits eating animals that are filthy and everything that is khabīth (foul).

"Khuṭuwāt" is the plural of khuṭwa, which is the distance between the two feet in walking. The meaning is a prohibition against following Satan and adopting his paths and ways. Ibn ʿAbbās said: "His khuṭuwāt are his deeds." Another said: (p-٤٠٧) "his traces." Mujāhid said: "his sins." Abū Mijlaz said: "They are vows and acts of disobedience." al-Ḥasan said: "It was revealed concerning what they instituted of the baḥīra (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released) and the sāʾiba (a freed camel) and the like." al-Naqqāsh said: "It was revealed concerning Thaqīf, Khuzāʿa, and the Banū al-Ḥārith ibn Kaʿb."

His saying, exalted is He:

﴿O you who believe, eat of the good things We have provided for you, and give thanks to God, if it is Him you worship.﴾ ﴿He has forbidden you only carrion, blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which other than God has been invoked. But whoever is compelled, neither desiring nor transgressing, there is no sin upon him. Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what God has sent down of the Book and exchange it for a small price, those eat nothing into their bellies except the Fire. God will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and theirs is a painful punishment.﴾

Al-ṭayyib (the good, the wholesome) here comprises the lawful that is pleasing. The verse indicates, through the partitive "min" (some of), that the unlawful is not provision. He, exalted is He, urged gratitude, and the meaning applies in every circumstance. "In" (if) is a conditional particle, and the purpose of this condition is to affirm and stir the soul, as when you say: "Do such-and-such if you are a man."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He has forbidden you only﴾. "Innama" (only) here is restrictive. "Al-maytata" (carrion) is in the accusative, governed by "ḥarrama" (forbade). Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read "al-mayyitata" with the doubled letter. al-Ṭabarī and a group of philologists said: the form with and without doubling, "mayt" and "mayyit," are two dialects. Abu Ḥātim and others said: "mayt" and "mayyit" are both used of what has died, but of what has not yet died, "mayt" with the single letter is not said.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is the usage of the Arabs, and the poet's verse attests to it:

Not one who has died and found rest is a dead man;
rather, the dead man is the dead among the living.

"Istarāḥa" means he found rest (from rest, al-rāḥa); it was also said it is from "al-rā'iḥa" (scent). No one read with the lightened form in reference to what has not died, except what al-Bazzī related from Ibn Kathīr: "wa-mā huwa bi-mayyit" (Q. 14:17 / 19:... as transmitted), while the well-known reading from him is the doubled form. As for the poet's verse:

When a dead man (mayyit) of Tamīm dies,
and it pleases you that you live, bring provision (for your journey).

The most eloquent reading in invective is that he means one who is dead in actuality, though some people held that he meant one who is near death. The first is more well known. A group read "al-maytatu" with the nominative, taking "mā" as meaning "that which," with "inna" operating.

Abu 'Abd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī read "ḥarrama" in the passive voice, with what is mentioned as forbidden in the nominative. If "mā" is a restrictive particle (kāffa), then "al-maytatu" is the subject of the passive verb; if "mā" means "that which," then "al-maytatu" is the predicate.

The word "al-maytata" is general, but the meaning is restricted, because the fish and the locust never entered into this generality. "Al-maytata" is what has died without ritual slaughter (dhakāh) from among what has a flowing soul (nafs sā'ilah). Floating fish: Mālik and others permitted it, while the Iraqis forbade it. Regarding what dies of itself, without any cause from a locust, there is disagreement. Mālik and most of his companions forbade it; Ibn Nāfi' and Ibn 'Abd al-Ḥakam permitted it. Ibn Wahb said: if it is gathered in sacks, the gathering is its slaughter. Ibn al-Qāsim said: no, until something is done to it by which it dies, such as cutting off the heads, wings, or legs, or throwing it into water. Saḥnūn said: it should not be thrown into cold water. Ashhab said: if it dies from the cutting of a leg or wing, it is not eaten, because it is a state in which it might have lived and crawled away.

"Al-dam" (blood) is intended to mean what flows, because what mixes with the flesh is not forbidden by consensus. Regarding the blood of fish that separates from the fish there is disagreement; it is reported from al-Qābisī that it is pure, and it follows from its purity that it is not forbidden.

The mention of the flesh of swine is singled out to indicate the prohibition of its substance, whether slaughtered or not, and to include the fat and the cartilage and other such parts. The community has agreed on the prohibition of its fat.

Regarding the water-swine, Abu Mālik disliked answering about it, and said: "You say 'swine'." Most philologists held that the word khinzīr (swine) is quadriliteral. Ibn Sīdah related from some of them that it is derived from "khazr al-'ayn" (squinting of the eye), because it looks that way, so on this view the word is triliteral.

﴿and that over which other than God has been invoked﴾. Ibn 'Abbās and others said: what is intended is what was slaughtered for idols and images (anṣāb and awthān). "Uhilla" means it was cried out over; from it comes "istihlāl al-mawlūd" (the newborn's first cry). The custom of the Arabs was to cry out the name of the one intended by the sacrifice, and this became so prevalent in their usage that it was used to express the intention, which is the cause of the prohibition. Do you not see that 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may God be pleased with him, took account of the intention regarding the camels that Ghālib, Abu al-Farazdaq, slaughtered? He said: "They are of what was invoked over for other than God," so people left them. I have seen in the reports of al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan that he was asked about a wealthy woman who made a wedding feast for her idols and slaughtered a camel. al-Ḥasan said: "Its eating is not lawful, for it was slaughtered for an idol."

Regarding the slaughter of the Magians (majūs) there is disagreement, and Mālik did not permit it at all. The slaughter of the Christian and the Jew is permitted. There is disagreement regarding what was forbidden to them, such as the tendon and the fat, with permission and prohibition. Ibn Ḥabīb said: what was forbidden to them by the Book is not lawful for us from their slaughter, and what they forbade by their own reasoning is lawful for us. According to Mālik there is disliking regarding what the People of the Book invoked over the Messiah, or slaughtered for their church, and this does not reach the level of prohibition.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But whoever is compelled﴾, the verse. The nūn was given a ḍamma for the meeting of two consonants, following the ḍamma of the ṭā' according to the reading of the majority. Abu Ja'far and Abu al-Samāl read "fa-man iḍṭarra" with a kasra on the ṭā'; its origin is "iḍṭarara," and when it was assimilated the vowel of the rā' was transferred to the ṭā'. Ibn Muḥaysin read "fa-man iṭṭarra" with the assimilation of the ḍād into the ṭā', and so wherever it occurs in the Qur'an.

The meaning of "iḍṭurra" (compelled): one who is overcome by want and hunger. This is the correct view upon which the majority of scholars and jurists agree. It was also said: its meaning is that he is forced and overpowered to eat these prohibited things.

"Ghayra bāghin" (neither desiring) is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). The meaning, according to Qatādah, al-Rabī', Ibn Zayd, 'Ikrima and others, is: not intending corruption and transgression, by which he would find an alternative to these prohibited things and eat them anyway. These scholars permit eating from them in every journey along with necessity. Mujāhid, Ibn Jubayr and others said: the meaning is not rebelling against the Muslims and not being hostile towards them; this includes the highwayman, the one who rebels against the ruler, and the traveler who severs kinship or raids the Muslims and what resembles it; for others the concession applies. al-Suddī said: "ghayra bāghin" means not exceeding the limit of keeping the soul alive and preserving his strength, so that his eating is not for pleasure. "Wa-lā 'ādin" means not taking provision beyond need.

Mālik, may God have mercy on him, said: the compelled person eats his fill. In the Muwaṭṭa' (the collection of hadith by Mālik, which is held by many scholars) it is said that he may take provision if he fears necessity in the desert or wasteland ahead of him.

"ʿĀdin" means "ʿā'id" (one who turns back), and so it is from the inverted form (maqlūb), like "shākī al-silāḥ" (armed), whose origin is "shā'ik," and like "hārin," whose origin is "hā'ir," and "lā'iṭ" similarly.

"Bāghin" originally was "bāghī"; the kasra on the yā' was heavy, so it became sukūn, and since the tanwīn is also sākin, the yā' was dropped, and the kasra indicates it.

God removed the sin when He made the carrion lawful for the compelled, because prohibition in reality is connected to the act of eating, not to the substance of the forbidden thing; the prohibition is attributed to the substance only figuratively.

A group forbade taking provision from the carrion and said: once the strength of the eater is established, he becomes like one who was never afflicted by necessity before.

Among the scholars there are those who hold that the carrion of a human being and of swine does not have the concession of necessity, because no ritual slaughter is valid for them in any way; the concession applies only to what ritual slaughter is valid for in its kind.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal﴾, the verse. Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah, al-Rabī' and al-Suddī said: what is intended are the rabbis of the Jews, who concealed the matter of Muḥammad (ﷺ). "Al-Kitāb" (the Book) is the Torah and the Gospel. The pronoun in "bihi" refers to "al-Kitāb," and it is possible that it refers to "mā," which is part of the Book in which the matter of Muḥammad (ﷺ) is found, and in which the concealment occurred, not in the whole Book. It is also possible that it refers to the concealment itself.

"Al-thaman al-qalīl" (the small price) is the worldly life and its gains; it is described as "small" because it is transient and perishes. Although this verse was revealed concerning the rabbis, it encompasses those among the scholars of the Muslims who conceal the truth deliberately for the sake of a worldly benefit they obtain.

The bellies are mentioned in their eating that leads to the Fire, as an indication of the literal sense of eating, since it may be used figuratively, as in "Such-and-such ate my land" and the like. Mentioning the belly also serves as a rebuke of them, because they sold their Hereafter for their share of food, which has no value, and as a reproach of their baseness in obeying their bellies. al-Rabī' and others said: their food was called "fire" because it leads them to the Fire. It was also said: the meaning of the verse is that God punishes them for their concealment by eating fire in Hell in actuality.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿God will not speak to them﴾. It was said: this is an expression of His anger toward them and the removal of His approval of them, since in other places in the Qur'an there is what appears to indicate that God speaks to the disbelievers, such as His saying: "Begone therein, and do not speak to Me" (Q. 23:108) and similar. So this verse is like your saying: "So-and-so is not spoken to by the sultan, and he does not turn to him," and you are only expressing the lowering of his station before him. al-Ṭabarī and others said: the meaning is: He will not speak to them with what they love. Not one who has died and found rest is a dead man;

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 175–177:

The Exalted's saying:

﴿Those are the ones who have bought error in exchange for guidance, and punishment in exchange for forgiveness. How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ ﴿That is because Allah sent down the Book with truth; and indeed, those who differ concerning the Book are in far-reaching dissension.﴾ ﴿Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east and the west; but righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah, the Last Day, the angels, the Book, and the prophets, and gives wealth, despite love for it, to relatives, orphans, the needy, the traveler, those who ask, and for freeing captives; and [who] establishes prayer and gives zakah; and those who fulfill their promise when they promise; and the patient in poverty and hardship and during battle. Those are the ones who have been true, and those are the righteous.﴾

When they abandoned guidance, turned away from it, clung to error and earned it, while guidance was possible for them and made easy, that was like a sale and purchase, and this meaning has already been fully discussed. And since the punishment follows the error they bought, and forgiveness follows the guidance they discarded, both were included within the figurative use of buying and selling.

As for His saying, ﴿So how patient they are for the Fire!﴾, the majority of the exegetes said: "mā" is an exclamation (ta'ajjub), and it is within the domain of those addressed, meaning: they deserve that you be amazed at them and at how long they remain in the Fire. In the revelation there is ﴿Killed be man; how disbelieving he is!﴾ [Abasa: 17] and ﴿Hear them and see them!﴾ [Maryam: 38]. In this sense Abu 'Ali proceeded, and Qatadah, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and al-Rabi' said: He displayed amazement at their patience for the Fire, since they acted like one who has prepared himself for it. Its implied sense: how bold they are toward the Fire, in that they perform deeds that lead to it. It was also said: "mā" is interrogative, meaning: what is it that makes them so patient for the Fire? Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna went to this, but the first view is more apparent.

The meaning of "asbarahum" linguistically: he commanded them to be patient, and it also means: he made them people of patience. Both meanings are fitting in the verse on the interrogative reading. Al-Mubarrad, in the chapter on exclamation in "al-Muqtadab", held that this verse is an affirmation and interrogation, not an exclamation, and that the word "uṣbir" means "compelled and confined," as you say: "aṣbartu Zaydan 'alā al-qatl" (I compelled Zayd to be killed). From this is the Prophet's ﷺ prohibition that animals be made to stand still (for slaughter/killing). He said, and similar to it is the saying of the poet:

"I said to her, 'I keep compelling her constantly, like the likes of Bisṭām ibn Qays, few'"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The vocalization according to al-Mubarrad is with a damma on the hamza and a kasra on the bā', and he refuted him on this, for it is not known in the language that "uṣbira" means "ṣabara." Rather, the verse is "uṣubiruhā" with a fatḥa on the hamza and a ḍamma on the bā', its past tense being "ṣabara," and from it comes "al-maṣbūrah" (the one tied to be shot at). Abu al-'Abbas's statement only refutes the meaning: "make her one of patience."

His saying, ﴿That is because Allah﴾ and the rest of the verse: the meaning is: that matter, or the matter is that, because Allah sent down the Book with truth, so they disbelieved in it. The reference, according to this, is to the obligation of the Fire upon them. It is possible to estimate: "We did that," and it is possible to estimate: "that became obligatory," and "the Book" would then be the whole of the Qur'an under these estimations. It was said: the reference by "the Book" is to His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6], meaning: the Fire became obligatory for them by what Allah has sent down in the Book of the report about it.
