His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿O you who believe, retaliation (qisas) is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother, let there be the following up with fairness and payment to him with good conduct. That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy. Whoever transgresses after that, for him is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous.﴾ ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is the bequest to parents and relatives in a fair manner, a duty upon the righteous.﴾

"Kutiba" means "it was obligated and established." "Kutiba" is frequently used for matters that are lasting and permanent. It was said that "kutiba" in such a context is an informing of what was written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) and what preceding decree had determined.

The form of the obligation of retaliation is that the killer is obligated, when the guardian (wali) seeks retaliation, to submit to the command of God and to comply with the lawful retaliation against him. The guardian is obligated to stop at killing the killer of his relative and to refrain from transgressing against others, as the Arabs used to transgress, killing a man from the tribe of the killer for their slain. The rulers and those in authority are obligated to carry out retaliation and to enforce the prescribed punishments. Retaliation is not compulsory in itself; what is compulsory is that it not exceed retaliation into aggression. As for when mutual consent is reached without retaliation, through blood money (diyya) or pardon, that is permissible. Thus the verse makes clear that retaliation is the ultimate recourse in case of contention.

"Qisas" is derived from "qassa al-athar" (he traced the track), as if the killer had taken a path of killing and the avenger traced his trail along it and followed his way in that.

"Al-qatla" is the plural of "qatil," a word that takes the feminine form as a collective noun, and it is among the things that befall people unwillingly (kurhan). For this reason it came in this pattern, like jarha, zamna, hamqa, sar'a, and gharqa.

There is a difference regarding the cause of this verse. Al-Sha'bi said: The Arabs, among them those of power and strength, when a slave of theirs was killed, they would kill a free person in return, and when a woman was killed, they would kill a male in return. So the verse was revealed concerning that, so that God the Exalted would establish equality and remove the matter of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance).

It is related that a group of the Arabs fought a battle of blind fury ('amiyya), then some of them said: "We will kill free men in return for our slaves." So the verse was revealed.

It was also said: it was revealed because of a fight that took place between two tribes of the Ansar, and it was said: from other than them. These killed men, slaves, and women from the others, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded that he reconcile between them and settle their dues among themselves by blood money on an equal basis: free for free, women for women, and slaves for slaves.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed requiring that a man not be killed for a woman, nor a woman for a man, and that no category be applied to another category. Then it was abrogated (nusikhat) by the verse of al-Ma'ida: ﴿that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
This is how it has been related. But the verse of al-Ma'ida is only an informing of what was prescribed for the Children of Israel. Abrogation (naskh) does not hold except by what was received from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that our ruling in our law is like their ruling.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, as Abu 'Ubayd mentioned, and from others, that this verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and that in it there is a general statement (ijmal) which the verse of al-Ma'ida explained, and that His saying here: ﴿the free for the free﴾ includes men and women. This was said by Mujahid.

(p-424) Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: The best I have heard regarding this verse is that what is intended by it is the category (jins), with male and female equal in it, and the mention of the female was repeated for emphasis and concern, to eliminate the matter of the Jahiliyya.

It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, that the verse was revealed clarifying the ruling for those mentioned, so that this would indicate the distinction between them and a free man killing a slave, or a slave killing a free man, or a male killing a female, or a female killing a male. They both said: If a man kills a woman, then if her guardians wish, they kill their companion (the killer), and they pay the killer's guardians half the blood money from him. If they wish to spare him, they take from him the blood money of a woman. And if a woman kills a man, then if his guardians wish, they kill her and take half the blood money. Otherwise they take the blood money of their companion and spare her. If a free man kills a slave, then if the master of the slave wishes, he (the killer) is killed and gives the blood money of a free man minus the value of the slave. If he wishes, he spares him and takes the value of the slave. This is reported from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and from al-Hasan. But this has also been denied as coming from them both.

The community (umma) agreed (ajma'at) on the killing of a man for a woman and of a woman for a man. The majority do not hold that there is any reduction (ruju') in payment, and a group holds that there is following up with the excess of the blood money. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: Likewise retaliation between them (man and woman) applies to injuries below the soul. Abu Hanifa said: There is no retaliation between them for injuries below the soul; it applies only to the soul for the soul. Al-Nakha'i, Qatada, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and Abu Yusuf said: a free man is killed for a slave. Malik, may God have mercy on him, and the majority of scholars said: a free man is not killed for a slave. Their evidence is the consensus (ijma') of the community that a slave does not match a free man in injuries below the soul, so the soul is analogized to that. Also, there is consensus regarding one who kills a slave by mistake that he owes only the value (qima); just as the free man is not equivalent to the slave in mistake, he is not equivalent to him in intention. Also, the slave is a commodity among commodities, bought and sold. And if a man kills his son, intentionally, such as by laying him down and slaughtering him, or by holding him in a way for which he has no excuse and no doubt about a claim of error, then he is killed for him by unanimous opinion in the school of Malik. If he killed him in the course of shooting or striking and thereby killed him, then in the school there are two opinions: he is killed for him, or he is not killed and the blood money is made heavier.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But whoever is pardoned by his brother, something﴾ has four interpretations.

(p-425) The first: "min" (from) is intended to refer to the killer, "ufiya" (was pardoned) implies that the pardoner is the guardian of the blood, and "akh" (brother) is the slain. It is possible that the brother is the guardian in this interpretation, and it is the brotherhood of Islam. "Shay'" (something) is the blood that is pardoned, and it refers to taking the blood money. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and a group of scholars, and pardon in this view is in its proper sense. The two pronouns refer back to "man" in every interpretation.

The second interpretation, which is the saying of Malik, is that "min" is intended to refer to the guardian, "ufiya" carries the meaning of "yusshira" (was made easy), not in its proper sense of pardon, "akh" refers to the killer, "shay'" is the blood money, and the brotherhood in this case is the brotherhood of Islam. It is possible that by "akh" in this interpretation the slain is intended, meaning it was made easy for him by the side of his slain brother and because of him, so the brotherhood would then be a brotherhood of kinship and Islam. On this interpretation Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: If the guardian inclines toward pardon in exchange for blood money, then the killer is given the choice between giving it or surrendering himself. Sometimes it is made easy and sometimes it is not. Others than Malik say: If the guardians are content with blood money, the killer has no choice; rather it is binding on him. This view has also been related from Malik, and many of his companions preferred it.

The third interpretation is that these words concern the specific persons about whom the verse was revealed, all of them, and that they dropped the blood money among themselves by mutual offset, as we mentioned just before. So the meaning of the verse is: whoever from the two groups has an excess over the other of something from those blood moneys. "Ufiya" would then mean "excess," from their saying "afa al-shay'" when it increased, meaning the situation or the reckoning or the measure became abundant for him.

The fourth interpretation follows the saying of 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, regarding the excess between the blood money of a woman and a man, and between a free man and a slave. That is, whoever has that excess, then there is following up (ittiba') with fairness (p-426). "Ufiya" in this place also carries the meaning of "afdala" (was given excess). It is as if the verse from its beginning explained the ruling when the categories are not mixed, then the rulings when they are mixed. "Shay'" in this verse is a subject that was not named as agent, and that is permissible. "Ufiya" does not transitively govern the past form from which it is derived, in that "shay'" may be estimated as a verbal noun (masdar), as if the sentence meant: "pardon was made for him from his brother." Or "shay'" is a general name for this and for other things. Or "ufiya" is estimated with the meaning of "tarak" (left), so it operates as that. The first is better. There are parallels in the Book of God, among them His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they will not harm Him at all﴾ [Hud: 57]. Al-Akhfash said: the estimate is "la tadurrunahu durran" (you will not harm Him harm). Among that is the saying of Abu Khirash:
"So I was hostile to something, while the dust-blown trail was as if shaken by a wind-driven rain of the burning mum."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-ittiba'un﴾ is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "so the obligation and the ruling is following up." This is the path of obligatory matters, like His saying: ﴿then retention in fairness﴾ [al-Baqara: 229]. As for what is recommended, it comes in the accusative, like His saying: ﴿then striking of the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4]. This verse is an exhortation from God the Exalted to good conduct in making the demand on the part of the creditor, and to good conduct in payment on the part of the debtor (p-427). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "fa-ittiba'an" with the accusative.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is a lightening from your Lord﴾ refers to what He legislated for this community regarding taking the blood money. The Children of Israel had no blood money; for them there was only retaliation.

The threatened transgression (i'tida') in this verse is that a man takes the blood money from his guardian and then kills the killer after the blood has been dropped. There is a difference regarding the painful punishment that befalls him. A group of scholars, including Malik, said: he is treated as one who killed from the outset: if the guardian wishes, he kills him, and if he wishes, he pardons him, and his punishment is in the Hereafter. Qatada, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi, and others said: his punishment is that he is killed definitively, and the ruler does not permit the guardian to pardon. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "We swear that a man who pardons regarding blood, takes the blood money, then transgresses and kills, will not be pardoned." al-Hasan said: his punishment is that he returns the blood money only, and his sin remains until the punishment of the Hereafter. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: His matter is referred to the Imam, who does with him what he sees fit.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life﴾. Similar to this is the saying of the Arabs in such things as: "Killing is more protective against killing." It is related as "abqa" with a ba' and qaf, and it is related as "anfa" with a nun and fa'. The meaning is that when retaliation is carried out and the ruling regarding it is realized, it restrains whoever wishes to kill someone, for fear that retaliation will be taken from him, and thus both are given life. This arrangement (p-428) was preceded for both in eternity. Also, when a man killed another, the Arabs' two tribes would become incensed and fight, and that would lead to the death of a great number. So when God legislated retaliation, everyone was content with it and stopped there, and they abandoned fighting, so there is life for them in that.

"Ulu al-albab" (people of understanding) is singled out for mention as an alert to them, because they are the ones who know and accept the commands and prohibitions, and others follow them.

"Tattaqun" (you may become righteous) means: that you refrain from killing, so that you are safe from retaliation. Then this becomes a motive toward various kinds of piety in other matters, since God the Exalted rewards obedience with obedience. Abu al-Jawza' Aws ibn 'Abd Allah al-Rib'i read: "wa-lakum fi al-qisas" (in the stories), meaning in the Book of God in which He legislated retaliation and ruled on it. It is possible that it is a verbal noun like "qisas," meaning that he traced the killer's track in tracing, so he was killed as he killed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Prescribed for you﴾ and the verse. It is as if the verse is connected to His saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾, which is why the conjunctive waw dropped out. "Kutiba" means "it was obligated and established." Some people of knowledge said: the bequest (wasiyya) is obligatory. Some said: it was obligatory and then abrogated. A group said: it is recommended. "Kutiba" governs the raising of "al-wasiyya" as the non-named agent in some estimates, and the feminine marker was dropped from "kutiba" because of the length of the speech, so its dropping was good. Sibawayh related: "qama imra'atan" (a woman stood up), but its goodness is only with a long intervening element.

(p. 429) According to the majority of grammarians, the *wasiyya* (bequest) cannot govern *idha* (when), because *idha* functions as a complement to the verbal noun *al-wasiyya*, and since the complement has already been placed before it, the noun cannot govern what precedes it. The construction that is sound in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this verse is that *kutiba* (was prescribed) is the governing element of *idha*. The meaning is: God's obligation is directed at you, and its requirement, when death approaches, is in His Book. He expressed the directing of the obligation with *kutiba* so that, alongside this meaning, it would also convey that it is written in eternity. *Al-wasiyya* is the object that has not been named as its agent, with *kutiba* as its verb. The response (*jawab*) to the two conditionals, *idha* and *in*, is omitted, and what precedes it, His saying ﴿prescribed for you﴾, indicates it, as when you say: "I thank you for your deed if you come to me when such-and-such is the case."

It is also sound in its i'rab that the implied meaning is: "He prescribed for you the bequeathing," and this implied bequeathing, which the later mention of *al-wasiyya* indicates, is the governing element of *idha*. *Al-wasiyya* is then in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*). The response to the two conditionals is contained in it, in the manner of what Sibawayh recited:

"Whoever does righteous deeds, God preserves them ..........................."

(p. 430) Alternatively, its nominative case may be as the subject, with the implied phrase: "then upon him is the bequest," or with only the implied *fa'* (the particle of consequence), as if it were said: "So the bequest is for the two parents."

It is also sound in its i'rab that *al-wasiyya* be in the nominative case governed by *kutiba*, as the object that has not been named as its agent, and that *al-wasiyya* itself be the governing element of *idha*. This is according to the opinion of Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash, for he permits what is within the complement of the relative construction (*al-mawsul*) to precede it under two conditions, both of which are present in this verse. The first is that the relative word is not a pure relative but resembles one, such as the definite article *al-*, which is treated as connected, or like a verbal noun; in this verse, *al-wasiyya* is a verbal noun. The second condition is that the element that precedes is an adverbial of time or place (*zarf*), for there is greater latitude with adverbials, and *idha* is an adverbial. This is Abu al-Hasan's view on the words of the poet:

"She says, and struck her face with her right hand: 'Is this husband of mine the one who is slow with the millstone?'"

For he holds that *bil-ra'a* (with the millstone) is related to *al-mutaqa'is* (the one who is slow), as if he had said: "Is this husband of mine the one who is slow with the millstone?" The response to the two conditionals in this statement is as we mentioned in the first statement.

In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when death approaches﴾, there is a metaphor (*majaz*), because the meaning is: when one fears death and its signs appear. The "good" (*khayr*) in this verse is wealth.

The scholars who require bequests differed about the amount from which it is obligatory. Al-Zuhri and others said: it is obligatory for a little or for a lot. Al-Nakha'i said: it is obligatory for five hundred dirhams and above. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and Qatada said: for a thousand and above.

(p. 431) The scholars differed concerning this verse. One group said: it is *muhkama* (decisive, not abrogated), its apparent meaning is general, but its meaning is specific to the parents who do not inherit, such as non-Muslim parents or enslaved parents, and to relatives who are not heirs. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada said: the verse is general, and the ruling was affirmed by it for a time, and from it every person who inherits was abrogated (*nusikha*) by the verse of the inheritance shares. Within this formulation falls the statement of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and others that the parents were abrogated from it, and the nearest relatives who do not inherit remained. He explained that the verse of the shares in Surat al-Nisa' abrogates this one, based on the widely transmitted hadith: "God has given every rightful person his right, so there is no bequest to an heir." Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas also, and Ibn Zayd said: the whole verse is abrogated, and the bequest remained as a recommendation (*nadban*). Malik, may God have mercy on him, held a similar view. Al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and others said: there is no bequest to an heir. Urwa ibn Thabit said to al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym: "Bequeath to me your copy of the Qur'an." Al-Rabi' looked at his son and recited: ﴿And those of blood-relationship are closer to one another in the Book of God﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with him, did something similar. Some scholars said: the abrogating element of this verse is the widely transmitted Sunnah in the hadith mentioned earlier, and the justification for the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah has already been discussed (p. 432) in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqara: 106]. Some scholars said: the bequest to relatives takes priority; if it is to a stranger, it is with them (the relatives), and it is not permitted to others while they (the relatives) are left out. When Abu al-'Aliya died, people said: "How strange! A woman of the Riyah tribe freed him, and he bequeathed his wealth to the Banu Hashim." Al-Sha'bi said: that was not for him, nor was it an honour. Tawus said: if one bequeaths to someone other than his relatives, the bequest is returned to his relatives and his action is annulled. Jabir ibn Zayd said the same. Al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd also, and Abd al-Malik ibn Ya'la said: a third of the bequest remains where he placed it, and two-thirds are returned to his relatives. Malik, may God have mercy on him, and a group of scholars said: the bequest is valid wherever the deceased placed it.

*Al-aqrabun* (the nearest) is the plural of *aqrab* (nearest). *Bil-ma'ruf* (with fairness) means: with the moderation that people recognize, without harm to the heirs and without extravagance in the bequest. *Haqqan* (as a duty) is an emphatic verbal noun, and the *muttaqun* (God-conscious) were singled out for mention to honour their rank, so that people would be drawn toward it.

The fourth interpretation follows the saying of 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, regarding the excess between the blood money of a woman and a man, and between a free man and a slave. That is, whoever has that excess, then there is following up (ittiba') with fairness (p-426). "Ufiya" in this place also carries the meaning of "afdala" (was given excess). It is as if the verse from its beginning explained the ruling when the categories are not mixed, then the rulings when they are mixed. "Shay'" in this verse is a subject that was not named as agent, and that is permissible. "Ufiya" does not transitively govern the past form from which it is derived, in that "shay'" may be estimated as a verbal noun (masdar), as if the sentence meant: "pardon was made for him from his brother." Or "shay'" is a general name for this and for other things. Or "ufiya" is estimated with the meaning of "tarak" (left), so it operates as that. The first is better. There are parallels in the Book of God, among them His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and they will not harm Him at all﴾ [Hud: 57]. Al-Akhfash said: the estimate is "la tadurrunahu durran" (you will not harm Him harm). Among that is the saying of Abu Khirash:
"So I was hostile to something, while the dust-blown trail was as if shaken by a wind-driven rain of the burning mum."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-ittiba'un﴾ is in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, its estimate being: "so the obligation and the ruling is following up." This is the path of obligatory matters, like His saying: ﴿then retention in fairness﴾ [al-Baqara: 229]. As for what is recommended, it comes in the accusative, like His saying: ﴿then striking of the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4]. This verse is an exhortation from God the Exalted to good conduct in making the demand on the part of the creditor, and to good conduct in payment on the part of the debtor (p-427). Ibn Abi 'Abla read "fa-ittiba'an" with the accusative.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is a lightening from your Lord﴾ refers to what He legislated for this community regarding taking the blood money. The Children of Israel had no blood money; for them there was only retaliation.

The threatened transgression (i'tida') in this verse is that a man takes the blood money from his guardian and then kills the killer after the blood has been dropped. There is a difference regarding the painful punishment that befalls him. A group of scholars, including Malik, said: he is treated as one who killed from the outset: if the guardian wishes, he kills him, and if he wishes, he pardons him, and his punishment is in the Hereafter. Qatada, 'Ikrima, al-Suddi, and others said: his punishment is that he is killed definitively, and the ruler does not permit the guardian to pardon. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "We swear that a man who pardons regarding blood, takes the blood money, then transgresses and kills, will not be pardoned." al-Hasan said: his punishment is that he returns the blood money only, and his sin remains until the punishment of the Hereafter. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: His matter is referred to the Imam, who does with him what he sees fit.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life﴾. Similar to this is the saying of the Arabs in such things as: "Killing is more protective against killing." It is related as "abqa" with a ba' and qaf, and it is related as "anfa" with a nun and fa'. The meaning is that when retaliation is carried out and the ruling regarding it is realized, it restrains whoever wishes to kill someone, for fear that retaliation will be taken from him, and thus both are given life. This arrangement (p-428) was preceded for both in eternity. Also, when a man killed another, the Arabs' two tribes would become incensed and fight, and that would lead to the death of a great number. So when God legislated retaliation, everyone was content with it and stopped there, and they abandoned fighting, so there is life for them in that.

"Ulu al-albab" (people of understanding) is singled out for mention as an alert to them, because they are the ones who know and accept the commands and prohibitions, and others follow them.

"Tattaqun" (you may become righteous) means: that you refrain from killing, so that you are safe from retaliation. Then this becomes a motive toward various kinds of piety in other matters, since God the Exalted rewards obedience with obedience. Abu al-Jawza' Aws ibn 'Abd Allah al-Rib'i read: "wa-lakum fi al-qisas" (in the stories), meaning in the Book of God in which He legislated retaliation and ruled on it. It is possible that it is a verbal noun like "qisas," meaning that he traced the killer's track in tracing, so he was killed as he killed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Prescribed for you﴾ and the verse. It is as if the verse is connected to His saying: ﴿O you who believe﴾, which is why the conjunctive waw dropped out. "Kutiba" means "it was obligated and established." Some people of knowledge said: the bequest (wasiyya) is obligatory. Some said: it was obligatory and then abrogated. A group said: it is recommended. "Kutiba" governs the raising of "al-wasiyya" as the non-named agent in some estimates, and the feminine marker was dropped from "kutiba" because of the length of the speech, so its dropping was good. Sibawayh related: "qama imra'atan" (a woman stood up), but its goodness is only with a long intervening element.

(p. 429) According to the majority of grammarians, the *wasiyya* (bequest) cannot govern *idha* (when), because *idha* functions as a complement to the verbal noun *al-wasiyya*, and since the complement has already been placed before it, the noun cannot govern what precedes it. The construction that is sound in the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of this verse is that *kutiba* (was prescribed) is the governing element of *idha*. The meaning is: God's obligation is directed at you, and its requirement, when death approaches, is in His Book. He expressed the directing of the obligation with *kutiba* so that, alongside this meaning, it would also convey that it is written in eternity. *Al-wasiyya* is the object that has not been named as its agent, with *kutiba* as its verb. The response (*jawab*) to the two conditionals, *idha* and *in*, is omitted, and what precedes it, His saying ﴿prescribed for you﴾, indicates it, as when you say: "I thank you for your deed if you come to me when such-and-such is the case."

It is also sound in its i'rab that the implied meaning is: "He prescribed for you the bequeathing," and this implied bequeathing, which the later mention of *al-wasiyya* indicates, is the governing element of *idha*. *Al-wasiyya* is then in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*). The response to the two conditionals is contained in it, in the manner of what Sibawayh recited:

"Whoever does righteous deeds, God preserves them ..........................."

(p. 430) Alternatively, its nominative case may be as the subject, with the implied phrase: "then upon him is the bequest," or with only the implied *fa'* (the particle of consequence), as if it were said: "So the bequest is for the two parents."

It is also sound in its i'rab that *al-wasiyya* be in the nominative case governed by *kutiba*, as the object that has not been named as its agent, and that *al-wasiyya* itself be the governing element of *idha*. The first is that the relative word is not a pure relative but resembles one, such as the definite article *al-*, which is treated as connected, or like a verbal noun; in this verse, *al-wasiyya* is a verbal noun. The second condition is that the element that precedes is an adverbial of time or place (*zarf*), for there is greater latitude with adverbials, and *idha* is an adverbial. This is Abu al-Hasan's view on the words of the poet:

"She says, and struck her face with her right hand: 'Is this husband of mine the one who is slow with the millstone?'"

For he holds that *bil-ra'a* (with the millstone) is related to *al-mutaqa'is* (the one who is slow), as if he had said: "Is this husband of mine the one who is slow with the millstone?" The response to the two conditionals in this statement is as we mentioned in the first statement.

In His saying, exalted is He, ﴿when death approaches﴾, there is a metaphor (*majaz*), because the meaning is: when one fears death and its signs appear. The "good" (*khayr*) in this verse is wealth.

The scholars who require bequests differed about the amount from which it is obligatory. Al-Zuhri and others said: it is obligatory for a little or for a lot. Al-Nakha'i said: it is obligatory for five hundred dirhams and above. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and Qatada said: for a thousand and above.

(p. 431) The scholars differed concerning this verse. One group said: it is *muhkama* (decisive, not abrogated), its apparent meaning is general, but its meaning is specific to the parents who do not inherit, such as non-Muslim parents or enslaved parents, and to relatives who are not heirs. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada said: the verse is general, and the ruling was affirmed by it for a time, and from it every person who inherits was abrogated (*nusikha*) by the verse of the inheritance shares. Within this formulation falls the statement of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and others that the parents were abrogated from it, and the nearest relatives who do not inherit remained. He explained that the verse of the shares in Surat al-Nisa' abrogates this one, based on the widely transmitted hadith: "God has given every rightful person his right, so there is no bequest to an heir." Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas also, and Ibn Zayd said: the whole verse is abrogated, and the bequest remained as a recommendation (*nadban*). Malik, may God have mercy on him, held a similar view. Al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and others said: there is no bequest to an heir. Urwa ibn Thabit said to al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym: "Bequeath to me your copy of the Qur'an." Al-Rabi' looked at his son and recited: ﴿And those of blood-relationship are closer to one another in the Book of God﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with him, did something similar. Some scholars said: the abrogating element of this verse is the widely transmitted Sunnah in the hadith mentioned earlier, and the justification for the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah has already been discussed (p. 432) in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqara: 106]. When Abu al-'Aliya died, people said: "How strange! A woman of the Riyah tribe freed him, and he bequeathed his wealth to the Banu Hashim." Al-Sha'bi said: that was not for him, nor was it an honour. Tawus said: if one bequeaths to someone other than his relatives, the bequest is returned to his relatives and his action is annulled. Jabir ibn Zayd said the same. Al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd also, and Abd al-Malik ibn Ya'la said: a third of the bequest remains where he placed it, and two-thirds are returned to his relatives. Malik, may God have mercy on him, and a group of scholars said: the bequest is valid wherever the deceased placed it.

*Al-aqrabun* (the nearest) is the plural of *aqrab* (nearest). *Bil-ma'ruf* (with fairness) means: with the moderation that people recognize, without harm to the heirs and without extravagance in the bequest. *Haqqan* (as a duty) is an emphatic verbal noun, and the *muttaqun* (God-conscious) were singled out for mention to honour their rank, so that people would be drawn toward it.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 2, verses 178–180 (part 1 of 2)**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿O you who believe, retaliation (qisas) is prescribed for you regarding the slain: the free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female. But whoever is pardoned by his brother, let there be the following up with fairness and payment to him with good conduct. That is a lightening from your Lord and a mercy. Whoever transgresses after that, for him is a painful punishment.﴾ ﴿And for you in retaliation there is life, O people of understanding, that you may become righteous.﴾ ﴿Prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you, if he leaves wealth, is the bequest to parents and relatives in a fair manner, a duty upon the righteous.﴾

"Kutiba" means "it was obligated and established." "Kutiba" is frequently used for matters that are lasting and permanent. It was said that "kutiba" in such a context is an informing of what was written in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz) and what preceding decree had determined.

The form of the obligation of retaliation is that the killer is obligated, when the guardian (wali) seeks retaliation, to submit to the command of God and to comply with the lawful retaliation against him. The guardian is obligated to stop at killing the killer of his relative and to refrain from transgressing against others, as the Arabs used to transgress, killing a man from the tribe of the killer for their slain. The rulers and those in authority are obligated to carry out retaliation and to enforce the prescribed punishments. Retaliation is not compulsory in itself; what is compulsory is that it not exceed retaliation into aggression. As for when mutual consent is reached without retaliation, through blood money (diyya) or pardon, that is permissible. Thus the verse makes clear that retaliation is the ultimate recourse in case of contention.

"Qisas" is derived from "qassa al-athar" (he traced the track), as if the killer had taken a path of killing and the avenger traced his trail along it and followed his way in that.

"Al-qatla" is the plural of "qatil," a word that takes the feminine form as a collective noun, and it is among the things that befall people unwillingly (kurhan). For this reason it came in this pattern, like jarha, zamna, hamqa, sar'a, and gharqa.

There is a difference regarding the cause of this verse. Al-Sha'bi said: The Arabs, among them those of power and strength, when a slave of theirs was killed, they would kill a free person in return, and when a woman was killed, they would kill a male in return. So the verse was revealed concerning that, so that God the Exalted would establish equality and remove the matter of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance).

It is related that a group of the Arabs fought a battle of blind fury ('amiyya), then some of them said: "We will kill free men in return for our slaves." So the verse was revealed.

It was also said: it was revealed because of a fight that took place between two tribes of the Ansar, and it was said: from other than them. These killed men, slaves, and women from the others, so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) commanded that he reconcile between them and settle their dues among themselves by blood money on an equal basis: free for free, women for women, and slaves for slaves.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that the verse was revealed requiring that a man not be killed for a woman, nor a woman for a man, and that no category be applied to another category. Then it was abrogated (nusikhat) by the verse of al-Ma'ida: ﴿that the soul is for the soul﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 45].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
This is how it has been related. But the verse of al-Ma'ida is only an informing of what was prescribed for the Children of Israel. Abrogation (naskh) does not hold except by what was received from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), that our ruling in our law is like their ruling.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, as Abu 'Ubayd mentioned, and from others, that this verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated), and that in it there is a general statement (ijmal) which the verse of al-Ma'ida explained, and that His saying here: ﴿the free for the free﴾ includes men and women. This was said by Mujahid.

(p-424) Malik, may God have mercy on him, said: The best I have heard regarding this verse is that what is intended by it is the category (jins), with male and female equal in it, and the mention of the female was repeated for emphasis and concern, to eliminate the matter of the Jahiliyya.

It is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and from al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, that the verse was revealed clarifying the ruling for those mentioned, so that this would indicate the distinction between them and a free man killing a slave, or a slave killing a free man, or a male killing a female, or a female killing a male. They both said: If a man kills a woman, then if her guardians wish, they kill their companion (the killer), and they pay the killer's guardians half the blood money from him. If they wish to spare him, they take from him the blood money of a woman. And if a woman kills a man, then if his guardians wish, they kill her and take half the blood money. Otherwise they take the blood money of their companion and spare her. If a free man kills a slave, then if the master of the slave wishes, he (the killer) is killed and gives the blood money of a free man minus the value of the slave. If he wishes, he spares him and takes the value of the slave. This is reported from 'Ali, may God be pleased with him, and from al-Hasan. But this has also been denied as coming from them both.

The community (umma) agreed (ajma'at) on the killing of a man for a woman and of a woman for a man. The majority do not hold that there is any reduction (ruju') in payment, and a group holds that there is following up with the excess of the blood money. Malik and al-Shafi'i said: Likewise retaliation between them (man and woman) applies to injuries below the soul. Abu Hanifa said: There is no retaliation between them for injuries below the soul; it applies only to the soul for the soul. Al-Nakha'i, Qatada, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, al-Sha'bi, al-Thawri, Abu Hanifa, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and Abu Yusuf said: a free man is killed for a slave. Malik, may God have mercy on him, and the majority of scholars said: a free man is not killed for a slave. Their evidence is the consensus (ijma') of the community that a slave does not match a free man in injuries below the soul, so the soul is analogized to that. Also, there is consensus regarding one who kills a slave by mistake that he owes only the value (qima); just as the free man is not equivalent to the slave in mistake, he is not equivalent to him in intention. Also, the slave is a commodity among commodities, bought and sold. And if a man kills his son, intentionally, such as by laying him down and slaughtering him, or by holding him in a way for which he has no excuse and no doubt about a claim of error, then he is killed for him by unanimous opinion in the school of Malik. If he killed him in the course of shooting or striking and thereby killed him, then in the school there are two opinions: he is killed for him, or he is not killed and the blood money is made heavier.

This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and a group of scholars, and pardon in this view is in its proper sense. The two pronouns refer back to "man" in every interpretation.

The scholars who require bequests differed about the amount from which it is obligatory. Al-Zuhri and others said: it is obligatory for a little or for a lot. Al-Nakha'i said: it is obligatory for five hundred dirhams and above. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, and Qatada said: for a thousand and above.

(p. 431) The scholars differed concerning this verse. One group said: it is *muhkama* (decisive, not abrogated), its apparent meaning is general, but its meaning is specific to the parents who do not inherit, such as non-Muslim parents or enslaved parents, and to relatives who are not heirs. Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and Qatada said: the verse is general, and the ruling was affirmed by it for a time, and from it every person who inherits was abrogated (*nusikha*) by the verse of the inheritance shares. Within this formulation falls the statement of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, and others that the parents were abrogated from it, and the nearest relatives who do not inherit remained. He explained that the verse of the shares in Surat al-Nisa' abrogates this one, based on the widely transmitted hadith: "God has given every rightful person his right, so there is no bequest to an heir." Ibn Umar, Ibn Abbas also, and Ibn Zayd said: the whole verse is abrogated, and the bequest remained as a recommendation (*nadban*). Malik, may God have mercy on him, held a similar view. Al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym and others said: there is no bequest to an heir. Urwa ibn Thabit said to al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym: "Bequeath to me your copy of the Qur'an." Al-Rabi' looked at his son and recited: ﴿And those of blood-relationship are closer to one another in the Book of God﴾ [al-Anfal: 75]. Ibn Umar, may God be pleased with him, did something similar. Some scholars said: the abrogating element of this verse is the widely transmitted Sunnah in the hadith mentioned earlier, and the justification for the abrogation of the Qur'an by the Sunnah has already been discussed (p. 432) in the commentary on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whatever verse We abrogate﴾ [al-Baqara: 106]. Some scholars said: the bequest to relatives takes priority; if it is to a stranger, it is with them (the relatives), and it is not permitted to others while they (the relatives) are left out. When Abu al-'Aliya died, people said: "How strange! A woman of the Riyah tribe freed him, and he bequeathed his wealth to the Banu Hashim." Al-Sha'bi said: that was not for him, nor was it an honour. Tawus said: if one bequeaths to someone other than his relatives, the bequest is returned to his relatives and his action is annulled. Jabir ibn Zayd said the same. Al-Hasan, Jabir ibn Zayd also, and Abd al-Malik ibn Ya'la said: a third of the bequest remains where he placed it, and two-thirds are returned to his relatives. Malik, may God have mercy on him, and a group of scholars said: the bequest is valid wherever the deceased placed it.

*Al-aqrabun* (the nearest) is the plural of *aqrab* (nearest). *Bil-ma'ruf* (with fairness) means: with the moderation that people recognize, without harm to the heirs and without extravagance in the bequest. *Haqqan* (as a duty) is an emphatic verbal noun, and the *muttaqun* (God-conscious) were singled out for mention to honour their rank, so that people would be drawn toward it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 181–184 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted and Majestic said:
﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it, the sin thereof is only upon those who alter it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾ ﴿But whoever fears from a testator an error or sin and brings about reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you that you may become righteous.﴾ ﴿[For] a limited number of days. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey [during them]—then an equal number of other days. And upon those who are able to fast [with difficulty] is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man. And whoever volunteers good—it is better for him. But to fast is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

The pronoun in "بَدَّلَهُ" (baddalahu, "altered it") refers to the bequest and the testator's instruction, and likewise in "سَمِعَهُ" (sami'ahu, "heard it"). It is possible that the pronoun in "سَمِعَهُ" refers to the command of Allah the Exalted in this verse, but the first opinion is more immediate for the reader. However, implicit in it is that the one who alters is aware of the prohibition and deliberately opposes it. The pronoun in "إثْمُهُ" (ithmuhu, "its sin") refers to the alteration (al-tabdil), and ﴿Hearing, Knowing﴾ are two attributes, with which nothing is hidden of the deviation of testators or the alteration of transgressors.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "مِن مُوصٍ" (min mūṣin) with a fatḥa on the wāw and a shadda on the ṣād. The rest read it with a sukūn on the wāw.

Al-janaf (الجَنَفُ) means inclination. al-A'sha said:
"It deviates from the stone of al-Yamamah, my she-camel, and I did not aim from its people for other than you."
And 'Amir al-Ramī al-Ḥaḍramī al-Muḥāribī said:
"The master intended, and they had deviated against us, and indeed we are visitors from their hostilities."

The meaning of the verse, according to Mujahid, is: whoever fears that the testator will act unjustly and cut off the inheritance of a group, and deliberately intends harm or does so without deliberate intent—this is janaf without sin. If he does it deliberately, it is janaf with sin. So the meaning is: whoever admonishes him in this matter and turns him back from it, thereby reconciling what is between him and his heirs, and what is among the heirs themselves, ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ toward the testator when the admonition takes effect and he returns from what he intended of harm, ﴿Merciful﴾ to him.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Qatadah, and al-Rabi' said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever fears—that is, knows, sees, and his knowledge reaches him after the death of the testator—that the testator has acted unjustly, deviated, and deliberately intended harm to some of his heirs, then he reconciles what has occurred among the heirs of disorder and discord, ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾, that is, the sin of the aforementioned alterer does not befall him, even though in his act there is some alteration and it is unavoidable, but it is an alteration for a benefit. The alteration that carries sin is only the alteration of desire. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar read "فَلا إثْمَ" ("then there is no sin") with the alif omitted from "عَلَيْهِ".

"Kutiba" (كُتِبَ) means it was obligated. "Al-siyam" (الصِيامُ, fasting) linguistically means abstention and leaving off moving from one state to another, and from it is the saying of al-Nabigha:
"Horses standing still and horses not standing still, under the dust, and horses chewing their bits."
That is: horses firm and holding still. And from it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26], that is, abstention from speech. And from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
"As if al-Thurayya were suspended in its station..."
That is, in the place of its settling and holding. And from it is his saying:
"So leave this, and drive away worry from yourself with a swift she-camel, steady when the day stands still and it travels in the heat..."
That is: the sun stood still from moving and remained fixed.

In the Shari'ah, fasting (al-siyam) is abstention from food and drink, accompanied by conditions, such as observing certain times and other things. Therefore it is among the unspecified (mujmal) terms of the Qur'an according to the scholars.

The kaf in His saying "kama" (كَما, "as") is in the accusative position as a description (na't), its estimate being: "kutiba ... [ṣiyāman] kamā", or as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if the statement were: "fasting has been prescribed for you, resembling what was prescribed for those before you."

Some grammarians said: the kaf is in the nominative position as a description of al-siyam, since its definiteness is not pure, because of the generality it contains, which the Shari'ah has explained; therefore it is permissible to describe it with "kamā", since only indefinites are described with it. It is thus like: "Fasting has been prescribed for you [ṣiyām]." This view is weak.

The interpreters differed on the point of the comparison. Al-Sha'bi and others said: the meaning is: "Ramadan has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for the Christians." He said: Ramadan was prescribed for them, but they altered it, because they were cautious about it, by adding a day at its beginning and a day at its end, generation after generation, until they reached fifty days. It then became difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to the winter season. Al-Naqqash said: "There is a report about this from Dughfal ibn Handhalah, al-Hasan al-Basri, and al-Suddi." It was also said: a king of theirs fell ill and vowed that if he recovered he would add ten days to it, then the last seven, then the last three, and they considered the addition good in exchange for the error in transmitting it.

Al-Suddi and al-Rabi' said: the comparison is that from iftar to its like, one does not eat, drink, or approach one's spouse; and when iftar time comes, one does not do these things if one has slept. Likewise it was for the Christians at first, and it was so at the beginning of Islam, then Allah abrogated it, by means of 'Umar and Qays ibn Sirmah, with the verses that come on that matter.

'Ata' said: the comparison is: "Fasting has been prescribed for you three days of every month."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
In some transmissions: "and the day of 'Ashura', as it was prescribed for those before you, three days of every month and the day of 'Ashura'." Then this was abrogated for this community by the month of Ramadan.

A group said: the comparison is "kutiba 'alaykum ka-ṣiyām" in general, that is, it has already been prescribed in the law of others. So "alladhīna" is general, covering the Christians and others. "La'allakum" expresses hope regarding them, and "tattaqūn" (you may become righteous). Al-Suddi said: its meaning is that you may be wary of eating, drinking, and intercourse after sleep, according to the view of those who interpreted it so. It was also said: "tattaqūn" is general, because fasting, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said, is a shield and protection and a cause of piety, since it kills desires.

"Ayyāman" is a second object of "kutiba", said by al-Farra'. It was also said: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time. It was also said: its accusative is governed by "al-siyām", but this is not good except on the view that "al-siyām" governs the kaf in "kamā", according to the one who estimates "ṣawman kamā". If "al-siyām" does not govern the kaf, it is ugly to separate the verbal noun from what it governs by something governed by another, and this is the case when the governing verb of the kaf is "kutiba". Some permitted that "ayyāman" be an adverb of time governed by "al-siyām". "Ma'dūdāt" (limited) was said to refer to Ramadan, and it was said to refer to the three days.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey﴾, the estimate is: "then he breaks his fast, and [owes] an equal number of other days." This is what they call fahwā al-khiṭāb (the implication of the address).

The scholars differed about the limit of the illness that permits breaking the fast. Some people said: whenever a person is in a state that makes him deserve the name "ill," breaking the fast is valid, by analogy with the traveler, who breaks his fast because of the cause of travel, even if it does not compel him to break it by necessity. This was said by Ibn Sirin. Most scholars said: if he has an illness that harms him and causes him pain, or he fears its prolongation, or he fears that fasting will increase it, breaking the fast is valid for him. This is the position of the leading companions of Malik, and by it they debate; as for the wording of Malik himself, it is: "the illness that is hard on a person and by which he is kept going." Al-Hasan said: if due to the illness he cannot pray standing, he breaks his fast. A group said: one breaks the fast due to illness only if the necessity of the illness itself compels him to break it; and whenever he can bear the necessity with it, he does not break it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him.

The scholars differed about which is better, breaking the fast or fasting, during travel. A group, al-Shafi'i, and Malik in some of what is narrated from him, said: fasting is better for one who is able. The bulk of Malik's school is free choice (al-takhyir). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, and others said: breaking the fast is better. Mujahid, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and others said: whichever of the two is easier is better. Ibn Hanbal and others disliked fasting while travelling. Ibn 'Umar said: whoever fasts while travelling must make it up while resident, and this is the position of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

Malik's position on recommending fasting for one who is able to do so, and shortening the prayer is good, because the obligation is discharged by the concession of the prayer while it remains occupied with the matter of fasting, and the correct course is to hasten to deeds. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: breaking the fast during travel is a firm obligation. Anas ibn Malik went to fasting and said: the concession was revealed only when we were hungry, setting out into hunger and rising into hunger.

The journey that is a journey of obedience, such as Hajj and jihad, is agreed upon. Connected to these two is the journey of maintaining family ties and seeking essential livelihood. As for travel for trade and permissible purposes, it is disputed between prohibition and permission, and the view of permission is more preponderant. As for travel for sinful purposes, it is disputed between permission and prohibition, and the view of prohibition is more preponderant. The distance of travel for breaking the fast according to Malik is where the prayer is shortened. The amount of that was disputed. Malik said: a day and a night; then he returned and said: forty-eight miles. It was also narrated from him: two days; and it was narrated from him in al-'Utbiyya: forty-five miles; in al-Mabsut: forty miles; in al-Madhhab: thirty-six miles; and in it: thirty. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Thawri said: breaking the fast is for a journey of three days; and outside the madhhab, one shortens [the prayer] at three miles or more.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-'iddatun﴾ (then a number) is nominative as the predicate of an inchoative; its estimate is: "so the ruling is, or so what is obligatory is, a number." It may also be nominative as an inchoative with the predicate following: the estimate is "so the number of the like of it is incumbent," and it may be: "so upon him is a number." It was disputed whether consecutiveness of these days is obligatory, on two views. "Ukhar" (other) does not take nunation according to Sibawayh, because it is diverted from al-alif wa-l-lam, since this form comes with alif and lam, as you say: "al-fadl" and "al-kibar," in which both diversion (al-'adl) and description (al-ṣifa) are combined. "Ukhar" is used in the verse, and "ukhrā" is not used, lest it be problematic as an attribute of "'iddah," and the rule is that the plural of non-rational things in such a case follows the pattern of the feminine singular, and from it is His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba': 10], and so on.

The majority of people read "yuṭīqūnahu" with a kasra on the ṭā' and sukūn on the yā'; the original is "yuṭawwiqūnahu," the vowel of the wāw was moved to the ṭā' and it was changed to yā' because of the kasra before it. Ḥumayd read "yaṭūqūnahu," which is on the original form, while the regular rule is the altered form. Ibn 'Abbas read "yuṭawwaqūnahu," meaning "they are charged with it." 'A'isha, Ṭawus, and 'Amr ibn Dinar read "yaṭṭawwaqūnahu" with a fatḥa on the yā' and a shadda on the ṭā' with fatḥa.

A group read "yuṭayyiqūnahu" with a ḍamma on the yā' and fatḥa on the ṭā' and shadda on the fatḥa-marked yā'. Ibn 'Abbas read "yuṭṭayyiqūnahu" with a fatḥa on the yā' and shadda on the ṭā' and shadda on the fatḥa-marked yā', meaning "they strain at it." al-Naqqash related it from 'Ikrimah. The doubling of the yā' in this word is weak.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, through the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, read "fidyatu ṭa'āmi masākīn" with the ransom construct-annexed. Hashim, from Ibn 'Amir, read "fidyatu ṭa'āmi masākīna" with nunation of "fidyah." The rest read "fidyatun" with nunation, "ṭa'āmu miskīn" in the singular, and this is a good reading because it clarifies the ruling regarding the day, since the plural "masākīn" would not reveal how many of them are due per day except from outside the verse. Abu 'Ali said: If you say, why is "miskīn" singular when the meaning is plural, since those who are able are plural and each one of them is obligated to a miskīn, so it would seem appropriate to make it plural as the able ones are plural? The answer is that the singular is good, because it is understood from the meaning that each one has a miskīn. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses—flog them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4]; the eighty are not distributed among all of them, rather each one receives eighty.

The interpreters differed about what is meant by the verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 181–184 (part 2 of 2):

(p-440) Mu'adh ibn Jabal, 'Alqama, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn 'Umar, al-Sha'bi, Salama ibn al-Akwa', and Ibn Shihab said: The obligation of fasting was thus upon people: whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished fed a poor person and broke the fast. Then this was abrogated (naskh) by the words of God Most High: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]. A group said: ﴿And upon those who are able to do it﴾ means: upon the elderly and the infirm who are able to do it, but with severe strain. So God permitted them the ransom (fidya) and breaking the fast. According to those who hold this view, the ruling is muhkam (firm, not abrogated). On this interpretation, the readings "yutiqunahu" and "yuttawwaqunahu" also fit.

Ibn 'Abbas said: This concession was revealed specifically for the elderly and the infirm, when they break the fast while they are still able to fast. Then it was abrogated by the words of God Most High: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], so the concession was removed, except for those among them who are incapable. Al-Suddi said: ﴿And upon those who are able to do it﴾ means: upon those who were able to do it while in the state of youth, then they became old and are no longer able to fast. In his view the ruling is muhkam, and according to him the elderly must pay the ransom if they break the fast; and similarly from Ibn 'Abbas.

Malik said: I do not consider the ransom obligatory upon the weak elderly person; it is recommended for one who is able to pay it. According to him, the verse refers only to one whom Ramadan reaches while owing a fast from a previous time, for he was able during that period to fast but neglected it; so for him there is a ransom. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: the incapable elderly person must feed (a poor person). Al-Tabari transmitted from 'Ikrima that he used to read it: "And upon those who are able to do it, but they broke the fast."

The position of Malik, may God have mercy on him, and a group of scholars is that the measure of the ransom is one mudd for each poor person. Some said: the daily sustenance. Some said: a supper and a predawn meal. Sufyan al-Thawri said: half a sa' of wheat, or a sa' of dates or raisins.

The pronoun in "yutiqunahu" refers to "al-siyam" (fasting). It was also said that it refers to "al-ta'am" (food), but this is a weak view.

Scholars differed concerning the pregnant woman. Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas said: she pays the ransom and breaks the fast, with no make-up fast (qada') upon her. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Zuhri, Rabi'a, and Malik said: a pregnant woman makes up the fast when she breaks it, with no ransom upon her. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Mujahid said: she makes up the fast and pays the ransom when she breaks it. Likewise Malik said of the nursing woman that when she breaks the fast she makes up the fast and pays the ransom; this is the well-known position. In Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam's Mukhtasar, however, he said: there is no feeding upon the nursing woman.

As for God's words: ﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾, [the verse continues], Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, 'Ata', and al-Suddi said: what is meant is one who feeds two poor persons or more. Ibn Shihab said: one who adds feeding to fasting. Mujahid said: one who exceeds the mudd in feeding.

The second "khayr" is a comparative adjective (superlative sense of "better"), and likewise the third; the first "khayr" has taken the place of "maal" (wealth) or "naf' " (benefit). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "And fasting is better for you" as a substitute for ﴿and that you fast﴾. God's words ﴿if you know﴾ imply an urging to fast, that is: know this and fast.

Al-Suddi and al-Rabi' said: the comparison is that from iftar to its like, one does not eat, drink, or approach one's spouse; and when iftar time comes, one does not do these things if one has slept. Likewise it was for the Christians at first, and it was so at the beginning of Islam, then Allah abrogated it, by means of 'Umar and Qays ibn Sirmah, with the verses that come on that matter.

'Ata' said: the comparison is: "Fasting has been prescribed for you three days of every month."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
In some transmissions: "and the day of 'Ashura', as it was prescribed for those before you, three days of every month and the day of 'Ashura'." Then this was abrogated for this community by the month of Ramadan.

A group said: the comparison is "kutiba 'alaykum ka-ṣiyām" in general, that is, it has already been prescribed in the law of others. So "alladhīna" is general, covering the Christians and others. "La'allakum" expresses hope regarding them, and "tattaqūn" (you may become righteous). Al-Suddi said: its meaning is that you may be wary of eating, drinking, and intercourse after sleep, according to the view of those who interpreted it so. It was also said: "tattaqūn" is general, because fasting, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said, is a shield and protection and a cause of piety, since it kills desires.

"Ayyāman" is a second object of "kutiba", said by al-Farra'. It was also said: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time. It was also said: its accusative is governed by "al-siyām", but this is not good except on the view that "al-siyām" governs the kaf in "kamā", according to the one who estimates "ṣawman kamā". If "al-siyām" does not govern the kaf, it is ugly to separate the verbal noun from what it governs by something governed by another, and this is the case when the governing verb of the kaf is "kutiba". Some permitted that "ayyāman" be an adverb of time governed by "al-siyām". "Ma'dūdāt" (limited) was said to refer to Ramadan, and it was said to refer to the three days.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey﴾, the estimate is: "then he breaks his fast, and [owes] an equal number of other days." This is what they call fahwā al-khiṭāb (the implication of the address).

The scholars differed about the limit of the illness that permits breaking the fast. Some people said: whenever a person is in a state that makes him deserve the name "ill," breaking the fast is valid, by analogy with the traveler, who breaks his fast because of the cause of travel, even if it does not compel him to break it by necessity. This was said by Ibn Sirin. Most scholars said: if he has an illness that harms him and causes him pain, or he fears its prolongation, or he fears that fasting will increase it, breaking the fast is valid for him. This is the position of the leading companions of Malik, and by it they debate; as for the wording of Malik himself, it is: "the illness that is hard on a person and by which he is kept going." Al-Hasan said: if due to the illness he cannot pray standing, he breaks his fast. A group said: one breaks the fast due to illness only if the necessity of the illness itself compels him to break it; and whenever he can bear the necessity with it, he does not break it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him.

The scholars differed about which is better, breaking the fast or fasting, during travel. A group, al-Shafi'i, and Malik in some of what is narrated from him, said: fasting is better for one who is able. The bulk of Malik's school is free choice (al-takhyir). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, and others said: breaking the fast is better. Mujahid, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and others said: whichever of the two is easier is better. Ibn Hanbal and others disliked fasting while travelling. Ibn 'Umar said: whoever fasts while travelling must make it up while resident, and this is the position of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

Malik's position on recommending fasting for one who is able to do so, and shortening the prayer is good, because the obligation is discharged by the concession of the prayer while it remains occupied with the matter of fasting, and the correct course is to hasten to deeds. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: breaking the fast during travel is a firm obligation. Anas ibn Malik went to fasting and said: the concession was revealed only when we were hungry, setting out into hunger and rising into hunger.

The journey that is a journey of obedience, such as Hajj and jihad, is agreed upon. Connected to these two is the journey of maintaining family ties and seeking essential livelihood. As for travel for trade and permissible purposes, it is disputed between prohibition and permission, and the view of permission is more preponderant. As for travel for sinful purposes, it is disputed between permission and prohibition, and the view of prohibition is more preponderant. The distance of travel for breaking the fast according to Malik is where the prayer is shortened. The amount of that was disputed. Malik said: a day and a night; then he returned and said: forty-eight miles. It was also narrated from him: two days; and it was narrated from him in al-'Utbiyya: forty-five miles; in al-Mabsut: forty miles; in al-Madhhab: thirty-six miles; and in it: thirty. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Thawri said: breaking the fast is for a journey of three days; and outside the madhhab, one shortens [the prayer] at three miles or more.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-'iddatun﴾ (then a number) is nominative as the predicate of an inchoative; its estimate is: "so the ruling is, or so what is obligatory is, a number." It may also be nominative as an inchoative with the predicate following: the estimate is "so the number of the like of it is incumbent," and it may be: "so upon him is a number." It was disputed whether consecutiveness of these days is obligatory, on two views. "Ukhar" (other) does not take nunation according to Sibawayh, because it is diverted from al-alif wa-l-lam, since this form comes with alif and lam, as you say: "al-fadl" and "al-kibar," in which both diversion (al-'adl) and description (al-ṣifa) are combined. "Ukhar" is used in the verse, and "ukhrā" is not used, lest it be problematic as an attribute of "'iddah," and the rule is that the plural of non-rational things in such a case follows the pattern of the feminine singular, and from it is His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba': 10], and so on.

The majority of people read "yuṭīqūnahu" with a kasra on the ṭā' and sukūn on the yā'; the original is "yuṭawwiqūnahu," the vowel of the wāw was moved to the ṭā' and it was changed to yā' because of the kasra before it. Ḥumayd read "yaṭūqūnahu," which is on the original form, while the regular rule is the altered form. Ibn 'Abbas read "yuṭawwaqūnahu," meaning "they are charged with it." 'A'isha, Ṭawus, and 'Amr ibn Dinar read "yaṭṭawwaqūnahu" with a fatḥa on the yā' and a shadda on the ṭā' with fatḥa.

A group read "yuṭayyiqūnahu" with a ḍamma on the yā' and fatḥa on the ṭā' and shadda on the fatḥa-marked yā'. Ibn 'Abbas read "yuṭṭayyiqūnahu" with a fatḥa on the yā' and shadda on the ṭā' and shadda on the fatḥa-marked yā', meaning "they strain at it." al-Naqqash related it from 'Ikrimah. The doubling of the yā' in this word is weak.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, through the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, read "fidyatu ṭa'āmi masākīn" with the ransom construct-annexed. Hashim, from Ibn 'Amir, read "fidyatu ṭa'āmi masākīna" with nunation of "fidyah." The rest read "fidyatun" with nunation, "ṭa'āmu miskīn" in the singular, and this is a good reading because it clarifies the ruling regarding the day, since the plural "masākīn" would not reveal how many of them are due per day except from outside the verse. Abu 'Ali said: If you say, why is "miskīn" singular when the meaning is plural, since those who are able are plural and each one of them is obligated to a miskīn, so it would seem appropriate to make it plural as the able ones are plural? The answer is that the singular is good, because it is understood from the meaning that each one has a miskīn. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses—flog them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4]; the eighty are not distributed among all of them, rather each one receives eighty.

The interpreters differed about what is meant by the verse.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 181–184 (part 2 of 2):

(p-440) Mu'adh ibn Jabal, 'Alqama, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn 'Umar, al-Sha'bi, Salama ibn al-Akwa', and Ibn Shihab said: The obligation of fasting was thus upon people: whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished fed a poor person and broke the fast. Then this was abrogated (naskh) by the words of God Most High: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾ [al-Baqara: 185]. A group said: ﴿And upon those who are able to do it﴾ means: upon the elderly and the infirm who are able to do it, but with severe strain. So God permitted them the ransom (fidya) and breaking the fast. According to those who hold this view, the ruling is muhkam (firm, not abrogated). On this interpretation, the readings "yutiqunahu" and "yuttawwaqunahu" also fit.

Ibn 'Abbas said: This concession was revealed specifically for the elderly and the infirm, when they break the fast while they are still able to fast. Then it was abrogated by the words of God Most High: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], so the concession was removed, except for those among them who are incapable. Al-Suddi said: ﴿And upon those who are able to do it﴾ means: upon those who were able to do it while in the state of youth, then they became old and are no longer able to fast. In his view the ruling is muhkam, and according to him the elderly must pay the ransom if they break the fast; and similarly from Ibn 'Abbas.

Malik said: I do not consider the ransom obligatory upon the weak elderly person; it is recommended for one who is able to pay it. According to him, the verse refers only to one whom Ramadan reaches while owing a fast from a previous time, for he was able during that period to fast but neglected it; so for him there is a ransom. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: the incapable elderly person must feed (a poor person). Al-Tabari transmitted from 'Ikrima that he used to read it: "And upon those who are able to do it, but they broke the fast."

The position of Malik, may God have mercy on him, and a group of scholars is that the measure of the ransom is one mudd for each poor person. Some said: the daily sustenance. Some said: a supper and a predawn meal. Sufyan al-Thawri said: half a sa' of wheat, or a sa' of dates or raisins.

The pronoun in "yutiqunahu" refers to "al-siyam" (fasting). It was also said that it refers to "al-ta'am" (food), but this is a weak view.

Scholars differed concerning the pregnant woman. Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas said: she pays the ransom and breaks the fast, with no make-up fast (qada') upon her. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Zuhri, Rabi'a, and Malik said: a pregnant woman makes up the fast when she breaks it, with no ransom upon her. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Mujahid said: she makes up the fast and pays the ransom when she breaks it. Likewise Malik said of the nursing woman that when she breaks the fast she makes up the fast and pays the ransom; this is the well-known position. In Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam's Mukhtasar, however, he said: there is no feeding upon the nursing woman.

As for God's words: ﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾, [the verse continues], Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, 'Ata', and al-Suddi said: what is meant is one who feeds two poor persons or more. Ibn Shihab said: one who adds feeding to fasting. Mujahid said: one who exceeds the mudd in feeding.

The second "khayr" is a comparative adjective (superlative sense of "better"), and likewise the third; the first "khayr" has taken the place of "maal" (wealth) or "naf' " (benefit). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "And fasting is better for you" as a substitute for ﴿and that you fast﴾. God's words ﴿if you know﴾ imply an urging to fast, that is: know this and fast.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 181–184 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted and Majestic said:
﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it, the sin thereof is only upon those who alter it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾ ﴿But whoever fears from a testator an error or sin and brings about reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you that you may become righteous.﴾ ﴿[For] a limited number of days. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey [during them]—then an equal number of other days. And upon those who are able to fast [with difficulty] is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man. And whoever volunteers good—it is better for him. But to fast is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

The pronoun in "بَدَّلَهُ" (baddalahu, "altered it") refers to the bequest and the testator's instruction, and likewise in "سَمِعَهُ" (sami'ahu, "heard it"). It is possible that the pronoun in "سَمِعَهُ" refers to the command of Allah the Exalted in this verse, but the first opinion is more immediate for the reader. However, implicit in it is that the one who alters is aware of the prohibition and deliberately opposes it. The pronoun in "إثْمُهُ" (ithmuhu, "its sin") refers to the alteration (al-tabdil), and ﴿Hearing, Knowing﴾ are two attributes, with which nothing is hidden of the deviation of testators or the alteration of transgressors.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "مِن مُوصٍ" (min mūṣin) with a fatḥa on the wāw and a shadda on the ṣād. The rest read it with a sukūn on the wāw.

Al-janaf (الجَنَفُ) means inclination. al-A'sha said:
"It deviates from the stone of al-Yamamah, my she-camel, and I did not aim from its people for other than you."
And 'Amir al-Ramī al-Ḥaḍramī al-Muḥāribī said:
"The master intended, and they had deviated against us, and indeed we are visitors from their hostilities."

The meaning of the verse, according to Mujahid, is: whoever fears that the testator will act unjustly and cut off the inheritance of a group, and deliberately intends harm or does so without deliberate intent—this is janaf without sin. If he does it deliberately, it is janaf with sin. So the meaning is: whoever admonishes him in this matter and turns him back from it, thereby reconciling what is between him and his heirs, and what is among the heirs themselves, ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ toward the testator when the admonition takes effect and he returns from what he intended of harm, ﴿Merciful﴾ to him.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Qatadah, and al-Rabi' said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever fears—that is, knows, sees, and his knowledge reaches him after the death of the testator—that the testator has acted unjustly, deviated, and deliberately intended harm to some of his heirs, then he reconciles what has occurred among the heirs of disorder and discord, ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾, that is, the sin of the aforementioned alterer does not befall him, even though in his act there is some alteration and it is unavoidable, but it is an alteration for a benefit. The alteration that carries sin is only the alteration of desire. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar read "فَلا إثْمَ" ("then there is no sin") with the alif omitted from "عَلَيْهِ".

"Kutiba" (كُتِبَ) means it was obligated. "Al-siyam" (الصِيامُ, fasting) linguistically means abstention and leaving off moving from one state to another, and from it is the saying of al-Nabigha:
"Horses standing still and horses not standing still, under the dust, and horses chewing their bits."
That is: horses firm and holding still. And from it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26], that is, abstention from speech. And from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
"As if al-Thurayya were suspended in its station..."
That is, in the place of its settling and holding. And from it is his saying:
"So leave this, and drive away worry from yourself with a swift she-camel, steady when the day stands still and it travels in the heat..."
That is: the sun stood still from moving and remained fixed.

In the Shari'ah, fasting (al-siyam) is abstention from food and drink, accompanied by conditions, such as observing certain times and other things. Therefore it is among the unspecified (mujmal) terms of the Qur'an according to the scholars.
