A group said: ﴿And upon those who are able to do it﴾ means: upon the elderly and the infirm who are able to do it, but with severe strain. So God permitted them the ransom (fidya) and breaking the fast. According to those who hold this view, the ruling is muhkam (firm, not abrogated). On this interpretation, the readings "yutiqunahu" and "yuttawwaqunahu" also fit.

Ibn 'Abbas said: This concession was revealed specifically for the elderly and the infirm, when they break the fast while they are still able to fast. Then it was abrogated by the words of God Most High: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month﴾ [al-Baqara: 185], so the concession was removed, except for those among them who are incapable. Al-Suddi said: ﴿And upon those who are able to do it﴾ means: upon those who were able to do it while in the state of youth, then they became old and are no longer able to fast. In his view the ruling is muhkam, and according to him the elderly must pay the ransom if they break the fast; and similarly from Ibn 'Abbas.

Malik said: I do not consider the ransom obligatory upon the weak elderly person; it is recommended for one who is able to pay it. According to him, the verse refers only to one whom Ramadan reaches while owing a fast from a previous time, for he was able during that period to fast but neglected it; so for him there is a ransom. Al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa said: the incapable elderly person must feed (a poor person). Al-Tabari transmitted from 'Ikrima that he used to read it: "And upon those who are able to do it, but they broke the fast."

The position of Malik, may God have mercy on him, and a group of scholars is that the measure of the ransom is one mudd for each poor person. Some said: the daily sustenance. Some said: a supper and a predawn meal. Sufyan al-Thawri said: half a sa' of wheat, or a sa' of dates or raisins.

The pronoun in "yutiqunahu" refers to "al-siyam" (fasting). It was also said that it refers to "al-ta'am" (food), but this is a weak view.

Scholars differed concerning the pregnant woman. Ibn 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas said: she pays the ransom and breaks the fast, with no make-up fast (qada') upon her. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, al-Zuhri, Rabi'a, and Malik said: a pregnant woman makes up the fast when she breaks it, with no ransom upon her. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Mujahid said: she makes up the fast and pays the ransom when she breaks it. Likewise Malik said of the nursing woman that when she breaks the fast she makes up the fast and pays the ransom; this is the well-known position. In Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam's Mukhtasar, however, he said: there is no feeding upon the nursing woman.

As for God's words: ﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾, [the verse continues], Ibn 'Abbas, Tawus, 'Ata', and al-Suddi said: what is meant is one who feeds two poor persons or more. Ibn Shihab said: one who adds feeding to fasting. Mujahid said: one who exceeds the mudd in feeding.

The second "khayr" is a comparative adjective (superlative sense of "better"), and likewise the third; the first "khayr" has taken the place of "maal" (wealth) or "naf' " (benefit). Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "And fasting is better for you" as a substitute for ﴿and that you fast﴾. God's words ﴿if you know﴾ imply an urging to fast, that is: know this and fast.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 181–184 (part 1 of 2):

The Exalted and Majestic said:
﴿Then whoever alters it after he has heard it, the sin thereof is only upon those who alter it. Indeed, Allah is Hearing, Knowing.﴾ ﴿But whoever fears from a testator an error or sin and brings about reconciliation between them, there is no sin upon him. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for those before you that you may become righteous.﴾ ﴿[For] a limited number of days. So whoever among you is ill or on a journey [during them]—then an equal number of other days. And upon those who are able to fast [with difficulty] is a ransom: the feeding of a poor man. And whoever volunteers good—it is better for him. But to fast is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

The pronoun in "بَدَّلَهُ" (baddalahu, "altered it") refers to the bequest and the testator's instruction, and likewise in "سَمِعَهُ" (sami'ahu, "heard it"). It is possible that the pronoun in "سَمِعَهُ" refers to the command of Allah the Exalted in this verse, but the first opinion is more immediate for the reader. However, implicit in it is that the one who alters is aware of the prohibition and deliberately opposes it. The pronoun in "إثْمُهُ" (ithmuhu, "its sin") refers to the alteration (al-tabdil), and ﴿Hearing, Knowing﴾ are two attributes, with which nothing is hidden of the deviation of testators or the alteration of transgressors.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "مِن مُوصٍ" (min mūṣin) with a fatḥa on the wāw and a shadda on the ṣād. The rest read it with a sukūn on the wāw.

Al-janaf (الجَنَفُ) means inclination. al-A'sha said:
"It deviates from the stone of al-Yamamah, my she-camel, and I did not aim from its people for other than you."
And 'Amir al-Ramī al-Ḥaḍramī al-Muḥāribī said:
"The master intended, and they had deviated against us, and indeed we are visitors from their hostilities."

The meaning of the verse, according to Mujahid, is: whoever fears that the testator will act unjustly and cut off the inheritance of a group, and deliberately intends harm or does so without deliberate intent—this is janaf without sin. If he does it deliberately, it is janaf with sin. So the meaning is: whoever admonishes him in this matter and turns him back from it, thereby reconciling what is between him and his heirs, and what is among the heirs themselves, ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ toward the testator when the admonition takes effect and he returns from what he intended of harm, ﴿Merciful﴾ to him.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, Qatadah, and al-Rabi' said: the meaning of the verse is: whoever fears—that is, knows, sees, and his knowledge reaches him after the death of the testator—that the testator has acted unjustly, deviated, and deliberately intended harm to some of his heirs, then he reconciles what has occurred among the heirs of disorder and discord, ﴿then there is no sin upon him﴾, that is, the sin of the aforementioned alterer does not befall him, even though in his act there is some alteration and it is unavoidable, but it is an alteration for a benefit. The alteration that carries sin is only the alteration of desire. 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar read "فَلا إثْمَ" ("then there is no sin") with the alif omitted from "عَلَيْهِ".

"Kutiba" (كُتِبَ) means it was obligated. "Al-siyam" (الصِيامُ, fasting) linguistically means abstention and leaving off moving from one state to another, and from it is the saying of al-Nabigha:
"Horses standing still and horses not standing still, under the dust, and horses chewing their bits."
That is: horses firm and holding still. And from it is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾ [Maryam: 26], that is, abstention from speech. And from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:
"As if al-Thurayya were suspended in its station..."
That is, in the place of its settling and holding. And from it is his saying:
"So leave this, and drive away worry from yourself with a swift she-camel, steady when the day stands still and it travels in the heat..."
That is: the sun stood still from moving and remained fixed.

In the Shari'ah, fasting (al-siyam) is abstention from food and drink, accompanied by conditions, such as observing certain times and other things. Therefore it is among the unspecified (mujmal) terms of the Qur'an according to the scholars.

The kaf in His saying "kama" (كَما, "as") is in the accusative position as a description (na't), its estimate being: "kutiba ... [ṣiyāman] kamā", or as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), as if the statement were: "fasting has been prescribed for you, resembling what was prescribed for those before you."

Some grammarians said: the kaf is in the nominative position as a description of al-siyam, since its definiteness is not pure, because of the generality it contains, which the Shari'ah has explained; therefore it is permissible to describe it with "kamā", since only indefinites are described with it. It is thus like: "Fasting has been prescribed for you [ṣiyām]." This view is weak.

The interpreters differed on the point of the comparison. Al-Sha'bi and others said: the meaning is: "Ramadan has been prescribed for you as it was prescribed for the Christians." He said: Ramadan was prescribed for them, but they altered it, because they were cautious about it, by adding a day at its beginning and a day at its end, generation after generation, until they reached fifty days. It then became difficult for them in the heat, so they moved it to the winter season. Al-Naqqash said: "There is a report about this from Dughfal ibn Handhalah, al-Hasan al-Basri, and al-Suddi." It was also said: a king of theirs fell ill and vowed that if he recovered he would add ten days to it, then the last seven, then the last three, and they considered the addition good in exchange for the error in transmitting it.

Al-Suddi and al-Rabi' said: the comparison is that from iftar to its like, one does not eat, drink, or approach one's spouse; and when iftar time comes, one does not do these things if one has slept. Likewise it was for the Christians at first, and it was so at the beginning of Islam, then Allah abrogated it, by means of 'Umar and Qays ibn Sirmah, with the verses that come on that matter.

'Ata' said: the comparison is: "Fasting has been prescribed for you three days of every month."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
In some transmissions: "and the day of 'Ashura', as it was prescribed for those before you, three days of every month and the day of 'Ashura'." Then this was abrogated for this community by the month of Ramadan.

A group said: the comparison is "kutiba 'alaykum ka-ṣiyām" in general, that is, it has already been prescribed in the law of others. So "alladhīna" is general, covering the Christians and others. "La'allakum" expresses hope regarding them, and "tattaqūn" (you may become righteous). Al-Suddi said: its meaning is that you may be wary of eating, drinking, and intercourse after sleep, according to the view of those who interpreted it so. It was also said: "tattaqūn" is general, because fasting, as the Prophet, peace be upon him, said, is a shield and protection and a cause of piety, since it kills desires.

"Ayyāman" is a second object of "kutiba", said by al-Farra'. It was also said: it is in the accusative as an adverb of time. It was also said: its accusative is governed by "al-siyām", but this is not good except on the view that "al-siyām" governs the kaf in "kamā", according to the one who estimates "ṣawman kamā". If "al-siyām" does not govern the kaf, it is ugly to separate the verbal noun from what it governs by something governed by another, and this is the case when the governing verb of the kaf is "kutiba". Some permitted that "ayyāman" be an adverb of time governed by "al-siyām". "Ma'dūdāt" (limited) was said to refer to Ramadan, and it was said to refer to the three days.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey﴾, the estimate is: "then he breaks his fast, and [owes] an equal number of other days." This is what they call fahwā al-khiṭāb (the implication of the address).

The scholars differed about the limit of the illness that permits breaking the fast. Some people said: whenever a person is in a state that makes him deserve the name "ill," breaking the fast is valid, by analogy with the traveler, who breaks his fast because of the cause of travel, even if it does not compel him to break it by necessity. This was said by Ibn Sirin. Most scholars said: if he has an illness that harms him and causes him pain, or he fears its prolongation, or he fears that fasting will increase it, breaking the fast is valid for him. This is the position of the leading companions of Malik, and by it they debate; as for the wording of Malik himself, it is: "the illness that is hard on a person and by which he is kept going." Al-Hasan said: if due to the illness he cannot pray standing, he breaks his fast. A group said: one breaks the fast due to illness only if the necessity of the illness itself compels him to break it; and whenever he can bear the necessity with it, he does not break it. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him.

The scholars differed about which is better, breaking the fast or fasting, during travel. A group, al-Shafi'i, and Malik in some of what is narrated from him, said: fasting is better for one who is able. The bulk of Malik's school is free choice (al-takhyir). Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, and others said: breaking the fast is better. Mujahid, 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, and others said: whichever of the two is easier is better. Ibn Hanbal and others disliked fasting while travelling. Ibn 'Umar said: whoever fasts while travelling must make it up while resident, and this is the position of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

Malik's position on recommending fasting for one who is able to do so, and shortening the prayer is good, because the obligation is discharged by the concession of the prayer while it remains occupied with the matter of fasting, and the correct course is to hasten to deeds. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: breaking the fast during travel is a firm obligation. Anas ibn Malik went to fasting and said: the concession was revealed only when we were hungry, setting out into hunger and rising into hunger.

The journey that is a journey of obedience, such as Hajj and jihad, is agreed upon. Connected to these two is the journey of maintaining family ties and seeking essential livelihood. As for travel for trade and permissible purposes, it is disputed between prohibition and permission, and the view of permission is more preponderant. As for travel for sinful purposes, it is disputed between permission and prohibition, and the view of prohibition is more preponderant. The distance of travel for breaking the fast according to Malik is where the prayer is shortened. The amount of that was disputed. Malik said: a day and a night; then he returned and said: forty-eight miles. It was also narrated from him: two days; and it was narrated from him in al-'Utbiyya: forty-five miles; in al-Mabsut: forty miles; in al-Madhhab: thirty-six miles; and in it: thirty. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Thawri said: breaking the fast is for a journey of three days; and outside the madhhab, one shortens [the prayer] at three miles or more.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-'iddatun﴾ (then a number) is nominative as the predicate of an inchoative; its estimate is: "so the ruling is, or so what is obligatory is, a number." It may also be nominative as an inchoative with the predicate following: the estimate is "so the number of the like of it is incumbent," and it may be: "so upon him is a number." It was disputed whether consecutiveness of these days is obligatory, on two views. "Ukhar" (other) does not take nunation according to Sibawayh, because it is diverted from al-alif wa-l-lam, since this form comes with alif and lam, as you say: "al-fadl" and "al-kibar," in which both diversion (al-'adl) and description (al-ṣifa) are combined. "Ukhar" is used in the verse, and "ukhrā" is not used, lest it be problematic as an attribute of "'iddah," and the rule is that the plural of non-rational things in such a case follows the pattern of the feminine singular, and from it is His saying: ﴿O mountains, echo with him﴾ [Saba': 10], and so on.

The majority of people read "yuṭīqūnahu" with a kasra on the ṭā' and sukūn on the yā'; the original is "yuṭawwiqūnahu," the vowel of the wāw was moved to the ṭā' and it was changed to yā' because of the kasra before it. Ḥumayd read "yaṭūqūnahu," which is on the original form, while the regular rule is the altered form. Ibn 'Abbas read "yuṭawwaqūnahu," meaning "they are charged with it." 'A'isha, Ṭawus, and 'Amr ibn Dinar read "yaṭṭawwaqūnahu" with a fatḥa on the yā' and a shadda on the ṭā' with fatḥa.

A group read "yuṭayyiqūnahu" with a ḍamma on the yā' and fatḥa on the ṭā' and shadda on the fatḥa-marked yā'. Ibn 'Abbas read "yuṭṭayyiqūnahu" with a fatḥa on the yā' and shadda on the ṭā' and shadda on the fatḥa-marked yā', meaning "they strain at it." al-Naqqash related it from 'Ikrimah. The doubling of the yā' in this word is weak.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, through the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, read "fidyatu ṭa'āmi masākīn" with the ransom construct-annexed. Hashim, from Ibn 'Amir, read "fidyatu ṭa'āmi masākīna" with nunation of "fidyah." The rest read "fidyatun" with nunation, "ṭa'āmu miskīn" in the singular, and this is a good reading because it clarifies the ruling regarding the day, since the plural "masākīn" would not reveal how many of them are due per day except from outside the verse. Abu 'Ali said: If you say, why is "miskīn" singular when the meaning is plural, since those who are able are plural and each one of them is obligated to a miskīn, so it would seem appropriate to make it plural as the able ones are plural? The answer is that the singular is good, because it is understood from the meaning that each one has a miskīn. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses—flog them eighty lashes﴾ [al-Nur: 4]; the eighty are not distributed among all of them, rather each one receives eighty.

The interpreters differed about what is meant by the verse.

(p-440) Mu'adh ibn Jabal, 'Alqama, al-Nakha'i, al-Hasan al-Basri, Ibn 'Umar, al-Sha'bi, Salama ibn al-Akwa', and Ibn Shihab said: The obligation of fasting was thus upon people: whoever wished fasted, and whoever wished fed a poor person and broke the fast. Al-Shafi'i, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Mujahid said: she makes up the fast and pays the ransom when she breaks it. (p-442) His, Exalted and Glorified be He, saying:

﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down as guidance for mankind, and as clear proofs of guidance and the criterion. So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it; and whoever is ill or on a journey, then [let him fast] a number of other days. God desires ease for you, and does not desire hardship for you, and that you complete the period, and that you glorify God for having guided you, and that you may be thankful.﴾ ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near. I answer the supplication of the supplicant when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me, and let them believe in Me, that they may be rightly guided.﴾

"Shahr" (month): it is derived from "ishtihar" (fame), because it is well known and its knowledge is not difficult for anyone who seeks it. "Ramadan" has become the name, taken from a period in which there was "ramad" (scorching) and intense heat. Its name before that was "Natiq," just as "Rabi'" was named from the period of spring (rabi'), and "Jumada" from the period of freezing (jumud). Mujahid disliked saying "Ramadan" without saying "shahr Ramadan," as God Most High said, and he said: "Perhaps Ramadan is one of the names of God, Mighty and Majestic." The majority of readers read "shahrun" with a nominative ending (raf'), and its explanation is that it is the predicate of an inchoative (khabar mubtada'), i.e., "that is the month of..." It was also said that it is a substitute (badal) from "al-siyam," and it was said that it is an inchoative whose predicate is ﴿alladhi unzila fihi al-Qur'an﴾, and it was said that it is an inchoative whose predicate is ﴿fa-man shahida﴾, and ﴿alladhi unzila﴾ is an adjectival qualifier of it. Whoever says that the "siyam" in His saying ﴿kutiba 'alaykumu al-siyam﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183] refers to three days and 'Ashura', says here it is an inchoative; and whoever says that the "siyam" there is Ramadan, which is the counted days, says here it is either the predicate of the inchoative or a substitute for "al-siyam." Mujahid and Shahr ibn Hawshab read "shahra" with the accusative ending (nasb), and Abu 'Imara related it from Hafs from 'Asim, and Harun related it from Abu 'Amr; it is in the sense of an incitement (al-igra'), and it was said that it is governed by "tasumu" (you fast), and it was said that it is in the accusative of time (zarf). A group read with the assimilation of the "ra'" into the "ra'" (idghām), and this is not required by the rules, because two sukun letters would come together in it.

It was disputed concerning the sending down of the Qur'an in it. Al-Dahhak said: it was sent down concerning its obligation, its glorification, and its encouragement. It was said: the beginning of its revelation to the Prophet ﷺ was in it. Ibn 'Abbas said, as is related: it was sent down to the lowest heaven all at once on the night of the twenty-fourth of Ramadan, then Jibril used to bring it down piece by piece (rusulan rusulan) concerning commands, prohibitions and occasions. Wathila ibn al-Asqa' related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim descended on the first night of the month of Ramadan, the Torah on the sixth night of it passed, the Gospel on the thirteenth, and the Qur'an on the twenty-fourth."

Ibn Kathir omitted the hamza of "al-Qur'an" whether definite or indefinite wherever it occurs, and it has been said that its derivation in this reading is from "qarana," but that is weak.

"Huda" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "al-Qur'an," so the meaning is that the Qur'an in its entirety, consisting of the clear (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih), the abrogating (nasikh) and the abrogated (mansukh), is guidance. Then "al-bayyinat" from it were singled out and distinguished by mention, meaning the lawful and the unlawful, the admonitions, and all of the muhkam. The alif and lam in "al-huda" are for specific reference (al-'ahd), and the intended is the first sense. "Al-furqan" is that which differentiates between truth and falsehood. "Shahida" means "hadara" (was present), and "al-shahra" is in the accusative of time; the implied meaning is: whoever is present in the town during the month. Al-Hasan, 'Isa al-Thaqafi, al-Zuhri, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami and Abu Haywa read "fa-l-yasumhu" with the vowelling of the lam (taḥrik al-lam), and in the same way they read the imperative lam throughout the Qur'an on its original basis, which is kasra.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ubayda al-Salmani said: "man shahida" means whoever was present at the beginning of the month, having assumed he was resident at its start, shall complete his fasting, whether he travels afterwards or remains. One breaks the fast during travel only if Ramadan came upon him while he was on a journey. The majority of the community said: whoever witnesses the beginning or the end of the month shall fast for as long as he is resident. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: whoever witnesses the month, meeting the conditions of legal responsibility, not insane nor unconscious, shall fast it; and whoever Ramadan came upon while he was insane and he remained so throughout the month, there is no obligation of making up (qada') for him, because he did not witness the month in a state that requires fasting; and whoever became insane at the beginning or end of the month, he makes up the days of his insanity.

On this interpretation "al-shahr" is in the accusative as the direct object of "shahida." His saying, exalted is He, ﴿aw 'ala safar﴾, is in the sense of "aw musafiran," which is why it is conjoined to a noun. Mujahid and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said: "al-yusr" is breaking the fast during travel, and "al-'usr" is fasting during travel; the correct view is the general sense of the wording across all matters of religion, and the Prophet ﷺ explained this: "The religion of God is ease."

Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, and Abu 'Amr in some of what is related from him, read "wa-li-tukammilu" with a shadda on the mim, and it is related from both of them with the lightening (takhfif), as did the group. Or it is connected to a verb concealed after it, whose estimate is: "and so that you complete the period, this concession has been granted to you," and this is the view of some of the Kufans. It is also possible that this lam is the lam of command, and the waw is conjunctive, joining one sentence to another sentence.

Some people said: he magnifies from the sighting of the crescent until the imam leaves for the prayer. Sufyan said: it is the takbir on the day of al-Fitr. Malik said: it is from the moment a man leaves his house until the imam comes out.

Its wording according to Malik and a group of scholars is: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar" three times. Among the scholars are those who magnify, then recite tahlil and tasbih during the takbir, and among them are those who say: "Allahu akbaru kabira, wal-hamdu lillahi kathira, wa-subhana Allahi bukratan wa-asila." Other formulations have been said, and all are good with wide latitude, provided one begins with the takbir.

Then it was revealed." 'Ata' said: when ﴿And your Lord said: call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60] was revealed, some people said: "At what hour should we call?" Then ﴿wa-idha sa'alaka 'ibadi﴾ was revealed. This applies when the supplication is in what is permissible, without transgression, for transgression in supplication is forbidden. God Most High said: ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly; indeed He does not love the transgressors﴾ [al-A'raf: 55]. The exegetes said: that is, in supplication. The description of one whose supplication is answered is a description of good conduct, of keeping far from transgression, and of God's granting success to supplicate for what is within one's power. Consider that the best of mankind, the chosen Muhammad ﷺ, supplicated that his community's violence not be among them, and it was withheld from him, since the decree had already been determined otherwise.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is: let them seek that I answer them; this is the pattern of "istaf'ala," i.e., seeking a thing, except for what is irregular, such as "istaghna Allahu" (God is self-sufficient).

"A caller called: O you who answers to generosity, ∗∗∗ then no answerer answered him at that time."

That is: he did not answer him.

The majority read "yarshudun" with a fatha on the ya and a damma on the shin. A group read with a damma on the ya and a fatha on the shin. It is related from Ibn Abi 'Abla and Abu Haywa: a fatha on the ya and a kasra on the shin, with variation between them, and he read this reading and the one before it.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 187:**

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go to your wives. They are a garment for you, and you are a garment for them. Allah knows that you were deceiving yourselves, so He turned to you and pardoned you. So now, have relations with them and seek what Allah has decreed for you. Eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn. Then complete the fast until nightfall. And do not have relations with them while you are staying in devotion (i'tikaf) in the mosques. These are the limits of Allah, so do not approach them. Thus does Allah make His signs clear to the people, so that they may be mindful.﴾

The word "uhilla" (it is made lawful) implies that it was forbidden before that. "Layla" (night) is in the accusative as an adverb of time, and it is a generic noun (ism jins), which is why it is singular. Similar to this is the verse of 'Amir al-Ramiyy al-Hadrami al-Muharibi:

"They are the protectors, though they have acted unjustly against us, and we are truly visitors of their enmity."

"Al-rafath" is a metaphor for intercourse, because Allah, the Generous, speaks with indirect expressions. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. Ibn Mas'ud read it as "al-rufuth." Outside of this context, "rafath" means obscene speech, as in the words of the poet:

"... from idle talk and obscene speech..."

Abu Ishaq said: "Rafath" is everything that a man does with a woman, such as kissing, touching, and intercourse.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Or it is speech about these meanings. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Whoever performs this House's pilgrimage and does not commit rafath or sin, will return free of his sins as on the day his mother bore him."

The cause of this verse, according to Ibn 'Abbas and others, is that a group of Muslims deceived themselves and had relations with their wives after sleeping, or after the 'Isha' prayer, according to the differing reports. Among them was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who came to his wife and wanted her, but she said to him: "I have already slept." He thought she was pretending, so he had relations with her, and then he realized that she had indeed been asleep. Intercourse after one of the two had slept was forbidden. Al-Suddi said: this happened to him with a slave-girl of his. They said: 'Umar went and apologized to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Something similar happened to Ka'b ibn Malik al-Ansari, and so the beginning of the verse was revealed concerning them. Therefore it is abrogating (nasikha) the ruling, established in the prohibition of intercourse after sleep.

Al-Nahhas and Makki related that 'Umar slept and then had relations with his wife. In my view, this is far-fetched for 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. It is also reported that Surma ibn Qays (it is said: Surma ibn Malik, and it is said: Abu Anas Qays ibn Surma) slept before eating, and remained so without eating until he fainted during the following day, so the words of the Exalted, ﴿And eat and drink﴾, were revealed concerning him.

"Libas" (garment) originally refers to clothing. Then the closeness of a man and a woman, their mingling and their being bound together, was likened to this, as al-Nabigha said:

"When the bedfellow turns her neck, she falls toward him and becomes a garment upon him."

Al-Nabigha also said:

"I have worn people and wasted them, and after people I have wasted people."

He likened his mixing with them to garments. Al-Rabi' and others took this same direction in explaining "libas." Mujahid and al-Suddi said: "libas" means "sakan" (repose), i.e., some of them find repose in others.

These acts were named "ikhtiyan" (betrayal) because of the consequence and recompense of disobedience, since the one who commits them betrays himself and harms it.

"Wa tâba 'alaykum" means: from the disobedience in which you engaged. "Wa 'afa 'anku" may mean that He pardoned the very disobedience itself, which would be an affirmation and reassurance added to repentance. It may also mean that He pardoned what had obligated you to abstain from women in what follows, meaning He left it for you, as one says: "something is pardoned" (ma'fu 'anhu), i.e., left aside.

Ibn 'Abbas and others said: "Bashiruhunna" is a metaphor for intercourse, taken from the skin (bashra). We have already mentioned the word "al-an" (now) in the earlier account of the cow. ﴿And seek what Allah has decreed for you﴾: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba, 'Ikrima, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, al-Rabi', and al-Dahhak said its meaning is: seek offspring. It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and others that the meaning is: seek the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr). It was also said: the meaning is: seek leniency and ease. This was said by Qatada, and it is a good view. Al-Hasan, as reported from him, and Mu'awiya ibn Qurra read "wa-ittaba'u" (follow) from "ittiba'" (following). Ibn 'Abbas permitted this reading, but he preferred "ibtaghu" from "ibtighaa" (seeking).

﴿And eat and drink until it becomes distinct﴾: This was revealed because of Surma ibn Qays. "Hatta" (until) indicates the limit of the distinction. It is not valid for distinction to occur for someone, and eating to become forbidden for him, unless a measure of time has passed since the rising of dawn. "Al-khayt" (thread) is a metaphor and a comparison for the delicacy of the whiteness at first, and the thinness of the blackness bordering it. From this is the verse of Abu Dawud:

"When they saw him at dawn, and there appeared from the dawn a thread that shone..."

It is also narrated as "fa-nāran" (then it shone). Some exegetes said: "al-khayt" means the color. This does not hold in the language. What is meant, according to all scholars, is the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night. This is the explicit statement of the Prophet's ﷺ words to 'Adi ibn Hatim in his well-known hadith. The first "min" (from) indicates the starting point, and the second "min" indicates partitive meaning. "Al-fajr" (dawn) is derived from "tafajjur al-ma'" (the gushing of water), because it gushes forth little by little.

It is reported from Sahl ibn Sa'd and others among the Companions that the verse was revealed without the words "min al-fajr" (from the dawn). So some people made two threads, a white and a black one, until the words of the Exalted were revealed: "from the dawn." It is also reported that between the two ends of the period there was a year from one Ramadan to the next, the clarification being delayed until the time of need. 'Adi ibn Hatim placed two threads under his pillow and informed the Prophet ﷺ, who said to him: "Indeed your pillow is broad." It is also reported that he said to him: "Indeed you have a broad nape." These expressions have two interpretations.

Scholars differ regarding the limit by whose distinction abstention becomes obligatory. The majority said, and by this people acted, and the cities and generations followed it, and sound hadiths were transmitted about it: it is the spreading dawn that extends across the horizon to the right and to the left. Thus, with the rising of its beginning on the horizon, abstention becomes obligatory. This is what is implied by the hadiths of Ibn Mas'ud and Samura ibn Jundub.

It is reported from 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, Ibn 'Abbas, Talq ibn 'Ali, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-A'mash, and others that abstention becomes obligatory upon the distinction of dawn in the roads and on the tops of mountains. It is mentioned from Hudhayfa that he said: "I ate the pre-dawn meal with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and it was (like) day, except that the sun had not risen." It is also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he led the people in the dawn prayer and then said: "Now the white thread has become distinct from the black thread." Al-Tabari said: "What led them to this view is that they see that fasting is only in the daytime, and the day, for them, is from sunrise, because its end is its setting, so likewise its beginning is its rising."

Al-Naqqash related from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad that the day begins from the rising of dawn, and the words of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, indicate this: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114].

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The view in itself is sound, and its argument has been mentioned in the commentary on the words of the Exalted: ﴿and the alternation of the night and the day﴾ [al-Baqarah: 164]. But there is room for scrutiny in using this verse as evidence. As for one who eats while in doubt whether dawn has risen or not, according to Malik he must make up the fast.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾ are a command that implies obligation. "Ila" (until) indicates a limit. If what comes after it is of the same kind as what comes before it, then it is included in its ruling, as when you say: "I bought the farm up to its boundary." But if it is not of the same kind, as when you say: "I bought the farm up to the house," then what follows "ila" is not included in the limited thing.

'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, held that the words "until the night" imply a prohibition against continuous fasting (wisal). The Prophet ﷺ himself fasted continuously and forbade people from continuous fasting, and a group of scholars also fasted continuously.

It has already been stated that this verse abrogated the ruling in the words: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 183], according to the view of those who saw a resemblance in the prohibition of intercourse and eating after sleep, according to some of them, and after the 'Isha' prayer, according to others.

The night by which the fast is completed is the setting of the disk of the sun. Whoever breaks his fast while in doubt whether the sun has set, the well-known position of the school is that he must make up the fast and pay the expiation (kaffara). In the Thamaniya of Abu Zayd, he must only make up the fast, by analogy with doubt about dawn, and this is the view of a group of scholars. Ishaq and al-Hasan said: he has no obligation to make it up, like one who forgets.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And do not have relations with them while you are staying in devotion in the mosques﴾: a group said the meaning is: do not have intercourse with them. The majority said this applies to intercourse and what is less than it of the enjoyments one takes from women.

"'Akifun" means dwelling constantly, as one says: "'akafa 'ala al-shay'" when one persists at a thing, attentive to it. The rajaz poet said:

"... the Nabateans bent over playing al-fanzaja..."

Another poet said:

"And the daughters of the night remained around me, bent, like the bending of weeping women, among them is one thrown down..."

Abu 'Amr and Abu Hatim said: Qatada read "'akifun" without an alif, and i'tikaf is a sunna. Al-A'mash read "fi al-masjid" in the singular, and said: it is al-Masjid al-Haram.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and a group with him, said: there is no i'tikaf except in the mosques where Friday prayer is held. It is also reported from Malik that it is valid in every mosque, and one goes out to the Friday prayer as one goes out for necessary business. Some said: there is no i'tikaf except in one of the three mosques to which journeys are undertaken. Another group said: there is no i'tikaf except in the mosque of a prophet. Malik said: one does not perform i'tikaf for less than a day and a night, and whoever vows one of them is bound to the other. Sahnun said: whoever vows i'tikaf for a single night is not bound to anything. Another group said: whichever of the two one vows, one performs it, and nothing more is required.

Malik said: there is no i'tikaf except with fasting. Others said: one may perform i'tikaf without fasting. It is reported from 'A'isha that one may perform i'tikaf in any mosque.

"Tilka" (those) refers to these commands and prohibitions. "Al-hudud" (limits) are barriers between permission and prohibition. From this, the doorkeeper was called "haddad," because he prevents. From this also comes "al-hadd" (the widow in mourning), because she is prevented from adornment.

"Al-ayat" (signs) are the indicators guiding to the truth. "La'allahum" (so that they may) expresses hope concerning them. Its apparent meaning is general, but its meaning is specific to those whom Allah has facilitated for guidance, by the evidence of the verses which contain that Allah leads astray whom He wills.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 188–190:**

The Almighty said:

﴿And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, nor send it [as a bribe] to the rulers in order to consume a portion of people's wealth sinfully while you know [it to be wrong].﴾ ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons. Say: "They are times marked out for people and for the Hajj. Righteousness does not lie in entering houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah. Enter houses through their doors, and fear Allah that you may be successful."﴾ ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you, but do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors.﴾

The address is to the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is: "Let none of you consume another's property." The wealth is attributed to the pronoun of those being addressed, since each of them is forbidden from it. This is like the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿you kill yourselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 85].

This verse includes gambling, deception, usurpation, denying rightful dues, and other such things. It does not include cheating in a sale where the seller knows the true nature of what he is selling, because such cheating is, as it were, a gift from him.

Some said: the meaning of "﴿Do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly﴾" is: in frivolous pursuits, in singing-girls, in drink, and in idleness. On this view, the attribution of wealth is to the pronoun of its owners.

As for Allah's saying ﴿and send it [to the rulers]﴾: one says "adla al-rajul bil-hujjah" (the man put forward his argument), or "bil-amr alladhi yarju al-najah bihi" (with the matter by which he hopes for success), by way of comparison with one who lowers a bucket (dalw) into a well hoping to draw water with it.

Some said: the meaning of the verse is: you hasten to litigation over property when you know that the proof will stand for you, either because there is no evidence against the one who denies the claim, or because it is property held in trust, such as an orphan's wealth or the like, where the word of the one holding it is taken. On this view, the bā' in "bihā" (with it) is the bā' of cause.

It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is: you bribe the rulers with them in order to consume more of them. On this view, the bā' is the bā' of mere adherence (ilsāq mujarrad). This view is preferred, because rulers are the typical place of bribery, except for one who is protected (from it), and such people are few. Moreover, the two words are well-matched: "tudlū" (you lower) derives from "arsala al-dalw" (he lowered the bucket), and "al-rishwah" (bribe) derives from "al-rishā'" (the rope), as though the bribe is drawn out by it so that the need may be fulfilled.

"Tudlū" is in the jussive position, in coordination with "ta'kulū" (you consume). In the codex of Ubayy, it reads "wa-lā tudlū" (and do not send), with the negative particle repeated, and this reading supports the jussive form of "tudlū" in the recitation of the majority.

It has also been said that "tudlū" is in the accusative position as an adverbial of time (ẓarf). This is the doctrine of the Kufans, that the meaning of the adverb itself is what governs the accusative, whereas according to Sībawayh, what is put in the accusative in such a case is "an" (that) implied.

"Al-farīq" means a piece and a part. "Bil-ithm" means: with wrongdoing and transgression. It is called "ithm" because sin (ithm) is a meaning that attaches to its doer. "﴿And you know﴾" means: you are wrongdoers and sinners. This is an emphasis on disobedience and audacity.

As for Allah's saying ﴿They ask you about the crescent moons﴾: Ibn 'Abbās, Qatādah, al-Rabī' and others said: it was revealed in response to a question from some Muslim people to the Prophet (ﷺ) about the crescent. What is the benefit of its waning, its fullness, and its difference from the state of the sun?

The crescent, though one in reality, is a multiplicity in terms of its being a crescent in one month and not in another; so the crescent's states are gathered together in the sense of being crescent. The crescent lasts for two nights without disagreement, then it becomes a half moon (yaqmuru). It has been said: three nights. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: it remains a crescent until it becomes thin and curved like a fine thread. It has also been said: it remains a crescent until its light fills the sky, and this is on the seventh night.

As for his saying "mawāqīt" (times): its meaning is: for the due dates of debts, the expiry of waiting periods (ʿiddah), leases, and what is similar to these of the interests of servants. The appointed times of the Hajj are also known by them, and its months.

"Mawāqīt" is not declined (lā yanṣarif), because it is a plural with no singular counterpart, so it is a plural and the final limit of plurals, since it cannot be pluralised further. Ibn Abī Isḥāq recited "wal-ḥijj" with a kasrah on the ḥā' throughout the Qur'an. Regarding the phrase ﴿the pilgrimage to the House﴾ [al-Baqarah: 158] in Āl ʿImrān, Sībawayh said: "al-ḥajj" (with fatḥah) is like "al-radd" and "al-shadd", and "al-ḥijj" (with kasrah) is like "al-dhikr", and both are verbal nouns with the same meaning. It has also been said: the fatḥah is the verbal noun, and the kasrah is the noun.

As for Allah's saying ﴿Righteousness does not lie﴾: al-Barā' ibn ʿĀzib, al-Zuhrī, and Qatādah said: its occasion was that when the Anṣār performed Hajj or ʿumrah, they would bind themselves, by way of religious strictness, that nothing should come between them and the sky. So they would climb onto the roofs of their houses over the walls. It was also said that they would make openings in the backs of their houses, which they would enter through, and they would not enter by the doors. It was also said other things similar to this, which I have abridged. A man among them then came and entered through the door of his house, and he was reproached for it, and so the verse was revealed.

Ibrāhīm said: the people of the Ḥijāz used to do what was mentioned by a people. Al-Suddī said: "Some Arabs, who are called the Ḥums, did this. He said: The Prophet (ﷺ) entered through a door, and with him was a man of them, and that man stopped and said: 'I am a Ḥumsī (one who observes this custom).' The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: 'And I am a Ḥumsī,' and so the verse was revealed." Al-Rabī' narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered, and behind him was a man of the Anṣār, who entered and broke the custom of his people. The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Why did you enter while you are in iḥrām?" He said: "You entered, so I entered by your entering." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "I am a Ḥumsī," meaning: of a people who do not hold to this. The man said: "And my religion is your religion," and so the verse was revealed.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: the verse is a parable. The meaning is: righteousness is not that you ask the ignorant, but rather fear Allah and ask the scholars. This is like the saying: "I came to this matter by its door." Others than Abū ʿUbaydah said: the meaning is: righteousness is not that you go to extremes in asking questions about the crescents and other things, so that you approach matters in a way other than what is required. This is possible, but the first view is firmer. As for what al-Mahdawī and Makkī related from Ibn al-Anbārī, that the verse is a parable for sexual intercourse, it is far-fetched and alters the style of the speech.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī, and Nāfiʿ (with a variant from him) recited "al-buyūt" (the houses) with a kasrah on the bāʾ. Some readers recited "wa-lākinna al-birra" with the tashdīd of the nūn of "lākinna" and the naṣb of "al-birra". The discussion of "man" has already been given in His saying ﴿whoever believes in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. "Ittaqū" means: make between yourselves and His punishment a shield. "Laʿallakum" (so that you may) indicates hope with regard to humans. "Al-falāḥ" (success) is attaining the desired goal.

As for Allah's saying ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾: this is the first verse revealed about the command to fight. Ibn Zayd and al-Rabī' said: its meaning is: fight those who fight you, and refrain from those who refrain from you, and do not transgress in fighting those who do not fight you. This ceasefire is abrogated by the verse of Barāʾah and by His saying: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36].

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: fight those who are in the state of those who fight you, and do not transgress by killing women, children, monks, and their likes. On this view, the verse is muḥkam (not abrogated). Others said: the meaning is: do not transgress in fighting for other than the sake of Allah, such as for zealotry or for the pursuit of renown.

Abū ʿUbaydah said: the verse is a parable. The meaning is: righteousness is not that you ask the ignorant, but rather fear Allah and ask the scholars. This is like the saying: "I came to this matter by its door." Others than Abū ʿUbaydah said: the meaning is: righteousness is not that you go to extremes in asking questions about the crescents and other things, so that you approach matters in a way other than what is required. This is possible, but the first view is firmer. As for what al-Mahdawī and Makkī related from Ibn al-Anbārī, that the verse is a parable for sexual intercourse, it is far-fetched and alters the style of the speech.

Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir, al-Kisāʾī, and Nāfiʿ (with a variant from him) recited "al-buyūt" (the houses) with a kasrah on the bāʾ. Some readers recited "wa-lākinna al-birra" with the tashdīd of the nūn of "lākinna" and the naṣb of "al-birra". The discussion of "man" has already been given in His saying ﴿whoever believes in Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. "Ittaqū" means: make between yourselves and His punishment a shield. "Laʿallakum" (so that you may) indicates hope with regard to humans. "Al-falāḥ" (success) is attaining the desired goal.

As for Allah's saying ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾: this is the first verse revealed about the command to fight. Ibn Zayd and al-Rabī' said: its meaning is: fight those who fight you, and refrain from those who refrain from you, and do not transgress in fighting those who do not fight you. This ceasefire is abrogated by the verse of Barāʾah and by His saying: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36].

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and Mujāhid said: the meaning of the verse is: fight those who are in the state of those who fight you, and do not transgress by killing women, children, monks, and their likes. On this view, the verse is muḥkam (not abrogated). Others said: the meaning is: do not transgress in fighting for other than the sake of Allah, such as for zealotry or for the pursuit of renown.

قوله عزّ وجلّ:

﴿واقْتُلُوهم حَيْثُ ثَقِفْتُمُوهم وأخْرِجُوهم مِن حَيْثُ أخْرَجُوكم والفِتْنَةُ أشَدُّ مِن القَتْلِ ولا تُقاتِلُوهم عِنْدَ المَسْجِدِ الحَرامِ حَتّى يُقاتِلُوكم فِيهِ فَإنْ قاتَلُوكم فاقْتُلُوهم كَذَلِكَ جَزاءُ الكافِرِينَ﴾ ﴿فَإنِ انْتَهَوْا فَإنِ اللهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ ﴿وَقاتِلُوهم حَتّى لا تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌ ويَكُونَ الدِينُ لِلَّهِ فَإنِ انْتَهَوْا فَلا عُدْوانَ إلا عَلى الظالِمِينَ﴾ ﴿الشَهْرُ الحَرامُ بِالشَهْرِ الحَرامُ والحُرُماتُ قِصاصٌ فَمَنِ اعْتَدى عَلَيْكم فاعْتَدُوا عَلَيْهِ بِمِثْلِ ما اعْتَدى عَلَيْكم واتَّقُوا اللهَ واعْلَمُوا أنَّ اللهَ مَعَ المُتَّقِينَ﴾

Ibn Ishaq and others said: These verses were revealed concerning ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī and Wāqid, and this was the expedition (sariyya) of ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh. "Thaqiftumūhum" means: you gained decisive control over them, and you encountered them having power over them. It is said: "rajulun thaqifun laqif" when a man is firm (muḥkam, decisive) in handling the affairs he deals with. As for "akhrijūhum," al-Ṭabarī said: the address is to the Muhajirun, and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Rather, the address is to all the believers. It is said, "akhrajūkum" when they expelled some of them who are greater in rank, and they are the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muhajirun.

﴿Wal-fitnatu ashaddu minal-qatl﴾ means: the sedition (fitna) with which they came upon you, and which they sought to make you use to return to disbelief, is worse than killing.

(p-464) Mujahid said: that is, worse than the believer killing; for killing is lighter on him than sedition. Others said: rather, the meaning is: the sedition which they committed is more severe in violating the sanctities of truth than the killing which has been permitted to you, O believers, to inflict upon them.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "wal-fitna," that is, the disbelief and misguidance in which they are, is more severe in the Sacred Precinct and greater in crime than the killing about which they reproached you in the matter of Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ and the verse, the majority said: this was a ruling which was then abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of an earlier ruling by a later one), and they were commanded to fight in every place. Al-Rabīʿ said: it was abrogated by ﴿And fight them until there is no fitna﴾. Qatada said: it was abrogated by His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. Mujahid said: the verse is muḥkam (decisive, not abrogated), and it is not permissible to fight anyone in al-Masjid al-Haram unless he has fought first. Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Aʿmash recited: ﴿And do not kill them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they kill you therein. If they kill you, then kill them﴾, using "taqtulūhum" with qatl (killing) in the four [other] (readings) and there is no disagreement about the last, that it is "faqtulūhum." The meaning according to the reading of Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Aʿmash is: if some of you are killed, then kill them, you who remain. This is like His words: ﴿Many devoted followers fought alongside him, and they did not weaken﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 146], meaning: the rest did not weaken.

The "intihāʾ" (desisting) in this verse is entering into Islam, because the forgiveness and mercy of Allah are only with that.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitna﴾, He commanded fighting every polytheist in every place according to the view of those who regard it as abrogating. As for those who do not regard it as abrogating, they say: the meaning is: fight those about whom Allah said: ﴿If they fight you﴾. The first view is more evident, and it is a command to fight without condition, not conditional on the disbelievers initiating. The proof of this is His words: ﴿and the religion becomes entirely for Allah﴾. The fitna here is shirk and what follows it of harm to the believers, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatada, al-Rabīʿ, and al-Suddī said. And "al-dīn" here means obedience and the sharīʿa (law). Al-Aʿshā Maymūn ibn Qays said:

He subdued the Rabāb when they hated the religion,
Overtaking them with a raid and a charge.

The "intihāʾ" in this place, consistent with the general application of the verse to the disbelievers, may mean entering Islam, and it may also mean paying the jizya (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects under Muslim rule).

He called what is done to the wrongdoers "ʿudwān" (transgression) insofar as it is the recompense of transgression, since wrongdoing (ẓulm) includes transgression, and punishment is called by the name of the sin in more than one place. The wrongdoers are, according to one of the two interpretations, those who initiated fighting, and according to the other interpretation, those who remained in disbelief and fitna.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾ and the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujahid, Qatada, Muqsim, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others said: it was revealed concerning the ʿUmra of al-Qaḍiyya (p-466) and the year of al-Ḥudaybiya, because "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out performing ʿUmra until he reached al-Ḥudaybiya in the sixth year, and the disbelievers of Quraysh prevented him from the House, so he turned back. Allah promised him that He would cause him to enter it over them, and he entered it in the seventh year, and the verse was revealed about that." That is: the sacred month in which Allah gave you victory and admitted you into the Sanctuary over them is (the equivalent of) the sacred month in which they prevented you.

The meaning of "al-ḥurumāt qiṣāṣ" (the sacred violations are subject to retaliation) according to this interpretation is: the sanctity of the month, the sanctity of the city, and the sanctity of those in ihram when you were barred, are (answered) by the sanctity of the city and the month, and the people of the sanctuary when you entered.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: the verse was revealed because "the disbelievers asked the Prophet (ﷺ): Is fighting permitted in the sacred month? He informed them that it is not permitted to fight in it. They then intended to attack him in it, and those with him were killed when they expected that he would not defend himself in it. So the verse was revealed: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and the sacred violations are subject to retaliation﴾." That is, it is upon you in refraining from fighting, or in permitting (the sacred month) against them, in both respects. So whichever course they take, take it too. And "al-ḥurumāt" according to this view is the plural of ḥurma, in general: life, property, honour, and other things. So Allah permitted repelling them by the verse.

The first view is more prevalent.

A group said: His words: ﴿and the sacred violations are subject to retaliation﴾ are separate from what precedes them, and it is the beginning of a ruling which existed at the start of Islam, that whoever violated your sanctity, you could inflict upon him the like of what he inflicted upon you. Then that was abrogated by fighting.

Another group said: what the verse covers of transgression among the community of Muhammad, such as injuries and the like, has not been abrogated, and it is permissible for one who has been transgressed against in property or a wound to transgress in the like of what was done to him if that is concealed from him, and there is nothing between him and Allah in that. This was said by al-Shāfiʿī and others, and it is a narration in the Mālikī school.

Another group, among them Mālik, said: that is not permitted for him; matters of retaliation are reserved for the rulers. As for property, what covers it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you."

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan recited "wal-ḥurmāt" with a sukūn on the rāʾ.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you﴾ and the verse. There has been disagreement about the abrogation of this verse according to what has preceded. The retaliation for transgression is called transgression, as He said: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15], and so on in other places.

﴿And be mindful of Allah﴾: it was said that the meaning is: in not transgressing. It was also said: in not exceeding the like.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: this verse and what is similar in meaning were revealed in Mecca when Islam had not been made strong. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated and his religion became strong, the Muslims were commanded to refer their affairs to their rulers, and they were commanded to fight the disbelievers. Mujahid said: rather, this verse was revealed in Medina after the ʿUmra of al-Qaḍāʾ, and it is part of the gradual revelation (tadrīj) of the command to fight.

If they kill you, then kill them﴾, using "taqtulūhum" with qatl (killing) in the four [other] (readings) and there is no disagreement about the last, that it is "faqtulūhum." The meaning according to the reading of Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and al-Aʿmash is: if some of you are killed, then kill them, you who remain. This is like His words: ﴿Many devoted followers fought alongside him, and they did not weaken﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 146], meaning: the rest did not weaken.

The "intihāʾ" (desisting) in this verse is entering into Islam, because the forgiveness and mercy of Allah are only with that.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitna﴾, He commanded fighting every polytheist in every place according to the view of those who regard it as abrogating. As for those who do not regard it as abrogating, they say: the meaning is: fight those about whom Allah said: ﴿If they fight you﴾. The first view is more evident, and it is a command to fight without condition, not conditional on the disbelievers initiating. The proof of this is His words: ﴿and the religion becomes entirely for Allah﴾. The fitna here is shirk and what follows it of harm to the believers, as Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatada, al-Rabīʿ, and al-Suddī said. And "al-dīn" here means obedience and the sharīʿa (law). Al-Aʿshā Maymūn ibn Qays said:

He subdued the Rabāb when they hated the religion,
Overtaking them with a raid and a charge.

The "intihāʾ" in this place, consistent with the general application of the verse to the disbelievers, may mean entering Islam, and it may also mean paying the jizya (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects under Muslim rule).

He called what is done to the wrongdoers "ʿudwān" (transgression) insofar as it is the recompense of transgression, since wrongdoing (ẓulm) includes transgression, and punishment is called by the name of the sin in more than one place. The wrongdoers are, according to one of the two interpretations, those who initiated fighting, and according to the other interpretation, those who remained in disbelief and fitna.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾ and the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujahid, Qatada, Muqsim, al-Suddī, al-Rabīʿ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, and others said: it was revealed concerning the ʿUmra of al-Qaḍiyya (p-466) and the year of al-Ḥudaybiya, because "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out performing ʿUmra until he reached al-Ḥudaybiya in the sixth year, and the disbelievers of Quraysh prevented him from the House, so he turned back. Allah promised him that He would cause him to enter it over them, and he entered it in the seventh year, and the verse was revealed about that." That is: the sacred month in which Allah gave you victory and admitted you into the Sanctuary over them is (the equivalent of) the sacred month in which they prevented you.

The meaning of "al-ḥurumāt qiṣāṣ" (the sacred violations are subject to retaliation) according to this interpretation is: the sanctity of the month, the sanctity of the city, and the sanctity of those in ihram when you were barred, are (answered) by the sanctity of the city and the month, and the people of the sanctuary when you entered.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: the verse was revealed because "the disbelievers asked the Prophet (ﷺ): Is fighting permitted in the sacred month? He informed them that it is not permitted to fight in it. They then intended to attack him in it, and those with him were killed when they expected that he would not defend himself in it. So the verse was revealed: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and the sacred violations are subject to retaliation﴾." That is, it is upon you in refraining from fighting, or in permitting (the sacred month) against them, in both respects. So whichever course they take, take it too. And "al-ḥurumāt" according to this view is the plural of ḥurma, in general: life, property, honour, and other things. So Allah permitted repelling them by the verse.

The first view is more prevalent.

A group said: His words: ﴿and the sacred violations are subject to retaliation﴾ are separate from what precedes them, and it is the beginning of a ruling which existed at the start of Islam, that whoever violated your sanctity, you could inflict upon him the like of what he inflicted upon you. Then that was abrogated by fighting.

Another group said: what the verse covers of transgression among the community of Muhammad, such as injuries and the like, has not been abrogated, and it is permissible for one who has been transgressed against in property or a wound to transgress in the like of what was done to him if that is concealed from him, and there is nothing between him and Allah in that. This was said by al-Shāfiʿī and others, and it is a narration in the Mālikī school.

Another group, among them Mālik, said: that is not permitted for him; matters of retaliation are reserved for the rulers. As for property, what covers it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Return the trust to the one who entrusted you, and do not betray the one who betrayed you."

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan recited "wal-ḥurmāt" with a sukūn on the rāʾ.

As for His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you﴾ and the verse. There has been disagreement about the abrogation of this verse according to what has preceded. The retaliation for transgression is called transgression, as He said: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15], and so on in other places.

﴿And be mindful of Allah﴾: it was said that the meaning is: in not transgressing. It was also said: in not exceeding the like.

Ibn ʿAbbās said: this verse and what is similar in meaning were revealed in Mecca when Islam had not been made strong. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) emigrated and his religion became strong, the Muslims were commanded to refer their affairs to their rulers, and they were commanded to fight the disbelievers. Mujahid said: rather, this verse was revealed in Medina after the ʿUmra of al-Qaḍāʾ, and it is part of the gradual revelation (tadrīj) of the command to fight.

Ibn Ishaq and others said: These verses were revealed concerning ʿAmr ibn al-Ḥaḍramī and Wāqid, and this was the expedition (sariyya) of ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaḥsh. "Thaqiftumūhum" means: you gained decisive control over them, and you encountered them having power over them. It is said: "rajulun thaqifun laqif" when a man is firm (muḥkam, decisive) in handling the affairs he deals with. As for "akhrijūhum," al-Ṭabarī said: the address is to the Muhajirun, and the pronoun refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Rather, the address is to all the believers. It is said, "akhrajūkum" when they expelled some of them who are greater in rank, and they are the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muhajirun.

﴿Wal-fitnatu ashaddu minal-qatl﴾ means: the sedition (fitna) with which they came upon you, and which they sought to make you use to return to disbelief, is worse than killing.

(p-464) Mujahid said: that is, worse than the believer killing; for killing is lighter on him than sedition. Others said: rather, the meaning is: the sedition which they committed is more severe in violating the sanctities of truth than the killing which has been permitted to you, O believers, to inflict upon them.

It is also possible that the meaning is: "wal-fitna," that is, the disbelief and misguidance in which they are, is more severe in the Sacred Precinct and greater in crime than the killing about which they reproached you in the matter of Ibn al-Ḥaḍramī.

Al-Rabīʿ said: it was abrogated by ﴿And fight them until there is no fitna﴾. Qatada said: it was abrogated by His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5].
