(p-468) Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿And spend in the way of Allah, and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction. And do good; indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah. But if you are prevented, then [offer] what is easy of the hady (sacrificial animal). And do not shave your heads until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice. But whoever among you is ill, or has an ailment of the head, then [he must give] a ransom of fasting, or charity, or an act of worship (nusuk). And when you are safe, whoever enjoys [the benefit of] 'Umrah until Hajj, then [offer] what is easy of the hady. But whoever cannot find [one], then fast three days during the Hajj and seven when you return; those are ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

"Sabil Allah" (the way of Allah) here means jihad, but the wording extends afterwards to all of its paths.

Abu 'Ubaydah and a group said: the "ba'" in His words "bi-aydikum" is superfluous. The meaning is: "do not throw your hands into destruction."

The majority said: this is a figure of speech. One says: "So-and-so threw his hand into such-and-such a matter" when he surrenders, because the one who surrenders in battle throws down his weapon with his hand. Likewise, every helpless person does so in any act whatsoever. From this is the saying of 'Abd al-Muttalib: "By Allah, our throwing ourselves with our hands into death is indeed helplessness."

Others said: the meaning is: do not throw your souls into destruction with your hands, just as you say: "Do not spoil your condition by your own opinion."

"Al-tahlukah" with a damma on the lam is a verbal noun from halaka (to perish). Al-Khalil read "al-tahlikah" with a kasra on the lam; it is on the pattern mif'alah from hallaka with a shadda on the lam.

It is narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari that he was at Constantinople when a man charged into the enemy's army. Some people said: "He has thrown himself with his hand into destruction." Abu Ayyub said: "No. This verse was revealed about the Ansar when Islam had become dominant and they wanted to abandon jihad and tend to their wealth. As for this man, he is the one of whom Allah said: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207]."

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, and the majority of people said: the meaning is: do not throw yourselves with your hands by abandoning spending in the way of Allah and fearing poverty, so that a man says, "I have nothing to spend."

Others said: the meaning is: do not despair of repentance.

al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and 'Ubaydah al-Salmani said: the verse concerns a man who says, "I have gone too far in sins, so there is no benefit in repentance," and so he plunges further after that.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: the meaning is: do not travel in jihad without provisions. Some people did this, and it led them to being cut off on the road or becoming a burden on people.

As for His words "and do good": it has been said that its meaning is: in your deeds, by complying with acts of obedience, and this has been narrated from some of the Companions.

It has also been said: the meaning is: be good in spending in the way of Allah and in charities. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

'Ikrimah said: the meaning is: think well of Allah.

(p-470) As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾, Ibn Zayd, al-Sha'bi, and others said: completing them is that you do not cancel them, and that you complete them once you have begun them. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: completing them is that you enter into ihram for both from the dwelling of your family. 'Imran ibn Husayn did this. Sufyan al-Thawri said: completing them is that you set out intending them alone, not for trade or any other purpose, and this is supported by His words "for Allah." Qatadah and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: completing them is that you enter into ihram for 'Umrah and perform it outside the months of Hajj, and that you complete the Hajj without deficiency and without compensating with a sacrifice (dam).

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, says:

This is based on the view that the dam in Hajj and 'Umrah is a compensation for a deficiency, which is the view of Malik and a group of scholars. Abu Hanifah and his companions hold that a large number of sacrifices is a perfection and an addition, and the more sacrifices that are incumbent on them, the better it is. They argued with the report that it was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which Hajj is best?" He said: "The 'ajj and the thajj" (raising the voice in talbiyah and shedding blood through sacrifice). Malik and those who follow his view consider the thajj to be voluntary.

A sect said: completing them is that you perform each of them separately, Hajj alone and 'Umrah alone, without combining them (qiran). This is based on the view that ifrad (performing Hajj alone) is the best. Another sect said: qiran is best, and that is completion according to them. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Alqamah, Ibrahim, and others said: completing them is that you perform their rites fully, including the sacrifices that are required in them.

The obligatory acts (furud) of Hajj are: the intention, the ihram, the tawaf connected to the sa'y, the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah according to us (contrary to Abu Hanifah), standing at 'Arafah, and the stoning of the jamrah according to the view of Ibn al-Majishun.

As for the acts of 'Umrah: intention, ihram, tawaf and sa'y. Scholars differed about whether 'Umrah is obligatory.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is a obligatory sunnah which should not be abandoned, like witr (the odd prayer), and according to us it is once a year. This is the view of the majority of his companions.

Ibn al-Mundhir in al-Ishraf narrated from the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) that it is not obligatory according to them.

Some scholars of Qayrawan and Baghdad narrated from Abu Hanifah that he considers it obligatory like Hajj, and that it is a sunnah. Ibn Mas'ud and the majority of scholars said so, and al-Tabari reported an explicit text from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on this. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Sha'bi, and a group of the Successors that it is obligatory like the fard. Ibn al-Jahm of the Malikis said the same. Masruq said: Hajj and 'Umrah are both fard; 'Umrah was revealed alongside Hajj in the same way that zakat is alongside prayer.

al-Sha'bi and Abu Hayawah read "wa-al-'umrata lillah" with a raised 'umrah, as a new sentence (qat' wa-ibtida'). Ibn Abi Ishaq read "al-Hijj" with a kasra on the ha'. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is: "And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah to the House for Allah," and it was narrated from him: "And establish the Hajj and the 'Umrah to the House," and other readings were narrated from him which are like tafsir.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But if you are prevented, then [offer] what is easy of the hady﴾. 'Alqamah, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, and others said: the verse concerns one who is prevented by sickness, not by an enemy. Ibn 'Abbas and others said the opposite. The well-known usage in the language is: uhsira (passive) by sickness and hasira by the enemy. In al-Mujmal by Ibn Faris: hussira by sickness and uhsira by the enemy. Al-Farra' said: they have the same meaning for sickness and enemy.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, says:

The correct view is that "hasira" is only used for what surrounds and encompasses, so an enemy or water or the like may be the one who "hasira" (encloses), but sickness does not enclose. "Uhsira" means: the thing was made to have an enclosure, like "aqbara" (made into a grave) and "ahma" (made into a protected place) and the like. So sickness, water, the enemy, and other things may be "muhsar" (one who is made to be enclosed), not one who encloses. Do you not see that the enemy was the one who "muhsar" (enclosed the Muslims) in the year of al-Hudaybiyah? This verse was revealed about that, according to the majority of the exegetes. The majority of people agreed that one who is prevented by an enemy is released from ihram where he is prevented and slaughters his hady if he has one, and shaves his head. Qatadah and Ibrahim said: he sends his hady if he is able, and when it reaches its place he becomes free, and there is no qada' (making up) upon him according to all, except that if it was a necessity, then the obligation of Islam (Hajj) falls upon him. Ibn al-Majishun said: the obligation of Islam does not fall upon him, since he performed it when he was prevented; this view is weak and has no basis. Ashhab said: one who is prevented by an enemy must give a hady because of the prevention. Ibn al-Qasim said: he does not give any hady unless he had a hady with him and wanted to slaughter it. This was mentioned by Ibn Abi Zayd. 'Ata' and others said: one prevented by sickness is like one prevented by an enemy.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and the majority of scholars said: one prevented by sickness is released only by the House (the Ka'bah), and he remains [in ihram] until he recovers, even if this takes years. When he reaches the House after the Hajj has passed, he stops the talbiyah at the beginning of the Haram and releases himself by 'Umrah. Then he has an obligation of qada' Hajj, and in it there is the hady. It has also been said that the hady is obligatory at the time of the prevention first. Ibn 'Abbas did not consider one prevented by sickness to be included in this verse, and he said: if the sick person has no hady with him, he is released where he is detained; if he has a hady with him, he is not released until the hady reaches its place, and then there is no qada' upon him. He said: Allah only said ﴿And when you are safe﴾, and safety is only from the enemy, so the sick person is not in the verse.

"Ma" is in the nominative position, meaning: then what is obligatory is what is easy, or: upon you is what is easy. It may also be in the accusative position, meaning: then slaughter, or: then give hady.

﴿Fa-ma istaysara﴾ according to the majority of scholars means: a sheep (shah). Ibn 'Umar and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: "what is easy" is a camel, not less than a camel, or a cow, not less than a cow.

al-Hasan said: the highest hady is a camel, its middle is a cow, and its lowest is a sheep.

"Al-hady" is the plural of hadyah, like jadyat al-sarj (the knob of a saddle), and it is the brad (a kind of small nail), whose plural is judy. It is possible that "al-hady" is a verbal noun named as such, like "al-rahn" and the like, so it applies to the singular and the plural. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: I know of no parallel to this word.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not shave your heads﴾ and what follows, the address is to the whole community: the one prevented and the one not prevented. Some scholars consider it addressed to those who are prevented only.

The place of the hady is where its slaughter is permitted. That is for one not prevented: at Mina; and for one prevented by an enemy: where he is prevented, if it is not possible to send it.

As for the sick: if he has a hady, he sends it to its place.

The order is: the pilgrim throws the jamrah, then slaughters, then shaves, then performs the tawaf al-ifadah. If a man slaughters before the stoning or shaves before slaughtering, there is no blame, according to the hadith, and no dam. Some said: there is no blame in Hajj, but he sheds a dam. 'Abd al-Malik ibn al-Majishun, one of our companions, said: if he shaves before he slaughters, let him give a hady. If a man shaves before he stones, there is a dam according to a single opinion in the school (madhhab). Ibn al-Mawwaz said, from Malik: the razor passes over his head after the stoning, and there is no dam in that according to Abu Hanifah and a group with him. al-Zuhri, al-A'raj, and Abu Hayawah read "al-hadiyy" with a kasra on the dal and a shadda on the ya' in both places; its singular is hadiyyah. This reading was narrated from 'Asim.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But whoever among you is ill﴾ and what follows, the meaning is: so he shaves to remove the harm, then there is a ransom (fidyah). This is the implication of the address according to most of the usulis (scholars of legal theory).

"This verse was revealed about Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw him with his head covered with lice, and he ordered him to shave, and the concession was revealed."

"Fidyah" is in the nominative case as the predicate of the subject.

Fasting, according to Malik, 'Ata', Mujahid, Ibrahim, and others, and all the companions of Malik, is three days. Charity is six poor persons, each poor person receiving half a sa', which is two mudds by the mudd of the Prophet (ﷺ). The nusuk is a sheep, by consensus, and whoever sacrifices something better than it, it is better.

al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: fasting is ten days and feeding is ten poor persons. al-Zuhri read "aw nusukun" with a sukun on the sin. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid said: the nusuk is a sheep; if he does not find one, its value is taken, and with it food is bought and given to the poor, two mudds for each poor person; if he does not find the value, he makes it known, and makes known what food is bought with it, and fasts one day for each mudd.

'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: all of that is wherever he wishes. Ibrahim said the same, and this is the position of Malik and his companions, except Ibn al-Jahm, who said: nusuk is only in Makkah. 'Ata', in some of what was narrated from him, and the people of opinion, said: the nusuk is in Makkah, and fasting and feeding are wherever he wishes. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Tawus, 'Ata' also, Mujahid, and al-Shafi'i said: the nusuk and feeding are in Makkah, and fasting is wherever he wishes. The one who pays the ransom has the choice among these three, as Malik and others said regarding everything in the Qur'an, or that it is by choice.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when you are safe﴾. 'Alqamah and 'Urwah said: the meaning is: when you recover from your sickness. Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and others said: when you are safe from your fear of the enemy that prevents you. This is closer to the wording, unless one imagines fear of sickness, in which case safety is from it.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever enjoys [the benefit of] 'Umrah until Hajj﴾ and what follows.

Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, 'Alqama and Ibrahim said: The verse concerns those who are prevented (al-muhsarun) rather than those who are free to go their way (al-mukhalla sabiluhum). The form of the tamattu' (the combining of 'umrah and hajj, lit. "enjoyment") according to Ibn al-Zubayr is that a man is prevented until the hajj passes him by; then he reaches the House, exits ihram by means of 'umrah, and performs the hajj in the following year as a make-up (qada'). So he has enjoyed the period between the 'umrah and the make-up hajj. The form of the muhsar tamattu' according to others is that he is prevented, exits ihram without 'umrah, and delays it until the next year, when he performs 'umrah in the months of hajj and performs hajj in that same year.

Ibn 'Abbas and a group of scholars said: The verse concerns those who are prevented and others who are free to go their way. The form of tamattu' is that the following six conditions come together in the person: that he performs 'umrah in the months of hajj; that he is not among the residents of al-Masjid al-Haram; that he exits ihram; that he initiates the hajj in that same year without returning to his homeland, or to something equal to it in distance. This is the view of Malik and his companions.

It has been disputed why it is called tamattu'. Ibn al-Qasim said: Because he enjoys everything that is forbidden to the one in ihram, from the time of his exit from ihram in 'umrah until the time he initiates the hajj. Others said: It is called tamattu' because he enjoys the dropping of one of the two journeys. This is because the proper form of 'umrah is that it be intended with a journey, and likewise the hajj; so when he enjoys by dropping one of them, God obligates him to an offering (hady), like the qarin who combines hajj and 'umrah in a single journey.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
This is a hardship upon one who comes to Makkah from the other regions, since he has dropped a journey; whereas the Makkan, his situation does not require a journey, either for 'umrah or for hajj, because he is in the place of hajj. Therefore he is not obligated to anything, because he has not dropped anything. And whoever says that the name tamattu' and its ruling arise only from enjoying women, perfume and other things, it is refuted by the fact that God's words "So whoever enjoys [the 'umrah] until the hajj" encompass the Makkan and others equally in analogy. How then would the hardship fall on the stranger, who is more excused, obligating him to an offering, while the Makkan is not required to do this? Thus by this consideration it is preferred that tamattu' is only for the sake of dropping one of the two journeys.

However, Abu 'Ubayd said in his book on the abrogating and abrogated (al-Nasikh wa'l-Mansukh): 'Umrah in the months of hajj is prohibited for the Makkan; it is not permitted for him, and God permitted it for the one arriving, due to the length of his remaining in ihram, and He attached the concession to the offering.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:
This is a hardship upon the people of Makkah. By this consideration it would be fitting that tamattu' is from the aspect of making lawful what is not permitted to the one in ihram; but this is an anomalous view on which no reliance is placed.

The majority of the community holds that 'umrah in the months of hajj is permissible for the Makkan, and there is no offering upon him. Abu 'Ubayd mentioned both views from Ibn 'Umar, and he relied on him regarding the view that agreed with his own. It has been related by al-Tabari from Ibn 'Abbas (p-477) that he said: "O people of Makkah, there is no tamattu' for you. God has made it lawful for the people of the distant lands and forbade it to you. Indeed one of you crosses a valley and then enters ihram for 'umrah." The meaning of this is that when they enter ihram they remain in it until the hajj.

Al-Suddi said: The one who enjoys is the one who turns the hajj into 'umrah (fasKh al-hajj fi'l-'umrah), and that is not permitted according to Malik. In Sahih Muslim is the hadith of Suraqa ibn Malik, who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, is the fasKh of hajj into 'umrah for us alone or forever? He said: 'Rather, forever and ever.'"

The condition for the tamattu' is only that he exit ihram in the months of hajj, because these are a period which the hajj possesses; so whoever is in ihram during them, his right is to connect the ihram to the hajj. In Sahih Muslim are the hadiths fully covering this meaning. The position of 'Umar, and the statement of Abu Dharr, that the enjoyment of women and the enjoyment of hajj are specific to the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), are also relevant. Tawus said: Whoever performs 'umrah outside the months of hajj and then remains until he performs hajj in the same year is a mutamatti'. Al-Hasan ibn Abi'l-Hasan said: "Whoever performs 'umrah after the Day of Sacrifice in the rest of the year is a mutamatti'." These two are anomalous views, which no scholar has agreed with. The discussion of what is easy of the offering (ma istaysara min al-hady) has already preceded.

(p-468) Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says:

﴿And spend in the way of Allah, and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction. And do good; indeed, Allah loves the doers of good.﴾ ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah. But if you are prevented, then [offer] what is easy of the hady (sacrificial animal). And do not shave your heads until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice. But whoever among you is ill, or has an ailment of the head, then [he must give] a ransom of fasting, or charity, or an act of worship (nusuk). And when you are safe, whoever enjoys [the benefit of] 'Umrah until Hajj, then [offer] what is easy of the hady. But whoever cannot find [one], then fast three days during the Hajj and seven when you return; those are ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

"Sabil Allah" (the way of Allah) here means jihad, but the wording extends afterwards to all of its paths.

Abu 'Ubaydah and a group said: the "ba'" in His words "bi-aydikum" is superfluous. The meaning is: "do not throw your hands into destruction."

The majority said: this is a figure of speech. One says: "So-and-so threw his hand into such-and-such a matter" when he surrenders, because the one who surrenders in battle throws down his weapon with his hand. Likewise, every helpless person does so in any act whatsoever. From this is the saying of 'Abd al-Muttalib: "By Allah, our throwing ourselves with our hands into death is indeed helplessness."

Others said: the meaning is: do not throw your souls into destruction with your hands, just as you say: "Do not spoil your condition by your own opinion."

"Al-tahlukah" with a damma on the lam is a verbal noun from halaka (to perish). Al-Khalil read "al-tahlikah" with a kasra on the lam; it is on the pattern mif'alah from hallaka with a shadda on the lam.

It is narrated from Abu Ayyub al-Ansari that he was at Constantinople when a man charged into the enemy's army. Some people said: "He has thrown himself with his hand into destruction." Abu Ayyub said: "No. This verse was revealed about the Ansar when Islam had become dominant and they wanted to abandon jihad and tend to their wealth. As for this man, he is the one of whom Allah said: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 207]."

Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, and the majority of people said: the meaning is: do not throw yourselves with your hands by abandoning spending in the way of Allah and fearing poverty, so that a man says, "I have nothing to spend."

Others said: the meaning is: do not despair of repentance.

al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and 'Ubaydah al-Salmani said: the verse concerns a man who says, "I have gone too far in sins, so there is no benefit in repentance," and so he plunges further after that.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: the meaning is: do not travel in jihad without provisions. Some people did this, and it led them to being cut off on the road or becoming a burden on people.

As for His words "and do good": it has been said that its meaning is: in your deeds, by complying with acts of obedience, and this has been narrated from some of the Companions.

It has also been said: the meaning is: be good in spending in the way of Allah and in charities. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

'Ikrimah said: the meaning is: think well of Allah.

(p-470) As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah for Allah﴾, Ibn Zayd, al-Sha'bi, and others said: completing them is that you do not cancel them, and that you complete them once you have begun them. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: completing them is that you enter into ihram for both from the dwelling of your family. 'Imran ibn Husayn did this. Sufyan al-Thawri said: completing them is that you set out intending them alone, not for trade or any other purpose, and this is supported by His words "for Allah." Qatadah and al-Qasim ibn Muhammad said: completing them is that you enter into ihram for 'Umrah and perform it outside the months of Hajj, and that you complete the Hajj without deficiency and without compensating with a sacrifice (dam).

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, says:

This is based on the view that the dam in Hajj and 'Umrah is a compensation for a deficiency, which is the view of Malik and a group of scholars. Abu Hanifah and his companions hold that a large number of sacrifices is a perfection and an addition, and the more sacrifices that are incumbent on them, the better it is. They argued with the report that it was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Which Hajj is best?" He said: "The 'ajj and the thajj" (raising the voice in talbiyah and shedding blood through sacrifice). Malik and those who follow his view consider the thajj to be voluntary.

A sect said: completing them is that you perform each of them separately, Hajj alone and 'Umrah alone, without combining them (qiran). This is based on the view that ifrad (performing Hajj alone) is the best. Another sect said: qiran is best, and that is completion according to them. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Alqamah, Ibrahim, and others said: completing them is that you perform their rites fully, including the sacrifices that are required in them.

The obligatory acts (furud) of Hajj are: the intention, the ihram, the tawaf connected to the sa'y, the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah according to us (contrary to Abu Hanifah), standing at 'Arafah, and the stoning of the jamrah according to the view of Ibn al-Majishun.

As for the acts of 'Umrah: intention, ihram, tawaf and sa'y. Scholars differed about whether 'Umrah is obligatory.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is a obligatory sunnah which should not be abandoned, like witr (the odd prayer), and according to us it is once a year. This is the view of the majority of his companions.

Ibn al-Mundhir in al-Ishraf narrated from the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) that it is not obligatory according to them.

Some scholars of Qayrawan and Baghdad narrated from Abu Hanifah that he considers it obligatory like Hajj, and that it is a sunnah. Ibn Mas'ud and the majority of scholars said so, and al-Tabari reported an explicit text from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on this. It is narrated from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Sha'bi, and a group of the Successors that it is obligatory like the fard. Ibn al-Jahm of the Malikis said the same. Masruq said: Hajj and 'Umrah are both fard; 'Umrah was revealed alongside Hajj in the same way that zakat is alongside prayer.

al-Sha'bi and Abu Hayawah read "wa-al-'umrata lillah" with a raised 'umrah, as a new sentence (qat' wa-ibtida'). Ibn Abi Ishaq read "al-Hijj" with a kasra on the ha'. In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud the reading is: "And complete the Hajj and the 'Umrah to the House for Allah," and it was narrated from him: "And establish the Hajj and the 'Umrah to the House," and other readings were narrated from him which are like tafsir.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿But if you are prevented, then [offer] what is easy of the hady﴾. 'Alqamah, 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr, and others said: the verse concerns one who is prevented by sickness, not by an enemy. Ibn 'Abbas and others said the opposite. The well-known usage in the language is: uhsira (passive) by sickness and hasira by the enemy. In al-Mujmal by Ibn Faris: hussira by sickness and uhsira by the enemy. Al-Farra' said: they have the same meaning for sickness and enemy.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, says:

The correct view is that "hasira" is only used for what surrounds and encompasses, so an enemy or water or the like may be the one who "hasira" (encloses), but sickness does not enclose. "Uhsira" means: the thing was made to have an enclosure, like "aqbara" (made into a grave) and "ahma" (made into a protected place) and the like. So sickness, water, the enemy, and other things may be "muhsar" (one who is made to be enclosed), not one who encloses. Do you not see that the enemy was the one who "muhsar" (enclosed the Muslims) in the year of al-Hudaybiyah? This verse was revealed about that, according to the majority of the exegetes. The majority of people agreed that one who is prevented by an enemy is released from ihram where he is prevented and slaughters his hady if he has one, and shaves his head. Qatadah and Ibrahim said: he sends his hady if he is able, and when it reaches its place he becomes free, and there is no qada' (making up) upon him according to all, except that if it was a necessity, then the obligation of Islam (Hajj) falls upon him. Ibn al-Majishun said: the obligation of Islam does not fall upon him, since he performed it when he was prevented; this view is weak and has no basis. Ashhab said: one who is prevented by an enemy must give a hady because of the prevention. Ibn al-Qasim said: he does not give any hady unless he had a hady with him and wanted to slaughter it. This was mentioned by Ibn Abi Zayd. 'Ata' and others said: one prevented by sickness is like one prevented by an enemy.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and the majority of scholars said: one prevented by sickness is released only by the House (the Ka'bah), and he remains [in ihram] until he recovers, even if this takes years. When he reaches the House after the Hajj has passed, he stops the talbiyah at the beginning of the Haram and releases himself by 'Umrah. Then he has an obligation of qada' Hajj, and in it there is the hady. It has also been said that the hady is obligatory at the time of the prevention first. Ibn 'Abbas did not consider one prevented by sickness to be included in this verse, and he said: if the sick person has no hady with him, he is released where he is detained; if he has a hady with him, he is not released until the hady reaches its place, and then there is no qada' upon him. He said: Allah only said ﴿And when you are safe﴾, and safety is only from the enemy, so the sick person is not in the verse.

"Ma" is in the nominative position, meaning: then what is obligatory is what is easy, or: upon you is what is easy. It may also be in the accusative position, meaning: then slaughter, or: then give hady.

﴿Fa-ma istaysara﴾ according to the majority of scholars means: a sheep (shah). Ibn 'Umar and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr said: "what is easy" is a camel, not less than a camel, or a cow, not less than a cow.

al-Hasan said: the highest hady is a camel, its middle is a cow, and its lowest is a sheep.

"Al-hady" is the plural of hadyah, like jadyat al-sarj (the knob of a saddle), and it is the brad (a kind of small nail), whose plural is judy. It is possible that "al-hady" is a verbal noun named as such, like "al-rahn" and the like, so it applies to the singular and the plural. Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: I know of no parallel to this word.

As for His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not shave your heads﴾ and what follows, the address is to the whole community: the one prevented and the one not prevented. Some scholars consider it addressed to those who are prevented only.

The place of the hady is where its slaughter is permitted. That is for one not prevented: at Mina; and for one prevented by an enemy: where he is prevented, if it is not possible to send it.

As for the sick: if he has a hady, he sends it to its place.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 197–198 (part 1 of 2):

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:
﴿Whoever cannot find [an animal], then let him fast three days during the Hajj and seven when you have returned; those are ten complete. That is for one whose family is not present at the Sacred Mosque. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is severe in punishment.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196] ﴿The Hajj is in known months. Whoever undertakes the Hajj therein, there shall be no sexual relations, no wickedness, and no quarreling during the Hajj. And whatever good you do, Allah knows it. And take provision, but the best provision is piety. And fear Me, O people of understanding.﴾ ﴿There is no sin upon you in seeking bounty from your Lord. And when you depart from 'Arafat, remember Allah at al-Mash'ar al-Haram, and remember Him as He has guided you, although you were before that among the astray.﴾

His saying "lam yajid" (he does not find) is either due to lack of wealth or lack of an animal. As for "fi al-Hajj" [al-Baqarah: 196], 'Ikrimah and 'Ata' said: he may fast them during the months of Hajj, even if he has not yet entered into ihram for Hajj. Ibn 'Abbas and Malik ibn Anas said: he may fast them from the time he enters into ihram for Hajj. 'Ata' also said, and Mujahid: he should only fast them during the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan and al-Hakam said: he fasts one day before the Day of Tarwiyah and the Day of 'Arafah. All of them say: it is not permissible to delay them beyond the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, because with their end the Hajj ends. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Umar, Malik ibn Anas and a group of scholars said: whoever misses fasting them before the Day of Sacrifice may fast them during the days of Tashriq, because they are among the days of Hajj. Some people said: he may begin delaying them until the days of Tashriq, because fasting is not obligatory upon him unless he does not find a sacrificial animal on the Day of Sacrifice.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and seven when you have returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. Mujahid, 'Ata' and Ibrahim said: the meaning is, when you have returned from Mina, whoever stays in Makkah fasts them, and whoever sets out for his land fasts them on the road. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: this is a concession from Allah, Exalted, and the meaning is: when you have returned to your homelands, then fasting the seven is not obligatory upon anyone until he reaches his homeland, unless he wishes to be strict, like one who fasts while travelling in Ramadan. Zayd ibn 'Ali read "wa sab'atan" with the accusative, meaning: and fast seven. Since someone might suppose an option between three days during Hajj and seven when he returns, this is removed by the phrase of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿those are ten complete﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196]. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the meaning is: complete in reward, like one who gave an offering. It was also said: complete in reward like one who did not perform tamattu'. This is based on the view that the Hajj in which blood-sacrifices are not numerous is more sincere and more excellent, contrary to Abu Hanifah. It was also said: "complete" is for emphasis, as you say: "I wrote with my hand," and like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the roof fell down upon them from above them﴾ [al-Nahl: 26]. It was also said: its wording is informative but its meaning is imperative, i.e., complete them, for that is their obligation.

Al-Ustadh al-Ajall Abu al-Hasan 'Ali ibn Ahmad said: the meaning is: "those are complete," and the subject was repeated for emphasis, as you say: "Zayd is a wise man."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is for one whose family is not present﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], the reference is to tamattu' and its offering and its ruling. This is according to the view of those who hold that the Makkan may not perform tamattu' in the months of Hajj. So the sentence means: that is the concession. This is reinforced by "li-man," because the lam is always used with concessions; you say: "It is permitted for you to do such-and-such," whereas with strictness the proper form is "'alayka" (upon you). As for those who hold that the Makkan may perform 'umrah and has no sacrifice upon him, since he has not cut short a journey, then the reference of "dhalika" in their view is to the "hady," i.e., that strictness and obligation.

People differed regarding ﴿present at the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqarah: 196], after agreement that it refers to the people of Makkah and what is connected to it. Al-Tabari said: after agreement that it refers to the people of the Haram; but this is not as he said. Some scholars said: whoever lives where the Friday prayer is obligatory for him in Makkah is a hadari (urban resident), and whoever is farther than that is a badawi (desert dweller). They thus took the term from hadarah (civilization) and badawah (nomadism). Some of them said: whoever is at a distance such that prayer is not shortened to his location is present, i.e., attending, and whoever is farther than that is absent. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: Makkah, Dajnan, Dhu Tuwa and what resembles them are present at the Sacred Mosque. Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said: the entire people of the Haram are present at the Sacred Mosque. Makhul and 'Ata' said: whoever is within the miqat boundaries from every direction are present at the Sacred Mosque. al-Zuhri said: whoever is a day or two days away is among those present at the Sacred Mosque.

Then Allah, exalted is He, commanded taqwa in general and warned of His severe punishment.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Hajj is in known months.﴾ In the speech there is an ellipsis, its estimate being: "the months of Hajj are months," or "the time of Hajj is months," or "the time of performing Hajj is months." The purpose is that the predicate about the subject should be the subject itself, while Hajj is not the months, so these estimates were needed. As for one who estimates the sentence as "the Hajj is in months," it would necessarily require, with the omission of the preposition, the accusative of "al-ashhur," but no one read it in the accusative.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Zuhri said: the months of Hajj are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and the whole of Dhu al-Hijjah. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi and Ibrahim said: they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah. Both opinions are attributed to Malik, may Allah have mercy on him; the latter was related by Ibn Habib.

On this last opinion, the plural is used for two and part of a third, as they did in forming the plural of "ten": they said "'ishrun" (twenty) for twenty, and two days of the third, just as Imru' al-Qays said:
"... thirty months in three states"

Whoever said that all of Dhu al-Hijjah is among the months of Hajj does not see a blood-sacrifice for what occurs of acts after the Day of Sacrifice, because they are within the months of Hajj. But according to the other view, the Hajj ends with the Day of Sacrifice, and a sacrifice is obligatory for what one does after that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever undertakes therein﴾, i.e., whoever obligates himself to it. The root of farḍ (obligation) is the notch found on arrows, bows and other things, and from it comes farḍat al-nahr and al-jabal (a gap in a river bank or mountain). So whoever commits himself to something and establishes it upon himself has, as it were, made it obligatory.

The obligating of Hajj occurs through intention and entering into ihram, and talbiyah follows from that. The word "man" is in the nominative as a subject, and its meaning is conditional, with the predicate being His saying "faradha" (undertakes), because "man" here is not a relative pronoun; it is as if he said: "then a man who undertakes [it]." His saying "fa-la rafath" (there shall be no sexual relations) may be the predicate, and "farḍ" would then be a qualifier.

His saying, exalted is He: "fihinna" (therein). The speech did not come as "fard fiha" (in it, singular). Some said: both are equivalent in usage. Abu 'Uthman al-Mazini said: the large plural of non-rational things takes the form of the feminine singular, whereas the small plural does not; you say: "al-ajdha' inkasarna" (the trunks broke), and "al-judhu' inkasarat" (the trunks broke). This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the number of months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], then He said: "minha" (of them).

Nafi' read "fa-la rafatha wa la fusuqa wa la jidala" with the accusative for all three, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "fa-la rafathu wa la fusuqu wa la jidalu" with the nominative in the first two and the accusative for "jidal." Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read the three in the nominative, and this is related from 'Asim in some transmissions.

With the nominative reading, "la" is in the sense of "laysa" (is not). The predicate is omitted according to Abu 'Amr's reading, and "fi al-Hajj" is the predicate of "la jidal." Omitting the predicate here is the view of Abu 'Ali. This has been opposed; rather, "fi al-Hajj" is the predicate of all, since it is in a nominative position in both readings, because "la" works on its own rules upon what follows it, and its predicate remains in the nominative as the predicate of the inchoative. Abu 'Ali thought that it is like "laysa" in putting the predicate in the accusative, but this is not so; rather, it and its noun in the inchoative position both require a predicate, and "fi al-Hajj" is the predicate in a reading that is entirely nominative and in a reading that is entirely accusative.

The verification is that "fi al-Hajj" is in an accusative position by the implied predicate, as if you said: "existing in the Hajj," and there is no difference between the verse and your saying: "Zayd is in the house."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Malik, Mujahid and others said: "rafath" is sexual intercourse. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Tawus, 'Ata' and others said: "rafath" is lewd talk and explicit speech about intercourse before women specifically; this is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and he recited while in ihram:
"They walk with us softly; if the bird speaks truly, we shall mate with them, O gentle one."
It was said to him: "Do you speak of that while in ihram?" He said: "Rafath is only what is said in the presence of women." Others said: "rafath" is explicit mention of women, whether it takes place in their presence or not. Ibn 'Umar said to the camel-driver: "Do not mention women," and this may be because a woman was present, which is why he forbade him; what strengthens this view is what is required of reverence for the Hajj.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "rafath" is idle speech, and he recited:
"Away from idle talk and the speech of rafath"
There is no proof in this line.

Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa la rufuth."

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', al-Hasan and others said: "fusuq" is all sins, not restricted to any particular one.

Ibn 'Umar and a group with him said: "fusuq" is sins within the context of Hajj, such as killing game and other things.

Ibn Zayd and Malik said: "fusuq" is slaughtering for idols, and from it is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿or a wickedness dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 145].

al-Dahhak said: "fusuq" is mutual insulting by nicknames, and from it is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

Ibn 'Umar also, Mujahid, 'Ata', and Ibrahim said: "fusuq" is cursing. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Cursing a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The generality of all sins is the most preferred of the opinions.

Qatadah and others said: "jidal" here is cursing.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid said: "jidal" here is that you dispute with a Muslim until you anger him.

Malik and Ibn Zayd said: "jidal" here is that people differ as to who will reach the standing place of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, when Quraysh would stand outside the standing place of the rest of the Arabs, and then dispute after that.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "jidal" is that one group says: "our Hajj is more righteous than your Hajj," and the other says the same.

A group said: "jidal" here is that one group says: "the Hajj is today," and another says: "rather, the Hajj is tomorrow." It was also said: "jidal" was in boasting about forefathers.

Mujahid and a group with him said: "jidal" is that the Arabs postpone the months as the intercalation (nasi') was practiced, so the Shari'ah established the time of Hajj, clarified it, and informed that it is decisive, with no dispute about it. This is the soundest and clearest of the opinions.

"Jidal" is derived from jadal, which is twisting, as if each disputant wrestles with his companion. As for what the intercalation consisted of, the apparent account of the biographies of Ibn Ishaq and other registers is that the intercalator would make the sacred month lawful so that three consecutive months would not pass for the Arabs without raiding, and he would make Safar sacred, and perhaps they called it the sacred month; and the rest of the months would remain with their names until their Hajj fell in Dhu al-Hijjah in reality.

al-Tabari reported from Mujahid that he said: they would drop the sacred month and then say: "Safarain for Safar, and Rabi' al-Awwal," and so on, transferring the names of the months, and the time of Hajj would shift in reality, but it would remain in Dhu al-Hijjah by name and not in the reality of the month. He said: so Abu Bakr's Hajj in the year nine was in Dhu al-Qa'dah in reality, then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed Hajj in the year ten in Dhu al-Hijjah in reality, and he said: "Indeed time has come full circle" — the hadith — and the verse was revealed: ﴿and no dispute in the Hajj﴾, meaning that its matter has become clear, so that no month shifts at all, ever.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾. The meaning: He will reward it. In this there is an emphasis upon doing good.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on verses 197–198 of Surah al-Baqarah (part 2 of 2):

Regarding His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And take provision, for indeed the best provision is piety﴾, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the verse was revealed concerning a group of the Arabs who used to come to the Hajj without provisions. Some of them would say, "We are those who rely upon God (al-mutawakkilun)," and some would say, "How can we make the Hajj to the House of God when He does not feed us?" So they would remain a burden upon the people, and they were forbidden from this and were commanded to take provision.

Some people said: "Take provision in the form of a good companion." This is a weak specification. The more correct meaning of the verse is: "And take provision for your return (ma'ad) in the form of righteous deeds."

In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿for indeed the best provision is piety﴾, there is an exhortation to piety (taqwa).

The address was specifically directed to "those of understanding" (ulu al-albab), although the command applies to everyone, because they are the ones upon whom the proof of God has been established, and they are the ones who respond to His commands and take them up. This is on the basis that "lubb" (understanding) means the lubb of experience and soundness of reasoning. If we take it to mean the lubb of legal responsibility (taklif), then the address "O people of understanding" is general to all who are legally responsible.

Al-lubb means al-'aql (reason, intellect). The Arabs say: "lababtu" (with the first letter of the root doubled, and its vowel), "alubbu" (with a damma on the lam), as Sibawayh related. There is no other verb in the language in which the 'ayn is pronounced with a damma in both forms except this word.

In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, the word "junah" (blame, sin) is more general than "ithm" (sin), because it applies to what requires punishment and to what requires reproach and rebuke. The word "tabtaghu" means: you seek, through your effort.

Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata' said: the verse was revealed because when Islam came, the Arabs felt uneasy about attending the markets of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period), such as 'Ukaz, Dhu al-Majaz and Majanna. So God permitted that. That is, there is no sin in your trading and seeking profit.

Mujahid said: some of the Arabs would not trade from the moment they entered the state of ihram (ihram being the sacred state of pilgrimage), so the verse was revealed to permit that.

Ibn 'Umar said, concerning one who hired (himself or a mount) for the Hajj: his Hajj is complete, and there is no blame upon him for seeking payment for the hire.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Zubayr read: "There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord" ﴿fi mawasim al-hajj﴾ ("during the seasons of the Hajj").

In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So when you pour forth from 'Arafat﴾, the scholars agreed that the Hajj of one who stood at 'Arafat after the decline of the sun (zawal) and departed during the day before night is complete, except Malik ibn Anas, who said: he must take some of the night. As for one who stood at 'Arafat at night, there is no disagreement among the community (ummah) regarding the completion of his Hajj.

"Afada al-qawm aw al-jaysh" means: the people or the army departed all together when they set off in a body. From this comes "afada al-rajul fi al-kalam" (he went on at length in speech), from this comes "fada al-ina' wa afadtuhu" (the vessel overflowed, and I poured it out), and from this comes "al-mufid" in the arrows (the one who draws the lots).

The tanwin in "'Arafat" is according to its rule, as in "muslimat" (the kasra corresponds to the ya' in "muslimin," and the tanwin corresponds to the nun). If you name a person with it, the tanwin is dropped, and it is then diptote (ghayr munsarif) according to its rule before you named anything with it.

If "'Arafat" is the name of that entire area, then it is as we have mentioned. If it is the plural of "'Arafah," then it is like "muslimat," without being named with it. Sibawayh related the kasra of the ta' in "'Arafat" without tanwin in the accusative and genitive cases, with definiteness. The Kufans related its fatha in the accusative and genitive cases, by analogy with the ta' of Fatimah and Talhah.

That area was called "'Arafat" because Ibrahim recognized it (ta'arrafa) when he saw it as it had been described to him; this is what al-Suddi said. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was named thus because Jibril (peace be upon him) would say to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): "This is the place of such-and-such," and he would say, "I have recognized it." It was also said: it was named thus because Adam recognized (ta'arafa) Hawwa' there when he met her in that place. The apparent view is that it is a proper name (ism murtajal), like the rest of the names of places.

'Arafah is Nu'man al-Arak (a place with arak trees). The poet says concerning it:

"I took from Nu'man a stick of arak wood
for Hind, but who will convey it to Hind?"

The phrase ﴿al-mash'ar al-haram﴾ (the sacred monument) is a collective noun in its entirety. It is the area between the two mountains of Muzdalifah, from the boundary that leads to the narrow passes (ma'zimayn) of 'Arafah to the bottom of Muhassir. This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Rabi' (ibn Anas), Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid: all of it is the mash'ar, up to the bottom of Muhassir, just as all of 'Arafah is a station (mawqif), except the valley of 'Uranah, which may be pronounced with a fatha or a damma on the ra'.

(p-489) It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "All of 'Arafah is a station except the valley of 'Uranah, and all of Muzdalifah is a mash'ar, and rise up from the valley of Muhassir." 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr mentioned this in his sermon. In Muzdalifah is Qarn Quzah, the place upon which the Quraysh used to stand.

Remembrance of God at al-mash'ar al-haram is recommended (nadb) according to the scholars. Malik said: whoever passes by it without stopping, upon him is a sacrifice (dam). Al-Shafi'i said: whoever leaves Muzdalifah before midnight, upon him is a sacrifice, and if it is after midnight, there is nothing upon him. Al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i said: whoever misses standing at Muzdalifah has missed the Hajj.

His saying, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, is an enumeration of the blessing and a command to thank for it. Then He reminded them of their state of misguidance so that the magnitude of the favour would become evident. The kaf in "kama" is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and "ma" is either a verbal (masdariyyah) particle or a restrictive particle (kaffah). The "in" is a lightened form of the heavy "inna," and what indicates this is the entry of the lam into the predicate. This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Farra' said: it is a negating particle in the sense of "ma," and the lam is in the sense of "illa" (except), and the pronoun in "qablihi" refers back to the guidance (al-hady).
