The purpose is that the predicate about the subject should be the subject itself, while Hajj is not the months, so these estimates were needed. As for one who estimates the sentence as "the Hajj is in months," it would necessarily require, with the omission of the preposition, the accusative of "al-ashhur," but no one read it in the accusative.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', al-Rabi', Mujahid and al-Zuhri said: the months of Hajj are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and the whole of Dhu al-Hijjah. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi and Ibrahim said: they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten of Dhu al-Hijjah. Both opinions are attributed to Malik, may Allah have mercy on him; the latter was related by Ibn Habib.

On this last opinion, the plural is used for two and part of a third, as they did in forming the plural of "ten": they said "'ishrun" (twenty) for twenty, and two days of the third, just as Imru' al-Qays said:
"... thirty months in three states"

Whoever said that all of Dhu al-Hijjah is among the months of Hajj does not see a blood-sacrifice for what occurs of acts after the Day of Sacrifice, because they are within the months of Hajj. But according to the other view, the Hajj ends with the Day of Sacrifice, and a sacrifice is obligatory for what one does after that.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Whoever undertakes therein﴾, i.e., whoever obligates himself to it. The root of farḍ (obligation) is the notch found on arrows, bows and other things, and from it comes farḍat al-nahr and al-jabal (a gap in a river bank or mountain). So whoever commits himself to something and establishes it upon himself has, as it were, made it obligatory.

The obligating of Hajj occurs through intention and entering into ihram, and talbiyah follows from that. The word "man" is in the nominative as a subject, and its meaning is conditional, with the predicate being His saying "faradha" (undertakes), because "man" here is not a relative pronoun; it is as if he said: "then a man who undertakes [it]." His saying "fa-la rafath" (there shall be no sexual relations) may be the predicate, and "farḍ" would then be a qualifier.

His saying, exalted is He: "fihinna" (therein). The speech did not come as "fard fiha" (in it, singular). Some said: both are equivalent in usage. Abu 'Uthman al-Mazini said: the large plural of non-rational things takes the form of the feminine singular, whereas the small plural does not; you say: "al-ajdha' inkasarna" (the trunks broke), and "al-judhu' inkasarat" (the trunks broke). This is supported by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed the number of months﴾ [al-Tawbah: 36], then He said: "minha" (of them).

Nafi' read "fa-la rafatha wa la fusuqa wa la jidala" with the accusative for all three, and this is the reading of Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "fa-la rafathu wa la fusuqu wa la jidalu" with the nominative in the first two and the accusative for "jidal." Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' read the three in the nominative, and this is related from 'Asim in some transmissions.

With the nominative reading, "la" is in the sense of "laysa" (is not). The predicate is omitted according to Abu 'Amr's reading, and "fi al-Hajj" is the predicate of "la jidal." Omitting the predicate here is the view of Abu 'Ali. This has been opposed; rather, "fi al-Hajj" is the predicate of all, since it is in a nominative position in both readings, because "la" works on its own rules upon what follows it, and its predicate remains in the nominative as the predicate of the inchoative. Abu 'Ali thought that it is like "laysa" in putting the predicate in the accusative, but this is not so; rather, it and its noun in the inchoative position both require a predicate, and "fi al-Hajj" is the predicate in a reading that is entirely nominative and in a reading that is entirely accusative.

The verification is that "fi al-Hajj" is in an accusative position by the implied predicate, as if you said: "existing in the Hajj," and there is no difference between the verse and your saying: "Zayd is in the house."

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Qatadah, Malik, Mujahid and others said: "rafath" is sexual intercourse. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, Tawus, 'Ata' and others said: "rafath" is lewd talk and explicit speech about intercourse before women specifically; this is also the view of Ibn 'Abbas, and he recited while in ihram:
"They walk with us softly; if the bird speaks truly, we shall mate with them, O gentle one."
It was said to him: "Do you speak of that while in ihram?" He said: "Rafath is only what is said in the presence of women." Others said: "rafath" is explicit mention of women, whether it takes place in their presence or not. Ibn 'Umar said to the camel-driver: "Do not mention women," and this may be because a woman was present, which is why he forbade him; what strengthens this view is what is required of reverence for the Hajj.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "rafath" is idle speech, and he recited:
"Away from idle talk and the speech of rafath"
There is no proof in this line.

Ibn Mas'ud read: "wa la rufuth."

Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata', al-Hasan and others said: "fusuq" is all sins, not restricted to any particular one.

Ibn 'Umar and a group with him said: "fusuq" is sins within the context of Hajj, such as killing game and other things.

Ibn Zayd and Malik said: "fusuq" is slaughtering for idols, and from it is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿or a wickedness dedicated to other than Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 145].

al-Dahhak said: "fusuq" is mutual insulting by nicknames, and from it is the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Wretched is the name of wickedness﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

Ibn 'Umar also, Mujahid, 'Ata', and Ibrahim said: "fusuq" is cursing. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Cursing a Muslim is wickedness, and fighting him is disbelief."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The generality of all sins is the most preferred of the opinions.

Qatadah and others said: "jidal" here is cursing.

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and Mujahid said: "jidal" here is that you dispute with a Muslim until you anger him.

Malik and Ibn Zayd said: "jidal" here is that people differ as to who will reach the standing place of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, as they used to do in the Jahiliyyah, when Quraysh would stand outside the standing place of the rest of the Arabs, and then dispute after that.

Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: "jidal" is that one group says: "our Hajj is more righteous than your Hajj," and the other says the same.

A group said: "jidal" here is that one group says: "the Hajj is today," and another says: "rather, the Hajj is tomorrow." It was also said: "jidal" was in boasting about forefathers.

Mujahid and a group with him said: "jidal" is that the Arabs postpone the months as the intercalation (nasi') was practiced, so the Shari'ah established the time of Hajj, clarified it, and informed that it is decisive, with no dispute about it. This is the soundest and clearest of the opinions.

"Jidal" is derived from jadal, which is twisting, as if each disputant wrestles with his companion. As for what the intercalation consisted of, the apparent account of the biographies of Ibn Ishaq and other registers is that the intercalator would make the sacred month lawful so that three consecutive months would not pass for the Arabs without raiding, and he would make Safar sacred, and perhaps they called it the sacred month; and the rest of the months would remain with their names until their Hajj fell in Dhu al-Hijjah in reality.

al-Tabari reported from Mujahid that he said: they would drop the sacred month and then say: "Safarain for Safar, and Rabi' al-Awwal," and so on, transferring the names of the months, and the time of Hajj would shift in reality, but it would remain in Dhu al-Hijjah by name and not in the reality of the month. He said: so Abu Bakr's Hajj in the year nine was in Dhu al-Qa'dah in reality, then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed Hajj in the year ten in Dhu al-Hijjah in reality, and he said: "Indeed time has come full circle" — the hadith — and the verse was revealed: ﴿and no dispute in the Hajj﴾, meaning that its matter has become clear, so that no month shifts at all, ever.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whatever good you do, Allah knows it﴾. The meaning: He will reward it. In this there is an emphasis upon doing good.

Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary on verses 197–198 of Surah al-Baqarah (part 2 of 2):

Regarding His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And take provision, for indeed the best provision is piety﴾, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Zayd said: the verse was revealed concerning a group of the Arabs who used to come to the Hajj without provisions. Some of them would say, "We are those who rely upon God (al-mutawakkilun)," and some would say, "How can we make the Hajj to the House of God when He does not feed us?" So they would remain a burden upon the people, and they were forbidden from this and were commanded to take provision.

Some people said: "Take provision in the form of a good companion." This is a weak specification. The more correct meaning of the verse is: "And take provision for your return (ma'ad) in the form of righteous deeds."

In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿for indeed the best provision is piety﴾, there is an exhortation to piety (taqwa).

The address was specifically directed to "those of understanding" (ulu al-albab), although the command applies to everyone, because they are the ones upon whom the proof of God has been established, and they are the ones who respond to His commands and take them up. This is on the basis that "lubb" (understanding) means the lubb of experience and soundness of reasoning. If we take it to mean the lubb of legal responsibility (taklif), then the address "O people of understanding" is general to all who are legally responsible.

Al-lubb means al-'aql (reason, intellect). The Arabs say: "lababtu" (with the first letter of the root doubled, and its vowel), "alubbu" (with a damma on the lam), as Sibawayh related. There is no other verb in the language in which the 'ayn is pronounced with a damma in both forms except this word.

In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, the word "junah" (blame, sin) is more general than "ithm" (sin), because it applies to what requires punishment and to what requires reproach and rebuke. The word "tabtaghu" means: you seek, through your effort.

Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata' said: the verse was revealed because when Islam came, the Arabs felt uneasy about attending the markets of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period), such as 'Ukaz, Dhu al-Majaz and Majanna. So God permitted that. That is, there is no sin in your trading and seeking profit.

Mujahid said: some of the Arabs would not trade from the moment they entered the state of ihram (ihram being the sacred state of pilgrimage), so the verse was revealed to permit that.

Ibn 'Umar said, concerning one who hired (himself or a mount) for the Hajj: his Hajj is complete, and there is no blame upon him for seeking payment for the hire.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Zubayr read: "There is no blame upon you that you seek bounty from your Lord" ﴿fi mawasim al-hajj﴾ ("during the seasons of the Hajj").

In His saying, the Exalted, ﴿So when you pour forth from 'Arafat﴾, the scholars agreed that the Hajj of one who stood at 'Arafat after the decline of the sun (zawal) and departed during the day before night is complete, except Malik ibn Anas, who said: he must take some of the night. As for one who stood at 'Arafat at night, there is no disagreement among the community (ummah) regarding the completion of his Hajj.

"Afada al-qawm aw al-jaysh" means: the people or the army departed all together when they set off in a body. From this comes "afada al-rajul fi al-kalam" (he went on at length in speech), from this comes "fada al-ina' wa afadtuhu" (the vessel overflowed, and I poured it out), and from this comes "al-mufid" in the arrows (the one who draws the lots).

The tanwin in "'Arafat" is according to its rule, as in "muslimat" (the kasra corresponds to the ya' in "muslimin," and the tanwin corresponds to the nun). If you name a person with it, the tanwin is dropped, and it is then diptote (ghayr munsarif) according to its rule before you named anything with it.

If "'Arafat" is the name of that entire area, then it is as we have mentioned. If it is the plural of "'Arafah," then it is like "muslimat," without being named with it. Sibawayh related the kasra of the ta' in "'Arafat" without tanwin in the accusative and genitive cases, with definiteness. The Kufans related its fatha in the accusative and genitive cases, by analogy with the ta' of Fatimah and Talhah.

That area was called "'Arafat" because Ibrahim recognized it (ta'arrafa) when he saw it as it had been described to him; this is what al-Suddi said. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was named thus because Jibril (peace be upon him) would say to Ibrahim (peace be upon him): "This is the place of such-and-such," and he would say, "I have recognized it." It was also said: it was named thus because Adam recognized (ta'arafa) Hawwa' there when he met her in that place. The apparent view is that it is a proper name (ism murtajal), like the rest of the names of places.

'Arafah is Nu'man al-Arak (a place with arak trees). The poet says concerning it:

"I took from Nu'man a stick of arak wood
for Hind, but who will convey it to Hind?"

The phrase ﴿al-mash'ar al-haram﴾ (the sacred monument) is a collective noun in its entirety. It is the area between the two mountains of Muzdalifah, from the boundary that leads to the narrow passes (ma'zimayn) of 'Arafah to the bottom of Muhassir. This was stated by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, al-Rabi' (ibn Anas), Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid: all of it is the mash'ar, up to the bottom of Muhassir, just as all of 'Arafah is a station (mawqif), except the valley of 'Uranah, which may be pronounced with a fatha or a damma on the ra'.

(p-489) It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "All of 'Arafah is a station except the valley of 'Uranah, and all of Muzdalifah is a mash'ar, and rise up from the valley of Muhassir." 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr mentioned this in his sermon. In Muzdalifah is Qarn Quzah, the place upon which the Quraysh used to stand.

Remembrance of God at al-mash'ar al-haram is recommended (nadb) according to the scholars. Malik said: whoever passes by it without stopping, upon him is a sacrifice (dam). Al-Shafi'i said: whoever leaves Muzdalifah before midnight, upon him is a sacrifice, and if it is after midnight, there is nothing upon him. Al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i said: whoever misses standing at Muzdalifah has missed the Hajj.

His saying, ﴿and remember Him as He has guided you﴾, is an enumeration of the blessing and a command to thank for it. Then He reminded them of their state of misguidance so that the magnitude of the favour would become evident. The kaf in "kama" is an adjective to an omitted verbal noun (masdar), and "ma" is either a verbal (masdariyyah) particle or a restrictive particle (kaffah). The "in" is a lightened form of the heavy "inna," and what indicates this is the entry of the lam into the predicate. This is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Farra' said: it is a negating particle in the sense of "ma," and the lam is in the sense of "illa" (except), and the pronoun in "qablihi" refers back to the guidance (al-hady).

[p-490] Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 199–203:

The Most High said:

﴿Then depart from where the people depart, and seek forgiveness from God. Indeed God is Forgiving, Merciful.﴾ ﴿So when you have completed your rites, remember God as you remember your fathers, or with even greater remembrance. Among the people there is one who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world," and he has no share in the Hereafter.﴾ ﴿And among them is one who says, "Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned, and God is swift in reckoning.﴾ ﴿And remember God during the numbered days. Whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him, for him who fears God. And fear God, and know that you will be gathered to Him.﴾

Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿĀʾishah, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid and others said: The addressees of this verse are the Quraysh and those born of them, and they are the Ḥums (the Ḥums, a group of Quraysh and their allies who considered themselves exempt from the general rites of the pilgrimage). This is because they used to say, "We are the people of God (qiṭṭīn Allāh), so it is fitting that we magnify the Sacred Precinct (al-Ḥaram) and do not magnify anything of the outside (al-Ḥill)." So they enacted the practice of tearing garments during circumambulation (ṭawāf) and other such things. Although they recognized and acknowledged that ʿArafa is the station of Ibrahim, they did not leave the Sacred Precinct, and they would stand at Jamʿ (Muzdalifah), depart from it, while the people stood at ʿArafa. So they were told to depart together with the general body of pilgrims.

"Thumma" (then) in this verse is not for sequence; rather, it is for conjoining one statement to another that is separate from it. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) was among the Ḥums, but he would stand at ʿArafa from the beginning, as guidance from God.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The addressees of the verse are the whole community, and by "the people" is meant Ibrahim (peace be upon him), as in His saying: ﴿those to whom the people said﴾ (Q. 3:173), and he meant one person. On this view it is possible that they were commanded to depart from ʿArafa, and it is possible that it refers to another departure, namely the one from Muzdalifah; then "thumma" remains on its proper meaning under this possibility, and al-Ṭabarī relied on this possibility.

Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read: "al-nāsī" (the forgetful one), and its interpretation is Adam (peace be upon him). Some have said it is permissible to lighten the yāʾ, so that one says "al-nās" like "al-qāḍḍ" and "al-hādd."

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said: As for its permissibility in Arabic, Sībawayh mentioned it; but as for its permissibility as a recited reading, I do not know of it.

God commanded seeking forgiveness because these are its places, the places where acceptance is hoped for and where mercy descends. And in the ḥadīth [p-491]: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) delivered a sermon on the evening of ʿArafa and said: O people! God has been generous to you in this your standing, so He accepted from your good-doers, and forgave your wrongdoers for the sake of your good-doers, except for wrongs committed among yourselves. Depart in the name of God." And when it was the morning of Jamʿ, he delivered a sermon and said: "O people! God has been bountiful to you, and He has compensated for the wrongs from Himself."

A group said: The meaning is: seek forgiveness from God for your action which was contrary to the Sunnah of Ibrahim in your standing at Quzaḥ in Muzdalifah.

As for His saying: ﴿So when you have completed your rites﴾ and the rest of the verse. Mujāhid said: "The manāsik (rites) are the sacrifices and the shedding of blood." In my view, the manāsik are the acts of worship at the landmarks of Ḥajj and the places of its rites. The meaning is: when you have finished your Ḥajj, which is the standing at ʿArafa, then remember God with His praises, and extol Him for His blessings upon you. This time was singled out for the completion because people complete their rites at one and the same time, whereas what comes before and after it is at different times: this one is at the ṭawāf, this one at the stoning (ramy), this one at the shaving (ḥalq), and other things.

It was the custom of the Arabs, when they had completed their Ḥajj, to stand at the Jamra (the pillar for stoning), boasting about their fathers, and mentioning the days of their forebears of valor, generosity and other things. So the verse was revealed to oblige them to keep the remembrance of God, the Most High, more than their remembrance of their fathers with the days of the Jāhiliyyah. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirīn). Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿAṭāʾ said: The meaning of the verse is: remember God as children remember their fathers and mothers, that is, call upon Him for help and turn to Him as you used to do with your fathers when you were young. And a group said: The meaning of the verse is: remember God, glorify Him, defend His Sacred Precinct, and repel whoever wishes to associate partners with Him or to diminish His religion and His sacred places, just as you mention your fathers with good when someone disparages them, and you protect their sides and defend them.

Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī read: "kadhikrikum ābāʾukum" (as your fathers are remembered by you), meaning: be earnest in remembering Him as a man is earnest in remembering his son. The verbal noun in this reading is in the genitive (muḍāf) to the object. "Ashadda" (greater) is in the genitive position in coordination with "dhikrikum"; it may also be in the accusative position, the implied sense being: "or remember Him more intensely (ashadda dhikran)."

As for His saying: ﴿Among the people there is one who says﴾ and the rest of the verse. Abū Wāʾil, al-Suddī and Ibn Zayd said: Their custom in the Jāhiliyyah was to pray only for worldly interests, since they did not know the Hereafter. So they were forbidden from that specific supplication concerned only with worldly matters, and the prohibition came in the form of a report about them.

Al-khalāq means portion and share. The "min" (of "min khalāq") is extra (zāʾidah), because it follows a negation, and so it encompasses the whole category of shares.

Qatādah said: The good of this world is well-being in health and sufficiency of wealth. Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: The good of this world is knowledge and worship. Al-Suddī said: The good of this world is wealth. It was also said: The good of this world is a beautiful woman. The word implies all of this, and all the things of the world that are loved.

[p-493] As for the good of the Hereafter: it is Paradise, by consensus (ijmāʿ, the agreement of scholars). ﴿And protect us from the punishment of the Fire﴾ is a supplication that one not be among those who enter it because of their sins, and that intercession may bring them out of it. It is possible that it is a supplication emphasizing the request to enter Paradise, so that desire is directed toward both deliverance and success from both sides, as one of the Companions said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I only say in my supplication: O God, admit me into Paradise and grant me protection from the Fire. I do not know what your murmuring is, nor the murmuring of Muʿādh?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "Around it we murmur."

As for His saying: ﴿Those will have a share of what they have earned﴾ and the rest of the verse. The reward for righteous deeds is mentioned in the form of a plain report. The Lord, the Most High, is swift in reckoning because He has no need of counting, nor of exercising thought. It was said to ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may God be pleased with him): How does God reckon all creatures in one day? He said: As He provides for them in a day. It was also said: Reckoning here means recompense, as if the one who recompenses prepares the parts of the deed and then recompenses with their equivalent. It was also said the meaning of the verse is: swift is the coming of the Day of Reckoning. The purpose of the verse is therefore warning about the Day of Resurrection.

God commanded His servants to remember Him during the numbered days, which are the three days after the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Naḥr), namely the Days of Tashrīq (the days of drying meat). The Day of Sacrifice is not among the numbered days, and this is indicated by the consensus of people that no one departs on the Day of Qarr, which is the second day after the Day of Sacrifice. For the Day of Sacrifice is among the known days (al-maʿlūmāt). Had the Day of Sacrifice been among the numbered days, it would have been permissible for whoever wished to depart early on the Day of Qarr, since he had already taken two days from the numbered days. Makkī and al-Mahdawī narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: The numbered days are the days of the ten.

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

This is either a scribal error in the copy, or it means the ten days after the Day of Sacrifice, and that is far-fetched.

The known days are the Day of Sacrifice and the two days after it, since they agree that no one slaughters on the third day. The remembrance on the known days is over what God has provided of the beast of the livestock. Ibn Zayd said: The known days are the ten days of Dhū al-Ḥijjah and the days of Tashrīq, but this view is far-fetched.

God made the numbered days the days of remembrance of God, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "They are days of eating, drinking and the remembrance of God."

Among the remembrance is the takbīr (saying Allāhu akbar) after the prayers. There is disagreement about the two limits of the period of takbīr. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib and Ibn ʿAbbās said: One says takbīr from the dawn prayer on the Day of ʿArafa until the afternoon prayer on the last day of the Days of Tashrīq.

Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Ḥanīfah said: One says takbīr from the morning of ʿArafa until the afternoon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice.

Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said: One says takbīr from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the noon prayer on the last day of the Days of Tashrīq.

Mālik said: One says takbīr from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the dawn prayer on the last of the Days of Tashrīq, and al-Shāfiʿī said the same.

Ibn Shihāb said: One says takbīr from noon on the Day of Sacrifice until the afternoon prayer on the last of the Days of Tashrīq.

[p-495] Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: One says takbīr from noon on the Day of ʿArafa until the afternoon prayer on the last of the Days of Tashrīq.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: One says takbīr from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the noon prayer on the first day of departure (yawm al-nafar al-awwal). Abū Wāʾil said: One says takbīr from the noon prayer on the Day of ʿArafa until the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice.

The well-known position of the school of Mālik is that one says three takbīrs after each prayer. There is a narration in the school that after the three takbīrs one says: "There is no god but God, God is greatest, and to God belongs all praise."

As for His saying: ﴿So whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ and the rest of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid said: The meaning is: whoever departs on the second day of the numbered days, there is no blame on him, and whoever delays until the third, there is no blame on him. So the meaning of the verse is that all of this is permissible. It was expressed in this division out of concern and emphasis, since among the Arabs there were those who blamed the one who hastened and the reverse, so the verse came removing blame in both cases.

Among the scholars is one who holds that hastening is permitted only for one whose homeland is far away, not for the people of Makkah or those nearby, unless they have an excuse. This was said by Mālik and others. Among them is one who holds that it is permissible for all people. Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd said: One says takbīr from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the noon prayer on the last day of the Days of Tashrīq.

Mālik said: One says takbīr from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the dawn prayer on the last of the Days of Tashrīq, and al-Shāfiʿī said the same.

Ibn Shihāb said: One says takbīr from noon on the Day of Sacrifice until the afternoon prayer on the last of the Days of Tashrīq.

[p-495] Saʿīd ibn Jubayr said: One says takbīr from noon on the Day of ʿArafa until the afternoon prayer on the last of the Days of Tashrīq.

Al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan said: One says takbīr from the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the noon prayer on the first day of departure (yawm al-nafar al-awwal). Abū Wāʾil said: One says takbīr from the noon prayer on the Day of ʿArafa until the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice.

The well-known position of the school of Mālik is that one says three takbīrs after each prayer. There is a narration in the school that after the three takbīrs one says: "There is no god but God, God is greatest, and to God belongs all praise."

As for His saying: ﴿So whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾ and the rest of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrimah and Mujāhid said: The meaning is: whoever departs on the second day of the numbered days, there is no blame on him, and whoever delays until the third, there is no blame on him. So the meaning of the verse is that all of this is permissible. It was expressed in this division out of concern and emphasis, since among the Arabs there were those who blamed the one who hastened and the reverse, so the verse came removing blame in both cases.

Among the scholars is one who holds that hastening is permitted only for one whose homeland is far away, not for the people of Makkah or those nearby, unless they have an excuse. This was said by Mālik and others. Among them is one who holds that it is permissible for all people. This was said by ʿAṭāʾ and others. ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, Ibn Masʿūd and Ibrāhīm said: The meaning of the verse is: whoever hastens, he is forgiven, and whoever delays, he is forgiven. They based this on His (peace be upon him) saying: "Whoever performs this House of God and does not commit obscenity or transgression, he comes out of his sins like the day his mother bore him." So His saying "there is no sin" is a general negation and an absolute clearing.

Mujāhid also said: The meaning of the verse is: whoever hastens or delays, there is no sin upon him until the coming year, and in this view he cited a report (athar).

Abū al-ʿĀliyah said: The meaning of the verse is: there is no sin upon him for the one who fears God for the rest of his life, and the pilgrim is wholly forgiven.

Abū Ṣāliḥ and others said: The meaning of the verse is: there is no sin upon him who fears God regarding the hunting of game and what he must avoid during Ḥajj.

[p-496] He also said: for the one who fears God in his Ḥajj and performs it completely, until it is accepted (mabrūran).

The "lām" in His saying: ﴿for him who fears God﴾ is connected either to forgiveness according to some interpretations, or to the lifting of sin in Ḥajj according to others. It was said it is connected to the remembrance indicated by His saying "remember" (wa-dhkurū), meaning: the remembrance is for him who fears God. And the stoning of the third pillar is dropped for the one who hastens.

Ibn Abī Zamanayn said: He stones it on the first day of departure at the time he intends to hasten.

Ibn al-Mawwāz said: The one who hastens in two days stones with twenty-one pebbles, seven for each pillar, so that the total of his stoning is forty-nine pebbles.

Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

Because he has already stoned the pillar of al-ʿAqabah with seven on the Day of Sacrifice. Ibn al-Mawwāz said: and the stoning of the third day is dropped.

Sālim ibn ʿAbd Allāh read: "fa-lā ithm ʿalayhi" with the hamzah of connection (wasl). Then the Most High commanded piety, and reminded of the gathering and standing before Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 204–208 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:
﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life impresses you, and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents.﴾ ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock, and Allah does not love corruption.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him, so Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting-place.﴾ ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, and Allah is Kind to the servants.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace completely, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

Al-Suddi said: These verses were revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, whose name was Ubayy, and "al-Akhnas" was a nickname. The reason was that "he came to the Prophet ﷺ and displayed his Islam, and said, 'Allah knows that I am truthful.' Then he fled after that, and he passed by a group of Muslims, and he burned their crops and killed their donkeys, so these verses were revealed concerning him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
It has never been established at all that al-Akhnas embraced Islam.

Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who spoke about those who were killed at the expedition of al-Raji': 'Asim ibn Thabit, Khubayb, Ibn al-Dathina, and others. They said, "Woe to these people! They neither stayed in their houses, nor did they deliver the message of their companion." So these verses were revealed describing the characteristics of the hypocrites. Then he mentioned those who were martyred at the expedition of al-Raji' in His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾, and so on.

Qatada, Mujahid, and a group of scholars said: These verses were revealed concerning everyone who conceals disbelief, hypocrisy, lying, or harm, while outwardly displaying the opposite with his tongue. Thus it is general, and it resembles what is related in al-Tirmidhi: "Indeed, in some of the Books of Allah, the Exalted: 'Among the servants of Allah there are people whose tongues are sweeter than honey, while their hearts are more bitter than aloes. They wear sheep's skins over people for softness, they chew the world with religion. Allah, the Exalted, says: Do they deceive Me? Or do they dare against Me? I swear that I will surely send upon them a trial that leaves even the forbearing among them bewildered.'"

The meaning of ﴿and he calls Allah to witness﴾ is: he says, "Allah knows that I am saying the truth."

Abu Haywa and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-yashhadu Allah﴾ (with the verb attributed to Allah). The meaning is: his speech impresses you, while Allah knows from him the opposite of what he says. The recitation followed by the majority is more emphatic in condemning him, because he has bound himself to the discipline of fine speech, and then what is contrary to it appeared from his inner self. What is in his heart differs according to the two recitations. According to the recitation of the majority, it is the good that appears, that is, it is in his heart by his claim. According to the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin, it is the hidden evil.

Ibn 'Abbas recited: ﴿wa-llahu yashhadu 'ala ma fi qalbihi﴾. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿wa-yastashhidu Allah 'ala ma fi qalbihi﴾.

Al-aladd (الألد) means: one who is intensely contentious, stubborn in dispute, who twists arguments from every side. His deviation resembles walking in the two sides of a valley (ladiday al-wadi). From it come the words ladid al-fam (one with a sharp mouth) and al-ladud. It is said: from it, "ladidtu" (with a kasra on the 'ain) "aladdu." It is a dispraise. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The most hateful of men to Allah is the most contentious opponent (al-aladd al-khasm)." It is also said: "laddtuhu" (with a fatha on the 'ain), "aluddu-hu" (with a damma), when you overcome him in dispute. From the same word is the saying of the poet:

"Beneath the rocks there is resolve and determination, and an opponent most contentious, a man of stubborn grip."

(p. 499) As for al-khisam (الخصام) in the verse, it is a verbal noun of khasama. It was also said: it is the plural of khasm, like kalb and kilab, so the sentence would mean: "and he is the most contentious of the contentious ones," meaning their father.

(Note: "tawalla" and "sa'a" both allow two meanings. One is that they are verbs of the heart: "tawalla" then comes in the sense of going astray, becoming angry, and being offended within himself, so he strives with his schemes and intentions to plot against Islam. From this striving is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and from it: ﴿and strives for the Hereafter its striving﴾ [al-Isra': 19], and from it the saying of the poet:

"I strive on behalf of the tribe of Malik; every man is striving in his own affair."

Ibn Jurayj and others followed this direction in the meaning of the verse. The second meaning is that both are verbs of a person. Then "tawalla" comes in the sense of turning his back and departing from you, O Muhammad, and "sa'a" carries its meaning of moving on foot, so he cut the road and corrupted it. Ibn 'Abbas and others followed this direction. Both kinds of striving are corruption.)

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and destroy the crops and the offspring﴾, al-Tabari said: The intended one is al-Akhnas in his burning of the crops and his killing of the donkeys.

Mujahid said: The meaning is that the wrongdoer causes corruption on the earth, so Allah withholds the rain, and the crops and offspring are destroyed. It was also said: the meaning is that the corrupter kills people, so the cultivators of the crops and the ones who are taken away cease. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "al-harth" (crops) refers to women, and "al-nasl" (offspring) to their offspring.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The apparent meaning is that the verse is an expression of exaggeration in corruption, since all corruption in worldly affairs revolves around these two sections.

Most of the readers recite ﴿yuhlika﴾ with a damma on the yā', a kasra on the lām, and a fatha on the kāf, as a conjunction with ﴿li-yufsida﴾. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is ﴿wa-li-yahlika﴾. A group recited ﴿wa-yahlaka﴾ with a damma on the kāf, either as a conjunction with ﴿yu'jibuka﴾, or with ﴿sa'a﴾ because it carries the meaning of the future, or as a new independent statement. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-yahlikᵘ﴾ with a fatha on the yā', a kasra on the lām, a damma on the kāf, and the nominative on ﴿al-harth wa-l-nasl﴾. Ibn Salama related this from Ibn Kathir, as did 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr. Al-Mahdawi related that what Hammad ibn Salama related from Ibn Kathir is: ﴿wa-yuhlaku﴾ with a damma on the yā' and the kāf, and ﴿al-harth﴾ in the accusative. A group recited ﴿wa-yahlaku﴾ with a fatha on the yā' and the lām and the nominative on ﴿al-harth﴾, and this is the dialect of halaka yahlaku, which is classed among the irregular forms, like rakana yarkanu.

Al-harth (الحرث), linguistically, is the tilling of the earth for cultivation. The crop is called harth by association and congruity. Included in this, by analogy with crops, are all trees and plantings. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿when the two were judging concerning the field﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78], and it was a vineyard, as reported in the exegetical works.

Women have also been called harth by way of comparison. Al-nasl (النسل) is derived from nasala yansilu, when something comes out in succession. From it is nasal al-ta'ir (the falling of the bird's feathers one after another). From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and they will swarm from every elevation﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96]. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"......... so wipe from me the garments of your garments, which slip off (tansilu)."

(p. 501) As for ﴿la yuhibbu﴾, its meaning is: He does not love it from the people of righteousness, that is, He does not love it as a religion. Otherwise, nothing occurs except what Allah, the Exalted, loves to occur. Corruption does occur. This is in accordance with the view of the theologians that love (hubb) means will (irada).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Love, in the sense of will, has a distinction of preference. If someone were to say that the corruption intended lacks the distinction of preference, that would be valid, since Allah's love is only for what is good in all its aspects.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah"﴾ and so on: this is the description of the disbeliever or the hypocrite who goes off with himself in arrogance. It is disliked for a believer to bring someone into embarrassment in such a matter. Some scholars said: It is enough sin for a man that his brother says to him, "Fear Allah," and he replies, "Keep to yourself. Would someone like you advise me?"

Al-'izza (العزة) here means: power and strength of the self. That is, he became proud within himself and was puffed up, and that pride led him into sin when it seized him with it and bound him to his father. The wording of the verse may also be read as: "pride seized him along with the sin," so the meaning of the preposition bi- (الباء) differs according to the two interpretations.

Hasbuhu (حسبه) means: sufficient for him in punishment and recompense, just as you say to a man, "What has befallen you is enough for you," while you are magnifying and exaggerating over him what has befallen him. Al-mihad (المهاد) is what a man prepares for himself, as if it were a bed.

From this same category is the saying of the poet:

"......... a greeting among them is a painful blow."

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾ and so on, it encompasses every fighter in the way of Allah, or every martyr in his own person, or every one who changes wrong. The apparent sense of this division is that the verses before it concern the disbeliever in general, as is shown by the threat of the Fire, and that the sinners who have some of this disposition receive their share of the threat of the verse. As for the one who says that the preceding verses concern hypocrites who spoke about the expedition of al-Raji', he says: this verse concerns the martyrs of the expedition of al-Raji'.

As for the one who says that those (the earlier verses) concern al-Akhnas, he says: this one concerns the Ansar and the Muhajirun who hastened to faith. 'Ikrima and others said: this one concerns a group of the Muhajirun, and they mentioned the hadith of Suhayb, that he left Makkah to go to the Prophet ﷺ, and Quraysh followed him to turn him back. He shook out his quiver and said to them: "You know that by Allah I am among the best of you at archery. By Allah, I will shoot at you as long as I have an arrow left, and then I will strike with my sword as long as there is anything left in my hand." They said to him, "We will not let you go away from us wealthy, when you came to us poor. But show us where your wealth is, and we will leave you." So he showed them where his wealth was, and they left him. He migrated to the Prophet ﷺ, and when he saw him, he said to him, "The sale has profited, Abu Yahya." So this verse was revealed concerning him.

Whoever says that the first verses are meant in general says that this one is also meant in general.

Yashri (يشري) means "to sell," as in: ﴿and they sold him for a meagre price﴾ [Yusuf: 20]. From it is the saying of Yazid ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari:

"I sold a cloak, would that I had been, after that cloak, its owner."

Another said:

"He is offered a price for it, yet he refuses it, and his companion says: 'Will you not buy?'"

From this comes the name al-shurat (the Shurat), as if they are those who sold their souls to Allah, the Exalted.

Some people related that it is said: "shara" in the sense of "ishtara" (to buy). Whoever interprets the verse as concerning Suhayb will need this, because he bought his soul with his wealth and did not sell it. Unless it is said that Suhayb's resolve to fight them was a sale of his soul to Allah, the Exalted, so the word is correct in the sense of "baa" (to sell).

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, interpreted this verse concerning those who change wrong. Therefore 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas said: "The two men fought," meaning that the one who changes wrong said to the corrupter, "Fear Allah," but the corrupter refused, and pride seized him, so the one who changes wrong sold himself to Allah, the Exalted, fought him, and they fought each other.

It is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to gather young reciters on Friday, among them Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hurr ibn Qays and others. They would recite in his presence and with him. 'Umar heard Ibn 'Abbas say, "The two men fought," when he recited this verse. He asked him about what he had said, and he explained this interpretation to him. 'Umar said to him, "By Allah, your heritage is great, O Ibn 'Abbas!" (lillah taladuka ya Ibn 'Abbas).

Abu Hurayra and Abu Ayyub said, when Hisham ibn 'Amir charged into the ranks at Constantinople, and some people said, "He has thrown himself into destruction with his own hand," (that is not as they said). Rather, this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾ and so on.

Ibtighaʾ (ابتغاء) is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning "seeking." Hamza stopped on ﴿mardat﴾ with a ta' (مرضات), while the rest stopped with a ha' (مرضاه). Abu 'Ali said: The reason for Hamza's stopping with a ta' is either that it is in accordance with the dialect of those who say talhat and 'alqamat, from which is the saying of the poet:

"......... rather, the desert of Tayha, like the back of a shield (hajafat)."

Or it is because the genitive noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) is necessarily implied within the word, so he kept the ta' as it is kept in connected speech, so that it would be known that the genitive noun is intended.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Kind to the servants﴾, it is an expression of hope which implies urging toward complying with what the verse praised. Likewise, the saying: ﴿So Hell is sufficient for him﴾ is a warning that implies caution against what the verse condemned.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded the believers to enter into peace. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿al-salm﴾ with a fatha on the sin. The rest recited it with a kasra in this place. It was said: the two have the same meaning, and both refer to Islam and to peace-making (al-musalama). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: al-silm (with a kasra) means Islam, and al-salm (with a fatha) means peace-making. Al-Mubarrad rejected this distinction. Al-Tabari preferred interpreting the word in the sense of Islam, because the believers were never commanded to take the initiative to enter into peace-making. Rather, it was said to the Prophet ﷺ that he should incline to peace if they inclined to it, but not that he should initiate it.

Having taken the wording to refer to Islam, there is a dispute about who is being addressed. One group said: all the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is that He commanded them to remain steadfast in it and to increase in adhering to its limits. In this reading, *kaffatan* (entirely, all together) covers all the believers and all parts of the Sharia, so the circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) refers to two things at once. This is permissible, as in the Almighty's words: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him﴾ [Maryam: 27], along with other such examples.

'Ikrimah said: rather, the addressees are those among the Children of Israel who believed in the Prophet, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others. They had gone to the extent of exalting the day of Saturday (*as-Sabt*) and disliked eating camel meat, and they wanted to practise some of the rulings of the Tawrah (Torah) and mix that with Islam. So this verse was revealed concerning them. According to this view, *kaffatan* refers only to the parts of the Sharia.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book. The meaning is: O you who believe in Moses and Jesus, enter into Islam through Muhammad, entirely. According to this view, *kaffatan* refers to the parts of the Sharia and to the addressees. [Some] said, regarding one who understands *as-silm* as Islam, and one who understands it as peaceful coexistence, says: He commanded them to enter into it by paying the *jizyah* (the tax levied on non-Muslim subjects).

*Kaffatan* means "all of them." What is meant by *al-kaffah* is the group that restrains (*takuffu*) its opponent. It was also said that *kaffatan* is a qualifier (*na't*, adjective) of an elided verbal noun (*masdar*), as if the speech were "entered into it with entirety." When the described noun was elided, the qualifier remained in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*).

The discussion of *khutuwat* has already been given. The definite article in *ash-shaytan* is for the genus (*lil-jins*). *'Aduww* (enemy) applies to the singular, the dual, and the plural. *Mubin* may mean that it makes its enmity clear (*abana 'adawatahu*), or that it is evident in itself that he is an enemy, because the Arabs say *baana al-amr* and *abana al-amr* with one meaning.

(p-506)

Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "al-harth" (crops) refers to women, and "al-nasl" (offspring) to their offspring.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The apparent meaning is that the verse is an expression of exaggeration in corruption, since all corruption in worldly affairs revolves around these two sections.

Most of the readers recite ﴿yuhlika﴾ with a damma on the yā', a kasra on the lām, and a fatha on the kāf, as a conjunction with ﴿li-yufsida﴾. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is ﴿wa-li-yahlika﴾. A group recited ﴿wa-yahlaka﴾ with a damma on the kāf, either as a conjunction with ﴿yu'jibuka﴾, or with ﴿sa'a﴾ because it carries the meaning of the future, or as a new independent statement. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-yahlikᵘ﴾ with a fatha on the yā', a kasra on the lām, a damma on the kāf, and the nominative on ﴿al-harth wa-l-nasl﴾. Ibn Salama related this from Ibn Kathir, as did 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr. Al-Mahdawi related that what Hammad ibn Salama related from Ibn Kathir is: ﴿wa-yuhlaku﴾ with a damma on the yā' and the kāf, and ﴿al-harth﴾ in the accusative. A group recited ﴿wa-yahlaku﴾ with a fatha on the yā' and the lām and the nominative on ﴿al-harth﴾, and this is the dialect of halaka yahlaku, which is classed among the irregular forms, like rakana yarkanu.

Al-harth (الحرث), linguistically, is the tilling of the earth for cultivation. The crop is called harth by association and congruity. Included in this, by analogy with crops, are all trees and plantings. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿when the two were judging concerning the field﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78], and it was a vineyard, as reported in the exegetical works.

Women have also been called harth by way of comparison. Al-nasl (النسل) is derived from nasala yansilu, when something comes out in succession. From it is nasal al-ta'ir (the falling of the bird's feathers one after another). From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and they will swarm from every elevation﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96]. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"......... so wipe from me the garments of your garments, which slip off (tansilu)."

(p. 501) As for ﴿la yuhibbu﴾, its meaning is: He does not love it from the people of righteousness, that is, He does not love it as a religion. Otherwise, nothing occurs except what Allah, the Exalted, loves to occur. Corruption does occur. This is in accordance with the view of the theologians that love (hubb) means will (irada).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Love, in the sense of will, has a distinction of preference. If someone were to say that the corruption intended lacks the distinction of preference, that would be valid, since Allah's love is only for what is good in all its aspects.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah"﴾ and so on: this is the description of the disbeliever or the hypocrite who goes off with himself in arrogance. It is disliked for a believer to bring someone into embarrassment in such a matter. Some scholars said: It is enough sin for a man that his brother says to him, "Fear Allah," and he replies, "Keep to yourself. Would someone like you advise me?"

Al-'izza (العزة) here means: power and strength of the self. That is, he became proud within himself and was puffed up, and that pride led him into sin when it seized him with it and bound him to his father. The wording of the verse may also be read as: "pride seized him along with the sin," so the meaning of the preposition bi- (الباء) differs according to the two interpretations.

Hasbuhu (حسبه) means: sufficient for him in punishment and recompense, just as you say to a man, "What has befallen you is enough for you," while you are magnifying and exaggerating over him what has befallen him. Al-mihad (المهاد) is what a man prepares for himself, as if it were a bed.

From this same category is the saying of the poet:

"......... a greeting among them is a painful blow."

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾ and so on, it encompasses every fighter in the way of Allah, or every martyr in his own person, or every one who changes wrong. The apparent sense of this division is that the verses before it concern the disbeliever in general, as is shown by the threat of the Fire, and that the sinners who have some of this disposition receive their share of the threat of the verse. As for the one who says that the preceding verses concern hypocrites who spoke about the expedition of al-Raji', he says: this verse concerns the martyrs of the expedition of al-Raji'.

As for the one who says that those (the earlier verses) concern al-Akhnas, he says: this one concerns the Ansar and the Muhajirun who hastened to faith. 'Ikrima and others said: this one concerns a group of the Muhajirun, and they mentioned the hadith of Suhayb, that he left Makkah to go to the Prophet ﷺ, and Quraysh followed him to turn him back. He shook out his quiver and said to them: "You know that by Allah I am among the best of you at archery. By Allah, I will shoot at you as long as I have an arrow left, and then I will strike with my sword as long as there is anything left in my hand." They said to him, "We will not let you go away from us wealthy, when you came to us poor. But show us where your wealth is, and we will leave you." So he showed them where his wealth was, and they left him. He migrated to the Prophet ﷺ, and when he saw him, he said to him, "The sale has profited, Abu Yahya." So this verse was revealed concerning him.

Whoever says that the first verses are meant in general says that this one is also meant in general.

Yashri (يشري) means "to sell," as in: ﴿and they sold him for a meagre price﴾ [Yusuf: 20]. From it is the saying of Yazid ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari:

"I sold a cloak, would that I had been, after that cloak, its owner."

Another said:

"He is offered a price for it, yet he refuses it, and his companion says: 'Will you not buy?'"

From this comes the name al-shurat (the Shurat), as if they are those who sold their souls to Allah, the Exalted.

Some people related that it is said: "shara" in the sense of "ishtara" (to buy). Whoever interprets the verse as concerning Suhayb will need this, because he bought his soul with his wealth and did not sell it. Unless it is said that Suhayb's resolve to fight them was a sale of his soul to Allah, the Exalted, so the word is correct in the sense of "baa" (to sell).

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, interpreted this verse concerning those who change wrong. Therefore 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas said: "The two men fought," meaning that the one who changes wrong said to the corrupter, "Fear Allah," but the corrupter refused, and pride seized him, so the one who changes wrong sold himself to Allah, the Exalted, fought him, and they fought each other.

It is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to gather young reciters on Friday, among them Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hurr ibn Qays and others. They would recite in his presence and with him. 'Umar heard Ibn 'Abbas say, "The two men fought," when he recited this verse. He asked him about what he had said, and he explained this interpretation to him. 'Umar said to him, "By Allah, your heritage is great, O Ibn 'Abbas!" (lillah taladuka ya Ibn 'Abbas).

Abu Hurayra and Abu Ayyub said, when Hisham ibn 'Amir charged into the ranks at Constantinople, and some people said, "He has thrown himself into destruction with his own hand," (that is not as they said). Rather, this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾ and so on.

Ibtighaʾ (ابتغاء) is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning "seeking." Hamza stopped on ﴿mardat﴾ with a ta' (مرضات), while the rest stopped with a ha' (مرضاه). Abu 'Ali said: The reason for Hamza's stopping with a ta' is either that it is in accordance with the dialect of those who say talhat and 'alqamat, from which is the saying of the poet:

"......... rather, the desert of Tayha, like the back of a shield (hajafat)."

Or it is because the genitive noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) is necessarily implied within the word, so he kept the ta' as it is kept in connected speech, so that it would be known that the genitive noun is intended.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Kind to the servants﴾, it is an expression of hope which implies urging toward complying with what the verse praised. Likewise, the saying: ﴿So Hell is sufficient for him﴾ is a warning that implies caution against what the verse condemned.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded the believers to enter into peace. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿al-salm﴾ with a fatha on the sin. The rest recited it with a kasra in this place. It was said: the two have the same meaning, and both refer to Islam and to peace-making (al-musalama). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: al-silm (with a kasra) means Islam, and al-salm (with a fatha) means peace-making. Al-Mubarrad rejected this distinction. Al-Tabari preferred interpreting the word in the sense of Islam, because the believers were never commanded to take the initiative to enter into peace-making. Rather, it was said to the Prophet ﷺ that he should incline to peace if they inclined to it, but not that he should initiate it.

Having taken the wording to refer to Islam, there is a dispute about who is being addressed. One group said: all the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is that He commanded them to remain steadfast in it and to increase in adhering to its limits. In this reading, *kaffatan* (entirely, all together) covers all the believers and all parts of the Sharia, so the circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) refers to two things at once. This is permissible, as in the Almighty's words: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him﴾ [Maryam: 27], along with other such examples.

'Ikrimah said: rather, the addressees are those among the Children of Israel who believed in the Prophet, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others. They had gone to the extent of exalting the day of Saturday (*as-Sabt*) and disliked eating camel meat, and they wanted to practise some of the rulings of the Tawrah (Torah) and mix that with Islam. So this verse was revealed concerning them. According to this view, *kaffatan* refers only to the parts of the Sharia.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book. The meaning is: O you who believe in Moses and Jesus, enter into Islam through Muhammad, entirely. According to this view, *kaffatan* refers to the parts of the Sharia and to the addressees. [Some] said, regarding one who understands *as-silm* as Islam, and one who understands it as peaceful coexistence, says: He commanded them to enter into it by paying the *jizyah* (the tax levied on non-Muslim subjects).

*Kaffatan* means "all of them." What is meant by *al-kaffah* is the group that restrains (*takuffu*) its opponent. It was also said that *kaffatan* is a qualifier (*na't*, adjective) of an elided verbal noun (*masdar*), as if the speech were "entered into it with entirety." When the described noun was elided, the qualifier remained in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*).

The discussion of *khutuwat* has already been given. The definite article in *ash-shaytan* is for the genus (*lil-jins*). *'Aduww* (enemy) applies to the singular, the dual, and the plural. *Mubin* may mean that it makes its enmity clear (*abana 'adawatahu*), or that it is evident in itself that he is an enemy, because the Arabs say *baana al-amr* and *abana al-amr* with one meaning.

(p-506)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 204–208 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:
﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life impresses you, and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents.﴾ ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock, and Allah does not love corruption.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him, so Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting-place.﴾ ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, and Allah is Kind to the servants.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace completely, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

Al-Suddi said: These verses were revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, whose name was Ubayy, and "al-Akhnas" was a nickname. The reason was that "he came to the Prophet ﷺ and displayed his Islam, and said, 'Allah knows that I am truthful.' Then he fled after that, and he passed by a group of Muslims, and he burned their crops and killed their donkeys, so these verses were revealed concerning him."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
It has never been established at all that al-Akhnas embraced Islam.

Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who spoke about those who were killed at the expedition of al-Raji': 'Asim ibn Thabit, Khubayb, Ibn al-Dathina, and others. They said, "Woe to these people! They neither stayed in their houses, nor did they deliver the message of their companion." So these verses were revealed describing the characteristics of the hypocrites. Then he mentioned those who were martyred at the expedition of al-Raji' in His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾, and so on.

Qatada, Mujahid, and a group of scholars said: These verses were revealed concerning everyone who conceals disbelief, hypocrisy, lying, or harm, while outwardly displaying the opposite with his tongue. Thus it is general, and it resembles what is related in al-Tirmidhi: "Indeed, in some of the Books of Allah, the Exalted: 'Among the servants of Allah there are people whose tongues are sweeter than honey, while their hearts are more bitter than aloes. They wear sheep's skins over people for softness, they chew the world with religion. Allah, the Exalted, says: Do they deceive Me? Or do they dare against Me? I swear that I will surely send upon them a trial that leaves even the forbearing among them bewildered.'"

The meaning of ﴿and he calls Allah to witness﴾ is: he says, "Allah knows that I am saying the truth."

Abu Haywa and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-yashhadu Allah﴾ (with the verb attributed to Allah). The meaning is: his speech impresses you, while Allah knows from him the opposite of what he says. The recitation followed by the majority is more emphatic in condemning him, because he has bound himself to the discipline of fine speech, and then what is contrary to it appeared from his inner self. What is in his heart differs according to the two recitations. According to the recitation of the majority, it is the good that appears, that is, it is in his heart by his claim. According to the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin, it is the hidden evil.

Ibn 'Abbas recited: ﴿wa-llahu yashhadu 'ala ma fi qalbihi﴾. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿wa-yastashhidu Allah 'ala ma fi qalbihi﴾.

Al-aladd (الألد) means: one who is intensely contentious, stubborn in dispute, who twists arguments from every side. His deviation resembles walking in the two sides of a valley (ladiday al-wadi). From it come the words ladid al-fam (one with a sharp mouth) and al-ladud. It is said: from it, "ladidtu" (with a kasra on the 'ain) "aladdu." It is a dispraise. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The most hateful of men to Allah is the most contentious opponent (al-aladd al-khasm)." It is also said: "laddtuhu" (with a fatha on the 'ain), "aluddu-hu" (with a damma), when you overcome him in dispute. From the same word is the saying of the poet:

"Beneath the rocks there is resolve and determination, and an opponent most contentious, a man of stubborn grip."

(p. 499) As for al-khisam (الخصام) in the verse, it is a verbal noun of khasama. It was also said: it is the plural of khasm, like kalb and kilab, so the sentence would mean: "and he is the most contentious of the contentious ones," meaning their father.

(Note: "tawalla" and "sa'a" both allow two meanings. One is that they are verbs of the heart: "tawalla" then comes in the sense of going astray, becoming angry, and being offended within himself, so he strives with his schemes and intentions to plot against Islam. From this striving is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and from it: ﴿and strives for the Hereafter its striving﴾ [al-Isra': 19], and from it the saying of the poet:

"I strive on behalf of the tribe of Malik; every man is striving in his own affair."

Ibn Jurayj and others followed this direction in the meaning of the verse. The second meaning is that both are verbs of a person. Then "tawalla" comes in the sense of turning his back and departing from you, O Muhammad, and "sa'a" carries its meaning of moving on foot, so he cut the road and corrupted it. Ibn 'Abbas and others followed this direction. Both kinds of striving are corruption.)

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and destroy the crops and the offspring﴾, al-Tabari said: The intended one is al-Akhnas in his burning of the crops and his killing of the donkeys.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 204–208 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:
﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life impresses you, and he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart, yet he is the most contentious of opponents.﴾ ﴿And when he turns away, he strives throughout the land to cause corruption therein and to destroy crops and livestock, and Allah does not love corruption.﴾ ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him, so Hell is sufficient for him, and what an evil resting-place.﴾ ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah, and Allah is Kind to the servants.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace completely, and do not follow the footsteps of Satan. Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy.﴾

Al-Suddi said: These verses were revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, whose name was Ubayy, and "al-Akhnas" was a nickname. The reason was that "he came to the Prophet ﷺ and displayed his Islam, and said, 'Allah knows that I am truthful.' Then he fled after that, and he passed by a group of Muslims, and he burned their crops and killed their donkeys, so these verses were revealed concerning him."

It has never been established at all that al-Akhnas embraced Islam.

Ibn 'Abbas said: It was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who spoke about those who were killed at the expedition of al-Raji': 'Asim ibn Thabit, Khubayb, Ibn al-Dathina, and others. They said, "Woe to these people! They neither stayed in their houses, nor did they deliver the message of their companion." So these verses were revealed describing the characteristics of the hypocrites. Then he mentioned those who were martyred at the expedition of al-Raji' in His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾, and so on.

Qatada, Mujahid, and a group of scholars said: These verses were revealed concerning everyone who conceals disbelief, hypocrisy, lying, or harm, while outwardly displaying the opposite with his tongue. Thus it is general, and it resembles what is related in al-Tirmidhi: "Indeed, in some of the Books of Allah, the Exalted: 'Among the servants of Allah there are people whose tongues are sweeter than honey, while their hearts are more bitter than aloes. They wear sheep's skins over people for softness, they chew the world with religion. Allah, the Exalted, says: Do they deceive Me? Or do they dare against Me? I swear that I will surely send upon them a trial that leaves even the forbearing among them bewildered.'"

The meaning of ﴿and he calls Allah to witness﴾ is: he says, "Allah knows that I am saying the truth."

Abu Haywa and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-yashhadu Allah﴾ (with the verb attributed to Allah). The meaning is: his speech impresses you, while Allah knows from him the opposite of what he says. The recitation followed by the majority is more emphatic in condemning him, because he has bound himself to the discipline of fine speech, and then what is contrary to it appeared from his inner self. What is in his heart differs according to the two recitations. According to the recitation of the majority, it is the good that appears, that is, it is in his heart by his claim. According to the recitation of Ibn Muhaysin, it is the hidden evil.

Ibn 'Abbas recited: ﴿wa-llahu yashhadu 'ala ma fi qalbihi﴾. Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿wa-yastashhidu Allah 'ala ma fi qalbihi﴾.

Al-aladd (الألد) means: one who is intensely contentious, stubborn in dispute, who twists arguments from every side. His deviation resembles walking in the two sides of a valley (ladiday al-wadi). From it come the words ladid al-fam (one with a sharp mouth) and al-ladud. It is said: from it, "ladidtu" (with a kasra on the 'ain) "aladdu." It is a dispraise. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "The most hateful of men to Allah is the most contentious opponent (al-aladd al-khasm)." It is also said: "laddtuhu" (with a fatha on the 'ain), "aluddu-hu" (with a damma), when you overcome him in dispute. From the same word is the saying of the poet:

"Beneath the rocks there is resolve and determination, and an opponent most contentious, a man of stubborn grip."

(p. 499) As for al-khisam (الخصام) in the verse, it is a verbal noun of khasama. It was also said: it is the plural of khasm, like kalb and kilab, so the sentence would mean: "and he is the most contentious of the contentious ones," meaning their father.

(Note: "tawalla" and "sa'a" both allow two meanings. One is that they are verbs of the heart: "tawalla" then comes in the sense of going astray, becoming angry, and being offended within himself, so he strives with his schemes and intentions to plot against Islam. From this striving is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And that man will have nothing except what he strives for﴾ [al-Najm: 39], and from it: ﴿and strives for the Hereafter its striving﴾ [al-Isra': 19], and from it the saying of the poet:

"I strive on behalf of the tribe of Malik; every man is striving in his own affair."

Ibn Jurayj and others followed this direction in the meaning of the verse. The second meaning is that both are verbs of a person. Then "tawalla" comes in the sense of turning his back and departing from you, O Muhammad, and "sa'a" carries its meaning of moving on foot, so he cut the road and corrupted it. Ibn 'Abbas and others followed this direction. Both kinds of striving are corruption.)

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and destroy the crops and the offspring﴾, al-Tabari said: The intended one is al-Akhnas in his burning of the crops and his killing of the donkeys.

Mujahid said: The meaning is that the wrongdoer causes corruption on the earth, so Allah withholds the rain, and the crops and offspring are destroyed. It was also said: the meaning is that the corrupter kills people, so the cultivators of the crops and the ones who are taken away cease. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that "al-harth" (crops) refers to women, and "al-nasl" (offspring) to their offspring.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The apparent meaning is that the verse is an expression of exaggeration in corruption, since all corruption in worldly affairs revolves around these two sections.

Most of the readers recite ﴿yuhlika﴾ with a damma on the yā', a kasra on the lām, and a fatha on the kāf, as a conjunction with ﴿li-yufsida﴾. In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is ﴿wa-li-yahlika﴾. A group recited ﴿wa-yahlaka﴾ with a damma on the kāf, either as a conjunction with ﴿yu'jibuka﴾, or with ﴿sa'a﴾ because it carries the meaning of the future, or as a new independent statement. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq, Abu Haywa, and Ibn Muhaysin recited ﴿wa-yahlikᵘ﴾ with a fatha on the yā', a kasra on the lām, a damma on the kāf, and the nominative on ﴿al-harth wa-l-nasl﴾. Ibn Salama related this from Ibn Kathir, as did 'Abd al-Warith from Abu 'Amr. Al-Mahdawi related that what Hammad ibn Salama related from Ibn Kathir is: ﴿wa-yuhlaku﴾ with a damma on the yā' and the kāf, and ﴿al-harth﴾ in the accusative. A group recited ﴿wa-yahlaku﴾ with a fatha on the yā' and the lām and the nominative on ﴿al-harth﴾, and this is the dialect of halaka yahlaku, which is classed among the irregular forms, like rakana yarkanu.

Al-harth (الحرث), linguistically, is the tilling of the earth for cultivation. The crop is called harth by association and congruity. Included in this, by analogy with crops, are all trees and plantings. From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿when the two were judging concerning the field﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78], and it was a vineyard, as reported in the exegetical works.

Women have also been called harth by way of comparison. Al-nasl (النسل) is derived from nasala yansilu, when something comes out in succession. From it is nasal al-ta'ir (the falling of the bird's feathers one after another). From it is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿and they will swarm from every elevation﴾ [al-Anbiya': 96]. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"......... so wipe from me the garments of your garments, which slip off (tansilu)."

(p. 501) As for ﴿la yuhibbu﴾, its meaning is: He does not love it from the people of righteousness, that is, He does not love it as a religion. Otherwise, nothing occurs except what Allah, the Exalted, loves to occur. Corruption does occur. This is in accordance with the view of the theologians that love (hubb) means will (irada).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Love, in the sense of will, has a distinction of preference. If someone were to say that the corruption intended lacks the distinction of preference, that would be valid, since Allah's love is only for what is good in all its aspects.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah"﴾ and so on: this is the description of the disbeliever or the hypocrite who goes off with himself in arrogance. It is disliked for a believer to bring someone into embarrassment in such a matter. Some scholars said: It is enough sin for a man that his brother says to him, "Fear Allah," and he replies, "Keep to yourself. Would someone like you advise me?"

Al-'izza (العزة) here means: power and strength of the self. That is, he became proud within himself and was puffed up, and that pride led him into sin when it seized him with it and bound him to his father. The wording of the verse may also be read as: "pride seized him along with the sin," so the meaning of the preposition bi- (الباء) differs according to the two interpretations.

Hasbuhu (حسبه) means: sufficient for him in punishment and recompense, just as you say to a man, "What has befallen you is enough for you," while you are magnifying and exaggerating over him what has befallen him. Al-mihad (المهاد) is what a man prepares for himself, as if it were a bed.

From this same category is the saying of the poet:

"......... a greeting among them is a painful blow."

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾ and so on, it encompasses every fighter in the way of Allah, or every martyr in his own person, or every one who changes wrong. The apparent sense of this division is that the verses before it concern the disbeliever in general, as is shown by the threat of the Fire, and that the sinners who have some of this disposition receive their share of the threat of the verse. As for the one who says that the preceding verses concern hypocrites who spoke about the expedition of al-Raji', he says: this verse concerns the martyrs of the expedition of al-Raji'.

As for the one who says that those (the earlier verses) concern al-Akhnas, he says: this one concerns the Ansar and the Muhajirun who hastened to faith. 'Ikrima and others said: this one concerns a group of the Muhajirun, and they mentioned the hadith of Suhayb, that he left Makkah to go to the Prophet ﷺ, and Quraysh followed him to turn him back. He shook out his quiver and said to them: "You know that by Allah I am among the best of you at archery. By Allah, I will shoot at you as long as I have an arrow left, and then I will strike with my sword as long as there is anything left in my hand." They said to him, "We will not let you go away from us wealthy, when you came to us poor. But show us where your wealth is, and we will leave you." So he showed them where his wealth was, and they left him. He migrated to the Prophet ﷺ, and when he saw him, he said to him, "The sale has profited, Abu Yahya." So this verse was revealed concerning him.

Whoever says that the first verses are meant in general says that this one is also meant in general.

Yashri (يشري) means "to sell," as in: ﴿and they sold him for a meagre price﴾ [Yusuf: 20]. From it is the saying of Yazid ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari:

"I sold a cloak, would that I had been, after that cloak, its owner."

Another said:

"He is offered a price for it, yet he refuses it, and his companion says: 'Will you not buy?'"

From this comes the name al-shurat (the Shurat), as if they are those who sold their souls to Allah, the Exalted.

Some people related that it is said: "shara" in the sense of "ishtara" (to buy). Whoever interprets the verse as concerning Suhayb will need this, because he bought his soul with his wealth and did not sell it. Unless it is said that Suhayb's resolve to fight them was a sale of his soul to Allah, the Exalted, so the word is correct in the sense of "baa" (to sell).

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, interpreted this verse concerning those who change wrong. Therefore 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas said: "The two men fought," meaning that the one who changes wrong said to the corrupter, "Fear Allah," but the corrupter refused, and pride seized him, so the one who changes wrong sold himself to Allah, the Exalted, fought him, and they fought each other.
