'Umar said to him, "By Allah, your heritage is great, O Ibn 'Abbas!" (lillah taladuka ya Ibn 'Abbas).

Abu Hurayra and Abu Ayyub said, when Hisham ibn 'Amir charged into the ranks at Constantinople, and some people said, "He has thrown himself into destruction with his own hand," (that is not as they said). Rather, this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾ and so on.

Ibtighaʾ (ابتغاء) is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning "seeking." Hamza stopped on ﴿mardat﴾ with a ta' (مرضات), while the rest stopped with a ha' (مرضاه). Or it is because the genitive noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) is necessarily implied within the word, so he kept the ta' as it is kept in connected speech, so that it would be known that the genitive noun is intended.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
Love, in the sense of will, has a distinction of preference. If someone were to say that the corruption intended lacks the distinction of preference, that would be valid, since Allah's love is only for what is good in all its aspects.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah"﴾ and so on: this is the description of the disbeliever or the hypocrite who goes off with himself in arrogance. It is disliked for a believer to bring someone into embarrassment in such a matter. Some scholars said: It is enough sin for a man that his brother says to him, "Fear Allah," and he replies, "Keep to yourself. Would someone like you advise me?"

Al-'izza (العزة) here means: power and strength of the self. That is, he became proud within himself and was puffed up, and that pride led him into sin when it seized him with it and bound him to his father. The wording of the verse may also be read as: "pride seized him along with the sin," so the meaning of the preposition bi- (الباء) differs according to the two interpretations.

Hasbuhu (حسبه) means: sufficient for him in punishment and recompense, just as you say to a man, "What has befallen you is enough for you," while you are magnifying and exaggerating over him what has befallen him. Al-mihad (المهاد) is what a man prepares for himself, as if it were a bed.

From this same category is the saying of the poet:

"......... a greeting among them is a painful blow."

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾ and so on, it encompasses every fighter in the way of Allah, or every martyr in his own person, or every one who changes wrong. The apparent sense of this division is that the verses before it concern the disbeliever in general, as is shown by the threat of the Fire, and that the sinners who have some of this disposition receive their share of the threat of the verse. As for the one who says that the preceding verses concern hypocrites who spoke about the expedition of al-Raji', he says: this verse concerns the martyrs of the expedition of al-Raji'.

As for the one who says that those (the earlier verses) concern al-Akhnas, he says: this one concerns the Ansar and the Muhajirun who hastened to faith. 'Ikrima and others said: this one concerns a group of the Muhajirun, and they mentioned the hadith of Suhayb, that he left Makkah to go to the Prophet ﷺ, and Quraysh followed him to turn him back. He shook out his quiver and said to them: "You know that by Allah I am among the best of you at archery. By Allah, I will shoot at you as long as I have an arrow left, and then I will strike with my sword as long as there is anything left in my hand." They said to him, "We will not let you go away from us wealthy, when you came to us poor. But show us where your wealth is, and we will leave you." So he showed them where his wealth was, and they left him. He migrated to the Prophet ﷺ, and when he saw him, he said to him, "The sale has profited, Abu Yahya." So this verse was revealed concerning him.

Whoever says that the first verses are meant in general says that this one is also meant in general.

Yashri (يشري) means "to sell," as in: ﴿and they sold him for a meagre price﴾ [Yusuf: 20]. From it is the saying of Yazid ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari:

"I sold a cloak, would that I had been, after that cloak, its owner."

Another said:

"He is offered a price for it, yet he refuses it, and his companion says: 'Will you not buy?'"

From this comes the name al-shurat (the Shurat), as if they are those who sold their souls to Allah, the Exalted.

Some people related that it is said: "shara" in the sense of "ishtara" (to buy). Whoever interprets the verse as concerning Suhayb will need this, because he bought his soul with his wealth and did not sell it. Unless it is said that Suhayb's resolve to fight them was a sale of his soul to Allah, the Exalted, so the word is correct in the sense of "baa" (to sell).

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them, interpreted this verse concerning those who change wrong. Therefore 'Ali and Ibn 'Abbas said: "The two men fought," meaning that the one who changes wrong said to the corrupter, "Fear Allah," but the corrupter refused, and pride seized him, so the one who changes wrong sold himself to Allah, the Exalted, fought him, and they fought each other.

It is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab used to gather young reciters on Friday, among them Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hurr ibn Qays and others. They would recite in his presence and with him. 'Umar heard Ibn 'Abbas say, "The two men fought," when he recited this verse. He asked him about what he had said, and he explained this interpretation to him. 'Umar said to him, "By Allah, your heritage is great, O Ibn 'Abbas!" (lillah taladuka ya Ibn 'Abbas).

Abu Hurayra and Abu Ayyub said, when Hisham ibn 'Amir charged into the ranks at Constantinople, and some people said, "He has thrown himself into destruction with his own hand," (that is not as they said). Rather, this is the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself﴾ and so on.

Ibtighaʾ (ابتغاء) is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi), meaning "seeking." Hamza stopped on ﴿mardat﴾ with a ta' (مرضات), while the rest stopped with a ha' (مرضاه). Abu 'Ali said: The reason for Hamza's stopping with a ta' is either that it is in accordance with the dialect of those who say talhat and 'alqamat, from which is the saying of the poet:

"......... rather, the desert of Tayha, like the back of a shield (hajafat)."

Or it is because the genitive noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) is necessarily implied within the word, so he kept the ta' as it is kept in connected speech, so that it would be known that the genitive noun is intended.

As for the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Kind to the servants﴾, it is an expression of hope which implies urging toward complying with what the verse praised. Likewise, the saying: ﴿So Hell is sufficient for him﴾ is a warning that implies caution against what the verse condemned.

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded the believers to enter into peace. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿al-salm﴾ with a fatha on the sin. The rest recited it with a kasra in this place. It was said: the two have the same meaning, and both refer to Islam and to peace-making (al-musalama). Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: al-silm (with a kasra) means Islam, and al-salm (with a fatha) means peace-making. Al-Mubarrad rejected this distinction. Al-Tabari preferred interpreting the word in the sense of Islam, because the believers were never commanded to take the initiative to enter into peace-making. Rather, it was said to the Prophet ﷺ that he should incline to peace if they inclined to it, but not that he should initiate it.

Having taken the wording to refer to Islam, there is a dispute about who is being addressed. One group said: all the believers in Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is that He commanded them to remain steadfast in it and to increase in adhering to its limits. In this reading, *kaffatan* (entirely, all together) covers all the believers and all parts of the Sharia, so the circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) refers to two things at once. This is permissible, as in the Almighty's words: ﴿Then she brought him to her people, carrying him﴾ [Maryam: 27], along with other such examples.

'Ikrimah said: rather, the addressees are those among the Children of Israel who believed in the Prophet, such as 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others. They had gone to the extent of exalting the day of Saturday (*as-Sabt*) and disliked eating camel meat, and they wanted to practise some of the rulings of the Tawrah (Torah) and mix that with Islam. So this verse was revealed concerning them. According to this view, *kaffatan* refers only to the parts of the Sharia.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the verse was revealed concerning the People of the Book. The meaning is: O you who believe in Moses and Jesus, enter into Islam through Muhammad, entirely. According to this view, *kaffatan* refers to the parts of the Sharia and to the addressees. [Some] said, regarding one who understands *as-silm* as Islam, and one who understands it as peaceful coexistence, says: He commanded them to enter into it by paying the *jizyah* (the tax levied on non-Muslim subjects).

*Kaffatan* means "all of them." What is meant by *al-kaffah* is the group that restrains (*takuffu*) its opponent. It was also said that *kaffatan* is a qualifier (*na't*, adjective) of an elided verbal noun (*masdar*), as if the speech were "entered into it with entirety." When the described noun was elided, the qualifier remained in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*).

The discussion of *khutuwat* has already been given. The definite article in *ash-shaytan* is for the genus (*lil-jins*). *'Aduww* (enemy) applies to the singular, the dual, and the plural. *Mubin* may mean that it makes its enmity clear (*abana 'adawatahu*), or that it is evident in itself that he is an enemy, because the Arabs say *baana al-amr* and *abana al-amr* with one meaning.

(p-506)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 209–212:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And if you slip after the clear proofs have come to you, then know that Allah is Mighty, Wise.﴾ ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, with the angels, and the matter be decided? And to Allah all matters are returned.﴾ ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them. And whoever substitutes the favour of Allah after it has come to him—indeed, Allah is severe in penalty.﴾ ﴿The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve, and they mock those who believe. But those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection. And Allah provides for whom He wills without account.﴾

The majority of readers recited "zalaltum" (زَلَلْتُمْ) with a fatha on the lam. Abu al-Samal recited it with a kasra. The root meaning of zalal (الزَلَل) is slipping of the foot, then it is used for beliefs, opinions and other things. The meaning is: you went astray and deviated from the truth.

"Al-bayyinat" (الْبَيِّنَاتُ, the clear proofs) means Muhammad, his signs and his miracles, if the address is first to the community of believers. If the address is to the People of the Two Books, then "al-bayyinat" are what came in their laws of the information about Muhammad (ﷺ) and the description of him.

"'Aziz" (عَزِيزٌ, Mighty) is an attribute implying that He is able over you; you cannot overpower Him, and you cannot escape from Him. "Hakim" (حَكِيمٌ, Wise) means that He is precise in what He punishes you with for your slipping.

Al-Naqqash related that Ka'b al-Ahbar, when he embraced Islam, was learning the Qur'an, and the one who was teaching him recited to him, "fa'lamu anna Allaha ghafurun rahim" (فاعْلَمُوا أنَّ اللهَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ). Ka'b said, "I find it strange that it should be like this." A man passed by them, and Ka'b said, "How do you recite this verse?" The man recited, "fa'lamu anna Allaha 'azizun hakim," and Ka'b said, "This is how it should be."

His saying, the Exalted: "Do they await..." the verse. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). "Hal" (هَلْ) is among the particles of beginning, like "amma." "Yanzurun" (يَنْظُرُونَ) means "yantazirun" (they await). The intended people are those who slip.

"Zulal" (الظُلَلُ) is the plural of "zullah" (ظُلَّةٌ), which is what overshadows from above. Qatada and al-Dahhak recited "fi zilal" (فِي ظِلالِ), and Harun ibn Hatim related it from Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, here and in the two instances in al-Zumar. 'Ikrima said: "zulal" means canopies. Al-Hasan, Ibn al-Qa'qa', and Abu Haywa recited "wa'l-mala'ikati" (وَالْمَلائِكَةِ) in the genitive, as a conjunction with "al-ghamam" (the clouds). The majority of readers recited it in the nominative, as a conjunction with "Allah," and the meaning is that the judgment of Allah, His command, His prohibition and His punishment of them come to them. Ibn Jurayj and others held that this threat is about what occurs in this world. Some people said: rather, it is a threat about the Day of Resurrection. Some people said: His saying "unless Allah should come to them" is a threat about the Day of Resurrection, while as for the angels, the threat is about their coming at death.

"Al-ghamam" (الغَمامِ) is the finest, purest and most beautiful of clouds, and it is what the Children of Israel were shaded by. Al-Naqqash said it is white mist. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud: "illa an ya'tiyahumu Allahu wa'l-mala'ikatu fi zulalin mina'l-ghamam."

"Qudiya al-amr" (قُضِيَ الأمْرُ) means: the recompense has occurred and the people of disobedience have been punished. Mu'adh ibn Jabal recited "wa-qada'u al-amr" (وَقَضاءُ الأمْرِ). Yahya ibn Ya'mur recited "wa-qada al-umur" (وَقَضى الأُمُورَ) in the plural. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "tarji'u" (تَرْجِعُ) with the verb in the active voice. The rest recited "turja'u" (تُرْجَعُ) with the verb in the passive voice, and it returns to Him, the Exalted, before and after. The mention of this is made to alert to the Day of Resurrection, to the cessation of what was in the hands of kings in this world.

His saying, the Exalted: "Ask the Children of Israel..." the verse. The address is to Muhammad (ﷺ), and in it is permission to ask for whoever among his community wishes. The meaning of the verse is to rebuke them for their obstinacy after the clear signs. Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of 'Abbas from him, recited "isal" (اسْألْ) according to the original form. Some people recited "asal" (أسَلُ) with the movement transferred to the sin and the disregard of that, leaving the alif of connection in accordance with the dialect of those who say "al-humur." Whoever recited "sall" (سَلَّ) removed the alif of connection, since he transferred the movement and dispensed with it. "Kam" (كَمْ) is in the accusative position, either by a verb implied after it, because it has the front of the sentence, its estimate being "kam atayna" ("atayna-hum"), or by "atayna-hum."

His saying "min ayah" (مِن آيَةٍ) is, according to the first estimate, a second object of "atayna-hum," and according to the second, in the position of a specifier. It is possible that "kam" is in the nominative position as the subject, with the predicate being "atayna-hum," and in it there becomes a pronoun referring back to "kam," its estimate being "kam atayna-humuhu." The intended meaning of "ayah" is: how many signs came to them concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), identifying him and indicating him.

"Ni'mat Allah" (نِعْمَةَ اللهِ, the favour of Allah) is a general term for all of His bounties, but what strengthens the situation of the Prophet with them is that what is pointed to here is Muhammad (ﷺ). So the meaning is: whoever among the Children of Israel substitutes the attribute of the favour of Allah; then the wording came extending to every substituter of a favour of Allah, the Exalted.

Al-Tabari said: the favour here is Islam, and this is close to the first. The wording also includes the disbelievers of Quraysh, to whom Muhammad was sent as a favour, so they substituted accepting it and thanking for it with disbelief. The Torah is also a favour upon the Children of Israel, guiding and directing them, but they substituted it by distorting it and denying the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, the Exalted: "Indeed, Allah is severe in penalty" is a statement that implies and includes the threat.

"Al-'iqab" (العِقابِ) is derived from "al-'aqib" (the heel), as if the one punished walks, with the recompense for him, in the tracks of his heel. From it comes "'aqabat al-rakib" (the rider's stage) and "'aqabat al-qadar" (the consequence of fate).

His saying, the Exalted: "The life of this world has been made attractive to those who disbelieve" — the one who beautifies it is its Creator, its Originator, and the Creator of disbelief. Shaytan also beautifies it through his whisperings and his seduction. Mujahid, Humayd ibn Qays and Abu Haywa recited "zayyana" (زَيَّنَ) with the verb in the active voice and "al-hayat" in the accusative. Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited "zayyanat" (زَيَّنَتْ) with the sign shown, and the recitation without a sign is for the intervening word, and because the feminine is not real.

Those who disbelieve are singled out for mention because they accepted the beautification entirely, turned to this world, and turned away from the Hereafter on its account. The beautification from Allah, the Exalted, applies to all, and Allah has made what is on the earth an adornment for it, in order to test creation as to which of them is best in deed. So the believers who follow the ways of the Law are not seduced by the adornment, while the disbelievers are overcome by it, because they believe in nothing other than it. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, when wealth was brought to him, said: "O Allah, we cannot but rejoice in what You have adorned for us."

His saying "and they mock" refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh, because they used to magnify their state of worldly affairs, take pride in them, and mock the followers of the Prophet (ﷺ): such as Bilal, Suhayb, Ibn Mas'ud and others. Allah mentions the ugliness of their deed, and alerts to the lowliness of their station by His saying: "But those who fear Allah will be above them on the Day of Resurrection." The meaning of "above" here is in rank and standing, so it implies preference, even though the disbelievers have no share of standing, as He, the Exalted, said: "The companions of the Garden on that Day are better in resting place" (Al-Furqan: 24). And the verse allows that the righteous in the Hereafter are in luxury and in winning mercy above what these people are in their worldly life; and likewise, "better in resting place" than these in the blessing of this world. On this possibility, preference occurs in a matter in which there is sharing. And this verse may also mean that the place is above, in that Paradise is in the heavens and the Fire is in the lowest of the low, so from the arrangement of places one knows that these are in Paradise and those are in the Fire.

The two verses may also imply that the preference is according to what the disbelievers' claim includes, for they used to say: "If there is a resurrection, we will have more fortune than you." From this is the hadith of Khabbab with al-'As ibn Wa'il. All of this is among the possible interpretations, preserving the position of Sibawayh and al-Khalil that preference only comes in what involves sharing, while the Kufans permit it where there is no sharing.

His saying, the Exalted: "And Allah provides for whom He wills without account" may mean: Allah provides these disbelievers in this world, so do not be amazed at that, and do not measure the Hereafter by it, for provision is not in proportion to disbelief or belief, such that for this one his deed is reckoned and for that one his deed is reckoned, and they are provided according to that reckoning. Rather, provision is without reckoning of deeds, while deeds and their recompense are reckoned and returned, since the repaying of recompense corresponds to the repaying of the deed rewarded. So the meaning is that the believer, even if he is not provided in this world, is above on the Day of Resurrection.

The verse may also mean: Allah provides these weak ones with exalted rank by making them above, and with what is within that of bliss without reckoning, so the verse is an alert to the greatness of the blessing upon them, and to making their provision without reckoning, since it is lasting and does not end, for it does not run out.

It is also possible that "without account" is an attribute of the provision of Allah, the Exalted, however it is disposed, since His power is glorified and He does not spend less; so all His bounty is without account.

It is also possible that the meaning in the verse is: from where this one whom Allah wills does not reckon, as if He said: without reckoning by the one provided, as He said: "And He will provide for him from where he does not expect" (Al-Talaq: 3).

If an objector objects to this verse by His saying, the Exalted: "A gift from your Lord, a reckoning" (Al-Naba': 36), the meaning there is "muhsiban" (providing a sufficiency), and also, if it were a counting, the reckoning would be in the recompense and reward, since they are returned; while the absence of reckoning is in bounty and favour.

Misfortune and adversity touched them, and they were shaken, until the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When is the help of God?" Unquestionably, the help of God is near.﴾

(p-512) Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Zayd said: What is meant by "mankind" is the children of Adam, when God brought them forth as souls (nasam) from the loins of Adam, meaning they were upon the natural disposition (fitrah).

Mujahid said: "Mankind" is Adam alone. Some said: Adam and Eve.

Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said: "Mankind" refers to the generations that existed between Adam and Noah, and they were ten. They were upon the truth until they differed, so God sent Noah and those after him.

Some said: "Mankind" refers to Noah and those in his ark, who were Muslims, and after that they differed.

Ibn 'Abbas also said: Mankind was one community of disbelievers, meaning during the period of Noah, when God sent him.

According to these opinions, the verse remains on its original past tense, but the verse may bear a seventh meaning: that it informs about mankind as a whole, the entire species, that they were one community in their lack of laws and their ignorance of realities, had God not bestowed His favor upon them and graced them with messengers. On this reading, "kana" (was) denotes a permanent state and is not restricted to the past, like the saying of God, Exalted: "And God has always been Forgiving and Merciful."

The ummah (community) is a group united in one aim. One may also be called an ummah if he is alone in his aim. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ concerning Qiss ibn Sa'idah: "He will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as an ummah alone."

(p-513) Ubayy ibn Ka'b recited: "Mankind was one community" (kana al-bashar ummatan wahidah). Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Mankind was one community, then they differed, so He sent..." Whoever understood "mankind" in the verse as believers supplied "then they differed" in the sentence, and whoever understood them as disbelievers, the sending of the prophets was to them. The first of the messengers, according to what is related in the Sahih in the hadith of intercession, is Noah, because people say to him: "You are the first of the messengers." The meaning is: to rectify disbelievers. Otherwise, Adam was a messenger to his children, teaching them the religion and faith. "Bearers of good news" means with reward for obedience, and "warners" means from punishment for disobedience. Both words are in the accusative as circumstantial qualifiers (hal).

"Al-kitab" is a noun denoting a genus, and the meaning is all the books. Al-Tabari said: the alif and lam in "al-kitab" are for a known reference, and what is meant is the Torah. "Liyahkuma" (that He might judge) is attributed to the Book according to the majority view. Some said: the meaning is "that God might judge."

Al-Jahdari recited "liyuhkama" with the verb in the passive, and Makki reported from him "linahkuma" (that We might judge).

(p-514) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

I think this is a copyist's error, because he is not reported to have used the passive form as other people reported it.

The pronoun in "fihi" refers to "ma" in "fima" (concerning that). The second pronoun in "fihi" may refer to the Book, or to the preceding pronoun. "Alladhina utuhu" refers to those who were masters of knowledge of it and who studied it. God singled them out for mention to alert to the vileness of their deed and the ugliness of what they committed. "Bayyinat" means the proofs and arguments. "Baghyan" is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi). Baghy means transgression against truth through falsehood. "Huda" means guidance, and that is the creation of faith in their hearts. The aspects of guidance were mentioned earlier in the Surah al-Hamd. By "those who believed" is meant those who believed in Muhammad ﷺ. Some said: the meaning of the verse is that the nations denied each other's books, so God guided the community of Muhammad to affirm all of them. Others said: God guided the believers to the truth concerning what the People of the Two Books differed over, such as their claim that Ibrahim was a Jew or a Christian. Ibn Zayd said: this refers to their qibla, since the qibla of the Jews was toward Bayt al-Maqdis and that of the Christians toward the east. It also refers to the day of Friday, for the Prophet ﷺ said: "This is the day concerning which they differed, and God guided us to it: the Jews have Saturday and the Christians have Sunday," and [it refers to] their fasting and all that they differed over.

Al-Farra' said: there is inversion (qalb) in the sentence, and al-Tabari chose this view. He said: its intended sense is "So God guided those who believed to the truth from among what they differed over." What prompted this reading was the concern that the wording might be taken to mean that they differed about the truth itself, so God guided the believers to some of what they differed over, and perhaps the truth was altered in itself. Al-Tabari followed this in his report from al-Farra'.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

Claiming inversion in the wording of the Book of God without necessity, which is driven only by incapacity and poor reasoning, is not right. The sentence is intelligible in its own form and arrangement, because His saying "fahada" (so He guided) implies that they reached (p-515) the truth, and the meaning is complete at "fihi." The phrase "minal-haqq" clarifies the genus of that over which the disagreement occurred.

Al-Mahdawi said: The word "ikhtilaf" (disagreement) was placed before "al-haqq" for emphasis, since the concern is with mentioning the disagreement.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This, in my view, is not strong. In the recitation of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "lima ikhtalafu 'anhu minal-haqq," that is, "concerning Islam."

"Bi-idhnihi" (by His permission): al-Zajjaj said its meaning is "by His knowledge," and it was said: "by His command." Idhn is knowledge and enablement; if a command accompanies it, it becomes stronger than mere permission by an added quality.

In the saying of God, Exalted: "And God guides whom He wills," there is a refutation of the Mu'tazilah, who claim that the servant independently achieves guidance for himself.

As for His saying, "Or did you suppose" to the end of the verse: "am" may come to begin a new statement after another statement, even without being a division or an equivalence of the interrogative alif. Some philologists reported that it may function as the interrogative alif, beginning a sentence with it.

"Hasibtum" requires two objects. The grammarians said: "an tadkhulu" (that you enter) takes the place of both objects, since the clause following "an" is complete in meaning. It is also possible that the second object is omitted, its implied sense being: "Did you suppose your entering Paradise to be actual, and yet...?"

It does not seem right to posit the second object in His saying "wa lamma ya'tikum" by supposing: "Did you suppose your entering Paradise free from what befell those before you," because "khalaw" is a circumstantial clause, and a circumstantial clause here only comes after the two objects are complete, and the two objects are the subject and predicate before the entry of "hasiba."

"Al-ba'sa'" refers to wealth, and "al-darra'" refers to the body. "Khalaw" means they passed away, that is, they came to be in emptiness from the earth.

This verse was revealed concerning the episode of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), when they besieged the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions in Medina. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Suddi, and most exegetes. Another group said the verse was revealed to console the emigrants whose wealth was afflicted after they left, and who had been tested before that.

"Mathal" means "like" (shibh). The sense is: the like of those who "khalaw."

"Zalzalah" means intense shaking, which occurs in persons and in conditions. According to Sibawayh, "zulzila" is quadriliteral like "dahraja." Al-Zajjaj said it is a doubling of "zalla," so the doubling in this case falls on the first radical.

Al-A'mash recited "wa-zulzilu, wa-yaqulu al-rasul" with waw in place of "hatta."

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "wa-zulzilu thumma zulzilu wa-yaqulu al-rasul." Nafi' read "yaqulu" in the nominative, while the rest read it in the accusative. On Nafi's reading, it is as though a causal element is attached to it, so it is an inceptive particle that makes the verb nominative.

Most interpreters hold that the speech up to the end of the verse is from the words of the Messenger and the believers, and that this is the Messenger's saying in seeking to hasten victory, not out of doubt or suspicion.

(p-517) "Al-rasul" is a noun of genus, and God mentioned it to magnify the calamity that prompted the Messenger to say this.

Another group said: there is inversion and transposition in the speech, and the intended sense is: "until those who believed say, 'When is the help of God?' and then the Messenger says, 'Unquestionably, the help of God is near.'" The Messenger was placed first in rank for his station, and then the statement of the believers was placed first because it precedes in time.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This is arbitrary, and bearing the speech on its own proper sense is not difficult. It is possible that "Unquestionably, the help of God is near" is a report from God, Exalted, beginning a new statement after the completion of the quoted speech.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 215–217:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy and the wayfarer. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah knows it.﴾ ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is grave, but averting from the way of Allah, disbelieving in Him, and (barring access to) the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is graver with Allah. And fitnah (persecution, turning people from their religion) is graver than killing.﴾

[p-518] "Those who ask" (al-sa'iluna) are the believers. The meaning is: they ask you, "What are the ways in which they should spend, and where should they place what is obligatory to spend?" The word "ma" (what) may be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), with "dha" (this) as its predicate, so that it means "alladhi" (that which), "yunfiquna" is a relative clause (silah), and there is a returning pronoun (a'id) to "dha" in the sense of "yunfiquna-hu" (they spend it). It may also be that "madha" is a single compound noun in the accusative position, governed by "yunfiquna," and so it is stripped of the pronoun. When it is a compound noun it is in the accusative position, not in the case of what came in the verse of the poet:

"And what might the slanderers (al-washun) say, except that they say: Indeed I am in love with you?"

Since "'asa" (perhaps) does not govern what precedes it, "madha" is in the nominative position, and it is compound, since "dha" has no relative clause.

Some said: this verse concerns the obligatory zakat, and according to this, the parents and those who are like them among the relatives were abrogated from it (naskh, abrogation).

As-Suddi said: this verse was revealed before the obligation of zakat, and then the obligatory zakat abrogated it.

Al-Mahdawi erred regarding as-Suddi in this, attributing to him that he said: the verse concerns the obligatory zakat, then the parents were abrogated from it.

Ibn Juraij and others said: it is recommendation (nadb, a recommended act), and zakat is other than this spending. According to this, there is no abrogation in it.

Al-yutm (orphanhood) is the loss of the father before reaching puberty. The discussion of "al-miskin" (the needy) and "ibn al-sabil" (the wayfarer) has preceded.

"﴿Wa ma taf'alu﴾" (and whatever you do) is in the jussive mood by the conditional, and the answer of the condition is in the "fa" (then). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, read "yaf'alu" with the "ya'" (third person), in reference to the absent party. The apparent meaning of the verse is a statement of information, and it contains a promise of recompense.

[p-519] "Kutiba" (it was prescribed) means: it was made obligatory, and its like has been mentioned before. This is the obligation of jihad. Some read: "kutiba 'alaykumu al-qatlu" (killing was prescribed for you). 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: fighting was made obligatory upon the individuals of the Companions of Muhammad. Then, when the Law was established and became firm, it became a collective obligation (fard al-kifaya). The majority of the community said: its initial obligation was only a collective one, without specification.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The consensus (ijma') has continued that jihad upon the community of Muhammad is a collective obligation. When some of the Muslims undertake it, it is dropped from the rest. Except that if the enemy descends upon the territory of Islam, then it becomes an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) at that time.

Al-Mahdawi and others reported from ath-Thawri that he said: jihad is voluntary (tatawwu'). This expression, in my view, is only in response to the question of the questioner, and when [the community] was already engaged in jihad, it was said to him: that is voluntary.

"Al-kurh" with a damma on the kaf is the noun, and with a fatha it is the verbal noun. Some said: "al-kurh" with a fatha on the kaf is what a person is compelled to, and "al-kurh" is what he himself dislikes. Others said: both have one meaning.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And perhaps you dislike a thing﴾ to the end of the verse. Some said "'asa" from Allah is binding [p-520], and the meaning is: perhaps you dislike what there is in jihad of hardship, ﴿and it is good for you﴾ in that you will prevail, be victorious, gain booty, and be rewarded, and whoever dies, dies a martyr. ﴿And perhaps you love﴾ ease and abandoning fighting, ﴿and it is bad for you﴾ in that you will be overcome, humiliated, and your affair will be lost.

In the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah knows﴾ to the end of the verse there is an affirmation of the matter's strength.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ to the end of the verse were revealed concerning the story of 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami. This was because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment (sariyya) under the command of 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi, whose leader from the first Badr. They encountered 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami, with him 'Uthman ibn 'Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, and his brother Nawfal al-Makhzumiyyan, and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, on the last day of Rajab according to what Ibn Ishaq mentioned, and on the last day of Jumada al-Akhira according to what at-Tabari reported from as-Suddi and others. The first is more well known. However, Ibn 'Abbas has transmitted that this occurred on the first night of Rajab, while the Muslims thought it was Jumada, and that they had not intended killing in the sacred month. As for according to Ibn Ishaq's account, they said: if we leave them today they will enter the Sanctuary (al-Haram), so they resolved to fight them. Waqid ibn 'Abdullah shot 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami with an arrow and killed him. 'Uthman ibn 'Abdullah [p-521] and al-Hakam were captured, and Nawfal fled and escaped them. The Muslims considered this easy in the sacred month out of fear of missing them. Quraysh said: Muhammad has made lawful the sacred months, and they reproached him for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) hesitated and said: "I did not command you to fight in the sacred months." Then this verse was revealed.

Al-Mahdawi mentioned that the cause of this verse was that 'Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri killed two men of Banu Kilab in Rajab, and then it was revealed. This is a confusion on al-Mahdawi's part. The two companions of 'Amr had a covenant from the Prophet (ﷺ), and 'Amr had escaped from the incident of Bir Ma'una. Al-Sahib ibn 'Abbad mentioned in his well-known epistle called "al-Asadiyya" that 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh was named "Amir al-Mu'minin" (Commander of the Faithful) at that time, because he was appointed over a group of the believers.

"Qitalin" (fighting) is a substitute (badal) according to Sibawayh, and it is the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). Al-Farra' said: it is in the genitive by the implied "'an" (about). Abu 'Ubayda said: it is in the genitive by proximity (al-jiwar). This statement of his is an error. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, it reads: "yas'alunaka 'ani al-shahri al-haram 'an qitalin fihi" with the repetition of "'an," and likewise ar-Rabi' and al-A'mash read it. 'Ikrima read: "'ani al-shahri al-haram qatlun fihi, qul qatlun" without alif in both.

[p-522] "Al-shahr" (the month) in the verse is a generic noun (ism al-jins). The Arabs had been given by Allah the sacred month as a foundation, by which they maintained balance, so they did not shed blood, and did not alter in the sacred months. These are: Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, al-Muharram, and Rajab.

Jabir ibn 'Abdullah narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) did not go to war in them unless he was attacked." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾. "Sadd" (averting) is a nominative subject, separated from what precedes it, and its predicate is "akbar" (graver). "Al-Masjid" is conjoined to "sabil Allah," and this is the correct view.

Al-Farra' said: "sadd" is conjoined to "kabir" (grave). That is an error, because the meaning leads to the conclusion that His words "wa kufrun bihi" (and disbelief in Him) is also conjoined to "kabir," and from that it would follow that expelling the people of the Mosque from it is graver than disbelief with Allah, and the corruption of this is clear.

The meaning of the verse according to the view of the majority: indeed, you, O disbelievers of Quraysh, consider fighting in the sacred month to be a grave matter against us, while what you yourselves do of averting from the way of Allah toward whoever wishes to embrace Islam, and your disbelief in Allah, and your expulsion of the people of the Mosque from it, as they did to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions, is greater in offense with Allah.

Az-Zuhri, Mujahid, and others said: His words ﴿Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾ are abrogated by His words ﴿And fight the polytheists all together﴾ [al-Tawba: 36] and by His words ﴿Kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawba: 5]. 'Ata' said: it was not abrogated, and fighting in the sacred months is not appropriate; but this view is weak.

Mujahid and others said: "fitnah" here means disbelief, that is, your disbelief is worse than our killing of those people.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 215–217:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents, relatives, orphans, the needy and the wayfarer. And whatever good you do, indeed Allah knows it.﴾ ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, though it is hateful to you. But perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allah knows, while you know not.﴾ ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is grave, but averting from the way of Allah, disbelieving in Him, and (barring access to) the Sacred Mosque, and expelling its people from it, is graver with Allah. And fitnah (persecution, turning people from their religion) is graver than killing.﴾

[p-518] "Those who ask" (al-sa'iluna) are the believers. The meaning is: they ask you, "What are the ways in which they should spend, and where should they place what is obligatory to spend?" The word "ma" (what) may be in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), with "dha" (this) as its predicate, so that it means "alladhi" (that which), "yunfiquna" is a relative clause (silah), and there is a returning pronoun (a'id) to "dha" in the sense of "yunfiquna-hu" (they spend it). It may also be that "madha" is a single compound noun in the accusative position, governed by "yunfiquna," and so it is stripped of the pronoun. When it is a compound noun it is in the accusative position, not in the case of what came in the verse of the poet:

"And what might the slanderers (al-washun) say, except that they say: Indeed I am in love with you?"

Since "'asa" (perhaps) does not govern what precedes it, "madha" is in the nominative position, and it is compound, since "dha" has no relative clause.

Some said: this verse concerns the obligatory zakat, and according to this, the parents and those who are like them among the relatives were abrogated from it (naskh, abrogation).

As-Suddi said: this verse was revealed before the obligation of zakat, and then the obligatory zakat abrogated it.

Al-Mahdawi erred regarding as-Suddi in this, attributing to him that he said: the verse concerns the obligatory zakat, then the parents were abrogated from it.

Ibn Juraij and others said: it is recommendation (nadb, a recommended act), and zakat is other than this spending. According to this, there is no abrogation in it.

Al-yutm (orphanhood) is the loss of the father before reaching puberty. The discussion of "al-miskin" (the needy) and "ibn al-sabil" (the wayfarer) has preceded.

"﴿Wa ma taf'alu﴾" (and whatever you do) is in the jussive mood by the conditional, and the answer of the condition is in the "fa" (then). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, read "yaf'alu" with the "ya'" (third person), in reference to the absent party. The apparent meaning of the verse is a statement of information, and it contains a promise of recompense.

[p-519] "Kutiba" (it was prescribed) means: it was made obligatory, and its like has been mentioned before. This is the obligation of jihad. Some read: "kutiba 'alaykumu al-qatlu" (killing was prescribed for you). 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: fighting was made obligatory upon the individuals of the Companions of Muhammad. Then, when the Law was established and became firm, it became a collective obligation (fard al-kifaya). The majority of the community said: its initial obligation was only a collective one, without specification.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The consensus (ijma') has continued that jihad upon the community of Muhammad is a collective obligation. When some of the Muslims undertake it, it is dropped from the rest. Except that if the enemy descends upon the territory of Islam, then it becomes an individual obligation (fard 'ayn) at that time.

Al-Mahdawi and others reported from ath-Thawri that he said: jihad is voluntary (tatawwu'). This expression, in my view, is only in response to the question of the questioner, and when [the community] was already engaged in jihad, it was said to him: that is voluntary.

"Al-kurh" with a damma on the kaf is the noun, and with a fatha it is the verbal noun. Some said: "al-kurh" with a fatha on the kaf is what a person is compelled to, and "al-kurh" is what he himself dislikes. Others said: both have one meaning.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And perhaps you dislike a thing﴾ to the end of the verse. Some said "'asa" from Allah is binding [p-520], and the meaning is: perhaps you dislike what there is in jihad of hardship, ﴿and it is good for you﴾ in that you will prevail, be victorious, gain booty, and be rewarded, and whoever dies, dies a martyr. ﴿And perhaps you love﴾ ease and abandoning fighting, ﴿and it is bad for you﴾ in that you will be overcome, humiliated, and your affair will be lost.

In the words of the Exalted: ﴿And Allah knows﴾ to the end of the verse there is an affirmation of the matter's strength.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month﴾ to the end of the verse were revealed concerning the story of 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami. This was because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent a detachment (sariyya) under the command of 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh al-Asadi, whose leader from the first Badr. They encountered 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami, with him 'Uthman ibn 'Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, and his brother Nawfal al-Makhzumiyyan, and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan, on the last day of Rajab according to what Ibn Ishaq mentioned, and on the last day of Jumada al-Akhira according to what at-Tabari reported from as-Suddi and others. The first is more well known. However, Ibn 'Abbas has transmitted that this occurred on the first night of Rajab, while the Muslims thought it was Jumada, and that they had not intended killing in the sacred month. As for according to Ibn Ishaq's account, they said: if we leave them today they will enter the Sanctuary (al-Haram), so they resolved to fight them. Waqid ibn 'Abdullah shot 'Amr ibn al-Hadrami with an arrow and killed him. 'Uthman ibn 'Abdullah [p-521] and al-Hakam were captured, and Nawfal fled and escaped them. The Muslims considered this easy in the sacred month out of fear of missing them. Quraysh said: Muhammad has made lawful the sacred months, and they reproached him for it. The Prophet (ﷺ) hesitated and said: "I did not command you to fight in the sacred months." Then this verse was revealed.

Al-Mahdawi mentioned that the cause of this verse was that 'Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri killed two men of Banu Kilab in Rajab, and then it was revealed. This is a confusion on al-Mahdawi's part. The two companions of 'Amr had a covenant from the Prophet (ﷺ), and 'Amr had escaped from the incident of Bir Ma'una. Al-Sahib ibn 'Abbad mentioned in his well-known epistle called "al-Asadiyya" that 'Abdullah ibn Jahsh was named "Amir al-Mu'minin" (Commander of the Faithful) at that time, because he was appointed over a group of the believers.

"Qitalin" (fighting) is a substitute (badal) according to Sibawayh, and it is the substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal). Al-Farra' said: it is in the genitive by the implied "'an" (about). Abu 'Ubayda said: it is in the genitive by proximity (al-jiwar). This statement of his is an error. In the codex of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, it reads: "yas'alunaka 'ani al-shahri al-haram 'an qitalin fihi" with the repetition of "'an," and likewise ar-Rabi' and al-A'mash read it. 'Ikrima read: "'ani al-shahri al-haram qatlun fihi, qul qatlun" without alif in both.

[p-522] "Al-shahr" (the month) in the verse is a generic noun (ism al-jins). The Arabs had been given by Allah the sacred month as a foundation, by which they maintained balance, so they did not shed blood, and did not alter in the sacred months. These are: Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, al-Muharram, and Rajab.

Jabir ibn 'Abdullah narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) did not go to war in them unless he was attacked." This is the meaning of His words: ﴿Say: Fighting in it is grave﴾. "Sadd" (averting) is a nominative subject, separated from what precedes it, and its predicate is "akbar" (graver). "Al-Masjid" is conjoined to "sabil Allah," and this is the correct view.

Al-Farra' said: "sadd" is conjoined to "kabir" (grave). That is an error, because the meaning leads to the conclusion that His words "wa kufrun bihi" (and disbelief in Him) is also conjoined to "kabir," and from that it would follow that expelling the people of the Mosque from it is graver than disbelief with Allah, and the corruption of this is clear.

The meaning of the verse according to the view of the majority: indeed, you, O disbelievers of Quraysh, consider fighting in the sacred month to be a grave matter against us, while what you yourselves do of averting from the way of Allah toward whoever wishes to embrace Islam, and your disbelief in Allah, and your expulsion of the people of the Mosque from it, as they did to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions, is greater in offense with Allah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 218–219 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:
﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide eternally.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and striven in the way of Allah – those hope for the mercy of Allah, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, "In them is great sin and benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." And they ask you what they should spend. Say, "The excess." Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses that you may give thought.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And they will not cease fighting you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] is the beginning of a report from Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, and a warning from Him to the believers against the evil of the disbelievers. "Yaruddukum" (they turn you back) is in the accusative because of "hatta" (until), since it is a bare limit (ghayah mujarradah).

His saying, ﴿And whoever of you reverts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], meaning: returns from Islam to disbelief. A group of scholars said: the apostate (murtadd) is asked to repent; if he repents, well and good, otherwise he is killed. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Tawus, and al-Hasan said – with a difference of report from him – and al-Shafiʿi, in one of his two opinions, said: he is killed without being asked to repent. Something similar is reported from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari and Muʿadh ibn Jabal.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The implication of their statement is that he is told at that moment: "Return." If he refuses, he is killed. ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah said: if the apostate was born to Muslim parents, he is killed without being asked to repent; but if he had embraced Islam and then apostatized, he is asked to repent, because he is ignorant of the excellence of Islam to a degree that the child of Muslims is not ignorant of it.

Those who held the view of asking for repentance differed. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he is asked to repent for three days. This is the view of Malik, Ahmad, Ishaq, the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), and al-Shafiʿi in one of his two opinions. al-Zuhri said: he is invited to Islam; if he repents, well and good, otherwise he is killed. It is reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked an apostate to repent for a month, and when he refused, he killed him. al-Nakhaʿi and al-Thawri said: he is asked to repent while imprisoned, indefinitely. Ibn al-Mundhir said: the reports from ʿUmar on this matter differ.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, would carry out the ruling according to the gravity of the apostate's crime, or the slightness of his crime accompanying the apostasy.

"Habita al-ʿamalu" (the deed became void) means: when it is corrupted at its end, so it is nullified.

Abu al-Sammal recited "ḥabatat" with a fatḥa on the bāʾ throughout the Qur'an. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, al-Hakam, al-Layth, Abu Hanifa, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: the inheritance of the apostate goes to his heirs among the Muslims. Malik, Rabiʿa, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafiʿi, and Abu Thawr said: his inheritance goes to the public treasury (bayt al-mal). The people have agreed that his heirs from among the people of disbelief do not inherit from him, except for an anomalous view reported from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz and from Qatada; and a view contrary to it is also reported from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz.

His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated﴾, to the end of the verse. Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, and others said: "When Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Tamimi killed ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami in the sacred month, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held back from taking the fifth (khums) which ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh had been granted by lot as its share, and regarding the two captives." So the Muslims blamed ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions, until it grieved them. Then Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, consoled them with this verse concerning the sacred month, and then by mentioning them and pointing to them in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾. Then it remains applicable to everyone who does what Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, has mentioned.

"Hajara al-rajulu" (the man emigrated) means: he moved from one place to another, relocating to reside, intending to leave the first out of preference for the second. It is a form of mufaʿala from hajara (to abandon). Whoever says that hijra is moving from the desert to the settled town has made a mistake, on the basis that this was the more common case among the Arabs; but on his view the people of Makkah would not be emigrants.

"Jahada" (strove) is a form of mufaʿala from jahida, when one exerts effort. "Yarjūn" (they hope) means: they aspire and consider it near. Hope (rajaʾ) is a state of ease, and hope always involves fear, without fail, just as fear involves hope. Sometimes it is used figuratively, and rajaʾ comes to mean what accompanies it of fear, as al-Hudhali said:

"When the bee has stung him, he does not hope for its sting [to cease], and he swears to it in a tent of cloth, of many layers."

al-Asmaʿi said: when the negative particle is combined with rajaʾ, it carries the meaning of fear, like this verse, and like His saying, the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿those who do not hope for our meeting﴾, meaning: those who do not fear it. It has also been said: the word rajaʾ in the verse retains its usual meaning, i.e., they do not hope for reward in our meeting, and against that is the fear of punishment. Some people said: the word is one of the words with opposite meanings (addad), without figurative use in either direction; but this is not sound. al-Jahiz said in his book "al-Buldan": the meaning of his saying "lam yarujj lasʿahā" is: he does not hope for the healing and removal of its sting, so he endures it. The remainder of the verse is a promise.

His saying, ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾, to the end of the verse. Those who asked were the believers. "Khamr" (wine) is derived from khamara, meaning to cover. From it is the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying: "Cover the vessel" (khammirū al-inā'). From it also: khimar (the woman's head-covering). And khamr is whatever covers you of trees and other things. From it is the poet's verse:

"Ala ya Zayd wa al-Dahhak sayran, faqad jawaztumā khamara al-tariq."
("Look, O Zayd and al-Dahhak, go on, for you have passed the thicket of the road.")
That is: go on concealed, for you have passed the hollow in which the wolf and others hide. From it also is the verse of al-ʿAjjaj:

"In lami al-ʿaqbān la yamshī al-khamar..." 
(He describes an army that came with banners, not hidden.)

From it also is the expression: "So-and-so entered the crowd of people and their concealment (khimārihim)," meaning he is in a hidden place. Since wine covers the intellect and conceals it, it was named so. Khamr is the juice of grapes that has fermented and was not cooked, and whatever else covers the intellect is under its ruling.

Wine was prohibited in Madinah on the day it was prohibited, and it was made of honey, raisins, dates, barley, and wheat, and grape wine was not among them. The Ummah has agreed, regarding grape wine when it foams and froths, that it is forbidden, both its little and its much, and that the prescribed punishment (hadd) is obligatory for both little and much of it. The majority of the Ummah hold that whatever intoxicates in large quantity, other than grape wine, is forbidden in both its little and its much, and the hadd for it is obligatory. Abu Hanifa, Sufyan al-Thawri, Ibn Abi Layla, Ibn Shubruma, and a group of the jurists of Kufa said: "Whatever intoxicates in large quantity, other than grape wine, its small amount that does not intoxicate is permitted; and if anyone becomes intoxicated from it without deliberately aiming to reach the point of intoxication, there is no hadd upon him." This is a weak view, rejected by reasoning. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, ʿUmar al-Faruq, and the Companions are against it.

It is reported that the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Every intoxicant is khamr, and every khamr is forbidden, and whatever intoxicates in large quantity, its little is forbidden." Ibn al-Mundhir said in "al-Ishraf": this report leaves no opinion for any speaker, and no argument for any disputant.

It is reported that this verse was the first touching on the prohibition of wine, then after it: ﴿Do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisaʾ: 43]. Then His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Satan only wants to cause enmity and hatred between you through wine and gambling, and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 91]. Then His saying: ﴿Indeed, wine, gambling, stone altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 90]. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wine has been prohibited."

Nothing has been preserved from the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning the hadd for wine except that it is forty lashes. [This was] narrated by Muslim and Abu Dawud. It is also reported from him (ﷺ) that "he struck for it with a general striking," and Abu Bakr estimated it at forty lashes, and he acted accordingly, and then ʿUmar; then people became lax regarding it, so ʿUmar tightened the hadd upon them and made it like the lightest of the hadd punishments, eighty lashes. Malik held this view, while al-Shafiʿi held forty. According to a group of scholars, the striking for wine is not severe, such that the armpit of the one striking is not exposed. Malik said: all striking is the same; it is not lightened, nor does it leave a mark. And from the one struck, the face, the genitals, the heart, the brain, and the flanks are avoided, by consensus.

A group said: this verse has been abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿So avoid it that you may succeed﴾ [al-Maʾidah: 90]; they mean by it what is in His saying: ﴿and benefits for people﴾ of permissibility and the indication of leniency.

"Maysir" (gambling) is derived from yasara, meaning to slaughter a camel for division, and the yasir is the one who slaughters. From it is the poet's verse:

"His informer and their scheming never ceased against you until they divided the meat of the one whom they cut up by lot (yasarū)."

And from it is the other's verse:

"I say to them in the ravine, when they cast lots over me: 'Have you not despaired? I am the son of the horseman Zahdam.'"

The camel that is divided by lot is called "muyassar," because it is the place of ease (yusr). Then the arrows used in it were called "maysir" by association of meaning.

al-Tabari said: maysir is derived from yasara li hādhā, meaning when it became obligatory and was made possible. He attributed this view to Mujahid, but then quoted from Mujahid's own words something contrary to this view; rather, Mujahid meant the slaughtering.

"Yusr" is the one who participates in striking with the arrows; its plural is ayār. It was also said: yusr is the plural of yasir, like ḥāris and ḥaras and aḥrās.

The arrows of the maysir are seven, which have shares, and there are fixed portions according to the number of the shares; and three which have no shares and no fixed portions in them. They are: al-Fadhdh, al-Tawʾam, al-Raqib, al-Ḥils, al-Nafis, al-Musbil, and al-Muʿallā. The three that have no shares are: al-Munayyaḥ, al-Safiḥ, and al-Waghd. These three are added so that the arrows are multiplied and mixed up for the one who strikes with them (al-ḥurḍa), so that he finds no way to lean toward anyone.

It was the custom of the Arabs to strike with these arrows in the winter, in times of hardship and the bitter cold, for the poor. They would buy a camel, and the participants in the lot would guarantee its price. Then it would be slaughtered and divided into ten portions. al-Asmaʿi erred in the division of the camel, mentioning that it was divided according to the shares of the arrows, twenty-eight portions; but that is not so. Then they would strike with the arrows for the ten portions. Whoever's arrow won, by coming out first from the ribāba (the bag), took his allotments and gave them to the poor.

Sometimes they would gamble for themselves, and then the price was imposed on whoever's arrow did not win, and the poor of the tribe would live by this practice. From it is al-Aʿsha's verse:

"The feeders of guests when they are in winter, and those who place their sustenance upon the one who wins by lot."

And from it is the other's verse:

"In their hands are the marked arrows and the locking arrows; its gift returns to the sustenance of the petitioners."

(In this verse, "manīh" means the one who asks for a gift, because they used to borrow the arrow that had become smooth and had won often, and that is the praised "manīh.")

As for the manīh which is one of the three blank arrows, it is described only as "returning" (karr), and it is this that Jarir intended in his saying:

"Indeed they turned upon Fazara a turning, as the manīh returns, and they circled there in a circle."

And from the maysir is Labid's saying:

"When they cast lots, the ease did not leave among them any shameful deeds whose mention is recounted in the summer."

All of this is the benefit of the maysir, except that it devours wealth falsely, so in it is great sin.

Muhammad ibn Sirin, al-Hasan, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn al-Musayyab, and others said: every game of chance is maysir, such as backgammon (nard), chess (shatranj), and the like, even the children's game with nuts.

His saying, ﴿Say, "In them is great sin and benefit for people"﴾, to the end of the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Rabiʿ said: the sin in them is after prohibition, and the benefit in them is before it. A group said: the sin in wine is the loss of the intellect, insult, slander, harm, and the transgression that comes from its drinker. The benefit is the pleasure in it, as Hassan ibn Thabit said:

"We drink it, and it leaves us kings, and lions whom the encounter does not restrain."

And [there are] other joys from it. Mujahid said: "The benefit in it is the earning of its price. Then Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, informed that the sin is greater than the benefit and more harmful in the Hereafter. This is the preface to the prohibition."

Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "kathīr" with the triple-dotted thāʾ (kathīr, "great"). Their evidence is that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah cursed wine and cursed ten along with it: its seller, its buyer, the one for whom it is bought, its presser, the one for whom it is pressed, its server, its drinker, its carrier, the one to whom it is carried, and the consumer of its price." So these are many sins.

Also, the gathering of benefits is fittingly accompanied by the gathering of sins, and "kathīrun" with the three-dotted thā' conveys that.

The rest of the readers and the majority of people read "kabīrun" with the single-dotted bā'. Its argument is that the sin in gambling and drinking wine is among the major sins (al-kabā'ir), so describing it as "great" (kabīr) is more fitting.

Also, the consensus on "akbar" is an argument for "kabīr" with the bā' with one dot. They unanimously rejected "akthar" with the three-dotted thā', except what is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, where it reads: "Say: in both there is great sin, and their sin is greater" (qul fīhimā ithmun kathīrun wa-ithmuhumā akthar), with the thā' having three dots in both letters.

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿In both there is sin﴾, it may carry two meanings: one is that it refers to their use after the prohibition, and the other is that it refers to the evils that are in them.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: When the verse ﴿Say: In both there is great sin and benefits for people﴾ was revealed, some people disliked them because of the sin, and some people drank them for the benefits. Then when the verse ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] was revealed, they avoided them at the times of the prayers. Then when the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90], 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Ruined for you today, it has been joined with gambling and the altars." And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wine has been prohibited." When 'Umar ibn al-Khattab heard His words, ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], he said: "We have desisted, we have desisted."

Al-Farisi said, and some people of reflection said: Wine was prohibited by this verse, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin﴾ [al-A'raf: 33], and in this verse He informed that in it is sin, so it is prohibited.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This reasoning is not sound, because the sin that is in it is the prohibited thing, not the wine itself, as this reasoning would require.

Qatadah said: Allah censured wine by this verse but did not prohibit it.

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾: Qays ibn Sa'd said: This is the obligatory zakah. The majority of scholars said: Rather, it is voluntary spending. Some of them said: It was abrogated by zakah. Others said: It is muhkam (not abrogated), and there is a right in wealth besides zakah.

Al-'afw (the surplus) is what a person spends without straining himself and his wealth, and this is similar to the expression of the exegetes, and it is derived from "'afa al-shay'" when it increased. So the meaning is: spend what exceeds your needs, and do not harm yourselves by it so that you become dependent (ʿālah).

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a surplus, let him spend it on himself, then on those he supports, and if anything remains, let him give it in charity."

(p-535) He (ﷺ) also said: "The best charity is that which leaves one self-sufficient (ghinan)," and in another hadith: "That which is from a position of sufficiency (ghina)." The majority of people read "al-'afwa" with the accusative. Abu 'Amr alone read "al-'afwu" with the nominative. It was reported differently from Ibn Kathir. This is built upon "mādhā": whoever makes "mā" the subject and "dhā" its predicate in the sense of "alladhī," and takes the pronoun in "yunfiqūna" as referring back, reads "al-'afwu" with the nominative so that the clauses correspond; its nominative is then as a subject, its estimate being: the surplus is your spending, or what you spend is the surplus. Whoever makes "mādhā" a single word, object of "yunfiqūna," reads "qul al-'afwa" with the accusative, by supposing a verb, and the correspondence holds for him. Nominative "al-'afwa" with accusative "mādhā" is permissible but weak, and likewise accusative with nominative "mā".

(p-536) And according to their two positions, "perhaps you may reflect upon those signs." So His words, ﴿in this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220], are connected, on this interpretation, to "the signs." On the first interpretation, which is the well-known one from Ibn 'Abbas and others, "in this world" is connected to "you may reflect."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 218–219 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:
﴿And they will not cease fighting you until they turn you back from your religion, if they are able. And whoever of you reverts from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and those are the companions of the Fire, wherein they will abide eternally.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated and striven in the way of Allah – those hope for the mercy of Allah, and Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say, "In them is great sin and benefit for people, but their sin is greater than their benefit." And they ask you what they should spend. Say, "The excess." Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses that you may give thought.﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And they will not cease fighting you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217] is the beginning of a report from Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, and a warning from Him to the believers against the evil of the disbelievers. "Yaruddukum" (they turn you back) is in the accusative because of "hatta" (until), since it is a bare limit (ghayah mujarradah).

His saying, ﴿And whoever of you reverts﴾ [al-Baqarah: 217], meaning: returns from Islam to disbelief. A group of scholars said: the apostate (murtadd) is asked to repent; if he repents, well and good, otherwise he is killed. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Tawus, and al-Hasan said – with a difference of report from him – and al-Shafiʿi, in one of his two opinions, said: he is killed without being asked to repent. Something similar is reported from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari and Muʿadh ibn Jabal.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
The implication of their statement is that he is told at that moment: "Return." If he refuses, he is killed. ʿAtaʾ ibn Abi Rabah said: if the apostate was born to Muslim parents, he is killed without being asked to repent; but if he had embraced Islam and then apostatized, he is asked to repent, because he is ignorant of the excellence of Islam to a degree that the child of Muslims is not ignorant of it.

Those who held the view of asking for repentance differed. ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said: he is asked to repent for three days. This is the view of Malik, Ahmad, Ishaq, the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), and al-Shafiʿi in one of his two opinions. al-Zuhri said: he is invited to Islam; if he repents, well and good, otherwise he is killed. It is reported from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, that he asked an apostate to repent for a month, and when he refused, he killed him. al-Nakhaʿi and al-Thawri said: he is asked to repent while imprisoned, indefinitely. Ibn al-Mundhir said: the reports from ʿUmar on this matter differ.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, would carry out the ruling according to the gravity of the apostate's crime, or the slightness of his crime accompanying the apostasy.

"Habita al-ʿamalu" (the deed became void) means: when it is corrupted at its end, so it is nullified.

Abu al-Sammal recited "ḥabatat" with a fatḥa on the bāʾ throughout the Qur'an. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, al-Hakam, al-Layth, Abu Hanifa, and Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: the inheritance of the apostate goes to his heirs among the Muslims. Malik, Rabiʿa, Ibn Abi Layla, al-Shafiʿi, and Abu Thawr said: his inheritance goes to the public treasury (bayt al-mal). The people have agreed that his heirs from among the people of disbelief do not inherit from him, except for an anomalous view reported from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz and from Qatada; and a view contrary to it is also reported from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz.

His saying, ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and those who have emigrated﴾, to the end of the verse. Jundub ibn ʿAbd Allah, ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr, and others said: "When Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Tamimi killed ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami in the sacred month, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held back from taking the fifth (khums) which ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh had been granted by lot as its share, and regarding the two captives." So the Muslims blamed ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh and his companions, until it grieved them. Then Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, consoled them with this verse concerning the sacred month, and then by mentioning them and pointing to them in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed﴾. Then it remains applicable to everyone who does what Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, has mentioned.

It is a form of mufaʿala from hajara (to abandon). Whoever says that hijra is moving from the desert to the settled town has made a mistake, on the basis that this was the more common case among the Arabs; but on his view the people of Makkah would not be emigrants.

"Jahada" (strove) is a form of mufaʿala from jahida, when one exerts effort. "Yarjūn" (they hope) means: they aspire and consider it near. Hope (rajaʾ) is a state of ease, and hope always involves fear, without fail, just as fear involves hope. Sometimes it is used figuratively, and rajaʾ comes to mean what accompanies it of fear, as al-Hudhali said:

"When the bee has stung him, he does not hope for its sting [to cease], and he swears to it in a tent of cloth, of many layers."

al-Asmaʿi said: when the negative particle is combined with rajaʾ, it carries the meaning of fear, like this verse, and like His saying, the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿those who do not hope for our meeting﴾, meaning: those who do not fear it. It has also been said: the word rajaʾ in the verse retains its usual meaning, i.e., they do not hope for reward in our meeting, and against that is the fear of punishment.
