Their evidence is that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah cursed wine and cursed ten along with it: its seller, its buyer, the one for whom it is bought, its presser, the one for whom it is pressed, its server, its drinker, its carrier, the one to whom it is carried, and the consumer of its price." So these are many sins.

Also, the gathering of benefits is fittingly accompanied by the gathering of sins, and "kathīrun" with the three-dotted thā' conveys that.

The rest of the readers and the majority of people read "kabīrun" with the single-dotted bā'. Its argument is that the sin in gambling and drinking wine is among the major sins (al-kabā'ir), so describing it as "great" (kabīr) is more fitting.

Also, the consensus on "akbar" is an argument for "kabīr" with the bā' with one dot. They unanimously rejected "akthar" with the three-dotted thā', except what is in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud, where it reads: "Say: in both there is great sin, and their sin is greater" (qul fīhimā ithmun kathīrun wa-ithmuhumā akthar), with the thā' having three dots in both letters.

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿In both there is sin﴾, it may carry two meanings: one is that it refers to their use after the prohibition, and the other is that it refers to the evils that are in them.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: When the verse ﴿Say: In both there is great sin and benefits for people﴾ was revealed, some people disliked them because of the sin, and some people drank them for the benefits. Then when the verse ﴿Do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [al-Nisa': 43] was revealed, they avoided them at the times of the prayers. Then when the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90], 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "Ruined for you today, it has been joined with gambling and the altars." And the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Wine has been prohibited." When 'Umar ibn al-Khattab heard His words, ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 91], he said: "We have desisted, we have desisted."

Al-Farisi said, and some people of reflection said: Wine was prohibited by this verse, because Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: My Lord has only forbidden immoralities, what is apparent of them and what is concealed, and sin﴾ [al-A'raf: 33], and in this verse He informed that in it is sin, so it is prohibited.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
This reasoning is not sound, because the sin that is in it is the prohibited thing, not the wine itself, as this reasoning would require.

Qatadah said: Allah censured wine by this verse but did not prohibit it.

As for the words of the Exalted, ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾: Qays ibn Sa'd said: This is the obligatory zakah. The majority of scholars said: Rather, it is voluntary spending. Some of them said: It was abrogated by zakah. Others said: It is muhkam (not abrogated), and there is a right in wealth besides zakah.

Al-'afw (the surplus) is what a person spends without straining himself and his wealth, and this is similar to the expression of the exegetes, and it is derived from "'afa al-shay'" when it increased. So the meaning is: spend what exceeds your needs, and do not harm yourselves by it so that you become dependent (ʿālah).

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever has a surplus, let him spend it on himself, then on those he supports, and if anything remains, let him give it in charity."

(p-535) He (ﷺ) also said: "The best charity is that which leaves one self-sufficient (ghinan)," and in another hadith: "That which is from a position of sufficiency (ghina)." The majority of people read "al-'afwa" with the accusative. Abu 'Amr alone read "al-'afwu" with the nominative. It was reported differently from Ibn Kathir. This is built upon "mādhā": whoever makes "mā" the subject and "dhā" its predicate in the sense of "alladhī," and takes the pronoun in "yunfiqūna" as referring back, reads "al-'afwu" with the nominative so that the clauses correspond; its nominative is then as a subject, its estimate being: the surplus is your spending, or what you spend is the surplus. Whoever makes "mādhā" a single word, object of "yunfiqūna," reads "qul al-'afwa" with the accusative, by supposing a verb, and the correspondence holds for him. Nominative "al-'afwa" with accusative "mādhā" is permissible but weak, and likewise accusative with nominative "mā".

(p-536) And according to their two positions, "perhaps you may reflect upon those signs." So His words, ﴿in this world﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220], are connected, on this interpretation, to "the signs." On the first interpretation, which is the well-known one from Ibn 'Abbas and others, "in this world" is connected to "you may reflect."

[Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 220–221]

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿In this world and the Hereafter. And they ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is good. And if you mix with them, they are your brothers. Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer. Had Allah willed, He would have burdened you. Indeed Allah is Mighty, Wise.﴾

﴿And do not marry idolatresses until they believe. A believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even though she pleases you. And do not marry idolaters until they believe. A believing slave is better than an idolater, even though he pleases you. Those invite to the Fire, while Allah invites to the Garden and to forgiveness, by His leave, and He makes His signs clear to people that they may remember.﴾

His saying before this, "In this world," begins a verse. Its connection has already been discussed, and the fact that "you may reflect" (tatafakkarun) is a pause (waqf) strengthens the connection of "in this world" with "the signs." Tawus recited: "Say: Setting it right (aslah) for them is good."

The occasion of the revelation, according to al-Suddi and al-Dahhak, is that the Arabs customarily avoided the property of orphans and would not mix with it in food, drink, or anything else. That was a hardship for them, so they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about it. Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: its occasion was that when the Muslims heard, "And do not approach the property of the orphan" (6:152), and "Indeed those who devour the property of orphans unjustly" (4:10), they avoided orphans and their property and separated them from themselves, so this was revealed: "And if you mix with them, they are your brothers," and so on. It was also said that the questioner was 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha, and Allah commanded His Prophet to answer that whoever intends to set right the property of an orphan does well, and what is done after this intention, of mixing and sharing in a way that is repaid to the orphan, is not sinful. Allah removed the hardship of avoiding the orphan's food and drink, and permitted mixing in that matter when the intention is to set things right and to be gentle with the orphan.

An example of this: the orphan would be content, without mixing, with a certain amount for the month. If the guardian's mixing leads to that amount being increased, it is mixing of corruption; if it leads to reducing that amount, it is mixing of setting right.

His saying, may He be exalted, "then they are your brothers" (fa-ikhwanukum) is the predicate of an omitted subject. His saying, "Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer," is a warning.

Al-'anat is hardship. From it comes "the hardship of celibacy" (anat al-'azaba), and "a difficult (anut) steep path," meaning a laborious one. And 'anata al-ba'ir means the camel broke after being set. So the meaning is: "He would have made you toil in avoiding the matter of orphans, but He lightened it for you."

Ibn 'Abbas said: the meaning is: "He would have destroyed you (li-uwbiqakum) for what you had already taken of the orphans' property."

"Mighty" ('Aziz) implies that His command is not turned back. "Wise" (Hakim) means that what He carries out is firmly established.

His saying, may He be exalted: "And do not marry idolatresses until they believe," and so on. The majority of readers read "tankihu" with a fatha on the ta'. In the irregular reading it is read with a damma, as if the one who marries her has given her in marriage from himself. Nakaha originally means intercourse, and it is used for marriage figuratively and by extension.

A group said: "the idolatresses" here means those who associate another god with Allah. Therefore Jewish women and Christian women are not included in the wording of this verse or in its meaning.

Its occasion was the story of Abu Marthad Kinaz ibn Husayn with 'Anaq, who was in Mecca. Qatada and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: the wording of the verse is general for every disbelieving woman, and what is intended is specific, namely other than the women of the Book (kitabiyyat). The verse of al-Ma'ida specified it, and it never encompassed the women of the Book.

Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said: the general wording included them, then the verse of surah al-Ma'ida abrogated (naskh) part of the generality concerning the women of the Book. This is the view of Malik, may Allah have mercy on him. Ibn Habib transmitted it.

He said: marrying a Jewish or Christian woman, although Allah has made it lawful, is disliked and blameworthy. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, disliked marrying women of the abode of war (harbiyyat), for the reason of leaving offspring in the abode of war, and because of their handling of wine and pork. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, Talha, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, Ibn al-Musayyib, al-Hasan, Tawus, Ibn Jubayr, al-Zuhri, al-Shafi'i, and the common people of Medina and Kufa permitted marrying women of the Book. Among those who permitted marrying Magian women (majusiyya) were Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, al-Awza'i, and Ishaq. Ibn Hanbal said: "It does not please me." It is narrated that Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman married a Magian woman. Ibn al-Fassar said: some of our companions said: it is obligatory, according to one of the two opinions that they have a scripture, that marriage with them be permitted.

Ibn 'Abbas said, in some of what is narrated from him: the verse is general concerning idolatresses, Magian women, and women of the Book, and every woman who is not upon Islam is forbidden.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

On this view, it abrogates the verse in surah al-Ma'ida. To this refers the saying of Ibn 'Umar in the Muwatta': "I know of no association (shirk) greater than a woman saying her lord is 'Isa."

It is narrated from 'Umar that he separated between Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah and Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman and two women of the Book. They said: "O Commander of the Believers, we shall divorce them, so do not be angry." He said: "If their divorce were valid, their marriage would be valid. But a little stone of a pit (sighratu qam'a) separates you two." This does not rest on a sound basis. A stronger report is that 'Umar intended to separate them, and Hudhayfa said to him: "Do you claim that she is forbidden? Then I will release her, O Commander of the Believers?" He said: "I do not claim she is forbidden, but I fear that you will take up prostitutes from among them." Something similar is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, may He be exalted, "And a believing slave woman" (wa la'amatun mu'minatun) is an information that a believing slave woman is better than an idolatress, even if the idolatress is of noble lineage and wealth, and even if she pleases you in beauty or otherwise. This is the saying of al-Tabari and others.

Al-Suddi said: "It was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Rawaha. He had a black slave woman, and he struck her in anger. Then he regretted it and came to the Prophet ﷺ and told him. He said: 'She fasts, prays, and bears witness to the two testifications.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'This is a believer.' Ibn Rawaha said: 'I will surely free her and marry her.' He did so, and some people criticized him, so the verse was revealed concerning him."

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held that marrying a slave woman of the Book is not permitted. Ashhab said in the Kitab of Muhammad concerning a man who embraced Islam while under him was a slave woman of the Book: he does not separate the two. Ibn Wahb and others transmitted from Malik that a Magian slave woman may not be had by right of possession (bi-milk al-yamin).

Abu Hanifa and his companions permit marrying slave women of the Book.

His saying, may He be exalted, "And do not marry idolaters until they believe," and so on. The community is unanimous that an idolater may not have intercourse with a believing woman in any way, because of the disgrace this would bring upon the religion of Islam. The readers read "tunkihu" with a damma on the ta'.

Some scholars said: the guardianship (wilaya) in marriage is explicit in the wording of this verse. "And a believing slave is better than a free idolater, even if his beauty and wealth please you," as previously stated.

The preference here expressed by the word "khayr" is not only in terms of faith, because there is no sharing in faith. Rather, sharing exists in companionship, fellowship, the bond of marriage, and other things. This view follows the position of Sibawayh that the form af'al, which is used for comparison, is not valid where there is no sharing, as in your saying: "Ice is colder than fire," and "Light is brighter than darkness."

Al-Farra' and a group of the Kufans said: the form af'al is valid both where there is sharing and where there is no sharing. Makki transmitted from Niftawayh that the comparative form in the speech of the Arabs comes affirming the first and negating it of the second.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In my view the verse may bear that the mention of slave and free is an expression for all people, free and enslaved, as he ﷺ said: "Do not prevent the female servants of Allah from the mosques of Allah." And as we believe that all are servants of Allah. And as He, may He be exalted, said: "An excellent servant; indeed he is one who often turns (to Allah)" (38:30). So the meaning of the verse is as though it said: "And a woman and a man."

His saying, may He be exalted, "Those" (ulaika): the reference is to the idolatresses and the idolaters. That is, their companionship and their fellowship necessitate a decline in much of one's desires, together with their raising offspring. All of this is a call to the Fire, even though they do not explicitly call to their religion in their own words. Allah, may He be exalted, bestows guidance, makes the signs clear, and urges obedience, all of which are calls to the Garden.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan recited "wal-maghfiratu" with a raised ending, as a subject (mubtada').

Permission (idhn) means knowledge and enablement. If a command is added to that, it is stronger than mere permission, because when you say, "I permitted such-and-such," it does not necessarily follow that you commanded it. "La'allahum" (perhaps they) expresses hope regarding humans, and whoever remembers acts according to his remembrance and is saved.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah al-Baqarah, verses 222–224**

[p. 543]

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: It is a harm, so keep away from women during menstruation, and do not approach them until they have purified themselves. When they have purified themselves, then come to them from where Allah has commanded you. Indeed, Allah loves those who turn in repentance and loves those who purify themselves.﴾ ﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish, and send ahead for yourselves. Fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾ ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths that you be righteous, fear Allah, and make peace among the people. Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

al-Ṭabarī related, from al-Suddī, that the questioner was Thābit ibn al-Daḥdāḥ. Qatādah and others said: they asked because the Arabs in Madīnah and its surroundings had adopted the custom of the Children of Israel, avoiding eating with a menstruating woman and sharing a dwelling with her, so this verse was revealed. Mujāhid said: they used to avoid women during menstruation and would have intercourse with them in their rear passages, so the verse was revealed concerning that.

*Al-maḥīḍ* (the menstruation): a verbal noun like *al-ḥayḍ*, and similar to *al-maqīl* (the midday rest), from *qāla yaqīlu*. al-Rāʿī said:

> I built their elbows upon a slippery ground, where the tick cannot find a resting place.

al-Ṭabarī said: *al-maḥīḍ* is the name of the *ḥayḍ* (menstruation), and from it is the saying of Ruʾbah concerning life:

> To you I complain of the severity of livelihood, and of years that have plucked my feathers.

*Adhan* (harm) is a comprehensive term for things that cause harm, for it is blood, filth and foulness, and it comes from the path of urine. This is the phrasing of the commentators on this word.

His saying, may He be exalted, *fa-iʿtazilū* ("so keep away"), means: intercourse with them, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it: that a man should tie the wrapper of the menstruating woman and then do as he wishes above it. This is the most sound of what has been held concerning the matter, and it was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Shurayḥ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mālik, and a great body of scholars.

It is narrated from Mujāhid that he said: what must be avoided of the menstruating woman is the genitals alone.

This is also narrated from ʿĀʾishah, al-Shaʿbī and ʿIkrimah. It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUbaydah al-Salmānī that a man must keep away from his wife's bed when she is menstruating. This is an anomalous view. Ibn ʿAbbās's aunt Maymūnah, may Allah be pleased with them both, confronted him about it and said to him: "Are you turning away from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿*wa-lā taqrabūhunna ḥattā yaṭhurna*﴾ ("and do not approach them until they are purified"). Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Ḥafṣ from him read *yuṭhirna* (with the ṭāʾ sukūn and the hāʾ damma). The righteousness of a man, when the rule and lineage of it are attached to him, such as the pilgrim, the warrior, the scholar, and others, is the opposite of sin, since sin is the rule that attaches to disobedience. *Samīʿ* ("All-Hearing") means: of the words of the servants; *ʿAlīm* ("All-Knowing") means: of their intentions; and He will recompense for all of it.

As for the occasion of the verse, Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, when he swore to cut off his support from Mistaḥ ibn Uthāthah, when Mistaḥ spoke in the matter of the slander. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq together with his son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, in the story of the hospitality, when Abū Bakr swore that he would not eat the food. It was also said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah together with Bashīr ibn Saʿd, when he swore that he would not speak to him.

*Al-yamīn* ("the oath"): the pact. Its origin is that when the Arabs made alliances or covenants, a man would take the right hand of his companion with his own right hand; then this became so common that the oath and the covenant itself were called *yamīn*.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAṭiyya (al-Muḥarrar al-Wajīz) on Sūrah al-Baqarah, verses 222–224**

[p. 543]

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: It is a harm, so keep away from women during menstruation, and do not approach them until they have purified themselves. When they have purified themselves, then come to them from where Allah has commanded you. Indeed, Allah loves those who turn in repentance and loves those who purify themselves.﴾ ﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so go to your tilth as you wish, and send ahead for yourselves. Fear Allah, and know that you will meet Him. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾ ﴿And do not make Allah an obstacle for your oaths that you be righteous, fear Allah, and make peace among the people. Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

al-Ṭabarī related, from al-Suddī, that the questioner was Thābit ibn al-Daḥdāḥ. Qatādah and others said: they asked because the Arabs in Madīnah and its surroundings had adopted the custom of the Children of Israel, avoiding eating with a menstruating woman and sharing a dwelling with her, so this verse was revealed. Mujāhid said: they used to avoid women during menstruation and would have intercourse with them in their rear passages, so the verse was revealed concerning that.

*Al-maḥīḍ* (the menstruation): a verbal noun like *al-ḥayḍ*, and similar to *al-maqīl* (the midday rest), from *qāla yaqīlu*. al-Rāʿī said:

> I built their elbows upon a slippery ground, where the tick cannot find a resting place.

al-Ṭabarī said: *al-maḥīḍ* is the name of the *ḥayḍ* (menstruation), and from it is the saying of Ruʾbah concerning life:

> To you I complain of the severity of livelihood, and of years that have plucked my feathers.

*Adhan* (harm) is a comprehensive term for things that cause harm, for it is blood, filth and foulness, and it comes from the path of urine. This is the phrasing of the commentators on this word.

His saying, may He be exalted, *fa-iʿtazilū* ("so keep away"), means: intercourse with them, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) explained it: that a man should tie the wrapper of the menstruating woman and then do as he wishes above it. This is the most sound of what has been held concerning the matter, and it was the view of Ibn ʿAbbās, Shurayḥ, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Mālik, and a great body of scholars.

It is narrated from Mujāhid that he said: what must be avoided of the menstruating woman is the genitals alone.

This is also narrated from ʿĀʾishah, al-Shaʿbī and ʿIkrimah. It is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās and ʿUbaydah al-Salmānī that a man must keep away from his wife's bed when she is menstruating. This is an anomalous view. Ibn ʿAbbās's aunt Maymūnah, may Allah be pleased with them both, confronted him about it and said to him: "Are you turning away from the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?"

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿*wa-lā taqrabūhunna ḥattā yaṭhurna*﴾ ("and do not approach them until they are purified"). Nāfiʿ, Ibn Kathīr, Abū ʿAmr, Ibn ʿĀmir, and ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Ḥafṣ from him read *yuṭhirna* (with the ṭāʾ sukūn and the hāʾ damma). Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, and ʿĀṣim in the transmission of Abū Bakr and al-Mufaḍḍal from him read *yaṭṭahharna* (with the ṭāʾ and hāʾ shaddah and fatḥah).

In the *muṣḥaf* of Ubayy and ʿAbdullāh it is *ḥattā yatatahharna*. In the *muṣḥaf* of Anas ibn Mālik it is: "And do not approach the women during their menstruation, and keep away from them until they have purified themselves."

al-Ṭabarī preferred the reading with the doubled ṭāʾ, and said: it means *yaghtasilna* (they bathe), because all agree that it is forbidden for a man to approach his wife after the blood has stopped until she is purified. He said: the difference lies in what *purity* is. Some said it is bathing with water; some said it is a *wuḍūʾ* like the *wuḍūʾ* for prayer; and some said it is washing the genitals, and that makes her lawful to her husband even if she has not bathed from the menses.

Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī preferred the reading with the single ṭāʾ, since it is a triliteral verb opposed to *ṭamathat*, which is also triliteral.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: each of the two readings may be taken to mean bathing with water, and each may be taken to mean the cessation of the blood and the removal of its harm.

What al-Ṭabarī held, that the reading with the doubled ṭāʾ implies bathing and the reading with the single ṭāʾ implies the cessation of blood, is not a necessary conclusion; and likewise his claim of consensus. As for the matter, there is no disagreement about the disliked status of intercourse before bathing with water.

Al-Awzāʿī said: whoever does it gives in charity half a dīnār, and whoever has intercourse during the bleeding gives a dīnār in charity. Abū Dāwūd narrated with a chain to Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning one who comes to his wife while she is menstruating, that he said: "Let him give a dīnār or half a dīnār in charity." Ibn ʿAbbās said: the dīnār is for when the blood is flowing, and the half is for when it has stopped. Reports on the severity of this act have come down. The majority of scholars hold that it is a grave sin for which one repents, and that there is no expiation for it by means of wealth.

Mālik, may Allah have mercy on him, and the majority of scholars held that the purity which makes lawful intercourse with the menstruating woman, once the blood has gone from her, is her purification with water like the purification of one in a state of major impurity (*junub*); and nothing else suffices in place of it, not *tayammum* or anything other.

Yaḥyā ibn Bukayr and Ibn al-Qurazī said: when a menstruating woman has become pure and performs *tayammum* where there is no water, she becomes lawful to her husband even if she has not bathed. Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah and Ṭāwūs said: the cessation of the blood makes her lawful to her husband, but she must perform *wuḍūʾ*.

[p. 545]

*Ḥattā* here denotes only a limit, and nothing more. *Wa-taqrabūhunna* ("and approach them") means intercourse. This is an instance of *sadd al-dharāʾiʿ* (blocking the means that lead to what is forbidden).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿*fa-idhā taṭahharna*﴾ ("and when they have purified themselves"), and the verse continues. The reading is *taṭahharna* with an open tāʾ and a doubled hāʾ. The disagreement about its meaning, as already mentioned, is between purification by water and the cessation of the blood.

Mujāhid and a group of scholars say here that bathing with water is intended, without exception, because of the indication in the command to come to them. Even if approaching them before bathing is permissible, the form of command from Allah, exalted is He, is only directed to the most perfect manner.

*Fa-tūhunna* ("then come to them") is a permission. The meaning: "from where Allah has commanded you," that is, by keeping away from them, which is the genitals; or from the navel to the knees; or the whole body, as stated above. All of this is one opinion. Ibn ʿAbbās and Abū Razīn said: the meaning is "from before the purification, not from before the menstruation." Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same. Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyyah said: the meaning is "from before what is lawful, not from before fornication." It was also said: the meaning is "from before the state of permissibility, not while fasting, nor in the state of *iḥrām*, nor in other such states."

*Al-tawwābūn* (those who turn in repentance): those who return, and *ʿarafahu* ("he knew it") means: from evil to good.

*Al-mutaṭahhirūn* (those who purify themselves): ʿAṭāʾ and others said the meaning is with water. Mujāhid and others said the meaning is: from sins. Mujāhid also said the meaning is: from coming to women in their rear passages.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems he looked to the saying of Allah, exalted is He, relating the people of Lot: ﴿*Expel them from your town; indeed they are people who purify themselves*﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 82]. Ṭalḥah ibn Muṣarrif read *al-muṭahhirīn* with the doubled ṭāʾ and hāʾ.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿*Your women are a tilth for you*﴾ and the verse continues. Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh and al-Rabīʿ said its occasion was that the Jews said: if a man comes to his wife from her rear passage into her genitals, the child will be squint-eyed. They disparaged the Arabs for this. So the verse was revealed containing a refutation of their statement. Umm Salamah and others said its occasion was that the Quraysh used to come to women in the genitals in various postures. When they came to Madīnah and married Anṣārī women, they wanted to do that, but the women of Madīnah did not accept it, since the habit of their men was only to come in one posture, which is lying prone. This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and the talk of the people spread about it. So the verse was revealed permitting all postures, provided that the intercourse is in the place of the tilth.

*Ḥarth* (tilth) is a metaphor, for they are the field of offspring. So the word *ḥarth* indicates that the permission applies only to the genitals specifically, since that is the cultivated field.

His saying: ﴿*annā shi'tum*﴾ ("as you wish") means, according to the majority of scholars, from among the Companions, the Successors, and the Imams: in whatever manner you wish, facing or from behind, or lying on the side. *Annā* is used only in a question or in reporting about a matter that has multiple aspects; so it is more general in the language than *kayfa* ("how"), *ayna* ("where") and *matā* ("when"). This is the Arabic usage.

People have explained *annā* in this verse with these words. Sībawayh explained it as "how" and "from where" combined. A group among those who explained it as *ayna* ("where") held that intercourse in the rear passage is permissible. This was narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿUmar, and it was also narrated from him the opposite, and an expiation for doing it. This second view is the one fitting to him. Permissibility was also narrated from Ibn Abī Mulaykah and Muḥammad ibn al-Munkadir, and Mālik narrated it from Yazīd ibn Rūmān, from Sālim, from Ibn ʿUmar. Something similar is reported from Mālik, which occurs in *al-ʿUtbiyyah*, but that was falsely attributed to Mālik. Some narrated that a man did this during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), people spoke about it, and so this verse was revealed.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It has come down from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the *Muṣannaf* of al-Nasāʾī, and elsewhere, that he said: "Coming to women in their rear passages is forbidden." It has also come down from him that he said: "Cursed is he who comes to a woman in her rear passage." And it has come down from him that he said: "Whoever comes to a woman in her rear passage has disbelieved in what was revealed to the heart of Muḥammad (ﷺ)." This is the truth that is to be followed. It does not befit a believer in Allah and the Last Day to turn to the slip of a scholar concerning this matter after it has been authenticated from the Prophet. Allah is the Guide, there is no lord besides Him.

al-Suddī said: the meaning of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿*and send ahead for yourselves*﴾ is the reward for avoiding what you have been forbidden and for complying with what you have been commanded. Ibn ʿAbbās said: it is a reference to the mention of Allah at intercourse, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If one of you, when he comes to his wife, says: 'In the name of Allah. O Allah, keep Satan away from us, and keep Satan away from what You provide us,' then if a child is decreed between them, it will not be harmed."

It was also said: the meaning of *qaddimū li-anfusikum* ("send ahead for yourselves") is seeking offspring. ﴿*Fear Allah*﴾ is a warning. ﴿*And know that you will meet Him*﴾ is a statement implying emphasis in the warning, that is, He will recompense you for righteousness and sin. ﴿*And give good tidings to the believers*﴾ is a comfort to the doers of righteousness and the followers of the paths of guidance.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿*And do not make Allah an obstacle*﴾ and the verse continues. *ʿUrḍah* ("obstacle") is on the pattern *fuʿlah* in the passive form, meaning: something frequently exposed to what is mentioned. You say: a camel that is *ʿurḍah* for riding, a horse that is *ʿurḍah* for running. From this is the saying of Kaʿb ibn Zuhayr:

> From every sweating, perspiring camel, when it breaks into a sweat, its path is a road of effaced landmarks, unknown.

The purpose of the verse: do not make the name of Allah, exalted is He, a target for oaths by Him, and do not multiply oaths, for breaking them frequently, and that involves little regard for the right of Allah, exalted is He.

Then the interpreters differed. Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī, Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ and others said: the meaning is: in matters in which you desire severity, [such as] one who abandons kinship ties, righteousness, and reconciliation. al-Ṭabarī said: the estimated meaning is: "lest you be righteous, lest you fear Allah, lest you make peace." al-Mahdawī estimated it as: "out of dislike that you be righteous." Some of the interpreters said: the meaning is: do not swear by Allah falsely when you intend righteousness, piety, and reconciliation, so there is no need to estimate a *lā* after *an* ("that"). It is possible that this interpretation applies to one who intends to reconcile people, and so swears and breaks the oath in order to accomplish his aim. It is also possible that it refers to what is narrated from ʿĀʾishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: it was revealed concerning the multiplying of oaths by Allah, a prohibition against a man swearing by Him in a righteous matter, so how about [swearing by Him] in a wicked one? So the meaning is: when you want righteousness for yourselves.

al-Zajjāj and others said the meaning of the verse is: a man, when asked to do a good deed or the like, excuses himself by [invoking] Allah, exalted is He, saying: "An oath is upon me," though he has not sworn.

*An tabarrū* ("that you be righteous") is an object of purpose (*maf'ūl min ajlihi*). *Al-birr* ("righteousness") is the totality of aspects of good. The righteousness of a man, when the rule and lineage of it are attached to him, such as the pilgrim, the warrior, the scholar, and others, is the opposite of sin, since sin is the rule that attaches to disobedience. *Samīʿ* ("All-Hearing") means: of the words of the servants; *ʿAlīm* ("All-Knowing") means: of their intentions; and He will recompense for all of it.

As for the occasion of the verse, Ibn Jurayj said: it was revealed concerning Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, when he swore to cut off his support from Mistaḥ ibn Uthāthah, when Mistaḥ spoke in the matter of the slander. It was also said: it was revealed concerning Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq together with his son ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, in the story of the hospitality, when Abū Bakr swore that he would not eat the food. It was also said: it was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allāh ibn Rawāḥah together with Bashīr ibn Saʿd, when he swore that he would not speak to him.

*Al-yamīn* ("the oath"): the pact. Its origin is that when the Arabs made alliances or covenants, a man would take the right hand of his companion with his own right hand; then this became so common that the oath and the covenant itself were called *yamīn*.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 225–227**

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿Allah does not hold you accountable for what is vain in your oaths, but He holds you accountable for what your hearts have earned. And Allah is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾ ﴿For those who swear off [relations with] their wives, there is a waiting period of four months. So if they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if they resolve on divorce, then indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾

"Al-laghw" (vain speech, what is idle and void): speech that has fallen away and carries no ruling. It is used for abusive speech, obscene speech, and for oaths that carry no ruling, by way of comparison with a fallen part of speech. It is said: laghā yalghū laghwan, and laghiya yalghā laghyan. The Qur'anic usage is with a waw.

"Al-mu'akhadhah" (being held accountable) is taking [someone] to account by punishment.

The scholars differed concerning the oath that is laghw. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Aisha, 'Amir al-Sha'bi, Abu Salih and Mujahid said: the laghw of an oath is a man's saying, in the course of his speech and his haste in discussion, "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah," without intending an oath. It is related that a people were disputing with one another in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) while they were shooting arrows, and one of them swore, "By Allah, you were right and you were wrong, O so-and-so," and then the matter turned out to be otherwise. A man said, "He has broken his oath, O Messenger of Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The oaths of archers are laghw; there is no sin in them and no expiation."

Abu Hurayra, Ibn 'Abbas also, al-Hasan, Malik ibn Anas, and a group of scholars said: the laghw of an oath is what a man swears to upon his certainty, whereas the disclosure of the unseen is contrary to that.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This certainty is a predominant assumption, which the jurists called "certainty" by way of figurative usage. Malik said: an example of it is that a man sees another from a distance and believes him to be so-and-so, without doubt, and so he swears, and then the one sworn about turns out to be someone other than the one he was believed to be.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, and 'Abd Allah and 'Urwa, the two sons of al-Zubayr, said: the laghw of an oath is swearing to do sinful acts, such as the one who swears, "I will surely drink wine," or "I will surely sever the ties of kinship." Its fulfilment (birr) is abandoning that act, and there is no expiation for it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said the same, except that he said: "He disbelieves," and so his statement resembles the statement of those who do not regard it as laghw in the matter of expiation.

Ibn 'Abbas also, and Tawus said: the laghw of an oath is swearing in a state of anger. Ibn 'Abbas related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "There is no oath in anger." Makhul al-Dimashqi and a group of scholars said: the laghw of an oath is that a man prohibits for himself what Allah has made lawful, saying, "My wealth is forbidden to me if I do such-and-such," or "What is lawful is forbidden to me." Malik ibn Anas held this view, except regarding the wife, for in her case he obligated the prohibition unless the one swearing intends otherwise in his heart. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son said: the laghw of an oath is a man's invocation against himself: "May Allah blind his eye," "May Allah take away his wealth," "He is a Jew," "He is a polytheist," "He is a [...]" if he does such-and-such. Ibn 'Abbas also, and al-Dahhak said: the laghw of an oath is the expiation itself, meaning that when one expiates the oath, it then falls away and becomes laghw, and Allah does not hold one accountable for its expiation and returning to what is better. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: the laghw of an oath is that in which a man breaks his oath forgetfully. Ibn 'Abd al-Barr related an opinion: that laghw is the oaths of one who is compelled.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The method of reflection is to consider the word "laghw" and the word "kasb" (earning), and to judge their placement in the language. The earning of a person is what he intended and purposed, while laghw is what he did not deliberately intend, or what by its disgrace ought to fall away. By this method some of the preceding opinions become strong and some become weak.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, has lifted accountability in general for laghw, so its reality is that there is no sin in it and no expiation. Accountability in oaths is the punishment of the Hereafter for the false oath that is "ghamus" (plunging) and "masbura" (compelled), and for what one has neglected to expiate of that which has an expiation; and it is the punishment of this world in the imposition of expiation. Therefore the opinion that the accountable oath is the expiable one is weak, because accountability has already occurred in it; and restricting accountability to the Hereafter alone is an arbitrary judgment.

As for His statement, "But He holds you accountable for what your hearts have earned": Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, and others said: what the heart has earned is the false oath, the ghamus. In it there is accountability in the Hereafter, while expiation applies only to what is laghw when one expiates it.

Malik and a group of scholars said: the ghamus is not expiated; it is greater in sin than that. al-Shafi'i, Qatada, 'Ata' and al-Rabi' said: the ghamus oath is expiated, and expiation is a form of accountability. The ghamus is what a man intended in swearing by a lie, and likewise the "masbura" oath; the meaning in both is one, but the ghamus was so named because it plunges its swearer into sin, and the masbura was so named because its endurance is a struggle and an overpowering of it, just as an animal is made to endure being killed or shot at. Zayd ibn Aslam said that His statement, "But He holds you accountable for what your hearts have earned," concerns the man who says, "He is a polytheist if he does such-and-such," meaning this is laghw unless he firmly resolves on polytheism in his heart and earns it.

"Ghafur" (Forgiving) and "Halim" (Forbearing) are two attributes fitting to what was mentioned of the lifting of accountability, since this is a matter of gentleness and ease.

His statement, "For those who swear off [relations with] their wives": the verse. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read: "Li-alladhina yuqsimuna" (for those who swear). "Yu'lun" means: they swear. It is said: ālā al-rajulu yūlī īlā'an, and al-ulya is the oath; it is also said ulwa, with the hamza pronounced with a fatha, a damma, or a kasra.

Al-tarabbus means deliberation and delay. It was a custom of the Arabs for a man to swear that he would not have intercourse with his wife, intending by that to harm her at the time of quarrelling and the like. Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, set this limit so that men would not harm women, and for the one who swears, in this sense, there remains a respite for less than four months.

It is disputed who is intended to be subject to the ruling of ila'. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: it is the man who becomes angry with his wife and swears an oath, in breaking which a ruling applies, that he will not have intercourse with her for more than four months, out of harm to her, and does not intend by it the welfare of a suckling child or the like. 'Ata' and others held this view. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: it is the man who swears not to have intercourse with his wife in a manner of anger and quarrelling, whether or not this includes the welfare of a child. If it is not out of anger, then it is not ila'. Ibn 'Abbas said: there is no ila' except with anger. Ibn Sirin said: whether the oath is in anger or not, it is ila'. This was also said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Thawri, Malik, al-Shafi'i, and the people of Iraq, except that Malik said: so long as he does not intend the welfare of a child. al-Sha'bi, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, and Ibn al-Musayyib said: every oath that a man swears not to have intercourse with his wife, or not to speak to her, or to harm her, or to make her angry, all of that is ila'. Ibn al-Musayyib, among them, said: except that if he swears not to speak to her while he continues to have intercourse, then it is not ila'; rather, the oath on other than intercourse becomes ila' only when it is accompanied by abstention from intercourse.

The statements of those we have mentioned, together with Sa'id, are unclear: what Sa'id said is one possibility, and the other possibility is that the corruption of marital companionship is ila'. al-Tabari went in this last direction. Ibn 'Abbas also said: no one is called a mu'li except the one who swears not to have intercourse ever; this was related by Ibn al-Mundhir. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Abu Thawr said: one is not a mu'li unless he exceeds the four months.

'Ata', al-Thawri, and the people of opinion (ahl al-ra'y) said: ila' is to swear for four months or more. Qatada, al-Nakha'i, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, Ishaq, and Ibn Abi Layla said: whoever swears regarding a short or long period and then abstains for four months is a mu'li. Ibn al-Mundhir said: many people of knowledge rejected this opinion.

His statement, "from their wives," includes free women and slave-women when they are married.

A slave is subject to ila' with respect to his wife. al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, and Abu Thawr said: its term is four months. Malik, al-Zuhri, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Ishaq said: its term is two months. al-Hasan said: its term for a free wife is four months, and for a slave wife is two months; al-Nakha'i said the same. al-Sha'bi said: ila' with a slave-woman is half of ila' with a free woman.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, the people of opinion, al-Awza'i, al-Nakha'i, and others said: the one who has consummated the marriage and the one who has not are the same in being subject to ila'. al-Zuhri, 'Ata', and al-Thawri said: there is no ila' except after consummation. Malik said: there is no ila' from a young girl who has not reached puberty; if he swears ila' regarding her and she then reaches puberty, the ila' applies to him from the day of her puberty.

Malik, al-Zuhri, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, and Ishaq said: its term is two months. al-Hasan said: its term for a free wife is four months, and for a slave wife is two months; al-Nakha'i said the same. al-Sha'bi said: ila' with a slave-woman is half of ila' with a free woman.

Malik, al-Shafi'i, the people of opinion, al-Awza'i, al-Nakha'i, and others said: the one who has consummated the marriage and the one who has not are the same in being subject to ila'. al-Zuhri, 'Ata', and al-Thawri said: there is no ila' except after consummation. Malik said: there is no ila' from a young girl who has not reached puberty; if he swears ila' regarding her and she then reaches puberty, the ila' applies to him from the day of her puberty.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu al-Darda', Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Musayyib, Mujahid, Tawus, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Abu 'Ubayd said: when the four months have ended, he is held in suspension: either he returns, or he divorces; otherwise, divorce is pronounced against him. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Uthman, and also 'Ali, Zayd ibn Thabit, Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, and Masruq said: when the four months have ended, divorce takes effect upon him without any holding in suspension.

The scholars differed concerning the divorce that takes effect upon the one who has sworn ila'. 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, 'Ata', al-Nakha'i, al-Awza'i, and others said: it is a single irrevocable divorce, with no right of return for him in it. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Abu Bakr ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, Makhul, al-Zuhri, and Malik said: it is a revocable divorce.

"Fa'u" (they return) means: they came back. From it is His statement, "until it returns to the command of Allah" [al-Hujurat: 9]. "Al-fay'" is the shade that returns in the afternoon.

Al-Hasan and Ibrahim said: when the one who has sworn ila' returns and has intercourse, there is no expiation for him in his oath, based on His statement, "So if they return, then indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is built upon the premise that the laghw of an oath is what one swears in disobedience, and abandoning intercourse with one's wife is disobedience.

The majority said: when he returns, he must expiate. The fay' according to Ibn al-Musayyib and Ibn Jubayr is not achieved except by intercourse. If he is imprisoned or on a journey, the ruling of ila' remains upon him unless he has intercourse; he has no excuse, and the fay' is not by speech alone.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the fay' is not achieved except by intercourse, or by expiation in the case of an excuse such as one who is absent or imprisoned. Ibn al-Qasim said in the Mudawwana (the Mudawwana, a major Maliki legal compendium): unless his oath is one for which expiation is not applicable, because it does not take effect upon him except after breaking it; the speech then suffices for him so long as he has an excuse.

The position in the Mudawwana differs regarding an oath by Allah, the Exalted: is it sufficient for the fay' to be by speech and resolve to expiate, or is expiation necessary, and otherwise there is no fay'? al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, al-Nakha'i and others said: the fay' from one who is not excused is intercourse, and it is necessary; and for one who is excused, he must bear witness that he has returned in his heart.

al-Nakha'i also said: the fay' is valid by speech and witnessing alone, and the ruling of ila' falls away. "What do you think if he does not become aroused for intercourse?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

If he does not have intercourse, one returns regarding this statement to the category of harm.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "fa-inna fa'u fihinna" (then indeed they return regarding them). It is related from him: "fa-inna fa'u fiha" (then indeed they return regarding it).

His statement, "And if they resolve on divorce": the verse. Those who said that with the passing of four months the divorce takes effect said: the resolve to divorce is the abandonment of the fay' until the months end. Those who said that suspension after the completion of the months is necessary said: the resolve is the pronouncement of divorce or the separation at the time of suspension, until the judge pronounces divorce. Those who argued for suspension used His statement "Hearing" as evidence, because such perception pertains only to spoken matters.

Ibn 'Abbas read: "wa-in 'azamu al-sarah" (and if they resolve on release).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 228:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿Divorced women shall keep themselves in waiting for three qur'ū' (periods). It is not lawful for them to conceal what Allah has created in their wombs, if they believe in Allah and the Last Day. Their husbands have a better right to take them back in that period, if they desire reconciliation. And they have rights similar to those against them, according to what is reasonable. But men have a degree over them. And Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

The reciters, most of the people, read "qurū'" on the pattern of fu'ūl, with the lām being a hamza. It is narrated from Nafi' that the waw was doubled without a hamza. Al-Hasan recited "thalāthata qarw" with a fatha on the qāf, a sukūn on the rā', and tanwīn on the waw, lightly pronounced. The ruling of this verse is aimed at istibra' (ascertaining that the womb is clear), not at it being an act of worship ('ibadah), and for this reason it excludes the woman who has not yet been consummated with, unlike the 'iddat al-wafāh (waiting period on the death of a husband), which is an act of worship.

"Al-mutallaqāt" (divorced women) is a general term intended in a specific sense, referring to those who have been consummated with. The woman divorced before consummation is not included in the generality, nor is the pregnant woman, nor the one who has not menstruated, nor the one who has ceased to menstruate. Some people said: the generality included them and then they were abrogated (naskh). This is weak, for the verse concerns the woman who menstruates, which is the common custom of women and the case of most of them, so this made an explicit statement about the others unnecessary.

The word qur' in the language means a time that recurs at a regular interval. The qur' of a star is the time of its rising, and likewise the time of its setting. The qur' of the wind is the time of its blowing. From this is the verse of the rajaz poet:

Oh, many a one who harbours a grudge against a man who has a qur'ū' like the qur'ū' of a menstruating woman.

He meant the time of his anger. On this basis, menstruation is called qur', and from this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Leave off prayer during your days of iqrā'ik," meaning the days of your menstruation. Likewise, on this same reasoning, the state of purity is also called qur', because it is a time that recurs regularly and alternates with menstruation. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

And every year you are a sharer in a raid, whose far end is reached by the resolute strength of your resolve.

Leaving wealth as an inheritance, and there is nobility in the tribe, through what was lost in it of your women's qurū' (purity periods).

That is, from their periods of purity. Some people said: qur' is derived from qar' al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ (the gathering of water in the pool), which is its collecting. It is as if the womb gathers the blood at the time of menstruation, and the body gathers it at the time of purity.

They differed as to which of these two Allah, exalted is He, intended by the three that He specified for the divorced woman. Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, al-Rabi', Qatada, the people of ra'y (opinion), and a large group of the people of knowledge said: what is intended is menstruation. So if a man divorces his wife in a state of purity in which he has not had intercourse with her, she begins a menstrual period, then another, then another. When she has bathed from the third, she exits the 'iddah. Some of those who hold the view of menstruation said: if she becomes pure from the third, the 'iddah ends before bathing. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others. 'A'isha, Ibn 'Umar, a group of the Companions and the Successors, and those after them, among them Sulayman ibn Yasar and Malik, said: what is intended is the periods of purity. So if a man divorces his wife in a state of purity in which he has not had intercourse with her, she completes the 'iddah with what remains of that period, even if it is an hour. Then she enters a second period of purity after a menstruation, then a third after a second menstruation. When she sees blood from the third menstruation, she becomes lawful to other husbands and exits the 'iddah. If a divorcer divorces in a period of purity in which he has had intercourse, the divorce binds him, he has done wrong, and she completes the 'iddah with what remains of that purity. The view of Ibn al-Qasim and Malik is that when the divorced woman sees the first spot of the third menstruation, she leaves the bond of marriage (al-'isma), and this is the position of Zayd ibn Thabit and others. Ashhab said: the bond of marriage and inheritance do not end until it is certain that it is menstrual blood, lest it be a single discharge of blood other than menstruation.

The interpreters differed about the meaning of His saying: ﴿what He has created﴾. Ibn 'Umar, Mujahid, al-Rabi', Ibn Zayd, and al-Dahhak said: it is menstruation and pregnancy together. The meaning of the prohibition on concealment is the prohibition on harming the husband and removing his right. If the divorced woman says "I have menstruated" when she has not, she removes his right of return. If she says "I have not menstruated" when she has, she imposes upon him maintenance that is not obligatory for him, thereby harming him, or by her lie about the absence of menstruation she intends that he not return until the 'iddah is completed and the law cuts off his right. Likewise, the pregnant woman conceals the pregnancy so that his right of return is cut off.

Qatada said: their custom in the Jahiliyyah was to conceal pregnancy so that they could attribute the child to the new husband, and this verse was revealed concerning that. Al-Suddi said: the occasion of revelation is that when a man wanted to divorce his wife, he would ask her: "Are you pregnant?" fearing that separation would harm him and his child. So Allah commanded them to be truthful in that. Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and Ikrimah said: what is intended by "what He has created" is menstruation. It is narrated from 'Umar and Ibn 'Abbas that what is intended is pregnancy. The general meaning is preferred.

In His exalted saying: ﴿and it is not lawful for them﴾, there is an implication that they are entrusted with what is mentioned. Had investigation been permissible, concealment would not have been possible. Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd recited "fī arḥāmihinna" with a ḍamma on the hā'.

His saying: ﴿if they believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾ means: the right of faith, for that requires that they not conceal the truth. This is like when you say: "If you are free, then defend yourself," while addressing a free person.

His saying: ﴿and their husbands have a better right to take them back in that period if they desire reconciliation﴾. The ba'l is the husband, and its plural ba'ūlah is irregular and not analogous, but it is what is heard. Some people said: the hā' in it indicates the feminine plural, and it was said: it is a feminine hā' that entered upon bu'ūl, and bu'ūl has no irregularity.

Ibn Mas'ud recited "bi-riddatihinna" with an added tā'. Mubashshir ibn 'Ubayd recited "bi-raddihinna" with a ḍamma on the hā'. Allah, exalted is He, stated in this verse that the husband may take back his divorced wife as long as she is in the 'iddah. The reference by "that" is to the period. Then the husband's right of return is conjoined with the condition of desiring reconciliation and not harm, just as the women are strictly bound not to conceal what is in their wombs. This explains the rulings that Allah, exalted is He, has laid down between Himself and His servants: the women's not concealing, and the men's intending reconciliation. If anyone after this intends corruption, or a woman conceals what is in her womb, the rulings of this world are based on the outward, and the inward is with Allah, exalted is He, who will requite every doer of deeds. This verse weakens the view of the one who said concerning the one who makes an oath of abstention (al-mūlī): that when the four months pass, the bond is dissolved by an irrevocable single divorce with no return. For the most that the words of the Qur'an indicate is that leaving off the return within the four months is the resolve to divorce. If that is so, then the woman is among the divorced women who must wait, and their husbands have a better right to take them back.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they have rights similar to those against them, according to what is reasonable﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: that refers to beautifying oneself, adorning oneself, and being agreeable. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd recited: that refers to good companionship, each preserving the other, and fearing Allah regarding it. The verse encompasses all the rights of marriage.

His saying: ﴿but men have a degree over them﴾. Mujahid and Qatada said: this is an alert to the superiority of his share over hers in jihad, inheritance, and what is similar to them. Zayd ibn Aslam and his son said: this refers to obedience: it is incumbent upon her to obey him, and it is not incumbent upon him to obey her. 'Amir al-Sha'bi said: "That degree is the dowry that the man gives, and that he performs li'an if he accuses, while she receives the hadd (legal punishment) if she accuses." Ibn 'Abbas said: "That degree" is an indication of urging men toward good companionship and toward generosity to women in wealth and character, meaning that the better one should exert himself against his own self. This is a good and excellent view. Ibn Ishaq said: "The degree" is spending and that he is their guardian (qawwām). Ibn Zayd said: "The degree" is possession of the bond of marriage and that divorce is in his hand. Humayd said: "The degree" is the beard.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This, if it is correctly attributed to him, is weak, and neither the wording nor the meaning of the verse requires it. When you reflect on these aspects that the commentators mentioned, a degree results from their totality that necessitates preference. ﴿ʿAzīz﴾ (Mighty): none can overpower Him. ﴿Ḥakīm﴾ (Wise): in what He executes of rulings and affairs.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 229:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, statement:

﴿Divorce is twice; then either keep [her] in good fellowship or release [her] with kindness. And it is not lawful for you to take anything of what you have given them, unless both fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah. But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, then there is no blame upon them both for what she gives up to be released. These are the limits of Allah, so do not transgress them. And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah – it is those who are the wrongdoers.﴾

'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, Qatada, Ibn Zayd and others said: this verse was revealed to clarify the number of divorces after which the husband has the right to take her back without renewing the dowry (mahr) and the guardian (wali). That is because in the Jahiliyya they used to divorce and take back [their wives] without any end. A man said to his wife in the time of the Prophet ﷺ: "I will neither shelter you nor let you be free to remarry." She said: "How?" He said: "I will divorce you, and when your waiting period (iddah) is about to end, I will take you back." She complained of that, and the verse was revealed.

Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid and others said: the purpose of the verse is to explain the sunna of divorce, meaning: whoever divorces twice, let him fear Allah regarding the third, either by leaving her without wronging her of any of her rights, or by keeping her while treating her kindly in companionship.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The verse includes both of these meanings.

"Keeping [her] in good fellowship" (imsak bi-ma'ruf) means taking her back after the second [divorce] for good companionship and fulfilling the rights of marriage. As for "release" (tasrih), its wording may bear two meanings. The first: he leaves her to complete her iddah after the second, and she becomes more in control of herself; this is the view of al-Suddi and al-Dahhak. The other meaning: he divorces her a third time and thereby releases her; this is the view of Mujahid, 'Ata' and others. This latter view is strengthened in my opinion by three considerations. The first: it has been narrated that a man said to the Prophet ﷺ: "O Messenger of Allah, this [verse] mentions the two divorces, so where is the third?" The Prophet ﷺ said: "It is His saying: ﴿or release [her] with kindness﴾." The second consideration: "release" (tasrih) is among the words of divorce; do you not see that it has been recited as "wa in 'azamu al-sarah" [Qur'an 2:227 variant]? The third consideration: the form fa''ala with this doubling indicates that he has brought about a repeated act upon the second divorce, whereas leaving her does not involve bringing about an act that is expressed by the taf'il form.

"Imsak" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is "amthal" or "ahsan" (better or more excellent). It is also permissible for it to be nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, its implied meaning being: "then the obligation is imsak." His saying "bi-ihsan" means that he does not wrong her in any of her rights and does not transgress, according to one view.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And it is not lawful for you to take﴾ and so on, is addressed to the husbands; He forbids them from taking anything from their wives in a manner of harm. This is the khul' (divorce by compensation), which is not valid unless the man does not single out the harm.

What the husbands have given their wives is singled out for mention, because it is the custom among people that, at the time of discord and corruption, a man seeks back what has left his hand, and this is their main concern in most cases; therefore it is singled out for mention.

All of the Seven [Readers], except Hamza, recited "yakhafa" with a fatha on the ya', in the active form of the verb. Thus this is a verb (khafa) that transitively takes one object, namely "an" [clause]. Hamza alone recited "yukhafa" with a damma on the ya', in the passive form of the verb. Thus this is [the verb] khafa being transitive to two objects, one of which is the subject of the passive verb, and the other being "an" with an implied preposition omitted. The position of "an" is in the genitive by the omitted preposition according to Sibawayh and al-Kisa'i, and in the accusative according to others, because when the preposition is omitted and the verb reaches the second object, it is like "astaghfiru Allah dhanban" (I seek Allah's forgiveness for a sin) and "amartuka al-khayr" (I commanded you the good).

In the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "illa an yakhafu" with the ya' and the plural waw, and the pronoun on this reading refers to the judges and the mediators in people's affairs.

In this verse Allah, the Exalted, has forbidden the husband – [by the words] – to take [anything] except after the fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah, and He emphasised the prohibition with a threat for whoever exceeds the limit. The common scholars have agreed on the prohibition of taking her property, except where the disobedience (nushuz) and corruption of the marriage come from her side. Ibn al-Mundhir said: we have related this from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, 'Ata', al-Nakha'i, Ibn Sirin, al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, al-Zuhri, Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman, Qatada, Sufyan al-Thawri, Malik, Ishaq and Abu Thawr.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, al-Sha'bi, and a group with them said: if along with the corruption and disobedience of the wife there is corruption from the husband, and the discord between them has become severe, then the ransom (fidya) is permissible for the husband.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of that is that the husband – if he were to abandon his corruption – would still have her disobedience remaining.

As for if the husband alone is the source of corruption, I know of no one who permits him the ransom, except what has been narrated from Abu Hanifa, that he said: if the wrongdoing and disobedience come from his side and she then gives khul', it is permissible and valid, but he is sinful, and what he has done is not lawful, and he must not return what he has taken. Ibn al-Mundhir said: this contradicts the apparent meaning of the Book of Allah and the sunna of His Messenger ﷺ, and if someone were told: strive to find an error, he would find no matter greater than that the Qur'an speaks of the prohibition of something and he makes it lawful and permits it.

"The limits of Allah" (hudud Allah) in this place are what is binding upon the spouses of good companionship and the rights of the marital bond.

The incident of Habiba bint Sahl – it is said: Jamila bint Ubayy ibn Salul, and the first is more sound – [concerning her] with Thabit ibn Qays, when the Prophet ﷺ permitted him to take the ransom from her: the transgression in it came only from the woman, because she praised him with every good quality, while she did not love remaining with him.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿But if you fear that they will not keep within the limits of Allah﴾ is addressed to the judges and the mediators in such a matter, even if he is not a judge. Abandoning the keeping of Allah's limits is the wife's disdain for her husband's right and her poor obedience to him. This is said by Ibn 'Abbas, Malik ibn Anas, and the majority of jurists. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and a group with him said: if she says to him, "I will not obey you in any matter, nor will I bathe for you from janaba, nor will I fulfil your oath," the khul' becomes lawful. al-Sha'bi said: "They will not keep the limits of Allah" means: they will not obey Allah, because estrangement calls to abandoning obedience. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: the khul' and the taking are lawful if the woman says to her husband, "I truly dislike you and do not love you," and the like.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿then there is no blame upon them both for what she gives up to be released﴾ is a permission of the ransom, and both sharing in the lifting of blame, because it is not permissible for her to give him her property where it is not permissible for him to take it, and she is able to contest. So if the aforementioned fear exists, it is permissible for him to take and for her to give; and whenever the fear does not occur, it is not permissible for her to give to one who seeks separation.

Ibn 'Umar, al-Nakha'i, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, may Allah be pleased with him, Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifa, 'Ikrima, Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb, Abu Thawr and others said: it is permissible for the husband to take from the woman in the ransom everything she owns, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab judged accordingly. Tawus, al-Zuhri, 'Ata', 'Umar ibn Shu'ayb, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, al-Hakam, Hammad, Ahmad and Ishaq said: it is not permissible for him to take more than the mahr which he gave her. al-Rabi' said likewise, and al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan used to recite with him: "fima iftadat bihi minhu" with the addition of "minhu", meaning: of what you have given them, which is the mahr. Makki related this view from Abu Hanifa, but Ibn al-Mundhir is more reliable. Ibn al-Musayyab said: I do not think he should take all of her property, but he should leave something for her. Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah al-Muzani said: it is not permissible for a man to take from his wife anything as khul', whether little or much. He said: this verse is abrogated by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And if you intend to replace a wife with another and you have given one of them a great amount, do not take anything from it﴾ [al-Nisa': 20].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is weak, because the community (umma) is unanimous on the permissibility of the ransom, and because the meaning associated with the verse of the ransom is not the meaning in the verse of intending replacement.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾ and so on means: these commands and prohibitions are the markers between truth and falsehood, and between obedience and disobedience, so do not overstep them. Then the Exalted threatened for transgressing the limit, and described the transgressor with wrongdoing (zulm), which is placing a thing in other than its proper place, and wrongdoing brings punishment upon its doer. As he ﷺ said: "Wrongdoing will be darkness on the Day of Resurrection."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 230–231:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And if he divorces her [a third time], she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband. And if he divorces her, there is no blame on them both if they return to one another, provided they think they can keep within the limits of Allah. These are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear to a people who have knowledge.﴾ ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, then either retain them in kindness or release them in kindness. And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself.﴾

(p-566) Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: this is the beginning of the third divorce, so the earlier "release" (tasrih) is leaving the woman to complete her waiting period (iddah) from the second.

From the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that khul' (divorce by compensation) is a dissolution of the marriage bond (fash' 'isma) and not a divorce (talaq), he argued from this verse by Allah's mention of two divorces, then His mention of khul', then His mention of the third after the two divorces, and khul' has no ruling that is counted. This was reported by Ibn al-Mundhir in al-Ishraf from him, and from 'Ikrimah, Tawus, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr. He also reported the view of the majority contrary to their opinion.

Mujahid said: this verse explains what is binding upon the one who releases, and the release (tasrih) is the third divorce.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or release with kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] admits of both interpretations: either leaving her to complete the waiting period, or following up with a third divorce. Then in this verse He clarified the ruling for one of the two possibilities, since the second possibility is already known to have no ruling over her after the waiting period has ended.

"Tankiha" (to marry) in the language is literally applied to intercourse (wat') and metaphorically to the contract ('aqd).

The community agreed in this case upon following the sound hadith concerning "the daughter of Samaw'al (p-567), the wife of Rifa'ah, when 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr married her, and Rifa'ah had divorced her three times. She said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'I do not wish to remain with 'Abd al-Rahman; with him is only like the tip of a garment (hudbah).' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to her: 'Perhaps you wish to return to Rifa'ah? No, not until he tastes your 'usaylah (sweetness) and you taste his.'" The scholars held that the marriage which makes her lawful is only entry and intercourse (dukhul and wat'). All of them agree that the penetration of the glans (hashafah) makes her lawful, except al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, who said: "It makes her lawful only by emission (inzal), which is tasting the 'usaylah." Some jurists said: the meeting of the two circumcised parts (iltiqa' al-khitanayn) makes her lawful.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is one, since the two circumcised parts do not meet except with the penetration on which the majority agree.

It is reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that the contract alone upon her makes her lawful to the first husband. This view was deemed erroneous because it contradicts the sound hadith. It is interpreted for Sa'id, may Allah have mercy on him, that the hadith did not reach him. Since he saw that the contract is effective in prohibiting a man from marrying a woman upon whom his father has contracted, he analogized on it, that the contract is effective in making the divorced woman lawful; and the making lawful of a divorced woman is a concession (tarkhis), so it is not completed except by the most complete means. He also prevented the son from [the father's oath] by the strictest of the means of interference, on their principle regarding oaths of piety and breaking them.

According to Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, what makes her lawful is a valid marriage and permissible intercourse. If the one who makes her lawful (muhallil) agrees with the woman [beforehand], then she has not truly been married, and that does not make her lawful; and I know of no disagreement about his agreement with the wife.

(p-568) 'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: if the muhallil intends only to make her lawful, she is not made lawful; and likewise if the woman intends it alone. Ibrahim and al-Sha'bi permitted it even with the woman's intention alone, provided the husband did not order it.

al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: if any of the three intends the making lawful, she is not made lawful to the first husband; and this is an anomalous view. Salim and al-Qasim said: there is no harm in his marrying her in order to make her lawful, provided the two spouses do not know [of the arrangement].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if he divorces her, there is no blame﴾ the verse. The meaning: if the second husband divorces her, there is no blame upon the two of them, i.e. the woman and the first husband. Ibn 'Abbas said this, and there is no disagreement about it. The word "zann" (thought) here is in its usual sense of preferring one of two possibilities. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "ayqanna" (we are certain). His statement on this is weak. "The limits of Allah" are the matters which He commanded not to be transgressed.

He singled out "those who know" for mention, to honour them, since they are the ones who benefit from what He made clear, i.e. set up as a lesson, whether by word or by deed.

If by "making clear" we mean creating understanding in the heart, then that requires specifying "those who know" for mention, because whoever has a seal set upon his heart has nothing made clear to him. The Seven Readers read "yubayyinuha" with the yā'. 'Asim, as reported from him, read "nubayyinuha" with the nūn.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you divorce women﴾ the verse. It is addressed to men; its ruling does not specifically concern anyone but husbands. It is a prohibition on a man from prolonging the waiting period over the woman in order to harm her, by taking her back close to its end and then divorcing her again after that. This was said by al-Dahhak and others, and there is no disagreement about it.

The meaning of "balaghna ajalahunna" (they reach their term) is "qaraba" (they approach it), because the sense necessitates this, since after the term has truly arrived he has no choice in retaining her.

(p-569) The meaning of "amsikuhunna" is "raji'uhunna" (take them back). "Bi-ma'ruf" was said to mean witnessing (al-ishhad). "Wa la tumsikuhunna" means do not take them back to harm them. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 230–231:

His saying, may He be exalted:

﴿And if he divorces her [a third time], she is not lawful to him after that until she marries another husband. And if he divorces her, there is no blame on them both if they return to one another, provided they think they can keep within the limits of Allah. These are the limits of Allah, which He makes clear to a people who have knowledge.﴾ ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, then either retain them in kindness or release them in kindness. And do not retain them to harm them, so that you transgress. Whoever does that has wronged himself.﴾

(p-566) Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: this is the beginning of the third divorce, so the earlier "release" (tasrih) is leaving the woman to complete her waiting period (iddah) from the second.

From the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that khul' (divorce by compensation) is a dissolution of the marriage bond (fash' 'isma) and not a divorce (talaq), he argued from this verse by Allah's mention of two divorces, then His mention of khul', then His mention of the third after the two divorces, and khul' has no ruling that is counted. This was reported by Ibn al-Mundhir in al-Ishraf from him, and from 'Ikrimah, Tawus, Ahmad, Ishaq and Abu Thawr. He also reported the view of the majority contrary to their opinion.

Mujahid said: this verse explains what is binding upon the one who releases, and the release (tasrih) is the third divorce.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or release with kindness﴾ [al-Baqarah: 229] admits of both interpretations: either leaving her to complete the waiting period, or following up with a third divorce. Then in this verse He clarified the ruling for one of the two possibilities, since the second possibility is already known to have no ruling over her after the waiting period has ended.

"Tankiha" (to marry) in the language is literally applied to intercourse (wat') and metaphorically to the contract ('aqd).

The community agreed in this case upon following the sound hadith concerning "the daughter of Samaw'al (p-567), the wife of Rifa'ah, when 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Zubayr married her, and Rifa'ah had divorced her three times.
