She said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'I do not wish to remain with 'Abd al-Rahman; with him is only like the tip of a garment (hudbah).' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to her: 'Perhaps you wish to return to Rifa'ah? No, not until he tastes your 'usaylah (sweetness) and you taste his.'" The scholars held that the marriage which makes her lawful is only entry and intercourse (dukhul and wat'). All of them agree that the penetration of the glans (hashafah) makes her lawful, except al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, who said: "It makes her lawful only by emission (inzal), which is tasting the 'usaylah." Some jurists said: the meeting of the two circumcised parts (iltiqa' al-khitanayn) makes her lawful.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning is one, since the two circumcised parts do not meet except with the penetration on which the majority agree.

It is reported from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib that the contract alone upon her makes her lawful to the first husband. This view was deemed erroneous because it contradicts the sound hadith. It is interpreted for Sa'id, may Allah have mercy on him, that the hadith did not reach him. Since he saw that the contract is effective in prohibiting a man from marrying a woman upon whom his father has contracted, he analogized on it, that the contract is effective in making the divorced woman lawful; and the making lawful of a divorced woman is a concession (tarkhis), so it is not completed except by the most complete means. He also prevented the son from [the father's oath] by the strictest of the means of interference, on their principle regarding oaths of piety and breaking them.

According to Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, what makes her lawful is a valid marriage and permissible intercourse. If the one who makes her lawful (muhallil) agrees with the woman [beforehand], then she has not truly been married, and that does not make her lawful; and I know of no disagreement about his agreement with the wife.

(p-568) 'Uthman ibn 'Affan said: if the muhallil intends only to make her lawful, she is not made lawful; and likewise if the woman intends it alone. Ibrahim and al-Sha'bi permitted it even with the woman's intention alone, provided the husband did not order it.

al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: if any of the three intends the making lawful, she is not made lawful to the first husband; and this is an anomalous view. Salim and al-Qasim said: there is no harm in his marrying her in order to make her lawful, provided the two spouses do not know [of the arrangement].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if he divorces her, there is no blame﴾ the verse. The meaning: if the second husband divorces her, there is no blame upon the two of them, i.e. the woman and the first husband. Ibn 'Abbas said this, and there is no disagreement about it. The word "zann" (thought) here is in its usual sense of preferring one of two possibilities. Abu 'Ubaydah said: "ayqanna" (we are certain). His statement on this is weak. "The limits of Allah" are the matters which He commanded not to be transgressed.

He singled out "those who know" for mention, to honour them, since they are the ones who benefit from what He made clear, i.e. set up as a lesson, whether by word or by deed.

If by "making clear" we mean creating understanding in the heart, then that requires specifying "those who know" for mention, because whoever has a seal set upon his heart has nothing made clear to him. The Seven Readers read "yubayyinuha" with the yā'. 'Asim, as reported from him, read "nubayyinuha" with the nūn.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when you divorce women﴾ the verse. It is addressed to men; its ruling does not specifically concern anyone but husbands. It is a prohibition on a man from prolonging the waiting period over the woman in order to harm her, by taking her back close to its end and then divorcing her again after that. This was said by al-Dahhak and others, and there is no disagreement about it.

The meaning of "balaghna ajalahunna" (they reach their term) is "qaraba" (they approach it), because the sense necessitates this, since after the term has truly arrived he has no choice in retaining her.

(p-569) The meaning of "amsikuhunna" is "raji'uhunna" (take them back). "Bi-ma'ruf" was said to mean witnessing (al-ishhad). "Wa la tumsikuhunna" means do not take them back to harm them. The rest of the verse is clear.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 232:

His Exalted and Majestic words:

﴿And do not take the signs of Allah in jest, and remember the favour of Allah upon you and what He has sent down to you of the Book and wisdom, by which He admonishes you. And fear Allah and know that Allah is Knowing of all things﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231] ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them from marrying their husbands when they have agreed among themselves in a proper manner. This is admonished to whoever among you believes in Allah and the Last Day. That is more virtuous for you and purer. And Allah knows, while you do not know﴾

The intended meaning: His signs revealed in the commands and prohibitions.

Al-Hasan said: this verse was revealed concerning one who divorces in jest or in play, or who takes back (his wife) in the same manner. 'A'isha said the same, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Three things are serious whether done seriously or in jest: marriage, divorce, and taking back (a wife)." This hadith occurs in al-Mudawwana as a saying of Ibn al-Musayyab: "Marriage, divorce, and manumission." Then Allah reminded His servants of His bounty upon them through the Qur'an and the Sunnah.

"Wisdom" (al-hikmah) is the Sunnah that explains, on the tongue of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the intent of Allah regarding what is not explicitly stated in the Book. The description "Knowing" (ʿalim) is required by what preceded of actions whose outward form differs from the intention behind them, such as the one who performs a legal device (muhallil) and the one who takes back (a wife) with the intent of harm (mudarrah).

As for His Exalted words: ﴿And when you divorce women and they reach their term, do not prevent them﴾ — the verse is addressed to the believers, among whom are the husbands and among whom are the guardians (awliya'), since they are the intended ones in "do not prevent them" (ta'dulu-hunna).

The reaching of the term (bulugh al-ajal) in this place means its completion, because the meaning requires that. Some people have said in this place that the intended subject of "do not prevent them" (ta'dulu-hunna) is the husbands, namely by taking them back as a harm that amounts to preventing them from marrying others. According to this view, "their husbands" (azwajahunna) refers to the men, since among them are the husbands. But on the view that the intended subject of "do not prevent them" is the guardians, then "the husbands" are those who had them in their marital bond.

Al-'adl (prevention) means preventing marriage. It carries the sense of constraint and difficulty, as one says: "a'dalat al-dajajah" when the hen's egg is difficult to lay, and "al-da' al-'udal" is a disease that is difficult to cure.

This verse was revealed concerning Ma'qil ibn Yasar and his sister. It was also said: concerning Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah. The circumstance was that a man divorced his sister, or it was said his paternal cousin, and left her until her waiting period was complete. Then he wished to take her back, but Jabir became jealous and said: "You left her while you had the right to her; I will never marry her to you." So the verse was revealed. This verse requires the establishment of the guardian's right to arrange the marriage of the one under his guardianship, and that marriage requires a guardian, contrary to the view of Abu Hanifa that the guardian is not a condition of marriage.

His words "in a proper manner" (bil-ma'ruf) mean the dower (mahr) and witnessing (ishhad).

His Exalted words: ﴿This is admonished to whoever among you﴾ are addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), then a return to addressing the community. The reference in "this" (dhalika) is to abstaining from preventing. The phrase "more virtuous and purer" (azka wa-athar) means: better for the soul, and purer for honour and religion, because of the relations that occur between spouses; the guardian may not know of them, so preventing may lead to corruption and mingling in ways that are not proper. Allah Exalted knows of this what humankind does not know.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 233:

(p-571) His statement, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And the mothers shall suckle their children for two full years, for whoever wishes to complete the suckling.﴾

﴿Yurdi'na awladahunna﴾ ("shall suckle their children") is a report whose meaning is a command, obligatory for some mothers, and a command in the manner of recommendation and option for others. As for the woman who is in marriage (al-'isma), suckling is incumbent upon her, and it is a customary obligation (ʿurf yalzam), since it has become like a condition, except that if she is a noblewoman of luxury, her custom is not to suckle, and that too is like a condition. If the father dies and the child has no property, the position of Malik in al-Mudawwana is that suckling is binding on the mother, unlike maintenance (nafaqa). In the Kitab of Ibn al-Jallab: its suckling is from the treasury (bayt al-mal). ʿAbd al-Wahhab said: he is among the poor Muslims. As for the divorced woman with irrevocable divorce (talaq bayna), there is no suckling obligation upon her; the suckling is upon the husband, unless she herself wishes, in which case she has more right to it at the wage of the like (ujrat al-mithl). This is with the husband being well-off; if he is destitute, suckling is not binding upon her unless the newborn will not accept any other, in which case she is compelled to suckle at that time, and she has the wage of the like according to the husband's ease. Whenever suckling becomes binding upon her and some excuse prevents her from it, the suckling reverts to the father. It is narrated from Malik that if the father is destitute and the child has no property, the suckling is upon the mother; if she has an excuse and has property, then suckling is upon her from her property.

This verse concerns divorced women, as said by al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and others. Allah made it a limit at the point of disagreement between the spouses about the period of suckling, so whichever of them calls for completing the two years, that is his/her right. The majority of exegetes said: these two years are for every child.

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: it concerns the child who remains in the womb for six months; if he remains seven months, his suckling is twenty-three months; if he remains eight months, his suckling is twenty-two months; if he remains nine months, his suckling is twenty-one months.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It seems this view is built upon His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And his carrying and his weaning are thirty months﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15], except that this is a ruling on humankind in general. The year is called ḥawl because affairs change within it for the most part.

Describing them as "full" (kamilayn) is because it is customary, by way of figurative usage, to say: "a year and part of another," and "two days" for a day and part of another, "I walked two days," and "I endured for you in my debt two days and two months."

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿for whoever wishes to complete the suckling﴾ is based on the premise that the two years are not an obligation that may not be exceeded. The Seven readers read: "an yutimma al-rada'ah" with a dammah on the yaʾ and nasb on al-raḍāʿa. Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, Humayd, al-Hasan, and Abu Raja' read: "tatimmu al-raḍāʿatu" with a fatḥa on the first tāʾ and raf' on al-raḍāʿa, attributing the verb to it. Abu Haywa, Ibn Abi ʿAbla, and al-Jarud ibn Abi Sabra read likewise, except that they kasrated the rāʾ of "al-riḍāʿa," and this is a dialect like al-ḥaḍāra and al-ḥiḍāra, and other such forms. It is narrated from Mujahid that he read "al-Rad'a" on the pattern of al-fa'la. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he read: "an yukmila al-raḍāʿa" with a dammed yaʾ.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and a group of scholars derived from this verse that the prohibited suckling which takes the place of kinship is only that which occurred within the two years, because with the completion of the two years, suckling is complete, so there is no suckling thereafter. It is narrated from Qatada that he said: this verse contained an obligation of suckling upon mothers, then this was eased and lightened by the option in His statement: ﴿for whoever wishes﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is an innovated view (qawl mubtada').

**

(p-573) His statement, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And upon the one born to him (al-mawlud lahu) is their provision and their clothing according to what is customary. No soul is burdened except according to its capacity. No mother shall be harmed through her child, nor a father through his child. And upon the heir is the like of that.﴾

"Al-mawlud": a generic noun and a category of men. Provision (al-rizq) in this ruling means sufficient food.

His statement "bil-maʿruf" ("according to what is customary") encompasses good measure in the food, goodness in its delivery, and good demand from the woman. Then He, the Exalted, made clear that spending is according to the husband's wealth and her status with His statement: ﴿No soul is burdened except according to its capacity﴾. The majority of people read "tukallafu" with a ḍammah on the tāʾ, "nafs" as the unnamed subject (maf'ul lam yusamma fa'iluh). Abu Raja' read "takallafu" with a fatḥa on the tāʾ, meaning "tatakallafu," with "nafs" as its subject. Abu al-Ashhab related from him: "la nukallifu" with nūn, "nafsan" with nasb. Abu ʿAmr, Ibn Kathir, and Aban from ʿAsim read: "la tuḍārru wālidatun" with raf' on the rāʾ, and this is a report whose meaning is a command. It is possible the original is "la tuḍārir" with kasra on the first rāʾ, so "wālidatun" is the unnamed subject, and "mawlud" is conjoined to it on this basis in both possibilities. Nafi', Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and ʿAsim read "la tuḍārra" with fatḥa on the shaddāh rāʾ, and this is in the sense of prohibition; its original may be what we mentioned in the first.

The meaning of the verse, in every reading, is the prohibition of the mother harming her divorced husband because of her child, and of him harming her because of the child, or harming the wet-nurse (al-ẓi'r); for the wording of His prohibition encompasses the wet-nurse. ʿIkrima said regarding His statement: ﴿No mother shall be harmed﴾: it means the wet-nurse.

The forms of harm are not limited, and all that is mentioned of them in the exegeses is an example.

(p-574) It is narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read: "la tuḍārir" with two rāʾs, the first fatḥa. Abu Jaʿfar ibn al-Qaʿqaʿ read: "la tuḍārr" with sukun on the first rāʾ.

The scholars differed concerning the meaning of His statement: ﴿And upon the heir is the like of that﴾. Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Hasan, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and others said: it is the heir of the child if he were to die. Some of them said: his heir among men specifically is obligated to suckle as the child's father would have been obligated had he been alive; this was said by Mujahid and ʿAtaʾ. Qatada and others also said: it is the heir of the child, whether men or women, and they are obligated to suckle him according to the proportion of their inheritance from him. Al-Tabari related from Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan that they said: the heir obligated to suckle the child is his guardian and heir if he is a blood relative within the prohibited degrees; if he is a paternal cousin or other, not a mahram relative, nothing is binding on him.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

In this view there is arbitrariness (tahakkum). Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb, al-Dahhak, and Bashir ibn Nasr, judge of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-Aziz, said: the heir is the child himself, meaning that upon his property, when he inherits his father, is the suckling of himself. Sufyan, may Allah have mercy on him, said: the heir is the surviving one of the child's two parents after the death of the other, and he holds, in addition, that if the mother is the surviving one, the paternal relative (al-'asib) shares with her in suckling the child in proportion to his share of the inheritance.

Those whose views were mentioned stated explicitly that what is meant by His statement, ﴿the like of that﴾, is the provision (p-575) and the clothing. Among the scholars, Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, ʿUbayd Allah ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUtba ibn Mas'ud, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Ibn ʿAbbas, and others also mentioned this.

Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said in "al-Mudawwana," and all his companions, as did al-Sha'bi, al-Zuhri, al-Dahhak, and a group of scholars: rather, what is meant by His statement, ﴿the like of that﴾, is that he not harm; as for provision and clothing, nothing is upon him concerning it.

Ibn al-Qasim related from Malik that the verse contained that provision and clothing are upon the heir, then this was abrogated.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Thus there is consensus of the Ummah that the heir must not harm, and the disagreement is whether upon him is provision and clothing or not. Yahya ibn Yaʿmar read: "wa ʿala al-warathati mithlu dhalik" in the plural.

**

His statement, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And if they both wish weaning by mutual consent and consultation, there is no blame upon them. And if you wish to seek wet-nurses for your children, there is no blame upon you, provided you hand over what you gave in accordance with what is customary. And fear Allah, and know that Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

The pronoun in "aradā" (they both wish) refers to the two parents, and "fiṣālan" (weaning) means weaning from suckling. Consultation does not occur, and mutual consent is not permitted, except with what involves no harm to the child. So when it becomes apparent from his condition that he is independent of milk before the completion of the two years, there is no blame upon the two parents in weaning him. This is the meaning of the verse. Mujahid, Qatada, Ibn Zayd, Sufyan, and others said this. Ibn ʿAbbas said: there is no blame with mutual consent in weaning him before the two years and after them.

(p-576) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The precise statement on this is that weaning him before the two years is valid only with the consent of both of them and that there be no harm to the child. As for after their completion, whoever calls for weaning, that is his right, unless there is harm to the child in it.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And if you wish to seek wet-nurses﴾ addresses all people, including fathers and mothers; that is, it is permitted for them to take a wet-nurse with agreement upon that.

As for His statement, the Exalted: ﴿provided you hand over﴾, it addresses men specifically, except—according to one of the two interpretations—in the reading of whoever reads "ataytum." Six of the Seven read: "ataytum" with madd. The meaning: you gave. Ibn Kathir read "ataytum" in the sense of "what you brought and did," as Zuhayr said:

Whatever good they brought, it is only what the fathers of their fathers inherited before.

Abu ʿAli said: the meaning is: when you hand over what you gave of its payment, or its giving, or its sale, so the governed noun was omitted, the pronoun was placed in its stead, so the estimate was: "what you gave it," then the pronoun was omitted from the relative clause. The wording may bear another meaning, said by Qatada: when you hand over what you brought of the intention to seek suckling, that is, each of the two parents surrenders and is content, and this was by agreement between them, with the intent of good and the desire of what is customary in the matter.

According to this possibility, men and women both enter into the address "salamtum." According to the interpretation Abu ʿAli and others mentioned, the address is to men, because they are the ones who are given the wage of suckling. Abu ʿAli said: it is possible that "ma" is verbal (maṣdariyya), meaning: when you hand over the coming (al-ityan), and the meaning is as the first, but one is spared the artifice of omitting the governed noun and then the pronoun.

Mujahid said: the meaning is: when you hand over to the mothers their wage, in accordance with the amount they suckled up to (p-577) the time of seeking suckling. Sufyan said: the meaning is: when you hand over to the wet-nurse, who is the suckler, her wage in accordance with what is customary.

The rest of the verse is a command to piety, and a reminder that Allah, the Exalted, is Seeing of every deed; in this there is a warning and admonition, that is, He will recompense you according to your deeds.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 234:

His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying:

﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves for four months and ten days.﴾

Some of the Kufan grammarians said: the predicate for "those who" (alladhina) is omitted, and the intended meaning is to inform about their wives, that they "shall wait." The position of the Basran grammarians is that the predicate of "alladhina" is implied in meaning, since the sentence's implied wording is: (their wives shall wait). If you wish, you may estimate it as: (and the wives of those among you who die shall wait). The expression thus came in the utmost brevity, and its grammatical analysis is built upon this meaning, which is its governing and established sense.

al-Mahdawi related from Sibawayh that the meaning is: "And among what is recited to you is: those who die..." I do not know this which he related, because that would only be correct if the sentence contained a word of command after it, like His saying: ﴿As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 38]. This verse contains the sense of a command but not its wording. So with this estimate one would need another estimate, which is dispensed with when a word of command is present. The beauty of the verse's arrangement in this way is that it serves as a preparation for His saying: ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾, since the address from the beginning of the verse to its end is directed to the men among whom are the rulers and the judges. The phrasing of al-Mubarrad and al-Akhfash is what we have mentioned.

This verse concerns the waiting period of a woman whose husband has died. Its apparent wording is general, but its meaning is specific to free women who are not pregnant (p-578), and the verse does not refer to the rare exceptions such as one who is doubtful and the like.

al-Mahdawi related from some scholars that the verse included pregnant women, then this was abrogated by His saying: ﴿and those who carry burdens, their term is that they lay down their burden﴾ [al-Talaq: 4]. The waiting period of a pregnant woman is the delivery of her child according to the majority of scholars, and it is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, and others that the complete period for her is the later of the two terms.

Al-tarabbus (waiting): patient restraint and deliberate staying with a person in a place or state. God has clarified this by His saying: "by themselves." The reports from the Prophet ﷺ are widely attested that the waiting with mourning (ihdad) is abstaining from adornment, wearing dyed and beautiful clothing, perfume and the like, and committing to remain in her dwelling, wherever she was at the time of the husband's death. This is the view of the majority of scholars, and it is the view of Malik and his companions.

Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hanifa (according to what is related from him), and others said: staying the night in the dwelling is not required; she may spend the night wherever she wishes.

al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: mourning is nothing; she only waits from marriage, and she may adorn herself and perfume herself.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

This view is weak. The majority of people recited "yutawaffawna" with a damma on the yā'. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God be pleased with him, recited "yatawaffawna" with a fatha on the yā', and likewise al-Mufaddal related it from 'Asim, and its meaning is: they fulfil their terms (ajal).

(p-579) God made the four months and ten days a worship within the waiting period, in which there is a determination of the womb's emptiness, since in them the forty, forty, forty are completed, according to the hadith related by Ibn Mas'ud and others, after which the spirit is breathed in.

God, exalted, made the ten days a completion, since it is the time when the movement of the fetus is likely to appear, whether the months are complete or deficient, and because of the swiftness or slowness of the fetus's movement; this was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Abu al-'Aliya, and others.

He, exalted, said: "ashra" and did not say "ashratan," giving precedence to the rule of nights, since the night precedes the day, and the days are included within it; and "ashr" is lighter in pronunciation. The majority of scholars said: the tenth day is included in this, and it is part of the waiting period, since the days are together with the nights. Mundhir ibn Sa'id related, and it is also reported from al-Awza'i, that the tenth day is not part of the waiting period, but the period is completed with the completion of ten nights. al-Mahdawi said: it has been said that the meaning is: "and ten periods, each period being a day and a night."

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he recited: "arba'ata ashhurin wa 'ashra layalin" (four months and ten nights).

**

His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying:

﴿So when they have reached their term, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves in an honourable manner. And God is Aware of what you do.﴾

He, exalted, attributed the term (ajal) to them, since it is a defined period set for their affair.

The address in His saying "there is no blame upon you" is general to all people, and the one charged with this ruling is the rulers and the close guardians, and the women observing the waiting period.

His saying, exalted and majestic: "what they do" intends marriage and what is less than it, such as adornment and abandoning mourning. Mujahid, Ibn Shihab, and others said: by "what they do" is meant marriage to whomever they wish, provided it is honourable and not reprehensible. The aspects of what is reprehensible in this are many.

(p-580) Some exegetes said: "in an honourable manner" means with witnesses.

His saying, exalted: ﴿And God is Aware of what you do﴾ is a warning containing a caution, and "khabir" is an active participle from "khabara," when one thoroughly investigates the knowledge of a thing.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 235:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿There is no blame upon you for what you hint at in the proposal to women, or for what you conceal within yourselves. God knows that you will remember them. But do not make a secret promise with them, except that you speak a fitting word. And do not resolve upon the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end. Know that God knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that God is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

The address of this verse is to all people, and the one who directly applies its ruling is the man who has in mind marrying a woman in her waiting period (ʿiddah).

Ta'rid (allusion) is speech that contains no explicit statement, as if it presents itself to the mind of the one who speaks it. The community (ummah) has agreed that speaking to a woman in her waiting period with words that are explicit about her marriage, or that point clearly to it, is not permitted. Likewise they agreed that speaking to her with words that are sexual (rafath), or that mention intercourse, or that incite to it, is not permitted. Anything beyond that is permitted.

Among the strongest forms of allusion that come close to explicitness is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Fatimah bint Qays: "Stay at the house of Umm Shurayk, and do not get ahead of me with yourself." Among what is permitted is a man's saying: "You are good, you are desirable, and I hope to marry you; if something is decreed, it will be." This is the example given by Malik, Ibn Shihab, and many of the scholars in this matter.

It is permissible for a man to praise himself and mention his good qualities by way of allusion to marriage. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Husayn did this, and he argued that the Prophet (ﷺ) did it with Umm Salamah.

Giving a gift to a woman in her waiting period is permitted, and it is a form of allusion; this was said by Sahnun and many scholars. Mujahid disliked saying "do not get ahead of me with yourself," and he regarded it as a secret promise.

In my view, this is to be interpreted as follows: the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to Fatimah bint Qays was given as an opinion (ra'y) on her behalf concerning whom she should marry, not that he himself desired her for himself. Otherwise it would contradict his own saying (ﷺ).

Khitbah (proposal), with a kasrah on the kha', is the action of the one proposing, consisting of speech, intention, and seeking to win favour through an action or a word. One says: he proposed to her (khataba-ha yakhtibu-ha khatban wa khitbatan), and a man who is a khattab is one who is much engaged in proposals. From this is the saying of the poet:

Ba-raḥa bil-ʿaynayni khaṭṭābu al-kuthab
Yaqūlu innī khāṭibun wa qad kadhab

(He was bewitching in the eyes, the suitor of the sand-hills; he says, "I am a suitor," and he has lied.)

And:

Wa innamā yakhṭubu ʿassan man ḥalab

(He who proposes is only one who has milked.)

Khitbah is on the pattern of jilsah and qi'dah. Khutbah, with a damma on the kha', is the speech that is spoken in marriage and other matters. "Akinnatum" means: you concealed and hid. The Arabs say: "I concealed (kanantu) the thing" of physical objects when I covered it in a house, a garment, or land and the like, and "I concealed (akanantu) the matter within myself." It is not heard from the Arabs that they said "kanantuhu fi nafsi" (in my soul). And they say: "The house concealed (akanna) the person" and the like.

God therefore lifted blame from those who wish to marry a woman in her waiting period, both by allusion and by concealment within themselves, and He forbade the secret promise, which is an explicit statement about marriage, a building upon it, and an agreement upon a pledge. Thus He granted leniency, knowing (ta'ala) the overpowering of souls, their aspirations, and the weakness of humans in controlling them.

His saying, "you will remember them": al-Hasan said: "you will propose to them," as if He said: "if you are not forbidden." Others than al-Hasan said: its meaning is that God knows you will mention the women in waiting periods in your souls and with your tongues to those whom you find light (lenient) about them. So He forbade that a means be made to a secret promise with them, because that involves violating the sanctity of the waiting period.

His saying: ﴿But do not make a secret promise with them﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Malik and his companions, al-Sha'bi, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Suddi, and the majority of the scholars held that the meaning is: do not agree with them on a promise, a binding commitment, and taking pledges, in secret from you and hidden. So "sirran" (secretly), on this interpretation, is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: keeping it secret. Jabir ibn Zayd, Abu Mijlaz Lahiq ibn Humayd, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i said: "sirr" in this verse means fornication (zina), that is: do not promise them fornication.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

This is how these scholars phrased the interpretation of "sirr," and in my view there is an issue with it. The word sirr in the language applies to sexual intercourse, lawful and unlawful, but the meaning of the statement and its context must be referred to one of the two aspects. Among the evidence is the verse of al-Hutay'ah:

Wa yaḥrumu sirru jārihim ʿalayhim
Wa ya'kulu jāruhum anfa al-qiṣā'

(The secret (intercourse) with their neighbour's wife is forbidden to them, while their neighbour eats the best of the dishes.)

The context of this verse indicates that sirr is intended to mean unlawful intercourse, for if the neighbour had married her, as is proper, there would be no shame in that. Among the evidence is another poet's saying:

Akhālatunā sirru al-nisā'i muḥarramun
ʿalayya wa-tashhādu al-nadāmā maʿa al-khamri

(O our maternal aunt, the secret of women is forbidden to me, and the witnessing of drinking companions alongside wine.)

La'in lam uṣabbiḥ dāhinan wa-lafīfahā
wa-nā'iba-hā yawman bi-rāghiyat al-bikr

(If I do not wake up in the morning, greasing (myself) and the one who wraps her, and calling her one day with the young camel's rumble...)

The context of this poetry indicates that he meant the prohibition of intercourse with women in general, lawful and unlawful, until he takes his revenge.

The verse gives the prohibition of a man promising a woman in her waiting period that he will have intercourse with her after the waiting period by way of marriage. As for a promise of fornication, it is forbidden to a Muslim with a woman in her waiting period and with other women.

Makki transmitted from Ibn Jubayr that he said: "sirran": marriage (nikah). This is a clear expression. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of His saying, "But do not make a secret promise with them," is: do not marry them secretly and conceal that; when she is free (from the waiting period), you make it public and consummate with her.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad said:

Ibn Zayd's interpretation of sirr, along with the first view, means secretly. He stood alone in calling the contract a promise, and this is problematic, for once the contract is concluded, even if concealed, it is only in the resolution of the tie.

Makki transmitted from him that he said: the verse is abrogated by His saying, "And do not resolve upon the tie of marriage."

The community agreed on the disliked nature of making a promise during the waiting period, for the woman herself, for the father concerning his virgin daughter, and for the master concerning his slave-woman. Ibn al-Mawwaz said: "As for the guardian who does not have the power of compulsion, I dislike it, and if it happens, I will not annul it." Malik (may God have mercy on him) said concerning one who makes a promise during the waiting period and then marries after it: "Separating them is more beloved to me, whether he consummated with her or not, and it is a single divorce; when she is freed, he proposes to her along with the proposers." This is the narration of Ibn Wahb. Ashhab narrated from Malik that he separates them as an obligation. This was also said by Ibn al-Qasim, and Ibn Harith transmitted the like from Ibn al-Majishun, adding what implies that the prohibition is permanent.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except that you speak a fitting word﴾ is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'). The "fitting word" is what is permitted of allusion. Al-Dahhak mentioned that among the fitting word is that a man says to the woman in her waiting period: "Hold yourself for me, for I have a desire for you," and she says: "And I am the same."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

In my view this is a promise, whereas allusion is the man's saying: "You are indeed noble and worthy, and what is decreed will be; and indeed you are admirable," and the like.

**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And do not resolve upon the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end. Know that God knows what is in your souls, so beware of Him. And know that God is Forgiving and Forbearing.﴾

The resolution of the tie ('azm al-'uqdah) is concluding it by witnesses and the guardian, and then it is called a "tie" ('uqdah).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿until the prescribed term reaches its end﴾. He means the completion of the waiting period. "The Book" here is the limit that was set and the measure of time that was determined; He called it a book because God, Exalted, decreed and imposed it, as He said: ﴿the Book of God upon you﴾ [An-Nisa: 24] and as He said: ﴿Indeed, prayer has been upon the believers a decreed Book﴾ [An-Nisa: 103]. In my view, the sentence does not need an omitted genitive; Abu Ishaq assumed an omitted genitive here, meaning "the obligation of the Book," and that is because he took the Book to mean the Qur'an.

The scholars differed about whether anyone who violated this prohibition and resolved the tie before the term reached its end.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad (may God have mercy on him) said:

I will detail this matter, God willing.

If he contracted during the waiting period and it was discovered, and the judge annulled his marriage before consummation, then the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and a group of scholars is that this does not make the prohibition permanent. Malik and Ibn al-Qasim said this in the Mudawwanah at the end of the chapter that follows it, concerning setting the term for the wife of a missing man. All of them said: he is one of the proposers.

Ibn al-Jallab transmitted from Malik a narration that the prohibition becomes permanent with a contract during the waiting period, even if it is annulled before consummation.

As for one who contracts during the waiting period and consummates after its end, some scholars said: that is like consummation during the waiting period, and the prohibition between them becomes permanent. Other scholars said: the prohibition is not made permanent by that. Malik once said it makes the prohibition permanent, and once said: "The prohibition is not established by that, by itself." Both views are found in the Mudawwanah in the chapter on the Sunnah divorce.

As for one who consummates during the waiting period, the view of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Malik, a group of his companions, al-Awza'i, al-Layth, and other scholars is that the prohibition becomes permanent. The view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may God be pleased with him), Ibn Mas'ud, Ibrahim, Abu Hanifah, al-Shafi'i, a group of scholars, and 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Abi Salamah is that the prohibition does not become permanent even if he had intercourse during the waiting period; rather, they are separated, she observes a waiting period from him, and then he is one of the proposers.

Abu Hanifah and al-Shafi'i said: she observes the waiting period from the first husband, and when the waiting period is over, there is no harm in the second man marrying her.

Ibn al-Jallab transmitted a narration within the school that the prohibition is not made permanent with consummation during the waiting period; he mentioned this regarding the one who knows the prohibition and is bold in it, because he is an adulterer. As for the ignorant person, I know of no disagreement about it within the school.

Abu 'Ali al-Husayn ibn Muhammad al-Ghassani narrated to me by licence (munawalah), saying: Abu 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-Barr narrated to us, 'Abd al-Warith ibn Sufyan narrated to us, Qasim ibn Asbagh narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Nu'aym ibn Hammad, from Ibn al-Mubarak, from Ash'ath, from al-Sha'bi, from Masruq, who said: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab learned that a woman of Quraysh had been married by a man of Thaqif during her waiting period. He sent for them both, separated them, punished them, and said: "Never marry her." He placed her dowry in the public treasury (bayt al-mal). This spread among the people, and it reached 'Ali, who said: "May God have mercy on the Commander of the Faithful. What is the matter with the dowry and the public treasury? They were only ignorant, and it is proper for the imam to return them to the Sunnah." It was said to him: "What do you say about it?" He said: "She has the dowry for what he made lawful of her private parts; they are separated, there is no lashing upon them, she completes her waiting period from the first, then observes a complete waiting period of three cycles from the second, and then he may propose to her if he wishes." When this reached 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, he addressed the people and said: "O people, return the ignorant practices to the Sunnah."

This is the view of al-Shafi'i and al-Layth regarding the waiting period from two men.

Malik, the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y), al-Awza'i, and al-Thawri said: one waiting period suffices for both of them, whether it is by pregnancy, by menstrual cycles, or by months.

The Madinan scholars narrated from Malik the view like that of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and al-Shafi'i, that both waiting periods must be completed. Malik's view varied concerning one who enters into a waiting period while knowing the prohibition and is bold in it. Once he said: the knowledgeable and the ignorant are alike in this; there is no hadd punishment upon him, the dowry is binding upon him, the child is attributed to him, they are both punished, and they are never to marry one another. And once he said: the one who knows the prohibition is like an adulterer; he is punished by hadd, the child is not attributed to him, and he may marry her after the purification (istibra'). The first view is the more famous from Malik (may God have mercy on him).

His saying, Exalted is He: "And know," to the end of the verse, is a warning against falling into what He forbade, and a reminder of His forgiveness and forbearance in these rulings, which He clarified and made broad, including the permission of allusion and the like.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 236:

(p-589) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women before you have touched them or specified for them a bridal payment. But provide for them, the wealthy according to his means and the poor according to his means, a provision according to what is reasonable, a duty upon the doers of good.﴾

This is the beginning of a report that the blame is lifted from the one who divorces before consummation (al-bina') and intercourse (al-jima'), whether he has specified a dower (mahr) or not. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade marrying for the sake of mere pleasure and the satisfaction of desire, and commanded marriage for the sake of seeking chastity, seeking the reward of Allah, and intending lasting companionship, it entered the minds of the believers that whoever divorces before consummation has committed a part of this disliked matter. So the verse came, lifting the blame in that case when the basis of the marriage was on a good intention.

Some said: "There is no blame upon you" means: there is no claim for the full dower; rather, upon you is half of what was specified for her for whom it was specified, and provision (mut'ah) for her for whom nothing was specified.

Some said: "There is no blame upon you" means: in sending the divorce during a menstrual period, unlike with one who has been consummated.

Makki said: the meaning of "there is no blame upon you" is in divorce before consummation, because blame may fall upon the divorcer after he had intended pleasure, and that is safe before touching (al-masis).

The address of the verse is to all people.

(p-590) Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "tamassuhunna" without an alif. Al-Kisa'i and Hamza read "tumasshunna" with an alif and a damma on the ta'. The latter reading conveys touching from both spouses, while the first reading implies that through the meaning understood from touching (al-mass). Abu 'Ali preferred it, because the verbs of this meaning came in trilateral form on this pattern: nakaha, safada, qara'a, dhaqata, and darab al-fahl. Both readings are good. "Tafridu" is coordinated with "tamassu". Imposing the dower (fard al-mahr) is affirming and specifying it.

This verse indicates the permissibility of a contract based on tafwid (delegation of the dower), because it is a marriage established in the verse, explaining the ruling of divorce in it. Malik said this in al-Mudawwana.

Al-faridah: the dower (al-sadaq).

His saying, exalted is He: "wa-matti'uhunna" means: give them something that will be a provision (mata') for them. Ibn 'Umar, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Qilaba, al-Zuhri, Qatada, and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim took it as obligatory. Abu 'Ubayd, Malik ibn Anas and his companions, Shurayh, and others took it as recommended (nadb). Then they differed regarding the pronoun attached to "matti'u": which women is meant? Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, 'Ata', Jabir ibn Zayd, al-Hasan, al-Shafi'i, Ahmad, Ishaq, and the people of opinion (ashab al-ra'y) said: provision is obligatory for the divorced woman before consummation and specification of the dower, and recommended in other cases.

Malik and his companions said: provision is recommended for every divorced woman even if he had consummated with her, except the one he did not consummate with and for whom he specified a dower; for her, what was specified suffices, and she has no provision.

Abu Thawr said: she has provision, and so does every divorced woman.

The scholars agreed that the one for whom no dower was specified and with whom he did not consummate has nothing except the provision (p-591). Al-Zuhri said: the judge rules for her with it. The majority of people said: the judge does not rule with it; this was said by Shurayh, and it is said to the husband: if you are of the God-fearing and the good-doers, then give provision, and he is not compelled.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is with the application of the term "obligatory" according to some of them. As for linking the school of Malik: Ibn Sha'ban said: the provision is in exchange for the distress of divorce, and therefore the woman who obtains khul', the one divorced by mubara'a, and the one subjected to li'an have no provision. al-Tirmidhi, 'Ata', and al-Nakha'i said: the woman who obtains khul' has provision. The people of opinion said: the woman subjected to li'an has provision.

Ibn al-Qasim said: there is no provision in a marriage that has been annulled.

Ibn al-Mawwaz said: nor in what is subject to annulment after the validity of the contract, such as one spouse owning the other.

Ibn Wahb narrated from Malik that the woman given choice (al-mukhayyara) has provision, unlike the slave woman freed while under a slave husband who then chooses; for her there is no provision. As for the free woman who is given choice, or is given ownership of her divorce, or whose husband marries a slave woman over her, and she chooses herself in all of that, she has provision, because the husband is the cause of separation, and for her it would be a humiliation not to choose herself.

People differed about the amount of the provision. Ibn 'Umar said: the least that suffices as provision is thirty dirhams or its equivalent. It is narrated that Ibn Muhayriz used to rule against the treasurer of the register for three (p-592) dinars. Ibn 'Abbas said: the highest provision is a servant, then clothing, then maintenance. 'Ata' said: the middle of that is a shirt, a veil, and a wrap. al-Hasan said: each is provided according to his means: this one with a servant, that one with garments, this one with a garment, and that one with maintenance; and so Malik ibn Anas says. al-Hasan ibn 'Ali provided twenty thousand and a jar of honey; Shurayh provided five hundred dirhams. The mother of Humayd ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf said: "It is as if I am looking at a black servant woman with whom 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf provided his wife, the mother of Abu Salama." The people of opinion and others said: the provision of the woman divorced before consummation, when the dower was specified, is only half of the dower of her equal.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿according to the wealthy his means and according to the poor his means﴾ is evidence for rejecting fixed determination. Al-Jumhur read "'ala al-mus'i" with a sukun on the waw and a kasra on the sin, meaning "the one who is wealthy," that is, his circumstances have become broad. Abu Haywa read "al-muwassa'" with a fatha on the waw and a shadda on the sin, with fatha. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim in the narration of Abu Bakr read "qadruhu" with a sukun on the dal in both places. Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim in the narration of Hafs read "qadaruhu" with a fatha on the dal in both places. Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash and others said: they have the same meaning; both are eloquent dialects. Likewise Abu Zayd reported: you say "khudh qadra kadha" and "qadra kadha" with the same meaning, and it is read in the Book of Allah: ﴿So the valleys flowed according to their measure﴾ [al-Ra'd: 17], and He said: ﴿And they did not measure Allah with His true measure﴾ [al-An'am: 91]; and if the dal were moved it would be permissible.

And "al-muqtir": the one who is poor, the one of little wealth.

And "mata'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar).

His saying, exalted is He: "bil-ma'ruf" means: there is no burden in it and no excess on either side. So it is an emphasis on the meaning of His saying: ﴿according to the wealthy his means and according to the poor his means﴾.

(p-593) Then Allah, exalted is He, emphasized the recommendation with His saying: ﴿a duty upon the doers of good﴾, meaning: in this matter of providing, they are the doers of good. And whoever said that provision is obligatory said: this is an emphasis of obligation, that is, upon the doers of good by faith and Islam, so no one may say "you are not a doer of good" under this interpretation. "Haqqan" is an attribute of "mata'an", or it is in the accusative as a verbal noun, and that is more emphatic for the command.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 237:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, and you have already specified for them a obligation, then half of what you have specified [is due], unless they waive it or the one in whose hand is the marriage tie waives it. And that you waive is nearer to righteousness. And do not forget graciousness between you. Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

The people have differed concerning this verse.

A group, among them Malik and others, said: it excludes the divorced woman after the specification [of a dower] from the ruling of provision (tamti'), since the words of the Exalted, ﴿And provide for them﴾ [al-Baqarah: 236], would otherwise apply to her.

Ibn al-Musayyib said: this verse abrogated the verse in al-Ahzab, because that one included the provision of every woman who had not been consummated with.

Qatadah said: this verse abrogated the verse before it.

Ibn al-Qasim said in al-Mudawwana: the provision was for every divorced woman by the words of the Exalted, ﴿And for divorced women is provision according to what is reasonable﴾ [al-Baqarah: 241], and for the one not consummated with by the verse in Surah al-Ahzab. Then Allah made an exception from it, for the one for whom a dower was specified before consummation, by this verse, and established for the one for whom a dower was specified only half of what was specified.

Zayd ibn Aslam claimed that it is abrogated by this verse; this was related in al-Mudawwana from Zayd ibn Aslam as an assertion.

Ibn al-Qasim also said: it is an exception (istithna'), and the clarification is to return that to the abrogation which Zayd spoke of, because Ibn al-Qasim said: the words of the Exalted, ﴿And for divorced women is provision﴾ [al-Baqarah: 241], are general to all, then Allah made an exception from it, this one for whom a dower was specified before touching.

A group of scholars, among them Abu Thawr, said: the provision is for every divorced woman in general, and this verse only clarifies that the one for whom a dower was specified takes half of what was specified; the verse was not meant to cancel her provision, rather she has the provision and half of the specified dower.

The majority read "fa-nisfu" (فَنِصْفُ) with a raised (ḍammah) ending, and the meaning: then what is due is half of what you specified. A group read "fa-nisfa" (فَنِصْفَ) with the fa' in the accusative, and the meaning: then pay half. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Zayd ibn Thabit read "fa-naṣifu" (فَنَصِفُ) with a ḍammah on the nun throughout the Qur'an, and this is a dialect; similarly al-Asma'i transmitted it as a reading from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿unless they waive it﴾ is a discontinuous exception (istithna' munqati'), because their waiving of half is not of the same kind as their taking it. "Ya'fu-na" (يَعْفُونَ) means: they leave aside and pardon; its form is yaf'ulna. The meaning: unless they leave aside the half that was due to them from the husband.

Al-'afiyat in this verse means every woman who controls her own affair. Ibn 'Abbas and a group of jurists and Successors said: the waiver of a virgin who has no guardian is permissible. Sahnun related this in al-Mudawwana from other than Ibn al-Qasim, after he had mentioned to Ibn al-Qasim that her waiving of half the dower is not permissible.

As for the one under the guardianship of a father or a guardian (wasi), her waiving of half her dower is not permissible, by one opinion, as far as I recall.

People differed concerning the intended meaning of his saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or the one in whose hand is the marriage tie﴾.

(p-595) Ibn 'Abbas, 'Alqamah, Tawus, Mujahid, Shurayh, al-Hasan, Ibrahim, al-Sha'bi, Abu Salih, 'Ikrimah, al-Zuhri, Malik and others said: it is the guardian (wali) in whose charge the woman is; so it is the father regarding his daughter who does not control her own affair, and the master regarding his slave-woman. As for Shurayh, he permitted the waiver of a brother regarding half the dower, and said: "I waive the dowers of the Banu Murrah even if they dislike it." Likewise 'Ikrimah said: the waiver of the one who concluded the marriage contract between them is permissible, whether he was a paternal uncle, a brother, or a father, even if she dislikes it.

A group of scholars said: the one in whose hand is the marriage tie is the husband. This was said by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, and also said by Ibn 'Abbas; Shurayh also returned to it; and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said it, as did many jurists of the cities.

According to the first view, the recommendation for both parties applies to the half which is due to the woman: either she waives it, or her guardian waives it. According to the second view, the recommendation applies to both sides: either she waives her half, so that she takes nothing from the husband; or the husband waives the half which he reduces, so that he pays the whole dower. This is the grace from both of them, and according to the condition of the spouses, forbearance and gracious conduct are fitting.

It is related that Jubayr ibn Mut'im entered upon Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and offered him a daughter of his, and he married her. When he went out he divorced her and sent her the dower. It was said to him: "Why did you marry her?" He said: "She was offered to me and I disliked refusing her." It was said: "Then why did you send the dower?" He said: "Then where is the grace?"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Those who argue that the one in whose hand is the marriage tie is the husband argue that this guardian is not permitted to forgo any part of her dower before the divorce, so there is no difference after the divorce. Also, he is not permitted to forgo anything of her property which is not part of the dower, so why would he forgo half of the dower? Also, if it is said that it is the guardian, what singles out some guardians over others, when all of them hold the marriage tie, whether he be a guardian for support (kafil), or a legal guardian (wasi), or the judge, or a man of the clan? (p-596) Those who argue that it is the guardian who is restrained (al-hajir) argue by the wording of the verse, because the words "the one in whose hand is the marriage tie" are firmly applicable to the guardian, whereas for the husband they are somewhat strained. The matter is not as al-Tabari and Makki said, that the divorcer has no tie in his hand; rather the attribution of the tie to him remains, inasmuch as he concluded it before. Also, the words "unless they waive it" do not include one who does not control her affair, since she has no waiver; so likewise women are not to be disadvantaged by the waiver of one who controls the affair of one who does not control her affair. Also, the verse is only a recommendation to leave aside something which has become due upon the husband's wealth; the wording of waiver, which is leaving aside and dropping, gives that; but the husband's giving the full dower is not called a waiver, it is only a call to excellence. Except that the woman may be considered to have already received it. And this is a weak argument which is not relied upon. Makki said: Also, Allah mentioned the husbands in His saying, ﴿then half of what you specified﴾, then mentioned the wives by His saying "they waive"; so how can the husbands be described afterwards as "the one in whose hand is the marriage tie"? Rather it is a third degree, and there remains for it only the guardian.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this there is room for consideration.

The majority read "aw ya'fuwa" (أَوْ يَعْفُوَ) with a fatḥah on the waw because the verb is in the subjunctive. Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan read "aw ya'fu alladhi" (أَوْ يَعْفُو الَّذِي) with a quiescent waw. Al-Mahdawi said this is by analogy with the alif. From it is the verse of 'Amir ibn al-Tufayl:

> "'Amir did not blacken me by inheritance; God refused that I should rise through a mother or a father."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What appears to me is that he found the fatḥah on a final waw preceded by a moving letter heavy, owing to its rarity in the speech of the Arabs. Al-Khalil, may Allah have mercy on him, said: No final fatḥah-bearing waw preceded by a fatḥah has come in speech except in their saying "'afawah," which is the plural of "'afaw," meaning a donkey's foal; and likewise any vowel that precedes a fatḥah-bearing waw is heavy.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, addressed all of them recommending, by His saying: ﴿And that you waive is nearer to righteousness﴾, meaning: O all of mankind. This is the reading of the majority with the taʼ in the second person. Abu Nahik and al-Sha'bi read "wa-an ya'fuwa" with the yā', and this refers back to the one in whose hand is the marriage tie.

The majority read "wa-la tansawu al-fadl" (وَلا تَنْسَوُا الفَضْلَ). 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Mujahid, Abu Haywah and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "wa-la tanasaw al-fadl" (وَلا تَناسَوُا الفَضْلَ), which is a reading of firm meaning, because it is a place of mutual forgetting (tanasin), not of forgetting, except by way of figure of speech.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not forget graciousness﴾ is a recommendation to kindness. Mujahid said: the graciousness is the husband's completing the whole dower, or the woman's leaving aside the half which is hers.

His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ is a statement implying the promise of reward for the one who does good, and the deprivation for the one who does not.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 238:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Be watchful over the prayers, and over the middle prayer, and stand before Allah in devotion.﴾

The address is to the whole community, and the verse is a command to be vigilant in establishing the prayers at their appointed times and with all their conditions.

(p-598) The Exalted mentioned "the middle prayer" a second time, although it had already entered the general sense of His saying "the prayers," because the purpose is to honour it and to urge those who pray to observe it. Abu Ja'far al-Ru'asi read "wa-l-salata l-wusta" in the accusative, as an exhortation (al-igra'). Al-Halwani also read it thus.

People differed over which prayer is meant by this description.

One group held that it is the Dawn (Subh) prayer, and that the word "wusta" (middle) is meant in the sense of sequence, since before it are two night prayers in which recitation is audible, and after it are two day prayers in which recitation is silent. This view was held by 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas. [It is reported that] 'Ali once led the people in the Dawn prayer and performed the qunut before the bowing; when he finished he said: "This is the middle prayer which Allah commanded us to stand in devotedly." Abu al-'Aliyah also said this and transmitted it from a group of Companions. Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, 'Ikrimah, Mujahid, 'Abd Allah ibn Shaddad ibn al-Hadi, al-Rabi' and Malik ibn Anas also said it. Malik strengthened this by the fact that the Dawn prayer is not joined to any other, whereas the two Friday-type prayers (?) are before it and after it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If they knew what is in the 'Atamah (Isha') and the Dawn, they would come to them even crawling," and he said: "They are the heaviest of the prayers upon the hypocrites." The Dawn is preferred because it is like standing in prayer for the night for one who attends it. (p-599) The 'Atamah is half the night. Allah said: "Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed" [al-Isra' 78]. All of this strengthens the position concerning the Dawn.

Another group said: it is the Noon (Zuhr) prayer. This was said by Zayd ibn Thabit, who attributed a hadith to the Prophet (ﷺ) for it; it was also said by Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar. Those who held this view argued that it was the first prayer performed in Islam, so it is "middle" in the sense of "most excellent" (fuddhā), not in the sense of sequence. Also, it is reported that it was the hardest prayer for the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), since it fell in the midday heat, when they were occupied with their wealth. Also, what Hafsah and 'A'ishah said when they dictated "Be watchful over the prayers and the middle prayer, and the 'Asr prayer" points to this, for this is the pairing of Zuhr and 'Asr.

Another group said: "the middle prayer" is the 'Asr prayer, because before it are two day prayers and after it are two night prayers. This view is also reported from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Hurayrah, Ibn 'Umar, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. In the codex of 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) the verse reads "wa-l-salati l-wusta," and "wa-hiya l-'asr" [i.e., "that is, the 'Asr"], and this is her transmitted saying. It was also said by al-Hasan al-Basri and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i. In Hafsah's dictation too: "wa-l-salati l-wusta [wa-hiya salat al-'asr]." As for the one who narrates "wa-salati l-'asr," he interprets it as coordinating one attribute with another, both referring to one thing, as when you say: "Zayd the generous and the wise came to me." (p-600) It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he read "Be watchful over the prayers and the middle prayer [salat al-'asr]" as an apposition (badal). Samurah ibn Jundub also transmitted this view from the Prophet (ﷺ). The hadith is widely transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said on the day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab): "They occupied us from the middle prayer, the 'Asr prayer; may Allah fill their houses and their graves with fire." And 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "We used to think it was the Dawn, until the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said on the day of the Confederates: 'They occupied us from the middle prayer, the 'Asr prayer,' so we knew that it is the 'Asr."

Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "We used to recite in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Be watchful over the prayers and the 'Asr prayer,' then Allah abrogated it and we recited: 'Be watchful over the prayers and the middle prayer.' A man said to him: 'So it is the 'Asr?' He said: 'I have told you how we recited it and how it was abrogated.'" And Allah knows best.

Abu Malik al-Ash'ari transmitted that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The middle prayer is the 'Asr prayer."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Most people hold this view, and there are other sayings on it. And Allah knows best.

Qubaysah ibn Dhu'ayb said: "The middle prayer" is the Maghrib prayer, because it is intermediate in the number of its units (raka'at): it is neither two nor four. Also, before it are two silent prayers and after it are two audible prayers.

Abu 'Umar Yusuf ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Barr, in his commentary on the chapter of Jami' al-Wuquf and others, related from a group that "the middle prayer" is the late night ('Isha' al-Akhirah) prayer, because it falls at the time of sleep, and it is the heaviest of the prayers upon the hypocrites, and it is recommended to delay it, which is difficult; hence the emphasis on being watchful over it. Also, before it are two prayers and after it are two prayers.

Another group said: "The middle prayer" is a prayer which Allah the Exalted did not specify for us; it is among the five without being fixed, like the Night of Power among the nights of the last ten nights. Allah did this so that watchfulness would fall upon all of them. This was said by Nafi' from Ibn 'Umar, and al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym also said it.

Another group said: "The middle prayer" is the Friday (Jumu'ah) prayer, for it is "middle" in excellence, because of what is specific to it of congregation and sermon, and because it was made a festival. This was mentioned by Ibn Habib and Makki.

Some scholars said: "The middle prayer" is the obligatory five prayers. His earlier saying "over the prayers" encompasses both the supererogatory and the obligatory, then He singled out the obligatory by mention. The saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "They occupied us from the middle prayer," fits with this interpretation.

As for the Exalted's saying "and stand before Allah in devotion (qanitin)," its meaning is: in your prayers. People differed over the meaning of "qanitin." Al-Sha'bi said: its meaning is "obedient." Jabir ibn Zayd, 'Ata' and Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said it. Al-Dahhak said: "Every qunut in the Qur'an means obedience," and Abu Sa'id said it from the Prophet (ﷺ). The people of every religion today stand before Allah as worshippers, so this community was told: "and stand before Allah obediently." Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Tawus said something similar. Al-Suddi said: the meaning of "qanitin" is "silent."

This verse was revealed concerning the prohibition of speech during prayer, which had been permitted in the early period of Islam. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: "We used to speak during prayer, return greetings, and a man would ask his companion about his need." He said: "One day I entered while the Prophet (ﷺ) was leading the people in prayer, and I greeted him, but no one returned my greeting, and that weighed heavily on me. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) finished, he said: 'What prevented me from returning your greeting was only that we were commanded to stand devoutly (qanitin), not to speak in prayer.'"

(p-602) Qunut means silence. This was said by Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "We used to speak in prayer until the verse 'and stand before Allah in devotion (qanitin)' was revealed, and we were commanded to be silent." Mujahid said: "Humble (khashi'in). Qunut is prolonging the bowing and humility, lowering the gaze, lowering the wing, bringing awe and reflection into being before Allah the Exalted." Al-Rabi' said: "Qunut is prolonging the standing and the bowing, and standing upright before Him." Others said: "Qunut is supplication," and "qanitin" means "supplicating." This meaning is reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) performed qunut for a month, supplicating against Ri'l and Dhakwan." Some said its meaning is "he supplicated," and others said its meaning is "he prolonged his standing." There is no proof in this hadith for the meaning of supplication.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 239:

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And if you fear, then [pray] on foot or riding. But when you are secure, remember Allah as He taught you that which you did not know.﴾

Allah, the Exalted, commanded standing before Him in prayer in a state of qunut, which is dignity, tranquility, and stillness of the limbs. This is the predominant state of security and calm. Then He mentioned the state of fear that occurs at times, and He granted His servants a concession in prayer: "rijalan" (on foot), moving about on their feet, and "rukbanan" (riding) on horses, camels, and the like, signalling with the head wherever one is facing. This is the statement of all the scholars, and this is the prayer of the lone individual (al-fadh) whom fear may distress for his own self during close combat, or from a predatory beast that pursues him, or an enemy that follows him, or a flood that carries him away.

In sum, every matter feared for one's soul permits what this verse includes.

(p-603) As for the prayer of fear led by the imam with the people divided into groups, its ruling is not in this verse. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, differentiated between fear of an enemy who fights and fear of a beast or the like, in that he recommended, in the case of other than fear of an enemy, repeating the prayer within its time if security was restored. Most of the jurists of the metropolitan cities hold that the matter is the same.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿fa-rijalan﴾ is the plural of rajil, or of rajul, from their saying: "rajala al-insan yarjulu rajulan," when a person lacks a mount and walks on his feet. So he is rajil, rajil and rajul (with a damma on the jim), which is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz; they say: "Fulan walked to the House of Allah barefoot, rajlan (on foot)," reported by al-Tabari and others; also rajlan, rujayl, and rajl. Ibn al-A'rabi recited for rajlan:

"Upon me, when I meet Layla in privacy, that I visit the House of Allah on foot, barefoot."

It is pluralized as rijal, rujayla, rajali, rujali, rajjala, rujjal, rujjali, rujlan, rajla, rijala (with a fatha on the jim), arjila, aràjil and arajil. The word rajul, which is a noun of genus, is also pluralized as rijal. So this verse and His saying: ﴿They will come to you on foot (rijalan)﴾ [al-Hajj: 27] both derive from the word rajila, meaning the absence of a mount. His saying: ﴿two witnesses from among your men (rijalikum)﴾ [al-Baqarah: 282] is the plural of the well-known generic noun. Al-Mahdawi reported from Ikrimah and Abu Mijlaz that they both recited: "fa-rujjalan," with a damma on the ra' and a shadda on the jim with a fatha.

Also from Ikrimah, he recited: "fa-rijalan," with a damma on the ra' and a light jim.

Al-Tabari reported from some of them that he recited: "fa-rujjalan" without an alif, on the pattern fu'all, with a damma on the fa' and a shadda on the 'ayn.

The majority of reciters read: "aw rukbanan." Budayl ibn Maysara recited "fa-rijalan fa-rukbanan" with a fa'.

(p-604) Rukban is the plural of rakib. Within this concession, there is consensus among the scholars that a person may face in any direction, from the heavens, and turn and move as his view dictates for the salvation of his soul.

People differed on how many rak'ahs are to be prayed. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, and a group of scholars hold that the number of rak'ahs may not be reduced at all; rather the traveller prays two rak'ahs without fail.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Qatadah and others said: one prays one rak'ah by signalling. Mujahid narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: Allah prescribed the prayer through the tongue of your Prophet as four in residence, two in travel, and one in fear. Al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said: one who fears death in close combat or otherwise prays one rak'ah; if he is unable, he says the takbir twice. Ishaq ibn Rahawayh said: if he is unable except for one takbir, it suffices for him; Ibn al-Mundhir recorded this.

Interpreters differed regarding His saying: ﴿But when you are secure, remember Allah﴾, the verse. One group said: the meaning is: when the fear that compelled you to this prayer has passed, remember Allah with thanks for this blessing, in His teaching you this prayer by which sufficiency has been achieved, and no prayer of the prayers has escaped you; and this is what they did not know. Another group said: the meaning is: when you were secure before, or after, as if He said: "whenever you are in security, remember Allah," that is, pray the prayer you already know, i.e., pray as He taught you, a complete prayer. This was reported by al-Naqqash and others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

His saying according to this interpretation: ﴿as He taught you that which you did not know﴾ is a substitution for "ma" in His saying "kama"; otherwise the wording of the verse would not be coherent. According to the first interpretation, "ma" is the object of "allamakum."

(p-605) Mujahid said: the meaning of His saying: ﴿But when you are secure﴾ is: when you leave the abode of travel for the abode of residence. Al-Tabari rejected this view, and that involves much vagueness in meaning. The kaf in His saying "kama" is for comparison, between a person's remembrance of Allah and Allah's blessing upon him, in that they are equal; remembrance was akin to the blessing in measure and matching it. And whoever interprets "udhkuru" as meaning "pray," in accordance with what we have mentioned, then the kaf is for comparison between the servant's prayer and the form that Allah taught him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 240:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿Those of you who die and leave wives behind, let them bequeath for their wives a provision for a year, without eviction. But if they leave, there is no blame upon you for what they do with themselves of what is reasonable. And Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

"Alladhina" (those who) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is in the clause which is ﴿wasiyyatan li-azwajihim﴾ (a bequest for their wives).

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and 'Asim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, read "wasiyyatun" with the nominative case. This is on two possible readings. The first: it is the subject, and the predicate is the adverbial phrase which is his saying "li-azwajihim" (for their wives). The beginning with an indefinite noun is permissible inasmuch as it is a place of specification, just as "salamun 'alayka" (peace be upon you) and "khayrun bayna yadayka" (good lies before you) and "amtun fi hajarin, la fika" (a slave-girl in a stone, not in you) are in the nominative. For these are places of supplication. The other reading is that you supply for it a predicate that you estimate: "a bequest for their wives is upon them," and his saying "li-azwajihim" is then a qualifier (sifah).

Al-Tabari said: Some of the grammarians said: the meaning is, "a bequest has been prescribed upon them," and he said: likewise it is in the reading of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud.

Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and Ibn 'Amir read "wasiyyatan" in the accusative case, and this is treated as governed by the verb, as if he had said: "let them make a bequest" (li-yusu wasiyyatan). "Li-azwajihim," on this reading, is also a qualifier. Harun said: In the codex of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it is "wasiyyatun li-azwajihim, mata'un" in the nominative, and in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud: "al-wasiyyatu li-azwajihim mata'an." Al-Khifaf related that in the codex of Ubayy it is "fa-mata'un li-azwajihim" in place of "wasiyyatin."

The meaning of this verse is that when a man dies, his wife may remain in his house for a year, and he shall spend upon her from his property, and that is a bequest for her.

The scholars differed concerning: from whom is this bequest? One group said: It was a bequest from Allah, the Exalted, which becomes obligatory after the husband's death. Qatadah said: When a woman's husband died, she was entitled to lodging and maintenance for a year from her husband's property, so long as she did not leave of her own accord. Then what is in this verse concerning maintenance was abrogated by the quarter or the eighth which is in Surat al-Nisa', and the lodging of the year was abrogated by the four months and ten days. This was also the view of al-Rabi', Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak, 'Ata', and Ibn Zayd. Another group said: Rather, this bequest is from the husband. They had been encouraged to bequeath this to their wives, so "yutawaffawna" (who die), on this view, means: they approach death and are dying, because the dead person does not make a bequest. Qatadah also said this, as did al-Suddi, and Abu 'Ali al-Farisi in al-Hujjah interpreted the verse this way. Al-Suddi said: "Except that the 'idda was four months and ten days, and men would bequeath lodging for a year and its maintenance, so long as she did not leave. If she left after the end of the 'idda—the four months and ten days—the bequest lapsed. Then Allah, the Exalted, abrogated that with the revelation of the obligatory shares, so she took her quarter or her eighth, and she had no lodging nor maintenance, and bequests became for one who does not inherit." Al-Tabari related from Mujahid: this verse is muhkam (not abrogated), with no abrogation in it, and the 'idda had been established as four months and ten days; then Allah made for them a bequest from Him of lodging for seven months and twenty nights, so if the woman wished she could stay within her bequest, and if she wished she could leave; and this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿without eviction. But if they leave, there is no blame upon you﴾.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The expressions of Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him, which al-Tabari related from him, do not necessarily imply that the verse is muhkam, and Mujahid did not state that; rather it is possible that he meant: then that was abrogated afterwards by inheritance.

"Mata'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). This matter, up to the year, in terms of the general sense, is a known landmark of time, and it has taken a share of length.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ghayra ikhraj﴾ means: it is not permitted for the heirs of the deceased and the inheritors of the house to evict her. "Ghayra" is in the accusative as a verbal noun according to al-Akhfash, as if he had said: "not eviction." It was also said: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of those making the bequest. And it was said: it is a qualifier of his saying "mata'an."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿fa-in kharajna﴾ and the verse—its meaning is that if the leaving is from the wife's side, then there is no blame upon anyone—guardian, judge, or other—for what they do with themselves, such as marriage, abandoning mourning, and adornment, provided that this is of what is reasonable and not denounced.
