His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah is Mighty﴾ is a attribute that entails the threat of retribution for whoever transgresses the limit in this matter, so that he evicts the woman while she does not want to leave. "Hakim" (Wise): that is, He perfects what He commands His servants.

All of this has had its ruling removed by the abrogation agreed upon, except what al-Tabari attributed to Mujahid, may Allah have mercy on him. And there is consideration to be given regarding al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 241–242:

His Mighty and Majestic saying:

﴿And for divorced women is provision in kindness, a duty upon the righteous.﴾ ﴿Thus does Allah make clear to you His verses that you may understand.﴾

The scholars differed concerning this verse.

Abu Thawr said: It is muhkam (decisive, not abrogated), and the provision (mut'ah) is due to every divorced woman, whether he had consummated the marriage with her or not, whether a bridal gift had been fixed for her or not, by this verse.

Al-Zuhri said: Every divorced woman has a provision, and so does the slave-woman whose husband divorces her.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: Every divorced woman has a provision.

Ibn al-Qasim said, in Irkha' al-Sutur from the Mudawwana: Allah the Exalted made the provision due to every divorced woman by this verse, then He made an exception in the other verse concerning the one for whom a bridal gift was fixed and who was not consummated with, so He excluded her from the provision. Zayd ibn Aslam claimed that it abrogated it (this verse).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

Ibn al-Qasim fled from the word "abrogation" to the word "exception," but exception is not appropriate in this context; rather it is pure abrogation (naskh mahd), as Zayd ibn Aslam said. And when Ibn al-Qasim maintains that His saying "and for divorced women" covers every divorced woman, he is necessarily committed to the view of abrogation, without any escape.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah and others said: This verse concerns the thayyibat (women previously married) who have been cohabited with, since the provision for those not yet consummated has already been mentioned in another verse. This is a view that the one for whom a bridal gift was fixed before touching was never included in this general sense; so His saying, "And if you divorce them before you have touched them" [al-Baqarah 2:237], specifies this category of women. And whenever it is said that the general wording covers her, that is abrogation, not specification.

Ibn Zayd said: This verse was revealed to affirm the matter of the provision, since it came before "a duty upon the righteous," so that became obligatory upon them.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This obligation is from al-Tabari's interpretation, not from the wording of Ibn Zayd.

As for His saying, "haqqan" (a duty), it is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar). As for "al-muttaqin" (the righteous) here, its apparent meaning is that it refers to those who are clothed in the taqwa (God-consciousness) of Allah the Exalted. The kaf in His saying "thus" (kadhalika) is for comparison, and "dhalika" (that) refers to this explanation and to the division that occurred regarding women, and to the imposition of the provision upon them; that is, just as His making clear this account makes clear the rest of His verses. And "la'allakum" (that you may) expresses hope concerning humankind, and whoever sees this clarifier, hopes to understand what is made clear to him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 243:

The words of the Exalted and Majestic:

﴿Have you not considered those who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death? Then Allah said to them, "Die," and then He gave them life. Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward the people, but most of the people do not give thanks.﴾

This is seeing of the heart (ru'yat al-qalb), meaning: "Have you not known?" According to Sibawayh, the statement is meant to draw attention to the matter of "those who." This seeing does not require two objects (maf'ulayn).

As al-Dahhak reported, the account of these people is that they were a group from the Children of Israel who were ordered to fight in jihad, but they feared death by being killed in the fighting. So they left their homes fleeing from that. Allah caused them to die so that He would make clear to them that nothing saves them from death. Then He gave them life and ordered them to fight in jihad by His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190], and so on.

A group of Jews related to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that a company of the Children of Israel was struck by a plague, so they left their homes fleeing from it. Allah caused them to die, and then the rest of the Children of Israel built a wall around them. When their bones had decayed, Allah sent the Prophet Hizqil, peace be upon him, who supplicated to Allah, and He gave them life for him.

(p-610) al-Suddi said: "They were a nation that existed before Wasit, in a village called Dhawardan, where the plague struck them, so they fled from it. They were thirty-some thousand, in a long narrative. Concerning them the verse was revealed." He also said that al-Hasan and 'Amr ibn Dinar said they fled from the plague. Al-Naqqash related that they fled from fever. Concerning them Mujahid related that when they were brought back to life, they returned to their people, and the mark of death was upon their faces. None of them wore a garment without it turning into a greasy shroud, until they died at their appointed times that had been decreed for them.

Ibn Jurayj related from Ibn 'Abbas that they were from the Children of Israel, that they numbered forty-eight thousand, that they were made to die and then were brought back to life, and that the stench remained upon that tribe (sibt) of the Children of Israel until this day. So Allah ordered them to fight in jihad a second time. This is His saying: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah﴾ [al-Baqarah: 190], and so on.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

All of these narratives are weak in their chains of transmission (layyin al-asanid). What is necessarily implied by the verse is that Allah, the Exalted, informed His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) through an expression of alerting and questioning about a people from mankind who left their homes fleeing from death. Then Allah caused them to die and then gave them life, so that they would be seen by those who came after them, and so that every such person would know that causing death is only in the hand of Allah and not in the hand of anyone else. Therefore there is no point in a fearful person's fear, nor in a deluded person's delusion. Allah, the Exalted, placed this verse as an introduction before His command to the believers of the community of Muhammad to fight in jihad. This is the view of al-Tabari, and it is the apparent sense of the verse's arrangement. The narrators of these stories have additional details in this account, which I have abridged because of their weakness.

People differed concerning the word "uluf" (thousands). The majority said it is the plural of alf (a thousand). Some said they were eighty thousand. Ibn 'Abbas said they were forty thousand, and it was said they were thirty thousand. All of this fits with "uluf," since it is the plural of a large number. Ibn 'Abbas also said they were eight thousand, and also said four thousand. This is weakened by the word "uluf," because it is the plural of a large number. Ibn Zayd said concerning the word "uluf": its meaning is only "those who are in agreement (mu'talifun)," so this group departed, fleeing from death and seeking life, and Allah caused them to die at the place where they believed they would be saved.

(p-611) And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then Allah said to them, "Die,"﴾ and so on, is only an intensification of expression about His act toward them, as if what befell them was the act of one to whom it was said: "Die," and he died.

It is related that two angels shouted at them: "Die," and they died. So the meaning is that Allah said to them through the mediation of the two angels. This death is the apparent sense of the verse. As for what is related in its narratives, that it was a real death in which the souls departed from the bodies, then if that is so, it was not the death of their appointed terms. Rather, Allah made it, for these people, like an illness or an accident of the kind that befalls human beings.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward the people﴾ and so on, is an alert to Allah's bounty toward those people, whom He favored with blessings and ordered to fight in jihad, and ordered not to attribute power and strength except to Him, just as He ordered all the world to do. But they did not give thanks for His blessing in all of this. Rather, they acted presumptuously and thought that their own power and effort would save them. This verse is a warning to the rest of mankind against the like of this action. That is, people must give thanks for Allah's bounty in bringing them into existence, providing for them, and guiding them through commands and prohibitions. Thus it is incumbent upon them to hasten to comply with those commands, not to seek to escape them. His specifying "most" of the people indicates that the grateful are the minority.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 244–245:**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿And fight in the way of Allah, and know that Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾ ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan, so He will multiply it for him many times over? And Allah withholds and extends [provision], and to Him you will be returned.﴾

The *waw* (و) in this verse is conjunctive, joining a new statement to what preceded it. This is the view of the *jumhur* (the majority of scholars). According to it, this verse addresses the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) with the command to fight in the way of Allah, and the intention in it is that the Word of Allah be the highest, in line with the hadith. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak said: the command to fight is addressed to those among the Children of Israel who were brought back to life. On this view, the *waw* is conjunctive to the earlier command, and the meaning is: "and He said to them, 'Fight.'" Al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: there is no basis for the view that the command to fight was addressed to those who were brought back to life. "Hearing" means hearing the statements, and "Knowing" means knowing the intentions.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah...﴾, and the one who fights in the way of Allah is included in this, for he lends hoping for reward, as 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, did at the army of hardship (*jaysh al-'usra*).

It is related that when this verse was revealed, Abu al-Dahdah said: "O Messenger of Allah, does Allah want a loan from us?" He said: "Yes, O Abu al-Dahdah." He said: "Then I have lent my orchard to Allah." It was an orchard containing six hundred date palms. Then he came to the orchard, in which was Umm al-Dahdah, and said: "Come out, for I have lent my orchard to my Lord." The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "How many a dense cluster of dates [hanging] for Abu al-Dahdah in Paradise!"

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is also said Ibn al-Dahdah. The asking for a loan in this verse is only for the sake of making people comfortable and drawing them near with what they understand. Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy, but He, the Exalted, likened the giving of a believer in this world, in hope of its reward in the Hereafter, to a loan, just as He likened the giving of souls and wealth for the sake of entering Paradise to buying and selling. The Jews, in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), went to confuse the believers by the outward meaning of "borrowing," and they said: "Your God is in need and borrows." This is manifestly corrupt.

(p-613) His saying "*ḥasanan*" (goodly) means that the intention in it is made pure. It may also be an allusion to its abundance and excellence.

The readers differed concerning the doubling and non-doubling of the ʿayn, and the raising and putting in the accusative (*nasb*) of the fāʾ, and the omission and inclusion of the alif, in His saying: "*fayuḍāʿifahu*" (so He will multiply it). Ibn Kathir read "*fayuḍaʿʿifuhu*" with a *ḍamma* (raised) on the fāʾ, without an alif, and with a doubled ʿayn throughout the Qur'an. Ibn ʿAmir read likewise, except that he put the fāʾ in the accusative throughout the Qur'an. ʿĀṣim agreed with him on the accusative of the fāʾ, except that he included the alif in "*fayuḍāʿifuhu*" throughout the Qur'an. Abu ʿAmr did not omit the alif in all of this, except His saying: ﴿yuḍāʿaf lahā al-ʿadhāb﴾ (the punishment will be doubled for her) [al-Ahzab: 30] in Surat al-Ahzab, which he read without an alif. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Nafi' read all of it with the alif and the raising of the fāʾ.

The raised fāʾ can be explained in two ways. The first is that it is conjunctive to what is in the relative clause (*ṣila*), which is "*yuqriḍu*" (lends). The second is that the verb is resumed and cut off as a new clause. Abu ʿAli said: the raising in this verb is better, because the accusative is only with the fāʾ in answer to an interrogative (*istifhām*), and that occurs when the interrogation is about the first verb itself and the second then comes differing from it. You say: "Will you lend me so that I thank you?" Here, however, the interrogation is about the one who lends, not about the lending itself. But the reading of Ibn ʿAmir and ʿĀṣim in the accusative is borne out by meaning, for he only asked about the doer of the lending for the sake of the lending. It is as if the statement were: "Will anyone lend Allah so that He multiplies it for him?"

A parallel to this, in bearing [a reading] upon meaning, is the reading of one who read: "*man yuḍlili Allāhu fa-lā hādiya lahu, wa-yadharuhum*" with a jussive "*wa-yadharuhum*" (and He leaves them), since the meaning of His saying ﴿fa-lā hādiya lahu﴾ (there is no guide for him) [al-A'raf: 186] is "so He does not guide him." These many multiplications are up to the seven hundred that have been related, and it is given as the likeness of an ear of grain.

(p-614) Ibn Kathir read "*yabsuṭu*" (extends) with the sīn, and Nafi', according to the well-known report from him, with the ṣād. Al-Hulwani related from Qalun, from Nafi', that he did not mind how he read "*basṭatan wa-yabsuṭu*," whether with the sīn or with the ṣād.

Abu Qurra related from Nafi' "*yabsuṭu*" with the sīn. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked by him to fix prices because of a rise in prices that was feared for Madina, and he said: "Indeed Allah is the Extender, the Withholder, and I truly hope to meet Allah while no one holds me accountable for an injustice in person or in property."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 246:

The words of the Most High:

﴿Have you not considered the chiefs of the Children of Israel after Moses, when they said to a prophet of theirs: "Appoint for us a king, that we may fight in the way of Allah." He said: "Would you perhaps, if fighting were prescribed for you, not fight?"﴾

This verse is a report about a people of the Children of Israel who were struck by humiliation and the overpowering of an enemy. They asked for permission to fight in jihad and to be commanded to it. When they were commanded, most of them shrank back, and a few remained steadfast, so Allah granted them victory. In all of this there is an example for the believers, so that they may avoid what is disliked and emulate what is good.

The word "al-mala'" (the chiefs, or the assembly) in this verse refers to the whole people, because the meaning requires it, and this is the original sense of the term. The nobles are called "al-mala'" by way of metaphor.

His words "after Moses" mean: after his death and the end of his term. The commentators differed regarding the prophet to whom it was said "appoint" (ub'ath). Ibn Ishaq and others, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, said: he is Shamwil ibn Bali. As-Suddi said: he is Shim'un. Qatadah said: he is Yusha' ibn Nun.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is a weak opinion, because the period of Dawud comes after the period of Moses by many generations of people, and Yusha' was the young servant (fatan) of Moses. The Children of Israel used to prevail over whoever fought against them. It is related that they would place the Ark, which contained the tranquility (sakinah) and the remnant (baqiyyah), in the thick of battle, and they would not cease to prevail until they disobeyed; the young ones among them appeared, their kings opposed the prophets, and they followed their desires. Allah, exalted is He, had established their affairs by having their prophets guide their kings. When they did what we have mentioned, Allah set over them nations of disbelievers who overcame them, and in some of the battles they seized the Ark from them, so their affairs became abased. As-Suddi said: the one who overpowered them was Jalut (Goliath), and he was of the 'Amaliqah (Amalekites). When they saw that it meant total destruction and the vanishing of their remembrance, some of them were indignant, and they spoke about their situation, until their chiefs agreed to say to the prophet of the time: ﴿Appoint for us a king﴾, the verse. They only sought a king who would take charge of the matter of fighting. The kingship was in a tribe of the tribes of the Children of Israel called the Banu Yahudha (Judah), so the prophet knew by revelation that there was no one in the house of kingship who could take charge of the matter of war, and Allah facilitated Talut (Saul) for that purpose.

The majority of reciters read "nuqatil" with the nun and the lam jussed (jazm) as an answer to the imperative. Ad-Dahhak and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "yuqatil" with the ya' and the verb in the raf' (nominative), so it occupies the position of a description of the king.

The aforementioned prophet, upon him be peace, wished to secure a commitment from them, so he put them to the question in the form of an affirmation and tested what they had by his saying: ﴿Would you perhaps﴾ (hal 'asaytum). Nafi' read "'asaytum" with a kasrah on the 'ayn in both places, while the others pronounced the sin with a fatha. Abu 'Ali said: the fatha of the sin is more common and well known. The basis for the kasrah is the saying of the Arabs: "huwa 'assun bi-dhalika" (he is inclined to that), like "hurr" and "shajj," and the pattern fa'ala and fa'ila has come in words like naqama and naqima; so likewise 'asaytu and 'asitu. If the verb is attached to an explicit noun, the analogy for 'asaytum would be that one says "'asiya Zayd," like "radiya." If it is said, it is analogical; and if it is not said, it is permissible to take both dialects, so that one of them is used in the place of the other, as was done in other cases. The meaning of this statement is: "Are you close to turning away and fleeing if fighting is prescribed for you?"

**

The words of the Most High:

﴿They said: "What is the matter with us that we should not fight in the way of Allah, while we have been driven out of our homes and our children?" Yet when fighting was prescribed for them, they turned away, except for a few of them. And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾

The meaning: What is it that prevents us from not fighting, when we have been wronged and driven out of our homes? They said this statement, even though the speaker had not himself been driven out from the place from which one like him had been driven out, and he is in the same position. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about them that when fighting was enjoined upon them, and they saw the reality and their thoughts returned to direct engagement in war, they turned away, that is, their intentions became unsettled and their resolves weakened. This is the condition of nations given to luxury, inclined to ease, who wish for war in times of pride, but when war arrives they shrink back and yield to their nature.

On this meaning the Prophet ﷺ said: «Do not wish to meet the enemy, and ask Allah for well-being; but when you meet them, stand firm.»

Then Allah, exalted is He, informed about a few of them that they remained upon the first intention, and their resolve persisted in fighting in the way of Allah. Then He threatened the wrongdoers in the form of a report, which is His saying: ﴿And Allah is Knowing of the wrongdoers.﴾ Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "tawallaw illa an yakuna qalilun minhum" (they turned away, except that there should be a few of them).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 247:

(p-٥) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And their Prophet said to them, "Indeed, Allah has sent to you Ṭālūt (Saul) as a king." They said, "How can he have kingship over us while we are more deserving of kingship than him, and he has not been given a large amount of wealth?" He said, "Indeed, Allah has chosen him over you and increased him broadly in knowledge and physique."﴾

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When the chiefs of the Children of Israel said to Shamwīl (Samuel) ibn Bālī what they said, he asked Allah, exalted is He, to send them a king and to guide him to him. Allah, exalted is He, said to him: "Look at the horn that has the oil in your house. When a man enters upon you and bubbles the oil that is in the horn, then he is the king of the Children of Israel. Anoint his head with it and make him king over them."

He said: Ṭālūt was a tanner, and he was from the tribe of Binyāmīn ibn Ya'qūb, and his tribe had neither prophethood nor kingship in it. Ṭālūt went out in search of an animal of his that he had lost, so he headed to Shamwīl, hoping that he would supplicate for him regarding the matter of the animal, or find relief with him, and he bubbled the oil.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is the oil of holiness (dhuhn al-quds), as they claim. He said: So Shamwīl stood up to him, took it, and anointed Ṭālūt's head with it, and said to him: "You are the king of the Children of Israel whom Allah commanded me to appoint." Then he said to the Children of Israel: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent to you Ṭālūt as a king﴾. And "Ṭālūt" is a non-Arabic proper noun that has been Arabicized, and for this reason it is not declined.

As-Suddī said: Allah sent to Shamʿūn a staff and said to him: "Whoever of the Children of Israel enters upon you and is the height of this staff, he is their king." So the Children of Israel were measured by it, and they kept being taller than it, until Ṭālūt passed by them in search of his donkey on which he used to carry water, and he was a water-carrier. They called him and measured him with the staff, and he was its equal. So their Prophet said to them what he said.

(p-٦) Then the Children of Israel became stubborn and deviated from the command of Allah, exalted is He, and acted according to their customs, and they said: ﴿How can he have kingship over us while we are more deserving of kingship than him?﴾ That is, because he is not from the house of kings, and no precedence in it had preceded for him, and he was not given abundant wealth by which he could gather the hearts of men until he overcomes the people of pride with his wealth.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The people abandoned the strongest cause, which is the decree of Allah and His prior judgment, and that He is the Owner of sovereignty. So their Prophet, peace be upon him, argued against them with a decisive proof, and he explained to them, along with that, the reason for Ṭālūt's selection: that he has an abundance of knowledge, which is the foundation of a person, and of physique, which is his aid in war and his equipment at the encounter.

Ibn 'Abbās said:

Among the Children of Israel there were two tribes: one for prophethood and the other for kingship. A prophet is not sent except from the one, and a king is not appointed except from the other. So when Ṭālūt was sent from neither of them, they made their statement.

Mujāhid said: The meaning of "kingship" in this verse is command over the army, but they were troubled because it is the custom of whoever takes charge of war and prevails to continue as king.

"Iṣṭafā" (chose): it is of the form ifta'ala, derived from ṣafwa (choice). Nāfi' read "baṣṭatan" with ṣād. Abū 'Amr and Ibn Kathīr read "basṭatan" with sīn. The majority hold that "knowledge" in this verse is meant in general, covering all kinds of knowledge. Some of the commentators said: what is meant is knowledge of war. As for his physique, Wahb ibn Munabbih said: the tallest man among the Children of Israel would reach the shoulder of Ṭālūt.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 248:

(p-٧) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿And Allah gives His kingdom to whom He wills, and Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247] ﴿And their prophet said to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingship is that the chest (al-tabut) will come to you."﴾

When their prophet, peace be upon him, knew their obstinacy and their disputing over proofs, he concluded his speech with the certain matter to which there is no objection, which is his saying: ﴿And Allah gives His kingdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247].

The apparent meaning of the wording is that it is from the Prophet's saying to them, though some interpreters (mu'awwilun) have held that it is from the saying of Allah Most High to Muhammad ﷺ, and the first is more apparent. The kingship of the world is attributed to Allah Most High in the manner of the attribution of a possessed thing to its owner. And "All-Encompassing" (wasi') means: His power and His knowledge have encompassed everything.

As for the Prophet's saying to them, "Indeed, the sign of his kingship," al-Tabari held that the Children of Israel were obstinate and said to their prophet: "And what is the sign of the kingship of Talut?" This was by way of asking for evidence of the truth of his statement: ﴿Indeed, Allah has sent﴾ [al-Baqarah: 247].

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is possible that their prophet said this to them by way of exhortation and drawing attention to this blessing which Allah joined with the kingship of Talut, and made it a sign for him, without the Children of Israel being given to denying their prophet. This, in my view, is more apparent than the wording of the verse. And al-Tabari's interpretation is more fitting to the blameworthy character of the Children of Israel, for they are a people of denial, obstinacy and crookedness. Al-Tabari has related its meaning from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi.

The exegetes differed concerning the manner of the coming of the chest and how its beginning was.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The chest was with the Children of Israel, by which they overcame whoever fought them, until (p-٨) they disobeyed and were overcome, and the chest came to be with the people who had overcome them. They placed it in a church of theirs in which there were idols, and the idols would become overturned in the morning. So they moved it to the village of a people, and those people were afflicted with pains in their necks.

It was said: It was placed in the latrine of a people, and they were afflicted with fistula (nasur). When their affliction grew severe, however it was, they said: "This is nothing but because of this chest; let us return it to the land of the Children of Israel." They took a cart, placed the chest upon it, and tied it to two cows, and they sent them loose in the land toward the land of the Children of Israel. Allah sent angels driving the two cows until they entered with it upon the Children of Israel while they were in the matter of Talut, and they became certain of victory. This is the carrying of the angels of the chest in this narration.

Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: Rather, this chest was of what Musa had left with Yusha' ibn Nun, and Yusha' placed it in the wilderness, and ages passed over it until the time of Talut came. The matter of the chest was well known among them as part of the legacy of Musa, so Allah made its coming a sign of the kingship of Talut, and Allah sent angels who carried it to the Children of Israel. It is related that they saw the chest coming in the air until it descended among them, and it is related that the angels came bearing it until they placed it in the house of Talut; then the Children of Israel gathered in allegiance to Talut.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: The size of the chest was about three cubits by two cubits. Zayd ibn Thabit read "al-tabuh," and it is his dialect, while the people read it with a ta' (tabut).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The narrators have multiplied in the stories of the chest and the manner of its carrying with what I have not seen any ground for establishing, because of the weakness of its chain.

**

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿In it is tranquility from your Lord and a remnant of what the family of Musa and the family of Harun left behind, carried by the angels. Indeed in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.﴾

(p-٩) Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Al-sakinah is a gentle wind (rih haffafah) which has a face like the face of a human. It is also related from him that he said: It is a wind that is hollow (rih khajuj), and it has two heads. Mujahid said: Al-sakinah has a head like the head of a cat, and two wings and a tail. He said: al-Sakinah and al-Sarad and Jibril came with Ibrahim from al-Sham. Wahb ibn Munabbih said, from some scholars of the Children of Israel: Al-sakinah is the head of a dead cat, which, whenever it cried out in the chest with the cry of a cat, they became certain of victory. Ibn 'Abbas said: Al-sakinah is a basin of gold from Paradise, in which the hearts of the prophets were washed; al-Suddi also said so. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Al-sakinah is a spirit from Allah which speaks; whenever they disputed about a matter, it informed them with a clarification of what they wanted.

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: Al-sakinah is what they recognized of the signs, so they were at rest thereby. Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: ﴿tranquility from your Lord﴾ means mercy from your Lord. Qatadah said: ﴿tranquility from your Lord﴾ means dignity for you from your Lord.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The correct view is that the chest contained excellent things from the remnants of the prophets and their relics, so souls would find rest in that, be comforted by it, and be strengthened. The customary way is that Allah gives victory to truth and to matters that are excellent in His sight. And al-sakinah according to this is a form (fa'ilah) derived from al-sukun (stillness), as one says: "he resolved a resolution" (azama 'azimah) and "he cut a cutting" (qata'a qati'ah).

The exegetes differed concerning al-baqiyyah, what is it? Ibn 'Abbas said: It is the staff of Musa and the fragments of (p-١٠) the tablets. Al-Rabi' said: It is the staff of Musa and matters from the Torah. 'Ikrimah said: It is the Torah, the staff, and the fragments of the tablets.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of this is what is related: that when Musa came to his people with the tablets and found them having worshipped the calf, he threw the tablets in anger and they broke; he took from them what remained intact and gathered the fragments of what had broken and placed it in the chest. Abu Salih said: The baqiyyah is the staff of Musa and the staff of Harun, two tablets of the Torah, and the manna. 'Atiyyah ibn Sa'd said: It is the staff of Musa, the staff of Harun, their garments, and the fragments of the tablets.

al-Thawri said: Among the people is one who says: the baqiyyah is a qafiz of manna and fragments of the tablets, and among them is one who says: the staff and the two sandals. al-Dahhak said: The baqiyyah is jihad and fighting the enemies.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

That is, the command concerning that is in the chest: either it is written in it, or the very bringing of it is like a command concerning that. The leaving behind is attributed to the family of Musa and Harun because the command was transmitted from one people to another, and all of them are family of Musa and Harun. The "family" (al) of a man are his kinsmen and followers. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd said: The carrying of the angels is their driving the chest without anything else carrying it, until they placed it before the Children of Israel while they looked at it between heaven and earth. Wahb ibn Munabbih and al-Thawri said, from some of their shaykhs: their carrying of it is their driving the two bulls or the two cows which pulled the cart. Then Allah Most High established that the coming of the chest is a sign for them if they are among those who believe and see with the eye of truth.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 2, verse 249**

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿When Talut set out with the troops, he said: "Allah is going to test you with a river. Whoever drinks from it is not of me, and whoever does not taste it is of me, except one who scoops a handful with his hand." But they drank from it, except a few of them.﴾

Before this verse, some wording has been omitted, and the meaning of what is mentioned indicates it. It is: "The Children of Israel agreed on Talut as king, submitted to him, and prepared for war against their enemy." "Fasala" (set out) means: he went out with them from the land, and fasala (separated) the state of travel from the state of residence. As-Suddi and others said: they were eighty thousand.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Without doubt there were among them the believer, the hypocrite, the diligent, and the lazy. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: No one stayed behind except one with an excuse, whether from youth, old age, or illness.

The exegetes differed concerning the river. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: When Talut set out, they said to him: "The water will not carry us, so pray to Allah that He makes a river flow for us." So Talut said to them: ﴿Allah is going to test you﴾, the verse. Qatada said: The river by which Allah tested them is a river between the Jordan and Palestine. Ibn 'Abbas said the same, and he and as-Suddi also said: the river is the river of Palestine. The majority of reciters read "bi-nahar" (with a river) with a fatha on the ha'. Mujahid, Humayd al-A'raj, Abu as-Sammal, and others read "bi-nahr" with sukun on the ha' throughout the Qur'an.

The meaning of this testing is that it is a trial for them. Whoever's obedience appears in abstaining from the water is known to obey in other matters. Whoever overcame his desire for the water and disobeyed the command is more likely to disobey in hardships. It is narrated that they came to the river while thirst had afflicted them, and it was in the utmost sweetness and beauty. For this reason, the obedient were permitted a handful, so that the harm of thirst would be lifted from them to some degree, and so that they would break the soul's contention in this state by scooping with the hands, for its cleanliness and ease. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The palms are the cleanest vessels." From this is the saying of al-Hasan, may Allah have mercy on him:

*They do not approach water with vessels*
*except by scooping from the pools with the palm.*

And the apparent sense of Talut's words, ﴿Allah is going to test you with a river﴾, is that this was by revelation to the Prophet, and an announcement from the Prophet to Talut. It is possible that this was something Allah inspired in Talut, so he tested his troops with it, and the inspiration was made a trial from Allah for them. This is a course that every commander in war must take, for he fights only with obedient troops. From this is the saying of Mu'awiya: "'Ali is over the most corrupt and disobedient troops, while I am over the soundest and most obedient troops." From this is also the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "You have corrupted my opinion through disobedience."

It is clear that the handful suffices to ward off the harm of thirst for the resolute who are patient with the hardship of life, whose aspirations lie not in luxury, as 'Urwa said:

*................*
*And I sip the pure water, though the water is cold.*

So it seems that Talut wanted to test the people.

Some have held that 'Abdullah ibn Hudhafa as-Sahmi only ordered his companions to light a fire and enter it as a test of their obedience, but his joking led him to make the matter frightening, the task he had assigned them.

His words ﴿is not of me﴾ mean: is not among my companions in this war. He did not thereby take them out of faith. A similar saying is that of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever cheats us is not of us, whoever shoots at us with arrows is not of us, and not of us is the one who tears his garment and slaps his cheeks."

As for His words ﴿and whoever does not taste it﴾, it is a *sadd al-dhara'i* (blocking of the means to a prohibited act), because the least tasting enters into the meaning of "taste" (ta'm). When the prohibition on tasting is stated, there is no way for drinking to occur from one who avoids tasting. For the sake of these emphases, the speech did not come as "and whoever does not drink from it."

Abu 'Amr, Nafi', and Ibn Kathir read "ghurfatan" with a fatha on the ghayn. This is the verb transitive to the verbal noun, with an omitted object, meaning: except one who scoops the water of a handful. The rest read "ghurfatan" with a damma on the ghayn, which is the verb transitive to the direct object, because *ghurfa* (handful) is the scooped amount itself; this is equivalent to: except one who scoops water. Abu 'Ali preferred the damma on the ghayn, and at-Tabari also preferred it, on the ground that "ghurfa" with a fatha is a verbal noun not in the sense of scooping.

Then Allah, exalted, informed us that most of them drank and opposed what was intended. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, and others that the people drank according to the measure of their certainty. The disbelievers drank like thirsty camels, the disobedient drank less than that, and seventy-six thousand of the people withdrew. Some of the believers did not drink anything, and some took the handful. As for the one who drank, he was not quenched but thirst afflicted him severely. As for the one who left the water, his state was good, and he was stronger than the one who took the handful.

**

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿When he and those who believed with him crossed it, they said: "We have no strength today against Jalut and his troops." Those who were certain that they would meet Allah said: "How many a small company has overcome a large company by Allah's permission! And Allah is with the patient."﴾

*Jawaza* is *fa'ala* from *jaza*, yacuzu, and it is a *mufa'ala* (reciprocal form) from two parties in every place, because the river and what resembles it is as if it were crossing.

People differed about how many were with him who believed. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "We used to say that the number of the people of Badr was the same as the number of Talut's companions who crossed the river with him: three hundred and some ten men." In another narration: "and thirteen men," and none crossed with him except a believer.

Qatada said: It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions on the day of Badr: "You are the same in number as the companions of Talut." As-Suddi and Ibn 'Abbas said: "Rather, four thousand men crossed with him." Ibn 'Abbas said: "Among them were those who drank." Both said: When they looked at Jalut and his troops, they said: "We have no strength today." Of them, three thousand, six hundred, and some eighty returned. This is the text of as-Suddi's view, and the meaning of Ibn 'Abbas's view.

According to the first view, the ignorant ones said: "We have no strength today," out of regarding the enemy as too numerous. Those of firmness, resolve, and readiness for death among them said: ﴿How many a small company﴾, the verse. The meaning of "meeting Allah" on this view may well be a true *zann* (supposition) in its literal sense, i.e., they supposed that they would be martyred on that day because of their determination to fight truthfully, as happened to 'Abdullah ibn Haram at Uhud and to others.

According to the second view, many of the four thousand said: "We have no strength," out of cowardice and fear of death. They turned away from Talut. The believers, certain of the resurrection and of returning to Allah, who were the number of the people of Badr, said: ﴿How many a company﴾. The *zann* (supposition) on this view means certainty, and it concerns what has not yet occurred and has not come into the realm of the senses.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, that among the four thousand were those who drank, is refuted by His words: ﴿he and those who believed with him﴾.

Most exegetes hold that only those who took a handful crossed the river, and those who did not drink at all. Then their insights differed: some faltered, and a few stood firm.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b read: "ka'ayyin min fi'ah" (how many a company). *Fi'a* (company) is the group to which one returns in hardships, from their saying *fa'a yafi'u* when he returned. A single man may be called a *fi'a* by way of metaphor, and a king is the *fi'a* of the people, and a mountain is a *fi'a*, and a fortress is a *fi'a*; all of this is metaphor.

In their words, may Allah be pleased with them: "How many a company," the verse, there is encouragement through example, exhortation, and the rousing of patience, and imitation of one who was true to his Lord. Allah's *idhn* (permission) here means His enabling and His knowledge; all of that together is the *idhn*. ﴿And Allah is with the patient﴾, by His help and support.

**Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-Baqarah, verses 250–251:**

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿When they confronted Jalut and his troops, they said: "Our Lord, pour upon us patience, make our feet firm, and help us against the disbelieving people." So they routed them by the permission of Allah, and Dawud killed Jalut. Allah gave him the kingdom and the wisdom, and taught him what He willed.﴾

*Baarazu* means they went out into the *bараz* (open, clear ground), which is the wide, spacious part of the earth. *Jalut* is a non-Arabic name that has been Arabicized (*mu'arrab*). *Al-Ifraagh* (pouring) is the greatest form of pouring, as if it implies the all-encompassing nature of that which is poured upon. *Al-Hazm* (routing) originally means that something is struck so that one part enters into another; likewise an army that is driven back "rides" its own rear. Then the word was used with the meaning of defeating: *hazama*. Jalut was the commander and king of the Amalekites, and it is reported that he had three hundred thousand horsemen.

It is narrated concerning the story of Dawud and his killing of Jalut that among the companions of Talut were the brothers of Dawud, who were the sons of Ayshi. Dawud was a young boy who tended his father's sheep. When the war came, he said to himself: "I will certainly go to see this war." When he set out, he passed a stone on his way, and it called to him: "O Dawud, take me, for with me you will kill Jalut." Then another stone called to him, then another, then another. He took them and placed them in his shepherd's bag (*mikhlah*). He went on, and when the people had gathered, Jalut came out seeking a single combatant. The people shrank back from him until Talut said:

"Whoever will come out against him and kill him, I will marry him to my daughter and make him my steward over my wealth." Dawud came forward and said: "I will go out against him and kill him." Talut said to him: "Mount my horse and take my weapons." He did so and went out in the finest armor. When he had walked a little, he turned back. The people said: "The youth has become a coward." Dawud said: "If Allah has not decreed that he be killed by me and has not helped me against him, this horse will not benefit me, nor will this weapon. Rather, I want to fight him in my own way." He was among the best of people at using the sling (*miqla'*). So he dismounted, took his bag and hung it on himself, took his sling, and went out toward Jalut, who was armed. Jalut said to him: "Are you, O youth, coming out to me?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Like this, as one goes out to a dog?" He said: "Yes, and you are more contemptible." Jalut said: "Today I will feed your flesh to the birds and the beasts." Then they drew close. Dawud whirled his sling and put his hand into the stones, and it is narrated that they joined together and became one stone. He took it, placed it in the sling, invoked the name of Allah, whirled it, and threw it. It struck Jalut's head and killed him. He cut off his head, placed it in his bag, and the people were thrown into confusion. Talut's companions charged, and the enemy was routed.

Then Dawud came to Talut seeking the condition he had been promised. Talut said to him: "The daughters of kings have exceptional dowries, and you must kill two hundred of these Jarajima who harm the people and bring me their foreskins." Talut hoped to expose Dawud to death through this endeavor. Dawud killed two hundred of them, brought them back, and requested his wife, and Talut gave her to him. Dawud's position became great. It is related that Talut relinquished the kingship to him and Dawud became the king. It is also related that the Children of Israel overcame Talut in this matter because Dawud had killed Jalut, and that this was the cause of the victory. It is further narrated that Talut feared Dawud so much that he fled from him, and remained on a mountain until Talut died. Then the Children of Israel went to Dawud and made him their ruler.

It is also narrated that the Prophet of Allah, Shamwil (Samuel), was inspired by Allah to go to Ayshi and ask him to present his sons to him, so that the one indicated would be anointed with the holy oil (*duhn al-qudus*) and made king over the Children of Israel. And Allah knows best which of these accounts is correct. However, it is certain from the wording of the verse that Dawud became king of the Children of Israel.

It has also been narrated at the beginning of this story that Dawud was walking in the kitchen (*mutbakhah*) of Talut, and then a stone spoke to him, and he took it, and this was the cause of his killing Jalut and of his kingdom. People have greatly multiplied the narratives concerning the story of this verse, but all of them are weak in their chains of transmission (*layyin al-asaneed*). For this reason I have selected from them only what the verse depends upon and what reveals the stages of the event, and I have abridged the rest.

As for the wisdom that Allah gave him, it is prophethood and the Psalms (*Zabur*). Al-Suddi said: Allah gave him the kingdom of Talut and the prophethood of Shim'un. As for what He taught him, it is the craft of making coats of mail, the speech of birds, and other kinds of knowledge that He gave him (ﷺ).

Dawud whirled his sling and put his hand into the stones, and it is narrated that they joined together and became one stone. He took it, placed it in the sling, invoked the name of Allah, whirled it, and threw it. It struck Jalut's head and killed him. He cut off his head, placed it in his bag, and the people were thrown into confusion. Talut's companions charged, and the enemy was routed.

Then Dawud came to Talut seeking the condition he had been promised. Talut said to him: "The daughters of kings have exceptional dowries, and you must kill two hundred of these Jarajima who harm the people and bring me their foreskins." Talut hoped to expose Dawud to death through this endeavor. Dawud killed two hundred of them, brought them back, and requested his wife, and Talut gave her to him. Dawud's position became great. It is related that Talut relinquished the kingship to him and Dawud became the king. It is also related that the Children of Israel overcame Talut in this matter because Dawud had killed Jalut, and that this was the cause of the victory. It is further narrated that Talut feared Dawud so much that he fled from him, and remained on a mountain until Talut died. Then the Children of Israel went to Dawud and made him their ruler.

It is also narrated that the Prophet of Allah, Shamwil (Samuel), was inspired by Allah to go to Ayshi and ask him to present his sons to him, so that the one indicated would be anointed with the holy oil (*duhn al-qudus*) and made king over the Children of Israel. And Allah knows best which of these accounts is correct. However, it is certain from the wording of the verse that Dawud became king of the Children of Israel.

It has also been narrated at the beginning of this story that Dawud was walking in the kitchen (*mutbakhah*) of Talut, and then a stone spoke to him, and he took it, and this was the cause of his killing Jalut and of his kingdom. People have greatly multiplied the narratives concerning the story of this verse, but all of them are weak in their chains of transmission (*layyin al-asaneed*). For this reason I have selected from them only what the verse depends upon and what reveals the stages of the event, and I have abridged the rest.

As for the wisdom that Allah gave him, it is prophethood and the Psalms (*Zabur*). Al-Suddi said: Allah gave him the kingdom of Talut and the prophethood of Shim'un. As for what He taught him, it is the craft of making coats of mail, the speech of birds, and other kinds of knowledge that He gave him (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 252:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic says:

﴿And were it not for Allah's repelling some people by means of others, the earth would surely be corrupted; but Allah is full of bounty to the worlds.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 251] ﴿These are the verses of Allah; We recite them to you in truth, and indeed you are among the messengers.﴾

In this verse Allah informs us that were it not for His repelling, through the believers, the disbelievers' breasts over the course of time, the earth would be corrupted, because disbelief would have overspread it and spread throughout all its regions. But Allah, exalted is He, does not leave time devoid of one who stands upright in truth, one who calls to Allah, and one who fights for Him, until He placed that in the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) until the Hour is established. To Him belongs much praise.

Makki said: Most of the exegetes hold that the meaning is: were it not that Allah repels, through those who pray, from those who do not pray, and through those who are God-fearing, from those who are not God-fearing, He would have destroyed people for their sins.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is not the meaning of the verse, nor does it belong to its scope or its core sense. The hadith that Ibn 'Umar narrated is sound, but what Makki mentioned about Ibn 'Umar's argument from the verse against it is not sound in my view, because Ibn 'Umar was among the eloquent Arabs.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir recited: "wa-law-la daf'u Allah" (وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ اللهِ), and in al-Hajj: "inna Allah yadfa'u" (إنَّ اللهَ يَدْفَعُ). Nafi' recited: "wa-law-la difa'u Allah" (وَلَوْلا دِفاعُ اللهِ), and "wa-inna Allah yudafi'u" (وَإنَّ اللهَ يُدافِعُ). The rest recited: "wa-law-la daf'u Allah" (وَلَوْلا دَفْعُ اللهِ), and "wa-inna Allah yudafi'u" (وَإنَّ اللهَ يُدافِعُ), so they differentiated between the two. The word daf' (دفع, "repelling") may be the verbal noun of dafa'a, like kataba kitaban and laqiya liqa'an, and it may be the verbal noun of dafa'a, like qatala qitalan.

The demonstrative "tilka" (those) refers to the stories and reports that preceded. In this whole narrative there is a great example and lesson for the believers, and Muhammad's companions were prepared for war against the disbelievers, so for them in this event there is a lesson that calls for strengthening the souls, trust in Allah, and other aspects of the lesson.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 253:

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿Those messengers — We preferred some of them over others. Among them are those to whom God spoke, and some of them He raised in rank. And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, clear proofs and strengthened him with the Holy Spirit.﴾

"Tilka" is in the nominative as the subject (mubtada', the grammatical subject of a nominal sentence), and "al-Rusul" (the messengers) is its predicate (khabar). It is also permissible for "al-Rusul" to be an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayan), with "faddalna" (We preferred) as the predicate, and "tilka" is a demonstrative referring to a group that is feminine in form.

In this verse God explicitly states the preference of some prophets over others, but this is in general terms, without specifying which one is the lesser. Likewise are the hadiths from the Prophet, peace be upon him. He said: "I am the master of the descendants of Adam." He also said: "Do not make me superior to Musa." And he said: "It is not appropriate for anyone to say: 'I am better than Yunus ibn Matta.'" In this there is a strong prohibition against specifying the one who is lesser, because Yunus, peace be upon him, was a young man who buckled under the burdens of prophethood. If this prohibition applies to Muhammad ﷺ, then it applies to others all the more. The principle is that the preference among them is stated without specifying the lesser one. Abu Hurayrah said: "The best of the descendants of Adam are Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad, and they are the Ulu al-'Azm (those of firm resolve)." The one spoken to is Musa, peace be upon him. The Prophet ﷺ was asked about Adam: "Was he a messenger sent?" He said: "Yes, a prophet who was spoken to." Some people have interpreted that Adam's being spoken to took place in Paradise, and on this view the distinction remains specific to Musa.

His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿and some of them He raised in rank﴾. Mujahid and others said: it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, because he was sent to all of mankind, was given the five things that no one before him was given, is the greatest of nations, God sealed prophethood with him, and among his other noble character traits that God bestowed upon him, his miracles and his brilliant signs. The wording may also be taken to mean Muhammad and others whose signs were great, and the statement would then be an emphasis of the first. It is also possible that it means the elevation of Idris to a lofty place, and the ranks of the prophets in the heavens, so that "the degrees" refer to distance, and the preference mentioned at the beginning of the verse remains the only one stated.

The clear proofs of Isa, peace be upon him, are: the raising of the dead, the healing of the blind and the leper, and the creating of a bird from clay.

"Ruh al-Qudus" (the Holy Spirit) is Jibril, peace be upon him, and what the scholars have said about him has already been mentioned.

**

His, may He be exalted and glorified, saying:

﴿And had God willed, those who came after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them. But they differed: some of them believed and some of them disbelieved. And had God willed, they would not have fought one another, but God does what He wills.﴾

The apparent wording in His saying "min ba'dihim" (after them) suggests that He meant the people who came after all the messengers. That is not the intended meaning. Rather, what is meant is that people fought after each prophet. So the speech has been compressed (laffa al-kalam laffan), in a way the listener understands. This is like when you say: "I bought horses and then sold them," which is an acceptable expression, though you had actually bought one horse and sold it, then another and sold it, then another and sold it. Similarly, these events occurred only in that people differed after each prophet. Some of them believed and some disbelieved, out of rebellion and envy over the worldly goods. All of that is by divine decree and destiny, and by God's will, may He be exalted. Had He willed otherwise, it would have been, but He is the one who alone holds the secret of wisdom in this, the doer of what He wills. So they fought, with the believers fighting the disbelievers throughout the ages, and that is the meaning of God's repelling some people by means of others.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 254:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿O you who have believed, spend from what We have provided for you before there comes a Day in which there is no trade, nor close friendship, nor intercession; and the disbelievers are the wrongdoers.﴾

Ibn Jurayj said: "This verse encompasses zakah (obligatory almsgiving) and voluntary charity (tatawwu'). This is a correct statement: zakah is obligatory, and voluntary charity is recommended." The apparent meaning of this verse is that it intends all forms of righteousness: from the way of good, and the maintaining of family ties. However, what preceded of the verses concerning fighting, and that Allah repels [harm] through the believers from the breasts of the disbelievers, gives preference to the view that this exhortation is specifically in the way of Allah. This is reinforced by His saying at the end of the verse: ﴿and the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾, meaning: so confront them with fighting, with lives and with spending of wealth. Allah, exalted is He, has by this verse exhorted to spend some of what He has bestowed, and this is the utmost of bounty in deed and word. He, exalted is He, has warned against withholding before there comes a day on which trade and buying and the making up of expenditure in the cause of Allah are not possible, since it is an exchange of the kind we explained in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245]. Or [the meaning is that] trade is a ransom, for a person may buy himself and his wealth's purpose with it. The meaning of the verse is like the meaning of the other verses that contain [the rejection of] any ransom on the Day of Resurrection. Allah, exalted is He, also informed that there is no close friendship on the Day of Resurrection, meaning: a beneficial friendship that requires mutual contribution, as it was in this world. The people of piety will have friendship among themselves on that day, but it will not be needed by them, whereas the friendship of others will avail them nothing against Allah. He, exalted is He, also informed that intercession is likewise absent on that day. Al-Tabari took that to be a general wording with a specific meaning, namely that the intended sense is: "there is no intercession for the disbelievers." This is not necessary. Rather, the well-known intercession of this world, which is the appointing of an intercessor and his dominating over one on whom the interceded-for person has no desire, is absolutely lifted on the Day of Resurrection. Intercession only exists by the permission of Allah, exalted is He, so its reality is a mercy from Allah, exalted is He, but He honours the one to whom He grants permission to intercede. What is absent is only like the state of this world in trade, close friendship and intercession.

Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read: "lā bay'a fīhi wa-lā khullata wa-lā shafā'ata" with the accusative (naṣb), all without tanwin; and likewise in Surah Ibrahim: "lā bay'a fīhi wa-lā khilāl," and in al-Tur: "lā laghwa fīhā wa-lā ta'thīm." The rest read all of that with the nominative (raf') and tanwin.

"Al-ẓālimūn" are those who place a thing in other than its proper place. 'Ata' ibn Dinar said: "Praise be to Allah who said: ﴿and the disbelievers are the wrongdoers﴾ and did not say: 'the wrongdoers are the disbelievers.'"

[p. 23]

The commentary of Ibn ‘Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 2, verse 255:

God, the Exalted, says:

﴿Allah—there is no deity except Him, the Living, the Self-Subsisting. Neither drowsiness overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is it that can intercede with Him except by His permission? He knows what is before them and what is behind them.﴾

This verse is the master of the verses of the Qur’an. This is reported in the hadith, and it is reported that it equals a third of the Qur’an. It is also reported that whoever recites it at the beginning of his night, no devil will come near him, and likewise whoever recites it at the beginning of his day. It includes tawhid (the affirmation of God’s oneness) and the sublime attributes. “Allah” is a mubtada’ (subject), and “there is no deity” (lā ilāha) is a second mubtada’, whose khabar (predicate) is omitted; its estimated form is “worshipped” or “existent.” “Except Him” (illā huwa) is a badal (apposition) for the position of “lā ilāha.” “The Living” (al-Hayy) is one of God’s essential attributes. Al-Tabari reported from some people that they said: God is living, not by a life. This is the view of the Mu‘tazila, and it is a view to be avoided. It is also related from some people that He is living by a life which is an attribute of His. It is related from some people that it is said: “Living,” as He described Himself, and they accept this without examining it.

“Al-Qayyum” is fay‘ūl, from qiyām (standing). Its original form is qayyūm. The yā’ and wāw came together, and one of them was preceded by a sukūn, so the first was assimilated into the second after the wāw was changed to yā’. Qayyūm is a form of intensification (binā’ mubālagha), meaning: He is the one who stands over every matter with what it requires. Mujahid, al-Rabi‘ and al-Dahhak explained it in this sense.

Ibn Mas‘ud, ‘Alqama, Ibrahim al-Nakha‘i and al-A‘mash read: “al-Hayy al-Qayyām” with an alif.

Then, may He be exalted and glorified, negates that drowsiness or sleep overtakes Him. In the expression “overtake” (al-akhdh) there is a certain sense of overpowering, which is why negation is appropriate in this context. Drowsiness (al-sinah) is the onset of slumber, a lethargy that affects a person, and a drowsiness in his eyes; it does not wholly remove his mind. Sleep (al-nawm) is the deep sleep in which the mind departs.

The meaning of this verse is that no calamity reaches God, Exalted, and no defect affects Him in any state. So these were given as an example of that, and this mentioned category of afflictions stands in place of all of them. This is the understanding of the discourse, as God, Exalted, said: ﴿So do not say to them, “Uff”﴾ [al-Isra’: 23]. Among what distinguishes between wasan (light drowsiness) and sleep is the statement of ‘Adi ibn al-Riqa‘:

A drowsy man, whom slumber overcame, and it misted over
In his eyes a drowsiness, though he is not asleep.

In this sense of sinah, al-Dahhak and al-Suddi explained it. Ibn ‘Abbas and others said: sinah is slumber. Ibn Zayd said: the wasnān (drowsy person) is one who rises from sleep without understanding, to the point that he may draw his sword against his own family.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What Ibn Zayd said is open to question, and it is not an understanding derived from the speech of the Arabs.

Abu Hurayra reported that he said: “I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) relate from Musa on the pulpit, saying: ‘It occurred to Musa: Does Allah, may His praise be exalted, sleep? So Allah sent an angel to him, who kept him awake for three nights. Then He gave him two flasks, one in each hand, and commanded him to guard them. He said: So he began to sleep, and his hands were almost touching each other; then he would wake and withhold one from the other, until he slept a single sleep, and his hands jerked and the two flasks broke.’

He said: Allah struck a parable: if He were to sleep, the heavens and the earth would not remain firm.”

God, the Exalted, says: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning by ownership. He is the owner of all of them and their Lord. The expression uses “mā” (what), although among the whole there are those who have reason, because the intended meaning is the totality and what exists.

Then God, the Exalted, affirmed and established against whoever attempts to intercede with Him, unless He Himself grants permission, may He be exalted and glorified.

Al-Tabari said: This verse was revealed when the disbelievers said: “We worship these idols only so that they may bring us closer to Allah in nearness,” so Allah said: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, to the end of the verse. It is established in this verse that Allah grants permission to whomever He wills for intercession, and they are the prophets, the scholars, and others.

The permission here refers to a command concerning what has been explicitly stated, such as Muhammad (ﷺ) when it is said to him: “Intercede, and your intercession will be accepted.” And it refers to knowledge and empowerment, if any of the prophets or scholars interceded before being commanded to do so. What appears is that scholars and righteous people intercede for those who have not reached the Fire and are between the two abodes, or who have reached it but have righteous deeds.

In al-Bukhari, in the chapter on the remainder of the chapter on the vision (of God), it is reported: “The believers will say: ‘Our Lord, our brothers used to pray with us, fast with us, and act with us.’ So this is an intercession for those whose affair is near, just as the child who is stuck (al-muhabnati’) intercedes at the gate of Paradise.” The hadith continues.

This is only regarding their relatives and acquaintances. The prophets intercede for those among the disobedient of their communities who have entered the Fire because of sins, without kinship or acquaintance, but solely by the very fact of faith. Then the intercession of the Most Merciful of the merciful remains for those who are overwhelmed by sins and whom the intercession of the prophets has not reached.

As for the intercession of Muhammad (ﷺ) in hastening the reckoning, it is specific to him, and it is the fifth one mentioned in his saying: “And I have been given the intercession.” It is general for people, and its purpose is to give rest to the believers, while the disbelievers hasten toward their destination of punishment. Likewise, it is only the believers who ask the prophets for intercession.

The two pronouns in His saying “what is before them and what is behind them” refer to everyone who has reason and is included in His saying: ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.

Mujahid said: “What is before them” is this world, and “what is behind them” is the Hereafter. This is in itself correct at the time of death, because what is before a person (bayna al-yad) is everything that has preceded him, and what is behind him is everything that comes after him. Al-Suddi and others said similarly to Mujahid’s statement.

[p. 26]

God, the Exalted, says:

﴿And they do not encompass anything of His knowledge except what He wills. His Kursi (Footstool/Throne-seat) extends over the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not burden Him. And He is the Most High, the Most Great.﴾

His saying, “and they do not encompass anything of His knowledge,” means: of what is known to Him. This is like the saying of al-Khidr to Musa, peace be upon them both, when a sparrow pecked from the edge of the boat: “My knowledge and your knowledge have decreased from the knowledge of Allah only as much as this sparrow has decreased from this sea.” So this and what is similar to it refers to the things known, because God’s knowledge, which is an attribute of His essence, is not divisible. The meaning of the verse is: no one knows anything known except what Allah wills that he knows.

People differed concerning the Kursi, which God, Exalted, described as extending over the heavens and the earth.

Ibn ‘Abbas said: His Kursi is His knowledge. Al-Tabari preferred this and said: From it comes the karrāsa (notebook) for the pages that contain knowledge, and from it scholars are called karāsī, because they are relied upon, just as it is said: the pegs of the earth.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: These expressions give what was held, that the Kursi is knowledge. Al-Tabari said: From it is the saying of the poet:

Around them are white-faced ones and a band
Kursi-like in the events when calamities befall.

He means by this the scholars of the events of affairs and their occurrences.

Abu Musa al-Ash‘ari said: The Kursi is the place of the two feet, and it has a creak like the creak of a saddle.

Al-Suddi said: It is the place of His two feet. Abu Musa’s expression is sound, because he means that it is, relative to the Throne of the Merciful, like the place of the two feet on the beds of kings. So it is a great creation before the Throne, its relation to it being like the relation of the stool to the king’s throne, and the Kursi is the place of the two feet. As for al-Suddi’s expression, it is unstable, and Mundhir al-Balluti inclined toward it, interpreting it as “what has come forward from created things,” along the lines of what was interpreted in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: “Then the Almighty places His foot in it.” In my view this is a burden, because interpretation is only necessary for the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and for the Book of Allah. As for the expression of an exegete, it is not necessary.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: The Kursi is the Throne itself.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What the hadiths require is that the Kursi is a great creation before the Throne, and the Throne is greater than it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: “The seven heavens in the Kursi are like seven dirhams cast into a shield.” And Abu Dharr said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: “The Kursi in relation to the Throne is like a ring of iron cast into a desert of the earth.”

This verse indicates the greatness of God’s creations, and what is derived from that is the greatness of His power, since the preservation of this great matter does not burden Him.

“Ya’uduhu” means: it burdens him. It is said: ada‘ni al-shay’ meaning athqalani (it weighed on me), and tahammaltu minhu mashaqqatan (I bore hardship from it). Ibn ‘Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada and others explained the word in this way.

It is reported from al-Zuhri, Abu Ja‘far and al-A‘raj, with variation from them, that they softened the hamza on the first wāw, making it bayna bayn (an intermediate sound), neither clearly a pure wāw with damma nor a fully realized hamza, as is said in luʼm/lūm.

“Al-‘Aliyy” refers to loftiness of rank and station, not loftiness of place, because God is exalted above being situated in a place.

Al-Tabari related from some people that they said: He is “al-‘Aliyy” above His creation by the elevation of His place above the places of His creation.

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the saying of ignorant anthropomorphists, and the proper course was not to relate it. Likewise, “al-‘Azim” is an attribute meaning greatness of rank and dignity, not greatness of physical bodies.

Al-Tabari related from some people that “al-‘Azim” means the one who is magnified (al-mu‘azzam), as it is said: al-‘Atiq means al-mu‘attaq (the one freed/aged). He recited the verse of al-A‘sha:

And as if the old wine (al-‘atiq) from the sparkling vintage
Was mixed with clear water.

He reported that some people denied this and said: If it meant “magnified,” it would necessarily follow that He was not great before He created the creation and after their annihilation, since there would then be no one to magnify Him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 256:

His, may He be exalted and majestic, saying: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion. The right path has become clearly distinct from error. Whoever rejects false deities (al-taghut) and believes in God has grasped the firmest handhold, which will never break. God is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

The word "religion" (al-din) in this verse means belief and creed (al-mu'taqad wal-millah), as indicated by His saying: ﴿The right path has become clearly distinct from error.﴾ The compulsion that concerns legal rulings, such as oaths, sales, gifts and other transactions, is not its subject here. It belongs instead to the exegesis of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿except one who is compelled while his heart remains firm in faith﴾ [al-Nahl: 106]. Once it is established that the compulsion negated here concerns belief, meaning the creeds of the faiths and sects, people have differed on the meaning of the verse.

Al-Zuhri said: "I asked Zayd ibn Aslam about His saying, exalted is He: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ He said: The Messenger of God ﷺ remained in Makkah for ten years, not compelling anyone in religion. Then the polytheists refused except that he fight them, so he sought God's permission to fight them, and He permitted him." Al-Tabari said: The verse is abrogated (mansukhah) according to this view.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It follows from this that the verse is Meccan, and that it is one of the verses of truce which were abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim said: This verse is muhkamah (firm, not abrogated), specific to the People of the Book who pay the jizyah (poll tax) and pay it "with humility" (ʿan yadin sughrah). They said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ was commanded to fight the Arab people of idols, accepting from them nothing but 'There is no god but God' or the sword." Then he was commanded to accept the jizyah from others, and this verse was revealed concerning them: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: According to the school of Malik, the jizyah is accepted from every disbeliever other than the Quraysh, of whatever type he may be. The verse then applies specifically to whoever among all people gives the jizyah, and it is not restricted to the People of the Book, as Qatadah and al-Dahhak said.

Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: This verse was revealed only concerning a people from the Aws and the Khazraj. A woman would be barren, with no child surviving to her, so she would vow, if she bore a child, that she would make him a Jew. Among the Banu al-Nadir there was a group in this condition. When the Messenger of God ﷺ expelled the Banu al-Nadir, the Ansar said: "What shall we do with our sons? We only did what we did while we believed their religion to be better than what we are upon. Now that God has brought Islam, shall we compel them to it?" Then the verse was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion.﴾ The verse. Amir al-Sha'bi, Mujahid and al-Hasan said the same, except that he said the reason for their being among the Banu al-Nadir was fostering (al-istirda'). Al-Suddi said: The verse was revealed concerning a man of the Ansar called Abu Husayn, who had two sons. Merchants came from Syria to Madinah carrying olive oil. When they wished to return, the two sons of Abu Husayn went to them, and they invited them to Christianity, so both became Christians and went with them to Syria. Their father came to the Messenger of God ﷺ complaining of their situation and hoping that the Messenger of God ﷺ would send someone to bring them back. Then this verse was revealed: ﴿There is no compulsion in [the] religion.﴾ At that time the People of the Book had not yet been commanded to be fought. He (the Prophet) said: "May God remove them far away; they are the first to disbelieve." Abu Husayn was resentful toward the Messenger of God ﷺ because he did not send anyone to seek them. So God, whose praise is great, revealed: ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe until they make you judge in what is disputed between them﴾ [al-Nisa: 65]. Then He abrogated "There is no compulsion in religion" (naskh) and commanded the fighting of the People of the Book in Surat Bara'ah.

The sound account of the occasion of His saying, ﴿But no, by your Lord, they will not [truly] believe﴾ [al-Nisa: 65], is the hadith of al-Zubayr with his Ansari neighbour concerning the irrigation.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The right path has become clearly distinct from error﴾ means: through the establishment of proofs, the presence of the Messenger calling to God, and the luminous signs. Al-rushd (right guidance) is a verbal noun from your saying: rashida (with kasrah or dammah on the shin), yarshadu, rashadan, rushdan, and rashadan. Al-ghayy (error) is a verbal noun from ghawa, yaghwi, when one goes astray in creed or opinion; al-ghayy is not used for straying in general without restriction. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "al-rashad" with an alif. Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Mujahid read "al-rashad" with fathah on the ra and the shin. It is also reported from al-Hasan "al-rushd" with dammah on the ra and the shin.

Al-taghut is a form of intensification from taghā, yatghā. Al-Tabari recorded: yatghū, when one exceeds the limit, with an added letter, and its pattern is fa'lūt. Sibawayh's view is that it is a singular noun, as though it were a collective noun which applies to the many and the few. Abu 'Ali's view is that it is a verbal noun like rahabūt and jabarūt, which may be used as a description of the singular and the plural; its final radical was moved to the position of the middle radical and the middle radical to the position of the final, so it became taghūt. Al-Mubarrad said it is a plural, but this is rejected.

The exegetes differed on the meaning of al-taghut. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: al-taghut is the Satan. Ibn Sirin and Abu al-'Aliyah said: al-taghut is the sorcerer. Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Rafi', Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah and Ibn Jurayj said: al-taghut is the soothsayer.

The author, Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: It is clear that these are examples of al-taghut, because each of them has transgression (tughyan), and the Satan is the root of all of that. Others said: al-taghut is the idols. Some scholars said: whatever is worshipped besides God is al-taghut. This is a correct naming for every object of worship that approves of that, such as Pharaoh and Nimrod and the like. As for one who does not approve of it, such as 'Uzayr and 'Isa, peace be upon them both, and what does not understand, such as idols, they were named al-taghut with regard to their worshippers. That is metaphorical, since they are through the agency of al-taghut, which commands that worship and makes it appear good, and that is the Satan.

He, exalted is He, placed the mention of rejecting al-taghut before belief in God, to show the concern with the obligation of rejecting al-taghut.
