Al-'urwah (handhold) in physical objects is the point of gripping and tying the hands. "Istamsaka" means he grasped and tightened his hands. Al-wuthqa is the feminine form of al-wathaqah (firmness), and this verse is a simile. The exegetes differed in what the thing likened to the handhold is. Mujahid said: al-'urwah is faith (al-iman). Al-Suddi said: Islam. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak said: al-'urwah is: there is no god but God. These expressions return to one meaning.

Al-infisam is breaking without separation. When that is negated, there is no separation in any way. Al-fasm is a break with separation. The fasm may come with the letter fa' in the sense of separation. Among that is the verse of Dhu al-Rummah:

"As if it were a silver armlet, a nabah
in a playground among the maidens of the tribe, split apart."

Since rejecting al-taghut and believing in God are things which the tongue utters and the heart believes, it is fitting that the attributes be "All-Hearing" for the sake of utterance, and "All-Knowing" for the sake of belief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 257:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Allah is the Walī (Protector) of those who believe; He brings them out of darkness into light. And those who disbelieve, their protectors are the Ṭāghūt (false deities); they bring them out of light into darkness. Those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Al-walī: it is on the pattern fa'īl, from waliya al-shay' when one is adjacent to it and adheres to it. So when someone adheres to another with his support, affection and care, he is that person's walī. This is its usage in the language. Qatādah said: "al-ẓulumāt" (the darknesses) means misguidance, and "al-nūr" (the light) means guidance. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Rabī' said the same. Mujāhid and ʿAbdah ibn Abī Lubābah said: His saying ﴿Allah is the Walī of those who believe﴾, to the end of the verse, was revealed concerning a people who believed in ʿĪsā; when Muḥammad (ﷺ) came, they disbelieved in him, and that is their being brought out from the light into darkness.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: It seems this view considers that they had light in belief, from which they came out into darkness. But the wording of the verse does not need this restriction; rather, it applies to every disbelieving nation in which some believed, such as the Arabs, and it applies to people in general. That is because whoever among them believes, Allah is his Walī; He brings him out of the darknesses of disbelief into the light of faith. And whoever disbelieves after the summoner, the Prophet sent, has appeared, his devil and seducer is as if he had brought him out of (p-34) faith, since he was prepared and fit to enter it. This is like your saying to someone who prevented you from entering a matter: "You have expelled me from this matter, O so-and-so," even though you had never entered it at all. The word al-Ṭāghūt in this verse indicates that it is a noun of genus, which is why He said "their protectors" in the plural, since they are of various kinds. And al-Ḥasan ibn Abī al-Ḥasan read: "awliyāʾuhum al-ṭawāghīt" (their protectors are the ṭawāghīt), meaning the devils. He ruled that they abide in the Fire forever because of their disbelief.

قوله عزّ وجلّ ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, because Allah had given him kingship? When Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death," he said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west." So the disbeliever was overwhelmed, and Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

"ألَمْ تَرَ" (Have you not seen?) is an alert, and it refers to the seeing of the heart. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib recited "ألَمْ تَرْ" with the ra' vocalized with a jazm (sukun). The one who argued with Abraham was Nimrod ibn Kan'an ibn Kush ibn Ham ibn Nuh, king of his time and the owner of the fire and the gnat. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, Ibn Ishaq, Zayd ibn Aslam and others. Ibn Jurayj said he was the first king on earth, but this view is rejected. Qatadah said he was the first tyrant, and he is the owner of the ziggurat (al-sarh) in Babylon. It was said that he was the king of the whole world and his rule extended over it all, and that he was one of the two disbelieving kings, the other being Bukht Nasar (Nebuchadnezzar). It was also said that the one who argued with Abraham was Nimrud ibn Falikh ibn 'Amir ibn Shalikh ibn Arfakhshad ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

Regarding the narratives of this argument there are two reports. The first: Zayd ibn Aslam mentioned that this Nimrod sat ordering people to be given provisions (al-mirah). Whenever a people came, he would say, "Who is your Lord and your god?" They would say, "You." He would say, "Give them provisions." Abraham, peace be upon him, came seeking provisions, and he said to him, "Who is your Lord and your god?" Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." When Nimrod heard this he said, "I give life and cause death." Abraham countered him with the matter of the sun, so the disbeliever was overwhelmed, and he said, "Do not give provisions to him." Abraham returned to his family without anything. He passed by a heap of sand like flour, and he said, "If I fill my sacks with this, and when I enter with it the two boys rejoice, I will look after them." He took it, and when he reached his home the two boys rejoiced and began to play on top of the two sacks. He himself slept from exhaustion. His wife said, "If I prepared food for him, he would find it ready when he wakes." So she opened one of the two sacks and found the finest wheat flour, and she baked it. When he got up she placed it before him. He said, "From where is this?" She said, "From the flour you brought." Abraham then knew that Allah the Exalted had made this easy for them.

Al-Rabi' and others said in these narratives: when Nimrod said, "I give life and cause death," he brought two men, killed one of them, and released the other, and said, "I have given life to this one and caused death to this one." When Abraham answered him with the matter of the sun, he was overwhelmed.

The second report: al-Suddi mentioned that when Abraham came out of the fire, they brought him in to the king, having not entered upon him before that. He spoke to him and said, "Who is your Lord?" He said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." Nimrod said, "I give life and cause death. I take four men, put them in a house, and they are not fed anything or given anything to drink until they are hungry. Then I bring them out and feed two of them, and they live, and I leave two, and they die." Abraham countered him with the sun, so he was overwhelmed.

The scholars of legal theory (al-Usuliyyun, the scholars of foundational principles) mentioned regarding this verse that Abraham, peace be upon him, described his Lord, exalted is He, with what is one of His attributes, namely giving life and causing death. But this is a matter that has a literal meaning (haqiqah) and a figurative meaning (majaz). Abraham, peace be upon him, intended the literal meaning, so Nimrod resorted to the figurative meaning and used it to confuse his people. Abraham, peace be upon him, let him pass in the manner of debate, and moved on with him from the example and brought him a matter with no figurative meaning in it. So the disbeliever was overwhelmed, and he could not say, "I am the one who brings it from the east," because the people of understanding would have denied him.

His statement "حاجَّ" has the form فاعَلَ, from "الحُجَّة" (proof), meaning he drew him toward it (jadhabahu iyyaha). The pronoun in "رَبِّهِ" may refer to Abraham, peace be upon him, and it may refer to the one who argued. "أنْ" is a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlihi). The pronoun in "آتاهُ" refers to Nimrod, and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes. Al-Mahdawi said: it is possible that the pronoun refers to Abraham, so that "أنْ آتاهُ" means "that He gave him the kingship of prophethood." But this is a forced interpretation (tahamul min al-ta'wil).

The majority of reciters recited "أنَ أُحْيِي" by dropping the alif that follows the nun of "أنا" when they connect, throughout the Qur'an, except Nafi'. Warsh, Ibn Abi Uways, and Qalun saw that it is kept in connected speech when a hamza follows it throughout the Qur'an, such as "أنا أُحْيِي" and "أنا أخُوكَ", except in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿إنْ أنا إلا نَذِيرٌ﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:115], where they drop it in this place like the other reciters. His companions followed him in dropping it before a non-hamza. Abu 'Ali said: the first-person pronoun has the hamza and the nun in it; then the alif is attached in pause, just as the ha' is sometimes attached in pause. When the word in which it occurs is connected to something else, the ha' falls away, and so too the alif. It is like the alif of "حَيْهَلا", and this is like the alif that is added at the ends of lines of verse, so reflect on this. Abu 'Ali said: when the word is connected to something, the alif falls away, because the thing to which the word is connected takes the place of the alif. The alif has also come kept in connected speech in poetry. From that is the saying of the poet:

"I am the elder of the clan, so recognize me,
Hamid, for I have grown old and my hump has risen."

The majority recited "فَبُهِتَ الَّذِي" with a damma on the ba' and a kasra on the ha', and it is said: "بُهِتَ الرَجُلُ" when a man is cut off and the proof is established against him. Ibn Sida said: in this sense it is also said "بَهِتَ" with a fatha on the ba' and a kasra on the ha', and "بَهُتَ" with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on the ha'. Al-Tabari said: it has been reported from some Arabs in this sense: "بَهَتَ" with a fatha on the ba' and the ha'.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this word was vocalized thus in the copy of Ibn Malul without specification of a fatha on the ba' and the ha'. Ibn Jinni said: Abu Haywa recited "فَبَهُتَ" with a fatha on the ba' and a damma on the ha', and it is a dialect of "بُهِتَ" with a kasra on the ha'. He said: Ibn al-Sumayfa' recited "فَبَهَتَ" with a fatha on the ba' and the ha', meaning "so Abraham overwhelmed the one who disbelieved," so "الَّذِي" is in the accusative position. He said: it is also possible that "بَهَتَ" with a fatha on both is a dialect of "بُهِتَ". He said: Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash related the recitation "فَبُهِتَ" with a kasra on the ha', like "خُرِقَ" and "دُهِشَ". He said: the damma on the ha' is more common. Ibn Jinni said: he means that the damma is for emphasis (mubalaghah).

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: some people have interpreted the recitation of the one who read "فَبَهَتَ" with both fatha as meaning "he insulted and slandered," and that it was Nimrod who insulted Abraham when he was cut off and had no stratagem.

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿واللهُ لا يَهْدِي القَوْمَ الظالِمِينَ﴾ is an information addressed to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and his community. The meaning is: He does not guide them in their arguments while they persist in wrongdoing, because there is no guidance in wrongdoing. Its apparent meaning is general, but its intended meaning is specific, as we have mentioned, because Allah may guide wrongdoers through repentance and return to faith. It is also possible that the specificity applies to those who die as wrongdoers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 1 of 2):

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿Or like the one who passed by a town that was fallen upon its roofs. He said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years; then He resurrected him. He said, "How long have you remained?" He said, "I have remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you have remained a hundred years."﴾

The "aw" (or) in this verse is coordinated with the meaning, because the purpose of wonder in His saying, ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued﴾ [al-Baqarah: 258], implies the meaning: "Have you seen the likes of the one who argued?" Then His saying, ﴿Or like the one﴾, came as a coordination with that meaning.

Abu Sufyan ibn Husayn recited, "Awa ka-alladhi marra" with a fatha on the waw, and it is a waw of coordination into which the alif of confirmation (alif al-taqrir) has entered. Sulayman ibn Buraydah, Najiyah ibn Ka'b, Qatadah, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi', 'Ikrimah and al-Dahhak said: the one who passed by the town was 'Uzayr. Wahb ibn Munabbih, 'Abdullah ibn 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr, and Bakr ibn Mudar said: he was Armiya' (Jeremiah). Ibn Ishaq said: Armiya' is al-Khidr, and al-Naqqash related it from Wahb ibn Munabbih. This, as you see, is [weak], unless it is a name that coincides with another name, because al-Khidr was a contemporary of Musa, whereas this man who passed by the town was, according to what Wahb ibn Munabbih related, a long time after him, from the lineage of Harun. Makki related from Mujahid that he was a man from the Children of Israel, unnamed. Al-Naqqash said: it is also said that he was the servant (ghulam) of Lut, peace be upon him. There was disagreement about which town the town was. Al-Naqqash related that a people said it was al-Mu'tafikah. Ibn Zayd said: the people who left their homes, and they were thousands, fearing death, and Allah said to them, "Die," passed by them, and they were bones gleaming, so he stood looking and said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years. Al-Tabari gave this narration the heading that it is a statement that the town he passed by was the one in which Allah destroyed those who left their homes.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Ibn Zayd's statement does not fit the heading, because the demonstrative "this" (hadhihi), according to what the heading requires, refers to the place, whereas according to the statement itself it refers to the bones and bodies. This statement of Ibn Zayd contradicts the wording of the verse, since the verse only includes a fallen town in which there is no one, and the demonstrative "this" refers only to the town, and its bringing to life is only by building and the existence of buildings and inhabitants. Wahb ibn Munabbih, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, 'Ikrimah and al-Rabi' said: the town was Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), when Bukhtnassar the Babylonian ruined it. In the long hadith, when the Children of Israel committed their misdeeds, Armiya' or 'Uzayr stood by the town, which was like a great hill in the middle of Bayt al-Maqdis, because Bukhtnassar ordered his soldiers to carry the dust to it until he made it like a mountain. Armiya' saw the houses whose walls had fallen onto their roofs. The 'arish is the roof of the house, and everything prepared to give shade or shelter is an 'arish, and from it is the trellis of the vine and fruit, and from it is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and of what they trellis﴾ [al-Nahl: 68].

Al-Suddi said: it means it is fallen upon its roofs, i.e., the roofs fell and then the walls fell upon them. Other than al-Suddi said: its meaning is empty of people, upon the 'uroush, i.e., upon the houses, and their roofs are upon them, but they are empty of people while the houses are standing.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Observe the usage of 'arish with 'ala in the hadith, in His saying: "The mosque that day was upon an 'arish concerning the matter of Laylat al-Qadr."

And "khawiyah" means khaliyah (empty). It is said: the house became empty (khawat al-dar takhwa khawa'an), and it is also said khawiya. Al-Tabari said: the first is more eloquent. His saying, ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾ means: By what way? And by what cause? The apparent sense of the wording is a question about bringing the town to life through building and inhabitants, as is said now of ruined cities that are far from being rebuilt and inhabited. So this was a sorrowful lament from the one standing and reflecting upon his city in which he had known its people and his loved ones, and a parable was struck for him in himself with something greater than what he asked about. The parable struck for him in himself may be understood as his question being about the bringing back to life of the dead from the children of Adam, i.e., "How will Allah bring its dead to life?"

Al-Tabari related from some of them that he said: this statement was a doubt about Allah's power to give life, and therefore a parable was struck for him in himself.

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: No doubt enters into Allah's power to bring a town to life by bringing population to it, and doubt is only imaginable from an ignorant person in the other respect. The correct view is that no doubt should be attributed to the verse.

It is related in the narratives of this verse that when the Children of Israel committed their misdeeds, Allah sent against them Bukhtnassar the Babylonian, who killed them and expelled them from Bayt al-Maqdis and ruined it. When he left it, Armiya' came and stood over the city reflecting and said, "How will Allah bring this to life after its death?" He said: So Allah, Exalted, caused him to die. He had with him a donkey, which he had tied with a new rope, and he had with him a basket containing figs, which was his food; it is also said figs and grapes. He had with him a flask of wine, and it is also said of pressed juice, and it is also said a jug of water which was his drink. He remained dead for a hundred years. It is related that he decayed and his bones were scattered, he and his donkey. It is related that he decayed without the donkey, and that the donkey remained alive, tied, not dying, not eating anything, and its flesh did not decay. It is related that the donkey decayed and its joints were scattered, without 'Uzayr. It is related that Allah sent to that town one who rebuilt it and returned to it the group of the Children of Israel when it was completed at the end of a hundred years, and then 'Uzayr came to life. It is related that Allah returned his eyes to him and created for him a life by which he saw how the town was rebuilt and brought to life, from thirty years of the hundred's completion, because he had remained seventy years dead entirely. This is weak, and the wording of the verse refutes it.

His, Exalted is He, saying, ﴿then He resurrected him﴾ means: He gave him life, and gave him movement and ability to move. Allah, Exalted, asked him through an angel, ﴿How long have you remained?﴾, in the form of confirmation. "Kam" (how much) is in the accusative position as an adverb of time. He said, ﴿I have remained a day or part of a day.﴾ Ibn Jurayj, Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: Allah caused him to die at the beginning of a day, then he was resurrected before sunset, so he thought this day was one day and said, "I have remained a day." Then he saw a remnant of the sun and feared that he was lying, so he said, "or part of a day." Then it was said to him, "Rather, you have remained a hundred years" — and he saw from the building of the town, its trees and its structures, what indicated that.

Al-Naqqash said: 'am (year) is a verbal noun like 'awm (floating), and this measure of time was named after it, because it is one floating of the sun in the orbit, and 'awm is like sabh (swimming). Allah, Exalted, said: ﴿and each in an orbit swims﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40].

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: This is the meaning of al-Naqqash's statement, and 'am according to this is like qawl (saying) and qal (saying). The apparent sense of this death is that it was by the removal of the soul from the body. It is related in the narratives of this verse that Allah sent to it a king from among the kings who would rebuild it and strive in that, until the completion of its rebuilding came at the time of the speaker's resurrection: ﴿How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾

Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Nafi' recited "labithta" everywhere in the Qur'an with the tha' clearly pronounced, because the point of articulation of tha' differs from that of ta'. The ta', ta' and dal are from one region (hayyiz), and the zay, dhal and tha' are from another. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with idgham (assimilation) everywhere in the Qur'an, treating them like the similar letters, since the two letters agree in being from the tip of the tongue and the roots of the upper incisors, and in being voiceless (mahmusah). Abu 'Ali said: What strengthens this is that these two letters occur in the rhyme (rawiyy) of one single qasidah.

**

His, the Exalted and Majestic, saying:

﴿So look at your food and your drink; it has not spoiled. And look at your donkey; and We will make you a sign for the people. And look at the bones, how We raise them and then clothe them with flesh.﴾ Then when it became clear to him, he said, "I know that Allah is over all things competent."

In these words, he stood upon the preservation of his food and drink in their state, unchanged, and upon the preservation of his donkey alive at its tether, according to one of the two interpretations; and according to the second interpretation, he stood upon the donkey, how it would live and its bones would be gathered. Ibn Mas'ud recited: "And this is your food and your drink; it has not spoiled." Talhah ibn Musarrif and others recited: "And look at your food and your drink for a hundred years."

Abu 'Ali said: They differed about affirming the ha' in the verb in His saying, Exalted and Majestic: "lam yatasannah" and "iqtadih", and "ma aghna 'anni maliyah" and "sultaniyah", and "wa ma adraka ma hiyah" — and omitting it in continuous speech. They did not differ about affirming it in pause. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Umar recited all these letters with the ha' affirmed in continuous speech. Hamzah used to delete them in continuous speech. Al-Kisa'i used to delete it in "yatasannah" and "iqtadih" and affirm it in the rest. They did not differ about "hisabiyah" and "kitabiyah" that they have the ha' both in pause and in continuous speech.

"Yatasannah" may be from tasanna al-shay' when it changed and spoiled, and from it "al-hama' al-masnun" (the mud poured according to the ways of the earth). If it is from "tasannan," then it is: "lam yatasannan," the nun was changed into a ya' as was done in "tazannantu," until you say "lam atazzann." So tasannana becomes tasanna, then the ya' is deleted for jazm, so the imperfect becomes "lam yatasann." Whoever recited it with the ha' on this view, it is the ha' of pause (ha' al-sakt), and on this view its deletion in continuous speech is good.

"Yatasannah" may be from al-sanah, which is drought, famine and what resembles it; they name it so, and a verb has been derived from it, so it is said: "istannu" (they became afflicted by drought). If this is from al-sanah, which is the year, according to the opinion of those who make its plural sanawat, then on this also the ha' is the ha' of pause, and the meaning is: famine, dearth and the like have not changed your food, or years and seasons have not changed it.

As for one who says in the diminutive of sanah: "sunayhah," and in the plural: "sanahat," and says: "asnahtu 'inda bani fulan" — and this is the dialect of the Hijaz, and from it is the poet's saying:

"She is not one of the sanha' nor one of the rujabiyyah, but she is ʿarāyā in the years of calamities."

then the recitation on this dialect is with the affirmation of the ha' without fail, and it is the final radical of the verb, and in it the jazm appears with "lam." On this, it is the recitation of Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr, which has been mentioned. Talhah ibn Musarrif recited: "lam yassannah" with idgham.

al-Naqqash said: "lam yatasannah" means: it has not changed, from His saying, Exalted: ﴿of water unaltered (ghayr asin)﴾ [Muhammad: 15]. The grammarians rejected this view, because if it were from "asina al-ma'" (the water became foul), it would have come as "lam yata'assanh."

As for His saying, Exalted, ﴿And look at your donkey﴾, Wahb ibn Munabbih and others said: the meaning is: look at the joining of its bones and its revival piece by piece. It is related that Allah revived it in this way until it became bones joined together, then clothed it with flesh until it was complete as a donkey, then an angel came and blew the spirit into its nostril, and the donkey stood up braying. It is also related from al-Dahhak and Wahb ibn Munabbih that they both said: rather, it was said to him: "And look at your donkey standing at its tether; nothing has harmed it for a hundred years." They both said: and the bones he looked at were the bones of his own self. They said:

"And Allah blinded the eyes from Armiya' and his donkey for this period."

The qadi Abu Muhammad (may Allah have mercy on him) said: The people of the stories have expanded greatly on the details of this incident, which I have abridged because they are not sound.

His, Exalted, saying, ﴿and We will make you a sign for the people﴾ means: for this purpose, that you should be a sign, We have done this to you. Al-A'mash said: the point of his being a sign is that he came as a young man in his state of the day he died, and found his sons and grandchildren had become old men. 'Ikrimah said: he came being forty years old as he was the day he died, and found his sons had passed a hundred years. Other than al-A'mash said: rather, the point of his being a sign is that he came when everyone who knew him had perished, so he was a sign for whoever among his people was still alive, since they believed in his condition by hearsay.

(p-46) Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 259 (part 2 of 2)

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: In his being made to die for that period and then brought back to life there is the greatest sign, and his whole affair is a sign for mankind until the end of time. There is no need to restrict any part of it to the exclusion of another.

As for the bones that he was commanded to look at, we have already mentioned those who said they were the bones of his own body, and those who said they were the bones of the donkey. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "nanshuruha" (﻿نَنْشُرُها) with a fatha on the first nun, a damma on the shin, and a ra'. The Hasan, Ibn 'Abbas and Abu Haywa read it in the same way. Whoever reads "nunshiruha" (نُنْشِرُها) with a damma on the first nun and a ra' means: "nuhyiha" (we give them life). It is said: "anshara Allahu al-mawta" (God raised the dead). God the Exalted says: ﴿Then, when He wills, He will raise him up﴾ [Abasa: 22]. Al-A'sha said:

"... O wonder at the dead one who rises!"

The reading of 'Asim, "nanshuruha" with a fatha on the first nun and a damma on the shin, may be a dialectal usage for bringing to life. It is said: "nasharta al-mayyita" and "anshartuhu" (I raised the dead). So it becomes: "nashara al-mayyitu" (the dead one rose) and "nashartuhu" (I raised him), as one says: "hasirat al-dabbatu" (the animal became exhausted) and "hasartuha" (I exhausted it); "ghaya al-ma'u" (the water receded) and "ghidtuhu" (I made it recede); "raja'a Zayd" (Zayd returned) and "raja'tuhu" (I made him return). It may also be that the meaning is the opposite of folding (tayy), as if death were a folding of the bones and the limbs, and as if bringing to life and joining some of them to others were an unfolding (nashr).

As for whoever reads "nunshizuha" (نُنْشِزُها) with a za', its meaning is "narfa'uha" (we raise them). The "nashaz" is a raised place on the ground, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"You see the fox of the year in them, as if he were, when he rises upon a raised place, a horse covered with a blanket ..."

Abu 'Ali and others said: its sense is "nunshizuha" by raising some of them to others for bringing to life. From it comes "nushuz" (rebelliousness) of a woman. Al-A'sha said:

"... a Qudha'iyya who goes to the soothsayers, rebellious (nashiz)..."

It is said: "nashaza" and "anshaztuhu."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: What troubles me is that the meaning of "nushuz" should be raising bones to one another. Rather, "nushuz" is rising little by little, so it seems that he stood over the growth of the crumbled bones and the emergence of what is found of them at the moment of creation. Al-Naqqash said: "nunshizuha" means "nunbituha" (we make them grow). Consider the usage of the Arabs and you will find it as I have mentioned to you. Among that: "nashaza nab al-ba'ir" (the camel's tooth rose up), and "al-nashaz min al-ard" (the raised ground) by analogy with that.

"Nashazat al-mar'a" (the woman rebelled), as if she had departed from the state in which she ought to be.

The saying of God the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said: "Rise up, rise up"﴾ [al-Mujadila: 11], that is, rise a little at a time like the rising of the tooth. Thus there is room for expansion. So "nushuz" is a kind of rising. But it is unusual in usage to say of someone who has risen on a wall or an upper room that he "nashaza."

Al-Nakha'i read "nanshuzuha" with a fatha on the nun, a damma on the shin and a za', and this is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "kayfa nunshiha" (كَيْفَ نُنْشِيها) with a ya'.

The "kiswa" is what covers of garments, and flesh has been likened to it. Al-Nabigha used it as a metaphor for Islam, saying:

"Praise be to God, that my term did not come upon me until I was clothed in Islam as in a garment ..."

It is narrated that he (Ibrahim) saw the flesh, the sinews and the veins, how they come together and join. Al-Tabari said: the meaning of His saying: "falamma tabayyana lahu" (﻿فَلَمّا تَبَيَّنَ لَهُ), that is, when it became clear to him by direct vision what he had found strange regarding God's power before seeing it, "qala: a'lamu" (he said: "I know").

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is an error, because it imposes what the wording does not require, and it interprets according to an anomalous view and a weak possibility.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "a'lamu" (أعْلَمُ) with a cut alif and a damma on the mim. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "qala i'lam anna Allaha" (قالَ اعْلَمْ أنَّ اللهَ) with a connected alif and a sukun on the mim. Abu Raja' also read it so. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud and al-A'mash read "qila a'lamu" (قِيلَ أعْلَمُ).

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: As for this last reading, its meaning is clear, that is, the angel said to him. The first is also clear in meaning, that is, he himself said: "I know that God is over all things powerful" (﻿أعْلَمُ أنَّ اللهَ عَلى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ). In my view this is not an acknowledgement of what he had previously denied, as al-Tabari claimed. Rather, it is a saying prompted by reflection, as a believing person says when he sees some marvel of God's power: "There is no god but God," and the like. Abu 'Ali said: its meaning is: "I know this kind of knowledge which I had not known."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: He means the knowledge of direct observation. As for the reading of Hamza and al-Kisa'i, it allows two possibilities. One is that the angel said to him: "i'lam" (know). The other is that he placed himself in the position of a distant, separate addressee, so the meaning is: when it became clear to him, he said to himself: "i'lam" (know). Abu 'Ali cited in this sense the saying of al-A'sha:

"Bid farewell to Hurayra, for the caravan is departing..."

and his saying:

"Did your eyes not close during a night of sore eyes?..."

Examples of this are many. Abu 'Ali found support for this meaning in the saying of the poet:

"He remembers from where and whence his drink is, consulting his two selves, like the camel of a herd..."

[p. 49] *Ibn 'Atiyya's commentary (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah al-Baqarah, verse 260 (part 1 of 2)*

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at ease." He said, "Take four birds and incline them toward you. Then place on every mountain a portion of them, then call them; they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Mighty and Wise."﴾

The word that governs "idh" (when) is an implied verb whose estimated form is: "and remember." People have differed over why this statement came from Abraham (peace be upon him). The majority (al-jumhur) said: Abraham (peace be upon him) never at any time doubted that Allah gives life to the dead; he only sought direct observation (mu'aynah). Al-Tabari, in his tafsir, gave a heading and said: "Others said: he asked his Lord because he doubted Allah's power to give life to the dead." Under this heading he included, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he said: "There is no verse in the Qur'an more hopeful to me than this one." He also mentioned from 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah that he said: "Some of what enters the hearts of people entered the heart of Abraham, so he said: 'My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.'" He also mentioned the hadith of Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "We have more right to doubt than Abraham..." (the hadith). Then al-Tabari preferred this view, which accords with the apparent meaning of the hadith, and said: "When Abraham saw the carcass from which fish and land animals were eating, Satan cast into his soul, so he said: 'When will Allah gather these from the bellies of these creatures?'"

As for those who said that Abraham was not in doubt, they differed about the cause of his question. Qatadah said: Abraham saw an animal that had been torn apart among the beasts of prey, so he was amazed and asked this question. Al-Dahhak said something similar, and said: "He (peace be upon him) knew that Allah is able to give life to the dead." Ibn Zayd said: "He saw the animal being divided among the beasts of prey and the fish, because it was on the shore of the sea." Ibn Ishaq said: "Rather, its cause was that when he parted from Nimrod, who said to him, 'I give life and cause death,' he reflected on that reality and its metaphor, and so he asked this question." Al-Suddi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Rather, the cause of this question was that when he was given the good news that Allah had taken him as a close friend (khalil), he wished to seek assurance through this question, in order to test the truth of the friendship, for a close friend may seek assurance in what others may not. Sa'id ibn Jubayr also said: '"But so that my heart may be at ease" means: by friendship.'"

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: What al-Tabari headed with is, in my view, rejected, and what he included under the heading is an interpretation. As for the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, "It is the most hopeful verse," it is because in it there is reliance upon Allah, the Exalted, and a request for the giving of life in this world, though it is not the proper place for such a request. It is also permissible to say: "It is the most hopeful verse" because of His saying "Have you not believed?", meaning that faith is sufficient and needs no further refinement or inquiry after it. As for the saying of 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, "Some of what enters the hearts of people entered the heart of Abraham," its meaning is from love of direct observation, because souls are eager to see what they have been told of. For this reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "The report is not like direct observation." As for the saying of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): "We have more right to doubt than Abraham," its meaning is that if there were doubt, we would have more right to it; but we do not doubt, so Abraham is more deserving [p. 50] of not doubting. Thus the hadith is built upon negating doubt from Abraham. What was narrated from the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him), that he said, "That is the pure essence of faith," refers only to passing thoughts that do not remain. As for doubt, it is suspension between two matters with no preference of one over the other, and that is what is negated of the close friend (peace be upon him).

The giving of life to the dead is established only through revelation (al-sam'), and Abraham (peace be upon him) knew it better. What shows this is his saying: "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." Doubt is far-fetched even for one whose foot is firmly planted in faith alone, so how much more for the rank of prophethood and close friendship? Prophets are protected from major sins and from minor sins that involve baseness, by consensus (ijma').

If you reflect upon his question (peace be upon him) and the rest of the wording of the verse, it does not give any indication of doubt. The interrogative with "kayfa" (how) is only about the state of a thing that is existent and firmly established in the knowledge of both the questioner and the one questioned, like your saying: "How did Zayd know?" or "How did he weave the garment?" and the like. When you say, "How is your garment?" or "How is Zayd?", the question is only about one of his states. "Kayfa" may also be a report about something whose nature is that it is asked about with "kayfa," like your saying: "However you wish, so be it," and like al-Bukhari's phrase: "How did the beginning of revelation occur?"

"Kayfa" in this verse is an interrogative about the form (hay'ah) of giving life, while the giving of life is established. However, when we found that some who deny the existence of a thing may express their denial by asking about a state of that thing which they know to be unfitting, it follows that the thing itself is not valid. An example of this: someone claims, "I will lift this mountain," and the one who disbelieves him says, "Show me how you lift it." This is a figurative manner of speech, and its meaning is a dialectical concession, as if he were saying: "Suppose you lift it; show me how." Since this figurative shared usage was in the expression of the close friend (peace be upon him), Allah made it clear to him, and led him to clarify the reality, so He said to him: ﴿Have you not believed?﴾ He said: ﴿Yes﴾. Thus the matter was complete, and he was freed from every doubt. Then he (peace be upon him) gave the reason for his question as seeking tranquility.

His Exalted saying, ﴿Have you not believed?﴾, means: a faith without qualification, which includes the matter of giving life to the dead. The waw is a waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), upon which has entered the alif of affirmation (alif al-taqrir).

"Li-yatma'inna" means: so that his thought may settle. Tranquility (tuma'nina) is balance and stillness upon that balance. Tranquility of the limbs is well known, as he (peace be upon him) said: "Then bow until you are at rest in bowing," the hadith. Tranquility of the heart is that its thought come to rest upon the thing believed. Thinking about the form of giving life is not forbidden; just as we today may reflect upon it, indeed it is reflection that contains lessons. Abraham wished to see directly, so that his thought about the form of giving life would be settled, since what moved him to that was either the matter of the animal that was eaten, or the saying of Nimrod: "I give life and cause death."

Al-Tabari said: The meaning of "li-yatma'inna" is: so that he may be certain. Something similar is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and it is also related from him: "so that he may increase in certainty." Abraham said it, and Qatadah did too. Some said: "so that I may increase in faith along with my faith."

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: No increase is possible in this meaning except the calming of thought; otherwise certainty does not admit of degrees. It is related that the four birds that Abraham took were the rooster, the peacock, the dove, and the crow. Ibn Ishaq mentioned this from some of the early scholars of knowledge, and Mujahid, Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd said it likewise. Ibn 'Abbas said that in place of the crow it was the crane (al-kurki). [p. 53] It is related in the narratives about this verse that the close friend (peace be upon him) took these birds as he was commanded, slaughtered them, cut them into small pieces, and mixed that together with the blood and feathers. Then he placed a portion of that mixed collection on every mountain, and he stood from where he could see those portions, and held the heads of the birds in his hand. Then he said: "Come, by the permission of Allah!" The portions flew, blood flew to blood and feathers to feathers, until they were joined as they had been at first, and remained without heads. Then he repeated the call, and they came to him running, until their bodies were placed on their heads, and they flew by the permission of Allah, the Exalted.

Hamzah alone read "fa-sirhunna ilayka" with a kasrah on the sad (ṣād). The rest read it with a ḍammah. It is said: "ṣurtu al-shay'a aṣūruhu," meaning "I cut it," and from this is the saying of Ru'bah:

*"We cut the judgment by it, and the arbiter was helpless."*

From this is the saying of al-Khansa':

*"If it were to meet what you met, Ḥaḍan, the strong ones would be cut from it, while they were being severed."*

That is: they are cut apart. It is also said: "ṣurtu al-shay'a amaltuhu," meaning "I inclined it," and from this is the saying of the poet:

*"A dark, cut-tailed one, with its rump, inclines its young she-goat, and it roars as the debtor roars."*

From this is the saying of the Bedouin describing women: "They are images (ṣuwar) toward youth, and light away from wantonness." All of this is with a ḍammah on the sad.

It is also said, with these two meanings of "cutting and inclining": "ṣirtu al-shay'a" with a kasrah on the sad, "aṣīruhu." From this is the saying of the poet:

*"And a branch that makes the neck incline, as if on the nape the clusters of the bent vines..."*

So in the word there are two dialects, and both were read.

Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid said regarding this verse: "ṣurhunna" means "cut them up." 'Ikrimah and Ibn 'Abbas, in some of what is narrated from him, said that it is a Nabataean word meaning "cut them up." Al-Dahhak said the same. Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali said it is Syriac. Qatadah said: "ṣurhunna" means "separate them." Ibn Ishaq said: its meaning is "cut them up," and it is the ṣawr of Arabic speech. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: "fa-surhunna" means "gather them to you." Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is "gather them." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that its meaning is "bind them." So the commentators have interpreted the word in the sense of cutting and in the sense of inclining. Thus His saying "ilayka" (to you), on the interpretation of cutting, is connected to "khudh" (take); and on the interpretation of inclining and gathering, it is connected to "ṣurhunna." In the speech there is an omitted element indicated by the apparent meaning, its estimated form being: "so incline them to you, and cut them up."

A group read "fa-ṣurrahunna" with a ḍammah on the sad and a shaddah on the open rā', as if he were saying "fa-shuddahunna" (so bind them tight), and from this is "ṣurrat al-danānīr" (a purse of dinars).

A group read "fa-ṣirrahunna" with a kasrah on the sad and a shaddah on the open rā', meaning: "ṣayyihhunna" (make them cry out), from your saying: "ṣarra al-bābu wa al-qalamu" when it creaked. This was mentioned by al-Naqqash. Ibn Jinni said: this reading is strange, because yaf'ilu with a kasrah on the 'ayn in the doubled transitive verb is rare; its pattern is yaf'ulu with a ḍammah on the 'ayn, like "shadda yashuddu" and similar. But there has come from it: "nammma al-ḥadītha yanimmuhu and yanummuhu," and "harra al-ḥarba yahirruhā and yahurruhā," and from this is the saying of al-A'sha:

*"Let the speech turn you about until you are firmly held..."*

and other examples in a few letters. Ibn Jinni said: as for the reading of 'Ikrimah with a ḍammah on the sad, the rā' may be read with ḍammah, fatḥah, or kasrah, like "madda" and "shadda," and the preferred form is a ḍammah on the rā' because of the ḍammah on the hā' after it. Al-Mahdawi and others said: it is related from 'Ikrimah that he read with a fatḥah on the sad and a shaddah on the kasrah rā'. This carries the meaning of "fa-iḥbisḥunna" (hold them back), from their saying: "ṣaraa yaṣrī" when he held back, and from it the "muṣrāh" (a she-camel or ewe whose udder is held back from milking).

The interpreters differed about the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then place on every mountain a portion of them﴾. Abu Hamzah related from Ibn 'Abbas that the meaning is: place a portion on each quarter of the world, as if the meaning is: place them in the four corners of the earth. This view is far-fetched. Qatadah and al-Rabi' said: the meaning is: place on four mountains, on each mountain a portion of that gathered, divided mass; just as Allah raises these birds from these mountains, so He will raise creation on the Day of Resurrection from the quarters of the world and all its regions. The majority read "juz'an" with a hamzah. Abu Ja'far read "juzzan" with a shaddah on the zāy throughout the Qur'an; this is a dialect of pausing (waqf), and Abu Ja'far applied the connected reading to it. Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi said: he was commanded to place them on the mountains to which the birds and beasts of prey, when eating the animal, would fly and head, and disperse among. They said: there were seven mountains, so he divided that cut-up portion of bird flesh into seven parts. Mujahid said: rather, he was commanded to place on each mountain near him a portion. Al-Tabari said: the meaning is without restricting the mountains by number; rather, they are those which Abraham could reach at the time Allah charged him with dividing that among them, because the word "kull" (every) is a term indicating totality.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It is far-fetched that he was charged with all the mountains of the world, since his sight could not encompass that. Thus what al-Tabari went to is sound and well-founded. And Allah knows best which of these was the case.

The meaning of the verse is that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was positioned so that he could see the parts in their place and see how they came back together, and so the lesson was sound for him. His being commanded to call them while they were dead was only so that the verse would come close to him and be connected to his own state, and so that he would see that the display was directed at him. For this reason God made their coming to him a "sa'y" (ﺳَﻌْﻴًﺎ, running with effort), since it is the walk of one who is earnest and eager toward what he walks to. It was part of the emphasis that Ibrahim saw their eagerness in their intent and in answering his call. Had they come to him walking, this indication would have been lost, and had they come flying, that would have been in keeping with the usual manner of birds, so this (running) is more remarkable than that. Then, peace be upon him, he came to know, through the knowledge, the might (ʿizzah) that contains power within it, and the wisdom (ḥikmah) by which everything is perfectly made.

(p-57)

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 261–262:

The Exalted said:

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies for whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury, their reward is with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾

This verse, in its wording, is an explanation of a parable that shows the nobility and goodness of spending in the way of Allah, and it contains an exhortation to that. This verse concerns voluntary spending (nafaqat al-tatawwu'), and the ways (subul) of Allah are many. They include everything that is an act of obedience and that returns benefit to the Muslims and the community (milla). The most well-known and the greatest in benefit of these is jihad, so that the word of Allah may be the highest.

The word ḥabba (grain) is an ism jins (a collective noun for a kind), covering everything that the son of Adam sows and eats as food. The most well-known of these is wheat. The word ḥabb is often used to mean grain, and from it is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

"I have sworn that I will eat the grain of Iraq forever, while the weevil eats the grain in the village."

It is sometimes found that an ear of wheat contains a hundred grains, and in other grains the number is greater, but the parable was given with this amount. The Qur'an has stated that the good deed in all acts of righteousness is multiplied by ten times its like, and this verse indicates that the good reward for spending on jihad is seven hundred times, and the authentic hadith has clarified this.

The scholars differed regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾. One group said: it explains and emphasizes what came earlier about the seven hundred, and there is no multiplication beyond seven hundred. Another group of scholars said: rather, it is an announcement that Allah the Exalted multiplies for whom He wills more than seven hundred times. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the multiplication may reach, for whom Allah wills, two thousand (p-58) thousand, but this is not authentically transmitted from him. Ibn 'Umar said: "When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'My Lord, increase my ummah.' So it was revealed: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245]. He said: 'My Lord, increase my ummah.' So it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]."

The word sunbula is on the pattern fun'ula, from asbala al-zar' meaning it released what is in it, as a garment is let down (yusbalu). The plural is sanabil.

In the Exalted's saying ﴿The likeness of those who﴾ there is an omitted noun (ḥadhf mudāf, an elided word attached to a noun in the genitive). Its estimate is: "the likeness of the spending of those who," or its estimate is: "like the likeness of one possessing a grain."

Al-Tabari said regarding this verse: that His saying ﴿in each ear a hundred grains﴾ means: if that is found; otherwise, it is on the basis that we assume it. Then he cited from al-Dahhak that he said: ﴿in each ear a hundred grains﴾ means: every ear produced a hundred grains. So al-Tabari made the saying of al-Dahhak similar to what he himself said, but that is not necessarily what can be derived from the wording of al-Dahhak.

Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: some read "mi'ata" (a hundred) in the accusative, on the estimate: "it produced a hundred grains."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who spend their wealth﴾, the verse: since in the verse before this there was a mention of spending in the way of Allah in general, this verse makes clear that this ruling applies only to the one who does not follow (p-59) his spending with reminders of generosity or with injury. That is because the one who spends in the way of Allah is only in one of three states. Either he intends the face of Allah the Exalted and hopes for His reward; this one expects nothing from the recipient and does not look at his circumstances in any way except to observe his deserving. Or he intends from the recipient a return in some form; this one has not intended the face of Allah, but rather looked to this condition of the recipient, and this is the one who, whenever his expectation is disappointed, reminds of his giving and injures. Or he spends compelled, to repel a debt, either out of shame before the recipient or another reason such as the attention of the spender or similar; this one has looked at a condition that is not for the face of Allah, and this is the one who, whenever he is followed up on and is embarrassed in some way of embarrassment, injures.

So reminders of generosity and injury reveal, about the one from whom they appear, that he was acting upon the intentions we have mentioned, and that he did not sincerely seek the face of Allah. For this reason, reminders and injury invalidate the charity, since each of them makes clear that it was not a charity.

Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. It was also said: concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. Makki said: concerning 'Uthman and Ibn 'Awf.

Al-mann (reminder of generosity) is mentioning the favor in the sense of enumerating it and reproaching with it. Al-adha (injury) is abuse and complaining, and it is more general than al-mann, because al-mann is a part of al-adha, but it was specifically mentioned because of how frequently it occurs.

Ibn Zayd held that this verse concerns those who do not go out to jihad, but instead spend while sitting at home, and that the former verse before it concerns those who go out themselves and with their wealth. He said: (p-60) "For this reason the condition was placed upon these, and was not placed upon the first."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this statement there is something to consider, because the arbitrariness in it is apparent.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "If you think that your greeting weighs heavily upon the one you spent upon, while you intend the face of Allah, then do not greet him." A woman said to him: "O Abu Usama, direct me to a man who truly goes out in the way of Allah, for they only go out to eat fruit. I have arrows and a quiver." He said to her: "May Allah not bless your arrows and your quiver, for you have injured them before you give to them."

Allah guaranteed the reward for the one who spends in the way of Allah, and the reward is Paradise. He negated fear for him after his death concerning what lies ahead, and grief over what has passed of his worldly life, because he is content with his Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 261–262:

The Exalted said:

﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains. And Allah multiplies for whom He wills. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders of their generosity or with injury, their reward is with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve.﴾

This verse, in its wording, is an explanation of a parable that shows the nobility and goodness of spending in the way of Allah, and it contains an exhortation to that. This verse concerns voluntary spending (nafaqat al-tatawwu'), and the ways (subul) of Allah are many. They include everything that is an act of obedience and that returns benefit to the Muslims and the community (milla). The most well-known and the greatest in benefit of these is jihad, so that the word of Allah may be the highest.

The word ḥabba (grain) is an ism jins (a collective noun for a kind), covering everything that the son of Adam sows and eats as food. The most well-known of these is wheat. The word ḥabb is often used to mean grain, and from it is the saying of al-Mutalammis:

"I have sworn that I will eat the grain of Iraq forever, while the weevil eats the grain in the village."

It is sometimes found that an ear of wheat contains a hundred grains, and in other grains the number is greater, but the parable was given with this amount. The Qur'an has stated that the good deed in all acts of righteousness is multiplied by ten times its like, and this verse indicates that the good reward for spending on jihad is seven hundred times, and the authentic hadith has clarified this.

The scholars differed regarding the meaning of His saying: ﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾. One group said: it explains and emphasizes what came earlier about the seven hundred, and there is no multiplication beyond seven hundred. Another group of scholars said: rather, it is an announcement that Allah the Exalted multiplies for whom He wills more than seven hundred times. It has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that the multiplication may reach, for whom Allah wills, two thousand (p-58) thousand, but this is not authentically transmitted from him. Ibn 'Umar said: "When this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) said, 'My Lord, increase my ummah.' So it was revealed: ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan so He will multiply it for him?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 245]. He said: 'My Lord, increase my ummah.' So it was revealed: ﴿Indeed, the patient will be given their reward without account﴾ [al-Zumar: 10]."

The word sunbula is on the pattern fun'ula, from asbala al-zar' meaning it released what is in it, as a garment is let down (yusbalu). The plural is sanabil.

In the Exalted's saying ﴿The likeness of those who﴾ there is an omitted noun (ḥadhf mudāf, an elided word attached to a noun in the genitive). Its estimate is: "the likeness of the spending of those who," or its estimate is: "like the likeness of one possessing a grain."

Al-Tabari said regarding this verse: that His saying ﴿in each ear a hundred grains﴾ means: if that is found; otherwise, it is on the basis that we assume it. Then he cited from al-Dahhak that he said: ﴿in each ear a hundred grains﴾ means: every ear produced a hundred grains. So al-Tabari made the saying of al-Dahhak similar to what he himself said, but that is not necessarily what can be derived from the wording of al-Dahhak.

Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: some read "mi'ata" (a hundred) in the accusative, on the estimate: "it produced a hundred grains."

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those who spend their wealth﴾, the verse: since in the verse before this there was a mention of spending in the way of Allah in general, this verse makes clear that this ruling applies only to the one who does not follow (p-59) his spending with reminders of generosity or with injury. That is because the one who spends in the way of Allah is only in one of three states. Either he intends the face of Allah the Exalted and hopes for His reward; this one expects nothing from the recipient and does not look at his circumstances in any way except to observe his deserving. Or he intends from the recipient a return in some form; this one has not intended the face of Allah, but rather looked to this condition of the recipient, and this is the one who, whenever his expectation is disappointed, reminds of his giving and injures. Or he spends compelled, to repel a debt, either out of shame before the recipient or another reason such as the attention of the spender or similar; this one has looked at a condition that is not for the face of Allah, and this is the one who, whenever he is followed up on and is embarrassed in some way of embarrassment, injures.

So reminders of generosity and injury reveal, about the one from whom they appear, that he was acting upon the intentions we have mentioned, and that he did not sincerely seek the face of Allah. For this reason, reminders and injury invalidate the charity, since each of them makes clear that it was not a charity.

Al-Naqqash mentioned that it was said: this verse was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. It was also said: concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib. Makki said: concerning 'Uthman and Ibn 'Awf.

Al-mann (reminder of generosity) is mentioning the favor in the sense of enumerating it and reproaching with it. Al-adha (injury) is abuse and complaining, and it is more general than al-mann, because al-mann is a part of al-adha, but it was specifically mentioned because of how frequently it occurs.

Ibn Zayd held that this verse concerns those who do not go out to jihad, but instead spend while sitting at home, and that the former verse before it concerns those who go out themselves and with their wealth. He said: (p-60) "For this reason the condition was placed upon these, and was not placed upon the first."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this statement there is something to consider, because the arbitrariness in it is apparent.

Zayd ibn Aslam said: "If you think that your greeting weighs heavily upon the one you spent upon, while you intend the face of Allah, then do not greet him." A woman said to him: "O Abu Usama, direct me to a man who truly goes out in the way of Allah, for they only go out to eat fruit. I have arrows and a quiver." He said to her: "May Allah not bless your arrows and your quiver, for you have injured them before you give to them."

Allah guaranteed the reward for the one who spends in the way of Allah, and the reward is Paradise. He negated fear for him after his death concerning what lies ahead, and grief over what has passed of his worldly life, because he is content with his Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 263–264:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury. And Allah is Free of need, Forbearing.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders [of your generosity] and injury, like one who spends his wealth to be seen by people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His example is like that of a smooth rock with a layer of dust on it; a heavy rain strikes it and leaves it bare. They have no power over anything of what they have earned. And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people.﴾

This is a definitive statement from Allah, exalted is He, that a kind word, which is supplication, companionship, and encouragement with what is with Allah, is better than charity that outwardly is charity but inwardly is nothing, because that kind word carries a reward, whereas this [charity] carries no reward.

Al-Mahdawi and others said: The estimate in its i'rab (grammatical analysis) is: "A kind word is better, and forgiveness is better."

(p-61) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In this there is a departure from the splendour of the meaning. The implied [element] should be like the apparent one. Forgiveness (maghfirah) is the covering of the need and the bad condition of the one in want. From this is the saying of the Bedouin, when he asked a people with eloquent speech and someone said to him, "Who are you, man?" He replied: "O Allah, forgiveness! Poor earning prevents one from lineage." And al-Naqqash said: It is said its meaning is: "And forgiveness for the petitioner if he is harsh or rude when he is refused."

Then He, exalted is He, informed of His self-sufficiency regarding the charity of one whose condition is this, and of the outcome of his affair, and of His forbearance toward whoever among His servants may commit this and be given respite.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders and injury﴾ — the verse. The creed is that evil deeds do not invalidate good deeds. The majority of scholars said regarding this verse: the charity whose owner Allah knows reminds or injures, his charity is not accepted. It was also said: rather, Allah appoints for the angel a sign regarding it, so he does not record it.

Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is the better [view], because what we derive from rational consideration regarding the sons of Adam is that the one who reminds and injures explicitly reveals that his intention was not for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, according to what we mentioned earlier. Therefore no charity is recorded for him. This is the invalidation of charity by reminder and injury. Reminder and injury in one charity do not invalidate other charities, since that does not expose the intention in the sound [charities] nor cast doubt upon them.

Then Allah likened this one who reminds and injures, according to the preceding of his intention, to one who spends for show (riya') and not for the sake of Allah. Riya' is a verbal noun from the form of "fa'ala" from "ru'yah" (seeing), as if riya' is a display and boasting among people who have no good in them. Al-Mahdawi said: the estimate is: "like the invalidation of one who spends for show."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day﴾, it may be that He means the manifest disbeliever, since one may spend so as to be called generous and to be praised with all kinds of praise, and for other reasons. It may also be that He means the hypocrite who displays faith.

Then He likened this one who spends for show to a smooth rock with dust upon it; the observer thinks it is fertile, good earth, just as a people suppose that the charity of this showy person has some worth or meaning. When a heavy rain strikes the smooth rock, that dust is uncovered and it remains bare. Likewise this showy person, when the Day of Resurrection comes and deeds are presented, and his secret is exposed, it becomes clear that his charity has no worth and no meaning.

So reminder, injury and show reveal the intention, thereby invalidating the charity, just as the heavy rain strips away the rock, removing what was supposed to be earth.

Talhah ibn Musarrif recited: "riya'a al-nas" without hamzah, and it is narrated from 'Asim.

(p-64) Al-safwan: the large, smooth stone. It was said: it is a plural whose singular is safwanah; and some said its singular is safwah; and it was said: it is a singular form whose plural is safy, which al-Mubarrad denied, saying: it is only the plural of safa. From this meaning come al-safwa' and al-safa. Imru' al-Qays said:

A bay horse whose saddle-cloth slips from the state of its back, as the smooth rock slipped from the one descending upon it.

And Abu Dhu'ayb said:

Until it is as if I am, for calamities, a flint-stone, struck at every moment upon the rock of al-Mashaqqar.

Al-Zuhri and Ibn al-Musayyab recited "safawanin" with a fatha on the fa', and this is a dialect.

Al-wabil is the heavy, strong rain, which flows over the surface of the earth. Al-sald among stones is the smooth, hard one with nothing in it; it is used figuratively for a head without hair, and from it is the saying of Ru'bah:

... shining of the brow, bald-headed...

Al-Naqqash said: al-sald means bare, in the dialect of Hudhayl. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿they have no power﴾ means by it those who spend for show, i.e., they cannot benefit from the reward of anything of their spending. The expression came with "yaqdiruna" according to the meaning of "alladhi," while the speech had previously been construed according to the wording of "alladhi." This is the usual pattern of Arabic speech; and if it had been construed first according to the meaning, it would have been ugly afterwards to construe it according to the wording.

(p-65) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ is either a general statement intended in particular regarding those who die upon disbelief, or it means that He did not guide them in their disbelief but rather it is pure misguidance, or it means that He does not guide them in their charities and deeds while they are upon disbelief.

What I have mentioned regarding this verse, of linguistic explanation and establishing meaning, is transmitted from the exegetes, even if their wordings have not come summarized in an explanation of the invalidation of charity by reminder and injury.
