Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 265:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He:

﴿And the likeness of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah and for the strengthening of their own souls is like a garden on a height: a heavy rain strikes it, and it yields its produce twofold; and if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain. And Allah is Seeing of what you do.﴾

Among the eloquent methods of the Qur'an is that it mentions the opposite of what has just been mentioned, so that the state of contrast becomes clear by presenting it to the mind. When Allah mentioned the charities of the people whose charities have no merit (khalaq), and forbade the believers from engaging in anything resembling that in any way, He followed in this verse by mentioning the expenditures of the people who abandoned their charities, which were in their correct form according to the Sharia, and so He struck a parable for them.

The implied meaning of the speech is: "The likeness of the expenditure of those who spend is like the likeness of the planting of a garden," because what is intended by mentioning the garden is its plantings. Or you may supply the implied element at the end of the speech, without supplying "expenditure" at its beginning, as if He had said: "like the likeness of one who plants a garden."

"Ibtighā'" (seeking) means "seeking/desiring," and its grammatical case is the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl). It could also have been construed as the accusative of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi), but the accusative as a verbal noun is the correct reading because of the coordination of the verbal noun "tathbītan" with it. It is not valid to take "tathbītan" as an accusative of purpose, because spending is not for the sake of strengthening.

Makki said in "al-Mushkil": both are accusatives of purpose, and this is rejected by what we have explained. "Marḍāt" (pleasure) is a verbal noun from raḍiya yarḍā (to be pleased).

Al-Sha'bī, al-Suddī, Qatāda, Ibn Zayd and Abū Ṣāliḥ said: "tathbītan" means "and certainty," that is, their souls have firm insights, so they strengthen them in spending in obedience to Allah, a strengthening. Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan said: the meaning of His saying "wa-tathbītan" is that they are careful (yatathabbatūn) about where they place their charities. Al-Ḥasan said: when a man intended to give charity, he would be careful; if it was for Allah, he would carry it out, and if doubt mixed with it, he would refrain. The first opinion is more correct, because the meaning that Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan went to is expressed by "wa-tathabbutan" (with a different form), and if someone objects: this is among the verbal nouns that come out of the pattern of the verb, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And devote yourself to Him with complete devotion﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 8], and His saying: ﴿And Allah has brought you forth from the earth as plants﴾ [Nuh: 17], the answer is that this is only permissible when the verbal noun is mentioned and the preceding verb is expressed explicitly. But when no verb has been explicitly stated, you are not permitted to bring a verbal noun with a meaning other than its own and then say: I construe it as the verb of such-and-such for a verb that has not previously been mentioned. This is the established usage of the Arabs as far as I know. Qatāda said: "tathbītan" means: and goodness from their souls.

The qadi Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is close to the first opinion. "Janna" is an orchard, a piece of land in which trees have grown until they cover the ground; it is derived from the same root as janīn (fetus), janan (concealment), and jannah, and "janna al-layl" (the night covered).

"Rabwa" is the land that rises slightly, with which generally comes the density of soil, its goodness, and its depth, and what is like this has the best growth.

The gardens of al-Ḥazn are not from this, as al-Ṭabarī claimed; rather those are the gardens attributed to Najd, because they are better than the gardens of Tihama, the plants of Najd are more fragrant, and its breeze is cooler and gentler, and Najd is called al-Ḥazn. The air of Tihama rarely becomes good except at night, and for this reason the Bedouin woman said:

"My husband is the night-time of Tihama."

Ibn 'Abbas said: "al-Rabwa is the elevated place in which rivers do not flow."

The qadi Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: He only meant by this the rabwa mentioned in the Book of Allah, because His saying, exalted is He, ﴿a heavy rain strikes it﴾ to the end of the verse indicates that there is no flowing water in it. Ibn 'Abbas did not mean that the type of elevated ground does not have flowing water in it, because Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned a rabwa that has a settled place and a spring.

What is known in Arabic usage is that the rabwa is what is raised above what is adjacent to it, whether water flows in it or not. Al-Ḥasan said: the rabwa is level land that does not rise above the water. He also meant that it is not like a mountain or a rocky hill and the like.

Al-Khalil said: the rabwa is elevated, good land. Allah specified for mention the one in which water does not flow, because that is the custom in the lands of the Arabs, so He gave them an example from what they commonly perceive.

Al-Suddī said: "bi-rabwa" means "bi-rubāwa," which is what is low of the land, but this expression is unsound. The word rabwa is derived from raba yarbū, meaning to increase. It is said "rubwa" with a damma on the ra', and this is how Ibn Kathir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read. It is said "rabwa" with a fatha on the ra', and this is how 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read, and similarly their difference in Surat al-Mu'minun. It is said "ribwa" with a kasra on the ra', and this is how Ibn 'Abbas read, as reported from him. It is said "rabāwa" with a fatha on the ra' and the ba' and an alif after it, and this is how Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read. It is said "ribāwa" with a kasra on the ra', and this is how al-Ashhab al-'Uqayli read.

"Ātat" means "gave," and "al-ukl" with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf is the fruit that is eaten; the edible thing from anything is called ukl. Its attribution to the garden is an attribution of specificity, like the saddle of the animal and the door of the house, since the fruit is not something the garden itself eats.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "uklahā" with a damma on the hamza and a sukun on the kaf, and likewise every noun attributed to a feminine noun. Abu 'Amr differed in what is attributed to a masculine noun, such as "ukuluhu," or what is attributed to a collective noun, such as "ukulin khamt," where Abu 'Amr read it with a heavy vowel and they read it lightly.

'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read all of what we have mentioned with the heavy form. It is said: ukul and ukl have the same meaning, and it is from akala, in the sense of ṭu'ma from ṭa'ima, that is, the thing that is fed and eaten. "Ḍi'fayn" means "two," in terms of what is estimated for it and measured from its like. Then Allah, exalted is He, emphasized the praise of this rabwa by saying that if a heavy rain does not strike it, then a light rain suffices for it and takes the place of the heavy rain, and that is due to the nobility of the land.

Al-ṭall is the fine, light drizzle of rain; Ibn 'Abbas and others said so, and it is the well-known meaning in the language. Some people said: al-ṭall is dew, and this is a figurative usage and comparison, and this has been narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Mubarrad said: its estimate is: "then a light rain suffices for it." Others said: the estimate is: "so what strikes it is a light rain," likening the growth of the expenditures of these sincere people whom Allah makes their charities grow, as the raising of a foal or a young camel, according to the hadith, to the growth of the plants of this garden on the described height. All of that is in contrast to the smooth rock from which its dust has been swept away, leaving it bare.

In His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ there is both promise and warning. al-Zuhrī read "ya'malūn" with the ya', as if he meant all people together, or meant only the hypocrites, in which case it is a pure promise.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 266:

(p-69) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of palm trees and grapevines, with rivers flowing beneath it, in which he has every kind of fruit, and old age has overtaken him while he has weak offspring, and then a whirlwind containing fire strikes it and it is burned? Thus Allah makes the signs clear to you, that you may give thought.﴾

Al-Tabari related from al-Suddi that this verse is another parable for the spending of showing-off (riya'), and al-Tabari preferred this view. He related from Ibn Zayd that he recited the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury﴾ [al-Baqarah: 264], and the verse to its end. He said: "Then He struck in that a parable, saying: ﴿Would any of you like…﴾," the verse. This is clearer than what al-Tabari preferred, and this verse is not another parable for the spending of showing-off; this is what the context of the discourse requires.

As for the meaning outside this context, it resembles the state of every hypocrite or disbeliever who acts while thinking that he is doing good, but when the time of need comes he finds nothing. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, asked the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) about this verse, and they said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said, angrily: "Say: 'We know' or 'we do not know'." Ibn 'Abbas said to him: "It is a parable that Allah struck, as if He said: Would any of you like to spend his life doing the deeds of the people of goodness, and then, when his life has run out and his term has drawn near, he ends that with a deed of the people of wretchedness?" 'Umar was content with that.

Ibn Abi Mulayka related that 'Umar recited this verse, "Would any of you like…", and said: "This is a parable struck for a person who does a righteous deed until, when he is at the end of his life and most in need of it, he does a deed of evil." This is a view that carries the verse over to everything that falls under its wording, and Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Rabi' and others said something similar.

He singled out palm trees and grapevines for mention because of their nobility and their excellence over the rest of the trees. al-Hasan recited "jannat" in the plural.

His saying "from beneath it" refers to beneath the trees. The waw in His saying "wa-asabahu" is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), and likewise in His saying "wa-lahu," and "du'afa'" is the plural of da'if, and likewise "di'af."

Al-I'sar is a violent, sweeping wind in which there is burning for everything it passes over. That occurs in extreme heat and occurs in extreme cold, and all of it comes from the blaze (fayh) of Hell and its breath, as the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) includes: "When the heat is intense, delay the prayer until it cools, for the intensity of heat is from the blaze of Hell, and the Fire complained to its Lord..." — the hadith in full. Either it is fire in its literal sense, or else it is its breath, which is found from it as its effect.

al-Suddi said: al-I'sar is a wind and a scorching fire (al-samum). Ibn 'Abbas said: a wind in which there is intense samum. Ibn Mas'ud said: the samum from which Allah created the jinn is one part of seventy parts of the Fire, meaning the Fire of the Hereafter. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: "i'sar fihi nar": a wind in which there is cold (sirr) and frost, and al-Dahhak said the same.

(p-71) And in the proverb: "If you were a wind, you have met a whirlwind" — and the wind is an i'sar because it squeezes the cloud (ta'siru al-sahab), and the clouds are "mu'sirat," either because they are pregnant, in which case they are like the woman who is "mu'sir" (one who is about to conceive), who is liable to pregnancy, or because they are squeezed by the winds. Ubayd Allah ibn al-Hasan al-'Anbari the judge explained it this way.

Ibn Sidah related that some people explained "al-mu'sirat" as the winds rather than the clouds. al-Zajjaj said: al-I'sar is a violent wind that rises from the earth to the sky, and it is the one called al-zawba'a.

al-Mahdawi said: it was called i'sar because it coils like a garment when it is wrung out (u'sira), and this is weak. The reference of "dhalika" is to these explanatory parables, and "la'allakum" expresses hope regarding human beings: that is, if one who is shown this clarification reflects, there is hope that he will give thought, and that he is fit for it.

Ibn 'Abbas said: "tatafakkarun" refers to the passing away and annihilation of this world, and the advent and endurance of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 267:

His words, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿O you who believe, spend of the good things you have earned and of what We have brought forth for you from the earth. And do not aim at the defective therein to spend from it, while you would not accept it yourselves unless you overlook in it. And know that Allah is Rich and Praiseworthy.﴾

This address is to the entire community of Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is a form of command concerning spending. The commentators differed: is the intended spending here the obligatory zakat or voluntary charity? 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), 'Ubaydah al-Salmani and Muhammad ibn Sirin said: it concerns obligatory zakat. It forbids people from spending the inferior in it in place of the good. As for voluntary charity, just as a person may give voluntarily a little, so too he may give voluntarily something lower in quantity, and a counterfeit dirham is better than a date. According to this view, the command is for obligation.

(p-72) What appears from the statements of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan and Qatadah is that the verse concerns voluntary charity. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah related, in meaning, that "the Ansar used to hang clusters of dates on a rope between two pillars in the mosque during the harvest days, and the poor Emigrants would eat from them. A man hung a bundle of worthless dates, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw it and said: 'How bad is what this one has hung!' Then the verse was revealed." According to this view, the command is for recommendation (nadb), and likewise they were encouraged not to give voluntarily except what is good and choice.

The verse encompasses both aspects, but the owner of zakat receives it as an obligation, and the owner of voluntary charity receives it as a recommendation.

All of these, and the majority of commentators, said: the meaning of "min tayyibat" is: from the good and choice of what you have earned; and they took "al-khabith" to mean the inferior and worthless.

Ibn Zayd said: its meaning is: from the lawful (halal) of what you have earned. He said: "And do not aim at the khabith" means the unlawful (haram). But Ibn Zayd's statement is not strong from the standpoint of the verse's structure, though not in its meaning in itself.

The phrase ﴿min tayyibat ma kasabtum﴾ may be understood as not intending either "good" or "lawful." Rather the meaning would be as if He had said: "Spend of what you have earned," and it is then an exhortation to spending only. Then the mention of "good" was introduced to specify a good quality in what is earned in general, and to affirm the blessing, as you say: "I fed so-and-so from the most satisfying bread, and gave him to drink from the most quenching water." On this understanding, "tayyib" encompasses both excellence and lawfulness. (p-73) This possibility is supported by 'Abd Allah ibn Mughaffal's saying: "There is nothing khabith in the wealth of a believer."

"Kasabtum" means: you had effort in it, either through bodily toil or through engaging in trade. Inherited wealth is included in this, because the one who did not inherit it has earned it, since the pronoun in "kasabtum" refers to humankind or to the believers.

﴿And of what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾: plants, minerals, buried treasure (rikaz), and whatever resembles these. "Tayammamu" means: you intend and aim at. It is said: "tayammama al-rajul kadha" when he aimed at it. From this is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"She aimed at the spring that is by Darij, whose moss the shade shelters..."

And from it is the verse of al-A'sha:

"You aimed at Qays, and how far beyond him, across the land, through a desert of rough terrain..."

From the same root is tayammum, which is the substitute for ablution when water is unavailable. Thus the majority of people recite it. Al-Bazzi related from Ibn Kathir the doubling of the ta' in thirty-one places, the first of which is this word.

al-Tabari related that in the recitation of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it is: "wa la ta'ammamu al-khabith," from amamtu when I aimed at, and from it comes "imam al-bina'" (the foundation/plan of a building). The meaning in both readings is one. al-Zuhri and Muslim ibn Jundub recited: "wa la tuyammimu" with a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the mim, and this is according to the dialect of those who say: "yammamtu al-shay'," meaning I aimed at it.

There are several dialectal forms of the word: amamtu al-shay' with a light first mim, and ammamtu with a doubled mim, and yammamtuhu and tayammamtuhu. Abu 'Amr related that Ibn Mas'ud recited "wa la tu'ammimu" with a hamza after the ta', and this is according to the dialect of those who say: "amma'mtu" with a heavy mim. The discussion of the meaning of "khabith" has already passed.

Al-Jurjani said in the book Nazm al-Qur'an: A group of people said: the speech is complete at His words "al-khabith." Then another statement begins describing the khabith, saying: "minhu tunfiqun" (from it you spend), while you would not take it except when you overlook, i.e., you are lenient.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this meaning seems like a rebuke and reprimand to people. The pronoun in "minhu" refers to "al-khabith." Al-Jurjani said: another group said: rather, the speech continues to His words "fihi" (in it), so the pronoun in "minhu" refers to "ma kasabtum," and "tunfiqun" comes in a position of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), like His saying: "I go out fighting in the way of Allah."

(p-75) The commentators differed concerning the meaning of His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And you would not take it except by overlooking in it﴾. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Dahhak and others said: its meaning is: and you would not take it in your debts and rights owed to you from people except by being lenient in that, and giving up some of your rights, while you dislike it and do not approve of it. That is, do not do with Allah what you would not approve for yourselves. al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the meaning of the verse is: "and you would not take it, even if you found it in the market being sold, except that its price be reduced for you."

Something similar is related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him). These two views resemble the verse concerning obligatory zakat. al-Bara' ibn 'Azib also said: its meaning is: and you would not take it even if it were given to you as a gift, except that you overlook it, i.e., you feel shy before the giver and accept from him what you have no need for and which has no worth in itself. This resembles the verse concerning voluntary charity. Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of the verse is: and you would not take the unlawful except that you overlook its disliked aspect.

The majority of people recited "illa an tughmidu" with a damma on the ta', sukun on the ghain, and a kasra on the mim. al-Zuhri recited with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the mim, lightened, and it is also related from him "tughammidu" with a damma on the ta', fatha on the ghain, and a doubled kasra on the mim. Makki related from al-Hasan al-Basri: "tughammadu" with a doubled and fathaed mim. Qatadah recited with a damma on the ta', sukun on the ghain, fatha on the mim, lightened. Abu 'Amr said: its meaning is: unless it is overlooked for you.

The qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: this word is derived either from the Arab saying: "aghmada al-rajul fi amr kadha" when he was lenient in it, accepted part of his right and let it pass. From this is the verse of al-Tirimmah ibn Hakim:

"A people did not get ahead of us in vengeance, and among the generous are folk who accept overlooking..."

Or it is derived from "taghmis al-'ayn" (closing the eye), because one who wants to endure something disliked closes his eyes to it. From this is the verse of the poet:

"Until when, and how many things from you trouble me, that I overlook, while I am not blind to them?"

This is like overlooking at what is disliked. Al-Naqqash mentioned this meaning in this verse, and Makki pointed to it. Or it is derived from the Arab saying: "aghmada al-rajul" when he came to an obscure matter, as one says "a'man" when he came to 'Uman, "a'raqa" when he came to Iraq, and "anjada" and "aghwara" when he came to Najd and to al-Ghawr, which is Tihama. From this is the saying of the girl: "wa in dasara aghmada" (and if he was deceived, he went into obscurity).

So the recitation of the majority is explained as: by way of overlooking, and as closing the eye, because aghmada is like ghamuda; and as meaning until you come upon something obscure in interpretation and consideration regarding taking it, either because it is unlawful according to Ibn Zayd's view, or because it is a gift or taken in a debt according to others' view.

As for al-Zuhri's first recitation, its meaning is: that you cut down its price from the seller, so that he diminishes you. Abu 'Amr said the meaning of al-Zuhri's two recitations is: until you take with a deficiency. As for his second recitation, this is Abu 'Amr al-Dani's view of it, and it may be from closing the eye.

As for Qatadah's recitation, I have mentioned Abu 'Amr's explanation of it. Ibn Jinni said: its meaning is: you will be found to have been made to overlook the matter by your interpretation, or by your leniency, and you went along with what is not foremost to the souls. This is like when you say: "ahmadtu al-rajul" (I found the man praiseworthy), meaning I found him praised, and other similar examples.

Then He, may He be exalted, drew attention to the attribute of richness, that is, He has no need of your charities. Whoever draws near and seeks reward, let him do so with his wealth. And "Hamid" means: praiseworthy in every state, and it is an attribute of His essence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 268–269:

(p-77) His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty and commands you to indecency, while Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ ﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills, and whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good. And none will be reminded except those of understanding.﴾

This verse and what follows, although they are not a command to give charity, are conducive to souls giving charity. In them the Mighty and Majestic makes clear the incitements, whisperings and enmity of Shaytan. He reminds of His reward, for He has no Lord other than Himself; He reminds of His favour in giving wisdom, praises it, and points out that the people of intellect are the ones who remember, those who through wisdom assess the measure of spending in obedience to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and other than that.

Then He mentioned His knowledge of every expenditure and vow, and in that is both promise and warning. Then He explained the ruling on open and secret giving, and so on to the end of the meaning.

In the speech of the Arabs, a promise, when stated without qualification, is for good; but when the object promised is specified, it may be qualified by good or by evil, as with glad tidings. This verse is one in which the promise is qualified by something disliked, namely poverty.

Al-fahsha': everything that is shameful; and the mention of what is shameful is shameful, and all acts of disobedience to Allah are fahsha'. Ḥaywa narrated from a man from the people of the Ribāṭ that he recited "al-Fuqr" with a ḍamma on the fa', and this is a dialect (lugha). Ibn 'Abbas said: in the verse there are two from Shaytan and two from Allah the Exalted.

Ibn Mas'ud narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Indeed Shaytan has a whisper (lamma) into the son of Adam, and the angel has a whisper. As for the whisper of Shaytan, it is a promise of evil and denial of the truth; so whoever finds that, let him seek refuge. As for the whisper of the angel, it is a promise of good and affirmation of the truth; so whoever finds that, let him praise Allah." Then he (peace be upon him) recited: ﴿The Shaytan threatens you with poverty and commands you﴾, the verse.

Al-maghfira: it is the covering over of His servants in this world and the Hereafter. Al-fadl: it is provision in this world and expansion in it, and bliss in the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted has promised all of these.

Al-Naqqash mentioned that some people take comfort in this verse that poverty is better than wealth, because Shaytan only distances the servant from good, and by frightening him with poverty he keeps him far from it.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: There is no decisive proof in the verse, but the argument from it is strong. It is narrated that in the Torah: "My servant, spend from My provision, and I will extend My bounty upon you, for My hand is outstretched over every outstretched hand." And in the Qur'an is its confirmation, namely: ﴿And whatever you spend, He will replace it, and He is the best of providers﴾ [Saba: 39]. And "Wāsi'" (All-Encompassing) because He encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge.

Then He informed, exalted is He, about Himself that He ﴿gives wisdom﴾, i.e. He gives it to whom He wills of His servants, (p-79) and the interpreters differed regarding wisdom (ḥikma) in this place. Al-Suddi said: wisdom is prophethood. Ibn 'Abbas said: it is knowledge of the Qur'an, its jurisprudence (fiqh), its abrogating and abrogated (nasikh and mansukh), its clear and ambiguous verses, and its Arabic. Qatada said: wisdom is understanding (fiqh) of the Qur'an, as Mujahid also said. Mujahid also said: wisdom is correctness in speech and action. Ibn Zayd and his father Zayd ibn Aslam said: wisdom is intellect in religion. Malik said: wisdom is knowledge of the religion, understanding of it, and following it. Ibn al-Qasim narrated from him that he said: wisdom is reflection on the command of Allah and following it. He also said: wisdom is obedience to Allah, and understanding of the religion and acting upon it. Al-Rabi' said: wisdom is fear (khashya). From this is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The head of everything is the fear of Allah the Exalted." Ibrahim said: wisdom is understanding. Zayd ibn Aslam, and al-Hasan said: wisdom is scrupulousness (wara').

All these statements, apart from the statement of al-Suddi, are close to one another, because ḥikma is a verbal noun from iḥkām, which is perfection in an action or a speech. The Book of Allah is wisdom, and the Sunna of His Prophet is wisdom, and everything that has been mentioned is a part of wisdom, which is the genus. Al-Jumhur read "man yu'ta al-ḥikmata" with the verb in the passive. Al-Zuhri and Ya'qub read "wa man yu'ti" with a kasra on the ta', meaning: and whoever Allah gives wisdom to; so "man" is the first object, placed first, and "al-ḥikmata" is the second object. Al-Akhfash read "wa man yu'tihi al-ḥikmata". Al-Rabi' ibn Khuthaym read "tu'ti al-ḥikmata man tashā'" with the ta' on "tu'ti", and on "tashā'" with a dot above (the ta' is pointed from above), and "wa man yu'ta al-ḥikmata" with the ya'.

The rest of the verse is a clear reminder and an arousal of the aspirations of heedlessness. Al-albāb: intellects; its singular is lubb.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 270–271:

(p-80) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified:

﴿And whatever expenditure you spend, or whatever vow you vow, indeed Allah knows it. And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers.﴾ ﴿If you disclose your charities, then how excellent they are. But if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you, and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

Vows were among the customs of the Arabs, and they made them often. So God mentioned both kinds: that which a person does voluntarily, and that which he does after obligating himself to it. It is said: "nadhara al-rajul kadha" (the man vowed such-and-such) when he obligates himself to doing it; the verb is yanduru with a dammah on the dhal, and yandhiru with a kasrah.

As for His saying, ﴿indeed Allah knows it﴾, Mujahid said: its meaning is "He counts it." In the verse there is both promise and threat: whoever is sincere in intention is rewarded, and whoever spends for show or for another purpose that is revealed by reminding of favours and by harm and the like, he is a wrongdoer; his action goes to waste, and he finds no helper in it. He used the singular pronoun in "yaʻlamuhu" although two things were mentioned, because what is meant is what was mentioned or the one that was specified.

As for His saying, ﴿If you disclose the charities﴾, the verse... Most of the exegetes held that this verse concerns voluntary charity. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah made secret voluntary charity surpass its public form, said to be by seventy times, and made public obligatory charity better than its secret form, said to be by twenty-five times. He said: and likewise all obligatory and voluntary acts in all things."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is strengthened by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A man's prayer in his house is better than his prayer in the mosque, except the obligatory prayer," because obligatory acts are not open to show-off, whereas voluntary acts are liable to it.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: this verse concerns voluntary charity. Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: this verse was revealed only concerning charity to the Jews and the Christians, and he used to order that zakat be distributed in secret. This is rejected, especially by the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih). Al-Tabari said: the people are agreed that making obligatory charity manifest is better. Al-Mahdawi said: it has also been said that the verse refers to obligatory zakat and what is given voluntarily, and that concealment in both was better during the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him; then people's suspicions grew after that, so scholars regarded it as good to make obligatory charity public, lest anyone be suspected of withholding. This view contradicts the reports. In our time, it would be similar that it is good to conceal obligatory charity, since withholding has become widespread and publicizing it has become liable to show-off. Al-Naqqash said: this verse was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 274].

His saying ﴿fa-ni'immā hiya﴾ is praise of making charity public; then He judged that concealment is better than that disclosure.

The readers differed concerning His saying ﴿fa-ni'immā hiya﴾. Nafi', other than through the narration of Warsh, Abu 'Amr, and 'Asim through the narration of Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read "fa-ni'ma" with a kasrah on the nun and a sukun on the ayn.

'Asim through the narration of Hafs, Ibn Kathir, and Nafi' through the narration of Warsh read "fa-ni'imma" with a kasrah on the nun and on the ayn. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "fa-na'immā" with a fathah on the nun and a kasrah on the ayn. All of them doubled the mim.

Abu 'Ali said: whoever reads with a sukun on the ayn, his reading is not sound, because it joins two consecutive sukun letters, the first of which is not a letter of madd and lin. According to the grammarians, that is permissible only when the first is a letter of madd, since the madd takes the place of the vowel, as in dabbatin and dawallin and the like. Perhaps Abu 'Amr weakened the vowel and reduced it, as he does with the ikhfa' in "bari'kum" and "ya'murukum," so the listener thought it a sukun because of its subtlety and faintness in hearing.

As for whoever reads "ni'imma" with a kasrah on the nun and the ayn, his argument is that the original word is ni'im with a kasrah on the fa' because of the guttural letter, and it is not permissible that he be one who says "ni'ma," as you see that whoever says "hadha qadamu malikin" assimilates it in "ha'ulai qawmu malikin" and "jismu majidin."

Sibawayh said: "ni'imma" with a kasrah on the nun and the ayn is not in the dialect of the one who says "ni'ma" with a sukun on the ayn, but in the dialect of the one who says "ni'im" with a vowel on the ayn. Abu al-Khattab related to us that it is the dialect of Hudhayl, and its kasrah, as he said, is play; and if the one who said "ni'imma" were one who says "ni'ma" with a sukun on the ayn, the assimilation would not be permitted.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: It seems that this is ruled out because it leads to two consecutive sukuns.

Abu 'Ali said: As for whoever reads "na'immā" with a fathah on the nun and a kasrah on the ayn, he has brought the word according to its original form, which is na'im. From this is the poet's saying:

"What my two feet carried—indeed they,
how excellent were those who strove in the matter that is clear."

And it is not permissible that he be one who says before assimilation "ni'ma" with a sukun on the ayn. Al-Mahdawi said: that is permissible and possible, and the ayn is kasrah after assimilation because of the meeting of two sukuns.

Abu 'Ali said: The "ma" in His saying "ni'imma" is in the position of accusative, and His saying "hiya" is an explanation of the hidden subject mentioned before. The estimate is: "ni'ma shay'an ibda'uha" (how excellent a thing is its disclosure). The disclosure is the thing specified for praise, except that the mudaf (the governed noun) was omitted and the mudaf ilayh (the noun governing it) was put in its place. What indicates this is His saying: ﴿so it is better for you﴾, that is, concealment is better. Just as the pronoun here refers to concealment and not to the charities, so likewise at first the subject is disclosure, and it is what the pronoun was attached to; disclosure was omitted and the pronoun of the charities was put in its place.

The readers differed in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and He will remove﴾. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, and 'Asim through the narration of Abu Bakr read "wa-nukaffiru" with a nun and a raf' on the ra'. Nafi', Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-nukaffir" with a nun and a jazm on the ra'. The same is also related from 'Asim. Ibn 'Amir read "wa-yukaffiru" with a ya' and a raf' on the ra'. Ibn 'Abbas read "wa-tukaffir" with a ta' and a kasrah on the fa' and a jazm on the ra'. 'Ikrimah read "wa-tukaffar" with a ta' and a fathah on the fa' and a jazm on the ra'. Al-Hasan read "wa-yukaffir" with a ya' and a jazm on the ra'. It is related from al-A'mash that he read "wa-yukaffira" with a ya' and a nasb on the ra'. Abu Hatim said: al-A'mash read "yukaffir" with a ya' without a waw before it and with a jazm on the ra'.

Al-Mahdawi related from Ibn Hurmuz that he read "wa-tukaffaru" with a ta' and a raf' on the ra'. It is related from 'Ikrimah and Shahr ibn Hawshab that they both read with a ta' and a nasb on the ra'.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Whatever of these readings has a nun is the nun of majesty; whatever has a ta' is the charity acting, except that which is related from 'Ikrimah with a fathah on the fa', for the ta' in that reading belongs only to the misdeeds. Whatever has a ya' is that Allah, may He be exalted, is the One who expiates; and giving in secrecy is also what expiates, as Makki mentioned. As for the raf' on the ra', it has two aspects: one is that the verb is the predicate of a nominal sentence, its estimate being "wa-nahnu nukaffiru" (and We expiate), or "wa-hiya tukaffiru," meaning the charity, or "wallahu yukaffiru" (and Allah expiates). The second is cutting off and resuming, so that the waw is not conjunctive for sharing, but for coordinating one sentence with another. As for the jazm on the ra', it is treating the speech according to the position of His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so it is better﴾, since it is in the position of a jazm as the answer to the condition, as if He said: "And if you conceal them, it will be greater for your reward," then He coordinated it with this position, just as in the reading of one who read: "man yudlili Allahu fa-la hadiya lahu wa-nadharhum" with a jazm on the ra'. Examples of this are many.

As for the nasb on the ra', it is on the estimate of "an" (that), and consider this. Al-Mahdawi said: it is made similar to the nasb in answer to an interrogative, since the conditional requires one thing because another thing is required, as in the interrogative. The jazm on the ra' is the most eloquent of these readings, because it indicates that the expiation enters into the conditional, and that it is conditioned upon the concealment occurring; whereas the raf' on the ra' does not carry this meaning.

The "min" in His saying "min sayyi'atikum" is for pure partitiveness, and the meaning in that is firmly established. Al-Tabari related from a group that they said "min" is extra in this place, and that is an error on their part.

His saying ﴿And Allah is Acquainted with what you do﴾ is promise and threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 270–271:

But if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you, and He will remove from you some of your misdeeds. And Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾

In the verse there is both promise and threat: whoever is sincere in intention is rewarded, and whoever spends for show or for another purpose that is revealed by reminding of favours and by harm and the like, he is a wrongdoer; his action goes to waste, and he finds no helper in it. He used the singular pronoun in "yaʻlamuhu" although two things were mentioned, because what is meant is what was mentioned or the one that was specified.

As for His saying, ﴿If you disclose the charities﴾, the verse... Most of the exegetes held that this verse concerns voluntary charity. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah made secret voluntary charity surpass its public form, said to be by seventy times, and made public obligatory charity better than its secret form, said to be by twenty-five times. He said: and likewise all obligatory and voluntary acts in all things."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is strengthened by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A man's prayer in his house is better than his prayer in the mosque, except the obligatory prayer," because obligatory acts are not open to show-off, whereas voluntary acts are liable to it.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: this verse concerns voluntary charity. Yazid ibn Abi Habib said: this verse was revealed only concerning charity to the Jews and the Christians, and he used to order that zakat be distributed in secret. This is rejected, especially by the righteous predecessors (al-salaf al-salih). Al-Tabari said: the people are agreed that making obligatory charity manifest is better. Al-Mahdawi said: it has also been said that the verse refers to obligatory zakat and what is given voluntarily, and that concealment in both was better during the time of the Prophet, peace be upon him; then people's suspicions grew after that, so scholars regarded it as good to make obligatory charity public, lest anyone be suspected of withholding. This view contradicts the reports. In our time, it would be similar that it is good to conceal obligatory charity, since withholding has become widespread and publicizing it has become liable to show-off. Al-Naqqash said: this verse was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly﴾ [al-Baqarah: 274].

The Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on Surah 2, Verse 272:

Allah the Mighty and Majestic said:

﴿It is not upon you to guide them, but Allah guides whom He wills. Whatever good you spend is for yourselves, and you spend only seeking the Face of Allah. Whatever good you spend will be repaid to you in full, and you will not be wronged.﴾

It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse: "The Muslims used to give charity to the poor among the People of the Dhimma (non-Muslim protected subjects). When the poor among the Muslims increased, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Give charity only to the people of your religion.' So this verse was revealed," permitting charity to those who are not of the religion of Islam.

Al-Naqqash mentioned that "the Prophet, upon him be peace, received some charity, and a Jew came to him and said: 'Give me.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'You have no share of the charity of the Muslims.' The Jew went off not far, and then the verse was revealed: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him and gave him. Then Allah abrogated that by the verse of the alms (naskh, abrogation, by the verse on zakat)."

It is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that some of the Ansar had relatives among the Banu Qurayza and al-Nadir, and they would not give charity to them, out of desire that they would embrace Islam when they were in need. So the verse was revealed because of that.

Some exegetes (tafsir, interpretation of the Qur'an) related that Asma' bint Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with them both, wished to give to her grandfather Abu Quhafa, but then refrained from that because he was a disbeliever, and the verse was revealed concerning that.

Al-Tabari mentioned that the Prophet's ﷺ intention in withholding charity was only that they might become Muslims and enter the religion. So Allah said: ﴿It is not upon you to guide them﴾.

This charity which was permitted to them, according to what these reports include, is only voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'). As for obligatory charity (zakat), giving it to a disbeliever is not valid. This ruling is conceivable for Muslims today with their protected non-Muslims, and with the enslaved from among the enemy combatants.

Ibn al-Mundhir said: The scholars whom I know have agreed (ijma', scholarly consensus) that a dhimmi is not given anything from the zakat on wealth. Then he mentioned a group of those who stated this explicitly, and he did not mention any disagreement. Al-Mahdawi said: "It was permitted for Muslims to give to their polytheist relatives from the obligatory charity by this verse." This is rejected in my view.

The guidance which is not upon Muhammad ﷺ is the creation of faith in their hearts. As for the guidance which is the invitation (to the truth), it is upon him, but it is not what is meant in this verse. Then Allah, the Exalted, informed that He is the One who guides whom He wills, that is, He grants them right direction. In this there is a refutation of the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination) and the groups of the Mu'tazila.

Then He informed that a person's expenditure seeking reward is only for himself, so he should not care where it falls. Then Allah, the Exalted, made clear that the expenditure that is counted and accepted is only that which is done seeking the Face of Allah. This is one of the interpretations of His saying: ﴿and you spend only seeking the Face of Allah﴾. There is another interpretation of it, namely that it is a testimony from Allah, the Exalted, to the Companions that they spend only seeking His Face. So it is a report from Him to them, containing a commendation. According to the other interpretation, it is a condition placed upon them, and the condition includes others from the Ummah. The word "ibtighaa'" (seeking) is in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih).

Then He mentioned that the reward for spending will be paid in full to those who spend, meaning in the Hereafter, and they will not be deprived of anything of it, so that deprivation would be a wrong done to them. This is the explanation of His saying: ﴿Whatever good you spend is for yourselves﴾.

The "good" (khayr) in this verse is wealth, because it is connected with the mention of spending. This connection indicates that it is wealth. Where it is not connected with anything indicating that it means wealth, it does not necessarily mean wealth, such as His saying: ﴿better in dwelling﴾ [al-Furqan: 24] and His saying: ﴿whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ [al-Zalzala: 7], and so on.

What we have said is a precaution against the statement of 'Ikrima: "Every 'good' (khayr) in the Book of Allah means wealth."

[p. 88] The lām in His words "for the poor" (lil-fuqarā') is connected to an omitted element, its implied sense being: the spending or the charity is for the poor.

Mujāhid, al-Suddī and others said: by these poor are meant the poor among the Emigrants (muhājirūn) from Quraysh and others. Then the verse encompasses everyone who falls under the description of poverty until the end of time. God specified the poor Emigrants for mention only because there were no others there, since the Helpers (anṣār) were people of wealth and trade in their own land. [p. 88] Then God, by His words, "who have been confined in the way of God," clarified the circumstances of those poor Emigrants that make compassion toward them obligatory. The meaning of uḥṣirū is: they were held back and prevented. Some lexicographers held that uḥṣira and ḥuṣira have one meaning, namely being confined and prevented, whether this is by an enemy or by sickness or other excuses; this was related by Ibn Sīda and others.

Al-Suddī interpreted iḥṣār here as being caused by the enemy. Others held that uḥṣira is used for sickness and excuses, while ḥuṣira is used for the enemy. On this basis Ibn Zayd and Qatāda interpreted it, and al-Ṭabarī preferred it, and he construed in this verse that they are the ones who confine themselves by the bond of religion, the intention of jihad, and fear of the enemy, since disbelief had encircled them, so the fear of the enemy became an excuse by which they were confined.

The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This is a sound view, as if these excuses confined them, meaning they made them people who are confined, just as they say: qabarahu ("he buried him") means he placed him in his grave, and aqbarahu ("he made him a grave-owner") means he made him one who has a grave. Thus the enemy and every encircling thing confines, and the preventing excuses confine, with the tā' of uḥṣirū pronounced with a ḍamma and the ṣād with a kasra, meaning they make the person like one who is surrounded by it. God's words "in the way of God" may refer to jihad, and may refer to entering Islam, and the wording encompasses both.

Ḍarb fi'l-arḍ ("striking through the land") means engaging in trade, and ḍarb al-arḍ is walking to relieve a person's need in the open. They were unable to strike through the land because the lands were entirely disbelief, and this was at the beginning of the Emigration. Their small numbers prevented them from earning through jihad, and the disbelievers' denial of their Islam prevented them from engaging in trade, so they remained poor, except that they were withdrawn, abstaining from asking and relying upon God, such that the ignorant person who does not know their inner states supposes them to be wealthy.

[p. 89] Al-ta'affuf is a form of tafa''ul with the intensive tā', from ʿaffa ʿan al-shay' ("he refrained from the thing") when he withheld from it and kept himself free of seeking it. Qatāda and others interpreted it in this sense.

Nāfi', Abū ʿAmr and al-Kisā'ī read yaḥsibuhum with a kasra on the sīn, and this verb is so throughout the Qur'an. Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim and Ḥamza read yaḥsabuhum with a fatḥa on the sīn throughout the Qur'an. Both are dialectal forms of yaḥsab, like ʿahida yaʿhadu and yaʿhidu, with fatḥa and kasra of the hā' in many words that come in this pattern. Abū ʿAlī said: fatḥ the sīn in yaḥsab is more analogical, because the ʿayn of the past tense is kasra, so its pattern is that it should come in the present tense with fatḥa. The reading with kasra is good by virtue of its being transmitted, even though it is irregular with respect to analogy.

The "min" in His words "from [their] abstinence" (min al-ta'affuf) indicates the starting point, meaning: from their abstinence the ignorant person's supposing begins. It is not for indicating the kind, because the ignorant person regarding them does not suppose them rich with the richness of abstinence; rather he supposes them rich with the richness of wealth, and his supposing arises from their abstinence. This is on the understanding that they practise complete abstinence from begging, which is what the majority of exegetes hold, because in explaining His words, "they do not ask people insistently," they said: the meaning is: they do not ask at all. The verse may bear another meaning in which "min" indicates the kind, which we will mention later.

Al-sīmā, with a shortened vowel, means the sign. Some Arabs say al-sīmiyā' with an added yā' and with the long vowel, and from this is the poet's saying:

"... He has a sīmiyā' that does not strain the sight."

The exegetes differed in specifying this sīmiyā' by which these abstainers are recognized. Mujāhid said: it is humility and lowliness. Al-Suddī and al-Rabīʿ said: it is the effect of need and the distress of poverty on their faces, and scarcity of blessing. Ibn Zayd said: it is the wretchedness of condition. [p. 90] Some people, and Makkī related it, said: it is the mark of prostration, and this is the best view, because they were free, reliant upon God, with no occupation for the most part except prayer, so the mark of prostration was always upon them.

Al-ilḥāf and al-ilḥāḥ have one meaning. Some said: it is derived from alḥafa al-shay' when he covered it and enveloped it with covering, and from it comes al-liḥāf (the blanket), and from it is the saying of Ibn Aḥmar:

"He keeps surrounding them with his two wings,
and covers them, a fluttering, thick (wing)."

He describes the male ostrich sitting over eggs. So this insistent asker envelops people with his request, and so it covers them. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Zajjāj and others held that the meaning is: they do not ask at all. The verse bears both meanings: negation of asking altogether, and negation of insistent asking only. As for the first, it is on the basis that abstinence is a fixed attribute of theirs, and the ignorant person who does not know their poverty, because of their abstinence, supposes them rich in wealth, [p. 91] and "min" is for the starting point, and His words "they do not ask people insistently" do not mean that they ask without insistence; rather, the point is to draw attention to the bad state of the one who asks people insistently, as you say: "This is a good man who does not kill Muslims," where "good" implies that he does not kill and does not disobey, even in lesser matters; then by your saying "does not kill Muslims" you draw attention to the ugliness of the act of another who does kill. Such phrasing is often used when the one being drawn attention to is present in the matter, pointed to in the mind of the speaker and the listener. Insistent begging was never absent from a period of time, and it is something disliked, so attention was drawn to it. As for the second meaning, it is on the basis that abstinence falls within the supposing, meaning they do not appear to be asking; rather, it is rare.

In summary: the ignorant person, despite his knowledge of their poverty, supposes them rich in abstinence, so "min" indicates the kind on this interpretation. Then He negated insistent asking from them, and the rest of asking remains established for them according to what the implication of the discourse (dalīl al-khiṭāb, the argument from implied meaning) requires. This meaning, negating only insistent asking, is what al-Suddī's wording implies.

Al-Zajjāj, may God have mercy on him, said: the meaning is: there is no asking from them, so there is no insistence. This is like the statement of Imru' al-Qays:

"Upon a faint trail whose landmark cannot be followed..."

That is: there is no landmark, so there is no guidance.

[p. 92] The qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may God have mercy on him, said: If al-Zajjāj meant that there is no asking from them at all, the words after "lā" do not convey that, and asking is negated only if the meaning is controlled from the beginning of the verse as we have set forth. If he meant: there is no insistent asking from them, then that is the explicit text of the verse.

As for his comparing the verse to the verse of Imru' al-Qays, it is incorrect, because his saying:

"Upon a faint trail whose landmark cannot be followed..."

and his other saying:

"Halt by the abandoned campsites that antiquity has not effaced..."

and the saying of another:

"The one whose tyranny in judgment I feared,
I did not fear your tyranny, O ʿĀfiya!"

and what is similar to these, is an arrangement from which it is understood that the guidance by the landmark cannot occur even though the landmark exists. So [p. 93] only the meaning to which the particle of negation is attached is negated, and likewise effacement is negated even though antiquity exists, and likewise fear is negated even though tyranny exists. This arrangement does not apply in the verse.

It is possible that the poets meant that the second element is non-existent, and therefore they attached the particle of negation to the first, since the first is not valid except by the existence of the second: meaning, there is no landmark, so there is no guidance by a landmark; there is no antiquity, so there is no effacement; there is no tyranny, so there is no fear. His words, "they do not ask people insistently," do not carry anything of this, because the particle of negation has entered upon a general matter covering insistent asking and other asking, then the part of that general matter, namely insistent asking, was specified by His words "insistently." So it is not by the non-existence of insistent asking that asking is negated; and in the poetic verse the first is negated by the non-existence of the second, since the particle of negation entered upon something whose existence depends on the existence of that which is meant to be non-existent. Asking is not like this with insistence; rather, the matter is the reverse, since insistence may be absent from them while they still have asking without insistence.

Had the statement been, "they do not insistently ask people for anything," it would have come close to the preceding verses. Likewise, had the continuation been, "they do not ask anything, when the act of asking is absent," as if you said: "by earning" or something similar, the resemblance would have been valid. And God is the One sought for help.

His words, "And whatever good you spend, indeed God knows it," are a pure promise, meaning He knows it and counts it, in order to requite it and reward it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verses 274–275:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He:

﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, theirs is their reward with their Lord; there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve.﴾ ﴿Those who consume interest (ribā) will not stand except as one stands whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch. That is because they say, "Trade is only like interest," and Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest. So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists, he shall have what is past, and his affair is up to Allah. But whoever returns—those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein forever.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: This verse was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, who had four dirhams. He gave one dirham in charity at night, one by day, one secretly, and one openly. Ibn Juraij said: It was revealed concerning a man who did that, and he did not name 'Ali or anyone else. Ibn 'Abbas also said: This verse was revealed concerning the fodder of horses. This was also said by 'Abdullah ibn Bishr al-Ghafiqi, Abu Dhar, Abu Usama, al-Awza'i, and Abu al-Darda', who said: It concerns the fodder of horses and of those tethered in the way of Allah. Qatada said: This verse concerns those who spend in the way of Allah without extravagance or stinginess.

Although the verse was revealed concerning 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, its meaning encompasses everyone who does his deed and everyone who goes out at night with his charity seeking one in need. As for the fodder of horses and the expense upon them, the wording of the verse encompasses them firmly, and likewise the one who spends in jihad directly; his spending falls within the ranks of the verse.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The believers acted upon these verses from His saying, ﴿If you disclose your charities﴾ [al-Baqara: 271] up to His saying, ﴿nor shall they grieve﴾. When the surah of Bara'a was revealed with the detailed explanation of zakat, they restricted themselves to it. The discussion of the negation of fear and grief has already preceded.

The fa' (then) in His saying, "fa-lahum" (then for them), entered because of the indefiniteness in "alladhina" (those who). It resembles, in its indefiniteness, the indefiniteness found in the conditional, so the fa' is fitting in its response just as it is fitting in the conditional. The resemblance occurs only when "alladhi" is joined to a verb and when no governing particle enters upon "alladhi" that changes its meaning. If you say, "alladhi abuhu Zayd huwa 'Amr" (the one whose father is Zayd is 'Amr), the fa' is not fitting in your saying "fahuwa" (then he is), rather it would confuse the meaning. And if you say, "layta alladhi ja'ani ja'ani" (would that the one who came to me had come to me), the fa' has no place in the meaning. This mentioned fa' comes only to emphasize the meaning, and it may be dispensed with when emphasis is not intended, as in His saying after it, "la yaqumuna" (they do not stand).

His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿Those who consume interest﴾ and the rest of the verse. Ribā: it is excess, derived from "raba yarbu" when it grows and increases beyond what it was. Its most common form is what the Arabs used to do, saying to the debtor, "Will you pay or will you increase (turbi)?" The debtor would add to the amount of the wealth, and the creditor would be patient with him. Among clear forms of ribā is differential exchange in the same kind, because it is an increase. Likewise, most forbidden sales are prohibited only because of the meaning of an increase, either in the substance of the property or in a benefit for one of the two parties, such as delay and the like.

Among sales there are some that contain no meaning of increase, such as selling fruit before its ripening, and selling at the time of the call to prayer on Friday. If the doer of these is called "one who consumes ribā," it is by figurative usage and comparison.

Ribā is from the roots with waw, and its dual is "ribawān" according to Sibawayh; it is written with an alif. The Kufans said: it is written and made dual with a ya' because of the kasra at its beginning, and they say likewise of triliteral words from the waw roots when the first letter is kasra or damma, such as "duha". If it is fatha, as in "safa", then it follows what the Basrans said.

The meaning of this verse: those who earn ribā and practise it. He intended the word "consumption" (akl), because it is the strongest aim of a person regarding wealth, and because it indicates greed. So this part of the consequences of earning was put in place of the whole of earning. Clothing, housing, saving, and spending on dependants and other things are all included in His saying: ﴿those who consume﴾.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr, Qatada, al-Rabi', al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning of His saying "la yaqumuna" is that they will not rise from their graves on the Day of Resurrection. Some of them said: a devil will be made to accompany him, strangling him. And they all said: he will be raised like a madman as a punishment for him and as a disgrace at the gathering of the place of assembly. What strengthens this interpretation, on which there is consensus, is that in the reading of 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud: "la yaqumuna yawm al-qiyama illa kama yaqumu al-majnun" (they will not stand on the Day of Resurrection except as the madman stands). As for the wording of the verse, it could bear the comparison of the state of one who stands with eagerness and greed for the trade of ribā to the standing of a madman, because desire and longing agitate him until his limbs convulse. This is like what you say of one hastening in his walk, confused in the form of his movements, whether from fright or otherwise: "This one has gone mad." Al-A'sha compared his camel in her liveliness to madness in his saying:

"And she comes in the morning after the fatigue of travel, as if a madness of the jinn from a phantom had touched her."

But what the reading of Ibn Mas'ud transmitted, and what the statements of the exegetes concurred upon, weakens this interpretation.

"Yatakhabbatuhu" is of the form yatafa"alu from khabata yakhbitu, just as you say: tamallakahu, ta'abbadahu, and tahammalahu. "Al-mass" is madness, and likewise "al-awlaq", "al-als", and "al-zu'd".

His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿That is because they say, "Trade is only like interest"﴾ means, according to all the interpreters, concerning the disbelievers, and that it is a statement of denial of the Sharia and a rejection of it. The whole verse was revealed concerning the disbelieving usurers, and to them it was said, "he shall have what is past." This is not said to a sinning believer, but the sinners who engage in ribā take a portion of the threat of this verse.

Then He, Exalted is He, affirmed the statement in His saying: ﴿And Allah has permitted trade and forbidden interest.﴾ Some scholars said concerning His saying "And Allah has permitted trade": this is from the generality of the Qur'an, because the Arabs were able to act upon it, since taking and giving was trade among them, and whatever opposes the generality is a specification of it. Others said: "It is of the ambiguous (mujmal) part of the Qur'an, which was explained as: the lawful of trade, and the forbidden of ribā." My own view is that the first opinion is more correct. Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq said: "Allah forbade ribā so that people would lend to one another." Some scholars said: Allah forbade it because it destroys wealth and is a ruin for people.

The feminine marker was dropped in His saying "faman ja'ahu" (whoever has received), because the feminine of "mau'iza" (admonition) is not real, and it has the meaning of "wa'aza" (admonished). Al-Hasan read "faman ja'athu" with the marker retained.

His saying "fa-lahu ma salaf" means: what was of ribā is not pursued against him in this world or the Hereafter. This was said by al-Suddi and others. This is a ruling from Allah, Exalted is He, for those among the disbelievers of Quraysh and Thaqif who embraced Islam, and for those who used to trade there. "Salaf" means: it preceded in time and passed.

Concerning His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿and his affair is up to Allah﴾ there are four interpretations. The first: the pronoun returns to "ribā", meaning: the matter of ribā is up to Allah regarding the continuance of its prohibition or otherwise. The second: the pronoun returns to "what is past", meaning: his affair is up to Allah regarding pardoning it and dropping the consequence of it. The third: the pronoun returns to the one who practised ribā, meaning: his affair is up to Allah, that He may keep him firm in abstaining or return him to disobedience in ribā. The fourth: the pronoun returns to the one who desisted, but in the sense of giving him comfort and extending his hope for good, as you say: "his affair is toward obedience and good, and a place of hope," and as you say: "his affair is in growth or prosperity, turning to Allah and to His obedience." The word "amr" here is not limited to ribā alone, but includes the whole of his affairs.

His, Exalted is He, saying: ﴿But whoever returns﴾ means: returns to the practice of ribā and to the saying "trade is only like ribā." If we consider the verse as applying to a disbeliever, then "khulud" (abiding) is abiding without end in its true sense. If we consider it as applying to a sinning Muslim, then this is borrowed abiding, in the sense of intensification, as the Arabs say, "mulk khalid" (an everlasting dominion), an expression for some duration, not for true perpetuity.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿Allah deprives usury (ribā) of blessing, and makes charities grow. And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner.﴾ ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, establish the prayer and give zakah, for them is their reward with their Lord, and there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve.﴾

(p-99) "Yamḥaqu" means: it diminishes and removes. From it comes maḥāq al-qamar (the waning of the moon), which is its decrease. "Wa yurbī al-ṣadaqāt" means: He causes them to grow and increases their reward manifold. One says: rabat al-ṣadaqah (the charity grew), and Allah the Exalted made it grow (arbāhā) and nurtured it (rabbāhā), and that is the multiplying for whomever He wills. From it is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed, the charity of one of you falls into the hand of Allah, and He nurtures it for him as one of you nurtures his young camel or his foal, until it comes on the Day of Resurrection, and indeed a morsel is (as large) as Mount Uhud." Allah has made these two actions the reverse of what the greedy, avaricious son of Adam supposes: he supposes that usury enriches him, while in reality it is deprived of blessing, and he supposes that charity impoverishes him, while it is growth in this world and the Hereafter. (p-100) Ibn al-Zubayr recited: "Yumaḥḥiqu Allāhu" with a damma on the yā' and a kasra on the ḥā' with shadda, and "wa yurabbī" with a fatḥa on the rā' and shadda on the bā'; and these readings were also transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ.

It is also possible that it means: Allah does not love the granting of success (tawfīq) to the ungrateful sinner.

The Qāḍī Abū Muḥammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: These are strained interpretations. As for the first, it overextends the verb and assigns to it a meaning its wording does not bear; as for the second, its meaning is not sound, rather Allah the Exalted loves success in general and makes it beloved, and love in the observable sense involves inclination toward the beloved, gentleness toward him, and eagerness to preserve him, and the signs of this become evident. The occasion of revelation of this verse: "Interest (riba) was very widespread among the people at that time, and there was interest between Quraysh and Thaqif. Thus these owed to those and those owed to these. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, on the second day after the conquest he said in his sermon: 'Behold, every interest of the Jahiliyyah is annulled, and the first interest I annul is the interest of al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib.'" (p-102) So he ﷺ began with his paternal uncle and the person closest to him, and this is among the practices of justice for the leader: that he should spread justice upon himself and his close circle, so that it then extends to the people. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ returned to Madinah and appointed 'Attab ibn Asid over Makkah. When the people of Ta'if were later brought down to Islam, they stipulated conditions, some of which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted and some of which he did not. Among their conditions was that every interest owed to them by the people they would collect, and every interest owed by them would be annulled. It is related that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ confirmed these for them, then Allah annulled them with this verse, just as He annulled his agreement with the disbelievers of Quraysh regarding the return of women to them in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah.

Al-Naqqash mentioned the narration that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that it be written at the bottom of the document for Thaqif: 'What belongs to the Muslims belongs to you, and what is upon them is upon you.' When the due dates of their interest came, they sent to Makkah to demand payment. The debts were owed to the Banu Ghayrah, who are the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Umayr of Thaqif, and they were owed by the Banu al-Mughirah al-Makhzumiyyun. The Banu al-Mughirah said: 'We will not give anything, for interest has been annulled.' They raised their matter to 'Attab ibn Asid in Makkah, who wrote about it to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote with it to 'Attab, and Thaqif learned of it and desisted." This is the occasion of revelation in brief summary, compiled from what Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Jurayj, al-Suddi and others related. The meaning of the verse is: make between you and the punishment of Allah a shield by your leaving what remains of interest owed to you and your forgiving it.

His words ﴿if you are believers﴾ are a pure condition with regard to Thaqif, in its literal sense, because it was at the beginning of their entry into Islam. If we take the verse as addressing those whose faith is firmly established, then it is a figurative condition by way of emphasis, as you say to someone whom you want to rouse to dignity: "If you are a man, then do such-and-such."

Al-Naqqash related from Muqatil ibn Sulayman that he said: "'In' in this verse has the meaning of 'idh' (since)."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is rejected and is not known in the language. Ibn Fawrak said: it is possible that he means: O you who have believed in those prophets before Muhammad, leave what remains of interest, if you are believers in Muhammad, since the earlier faith is of no benefit except with this. This is rejected by what has been related regarding the occasion of revelation.

Then Allah, Exalted is He, threatened them, if they did not leave interest, with war from Allah and His Messenger, and war is a summons to killing. Ibn 'Abbas related that on the Day of Resurrection it will be said to the one who consumes interest: "Take your weapon for war." Ibn 'Abbas also said: whoever persists in interest and does not desist from it, it is incumbent upon the leader of the Muslims to call him to repentance, and if he desists, well and good, otherwise he should strike his neck. Qatadah said: Allah threatened the people of interest with killing, making them "bahraj" (outlawed), wherever they are found; then, Exalted is He, restored them upon repentance to their principal sums and said to them: "you wrong not" in taking interest, "nor are you wronged" in that anything of your principal sums be withheld so that your wealth is lost. It is possible that "you wrong not" refers to delay in payment, since "the delay of the wealthy is injustice," as the Prophet ﷺ said. So the meaning is that the repayment should be with the annulment of interest, and this is the practice of settlement; and this is most similar to settlement. Do you not see that when the Prophet ﷺ advised Ka'b ibn Malik regarding the debt of Ibn Abi Hadrad, to remit half of it, Ka'b said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah," and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to the other: "Stand up and pay him," so the scholars took his command to pay as a sunnah in settlements.

al-Hasan recited "ma baqiy" with a kasrah on the qaf and sukun on the ya', and this is like the line of Jarir:

﴿Hu al-khalifah, fa-rḍawā mā raḍiya lakum ∗∗∗ māḍī al-'azīmah mā fī ḥukmihi janaf﴾

Its basis is that he likened the ya' to the alif: just as the vowel does not reach the alif, so here it does not reach the ya'. In this there is room for consideration.

Abu al-Sammal recited "min al-ribw" with a kasrah on the doubled ra', a dammah on the ba', and sukun on the waw. Abu al-Fath said: this word is anomalous in two respects: first, the movement from kasrah to dammah as a fixed inflection; and second, a waw occurring after a dammah at the end of a noun, which is something that occurs only in verbs, such as yaghzu and yad'u. As for "dhu" in the Ta'i dialect meaning "alladhi," it is extremely rare, and some of them change its waw when it departs from the nominative case, saying: "I saw dha qama." The basis of this recitation is that he emphasized the alif and inclined toward the waw of which the alif is a substitute, in the manner of their saying al-salat wa al-zakat. In general it is an anomalous recitation.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i recited "fa-'dhanu" (in the short form, with fatha on the dhal). 'Asim, in the transmission of Abu Bakr, recited "fa-'adhinu" (with the long vowel and kasrah on the dhal). Sibawayh said: "adhantu" means "a'lamtu" (I informed), and "adhdhantu" means "nadaytu" (I called out and proclaimed with an announcement); he said: some use "adhantu" in the sense of "adhdhantu." Abu 'Ali said: whoever says "fa-'dhanu" in the short form means: "know the war from Allah." Ibn 'Abbas and other exegetes said: its meaning is: "be certain of the war from Allah, Exalted is He."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: In my view this is from the sense of permission (idhn), and when a person grants permission for something, he has established it and built his own position upon it. It is as if He said to them: establish war between yourselves and Allah and His Messenger. It follows from the wording of the verse that they are the ones who summon war and seek it, since they are the ones who grant permission for it and within it. Included in this meaning that I have mentioned is their knowledge that they are at war, and their certainty of that. Abu 'Ali said: whoever recites "fa-'adhinu" with the long vowel, its estimate is: "inform those who do not desist from this of war," and the object is omitted. This object has been confirmed in the words of the Exalted: ﴿Say: I have informed you on equal terms﴾ [al-Anbiya': 109]. When they are commanded to inform others, they will undoubtedly know it themselves. He said: thus in their informing is their knowledge, but in their knowledge is not necessarily their informing others. So the long recitation is more preponderant, because it is more emphatic and forceful. Al-Tabari said: the short recitation is more preponderant, because it is specific to them, whereas on the long recitation they are commanded to inform others.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The two recitations are equal in my view, because the addressee in the verse is restricted to every person who has not left what remains of interest. If it is said to them "fa-'dhanu," the command is general to them; and if it is said to them "fa-'adhinu" with the long vowel, the meaning is: inform yourselves and some of you inform others. It seems that this recitation allows them latitude for deliberation and reflection, i.e., inform yourselves of this, then consider which is more advantageous for you: leaving interest or war.

All the readers recited "la tazlimun" with fatha on the ta' and "la tuzlamun" with dammah on it, and its explanation has already passed. Al-Mufaddal related from 'Asim: "la tuzlamun" with dammah on the ta' in the first and fatha in the second. Abu 'Ali said: the recitation of the majority is preferred, because it accords with His words "fa-in tubtum" in the attribution of the two verbs to the agent; whereas "tazlimun" with fatha on the ta' is more incongruous with what precedes it.
