﴿If the debtor is in hardship, then let there be postponement until a time of ease. But if you give it as charity, that is better for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿And fear a Day on which you will be returned to Allah, then every soul will be paid in full what it earned, and they will not be wronged.﴾

God the Exalted ruled that the practitioners of usury (riba) may take back their principal (ru'us amwalihim) from those who have money, then He ruled that for the one in hardship there is postponement until a time of ease. Al-Mahdawi said: Some scholars said: this verse abrogates (nasikha, i.e. naskh, "abrogation") what was in the pre-Islamic period of selling a person who is in difficulty for a debt. Makki reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) commanded it at the beginning of Islam. If the action of the Prophet (ﷺ) is established, then it is abrogation (naskh); otherwise it is not abrogation.

Al-'Usra: hardship of circumstances due to lack of wealth, and from it comes "the army of hardship" (jaysh al-'usra).

Al-Nazira: postponement. Al-Maysara: a verbal noun meaning ease. "Dhu 'usra" is in the nominative because kana is the complete verb (kana al-tamma), meaning "existed" and "came to be." This is the view of Sibawayh, Abu 'Ali and others. From here it becomes clear (p-106) that the original state is wealth and the fullness of one's liability, and that poverty is an accidental, newly arising condition which must be established. Some of the Kufans, related by al-Tabari, said: rather kana is the incomplete verb (kana al-naqisa), and its predicate is omitted, its estimated form being: "if there is among your debtors one in hardship." "Fa-nazira" is nominative as the predicate of an implied subject, estimated as: "then what is required is postponement," or "then the ruling is postponement." Al-Tabari said: In the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads "wa-in kana dha 'usra," with the meaning: "if the one owed is..." Al-A'mash read "wa-in kana mu'siran fa-nazira." Abu 'Amr al-Dani said, from Ahmad ibn Musa: Likewise it is in the Mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b. Makki and al-Naqqash said: On this reading the wording of the verse is specific to the people of usury. On the reading "wa-in kana dhu," it is general to all who have a debt. This is not necessarily binding. Al-Mahdawi reported that in the Mushaf of 'Uthman it reads "fa-in kana" with fa, and "dhu 'usra" with waw.

The reading of the majority is "nazira" with a kasra on the zay. Mujahid, Abu Raja' and al-Hasan read "fa-nazrah" with a sukun on the zay, and likewise al-Dahhak read it; this is a Tamimi dialect, and they are the ones who say "karm Zayd" for "karuma," and "kibd" for "kabid," and "kitf" for "katif."

'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah read "fa-nazira" on the pattern fa'ila. Al-Zajjaj said: It is among the verbal nouns, like His saying: ﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 2], and His saying: ﴿Thinking that a calamity will be done to them﴾ [al-Qiyama: 25], and like ﴿the treachery of the eyes﴾ [Ghafir: 19], and others.

Nafi' alone read "maysurah" with a damma on the sin. The rest of the seven and the majority of people read "maysarah" with a fatha on the sin, on the pattern maf'alah. This reading is more common in the speech of the Arabs, because maf'ulah with a damma on the 'ayn is rare.

Abu 'Ali said: They have said "maskurah" and "mashrubah." But maf'alah with a fatha on the 'ayn is more common in their speech. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah also, and Mujahid, read "fa-nazirhu ila maysurih," as an imperative in "nazirhu," (p-107) and they made the hā' a pronoun referring to the debtor, and they gave the sin of "maysurih" a damma and the ra' a kasra, and they made the hā' a pronoun referring to the debtor. As for "nazirhu," its agent is from postponement, as you say "sammihu" (be lenient with him). As for "maysur," it is anomalous. Sibawayh said: There is no "maf'ul" pattern in speech. Abu 'Ali said: He means in singular nouns; but in the plural it has come, as in the words of 'Adi ibn Zayd:

Convey to al-Nu'man from me a refuge,
that my imprisonment and waiting have lasted long.

And the saying of Jamil:

Buthayna, persist in "no," for if you persist in it,
despite the multitude of slanderers, what helper is there?

The first is the plural of ma'lakah, and the second is the plural of ma'unah. Ibn Jinni said: 'Adi intended ma'lakah and omitted, and likewise Jamil intended: "ayyu ma'unah," and likewise the saying of the other:

........ for a day of terror or a noble deed

he intended makrumah and omitted. He said: It is possible that they are plurals, as Abu 'Ali said.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: If "maysur" is the plural of "maysurah," then it follows these examples. If its reciter intended the singular, then that is anomalous, and some people have deemed it erroneous, but Sibawayh's statement refutes that.

The scholars differed: Is this ruling of postponement until a time of ease restricted to the people of usury, or does it extend to every debtor whose debt is due? Ibn 'Abbas and Shurayh said: That ruling applies to usury specifically. As for ordinary debts and all trusts, there is no postponement in them; rather they must be paid to their owners. It seems that this view applies when there is no abject poverty (faqr mudqi'); but in the case of poverty and clear destitution, the ruling is postponement necessarily.

The majority of scholars said: Postponement until a time of ease is an established ruling for the one in hardship, whether the debt is usury, or from trade in one's liability, or from a trust. Al-Dahhak interpreted it this way.

God's saying ﴿And that you give charity﴾ is a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is "khayr" (better). God encouraged, by these words, charity to the one in hardship, and made it better than postponing for him. This was said by al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd, al-Dahhak, and the majority of people. Al-Tabari said: Others said: The meaning of the verse is: "And that you give charity to the rich and the poor is better for you." Then al-Tabari included under this heading statements of Qatada and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i which do not necessarily imply what his heading contains; rather they are like the statement of the majority of people. There is no room in the verse for the rich.

The majority of reciters read "tassaddaqu" with a shadda on the sad, as an assimilation of "tatasaddaqu." 'Asim read "wa-an tasaddaqu" with a light sad. In the Mushaf of 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud it reads "wa-an tatasaddaqu" without assimilation. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab reported from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he said: "The last of the Qur'an to be revealed was the verse of usury, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) died without explaining it to us, so leave usury and doubt." Ibn 'Abbas said: "The last revealed was the verse of usury."

(p-109) The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

The meaning of this, in my view, is that it is among the last revealed, because the majority of people, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj and others, said: The last verse revealed was His saying: ﴿And fear a Day on which you will be returned to Allah﴾.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: It has reached me that the most recent Qur'an with respect to the throne is the verse of debt. It is also reported that His saying "wa-ittaqu" was revealed nine nights before the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), after which nothing was revealed. It is reported as three nights, and it is also reported that it was revealed three hours before his death, and that he (peace be upon him) said: "Place it between the verse of usury and the verse of debt." Makki related that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Gabriel came to me and said: Place it at the head of two hundred and eighty verses of al-Baqara."

God's saying ﴿And fear﴾ is an admonition to all people, and a command that applies to each individual. "Yawman" (a day) is in the accusative as an object, not as an adverb of time.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' read "tarji'una" with a fatha on the ta' and a kasra on the jim. The rest of the seven read "turja'una" with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the jim. The reading of Abu 'Amr is like His saying: ﴿Indeed, to Us is their return﴾ [al-Ghashiya: 25], and the reading of the majority is like: ﴿Then they were returned to Allah﴾, and ﴿If I am returned to my Lord﴾. The address in both readings with the ta' is for the sake of emphasis in admonition and warning. Al-Hasan read "yarji'una" with a ya', meaning all people return. Ibn Jinni said: It is as if God, Exalted, was gentle with the believers so as not to confront them with mention of the return, since it is something at which hearts tremble; so He said to them: "And fear a day," then in mention of the return He shifted to the third person out of gentleness toward them. Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "yawman turaddun" with a damma on the ta'.

The majority of scholars hold that this day warned of is the Day of Resurrection, reckoning, and full recompense. Some people said it is the day of death, but the first is more correct by the wording of the verse. In His saying "ila Allah," there is an omitted noun, estimated as: "to the judgment of Allah and the decisive settlement of His decree." His saying "wa-hum" refers back to the meaning of "kullu nafs," not to its wording, except on the reading of al-Hasan "yarji'una," where "wa-hum" refers to the plural pronoun in "yarji'una."

In this verse there is an explicit statement that reward and punishment are tied to a person's acquisition (kasb), and this is a refutation of the Jabriyya (determinists).

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 1 of 3):

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:
﴿O you who have believed, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down. And let a scribe write [it] between you in justice. Let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him; so let him write﴾
Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: This verse was revealed specifically concerning salam (advance sale), meaning that the salam practice of the people of Madinah was the reason for this verse. Then it applies to all debts by consensus.

By His saying "with a debt" (bi-dayn), Allah the Exalted clarified what is shared in His saying "you contract" (tadayantum), since it may be said in the speech of the Arabs: "tadayanu" meaning: some of them repaid one another.

Describing the term as "specified" (musamma) is evidence that uncertainty is not permitted; it is as if the verse rejected it. If there is no specification and limit, then there is no term. Some people went to the view that writing down debts is obligatory upon their creditors, made obligatory by this verse. Al-Rabi' held that this was made obligatory by these words, then Allah the Exalted lightened it by His saying: ﴿But if one of you entrusts another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283]. Al-Sha'bi said: They used to see that His saying ﴿But if one of you entrusts another﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283] abrogates His command to write. Ibn Jurayj related something similar, Ibn Zayd said it, and it was narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. The majority of scholars said: The command to write is a recommendation (nadb) toward preserving wealth and removing doubt. If the debtor is pious, writing does not harm him; and if he is otherwise, then writing is a safeguard for his debt and for the need of the rightful creditor. Some of them said: If you call witnesses, that is prudence; and if you trust one another, then there is ease and latitude. This is the sound view, and no abrogation follows in this, because Allah the Exalted recommended writing in matters that a person may gift or leave aside, by consensus; so His recommendation is only for the sake of caution for people.

Then Allah the Exalted informed that trust would occur, so He said: If that occurs, then let him pay—the verse. This is an admonition to those upon whom debts lie, and Allah the Exalted did not explicitly make the command decisive that it should not be written when trust occurs.

As for al-Tabari, may Allah have mercy on him, he held that the command to write is an obligatory duty (fard wajib), and he extended the argument at length. The apparent sense of his words is that he holds commands to be for obligation until evidence indicates otherwise.

The people differed concerning His saying the Exalted: ﴿and let a scribe write between you﴾. 'Ata' and others said: It is obligatory upon the scribe to write. 'Ata' and al-Sha'bi also said: If no other scribe is found, then it is obligatory upon him to write. Al-Suddi said: It is obligatory when he is free. His saying the Exalted: ﴿in justice﴾ means: with truth and equity. The bi' (with) is connected to His saying ﴿and let [him] write﴾, and it is not connected to "scribe," because it would then follow that none may write a document except one who is just in himself; yet a child, a slave, or one of low standing may write it if they master its jurisprudence. As for those who are appointed for writing documents, it is not permitted for rulers to leave them except as just and approved persons. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: None of the people may write documents except one who knows them, who is just in himself and trustworthy, by His saying: ﴿and let a scribe write between you in justice﴾.

Then Allah the Exalted forbade the scribe from refusing (ibaya). "Aba ya'ba" is an irregular verb; it did not come except as qala yaqla and aba ya'ba, and the present of fa'ala with a fatha on the ayn does not come except when a throat letter (harf halq) is involved. Al-Zajjaj said: The view regarding aba is that its alif resembled the hamzah, so its present came as yaf'alu with a fatha on the ayn. Al-Mahdawi related from al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak that His saying ﴿and let him not refuse﴾ is abrogated by His saying: ﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾.

The kaf in His saying ﴿as Allah has taught him﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿to write﴾; the meaning is: writing as Allah has taught him. This is the view of some of them. It is possible that "kama" is connected to the sense in His saying ﴿and let him not refuse﴾, i.e., just as Allah has bestowed upon him the knowledge of writing, let him not refuse, and let him grant favor just as Allah has granted favor to him. It is also possible that the speech in this sense is complete at His saying ﴿to write﴾, and then His saying ﴿as Allah has taught him﴾ is a new beginning of speech, and the kaf is connected to His saying "so let him write."

When scribes are available, the writing is not obligatory upon a specific person, nor is it obligatory as a recommendation; rather he has the right to refrain, unless he is hired. When no scribe is found, the obligation of recommendation then falls upon the one present. As for writing in general, it is recommended, like His saying the Exalted: ﴿and do good﴾ [al-Hajj: 77], and it is of the category of helping the one who has lost [his way].

**
His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:
﴿Let the one upon whom the truth lies dictate, and let him fear Allah, his Lord, and not diminish anything from it. But if the one upon whom the truth lies is feeble-minded or weak or unable to dictate himself, then let his guardian dictate in justice﴾

Allah the Exalted commanded the one upon whom the truth lies to dictate, because testimony is only according to his acknowledgment, and when the document is written and he acknowledges it, it is as his dictation. Allah commanded piety regarding what he dictates, and forbade him from diminishing anything of the right. Bakhs is diminishment through a kind of deception and evasion. Those who were commanded to dictate are the ones who own themselves when present.

Then Allah the Exalted mentioned three types whose circumstances occur in every age, so He said: ﴿But if the one upon whom the truth lies is feeble-minded﴾. The right may be bound in aspects other than transactions, such as inheritances when divided, and other things. The safih (feeble-minded) is one whose judgment regarding wealth is loose, who does not know well how to take for himself or give from it, likened to a safih garment, which is thin in weave. Safah means lightness. From this is the saying of the poet, who is Dhu al-Rummah:
"They walked as spears sway, their tips made light by the passing of the gusty winds."
This attribute in the Shari'ah is not free from the guardianship (hajr) of a father or a guardian, and that is his walī. Then He said: "or weak," and the weak (da'if) is one whose intellect is corrupted and whose natural disposition is deficient; this also may have a father or guardian as his walī. "And one who is unable to dictate himself" is a minor child, whose walī is his guardian or his father; and one absent from the place of attestation, whether due to illness or another excuse, whose walī is his agent. As for the mute, it is permissible that he be among the weak, but the better view is that he is among those who are unable. These are categories that are distinguished, and you may find someone who falls under only one of them, and two of them may combine in one person, and perhaps all of them combine in one person. This order is derived from the words of Malik and other learned scholars.

Some people said: the safih is the young minor child, and this is an error. Some said: the da'if is the adult who is foolish, and this is a good view.

The verb appears doubled in His saying: ﴿an yumilla﴾, because if it were unfolded, many successive vowels would result. Unfolding in this verb is the dialect of Quraysh. "bil-'adl" means: with truth and aiming at correctness.

Al-Tabari held that the pronoun in "waliyyuhu" refers to the right (al-haqq), and he attributed this to al-Rabi' and Ibn 'Abbas.

The author Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This, in my view, is something not authentically related from Ibn 'Abbas, and how can testimony be given upon something and wealth be brought into the liability of the safih by the dictation of the one to whom the debt is owed? This is something not found in the Shari'ah, and the view is weak, unless its proponent means that the one who is unable to dictate due to illness, when incapable of dictating, then the creditor should dictate with justice, and make the one who is incapable hear it; then when the dictation is complete, he acknowledges it. This meaning is not what the verse intends, and this is valid only for one who is unable to dictate due to illness alone.

**
His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:
﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men; but if there are not two men, then a man and two women from those whom you accept as witnesses, so that if one of the two errs, the other may remind her﴾

Istishhad is seeking testimony. He expressed it with the intensive form in "two witnesses," indicating one who has testified and this has been repeated from him; it is as if it is an indication of justice.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿from among your men﴾ is explicit in excluding disbelievers, children, and women. As for slaves, the wording includes them, and the scholars differed concerning them. Shurayh, Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, and Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: the testimony of a slave is permissible if he is just, giving precedence to the wording of the verse. Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah, and the majority of scholars said: the testimony of a slave is not permissible, giving precedence to the deficiency of slavery.

The subject of "yakuna" is the pronoun in His saying "yakuna" (they be).

The meaning in the view of the majority: "If the one sought as witness is not two men," i.e., if the creditor overlooks this or intends it for some excuse. Some said: rather the meaning is: if two men are not found, and the testimony of two women is not permissible except when men are absent. This is a weak view, and the wording of the verse does not give it; rather the apparent meaning is the view of the majority.

His saying: ﴿then a man and two women﴾ is raised by one of three things: either you estimate: "then let a man and two women be called as witnesses," or: "then let there be a man and two women," and it is valid that this be complete and incomplete, but the complete is more similar, because omission is rare; or: "then a man and two women who testify." In every case, the supplied element is the governing factor in His saying: ﴿that one of the two errs﴾.

Hamid ibn 'Abd al-Rahman related from some people of Makkah that they read "wamra'tan" with the hamzah of the alif quiescent. Ibn Jinni said: there is no parallel for quiescing a moving hamzah without analogy; they only lightened the hamzah so that it approached the quiescent, then they exaggerated this so that the hamzah became a quiescent alif, as the poet said:
"They say in ignorance: the old man has no dependent; by my life, I have made dependents, and I am one who has been denied children."
He means: "wa-anā" (and I). Then after that they place the hamzah upon this alif as it is, while it is quiescent. From this is the reading of Ibn Kathir: "'an sa'qayha," and their saying: "ba'z" and "khi'tam." Abu al-Fath said: If it is said that the hamzah was made similar to the alif in that they equal it in voicing, increase, substitution, deletion, and closeness of point of articulation, then this is a rough statement with no craft in it, and one hardly is satisfied with its like.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿of those whom you accept among the witnesses﴾ is in the raised position as a description of His saying the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿then a man and two women﴾. Abu 'Ali said: The phrase "two witnesses" does not fall within this description because of difference in grammatical case, and this is a verbal ruling. As for the meaning, acceptance is a condition for the two witnesses as it is for the man and the two women.

Ibn Bakir and others said: His saying ﴿those whom you accept﴾ is addressed to the rulers. This is not noble; rather the address is to all people, but those engaged with this matter are the rulers. This is common in the Book of Allah, where the address is general concerning what some are engaged in. In His saying ﴿those whom you accept﴾ there is evidence that among witnesses there are some who are not accepted, from which it follows that people are not presumed to be just until their justice is established for them.

Hamzah alone read: "in tadilla" with a kasrah on the alif, fath on the ta', and kasrah on the dad, "fatudhakkiru" with a fatha on the dhal and raf' on the ra'; this is the reading of al-A'mash. The rest read: "an tadilla" with a fatha on the alif, "fatudhakkira" with nasb on the ra'; except that Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr lightened the dhal and the kaf, and the rest doubled them.

The discussion has already been presented concerning what governs His saying ﴿an tadilla﴾, and "an" is a object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih). The testimony did not occur for the sake of one of them erring; rather the testimony of two women occurred so that one may remind the other if the other errs. Sibawayh said: This is like saying: "I prepared this piece of wood so that this wall may lean, and I shall prop it up."

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 2 of 3):

The judge Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Since souls are eager to know the causes of events, in this verse he mentioned the cause of the matter intended before stating it. In this there is the anticipation of souls to being informed of its purpose, and this is one of the most skilful kinds of eloquence. For if a man said to you: "I have prepared this piece of wood to buttress this wall," the listener would say: "Why would you buttress a standing wall?" So it is necessary to mention the cause, saying: "When it leans." Thus in their speech the mention of the cause before the matter is found, more concisely than this exchange. Abu 'Ubayd said: The meaning of "tadilla" (that she forget) is "tansa" (she forgets). Going astray (al-dalal) regarding testimony is only forgetting a part of it, and recalling a part, while the person remains between that bewildered and astray. Whoever forgets the testimony entirely, it is not said that he went astray in it. As for the reading of Hamza, he made "an" (in) a conditional particle, and the fa' in his words "fa-tudhakkira" (then one reminds) the answer of the condition. The place of the condition and its answer is raised by being an attribute of what was mentioned, namely the two women. "Tudhakkiru" is raised just as the words of the Exalted are raised: ﴿And whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 95]. This is the saying of Sibawayh, and in this there is scrutiny. As for the accusative of "fa-tudhakkira" in the reading of the majority, it is by conjunction to the verb governed by "an".
The lightening of the kaf in the reading of Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir has the same meaning as its doubling, from dhikr (remembrance). It is said: dhakkara and adhkara, you transitive it by doubling or by the hamza. It is narrated from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna that they said: the meaning of his words "fa-tudhkira" with the lightening of the kaf is: she brings her back to remembrance of the testimony, because the testimony of a woman is half a testimony, so when the two of them testify, their combined testimony becomes like the testimony of a male. This is a distant interpretation, not eloquent, and it does not suit being set against going astray except with remembrance. And "dhakkarta" with the doubled kaf is transitive to two objects, and "one of them" in the verse is omitted; its estimate is: "fa-tudhakkira ihdahuma l-ukhra al-shahada allati dallat 'anha" (one of them reminds the other of the testimony about which she went astray). Al-Jahdari and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read: "an tudalla" with a damma on the ta' and a fatha on the dad, meaning "an tansa" (that she forget). Abu 'Amr al-Dani thus related from them, and al-Naqqash related from al-Jahdari a damma on the ta' and a kasra on the dad, meaning "an tudilla al-shahada" (that she cause the testimony to go astray), as you say: "adlaltu al-faras wa-l-ba'ir" (I lost the horse and the camel) when they perished for you and went away and you did not find them. Hamid ibn 'Abd al-Rahman and Mujahid read "fa-tudhkiru" with the lightening of the kaf, kasra on it, and a damma on the ra'. This verse includes the permissibility of the testimony of two women provided they are accompanied by a man. The saying of Malik differed regarding their testimony: Ibn Wahb related from him that the testimony of women is not permissible except where Allah mentioned it in debts, or in what none can witness except them, due to the necessity for that. Ibn al-Qasim related from him that it is permissible in wealth, in agencies over wealth, and in everything that leads to wealth; Ashhab and others disagreed with that.
And likewise if they testify concerning what leads to other than wealth; in this there are two opinions within the school.
**
The saying of the Mighty and Majestic:
﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called, and be not weary of writing it, whether it is small or large, for its term. That is more just in the sight of Allah, and more upright for testimony, and nearer to preventing doubt﴾
Qatada, al-Rabi' and others said: the meaning of the verse is: when they are called to testify so that a right is bound by their testimony. It was in this sense that it was revealed, for a man would go around among a numerous people seeking one who would testify for him, and they would be reluctant to testify, so none would go with him, and the verse was revealed concerning that.
Al-Hasan ibn Abi al-Hasan said: the verse combined two matters: do not refuse when you are called to obtain the testimony, nor when you are called to give it. Ibn 'Abbas also said this.
Mujahid said: the meaning of the verse is: do not refuse when you are called to give testimony which has already been obtained by you. Al-Naqqash traced to the Prophet ﷺ that he interpreted the verse thus. Mujahid said: as for when you are called to testify first, then if you wish go, and if you wish do not go. Lahiq ibn Humayd, 'Ata', Ibrahim, Ibn Jubayr, al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and others said likewise.
The verse, as al-Hasan said, combined two matters by way of recommendation. Muslims are recommended to help their brethren. So when there is leeway due to the abundance of witnesses and safety from the neglect of the right, the one called is recommended, and he may stay away for the slightest excuse; and if he stays away without an excuse, there is no sin upon him, nor reward for him. When there is necessity, and the neglect of the right is feared even to the slightest degree, the recommendation grows strong and comes close to obligation. And if he knows that the right will be lost and destroyed by the witness's delay in testifying, it is obligatory upon him to carry it out, especially if it has been secured and the call is to give it, for this condition is more emphatic, because it is a necklace around the neck and a trust which requires discharge.
"And be not weary" means "tamallu" (be bored). "Small or large" are two states of the pronoun in "tuktubuhu" (you write it). The small is placed first out of concern for it. This prohibition against weariness came only because borrowing and debt were frequent among them, so it was feared they would become bored with writing.
"Aqsatu" means "a'dalu" (more just). This is an af'al of the quadriliteral form, and there is an irregularity in it; consider whether it is from qasusa with a damma on the sin, as you say: "akramu" from "karuma". It is said: "aqsata" means "'adala" (to be just), and "qasata" means "jara" (to oppress). From this is the words of the Exalted: ﴿As for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 15]. Whoever estimates the words: ﴿and more upright for testimony﴾ to mean "wa-ashaddu iqamatan" (and firmer in establishing) then that is also an af'al of the quadriliteral form. Whoever estimates it from qama in the sense of "i'tadala" (to be straight) is free of the irregularity. "Wa-adna" means "aqrab" (nearer). "Tartabu" means "tashukku" (doubt). Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami read "yasam'u, yaktubuhu, and yartabu" all with the ya', as a relating of the absent third person.
**
The saying of the Mighty and Majestic:
﴿Except that it be a present trade which you conduct among yourselves; then there is no blame upon you that you do not write it. And take witnesses when you conclude a sale. Let no scribe or witness be harmed. If you do so, it is indeed a transgression on your part. And fear Allah; Allah teaches you, and Allah is Knowing of all things﴾
When Allah the Exalted knew the hardship of writing for them, He stated the dispensation from it and the lifting of blame in it in every sale for cash. That is mostly only in small things such as foodstuffs and the like, not in large things such as properties and the like. For this reason al-Suddi and al-Dahhak said: this is concerning what is hand to hand, you take and give. "An" is in the place of accusative by way of discontinuous exception.
The words of the Exalted: ﴿you conduct among yourselves﴾ require mutual exchange and immediate handing over of what is received. And since houses, land and many animals cannot be conducted in such exchange and are not faulted for it, writing is good for them, and they join in that to the sale on credit. 'Asim alone read "tijaratan" in the accusative, and the rest read "tijaratun" in the nominative. Abu 'Ali said: I doubt about Ibn 'Amir. When "kana" comes in the sense of "hadatha" and "waqa'a" (to happen, to occur), it is complete without a predicate. When the meaning of occurrence is removed from it, it requires an accusative predicate. The argument of whoever read "tijaratun" in the nominative is that "kana" means "hadatha" and "waqa'a". As for whoever read the accusative, it is as the predicate of "kana", and the subject is implied; its estimate, according to Abu 'Ali, is either: "al-mubaya'a" (the sale) which the preceding verses indicate, or: "illa an takuna al-tijaratu tijaratan" (unless the trade is a trade), and this is like the words of the poet:
Ransom for the sons of Dhuhl ibn Shayban is my she-camel, when there is a day of stars, dreadful.
That is: "idha kana al-yawmu yawman" (when the day is a day). Abu 'Ali recited the verse thus, and likewise Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad. Al-Tabari recited:
By Allah, my people, what a people, for a free woman ... when there is a day of stars, dreadful.
Sibawayh recited it with "yawmun" in the nominative:
When there is a day with stars...
As for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And take witnesses when you conclude a sale﴾, al-Tabari said: its meaning is: "and take witnesses over the small and large of that". People differed: is that obligatory or recommended? Al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and others said it is recommended. Ibn 'Amr and al-Dahhak said it is obligatory, and Ibn 'Umar did it in small and large things. 'Ata' also said it. Al-Tabari preferred this. Yet obligation in this is unsettled: in tiny matters it is difficult and hard, and in large matters a merchant may intend to win favour by leaving off witnessing; it may be a custom in some lands, and one may be shy before a scholar or a dignified, respected man and not call him as witness. All this falls under trust, and the command to witness remains recommended, due to the benefit in it for the most part, unless an excuse arises that prevents it, as we mentioned. Al-Mahdawi related from some people that they said: "wa-ashhidu idha tabaya'tum" is abrogated by His words: "fa-in amina" (if one of you trusts another). Makki related it from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri.
The people differed over the meaning of the words of the Exalted: ﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾. Al-Hasan, Qatada, Tawus, Ibn Zayd and others said the meaning is: let the scribe not be harmed by being made to write what was not dictated to him, and let the witness not be harmed by adding to or subtracting from the testimony. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and 'Ata' said the same, except that they said: let neither scribe nor witness be harmed by refusing. The wording of "harm" includes this and the first saying. The original of "yudarra" on these two sayings is "yudarir" with a kasra on the ra', then the assimilation occurred and the ra' was fathed in the jussive for the lightness of the fatha.
Ibn 'Abbas also said, as did Mujahid, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, Tawus and others: the meaning of the verse is: let no scribe or witness be harmed by the one seeking the writing or testimony harming them, saying: "write for me" or "testify for me" at a time of excuse or preoccupation for the scribe or witness; when they give their excuse, he presses and harms them and says: you have contradicted the command of Allah, and similar speech. The word "mudarra", being from two parties, requires all these meanings. For the scribe and witness on the first saying the verb is raised by their own action; on the second saying it is raised as the object not named as agent. The original of "yudarra" on the second saying is "yudarar" with a fatha on the ra'. It was related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn Mas'ud and Mujahid that they used to read: "wa-la yudarar" with unassimilated form and a fatha on the first ra'; this means that the one seeking the writing or testimony begins them with harm. Al-Tabari mentioned this from them in the rendering of this saying, and interpreted the reading in this sense, which indicates that the first ra' is fathed as we mentioned.
Abu 'Amr al-Dani related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Mujahid that the first ra' is kasra, and related from them also a fatha. Unassimilated form of the verb is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and assimilation is the dialect of Tamim. Abu Ja'far ibn al-Qa'qa' and 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd read "wa-la yudarr" with a jazm on the ra'. Abu al-Fath said: a sukun on the ra' with the doubling is questionable, but its way is that pause is applied to continuation. 'Ikrima read "wa-la yudarir" with a kasra on the first ra', "katiban wa-la shahidan" in the accusative, meaning the claimant of the right does not begin them with harm; and the aspects of harm are not limited. Miqsam related from 'Ikrima that he read "wa-la yudarr" with assimilation and a kasra on the ra' for the meeting of two consonants. Ibn Muhaysin read "wa-la yudarru" with a damma on the ra' doubled. Ibn Mujahid said: "I do not know what this reading is." Abu al-Fath said: what Ibn Mujahid denied is well known, and that is by making "la" a negation, meaning: it is not fitting that he be harmed, as the poet said:
Over the judge who comes one day, when he has decided, his decision is that he does not oppress and aims at justice.
So the raising of "wa-yaqsidu" is by intending "wa-yanbaghi an yaqsida" (and it is fitting that he aim), and likewise "wa-la yudarru" is raised by the meaning: "and it is fitting that he not be harmed." He said: and if you wish, it may be a declarative form with the meaning of a prohibition; this is close to the first view.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 282 (part 3 of 3):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you do it, then it is defiance (fusuq) in you﴾. Whoever takes the harm that is forbidden to be the addition by the scribe and the witness to what is dictated to them, or their reduction of it, then fusuq here carries its customary meaning in the Sharia, which is committing the major sins, because this is a kind of lying that harms wealth and bodies, and it involves nullifying the right. Whoever takes the forbidden harm to be causing distress to the scribe and the witness, by saying to them, "Respond, and do not oppose the command of God," or takes it to be their refusal when they are summoned, then fusuq retains its original linguistic meaning, which is going out from something, as one says: "The mouse fusaqat (came out) when it left its hole," and "the date fusaqat" (it burst out of its sheath). So the doer of this has departed (fasaqa) from what is right and true in this matter, and inasmuch as he has opposed God's command in this verse, the matter comes close to the customary Sharia meaning of fusuq.

His saying "bikum" (in you) is to be understood as: fusuq descends upon you (ḥāll bikum). The rest of the verse is admonition and an enumeration of blessing. And God is the One sought for help; there is no lord other than Him. It has also been said that the meaning of the verse is a promise that whoever has taqwa will be taught what is good and inspired with it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 283:

[p. 125] His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He:

﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then pledges taken in hand. But if one of you entrusts another, let the one who is entrusted discharge his trust and fear God, his Lord. And do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful. And God is Knowing of what you do.﴾

When God, exalted is He, mentioned the recommendation to call witnesses and to write down debts for the sake of preserving wealth and debts, He followed this with mention of the circumstances of the excuses that prevent writing, and made the pledge (rahn) a provision for them. He specified from among the circumstances of the pledge the journey, which is the most common of excuses, especially at that time because of the frequency of military expeditions (ghazw).

In meaning, every excuse is included in this. There are times when a scribe is unavailable in a settled place (hadar), such as times when people are busy, and at night. Also, the fear that the debtor's obligation (dhimma) will be ruined is an excuse that requires seeking a pledge. The Prophet ﷺ indeed "pledged his coat of mail to a Jew from whom he had requested a loan of barley. The Jew said: 'Muhammad only wants to take my property.' The Prophet ﷺ said: 'He lied. I am trustworthy on earth and trustworthy in heaven. Had he entrusted me, I would have repaid. Go to him with my coat of mail.'" Many scholars have said: the pledge during a journey is established in the Qur'an, and the pledge in a settled place is established in the hadith. This is good, except that he did not consider carefully the word "journey" in the verse. If the journey in the verse is an example of excuses, then the pledge in a settled place is present in the verse in meaning, since excuses may arise in a settled place. Al-Dahhak and Mujahid held that pledge and entrustment are only during a journey, and that in a settled place "nothing of that should be" [p. 126] done. Al-Tabari weakened their view regarding the pledge in light of the established hadith I have mentioned, and strengthened their view regarding entrustment. The correct position is the weakness of the view in both matters. Rather, entrustment occurs often in a settled place and is good.

The majority of reciters read "kātiban" (a scribe), meaning a man who writes. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn 'Abbas read "kitāban" with a kasra on the kaf, a light tā', and an alif after it, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar). Makki said: it has been said it is the plural of kātib, like qā'im and qiyām, and ṣāḥib and ṣiḥāb. Mujahid and Abu al-'Aliya read it this way and said: the meaning is: if the inkwell, the pen, or the page is absent.

Negation of the existence of writing (kitāb) occurs by the absence of any instrument whatsoever, so the negation of kitāb encompasses them all. The negation of the scribe also requires the negation of writing. The two readings are therefore good, except from the perspective of the script of the Muṣḥaf. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he read "kuttāban" with a ḍamma on the kāf, as the plural of kātib. This is good, since each incident has its own scribe, so it is said to the group: "and you do not find kuttāban." This is the category indicated by the reading of the one who reads "kātiban." Al-Mahdawi related from Abu al-'Aliya that he read "kutuban," which is the plural of kitāb, since incidents differ, and this is the category indicated by the reading of the one who reads "kitāban."

Nafi', 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and the majority of scholars read "fa-rihānun" (pledges). Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read "fa-ruhunun" with ḍamma on the rā' and hā'. It is related from them that the hā' is lightened, and a group other than them has read each form.

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: In the speech of the Arabs, "rahana al-shay'" means: it lasted and continued. It is said: "arhana lahum al-shurb" and other things (he made the drink continuous for them). Ibn Sida said: and "rahanahu" means: he made it last. From rahana in the sense of "lasted" is the poet's verse:

"The meat and the bread are constant for them, / and wine whose strainer is continually poured."

(That is, lasting.) Abu 'Ali said: Since the pledge means permanence and continuance, for this reason the pledge is void according to the jurists when it leaves the hand of the pledgee to the hand of the pledgor in any manner, because it has departed from what it was made for. It is said: "arhana fi al-silʿa" when he overpaid for it until he took it at a high price. From this is the poet's verse describing a she-camel:

"Ibn Salma folds up with her the distance of any rider, / a camel of the 'Iyd, for which dinars were pledged."

Al-'Id is a clan of Mahra, and the camels of Mahra are described as noble. It is said, regarding the meaning of pledge which is securing a right: "arhantu irhānan," as some have related. Abu 'Ali said: It is said: "arhantu" in overpayment, but in lending and selling it is "rahantu."

Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said:

It is said without disagreement in sale and loan: "rahantu rahnan," and then the thing that is handed over was named by this verbal noun and was transferred to the name. For this reason it is broken in the plural as names are broken, and as verbal nouns that are used as names are broken. Its verb governs its object like the accusative of the direct object, not the accusative of the verbal noun. You say: "rahantu rahnan," so that is like saying "rahantu thawban" (I pledged a garment), not like saying "rahantu al-thawba rahnan" or "darabtu darban." Abu 'Ali said: In this meaning it may also be said "arhantu," and "fa'altu" is more common in it. From this is the poet's verse:

"He pledges me against his sons, and I pledge him my sons, / by what I say."

And al-A'sha said:

"Until he gains from his sons a hostage, / and the Pleiades and the Bootes pledge you."

So these have been related from "rahana." As for "arhana," from it is the verse of Hammam ibn Murra:

"When I feared their claws, / I escaped and pledged my property to them."

Al-Zajjaj said: It is said regarding the pledge: "rahantu" and "arhantu," and Ibn al-A'rabi said the same. It is said: "rahantu lisani bi-kadha" (I pledged my tongue for such-and-such), and it is not said in this: "arhantu."

He said: whoever reads "fa-rihānun" it is the plural of rahn, like kabsh and kibāsh, ka'b and ki'āb, na'l and ni'āl, and baghl and bighāl. Whoever reads "fa-ruhunun" with ḍamma on the rā' and hā', it is the plural of rahn, like saqf and suqf, and asad and usud, since fa'l and fu'ul are close in their rulings. Whoever reads "fa-rahnun" with the hā' sukun, it is a lightening of ruhun, and it is a dialect in this whole category, like kutb, fakhdh, 'adhd, and other things.

Abu 'Ali said: The breaking of ruhun into the smallest number, I do not know it has come. If it had come, its analogy would be af'ul, like kalb and aklub, but they dispensed with the plural for the greater number in place of the smaller, as in their saying: thalāthatu shusūʿin (three sandals), and as the smaller form is dispensed with in favor of the larger in rusun and arsan.

So rahn is pluralized in two of the plural patterns: fu'ul and fi'āl. From what came in fu'ul is al-A'sha's verse:

"I swore I will not give to him from our sons / pledges, so that he corrupts them like one who has corrupted."

Al-Tabari said: Some people interpreted "ruhunan" with ḍamma on the rā' and hā' as the plural of rihān, so it is a plural of a plural, and al-Zajjaj related it from al-Farra'. Abu 'Ali directed a qiyās that requires that rihān be the plural of ruhun, by saying: fu'ul is pluralized into fi'āl, just as they pluralized fi'āl into fa'a'il in the saying of Dhu al-Rumma:

"And they brought near with the blue (lances) the camels, after / the marks had been pierced by the ribbed (feathers?) of their hindquarters..."

Then Abu 'Ali weakened this analogy and said that Sibawayh does not regard the plural of a plural as regular, so one should not proceed with it until it comes by transmission.

[p. 130] His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: "mqbūḍatun" (taken in hand) requires the separation of the pledgee from the pledge, and the people have agreed on the validity of the pledgee's taking possession, and likewise on the taking possession by his agent, as far as I know. They disagreed on the taking possession by a trustworthy person (ʿadl) on whose hands the pledge is placed. Mālik, all his companions, and the majority of scholars said: the taking possession by a trustworthy person is taking possession. Al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba, Abu al-Khattab Qatada ibn Di'ama, and others said: the taking possession by a trustworthy person is not taking possession. The view of the majority is more correct in terms of meaning regarding the pledge.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿But if one of you entrusts another﴾ and the rest of the verse, is a condition that ties the bequest of the one who owes the right to the discharge (of the debt). His statement, "let him discharge," is a command with the meaning of obligation, by the indication of the consensus on the obligation of paying debts, the establishment of the judge's ruling regarding it, and his compelling the creditors upon it, and by the indication of the sound hadiths on the prohibition of another's property. His statement, "trust" (amānatahu), is a verbal noun used as a name for the thing that is in the obligation (dhimma), and he attributed it to the one on whom the debt is because it has a relation to him. It is possible that by "trust" he means the verbal noun itself, as if he said: "let him guard his integrity (murū'a)," so the estimated meaning is: "let him discharge the debt of his trust."

'Asim, as transmitted from him by Abu Bakr, read "al-ladhu'tuumina" with ḍamma on the dhāl, and he indicates the ḍamma toward the hamza. Ahmad ibn Musa said: this rendering is a mistake. The rest read with the dhāl kasra, followed by a silent hamza without ishmām, and this is the correct reading which no other is permitted. Salim related from Hamza the ishmām of the hamza toward ḍamma, and this too is a mistake and not permitted. Abu 'Ali affirmed all of this view which belongs to Ahmad ibn Musa and argued for it. Ibn Muhayṣin read "al-ladhi ayutumina" with a silent yā' in place of the hamza, and likewise whatever is similar to it.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not conceal testimony﴾ is a prohibition with the force of obligation, by several indications, among them the threat. The locus of the prohibition is where the witness fears the loss of a right. Ibn 'Abbas said: The witness must testify wherever he is asked to testify, and inform wherever he is asked for information. He said: And do not say: "I informed him of it in the presence of the ruler," but rather inform him of it, perhaps he will return and be restrained.

[p. 131] Al-Qadi Abu Muhammad, may God have mercy on him, said: This, in my view, depends on the circumstances of the witness, the one witnessed about, and the case, especially with the corruption of the times, the baseness of people, the hypocrisy of stratagems, and the worldly concerns of rulers. Many a testimony, if it is stated in a place other than where it is effective, becomes a cause for serving falsehood by which the truth is obliterated.

"Āthimun" means: the ruling that follows the sin of concealing testimony has become attached to him. Its grammatical analysis is that it is the predicate of "inna" (indeed), and "qalbuhu" is the subject of "āthim." It is permissible that it be a subject-predicate beginning, with "qalbuhu" as the subject which takes the place of the predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "inna." It is permissible that "qalbuhu" be an apposition of the part to the whole (badal al-ba'ḍ min al-kull). God, Exalted is He, specified the mention of the heart because concealment is one of its actions, and because it is the lump of flesh upon whose soundness the body is sound, as he, peace be upon him, said. Ibn Abi 'Abla read "fa-innahu āthimun qalbahu" with the accusative on the bā', and Makki said: it is by way of explanation (tafsīr), then he weakened it because it is definite (ma'rifa). In His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And God is Knowing of what you do﴾ there is a warning, although its wording encompasses both promise and threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 284:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. And whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will bring you to account for it. Then He forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾

The meaning: all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth belongs to Allah and is subject to Him, because He is the Originator, the Creator, with no lord other than Him. He used the expression "mā" (what) although among them are those who have intellect, because the majority [of what is in the heavens and earth] is inanimate matter and animals, which lack intellect. Those who have intellect are few in terms of the number of their kinds, for they are three: angels, humankind, and jinn, whereas the kinds of the others are many. (p-132)

As for His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿And whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will bring you to account for it﴾, its meaning is that the matter is equal: concealment and hiding do not benefit in it, rather He knows it and calls to account for it. His saying ﴿within yourselves﴾ implies, by the strength of the wording, that it refers to what is established in the soul, believed, and whose thought is sustained upon it. As for the passing thoughts that cannot be repelled, they are not in the soul except in a figurative sense.

People differed concerning the meaning of this verse. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi said: it concerns the testimony which was forbidden to be concealed, and then in this verse He informed that the one who conceals it, who hides it in his soul, will be called to account. Ibn 'Abbas also, Abu Hurayrah, al-Sha'bi, and a group of the Companions and the Successors said: "When this verse was revealed, it grieved the companions of Muhammad ﷺ, and they said: 'We are destroyed, O Messenger of Allah, if we are called to account for the passing thoughts of our souls.' This also grieved the Prophet ﷺ. But he said to them: 'Do you wish to say what the Children of Israel said: We hear and we disobey? Rather say: We hear and we obey.' So they said it, and then Allah revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], and He relieved them of the distress, and Allah abrogated that [earlier ruling] by this verse." This is the meaning of the narration reported, and it has chains from various directions, and its wordings differ, and the wording of those who use the term naskh (abrogation) in this incident is settled.

Sa'id ibn Marjana said: I came to 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar, and he recited this verse: ﴿And whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it, Allah will bring you to account for it﴾, then said: "By Allah, if we are taken to account by this verse, we will surely perish." Then he wept until his tears flowed and his sobbing was heard. Ibn Marjana said: I stood up until I came to Ibn 'Abbas and informed him of what Ibn 'Umar had said and what he had done. He said: "May Allah have mercy on Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. The Muslims felt from it, when it was revealed, the same as what 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar felt. Then Allah revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ [al-Baqarah: 286], so it abrogated the whispering, and the statement and the action remained." Al-Tabari said, and others said: this verse is muhkam (definitive), not abrogated, and Allah, the Exalted, calls His creatures to account for what they did of deeds and for what they did not do of what was established in their souls, what they concealed, intended and wished; so He forgives the believers and holds to account the people of disbelief and hypocrisy. Then he (al-Tabari) cited from Ibn 'Abbas something resembling this meaning. Mujahid said: the verse concerns what arises in the souls of doubt and certainty. al-Hasan said: the verse is muhkam, not abrogated. Al-Tabari said: others said in a sense similar to the meaning mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas, except that they said the punishment which is the recompense for what occurs to the soul and accompanies thought is by the calamities of this world, its pains and all its hardships. Then he (al-Tabari) attributed, from 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, a similar meaning. Al-Tabari preferred that the verse is muhkam and not abrogated.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: That is because His saying, the Exalted, ﴿And whether you show what is within yourselves or conceal it﴾ means: concerning what is within your capacity and under your acquisition, and that is sustaining belief and thought upon it. Since the wording could include passing thoughts, the Companions and the Prophet ﷺ became apprehensive. So Allah, the Exalted, explained to them what He intended by the first verse and specified it, and affirmed His ruling that He does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. Passing thoughts are neither within capacity, nor is their repelling; rather it is an overwhelming matter, not something acquired or not acquired. In this explanation was their joy and the removal of their distress. The rest of the verse is muhkam, with no abrogation in it.

Among what refutes the matter of abrogation is that the verse is a report (khabar), and reports are not subject to abrogation. If someone insists on affirming abrogation, it applies only to the ruling that befell the Companions when they were alarmed by the verse, because the Prophet's ﷺ saying to them: "Say: We hear and we obey" implies a command to remain steadfast in this and to hold to it, and to await Allah's gentleness in forgiveness. Once this ruling is established, the occurrence of abrogation in it is valid, and the verse at that point resembles His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿If there are twenty steadfast among you, they will overcome two hundred﴾ [al-Anfal: 65]. This is the wording of a report, but its meaning is: adhere to this, remain firm upon it, and be patient according to it; then that was abrogated. People have agreed, as far as I know, that this verse concerning jihad was abrogated by the requirement that a hundred endure against two hundred. This verse in al-Baqarah is most similar to it.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "fa-yaghfir li-man yashā'u wa-yu'adhdhib" with jazm (apocopate, the verb in the jussive), while Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim read "fa-yaghfiru wa-yu'adhdhibu" with raf' (indicative). The justification for the jazm is that it follows what precedes it and is not cut off from it, and thus good parallelism is attained in their speech. The justification for the raf' is that it is cut off from the first clause, and this cutting is in one of two ways: either you make the verb a predicate of an omitted subject, so the verb takes the raf' because it occupies the place of the predicate of a subject; or you conjoin a clause consisting of verb and subject to what precedes it. Ibn 'Abbas, al-A'raj and Abu Haywah read "fa-yaghfira wa-yu'adhdhiba" with nasb, by hidden "an" (that), and it is coordinated on the meaning, as in His saying "fa-yudā'ifahu" (so that He may multiply it for him). al-Ju'fi, Khallad and Talhah ibn Musarrif read "yaghfir" without fa'. It is reported that it is thus in the codex of Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Jinni said: it is in apposition (badal) to "yuhasibukum," so it is an explanation of the reckoning. This is like the saying of the poet:

Slowly, O Banu Shayban, with some of your threats,
You will meet tomorrow my horses at Safawan.

You will meet horses that do not swerve from the battle,
When they run in the narrow, pressing place.

This is in apposition, and the poet repeated the verb because the benefit lies in what follows it of the speech.

His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾ means from among the disobedient upon whom the threat takes effect. al-Naqqash said: "He forgives whom He wills," that is, whoever refrains from it; and "punishes whom He wills," that is, whoever persists in it. Sufyan al-Thawri said: "He forgives whom He wills" the great (sin), and "punishes whom He wills" for the small. Some people who held the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne clung to this, and said: Allah has imposed on them the matter of passing thoughts, and that is something not bearable.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: This is not clear. The matter of passing thoughts was only an interpretation which the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ adopted, and it was not established as an obligation except in the manner we mentioned, from the Prophet's ﷺ affirmation of them in that. The question of imposing what cannot be borne we will discuss later, if Allah, the Exalted, wills.

When He mentioned forgiveness and punishment according to His will, the Exalted, He followed that with mention of power over all things, since what was mentioned is a part of them.

[p. 136]

The Exalted's saying:

﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord, and the believers too. Each one believes in Allah, His angels, His books, and His messengers. "We make no distinction between any of His messengers." And they say, "We hear and we obey. Your forgiveness, our Lord; to You is the final return."﴾

The occasion of this verse: when the verse ﴿Whether you show what is in your souls or conceal it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284] was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, became apprehensive about it. Then the matter was settled on their saying, "We hear and we obey." [p. 136] They then returned to supplication and humility. Allah praised them and commended them in this verse, and He placed this before His gentleness toward them and His removal of the distress that their overthinking had caused. Thus the Exalted combined for them the honour of praise, commendation, and the lifting of hardship concerning their inner thoughts. This is the fruit of obedience and of turning wholly to Allah, the Exalted. The opposite happened to the Children of Israel: they were blamed, and they were burdened with hardships of humiliation, wretchedness, and exile, when they said, "We hear and we disobey." This is the fruit of disobedience and rebellion against Allah. May Allah protect us from His vengeance.

*Āmana* means "he affirmed as true." *Al-Rasūl* is Muhammad (ﷺ). *Mā unzila ilayhi min rabbihi* is the Qur'an and all that was revealed to him, of which this verse, whose ruling they found severe, is part. It is related that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had this verse revealed to him, he said, "It is right that he should believe." Ibn Mas'ud recited *wa-āmana al-mu'minūn* ("and the believers believed"). Every expression that can convey encompassment may be used, and it may also be used without encompassment, by way of figurative likeness (*tashbīh*) to encompassment. Context makes this clear in every speech. Since it occurs here after *wa-al-mu'minūn*, this indicates that its encompassment extends to those mentioned.

Belief in Allah is affirming Him, affirming His attributes, and rejecting idols and every deity other than Him.

Belief in His angels is holding that they exist, that they are servants of Allah, and rejecting the beliefs of the Jahiliyyah about them. Belief in His books is affirming as true everything that was sent down to the prophets whose mention is contained in the Book of Allah revealed to Muhammad (ﷺ), or whatever he informed of.

Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim (according to the transmission of Abu Bakr), and Ibn 'Amir recited *wa-kutubihi* in the plural. In *al-Tahrim* they recited *wa-kitabihi* in the singular. Abu 'Amr recited here and in *al-Tahrim* *wa-kutubihi* in the plural. Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited *wa-kitabihi* in the singular in both places. Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, here and in *al-Tahrim*, recited *wa-kutubihi* like Abu 'Amr. Kharijah related from Nafi' the same as that. Most scholars read by each of these recitations (*qirā'āt*). Whoever used the plural meant the plurality of books, and whoever used the singular meant the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that encompasses every written scripture whose revelation was from Allah, the Exalted. This is the view of some scholars, and Abu 'Ali has explained it, and it is as they said: like "the weaving of Yemen" (*nasj al-Yaman*). Abu 'Ali said at the start of his discussion: As for the singular in the reading of whoever recited *wa-kitabihi*, it is not like how verbal nouns are used in the singular even when many is meant, as in the Exalted's saying, ﴿And call out for one destruction, and call out for many destructions﴾ [al-Furqan: 14], and similar. Rather, it is like how nouns are used in the singular when plurality is meant, as in their saying, "The dinar and the dirham increased," and similar. If you say, "These nouns that are meant to express plurality only come in the singular, whereas this is in the construct state (*muḍāf*)," it is answered: Indeed, in the construct state too there is what is meant to express plurality, as in the revelation, ﴿And if you count the favour of Allah, you will not enumerate it﴾ [Ibrahim: 34], and in the hadith, "Iraq has withheld its dirham and its qafiz." This is meant to express plurality, just as what has the definite article (*lām al-ta'rīf*) is meant. From this is the saying of Ibn al-Ruqa':

*He leaves the tribe in the evening ghirāthan (hungry),*
*while they are rich in their bread.*

The coming of generic nouns with the definite article *al-* is more frequent than their coming in the construct state.

The recitation of the majority is *wa-rusulihi* with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn*. Likewise *rusulunā*, *rusulukum*, and *rusulika*, except that Abu 'Amr is related to have lightened *rusulunā* and *rusulikum*. It is related from him in *rusulika* both the heavy and the light forms. Abu 'Ali said: Whoever recited *ʿalā rusulika* with the heavy form, that is the original form of the word. Whoever lightened it, it is like the lightening that occurs in singular nouns, such as *'unq* and *ṭunb*. When it is lightened in the singular, it is more fitting in the plural, which is heavier.

[p. 138] Yahya ibn Ya'mar recited *wa-kutbihi wa-rusulihi* with the *tā'* and *sīn* vowelless. Ibn Mas'ud recited *wa-kitabihi wa-liqā'ihi wa-rusulihi*. The majority of people recited *lā nufarriqu* with the *nūn*, meaning they say, "We do not distinguish." Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, Abu Zur'a ibn 'Umar ibn Jarir, and Ya'qub recited *lā yufarriqu* with the *yā'*, following the wording of *kullun*. Harun said: In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is *lā yufarriqūna* with the *yā'*. The meaning of this verse is that the believers are not like the Jews and Christians, who believe in some and disbelieve in others.

The Exalted's saying, ﴿And they say, "We hear and we obey"﴾, is a praise that implies encouragement to adopt this saying, and that the believer should hold to it for all time. Obedience is accepting commands.

*Ghufrānaka* is a verbal noun like *kufrān* and *khusrān*. It is in the accusative in the manner of verbal nouns, and its governing verb is an implied verb. Al-Zajjaj said its estimate is: "Forgive, (with) forgiveness from You." Others said: "We seek, or we ask, Your forgiveness." ﴿And to You is the final return﴾ is an affirmation of the Resurrection and of standing before Allah, the Exalted.

It is related that when this verse was revealed, the Prophet (ﷺ) was told by Jibril: "O Muhammad, Allah has exalted the praise of you and your community. So ask, and you will be given." Then he asked, up to the end of the surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 2, verse 286:

The words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity. It shall have what it earned, and it shall bear what it earned. Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err. Our Lord, do not place on us a burden like that You placed on those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so help us against the disbelieving people.﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ is a categorical statement, explicitly affirming that Allah does not impose on His servants, from the time this verse was revealed, any act of worship, whether of the heart or of the limbs, except what lies within the capacity of the one held accountable, in keeping with his understanding and his constitution. By this, the distress that had afflicted the Muslims concerning their interpretation of the matter of passing thoughts (al-khawatir) was lifted. Whoever denies the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne (taklif ma la yutaq) interprets this verse as meaning "He does not impose, and He did not impose." However, this is not explicit in the verse, nor does the wording exclude it, and for this reason the disagreement has been permissible.

The meaning we have mentioned in this verse accords with the meaning of His words: ﴿Allah intends ease for you and does not intend hardship for you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 185], His words: ﴿And He has not placed upon you any hardship in religion﴾ [al-Hajj: 78], and His words: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [al-Taghabun: 16].

People have disagreed about the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne in rulings that pertain to this world, after agreeing that it is not currently occurring in the Shari'ah, and that this verse indicates its absence. Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari and a group of theologians (mutakallimun) said: imposing what cannot be borne is rationally permissible, and this does not make any of the articles of the Shari'ah impermissible; and it would be a sign of the punishment of the one held accountable and a certainty of it. Based on this view, one may consider the case of the image-maker being commanded to breathe a soul into what he made, according to the hadith.

Those who held it permissible disagreed as to whether it occurred in the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) or not. One group said:

It occurred in the case of Abu Lahab, because it was decreed against him that his hands would perish and that he would burn in the Fire, and this indicates that he would not believe. The Shari'ah's obligation upon him to believe is constant, so it is as if he was obligated to believe while, in his belief, it was known that he would not believe, since if he believed, he would inevitably believe in the surah: ﴿Perish the hands of Abu Lahab﴾ [al-Masad: 1].

Another group said: it never occurred. His words: ﴿He will burn in a Fire of blazing flame﴾ [al-Masad: 3] mean only: if he dies in his disbelief.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

What cannot be borne is divided into kinds. Among it is what is impossible by reason, such as combining two opposites. Among it is what is impossible by habit, such as a man lifting a mountain. Among it is what cannot be borne because it is destructive, such as burning in fire and the like. Among it is what cannot be borne because of preoccupation with something else; and this is only said of it as "what cannot be borne" in a loose sense, with considerable figurative usage.

The verb "yukallifu" (He imposes) takes two objects, one of which is omitted, its estimated sense being: "an act of worship" or "something." Ibn Abi 'Abla read: "illa wus'ahā" with a fatha on the waw and a kasra on the sin (wasi'ahā), and this involves a figurative usage, since it is an inversion (maqlub). The original form of the wording would have been "illa wasi'athu," as He said: ﴿His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], and as He said: ﴿He has encompassed all things in knowledge﴾ [Ta-Ha: 98]. But this comes under the pattern of "I put the cap on my head" and "my mouth in the stone."

His words: ﴿It shall have what it earned﴾ refer to good deeds, and ﴿and it shall bear what it earned﴾ refer to bad deeds. This was said by al-Suddi and a group of exegetes (mufassirun). There is no disagreement about this. Passing thoughts and the like are not part of a person's earning. The expression for good deeds uses "la-ha" (for it), because such deeds are things a person is pleased and delighted to earn, so they are attributed to his possession. The expression for bad deeds uses "'alay-ha" (against it), because they are burdens, weights, and difficult responsibilities. This is like your saying: "I have wealth" (li mal), and "I have a debt upon me" ('alayya dayn). It is also like the words of the one who finds a lost item and gives its charity: "O Allah, on behalf of so-and-so; if he refuses, then it is for me and against me." The verb of earning is repeated, and the varying of its forms is good for the style of the speech, as He said: ﴿So give respite to the disbelievers, give them a little respite﴾ [al-Tariq: 17]. This is one view. What appears to me in this matter is that good deeds are what is earned without strain, since their earner is on the path of Allah's command and the outline of His Law. Bad deeds are earned through exaggeration, since their earner strains in their pursuit, breaking through the barrier of Allah's prohibition and going beyond it to them. So the use of both verb forms in the verse is fitting, to secure this meaning.

Al-Mahdawi and others said: it has been said that the meaning of the verse is: no one shall be seized for the sin of another.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

This is correct in itself, but it comes from other than this verse.

His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not hold us accountable﴾ mean: say this in your supplication.

People have disagreed about the meaning of His words: ﴿if we forget or err﴾. Al-Tabari and others held that it refers to forgetting in the sense of abandoning, that is, if we abandon some of Your obedience, and that it refers to deliberate error. They said: as for forgetting that overcomes a person, and error that results from ijtihad (independent effort), these are lifted from a person, so he is not commanded in supplication that he not be held accountable for them. Many scholars held that the supplication in this verse is only for prevalent forgetfulness and unintended error, and this is what I hold to be correct.

Qatadah said in explaining the verse: "It has reached me that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Allah has overlooked for my community their forgetfulness and their error.'" Al-Suddi said: "When this verse was revealed and they recited it, Jibril said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Allah has done that, O Muhammad.'" The apparent meaning of these two statements is what I have affirmed. This is because when the believers were relieved of what they feared in His words: ﴿Allah will call you to account for it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 284], they were commanded to supplicate for the averting of that category which is beyond a person's ability to avert, namely forgetting and error. "Al-isr" means a heavy weight and what cannot be borne in its most complete forms.

This verse, according to this view, requires the permissibility of imposing what cannot be borne, and for this reason the believers were commanded to supplicate that this difficult permissible matter not occur.

The position of al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj is that imposing what cannot be borne is impermissible. So forgetting, for them, is the abandoned acts of obedience, and error is the deliberate disobedience. "Al-isr" is the heavy acts of worship, like the obligations of the Children of Israel, such as killing themselves, cutting their bodies, their punishments in their bodies for their sins as was written on their doors, and their being charged with difficult covenants. "What no one has the strength to bear" is, in their view, used figuratively, as when you say: "I have no strength to deal with so-and-so," or for other matters that you find difficult though in reality you are able to bear them; or it may be what we cannot bear because it destroys us, such as the punishment of Hell and other things. As for the word "akhta'a" (to err), it may also be used of intentional acts and of acts done with ijtihad.

Qatadah said: "al-isr" means a covenant and a solemn pledge. This was also said by Mujahid, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Suddi, Ibn Juraij, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd. 'Ata' said: "al-isr" is being transformed into apes and swine. Ibn Zayd also said: "al-isr" is a sin for which there is no expiation and from which there is no repentance. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "al-isr" is a hard, difficult matter. In the language, "al-a'sira" is the binding matter of obligation, kinship, covenant, or the like. All these expressions tend toward this meaning. "Al-isar" is the rope with which loads and the like are bound, and "al-qidd" is what binds a man's upper arms. It is said: "asara yu'siru asran." "Al-isr" with a kasra on the hamza is from this; but there is scrutiny in this. It is narrated from 'Asim that he read: "uşran" with a damma on the hamza.

There is no disagreement that "those before us" refers to the Jews.

Al-Dahhak said: and the Christians.

As for the expressions of the exegetes on His words: ﴿Our Lord, do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾, Qatadah said: "Do not be harsh upon us as You were harsh upon those before us." Al-Dahhak said: "Do not burden us with deeds we cannot bear." Ibn Zayd said something similar. Ibn Juraij said: "Do not transform us into apes and swine."

Salam ibn Sabur said: "What we have no ability to bear is lust (al-ghulmah)." This was narrated by al-Naqqash from Mujahid, 'Ata' and Makhul. It is also narrated that Abu al-Darda' used to say in his supplication: "And I seek refuge with You from a lust for which there is no remedy." Al-Suddi said: it is the severity and the shackles that were upon the Children of Israel from the prohibitions.

Then He said, in what He commanded the believers to say: ﴿and pardon us﴾, that is, for what we have committed and what has come to light; ﴿and forgive us﴾, that is, conceal from us what You know of us; ﴿and have mercy on us﴾, that is, show favor, beginning with a mercy from You to us.

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

These are different avenues of supplication, even though the purpose intended by each one of them is one and the same: entry into Paradise.

﴿You are our Protector﴾ is praise, which includes drawing near to Him and thanking Him for His blessings. "Mawla" is from "waliya," so it is a noun of place (mafil), meaning the place of guardianship. Then the supplication was concluded with a request for victory over the disbelievers, which is the essential foundation of the establishment of the Shari'ah, the elevation of the Word, and the availability of the way to all kinds of acts of obedience.

It is narrated that "Jibril, peace be upon him, came to Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: 'Say: Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or err.' He said it, and Jibril said: 'Allah has done it.' Then he said: 'Say such-and-such,' and he said it, and Jibril said: 'Allah has done it,' until the end of the surah." Many hadiths corroborate this meaning.

It is narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that when he finished reciting this surah, he would say: "Amin."

The Qadi Abu Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on him, said:

It is thought that he narrated this from the Prophet (ﷺ). If so, it is perfect. If it was by analogy with Surat al-Hamd, since there is supplication there and supplication here, then it is good.

Abu Mas'ud 'Uqbah ibn 'Amr narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Whoever recites the two verses at the end of Surat al-Baqarah at night, they will suffice him," meaning for the night prayer. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I do not think anyone who has understanding and has reached Islam sleeps until he recites them."

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "These verses from the end of Surat al-Baqarah were given to me from a treasure beneath the Throne; no one before me was given them."

The Surah of al-Baqarah is complete, and praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings be upon our master Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets.
